answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the objection that the baraita prescribes thanks and praise for all these sites and answers by splitting the case into two blessings, "the true Judge" for the wife and "Who remembers the righteous" for Lot.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Berakhot 54b: "The language of the baraita should be emended and teach: Over Lot and his wife one recites two blessings.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question, and the page answers it outright by emending the baraita into two blessings for Lot and his wife. Ask something the page leaves standing, for example what it means that the mishna calls a prayer about a scream already heard "vain" while Rava tells a man to bless at the site of his rescue every time he passes, or why a place of judgment is worth returning to at all. Keep the summary's accurate framing of event-triggered blessings.

berakhot/55.summary: Rav Ḥisda says a dream left uninterpreted is like a letter never read, sealed and inert, and that a bad dream is better than a good one because it prompts remorse. Then the page tells of a man who brought one dream to twenty-four interpreters in Jerusalem; each gave a different reading, and every one came true. For someone shaken by a dream, the advice is not interpretation but three people who declare it good and recite nine verses over it.
berakhot/55.question: If twenty-four contradictory interpretations all came true, what was in the dream before anyone opened his mouth?

judge.reachNote: Whether a dream carries determinate content awaiting discovery or is a blank that the interpreter's word constitutes.

answer.quote: As long as it is not interpreted it cannot be fulfilled; the interpretation of a dream creates its meaning.
answer.explanation: The page holds that an uninterpreted dream has no operative content — meaning is conferred by the interpreter — and elsewhere adds that a dream contains only "the thoughts of his heart when he was awake" and that interpretation must be "akin to the dream," so the question is addressed but not settled.

berakhot/56.summary: Abaye and Rava bring bar Haddaya, a dream interpreter who works for a fee, one identical dream after another; Abaye pays and hears of profit and a yeshiva headship, Rava does not pay and hears of ruined wine, arrest, and a dead wife. Every interpretation comes true. Then a book falls from bar Haddaya as he boards a ship, and Rava reads in it that dreams follow the mouth of whoever explains them.
berakhot/56.question: Was bar Haddaya's offense inventing Rava's misfortunes, or having the power to decide them and selling that decision for a coin?

judge.reachNote: Whether an interpretation describes a fixed fate or creates it — and whether selling that creative power is fraud or something worse.

answer.quote: Scoundrel. It was dependent on you, and you caused me so much suffering. I forgive you for everything except for the daughter of Rav Ḥisda
answer.explanation: After reading the book's line that all dreams follow the mouth, Rava himself states the grievance: the outcomes were dependent on bar Haddaya, so the page settles the note's dichotomy in favor of the second horn — he held and exercised the power.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Berakhot 56a: "Scoundrel. It was dependent on you, and you caused me so much suffering. I forgive you for everything except for the daughter of Rav Ḥisda". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks which of two things bar Haddaya's offense was, but the page answers it outright: Rava, having read that all dreams follow the mouth, says "It was dependent on you, and you caused me so much suffering." Build the new question on top of that reveal rather than around it — for instance, why a fee should be able to move an outcome at all, or why Rava curses the interpreter instead of doubting the power he has just discovered. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

berakhot/57.summary: Wheat seen in a dream means peace, barley means iniquity taken away, and a goose means wisdom. A reciter of mishnayot teaches Rav Sheshet that killing a snake in a dream signals losing one's livelihood; Rav Sheshet reverses the ruling on the spot, and the Gemara notes he had just dreamed of killing a snake himself. Rabbi Yoḥanan likewise instructs a teacher to amend the rule so that wine is always a good sign for a Torah scholar.
berakhot/57.question: If an interpreter can flip the meaning of a snake the moment the dream is his own, what is the catalogue of omens actually good for?

judge.reachNote: Whether dream omens are fixed signs with objective meaning or are constituted by the interpreter's word, and what happens when the interpreter is the dreamer.

answer.quote: But that is not so. Rav Sheshet saw a snake in his dream and killed it, so he sought to interpret his dream positively.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself flags Rav Sheshet's reversal as self-interested and rejects it, which bears on the question without saying what the catalogue's authority ultimately rests on.

berakhot/58.summary: Ben Zoma, standing on a stair on the Temple Mount, sees a crowd of six hundred thousand and blesses God who knows all secrets, then adds a blessing that all these were created to serve him. He lists Adam's eleven steps from plowing to baking, against his own waking up to find bread already made. Later Rav Ḥanina tells two colleagues he counted them as a multitude worth three blessings; they stare at him and he dies.
berakhot/58.question: If Ben Zoma can look at a crowd and bless God for making them all to serve him, why does Rav Ḥanina's flattery of two men as six hundred thousand get him killed?

judge.reachNote: When does seeing the whole world's service in others count as gratitude, and when does it tip into flattery or self-display?

answer.quote: They said to him: Are you all that clever? They fixed their gaze upon him and he died.
answer.explanation: The page reports only the sages' rebuke of Rav Ḥanina's cleverness and his death, which bears on the question but never explains why his blessing over two men was punishable while Ben Zoma's was praised.

berakhot/59.summary: Rav Ketina was walking past the door of a necromancer, a man who claims to consult the dead, when an earthquake rumbled. The necromancer called out the cause: God sheds two tears into the great sea over His suffering children, and the sound shakes the earth. Rav Ketina calls him a liar, objecting that two tears would mean two quakes, and the Gemara quietly concedes that quakes do come in pairs, denying it so people would not follow the necromancer.
berakhot/59.question: If the necromancer had the earthquake right, what is lost by calling a true thing a lie because of who said it?

judge.reachNote: Whether truth should be suppressed because of the authority it would lend to its speaker, and what that costs.

answer.quote: the fact that Rav Ketina did not admit that the necromancer was correct was so that everyone would not mistakenly follow him
answer.explanation: The page states why Rav Ketina denied a claim it concedes was accurate, but it gives only the gain sought, not the cost the question asks about.

berakhot/60.summary: A man entering a Roman bathhouse, heated by a fire burning beneath the pool, prays to be saved from collapse and adds that if ruin comes, let his death atone for his sins. Abaye deletes that line, since naming disaster invites it, and he rewrites the bathroom prayer too, so the accompanying angels are asked to wait rather than to leave. The page closes with Rabbi Akiva in a field, candle blown out, rooster and donkey eaten.
berakhot/60.question: Akiva says it is all for the best because the town that refused him lodging was taken captive that night, but could the sentence be said by anyone inside that town?

judge.reachNote: Whether "all for the best" is a truth about providence or only a sentence available to whoever happened to be spared.

answer.quote: One must always accustom oneself to say: Everything that God does, He does for the best.
answer.explanation: The page states the formula as a standing obligation for everyone, and nearby lines add "even if God brings suffering to bear upon me, I will still praise Him," which bears on whether the harmed may say it, though the story itself only illustrates the saved man's case, so the question can still honestly be asked.

berakhot/61.summary: Rav and Shmuel argue over one word in Genesis, the tzela that God took from Adam to make Eve. One says it means a face, making Eve one whole side of a two-faced creature; the other says a tail, an appendage like a rib. The Gemara tests both readings verse by verse, and when the face side is asked which half walked in front, the answer arrives from a rule about not walking behind a woman on a path.
berakhot/61.question: If Adam and Eve were once one body with two faces, why is the question of who walked in front settled by a rule of conduct rather than by anything in the creation account?

judge.reachNote: A question about the primordial body is decided by a present-day rule of modesty, so lived propriety, not scripture, supplies the proof.

answer.quote: It is reasonable to say that the man walked in front, as it is taught in a baraita
answer.explanation: The page settles who walked in front by reasoning ("it is reasonable to say") from the baraita about not walking behind a woman, but never explains why no creation verse is brought.

berakhot/62.summary: Rabbi Akiva followed his teacher Rabbi Yehoshua into the bathroom and studied how he behaved; accused of impertinence, he answered that it is Torah and he must learn. The line repeats when Ben Azzai trails Akiva, and again when Rav Kahana lies under Rav's bed while Rav jokes with his wife and has relations with her. Later a eulogizer calls a dead man modest, and Rav Naḥman asks whether he ever went to the bathroom with him.
berakhot/62.question: If modesty is only real where nobody is watching, what exactly did Akiva and Rav Kahana manage to learn by watching?

judge.reachNote: If a virtue exists only unobserved, then teaching it by example is self-undermining — yet the Sages insist observation of private conduct is Torah.

answer.quote: I learned that one should not defecate while facing east and west, but rather while facing north and south
answer.explanation: The page spells out the three concrete practices Akiva (and Ben Azzai) learned by observation, though it never reconciles that with Rav Naḥman's rule that modesty is measured where no one is watching, nor says what Rav Kahana learned.

berakhot/63.summary: Ḥanina, the nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, went to Babylonia and began intercalating years and fixing months, work the Sages restricted to Eretz Yisrael. Two scholars sent after him contradicted every ruling he gave, pure for impure, permitted for prohibited, until the threat of a staged mass defection on a mountaintop, altar and lute included, brought the community to tears. The Gemara then notices the problem: one Sage may not permit what a colleague prohibited, and answers only that the emergency required it.
berakhot/63.question: If the pressure of the moment licenses two scholars to reverse a colleague's rulings on purity they may not even disagree about, what keeps the next faction from declaring its own emergency?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea under the case: when a horaat shaa suspends an ordinary rule of rabbinic deference, what prevents the exception from swallowing the rule.

answer.quote: They held that they must do so in this case, so that people would not be drawn after him; due to the exigencies of the time they overturned his rulings.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the emergency justification the note already names, and nearby grounds the Sages' authority in "For out of Zion shall go forth the Torah," but it never states any limit on who may invoke such an emergency, so the note's question survives.

berakhot/64.summary: The last page of Berakhot asks which scholar should head the yeshiva: Rav Yosef, called Sinai for his erudition, or Rabba, who uproots mountains with his sharpness. Eretz Yisrael answers that Sinai wins, since everyone needs the owner of the wheat, yet Rav Yosef steps aside and Rabba presides twenty-two years. The reason offered is not modesty but a forecast: Chaldean astrologers had told Rav Yosef he would serve only two years.
berakhot/64.question: If Rav Yosef declined the post because astrologers told him how long he would hold it, was he yielding to the moment or calculating it?

judge.reachNote: Whether renunciation made in light of foreknowledge of one's destiny still counts as self-effacement, or is just a longer-range grab.

answer.quote: Though he did not take advantage of the opportunity that presented itself, he ultimately fulfilled that for which he was destined.
answer.explanation: The Gemara frames the story as the proof-text for Rabbi Avin HaLevi's rule about yielding to the moment, so it classifies Rav Yosef's refusal as yielding, but it never addresses whether acting on the astrologers' forecast is itself a calculation.

shabbat/2.summary: Shabbat opens with a poor person standing in the street and a homeowner inside his house, passing an object between them through the doorway. The mishna sorts the transfer into eight cases: whoever lifts and sets down alone is liable, while when the two split the work, both go free. The Gemara then fights over the arithmetic, because a parallel mishna in tractate Shevuot counts the same Shabbat labor as only four.
shabbat/2.question: If each hand that lifts or receives counts as its own action, why does the mishna stop at eight rather than Rav Mattana's twelve or Abaye's sixteen?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.
the question brings in "Mattana's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Abaye's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: How a single prohibited labor is individuated: is an act counted per person's hand-motion, or per complete transfer from lifting to placing?

shabbat/3.summary: Rav asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about a man loaded with food on his back inside a private area who then walks out into the street on Shabbat, and is told he is liable, since a body is fixed in place while a hand is not. The same distinction runs into a man standing indoors with a fistful of fruit stuck out into the street, where one early teaching forbids pulling it back and another permits it. The Gemara notices the penalty falls on the riskier case.
shabbat/3.question: If forbidding the man to pull his hand back makes it likelier he drops the fruit and breaks the Torah prohibition outright, why does the page keep the penalty there rather than on the harmless case?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether the Sages' penalties are set by how blameworthy the act was rather than by how much Torah-level risk the penalty itself creates.

answer.quote: In resolving Abaye’s dilemma, the concern that one would likely throw the object from his hand, and thereby violate a Torah prohibition, was not taken into consideration.
answer.explanation: The page voices the note's objection ("On the contrary, the opposite is reasonable") and then states only that the dropping-risk was disregarded, from which it derives that a rabbinic prohibition may not be overridden — a principle rather than a justification of the asymmetry, after which the Gemara abandons the day/night distinction with several "if you wish, say instead" alternatives.

shabbat/4.summary: Someone sticks bread in an oven on Shabbat, and Rav Beivai bar Abaye asks whether he may pull it out before it bakes. Every version of the case falls apart: if he never realized, he would not ask; if he realized partway, that awareness already exempts him from the sin-offering brought for unwitting transgression. Rav Sheila moves the question to bystanders, and Rav Sheshet shuts that down: does one tell another person to sin?
shabbat/4.question: If a bystander may not break even a small rabbinic rule to stop a man from unknowingly committing a capital offense, what is the bystander supposed to do while the bread bakes?
gate: gloss "sin-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: May one commit a lesser transgression to spare another a graver one — the limit of 'sin so that another will benefit.'

answer.quote: the Sages permitted him to remove it from the oven on Shabbat before he comes to violate a prohibition punishable by stoning
answer.explanation: The page resolves the dilemma by relocating the permission to the intentional actor himself rather than to a bystander, which bears on the question but never says what an onlooker should do while an unwitting man's bread bakes.

shabbat/5.summary: Carrying on Shabbat requires lifting an object from a place and setting it down on one, and the Gemara wants that place to measure four handbreadths by four. A poor person's outstretched hand is nowhere near that size, so the Sages try baskets, a householder bending low, a man standing in a hole, a very short person whose hands hang near the ground. Rava waves the whole parade away: a hand simply counts as four by four.
shabbat/5.question: Is Rava's ruling that a hand counts as four by four handbreadths any less of an invention than the man standing in a hole, or only tidier?

judge.reachNote: Whether declaring a legal fiction (the hand counts as four by four) is more honest than contriving improbable facts to satisfy the measure.

answer.quote: when Ravin came from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, he said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: A person's hand is considered four by four handbreadths for him
answer.explanation: The page supports Rava's principle by citing it as an independent tradition from Rabbi Yoḥanan (and then applying it again to an object landing in another's hand), which bears on whether it is an ad hoc invention, though it never argues the point directly.

summaryProblems.claim: One of the proposed cases is a householder bending low.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The mishna here is referring to a case where the poor person lowered his hand below three handbreadths off the ground and received that object in his hand.

judge.feedback: The summary says "One of the proposed cases is a householder bending low.", but the page says "The mishna here is referring to a case where the poor person lowered his hand below three handbreadths off the ground and received that object in his hand.". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: it is the poor person outside who bends down, stands in a hole, or is a midget, not the householder. Keep the question and the shape of the summary, which otherwise tracks the sugya. You may also note that Rava's principle is backed by Ravin's report of Rabbi Yoḥanan, so the rewrite should ask what remains troubling even given that support.

shabbat/6.summary: The Gemara hunts for a case where a person is liable for carrying on Shabbat even though the object passed through a colonnade, a covered walkway where setting it down would carry no penalty at all. Three analogies are floated and two collapse under scrutiny. Then a baraita sorts all space into four domains, private, public, the in-between karmelit, and the exempt place, and Ben Azzai holds that a walker crossing the colonnade has effectively put the object down.
shabbat/6.question: If a person walking through a colonnade counts as having set the object down there, why does a hand stretched through that same space count as never stopping?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that liability tracks the continuity of the act rather than the status of the space crossed — but the page states that very distinction.

answer.quote: One who walks and carries out and one who walks and carries in are exempt, as he is considered to have come to rest in the colonnade. On the other hand, one who extends his hand
answer.explanation: The baraita itself gives Ben Azzai's reason for the distinction: walking involves coming to rest, while extending the hand or throwing are actions "whose actions are uninterrupted," and therefore liable.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 6a: "One who walks and carries out and one who walks and carries in are exempt, as he is considered to have come to rest in the colonnade. On the other hand, one who extends his hand". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim in the baraita on 6a, which says walking is exempt because he "is considered to have come to rest" while the hand and throw are liable because their "actions are uninterrupted." Rewrite the question to push past that label — for instance, ask why a walker's legal pause counts as a placement when he never intended to set the object down, or why a space that is exempt for placement can still ground liability when the movement through it is continuous. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

shabbat/7.summary: Much of the page sorts street-level patches into domains by asking whether people actually walk on them. An upright brick three handbreadths high is its own domain, since the crowd steps around it; thorns and shrubs are argued over; and Ḥiyya bar Rav says a spot fouled with feces is not part of the public domain, until Rav Ashi answers that hurried workers tread in it anyway. Convenience, not ownership, keeps deciding the case.
shabbat/7.question: If a corner counts as a karmelit because its use is inconvenient, and filth counts as public street because rushed people step in it regardless, whose habits set the boundary?

judge.reachNote: Whether a domain is defined by how a place invites use or by how people in fact treat it — a standard of convenience versus a standard of observed behavior.

answer.quote: There, the corner, its use is not convenient; here, the holes of the public domain, their use is convenient.
answer.explanation: Abaye's distinction supplies the operative criterion — convenience of use rather than any particular group's habits — but the page never settles whose behavior (the careful or the hurried) fixes that convenience, so the question survives.

shabbat/8.summary: A pillar nine handbreadths high stands in a public street, and passersby rest their shoulder loads on it; Ulla says that use makes it part of the public domain, so an object thrown onto it from a private courtyard brings liability. Abaye asks about a pit of the same depth, and Rava says no: stooping into a hole is awkward, and use under duress is not use. A muddy swamp, though, still counts as street, because people really do walk through it.
shabbat/8.question: If wading through mud in the rainy season is enough to make a swamp public street, why is reaching down into a pit too inconvenient to count?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether awkward, compelled use of a space still makes it public — which the page settles by splitting passage from usage.

answer.quote: passage, even when it is under duress, and not free and easy, is considered passage, but usage under duress is not considered usage
answer.explanation: The Gemara draws exactly the swamp/pit comparison the question raises and resolves it by distinguishing passage under duress (which counts) from usage under duress (which does not), concluding "Indeed conclude from this."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 8b: "passage, even when it is under duress, and not free and easy, is considered passage, but usage under duress is not considered usage". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks precisely what the Gemara asks and answers from the doubled "swamp" in the mishna, so it must be replaced. Write a question that starts from the page's own distinction — passage under duress counts, usage under duress does not — and presses on what remains unsettled, for instance why walking is judged by whether the multitudes actually pass while a pillar or pit is judged by convenience of use. Alternatively build the question off a different thread on the page, such as Rav Ashi's claim that partitions are made only for the inside of the barrel.

shabbat/9.summary: The mishna forbids sitting down before the barber, entering the bathhouse or the tannery, starting a meal, or opening a trial once the hour of the afternoon prayer draws near. The Gemara asks how a haircut could swallow an afternoon, and answers twice: either these are enormous versions, like ben Elasa's elaborate haircut, or the worry is that the scissors break and the time runs out. Then it pins down the exact moment each activity counts as already begun.
shabbat/9.question: If the afternoon prayer is obligatory for everyone, why should a loosened belt be enough to keep a man at his table?

judge.reachNote: Why a small token that an activity has begun should outweigh an admittedly obligatory prayer — where the line between 'not yet started' and 'already engaged' gets its force.

answer.quote: this, the statement of Rabbi Ḥanina, who said that the beginning of the meal is considered from when he loosens his belt, is for us, for the people of Babylonia
answer.explanation: The page explains why a loosened belt marks the meal's start for Babylonians, and it raises the very tension the question asks about — "Doesn't everyone agree that the afternoon prayer is obligatory?" — without resolving it on this daf.

shabbat/10.summary: Rav holds that one who gives a gift must tell the recipient, learned from God instructing Moses to inform Israel about Shabbat, a good gift in the treasure house. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies this to handing a child bread: the giver smears oil or eye shadow on him so the mother will notice and ask who fed him. Against the rule stands Moses, whose face shone without his knowing, and the two are split by whether the gift would surface on its own.
shabbat/10.question: If the mother only learns of the bread because oil was smeared on her child's face, whose benefit is the announcement really for?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that telling about a gift may serve the bond between giver and recipient rather than the recipient's material benefit, here refracted through a child who cannot register the telling.

shabbat/11.summary: A tailor may not step outside with his needle as Friday evening comes on, in case he forgets it and carries it after Shabbat begins. Abaye reads that as the Sages guarding one rabbinic decree with a second, and extends the logic to a karmelit, an in-between space that is neither public nor private domain. Rava refuses, asking whether a decree gets built on top of a decree, and every proof brought against him is reread as something else.
shabbat/11.question: If each proof for Abaye can be reassigned to Rabbi Yehuda's view or to the laws of tithes, what evidence could ever settle whether the Sages fence a fence?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Asks how a legal claim about the Sages' habits of legislating can ever be proven when every source can be reassigned to another tanna or another topic.

shabbat/12.summary: Reading a book by lamplight on Shabbat is barred because a reader might tilt the wick for more light. Rava says an important person is exempt, since he would never dirty his hands on an oily lamp, and then the Gemara produces Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha, who read, adjusted the wick, and wrote in his notebook that he owed a fat sin-offering, an atonement animal, when the Temple is rebuilt. Rabbi Abba rescues the exemption by calling Yishmael an exception.
shabbat/12.question: If Rava's exemption for important people survives only by ruling that Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha did not count as one, who is left inside it?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: An exemption keyed to a person's dignity collapses if the most dignified man on record is declared not to fit it.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha is different, since with regard to the study of Torah, he comports himself like a simple man with no air of importance
answer.explanation: Rabbi Abba limits the carve-out to Yishmael's self-effacement in Torah study, implying important people generally remain inside Rava's exemption, but the page never says who those people are.

shabbat/13.summary: A husband and his menstruating wife want to sleep in one bed, both fully dressed, and the Gemara asks whether the Sages forbade even that. It tests the case against a mishna where Beit Hillel bar fowl and cheese from sharing a table, then distinguishes: two people have two separate minds, and clothing is a visible reminder. A baraita overrides the distinction, and Elijah tells a grieving widow her scholar husband died young for exactly this.
shabbat/13.question: If Rabbi Pedat holds that the Torah forbids only relations themselves, on what grounds is the student's early death called a fitting punishment for lying beside his wife?
gate: the question brings in "Pedat", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a death-level punishment can rest on a prohibition broader than the Torah's bare ban on relations — the page reaches it and settles it against Rabbi Pedat.

answer.quote: And this conclusion disagrees with the opinion of Rabbi Pedat, as Rabbi Pedat said: The Torah only prohibited intimacy that involves engaging in prohibited sexual relations
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the accepted conclusion (from the Ezekiel baraita, that lying together clothed is forbidden) rejects Rabbi Pedat's narrow view, and 13b supplies the grounds in Eliyahu's words that "even mere affectionate contact is prohibited" so "since the matter is prohibited, that student was punished."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 13a: "And this conclusion disagrees with the opinion of Rabbi Pedat, as Rabbi Pedat said: The Torah only prohibited intimacy that involves engaging in prohibited sexual relations". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already settled on the page: the Gemara says the Ezekiel-based conclusion "disagrees with the opinion of Rabbi Pedat," and Eliyahu grounds the punishment in "even mere affectionate contact is prohibited." Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for example, why the two-consciousnesses-plus-noticeable-change reasoning, which would have permitted the clothed couple, is abandoned once the verse is cited, or why Ulla's own kissing of his sisters stands against his own adage. Keep the summary as it is; it is faithful.

shabbat/14.summary: Much of the page asks why the Sages declared certain things impure, and the answers are practical. Ignorant priests stored teruma, the portion of produce given to priests, beside Torah scrolls, saying both were sacred; mice came for the food and gnawed the scrolls, so the Sages ruled the scroll itself imparts impurity and the priests moved the food away. Later the page notes that hands touching a scroll were decreed impure before hands in general.
shabbat/14.question: Why would the very same decree about impure hands be refused when Hillel and Shammai issued it, and accepted when their students did?
gate: the question brings in "Hillel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Shammai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a rabbinic decree's force depends on the community's acceptance rather than the stature of the sage who issues it.

answer.quote: they came and issued a decree and the people did not accept the decree from them, and their disciples came and issued a decree and they accepted it from them
answer.explanation: The page states as fact that the people rejected the decree from Hillel and Shammai and accepted it from the disciples, but gives no reason for the difference in reception, so the question can still be asked.

shabbat/15.summary: Rav Huna counts only three places where Hillel and Shammai personally disagreed: how much dough requires halla, the portion given to a priest; how much drawn water ruins a ritual bath; and how far back a woman's impurity reaches once she finds blood. In all three the Rabbis rule like neither of them. The ritual bath measure stayed open until two weavers from the Dung Gate testified in the name of Shemaya and Avtalyon, and their number won.
shabbat/15.question: If the weavers' testimony was strong enough to beat both Hillel and Shammai, why does the page stop to tell you their trade was despised and their neighborhood contemptible?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that testimony's authority comes from its content, not the status of the witnesses — but the page says this explicitly.

answer.quote: The Gemara emphasized their occupation and the place that they lived to underscore that, despite the fact that their occupation was despised and their place was contemptible, there is no preferential treatment when it comes to Torah.
answer.explanation: The page states outright why it mentions the weavers' trade and neighborhood: to show that in Torah there is no preferential treatment by social standing.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 15a: "The Gemara emphasized their occupation and the place that they lived to underscore that, despite the fact that their occupation was despised and their place was contemptible, there is no preferential treatment when it comes to Torah.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same sentence the summary is drawing on: the Gemara says it mentioned their trade and place to show there is no preferential treatment in Torah. Write a question the page leaves open instead — for example, why the Rabbis needed testimony from Shemaya and Avtalyon at all rather than simply choosing between Hillel's and Shammai's measures, or why three log ends up below both of their figures. Keep the summary as it is.

shabbat/16.summary: Shimon ben Shataḥ's sister, Queen Shel Tziyyon, made a wedding feast for her son, and when all her metal vessels became ritually impure she broke them and had a smith weld them back together. The Sages said the maneuver failed, since recast metal takes up its old impurity again. Abaye explains the worry as an owner who loves his pot and will not smash it wide enough; Rava says bystanders will conclude a quick dip in water did the job.
shabbat/16.question: Should a repaired pot stay impure because of what a neighbor might wrongly conclude from watching it come clean?

judge.reachNote: Whether a public misimpression about how purity was achieved can justify imposing real impurity on an object that is in fact pure.

answer.quote: Rava said: It is a decree lest they say that immersion on the same day is sufficient for this vessel to be purified.
answer.explanation: The page states Rava's rationale and concludes "Therefore, the Sages decreed that repaired vessels retain previous impurity," but it asserts rather than defends the appearance-based logic the question probes, so the question can still be asked honestly.

shabbat/17.summary: Shammai and Hillel argue over whether juice seeping from harvested grapes makes them susceptible to ritual impurity, and Shammai threatens to decree the same for olives. The dispute ends with a sword planted in the study hall, no one permitted to leave until the vote, and Hillel sitting bowed before Shammai like a student. The Gemara calls that day as hard as the day of the Golden Calf, then notes the people refused the decree from the masters and accepted it from their students.
shabbat/17.question: Why would the same decree be rejected when Shammai and Hillel issued it, and accepted when their students issued it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a decree's binding force depends on popular acceptance rather than the stature of the sage who issues it.

shabbat/18.summary: A water mill left grinding wheat into Shabbat is forbidden, and the Gemara asks why. Rabba says the noise of the grinding advertises contempt for the day; Rav Yosef says the tool itself is obligated to rest. That second reason forces a line between tools that act and tools that do not: an oven drying bundles of flax just sits there, and a fish net stands still while the fish swims into it.
shabbat/18.question: If a cooking pot escapes the demand that utensils rest simply by being declared ownerless before dark, what is left of the demand?

judge.reachNote: Asks what an obligation of 'resting utensils' really demands if it can be dissolved by a costless formal renunciation of ownership.

shabbat/19.summary: An early teaching bars renting out utensils to a gentile on Friday and handing a letter to a gentile courier close to Shabbat, since the work done on Shabbat would look like it was done for the Jew. The fix is money: a fee fixed in advance makes the trip the courier's own business rather than an errand. Then comes Rabbi Yosei the priest, who broke no rule and still made sure a letter of his was never found in a gentile's hand.
shabbat/19.question: If a price agreed in advance really makes the delivery the courier's own affair, what was Rabbi Yosei avoiding by never sending a letter that way at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether a fixed fee truly severs the gentile's act from the Jew's agency, or only removes the appearance while the underlying unease remains, prompting piety beyond the letter of the rule.

answer.quote: a document in his handwriting was never found in the hand of a gentile, so that a gentile would not carry his letter on Shabbat
answer.explanation: The page states in so many words what Rabbi Yosei was avoiding — a gentile carrying his letter on Shabbat — though it never explains why a stipulated fee failed to satisfy him.

shabbat/20.summary: The measure for food left cooking into Shabbat is set by ben Drosai, a robber on the run who ate his meat only partly roasted. From there the argument turns to when a bonfire counts as lit: most of each branch, says Rav, or just enough that nobody calls for thinner sticks, says Shmuel. Then a mishna lists wicks and oils barred from the Shabbat lamp, and the Gemara discovers that half the names had been forgotten.
shabbat/20.question: Can a rule against lighting with kalakh be kept by people who have to ask sailors what kalakh is?

judge.reachNote: A prohibition can outlive knowledge of what it names; the question asks how law binds when its terms must be recovered by field inquiry.

answer.quote: Shmuel said: I asked all seafarers, and they said to me that the present-day name of kalakh mentioned in the mishna is kulka.
answer.explanation: The page shows the practical route by which a forgotten term is re-identified — asking those who trade in it — which bears on the question without directly settling whether the rule was keepable in the interim.

shabbat/21.summary: Rabba explains why certain wicks and oils are barred from the Shabbat lamp: the flame sputters on them, or the oil is not drawn up the wick. The same materials are then argued over for Hanukkah, where everything hinges on two unsettled questions, whether a lamp that goes out must be relit and whether its light may be used for anything. Rav Huna, Rav Ḥisda and Rav each answer differently, and the sputtering wick is forbidden or permitted accordingly.
shabbat/21.question: If a storekeeper puts his lamp outside because the Sages told him to, should the owner of the passing camel, and not he, pay for the flax that burns?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that acting under a rabbinic command can shift the cost of the resulting damage onto the other party — but the page itself already rules and explains this.

answer.quote: the storekeeper's Hanukkah lamp that he placed outside the entrance to his store, he is not liable, as in that case, it is permitted
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that the storekeeper who placed his Hanukkah lamp outside at the Sages' behest bears no liability for the burnt flax, and then gives two reasons for that exemption (the ten-handbreadth requirement, or not burdening the performer of the mitzva).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 21b: "the storekeeper's Hanukkah lamp that he placed outside the entrance to his store, he is not liable, as in that case, it is permitted". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what Rabbi Yehuda already rules on this page, and the Gemara even supplies two competing reasons for the exemption, so a reader finds the answer spelled out. Rewrite the question so it starts from that ruling and presses on what remains unsettled — for instance, whether the exemption rests on a height limit for the lamp or on the fear that too much liability would make people abandon the mitzva, and what that choice implies. Alternatively, build the question on the summary's own thread: the three-way dispute over relighting and using the Hanukkah light, which the page leaves genuinely open.

shabbat/22.summary: Rav says one may not light one Hanukkah lamp from another; Shmuel permits it. Two reasons for Rav circulate: that borrowing the flame demeans the mitzva, or that it weakens it, using up a little of the oil and wick set aside for the mitzva. Rav Sheshet presses with the Temple candelabrum, whose westernmost lamp was lit with the same measure of oil as the rest and kindled them all, and the objection is left standing.
shabbat/22.question: If the westernmost lamp lit every other lamp each day and still burned longest, why does the worry about weakening a lamp survive as an unanswered difficulty?

judge.reachNote: Whether spending a little of a mitzva's substance on another mitzva counts as diminishing it, and whether a lamp that never ran short can still be 'weakened'.

answer.quote: According to the one who said that Rav's reason is because he weakens the mitzva, lighting directly from lamp to lamp is also prohibited
answer.explanation: The page explains why Rav Pappa's long-wicks resolution rescues only the contempt reason — on the weakening reason even direct lamp-to-lamp lighting depletes the mitzva oil — though it states only that the difficulty "remains difficult" without further defending it.

shabbat/23.summary: The blessing over the Hanukkah light says God "has commanded us to light," and the Gemara stops to ask where, since no verse mentions Hanukkah at all. Rav Avya points to the command not to turn aside from what the Sages declare, making obedience to them itself a divine order. Rav Amram objects from demai, produce bought from someone who may not have tithed: the Sages let a man separate its tithe while naked, where no blessing is possible.
shabbat/23.question: If obeying the Sages counts as a divine command, why does the doubt about whether a farmer tithed strip the blessing away, while the doubt about which day the Festival falls on does not?
gate: the question brings in "Festival", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — when does rabbinic uncertainty still generate a blessing-worthy obligation — but the page states both answers a few lines later.

answer.quote: There, in the case of the second day of the Festival, the reason that blessings are required is so that people will not treat it with contempt.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's exact contrast between demai and the Diaspora second Festival day and answers it twice — by contempt, and by Rava's point that most an am ha'aretz do tithe, so demai is mere suspicion rather than true uncertainty.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 23a: "There, in the case of the second day of the Festival, the reason that blessings are required is so that people will not treat it with contempt.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved in the very passage the summary describes: the Gemara asks about the Diaspora second Festival day and answers with contempt, and Rava adds that demai is mere suspicion since most amei ha'aretz tithe. Rewrite the question to begin after those answers — for instance, probing why fear of contempt can manufacture a blessing where Abaye's definite/uncertain line would not, or what it means that 'most people tithe' downgrades doubt into suspicion. Keep the summary, which is accurate, but let it carry the reader to Abaye and Rava so the question has somewhere new to stand.

shabbat/24.summary: The Sages ask whether Hanukkah, being only a rabbinic obligation, should be mentioned in Grace after Meals at all, and whether the New Moon should be. The argument narrows to added prayers: if the extra Shabbat prayer exists only because it is Shabbat, does Hanukkah belong inside it? The ruling comes from Yom Kippur falling on Shabbat, where the day itself owes four prayers, while the evening repetition, instituted so latecomers would not walk dark roads alone, does not count.
shabbat/24.question: If a prayer's origin decides whether the day gets named in it, why does the repetition added for safety on the road home count as less a part of the day than the rest?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real principle — whether a prayer's source or the day's essential character governs mention — but the Gemara states that principle outright.

answer.quote: This repetition of the prayer does not stem from the obligation of the day but was instituted for another purpose.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly explains that the evening repetition is excluded because it was instituted for safety rather than arising from the day's own obligation, while Yom Kippur's four prayers are owed by the day itself.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 24b: "This repetition of the prayer does not stem from the obligation of the day but was instituted for another purpose.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim on the page: the repetition was instituted for safety and so does not stem from the day's obligation, unlike Yom Kippur's four prayers. Write a question that starts after that distinction rather than asking for it. For instance, press on why the same 'essence of the day' reasoning that includes ne'ila does not settle the earlier disputes about Hanukkah in the additional prayer or the New Moon in Grace after Meals.

shabbat/25.summary: Rabbi Yishmael bars tar as lamp fuel on Shabbat, and Rava explains the decree: the smell is bad, so a person might walk away from the light. Abaye pushes back, asking what obliges anyone to sit by a lamp at all. Rava answers that kindling the Shabbat lamp is an obligation and the meal must be eaten by its light, which pulls the page on to hot water, linen cloaks, and four sages defining wealth.
shabbat/25.question: If the Shabbat lamp exists so that a person eats by its light, is the obligation the kindling or the staying put?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether a mitzva of light is discharged by the act of lighting or only by using the light — but the page states both.

answer.quote: Because I say that kindling Shabbat lights is an obligation, and one is required to eat specifically by that light in deference to Shabbat.
answer.explanation: Rava's reply, which the summary itself paraphrases, states that the kindling is the obligation and that eating by that light is likewise required, so the either/or is resolved on the page.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 25b: "Because I say that kindling Shabbat lights is an obligation, and one is required to eat specifically by that light in deference to Shabbat.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered by the very line the summary quotes: Rava says kindling is an obligation and one must eat by that light, so both halves are stated. Write a question that starts after that answer — for example, why a bad smell needs a rabbinic decree at all if the duty to eat by the lamp already holds a person in place, or what it means that washing is called a mitzva yet not an obligation. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful to the page.

shabbat/26.summary: Balsam oil is flammable enough that the Gemara pauses on a mother-in-law who hated her daughter-in-law, told her to perfume herself with it, then sent her to light the lamp. The list of substances unfit for the Shabbat lamp then narrows, sage by sage, until Rabbi Tarfon permits olive oil alone. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri stands up and asks what Babylonia, Media, Alexandria, and Cappadocia are meant to burn, and the rule is recast as a closed list of forbidden oils.
shabbat/26.question: If Cappadocia has nothing but naphtha, does Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's answer actually leave them a lamp, or only a shorter list of things they cannot light?

judge.reachNote: A rule stated only as a closed list of prohibitions may not actually supply anyone with a permitted means; exclusion is not the same as provision.

answer.quote: And one may light with fish oil and tar. Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says: One may light with gourd oil and naphtha.
answer.explanation: The page does state that naphtha (at least per Rabbi Shimon Shezuri) may be used, and that the prohibition extends only to the listed substances, but the earlier baraita's ban on white naphtha as volatile leaves the Cappadocian case genuinely unresolved on the page.

shabbat/27.summary: Abaye and Rava argue over which fabrics can contract ritual impurity: wool and linen only, or also camel hair, rabbits' wool, and silk. A ruling given in Rav Pappa's name is tested, fails, and is taken back from him. The sharper turn is ritual fringes, the threads on a garment's four corners: "that you may look upon it" should exempt a blind man's garment, but it stays in, and a night garment is excluded instead.
shabbat/27.question: If the fringes are there so the wearer will look at them and remember, why is it enough that a blind man's garment can be seen by everyone else?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether the mitzva of fringes attaches to the garment as an object that is seen, or to the wearer's act of seeing and remembering.

answer.quote: I include the garment of a blind person because it is, at least, visible to others, and I exclude a night garment because it is not even visible to others.
answer.explanation: The Gemara states the operative criterion — visibility to others — but does not explain why that suffices given that the verse's stated purpose is the wearer's own looking and remembering, so the question can still be honestly asked.

shabbat/28.summary: Rabbi Elazar asks whether a hide from a non-kosher animal, spread over a corpse, counts as a tent and so picks up ritual impurity. The chase runs through the Tabernacle's coverings and the tahash, a creature nobody can identify, before Rava from Barnish settles it with goats' hair: goats' hair cannot become impure from leprosy yet counts as a tent, so non-kosher hide should too. The tahash stays a puzzle, one horn, wild or domesticated unknown.
shabbat/28.question: Once the ruling no longer depends on whether the tahash was kosher, why does the page keep pressing to identify the animal?

judge.reachNote: Whether the Gemara pursues a factual identification for its own sake once the halakhic outcome no longer turns on it.

answer.quote: Rav Yosef was certainly referring to straps when he said that all heavenly service must be performed with the hides of kosher animals.
answer.explanation: The page relocates the kosher-hide requirement to phylactery straps, showing where the kashrut of hides still matters, but it never states why it then goes on to press for the taḥash's identity, which it leaves unresolved.

shabbat/29.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalls a Shabbat in the upper story of Nit'za's house in Lod, where they pierced an eggshell, filled it with oil, and set it over a lamp to feed the flame longer. Rabbi Tarfon and other Elders were sitting right there and said nothing; the Rabbis answer that those men were vigilant, so their silence proves nothing about ordinary people. Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar, watching a bench dragged across a marble floor, refuses to stay quiet, saying silence itself did the damage.
shabbat/29.question: If the Elders' silence left Rabbi Yehuda with the wrong rule, is the mistake his for reading permission into it, or theirs for watching and saying nothing?

judge.reachNote: Whether a teacher's silence in the presence of an act functions as a ruling, and who bears the cost when it is read that way.

answer.quote: Had they told Rabbi Yehuda at that time that it is prohibited to puncture the eggshell, he would not have disagreed with the Rabbis.
answer.where: Shabbat 29b (Avin of Tzippori / Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar)
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar traces the damage to the Elders' silence, which bears directly on the note's question, though the Rabbis' retort "Do you bring proof from there?" still faults Rabbi Yehuda's inference, so blame is not finally allocated.

shabbat/30.summary: A question comes to Rabbi Tanhum of Nevi: may one extinguish a lamp on Shabbat so a sick person can sleep? Rather than answer, he sets Solomon against his father David and against himself on whether the dead are better off than the living, running through Moses' prayer, the Temple gates that refused to open, and David dying when a broken stair startled him into a moment's silence mid-study. Only at the close does the ruling arrive, as wordplay on the word ner, lamp.
shabbat/30.question: If one kingdom cannot overlap another by even a hairbreadth, how was David able to hold the Angel of Death off for hours simply by not pausing his study?
gate: the question brings in "Angel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Death", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the tension between a death fixed to the hairbreadth by decree and Torah study that can apparently hold death off within that day.

answer.quote: the Angel of Death stood before him and was unable to overcome him because his mouth did not pause from study
answer.explanation: The page states the mechanism of the delay — uninterrupted study shields him — but never reconciles that delay with the rule that kingdoms do not overlap by a hairbreadth, so the question survives.

shabbat/31.summary: Two men bet four hundred zuz, a serious sum of silver, that one of them could provoke Hillel into losing his temper; the man tries three times with questions about oval heads and wide feet, and fails. Then three gentiles arrive with impossible conditions: teach me only the Written Torah, teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot, make me High Priest. Shammai drives each away with his builder's measuring stick; Hillel accepts every condition and then works around it.
shabbat/31.question: Hillel converted the third man on condition that he be installed as High Priest, something Hillel never arranges; is a promise kept when the one who made it simply teaches you to stop wanting it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a condition is honored by satisfying the desire behind it or by curing the person of the desire.

answer.quote: Hillel the patient, may blessings rest upon your head as you brought me under the wings of the Divine Presence.
answer.explanation: The page has the convert himself, after retracting his demand, bless Hillel rather than accuse him of breaking faith, which bears on whether the condition was honored, but it never states that the promise was or was not kept.

summaryProblems.claim: Shammai drives each away with his builder's measuring stick.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Shammai scolded him and cast him out with reprimand.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Shammai drives each away with his builder's measuring stick.", but the page says "Shammai scolded him and cast him out with reprimand.". Say what the page says. Fix the claim that Shammai used the measuring stick on all three: the first gentile he simply "scolded him and cast him out with reprimand," and only the second and third were pushed with the builder's cubit. Also, the page never says Hillel accepted the High Priest condition in words — it says only "He came before Hillel; he converted him" — so the question should not assert a stated promise. Keep the promise-versus-changed-desire idea, which is the note's strength.

shabbat/32.summary: Rava, Abaye and Rav Hisda trade blunt folk sayings about why a woman's sins are reckoned at childbirth: if the ox falls, sharpen the knife. The talk turns to men, said to be examined when crossing a bridge, and Rav refused any ferry carrying a gentile while Shmuel boarded only if one was aboard. Then the roof parapet: the man who falls was marked as fallen since Creation, yet the negligent homeowner is still indicted.
shabbat/32.question: If the faller was destined to drop from that roof since the six days of Creation, what exactly is the homeowner being blamed for?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the tension between a fate fixed at Creation and personal liability for being the instrument of it.

answer.quote: Nevertheless, the owner of the house is indicted for this, as merit is engendered by means of the innocent and guilt by means of the guilty.
answer.explanation: The page states a principle that bears on why the homeowner is liable despite the predestined fall — misfortune is brought about through guilty agents — but it does not spell out what the homeowner's own culpable act consists of, so the question can still be honestly asked.

shabbat/33.summary: Rabbi Yehuda praises Rome for building marketplaces, bridges, and bathhouses; Rabbi Yosei stays silent; Rabbi Shimon bar Yoḥai answers that each was built for Roman purposes. The remark reaches the government: Yehuda is promoted, Yosei exiled, Shimon sentenced, so he hides twelve years in a cave with his son, sitting in sand, studying. When they emerge and burn farmers with a glance, a voice sends them back; later Shimon repays his rescue by repairing a town, as Jacob built marketplaces and bathhouses.
shabbat/33.question: If marketplaces and bathhouses were worth a death sentence when Rome built them, what makes them acts of kindness when Jacob or Rabbi Shimon builds them?

judge.reachNote: The same public works can be kindness or exploitation depending on whose benefit they serve — motive, not the deed, carries the moral weight.

answer.quote: Everything that they established, they established only for their own purposes. They established marketplaces, to place prostitutes in them; bathhouses, to pamper themselves
answer.explanation: Rabbi Shimon's own words locate the fault in Roman motive rather than in the buildings, and the page later calls Jacob's parallel works "gracious acts to benefit the city," which bears on the question without stating the comparison the note draws.

shabbat/34.summary: Three things have to be said at home just before dark on Friday: have you tithed the produce, have you placed the eiruv that lets neighbors carry in a shared courtyard, and light the lamp. Rabba bar Rav Huna adds that they must be said calmly, or the household may mislead him. Twilight itself stays undefined, carrying the strictures of both day and night, yet Rava lets two men each keep an eiruv that only one could have owned.
shabbat/34.question: If twilight gets the stringencies of both day and night, how do both men walk away with a valid eiruv when the same moment cannot have been day for one and night for the other?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that an uncertain moment can be treated leniently or strictly depending on whether the obligation is Torah-based or rabbinic.

answer.quote: The status of twilight is uncertain, as it is unknown whether it is day, or night, or both, and uncertainty in the case of a rabbinic ordinance is ruled leniently.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection ("Whichever way you look at it, this ruling is difficult") and resolves it by ruling twilight uncertainty leniently in rabbinic matters such as the joining of courtyards.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 34a: "The status of twilight is uncertain, as it is unknown whether it is day, or night, or both, and uncertainty in the case of a rabbinic ordinance is ruled leniently.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it outright by ruling twilight's uncertainty leniently because eiruv of courtyards is rabbinic. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer, for instance asking why the same uncertain moment carries the stringencies of both days for a zav's impurity yet is resolved leniently for the two eiruvin, or what it means that a single moment can count as day for one man and night for another. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

shabbat/35.summary: Twilight is the seam between Friday and Shabbat, and the page hunts for ways to catch it: the time it takes to walk half a mil, a dip in the sea while Mount Carmel still holds sunlight, one star, two stars, three. Rava tells his servant, who does not know the Sages' measures, to watch the roosters settling on their beams. Rabbi Yosei ben Zevida adds that working through both twilights, Friday's and Saturday night's, brings a sin-offering either way.
shabbat/35.question: If neither of the two acts can be shown to have fallen on Shabbat, what exactly is the sin-offering for?
gate: gloss "sin-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question uses "sin offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of liability grounded in certainty across alternatives rather than in an identified act — but the page states that rationale outright.

answer.quote: Whether we say that twilight is day or night, certainly one of those labors was performed on Shabbat.
answer.explanation: The page itself supplies the rationale for liability: although neither act can be pinned down, on either reckoning of twilight one of the two must have fallen on Shabbat.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 35b: "Whether we say that twilight is day or night, certainly one of those labors was performed on Shabbat.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very sentence the summary paraphrases: the page says that whichever way twilight is reckoned, one of the two labors certainly fell on Shabbat. Build the question on what remains hard after that answer — for example that the offender still cannot name which act he must atone for, or why this shared-certainty logic is not applied to other doubtful cases like immersion, where the page rules stringently instead. Alternatively pick a different thread on the page, such as why a community shofar becomes set-aside while an individual's stays permitted.

shabbat/36.summary: A shofar, a ram's horn, may be carried on Shabbat because its narrow end can pour water into a child's mouth, while a trumpet has no such permitted use. Sorting three conflicting early teachings leads Rav Hisda to a claim: after the Temple fell, the words shofar and trumpet swapped places, as did willow and tzaftzafa, and large table and small. Abaye adds the two stomachs of a cow; Rav Ashi adds Babylon, which came to mean Bursif.
shabbat/36.question: If names can trade places while the objects stay where they are, does a law about a willow branch bind the word or the branch?

judge.reachNote: Whether a halakhic term binds the name or the thing named once usage shifts — the page's own "what is the practical difference" refrain answers it for the object.

answer.quote: If one comes today and asks what instrument he should use to sound the requisite blasts, he should be told to use a trumpet.
answer.explanation: The page settles the word-versus-object issue directly: the mitzva follows the object, so today one is directed to what is now called a trumpet, and the parallel willow case likewise turns on which branch, "a willow branch, not a tzaftzafa."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 36a: "If one comes today and asks what instrument he should use to sound the requisite blasts, he should be told to use a trumpet.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already settled on the page: the Gemara's repeated "what is the practical halakhic difference" answers that the law tracks the object, telling a person today to sound what is now called a trumpet and to take a willow, not a tzaftzafa. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for instance, why the Gemara bothers to record name swaps at all rather than simply describing the required object, or what happens to a document or sale where the parties' words, not the objects, are what bind. Keep the summary's thread, which is faithful to the page.

shabbat/37.summary: The Sages keep hunting for proof about whether the mishna permits leaving a pot on a stove over Shabbat or returning one to it after removing it, and every proof gets rejected. The test then shifts from the stove to the food: if long cooking improves a dish, leaving it is forbidden, since someone might poke the coals; if it ruins the dish, it is fine. Rav Nahman's turnip stew switches categories depending on meat and on guests.
shabbat/37.question: If a turnip stew counts as improving or spoiling depending on whether guests are expected, whose appetite decides what may sit on the fire?

judge.reachNote: Whether a Shabbat prohibition tracks an objective property of the food or the shifting expectations of whoever will eat it.

answer.quote: when one needs it for guests, it shrivels and deteriorates because it is not polite to serve guests overcooked food, which is not aesthetic
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason the guest case flips the category — the food is judged by what would be fit to serve — but it never states whose standard of taste sets the measure, so the question can still be pressed.

shabbat/38.summary: A pot left on the stove before Shabbat keeps cooking into Shabbat, and the question is whether the food may be eaten. Rav reports that the rule once turned on intent, until so many people left pots on purpose and claimed they forgot that the Sages penalized the forgetful too. The page then argues about returning a pot to the stove, and whether holding it, setting it down, or hanging it on a stick matters.
shabbat/38.question: If the penalty exists only because liars claimed to have forgotten, what is it doing to the person who really did forget?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rule may burden the innocent in order to deny the guilty an excuse.

answer.quote: However, one who would come to deceive, intentionally leaving the pot on the stove and saying: I forgot it, the Sages penalize him and decree that if he did so unwittingly as well, he may not eat it.
answer.explanation: The page states the mechanism — the unwitting forgetter is penalized in order to close the loophole exploited by deceivers — but it never defends the justice of that penalty for the honest person, which is what the question presses on.

shabbat/39.summary: Everyone agrees an egg may be set in the sun to warm, and no one may set it on something heated by fire. The fight is over the middle case: cloths or sand warmed by the sun, which the Rabbis forbid lest people confuse them with fire-heated objects, and which Rabbi Yosei permits. When the Rabbis cite Tiberias, whose residents ran a cold-water pipe through the hot springs, Yosei answers that those springs pass over the entrance to Gehenna, so they count as fire.
shabbat/39.question: If the Rabbis' whole worry is that nobody can tell how a thing got hot, how does Rabbi Yosei know what heats the springs of Tiberias?

judge.reachNote: A decree built on the public's ignorance of how something got hot sits uneasily with a sage confidently classifying a spring's hidden heat source.

summaryProblems.claim: Sand warmed by the sun is part of the middle case that Rabbi Yosei permits.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabba said: Rabbi Yosei agrees with the opinion of the Rabbis in this case.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Sand warmed by the sun is part of the middle case that Rabbi Yosei permits.", but the page says "Rabba said: Rabbi Yosei agrees with the opinion of the Rabbis in this case.". Say what the page says. Fix the sand: the page says Rabbi Yosei does not permit insulating in sun-heated sand, either because he concedes the decree lest one use hot ashes (Rabba) or because insulating there displaces dirt (Rav Yosef). Keep the sun/fire/derivatives-of-the-sun framework and Tiberias, but let the disputed middle case be the cloths. The question can stay as it is.

shabbat/40.summary: Bathhouse attendants heated water on Shabbat and told customers it had been heated the day before. The Sages banned bathing and permitted sweating, so people bathed and called it sweating; ban followed ban, down to cold water only, until the Sages saw their decrees were ignored and reopened the hot springs of Tiberias. The sweating ban alone stayed, and Rava says someone who breaks a rabbinic decree can fairly be called a transgressor.
shabbat/40.question: If the Sages gave back the hot springs because people would not keep that decree, why did the ban on sweating survive the same disobedience?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: when a decree is widely ignored, what makes the Sages retreat on one prohibition and hold firm on another.

shabbat/41.summary: Rabbi Zeira watched Rabbi Abbahu bathe and could not tell whether he covered himself with his hands touching or not, since Rav had said that covering one's genitals looks like denying Abraham's covenant, hiding the mark of circumcision. The answer splits the moment: stand upright going down into the river, bend over coming out, when people on the bank are watching. Later Rabbi Zeira, dodging the teacher who called leaving Babylonia a transgression, finds Rav Yehuda in the bathhouse asking for natron, a washing powder, and a comb.
shabbat/41.question: What did Rabbi Zeira hear in "bring me natron, bring me a comb" that was worth seeking out the teacher he had been avoiding?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward whether holy speech and language belong in mundane, naked places — but the page states that lesson outright.

answer.quote: he was teaching us that mundane matters are permitted to be spoken in the bathhouse, even in the sacred language
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly explains the lesson Rabbi Zeira drew from Rav Yehuda's request for natron and a comb.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Zeira's uncertainty about whether Abbahu touched himself arose from Rav's statement that covering oneself looks like denying the covenant.
summaryProblems.pageSays: It is obvious that he did not touch his genitals, as it was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says: One who holds his penis and urinates

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 41a: "he was teaching us that mundane matters are permitted to be spoken in the bathhouse, even in the sacred language". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rabbi Zeira's uncertainty about whether Abbahu touched himself arose from Rav's statement that covering oneself looks like denying the covenant.", but the page says "It is obvious that he did not touch his genitals, as it was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says: One who holds his penis and urinates". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few lines later on the same page, which states that Rav Yehuda was teaching that mundane matters may be spoken in the bathhouse even in Hebrew; ask something the page leaves open instead, such as why drinking bathwater counts as a teaching worth travelling for, or what fear of the river does to the law of impure thoughts. The summary should also not present Rav's ruling about the covenant as the cause of Rabbi Zeira's uncertainty; on the page the uncertainty is challenged from Rabbi Eliezer's baraita, and Rav's statement is a separate objection to the whole story.

shabbat/42.summary: Rav Ḥisda says a vessel may not be placed under a hen about to lay, to catch the egg, but one may turn a vessel over an egg lying in a garbage dump. Rabba explains the line: rescues of a common kind were permitted, uncommon ones were not. Abaye pushes back with a barrel of untithed produce cracking on a roof and with sparks dripping from a lamp, and each time Rabba answers that those are common too.
shabbat/42.question: If a cracked barrel and falling sparks both turn out to be common, what rescue would still count as uncommon?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward whether the common/uncommon line does any real work once objections keep getting absorbed into 'common'.

answer.quote: And in an uncommon case of preservation, i.e., placing a vessel beneath a hen to receive its egg so that it would not roll down an inclined surface, they did not permit
answer.where: Shabbat 42b, Gemara on the lamp mishna
answer.explanation: The page itself names the rescue that stays uncommon — catching an egg from a hen on an inclined surface — so the question of what still counts as uncommon is answered in so many words.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 42b, Gemara on the lamp mishna: "And in an uncommon case of preservation, i.e., placing a vessel beneath a hen to receive its egg so that it would not roll down an inclined surface, they did not permit". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already supplies the answer: the hen on an inclined surface is Rabba's uncommon case, so asking what would still count as uncommon is settled by the text. Ask instead about the principle Rabba is using — why frequency of the mishap, rather than the value of what is saved or the fact that egg, tevel and lamp oil are all unusable on Shabbat, should decide whether the Sages permitted the rescue. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the passage accurately.

shabbat/43.summary: Rav Ḥisda lets a person cover an egg laid on Shabbat but not set a bowl under the hen to catch it, since a vessel holding an unusable egg becomes unusable itself. Abaye tests this against dripping oil sparks, a roof leak, chicks on an overturned basket, and a mat over a beehive. Later, two men shelter a corpse from the sun by sitting on beds, spreading a mat overhead for themselves, then standing the beds up and slipping away, leaving a canopy no one built for the dead.
shabbat/43.question: If setting a loaf of bread or an infant on a corpse makes it movable, what is the prohibition on moving it still holding back?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of a prohibition that a formal device (loaf, infant, indirect canopy) can lawfully dissolve, and asks what the rule is then protecting.

answer.quote: Apparently, the Sages did not permit carrying a mat to cover a corpse for the sake of the corpse. They only permitted doing so in an indirect manner
answer.explanation: The page shows what the prohibition still restrains — direct handling for the corpse's own sake — though it never says outright what remains forbidden once a loaf or infant is placed on it, so the question can still be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Abaye tests Rav Ḥisda's rule against a mat over a beehive.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Come and hear another proof for this from that which we learned: One may spread a mat over a beehive on Shabbat in the sun

judge.feedback: The summary says "Abaye tests Rav Ḥisda's rule against a mat over a beehive.", but the page says "Come and hear another proof for this from that which we learned: One may spread a mat over a beehive on Shabbat in the sun". Say what the page says. The beehive is not one of Abaye's objections to Rav Ḥisda; it belongs to the later 'come and hear' proofs tested against Rabbi Yitzḥak's rule that a vessel may be moved only for the sake of a movable object. Either drop it from Abaye's list or name it as part of the Rabbi Yitzḥak sequence. Keep the egg, sparks, leak and chicks as Abaye's objections, since the page states those explicitly.

shabbat/44.summary: A used oil lamp is covered in soot, so the mishna says it may not be carried on Shabbat, while a new one may. Rabbi Shimon drops the disgust rule and bars only a lamp still burning, then the Gemara narrows even that: a small lamp he expects to go out is fine, a big bowl or lantern of oil is not. The last move is stranger, a bed becomes untouchable all day because coins sat on it at twilight.
shabbat/44.question: If the coins slid off the bed hours ago, what is still clinging to it from that one moment of twilight?

judge.reachNote: An object's status can be fixed by a single moment at the onset of Shabbat and outlive the facts that created it.
