answer.quote: if the matter is as clear to you as the fact that your sister is forbidden to you, say it, and if not, do not say it
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan states the standard of certainty required for offering an explanation, and his own answers then meet it by resting on cited verses, but the page never says in so many words why his answers qualify as clear while theirs did not.

shabbat/146.summary: A mishna permits smashing open a barrel on Shabbat to get at the dried figs inside, so long as one is not fashioning a vessel. Students ask Rav Sheshet whether a man may spear a hole in a wine barrel; he answers that if the host truly wanted to be generous, he would pull out the plug instead. Rabba then argues that a hole made only to let wine out is not really an opening, and the whole prohibition rests on a chicken coop.
shabbat/146.question: If the size of the hole a host makes is taken as evidence of what he really wants, what else does the shape of a small convenience give away?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that the shape a person gives a permitted act is read as testimony about what he actually wants.

shabbat/147.summary: Shaking dust off a cloak on Shabbat can count as laundering, but only if the garment is new, only if it is black, and only if its owner is fussy about keeping it clean. Ulla, visiting Pumbedita, saw rabbis shaking their cloaks and said they were desecrating Shabbat; Rav Yehuda told them to go on shaking in front of him, since they did not care. Rav Yosef had Abaye shake dew off his hat on the same grounds.
shabbat/147.question: If one man's shake of a cloak is laundering and another's is nothing, because the first cares about a clean garment and the second does not, what exactly is the forbidden act?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibited labor is defined by the physical act or by the actor's standard of care about the result.

shabbat/148.summary: One may borrow a jug of wine or a loaf of bread on Shabbat, so long as one says "let me borrow" and not "loan me," since the second phrasing might make a lender reach for a pen and write. Rava bar Rav Ḥanan keeps pressing: people clap and dance on a Festival, women set down their jugs at an alleyway entrance, and nobody objects. Abaye's answer is to leave them be, unwitting rather than defiant.
shabbat/148.question: If the exact wording of a request for a borrowed jug is worth policing, why is the rule against clapping and dancing left quietly unenforced?

judge.reachNote: When does the law insist on precision and when does it accept that a rule will be ignored — enforcement versus formulation.

answer.quote: Leave the Jewish people alone, and do not rebuke them. It is better that they be unwitting in their halakhic violations
answer.explanation: The page states outright why clapping and dancing go unrebuked, though it never explains why the borrowing formula is nevertheless policed, so the comparative edge of the question survives.

summaryProblems.claim: Rava bar Rav Ḥanan raised the example of women setting down their jugs at the alleyway entrance as part of his pressing.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Abaye responded: And according to your reasoning, what about this halakha that Rava said: One may not sit on Shabbat at the entrance of a

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rava bar Rav Ḥanan raised the example of women setting down their jugs at the alleyway entrance as part of his pressing.", but the page says "Abaye responded: And according to your reasoning, what about this halakha that Rava said: One may not sit on Shabbat at the entrance of a". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: the clapping-and-dancing challenge is Rava bar Rav Ḥanan's, but the women sitting with their jugs at the alleyway entrance is Abaye's counter-example thrown back at him. Also make the question openly concede the page's "leave the Jewish people alone" answer, so it asks only what remains — why a rule nobody will obey is dropped while a rule about two nearly identical phrases is enforced.

shabbat/149.summary: A host wants to read the guest list written on his wall on Shabbat, and two reasons are offered for forbidding it: Rav Beivai fears he will erase a name he regrets, Abaye fears he will drift into reading business documents. The Gemara tests both against writing high up, writing low down, and letters engraved on a tablet. The same split returns with a metal mirror, banned because its sharp edge can trim a stray hair, unless it is fixed to the wall.
shabbat/149.question: If putting writing out of arm's reach settles the worry that someone will erase it, why does Rabba still forbid reading by a lamp ten houses high?
gate: the question brings in "Rabba", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether the practical difficulty of committing a violation reduces the need for a decree, but the page settles it as a tannaitic dispute.

answer.quote: that statement of Rabba is the subject of dispute between tanna'im, as it was taught in a baraita: One may count one's guests and one's appetizers from memory
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly resolves the Rabba objection by saying Rabba follows one tanna while Rabbi Aḥa, who permits reading writing raised high on a wall, disagrees, so height can matter.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 149a: "that statement of Rabba is the subject of dispute between tanna'im, as it was taught in a baraita: One may count one's guests and one's appetizers from memory". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later on the page: the Gemara says Rabba's lamp ruling is itself a tannaitic dispute, with Rabbi Aḥa permitting writing raised high on a wall. Rewrite the question so it takes that resolution as given, for instance asking what it costs to hold that likelihood of transgression sometimes matters and sometimes does not, or press on the mirror comparison instead. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

shabbat/150.summary: Hiring workers on Shabbat is forbidden, and the mishna also bars asking someone else to do the hiring, which the Gemara calls obvious until Rav Ashi rereads it as a rule about hinting: one may ask a neighbor, "Does it seem that you will join me this evening?" Rabbi Yoḥanan grounds this in Isaiah, speech about weekday business is out, silent contemplation is fine. Then comes a pious man who never repaired his broken field fence, because he once thought of mending it on Shabbat.
shabbat/150.question: If thinking about weekday work is permitted outright, why does the pious man's single thought about his fence cost him the fence forever?

judge.reachNote: The gap between what the law permits and what a pious person holds himself to: a thought that is technically allowed can still feel like a breach.

shabbat/151.summary: One may wash a corpse on Shabbat and smear it with oil, provided no limb is moved, and one may lay cold metal vessels on its stomach to keep it from swelling. The same page forbids closing the eyes of a person whose soul is still departing, and calls whoever does it a murderer: a finger on a guttering lamp puts out what might have burned longer. Then Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel explains how to shut a corpse's eyes.
shabbat/151.question: If the difference between tending a body and killing a man is the exact instant of death, who at the bedside is supposed to know when that instant has passed?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the whole distinction between permitted care and homicide rests on a boundary the page assumes is knowable but never says how to know.

shabbat/152.summary: The Gemara reads the last chapter of Ecclesiastes as a catalogue of an aging body: the trembling keepers of the house are the ribs, the grinders that cease are teeth, the failing caper berry is sexual desire. Barzilai the Gileadite told David at eighty that he could no longer taste food or hear singers, and Rav calls him a liar, citing a maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house who at ninety-two still tasted the cooking pots. Rava answers that promiscuity aged Barzilai early.
shabbat/152.question: If one maidservant could still taste the pots at ninety-two, does that make Barzilai a liar, or only a different man at eighty?

judge.reachNote: Whether one counterexample can refute a man's testimony about his own body, or only show that bodies age at different rates.

answer.quote: Rava said: Barzilai was speaking the truth, but Barzilai the Gileadite was steeped in promiscuity, and anyone who is steeped in promiscuity is overtaken by old age before his time.
answer.explanation: Rava explicitly resolves the question by holding Barzilai truthful and explaining that he was prematurely aged, i.e., simply a different man at eighty.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 152a: "Rava said: Barzilai was speaking the truth, but Barzilai the Gileadite was steeped in promiscuity, and anyone who is steeped in promiscuity is overtaken by old age before his time.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered on the page by Rava, and the summary itself quotes that answer in its last sentence, so the reader is told the resolution before being asked. Rewrite the question to probe something the page leaves unsettled, for example what it means that Rav treats a single ninety-two-year-old cook as proof against Scripture's own witness, or why Rava's explanation makes early aging a moral verdict on a person's past. Keep the summary's facts, which are accurate, but stop it from supplying the answer.

shabbat/153.summary: A traveler caught on the road as Shabbat begins hands his money pouch to a gentile walking with him, and if no gentile is there, loads it onto his donkey. The ranking keeps descending: the donkey comes before a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, because these are people and the donkey is not. When none of them is present, Rabbi Yitzhak says another permitted method existed, and the Sages deliberately kept quiet about it.
shabbat/153.question: If shifting the pouch in stretches shorter than four cubits breaks no Torah prohibition, what is gained by hiding that option from the one man stranded on the road with it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — why a permitted expedient is deliberately concealed — but the page states that very reason a few lines on.

answer.quote: If one were to move the pouch in this manner, there is concern lest he come to carry the object four cubits in the public domain.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks why the Sages withheld the incremental-carrying option and answers that publicizing it risks his carrying a full four cubits, a Torah violation.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 153b: "If one were to move the pouch in this manner, there is concern lest he come to carry the object four cubits in the public domain.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in so many words: the alternative was hidden lest he come to carry a full four cubits. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard — for instance, why concealing a leniency is safer than a decree, or how Rabbi Eliezer's and Rabbi Yehoshua's opposed verdicts on the eighteen decrees bear on it. The summary is accurate and can stand, though it could set up whichever new question you choose.

shabbat/154.summary: Rabban Gamliel's donkey stood all of Shabbat under jugs of spoiled honey, kept for rubbing on camels' wounds, and died of fatigue that night. The Gemara asks why he did not drop the jugs (they would crack) or slide cushions underneath (they would be soiled and unusable), and answers that animal suffering is only a rabbinic prohibition. Earlier, Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that a man who drives a laden animal on Shabbat is exempt entirely.
shabbat/154.question: If the objection that he should lose money rather than let the donkey suffer is answered by calling that suffering merely rabbinic, why does the story end with the animal dead?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether a ruling that is formally permitted can still be judged by the cost it produces — here a dead animal sitting alongside a clean legal answer.

shabbat/155.summary: A mishna allows untying bundles of grain in front of an animal on Shabbat but forbids crushing hay or carobs to make eating easier. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda read those same words into opposite rules: one permits effort spent on food an animal can already eat, the other permits only effort that makes inedible food edible. Later the page sorts creatures by who owes them dinner, with dogs in and pigs and dovecote doves out.
shabbat/155.question: If God stretches a dog's digestion to three days because its food is so scarce, why does Rav Mari say to give it an ear's worth and then strike it with a staff?
gate: the question brings in "Mari", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real tension between divine provision for the dog and the feeder's wish not to be followed home, but the page resolves it explicitly.

answer.quote: Give it the equivalent of the measure of its ear and strike it immediately thereafter with a staff so that the dog will not grow attached to the one who fed it.
answer.explanation: The page states Rav Mari's own reason for the blow in the same sentence, so the question is answered where it is asked.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 155b: "Give it the equivalent of the measure of its ear and strike it immediately thereafter with a staff so that the dog will not grow attached to the one who fed it.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line it quotes: the staff is so the dog will not grow attached, and the field/city distinction follows. Ask something the page leaves standing instead, for example why sustenance is said to be 'incumbent upon you' for the dog but not for the pig or the dovecote doves, or why the Gemara had to abandon Rav Ashi's water proof and fall back on water being found in lakes. A question built on the Rav Huna / Rav Yehuda dispute about exerting oneself with food versus rendering it edible would also work.

shabbat/156.summary: A notebook of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says a person born on Tuesday will be rich and promiscuous, because vegetation was created on the third day. Rabbi Yoḥanan counters that no constellation governs the Jewish people, and Abraham is told to step outside and stop reading his chart; two snakes fail to kill people who quietly fed someone hungry. Then Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, brought as proof against astrology, bites dates off a tree that is not his.
shabbat/156.question: If the astrologers told his mother he would be a thief, and he stole the dates anyway, what did the covered head actually change?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether upbringing and prayer cancel an astrological fate or merely restrain it, but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: Apparently, he had an inborn inclination to steal, but was able to overcome that inclination with proper education and prayer.
answer.explanation: The page's own closing gloss states exactly what the covered head changed: it enabled him to overcome an inborn inclination, which asserted itself only in the moment the cloak fell off.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shabbat 156b: "Apparently, he had an inborn inclination to steal, but was able to overcome that inclination with proper education and prayer.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in its final line, saying he had an inborn inclination to steal yet overcame it through education and prayer, with the lapse coming only when the cloak fell. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved, for example why a story in which the prediction half comes true is offered as proof that there is no constellation for Israel, or how Rabbi Ḥanina's 'constellation of the hour' stands beside Rabbi Yoḥanan's denial. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

shabbat/157.summary: The tractate's last mishna permits some measuring on Shabbat, of a rag to see if it is large enough to contract ritual impurity, and of a ritual bath to see if it holds enough water for immersion. Two sages plugged a window with an earthenware vessel and dangled a shard on a reed to test whether a crack in the roofing was a handbreadth wide. Shabbat closes with Ulla finding Rabba bar Rav Huna sitting in a tub of water, measuring it.
shabbat/157.question: If Rabba bar Rav Huna was measuring visibly enough for Ulla to catch him at it, what makes his claim that he was not interested in the numbers anything more than a convenient excuse?

judge.reachNote: Whether an act's permissibility turns on the doer's inner intent rather than on what the act visibly is.

answer.quote: I am merely acting unawares and am not at all interested in the measurements. Therefore, it is not prohibited.
answer.explanation: The page records Rabba bar Rav Huna's defense and its legal conclusion, but it never tests or vindicates the sincerity of the claim, which is what the question presses on.

eruvin/2.summary: Eruvin opens with an alleyway open at one end to the public street, where carrying on Shabbat is permitted only if a beam spans the entrance. A beam higher than twenty cubits must be lowered, a number the Gemara traces to the Sanctuary doorway in the Temple; Rabbi Yehuda, who permits higher, is said to measure by the forty-cubit Entrance Hall. Then a baraita reporting fifty cubits breaks the fit, and Rav Ḥisda says it misled Rav: Rabbi Yehuda was measuring by the doorways of kings.
eruvin/2.question: If Rabbi Yehuda was measuring by the doorways of kings all along, what made the Sanctuary so tempting a source that even Rav read it into him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward why Temple architecture supplies the default measure of a 'doorway,' but the page names the specific baraita that trapped Rav.

answer.quote: It was this baraita that misled Rav and led him to explain that Rabbi Yehuda derived the measurements of an entrance from the doorway
answer.explanation: Rav Ḥisda states exactly why Rav read the Sanctuary/Entrance Hall into Rabbi Yehuda — a baraita that glossed twenty cubits as 'higher than the doorway of the Sanctuary' — so the question is answered in so many words.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 2b: "It was this baraita that misled Rav and led him to explain that Rabbi Yehuda derived the measurements of an entrance from the doorway". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered on the daf: Rav Ḥisda says a baraita glossing twenty cubits as 'higher than the doorway of the Sanctuary' is what misled Rav. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on something still open — for instance, why the Rabbis get a verse-based doorway while Rabbi Yehuda is left with the merely customary practice of kings, or why the mishna's unqualified 'doorway' should be measured by the Sanctuary rather than the courtyard gate the Gemara rejects.

eruvin/3.summary: A cross beam over an alleyway higher than twenty cubits must be lowered, unless it has an amaltera, explained either as carvings shaped like birds' nests or as costly cedar poles, both eye-catching enough to be noticed high up. The page then asks about a beam or sukka roofing that straddles the twenty-cubit line, and Rabba's answer arrives in two flatly opposite versions. Rava from Parzakya's reasoning about shared responsibility is then run in both directions.
eruvin/3.question: When the same fact about an alleyway, that many people use it, can prove either that neighbors will remind each other or that each will leave it to the next man, what decides which way it is read?

judge.reachNote: It names the reversibility of sociological reasoning in halakha: the same social fact can be argued to produce either mutual reminding or mutual neglect, so the reasoning cannot be what settles the law.

eruvin/4.summary: A cubit is six handbreadths, or five, depending on whether it measures a sukka, a strip of mixed seeds, or the base of the altar. From there the discussion turns to Rav's claim that the measures for mitzvot, the rules of what interposes in a ritual bath, and the laws of partitions all reached Moses at Sinai unwritten. Challenged by a verse listing wheat, barley, figs and pomegranates, the answer is that the Sages attached those traditions to verses afterward.
eruvin/4.question: If the measures were already fixed at Sinai and the verses were found for them later, what work is the verse about wheat, barley, figs and pomegranates actually doing?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what scripture is for when a law's authority comes from unwritten tradition — support, mnemonic, or mere ornament.

answer.quote: Rather, they are halakhot that were transmitted to Moses from Sinai, and the Sages based them on verses in the Torah.
answer.explanation: The page states that the measures are Sinaitic traditions which the Sages anchored to verses, but it never says what function the verse itself then serves, which is what the question presses on.

eruvin/5.summary: A cross beam spanning an alleyway's entrance sits lower than the required ten handbreadths, so someone digs out the floor beneath it to make up the gap. Rav Yosef says the hollowed area need extend only four handbreadths into the alleyway; Abaye says four cubits, since a space that small could not have courtyards opening into it and would not be an alleyway at all. Later, a side post protruding four cubits stops being a post and becomes an alleyway itself.
eruvin/5.question: If a second side post placed beside the first only counts once it is made thicker or thinner than its neighbor, is a side post a measurement or something people have to notice?

judge.reachNote: Whether the demarcation of an alleyway works by satisfying a quantity or by being perceived as a distinct marker — the same tension as 'conspicuous marker' versus 'partition' earlier on the daf.

answer.quote: so long as he adds to it or diminishes from it in thickness or height, so that it will be noticeable that it is a side post of its own
answer.explanation: The page states the reason for altering the added post is noticeability, which leans toward the 'something people must notice' side of the question, though it does not settle whether a side post is essentially a measure or a marker (5a keeps both 'conspicuous marker' and 'partition' models live).

eruvin/6.summary: Whether carrying is permitted in a breached alleyway on Shabbat depends on where the gap is: ten cubits wide on the side wall, but only four handbreadths in the wall facing the street. Then a harder question arrives: can a genuine public domain be closed off at all, given that people in Jerusalem escaped liability only because the city's doors were locked at night? At the end, one crooked alleyway in Neharde'a gets both Rav's stringency and Shmuel's.
eruvin/6.question: If adopting Beit Shammai's stringencies alongside Beit Hillel's makes someone a fool walking in darkness, what were the people of Neharde'a doing when they loaded both Rav's stringency and Shmuel's onto a single bent alleyway?
gate: the question brings in "Beit", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Shammai's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Hillel's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of halakhic coherence: whether a ruling must follow one authority's whole system or may pile up unrelated stringencies.

eruvin/7.summary: The residents of Neharde'a held one alleyway to the strict rulings of both Rav and Shmuel at once, which looks like an illegal pick-and-mix of two authorities. Rav Sheizvi narrows the ban: two stringencies clash only when they answer the same question, like how many missing vertebrae make a spine incomplete. Then Rabbi Akiva, who picked citron fruit on the first of Shevat and separated both years' tithes, is explained away as merely unsure what Beit Hillel had said.
eruvin/7.question: Is Rabbi Akiva's double tithe really a lapse of memory, or is that reading chosen because the alternative would break the rule the Gemara just built?

judge.reachNote: Whether a resolution is chosen because it is true or because the governing principle would otherwise collapse.

answer.quote: Rabbi Akiva did not act in this way in order to be stringent in accordance with both opinions, but because he was in doubt with regard to his tradition
answer.explanation: The page does supply the doubt-about-tradition reading, but says nothing about whether that reading was adopted in order to protect Rav Sheizvi's newly built rule, which is what the question actually presses.

eruvin/8.summary: A blind alleyway that opened on one side to the sea and on the other to a refuse heap came before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and he said nothing at all, neither permitting nor forbidding carrying there on Shabbat. The worry is not the present but the future: the heap could be carted away, the sea could throw up a sandbank. The same logic reaches a backyard owned by one person, who might someday build houses in it.
eruvin/8.question: If a wall can be disqualified because someone might later haul the garbage away or build a house, what partition is ever secure enough to trust?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a partition's validity depends not on its present state but on its likely permanence, and asks what permanence can be relied upon.

answer.quote: Apparently, we distinguish between a public refuse heap and a private refuse heap, such that in the case of a private refuse heap we cannot assume that it will remain in place permanently
answer.explanation: The page supplies a criterion for when the fear of future change applies — private ownership makes a partition impermanent, communal ownership makes it trustworthy — but it does not settle the broader worry, since the sea itself is still distrusted (Mareimar's nets).

eruvin/9.summary: Rabbi Zakkai taught before Rabbi Yohanan that the space between an alleyway's two side posts counts as a karmelit, an in-between domain where carrying is forbidden by rabbinic decree, and Rabbi Yohanan told him to go teach that outside. Abaye and Rava then split over how much of the rejected line survives. The sharpest move comes later, when the Gemara decides that Rabbi Hiyya must agree with a ruling, since otherwise why would he teach it at all?
eruvin/9.question: If Rabbi Yohanan could hear a ruling and simply decline to repeat it, why does Rabbi Hiyya's repeating one prove that he holds by it?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether transmitting a teaching implies endorsing it — but the page itself draws the asymmetry between not teaching and teaching.

answer.quote: Granted, Rabbi Yoḥanan does not hold in accordance with that halakha. That is why he did not teach it. But Rabbi Ḥiyya, if it is true that he does not hold in accordance with it, why would he teach it?
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection ("Perhaps, then, Rabbi Ḥiyya also does not hold in accordance with it") and answers it by distinguishing silence from active teaching: declining to transmit fits rejection, but teaching a rule one rejects would be pointless.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 9b: "Granted, Rabbi Yoḥanan does not hold in accordance with that halakha. That is why he did not teach it. But Rabbi Ḥiyya, if it is true that he does not hold in accordance with it, why would he teach it?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it two lines later with "What is this comparison?" — silence fits rejection, teaching does not. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer, e.g. probing why Rabbi Yoḥanan's mere non-transmission is taken as evidence of his view at all, or how this reasoning sits with the fact that the Tosefta "was widely known." Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

eruvin/10.summary: A narrow post set against an alleyway wall can look like part of the wall from inside while standing out plainly from the street, and the argument here is whether it still counts as a side post. The Gemara works out a refutation of the lenient view, then rules in accordance with it anyway, on the strength of a baraita Rabbi Ḥiyya taught. Rav Yosef, ill and having forgotten his learning, hears Abaye quote back the very ruling he himself once gave.
eruvin/10.question: If the lenient view was conclusively refuted, what is the refutation worth once the ruling goes the other way?

judge.reachNote: What authority a dialectical refutation retains when halakha is decided from an explicit tannaitic statement instead.

answer.quote: Yes, it can because Rabbi Ḥiyya taught a baraita in accordance with it. Although the deductive analysis of the statements of other tanna'im led to different conclusions
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the objection that a refuted opinion cannot be the halakha and answers that an explicit baraita of Rabbi Ḥiyya outweighs deductive analysis, though it does not say what standing the refutation retains.

eruvin/11.summary: A man in the valley of Beit Ḥortan stuck four poles into his field, stretched a vine over the tops, and the Sages counted it as a sealed enclosure for planting. Much of the argument tests how little a doorway can be and still count: vines tied to the sides of posts, poles more than ten cubits apart, a top reed touching nothing. Rav Sheshet had Rav Naḥman's floating reeds torn down, then heard a teaching about arched gateways that undercut him.
eruvin/11.question: Once Rav Sheshet learns that the arched gateway ruling works against him, why does he ask Rabba bar Shmuel to keep it from the very household whose reeds he had thrown away?
gate: the question brings in "Rabba", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Shmuel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: A sage who acted forcefully on his ruling now shields the ruling from refutation before the very people he acted against — authority against truth.

answer.quote: do not say to the members of the Exilarch’s household anything with regard to this baraita of an arched gateway, as it is proof against my opinion
answer.explanation: The page gives Rav Sheshet's stated motive — the baraita refutes him — but does not address why he singles out that household or reconcile the suppression with his earlier action.

eruvin/12.summary: A courtyard whose wall is breached open to the street can still count as enclosed if upright boards remain at the gap's edges, either one board four handbreadths wide, a handbreadth being a palm, or two boards of any width. Rav Yosef cannot reconcile two things Shmuel said, and offers instead what he does know: a narrow sea inlet once broke a courtyard wall in a shepherds' village, and Rav Yehuda permitted it with a single board. Abaye is unimpressed, since water cases get easier rules.
eruvin/12.question: Is Rav Yosef's memory of one flooded courtyard an answer to the contradiction he admits he cannot solve, or a change of subject?

judge.reachNote: Whether a remembered ruling can stand in for legal reasoning — but the Gemara itself rules the memory out as inadmissible and leaves the contradiction standing.

answer.quote: In any case, it is difficult. The contradiction between the conflicting statements of Shmuel remains unresolved.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that Rav Yosef's incident settles nothing — Abaye dismisses it because "an inlet is different and nothing can be derived from that case," and the contradiction is only resolved later by Rav Pappa and Rav Huna.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 12a: "In any case, it is difficult. The contradiction between the conflicting statements of Shmuel remains unresolved.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: Abaye says the inlet case yields nothing, the Gemara concludes "it is difficult," and Rav Pappa and Rav Huna supply the real resolution later. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing — for instance why the Sages relax partition requirements specifically for water, or why a side post of minimal width serves an alleyway while a courtyard needs four handbreadths. Keep the summary's thread but let the question start after the page's own answer rather than before it.

eruvin/13.summary: Rabbi Meir, who wrote Torah scrolls, mixed iron sulfate into his ink so the letters could never be blotted out. Rabbi Yishmael warns him that one added or missing letter turns emet, truth, into met, death, then objects that the passage about the sota, a wife suspected of adultery, is written precisely in order to be erased into water. Two accounts flip which teacher banned the additive, and the Gemara admits it cannot settle which.
eruvin/13.question: If a scribe's care is measured by how permanent he can make the letters, what does he do with the one passage the Torah orders him to dissolve in water?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between a scribe's craft of permanence and a text whose whole purpose is to dissolve, but the page resolves it by carving out the sota passage.

answer.quote: One may place iron sulfate into the ink that is to be used for all sacred writings, except for the writing of the Torah passage with regard to a sota
answer.explanation: The baraita of Rabbi Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Meir states exactly what the scribe does with the sota passage: he omits the iron sulfate so it can be erased.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 13a: "One may place iron sulfate into the ink that is to be used for all sacred writings, except for the writing of the Torah passage with regard to a sota". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same daf: Rabbi Meir's own rule is that iron sulfate goes into all sacred writing except the sota passage. Rewrite the question to start from that carve-out rather than ask for it — for instance, about the later dispute over whether the sota passage may be erased out of an existing Torah scroll, or why writing need not be in her name while the erasing must be.

eruvin/14.summary: The mishna lets a cross beam over an alleyway count even if it is made of straw, curved, or round: one considers it as though it were metal, straight, and square. Squaring the round beam needs a ratio, three handbreadths of circumference for each handbreadth of diameter, which Rabbi Yoḥanan reads out of the bronze Sea in Solomon's Temple. When that Sea's volume fails to match the hundred and fifty ritual baths claimed for it, Rami bar Yeḥezkel makes its lower three cubits square.
eruvin/14.question: Why is it the shape of Solomon's Sea that gets adjusted to rescue the arithmetic, rather than the ratio of three that the same verse supplied?

judge.reachNote: Which datum is treated as unrevisable when a derivation and its source text conflict — the geometric constant or the described object.

answer.quote: From where are these matters, this ratio between circumference and diameter, derived? Rabbi Yoḥanan said that the verse said with regard to King Solomon
answer.explanation: The page shows the ratio is itself derived from Scripture (and likewise constrains the Sea's roundness: "you cannot say... the bottom of the sea was round, as it is written... its brim was round"), which bears on why the shape rather than the ratio is revised, but never states that trade-off explicitly.

eruvin/15.summary: Abaye and Rava argue about a side post, the post at an alleyway's entrance that lets residents carry there on Shabbat, when nobody put it up for that purpose. The Gemara tests the question with sukka walls made of trees and with branches hanging near the ground, but each time answers that the trees were planted for it; a natural mound and a rock cavity cannot be explained away that way. Rav froze his attendant mid-errand rather than trust a palm tree.
eruvin/15.question: If a palm tree already standing at the alleyway's entrance counts as a side post only when the residents decided in advance to rely on it, what did the deciding add to the tree?

judge.reachNote: Whether a physical object becomes a legal boundary through its form or through the community's prior intention to treat it as one.

answer.quote: The reason that the palm tree could not serve as a side post is because we did not rely on the palm tree from yesterday.
answer.explanation: The page establishes that prior reliance is the decisive factor and (via Abaye/Rava) that a side post works either as a partition or as a conspicuous marker, but it never says what the act of deciding adds to an already-standing tree, so the question survives.

eruvin/16.summary: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, argue over a fence whose gaps add up to exactly the width of its standing boards: enclosure or not? Proof texts about partitions between vines and seeds get read both ways, down to whether a gap is wide enough for a goat to leap through in one bound. A baraita finally refutes Rav Pappa outright, and the ruling goes with him anyway, on the strength of the mishna's precise wording.
eruvin/16.question: If the baraita really does refute Rav Pappa, what makes one phrase in the mishna heavy enough to outweigh it?

judge.reachNote: What kind of authority a mishna's exact phrasing carries against a baraita that logically defeats a position.

answer.quote: Yes, that is the case, because the precise reading of the mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rav Pappa.
answer.explanation: The page names the mishna's precise wording as the reason the halakha follows Rav Pappa despite the refutation, but it does not explain why that wording outweighs a conclusive refutation, so the question survives in part.

eruvin/17.summary: The Sages exempted a soldier in a military camp from four things: taking firewood from other people's land, washing the hands before eating, tithing produce bought from someone who may not have tithed it, and joining courtyards so people may carry between them on Shabbat. The Gemara then narrows each exemption. Washing after the meal stays obligatory, because a single grain of Sodomite salt in a whole kor of ordinary salt can blind the eyes.
eruvin/17.question: If the camp is loose enough that a soldier may take another man's dry wood and eat produce that may never have been tithed, why is the one grain of dangerous salt in a whole kor the thing that holds?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempted: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The idea is that camp exemptions relax ritual and property claims but not bodily danger — which the page already states outright.

answer.quote: It is due to the fact that there is the presence of Sodomite salt, which blinds the eyes even in a small amount.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks why final waters remain obligatory and answers that the danger of Sodomite salt blinding the eyes overrides the camp's leniencies, adding that soldiers too must maintain their health.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 17b: "It is due to the fact that there is the presence of Sodomite salt, which blinds the eyes even in a small amount.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates what the page already answers: Rav Ḥiyya bar Ashi gives the reason (Sodomite salt blinds the eyes) and the page adds that soldiers are obligated to maintain their health. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, about why a risk present in one grain per kor is treated as a standing obligation while outright theft of wood is waived, or about what kind of claim 'danger' is that property and tithe claims are not. The summary is accurate and can stand.

eruvin/18.summary: A caravan camped around a well may set up pairs of upright boards at the corners, and the page treats them as walls good enough for drawing water on Shabbat. After sorting out whose opinion the mishna follows, the Gemara stops on the word deyomadin and answers: two posts. That "two" pulls in a chain of sayings, ending with Rav and Shmuel splitting over whether Eve came from Adam's second face or from his tail.
eruvin/18.question: When every verse that troubles one reading can be turned into a moral lesson instead, what could ever decide between Adam's second face and Adam's tail?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that when every prooftext can be re-read homiletically, the verses stop functioning as evidence, so the dispute over Eve's origin cannot be decided by them.

eruvin/19.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar counts three entrances to Gehenna, the place of punishment: Korah's wilderness pit, the sea Jonah cried from, and a smoking spot near Jerusalem. Reish Lakish holds that the wicked never repent, reading Isaiah's "who rebel" as present tense and therefore endless, and the answer given is that this covers the nations only, since Abraham hauls circumcised sinners back out. Rav Kahana then attacks the grammar, since God is called "He Who brings out" of Egypt, long finished.
eruvin/19.question: If Rav Kahana is right that the present tense can describe something already over, what is left holding up the split between Jewish sinners who accept the verdict and gentile rebels who never do?

judge.reachNote: Whether a theological distinction rests on a reading of a verb's tense or on independent grounds that survive the collapse of that reading.

answer.quote: if you do not say so, there would be a contradiction between one statement of Reish Lakish and another statement of Reish Lakish
answer.explanation: The page grounds the Jew/gentile split not in the tense of "who rebel" but in the need to keep Reish Lakish consistent with his own teaching that Gehenna's fire has no power over Jewish sinners, which bears on the question without settling what survives Rav Kahana's grammatical attack.

eruvin/20.summary: Abaye asks Rabba about a courtyard whose open end runs into the area between the upright boards that surround a well and make it a private space for drawing water on Shabbat. Then the water dries up in the middle of Shabbat, and Rabba answers that the boards were a partition only on account of the water, so the walls go when it goes. If rain refills it later that day, the enclosure counts as a partition built on Shabbat, permitted unless it was put there deliberately.
eruvin/20.question: If the boards stop being walls the moment the well runs dry, what exactly was doing the enclosing?

judge.reachNote: Whether a partition is a physical fact or a permission granted for a need, so that it lapses when the need does.

answer.quote: The boards are considered a valid partition only on account of the water; since there is no longer any water here, there is also no longer a valid partition here.
answer.explanation: Rabba's reply states that the water is the condition of the boards' validity, which bears on the question but does not explain what the enclosing thing actually was.

eruvin/21.summary: Upright boards standing around a well in open country let travelers draw water on Shabbat, and the page insists the well must hold running spring water, fit for a person and not merely for cattle. Rav says the allowance does not apply outside Eretz Yisrael, since yeshivot are uncommon there and the concession was for those traveling to study. The discussion then swings to rabbinic decrees, ending with Rabbi Akiva in prison, given half a day's water, washing his hands with it.
eruvin/21.question: The boards exist so a thirsty traveler can drink, yet Akiva spends his last water on his hands and says he would rather die of thirst than skip a Sage's enactment; which of the two does the page actually admire?
gate: the question brings in "Sage's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: a concession made so scholars can travel and drink sits beside a story where rabbinic decree outweighs drinking itself — leniency for the sake of Torah versus fidelity unto death.

answer.quote: My son, be careful to fulfill the words of the Sages [soferim] even more than the words of the Torah.
answer.explanation: The page voices a clear preference for scrupulous obedience to rabbinic enactments, and follows it with the Sages' praise of Akiva, though it never reconciles this with the travelers' leniency of the boards.

eruvin/22.summary: Around a public well, upright boards set at the corners count as a fence, so water may be carried there on Shabbat. Rabbi Yehuda says a public path cutting through that space ruins the fence and must be diverted; the Rabbis say a crowd walking through does not break a partition. Rabbi Yohanan repeats the Rabbis' view without sharing it, since he holds that Jerusalem's walls would not help if its gates were left unlocked at night.
eruvin/22.question: If a crowd tramping through the boards around a well leaves the partition standing, why would Jerusalem's walls fail the moment its gates stay open?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a crowd's traffic defeats a formal partition, or whether formal walls hold regardless of how people use the space.

answer.quote: Rather, Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement must be understood as follows: Here, the Rabbis expressed this idea, although he does not agree with them.
answer.where: Eruvin 22a (Gemara on the mishna of the public path)
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the Jerusalem difficulty against Rabbi Yoḥanan and resolves it by saying he was only reporting the Rabbis' view, not holding it, so no single opinion says both things.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 22a (Gemara on the mishna of the public path): "Rather, Rabbi Yoḥanan’s statement must be understood as follows: Here, the Rabbis expressed this idea, although he does not agree with them.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page itself poses this Jerusalem difficulty and answers it: Rabbi Yoḥanan merely reported the Rabbis' view and does not agree with it, so ask something the page leaves standing. Better material is the convenience distinction Raḥava and Rava argue over — why the Rabbis' leniency at the well, where crossing is easy, does not settle the case of a steep mound or the paths of Beit Gilgul. Or ask about the asymmetry in the resolution: two real partitions suffice for Rabbi Yehuda while the Rabbis need a nominal set of four.

eruvin/23.summary: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava rules that a garden or a karpef, a walled yard used for storage, may be carried in on Shabbat only if it is no bigger than seventy cubits and a remainder square and holds something residential, like a watchman's booth. The measure comes from the Tabernacle courtyard, a hundred cubits by fifty, mentally reshaped into a square. The Gemara then asks what that verse was plainly describing, and Abaye answers by placing the tent inside the yard.
eruvin/23.question: If the verse's plain sense is only the layout of a desert sanctuary's courtyard, what makes its dimensions the right yardstick for the wall around someone's vegetable patch?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of how a verse's plain descriptive sense relates to the halakhic measure derived from it.

eruvin/24.summary: A karpef, a fenced yard larger than two beit se'a (roughly the space for sowing two measures of grain) that was never enclosed for living in, bars carrying inside. Shmuel's remedy is to breach the fence wider than ten cubits and then rebuild it into an entrance. Asked whether one could do this a cubit at a time, Rabbi Yoḥanan answers from a sandal whose straps broke and were mended one by one, and Ḥizkiya called him an angel.
eruvin/24.question: If at no moment was more than a single cubit of the fence open, what makes the finished wall a new thing rather than the old one patched?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of identity over time: when does piecemeal replacement of a thing's parts produce a different thing rather than the same thing repaired.

answer.quote: the reason it is no longer a utensil is because a new entity has arrived here
answer.explanation: The page states the very principle the question asks for — cumulative replacement makes the thing a new entity, "as the entire area of the hole is completely new" — and then applies it explicitly to breaching and fencing a cubit at a time.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 24a: "the reason it is no longer a utensil is because a new entity has arrived here". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what makes the rebuilt wall new, but the page answers it outright: "a new entity has arrived here, as the entire area of the hole is completely new." Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance why the sandal becomes a new entity only when the second strap is mended while the first was already replaced, or why newness counts for a fence built back cubit by cubit but a pile of fruit, however large, never strips a karpef of its status. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

eruvin/25.summary: An enclosure fenced not for the purpose of living in, a karpef, may be carried in on Shabbat only up to two beit se'a, so the page collects ways to shrink a larger one. Planting trees fails; a column ten handbreadths high works, and Rabba and Rava split over widths between three and four handbreadths. Rav Ḥisda lets a wall built on top of an existing wall count for Shabbat but not as an act of taking possession of a dead convert's land.
eruvin/25.question: If a wall built on top of a wall is real enough to permit carrying on Shabbat, why was it not real enough to give the woman who built it the convert's land?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a partition's 'reality' is domain-relative: for Shabbat it need only function as an enclosure, for acquisition it must be a recognizable human act of possession.

answer.quote: What can I do for you, as you did not take possession of the property in the manner that people take possession.
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman tells the woman why her partition-on-partition failed to acquire the convert's land — it was not a customary act of taking possession — though the page never explains why that same wall is nonetheless a real partition for Shabbat.

eruvin/26.summary: Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana put up reed fences in an orchard so people could carry there on Shabbat; Rava judged them unnecessary and tore them out on Friday, and his students gathered the reeds so they could not be put back. On Shabbat, three objections landed against Rava, one after another, including a fence built only for privacy and cattle ditches in Meḥoza. The Exilarch answered the whole affair with a verse from Jeremiah.
eruvin/26.question: If Ravina, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua all had objections ready by Saturday morning, why did two of them spend Friday collecting the reeds?
gate: the question brings in "Ravina", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Pappa", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yehoshua", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Saturday", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Deference to a teacher's ruling in the moment versus the duty to raise an objection you already hold — and the cost of timing dissent too late to help.

answer.quote: so as to prevent Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana from restoring the partitions, as they were Rava’s students and wanted to enforce his ruling
answer.explanation: The page states why the two collected the reeds — loyalty to their teacher's ruling — but it does not explain why they waited until Shabbat to voice objections they could have raised on Friday, a tension the Exilarch only rebukes rather than resolves.

eruvin/27.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan says a mishna that begins with "all" cannot be trusted as complete, even when it names exceptions. The proof: the rule exempting women from time-bound commandments, those that can only be done at a set time, has its own unlisted exceptions, eating matza on Passover among them. The same suspicion falls on the list of foods that may serve as an eiruv, the shared food that joins neighbors into one domain for carrying on Shabbat, which omits truffles and mushrooms.
eruvin/27.question: If listing exceptions still leaves the list incomplete, what is the word "except" doing in the mishna at all?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what an explicit exception clause is supposed to guarantee about a list's completeness, and what legal language does when it cannot be exhaustive.

eruvin/28.summary: Rav rules on what may serve as an eiruv, the portion of food set down at a boundary so a person may walk farther on Shabbat: cress and purslane yes, green grain and unripe dates no. Unripe dates can be sweetened by fire, which makes them food enough for tithes and for food impurity, but an eiruv needs something edible right now. Sweet clover still works, since food fit for someone else counts.
eruvin/28.question: If sweet clover a childless person must avoid still counts because someone else could eat it, why don't unripe dates count because fire could make them edible?

judge.reachNote: What kind of gap between food and eater may an eiruv tolerate: a different person's appetite, but not a future act of cooking.

answer.quote: However, with regard to an eiruv, we require food that is ready for consumption, and something that can be prepared to become food is not sufficient.
answer.explanation: The page states the eiruv standard of present edibility that blocks unripe dates, though it never directly explains why a shift of eater is tolerated while a shift of preparation is not.

eruvin/29.summary: Rava, in a good mood, boasts he can answer any question, and a Sage asks how many apples are needed for an eiruv, food set aside to extend one's Shabbat walking limit. The answer, a kav, sets off a run of measures: two-quarters of a log of wine, the same of beer because people breakfast on a cup of it, a kav of dates. Then Rabba and Rav Yosef split over roasted meat, whether it is relish eaten with bread or a meal on its own.
eruvin/29.question: If a scrap of cloth three fingerbreadths square counts as clothing because poor people treat it that way, why doesn't a Persian's plate of roasted meat count as a meal?
gate: the question brings in "Persian's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whose standards define a legal category — the practice of a subgroup that values a thing highly, or the custom of most of the world.

answer.quote: But are the Persians a majority of the world? The halakha follows the customary practice of most of the world and not that of particular locales.
answer.explanation: Abaye states the reason Persian eating habits do not set the measure — they are not the world's majority — though the page does not spell out how the poor-clothing baraita is reconciled with that principle, so the tension the question raises remains open.

eruvin/30.summary: Two meals' worth of food, left at the edge of town, sets a person's Shabbat boundary, and the argument here is whose appetite measures those meals. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar allows a smaller amount for someone ill or elderly who eats little, but refuses a glutton any more than the average. Against that, he rules that a giant like Og, king of the Bashan, needs a doorway sized to his own corpse, because there is no alternative.
eruvin/30.question: If a frail person's small appetite is allowed to set the measure, why is the glutton's large one dismissed as merely his own opinion?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a personal measure is set by the individual's real capacity or only when doing so is lenient.

answer.quote: because his opinion is rendered irrelevant by the opinions of all other people. Therefore, there is no reason to be stringent with him and determine the measure according to his particular needs
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly explains the asymmetry: the ill person's smaller measure is a leniency, while the glutton's appetite is disregarded because his view is nullified by everyone else's and there is no cause for stringency.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 30b: "because his opinion is rendered irrelevant by the opinions of all other people. Therefore, there is no reason to be stringent with him and determine the measure according to his particular needs". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: it says the glutton's view "is rendered irrelevant by the opinions of all other people" and that there is no reason to be stringent with him, so the question is closed a few lines later. Rewrite the question around something the page leaves unsettled — for instance whether measures like the priest's handful or the giant's doorway are personal because of need or because of physical necessity, or why Abaye's "what should we do?" reasoning does not equally excuse the glutton. Keep the summary; it holds up.

eruvin/31.summary: An eiruv teḥumin is food set down before Shabbat so that a person's Shabbat starting point shifts to that spot, and Rabbi Yehuda permits a priest to place his, made of teruma, the priest's portion of produce, on a grave. The Gemara works to keep that food edible: produce never touched by liquid cannot become impure, and a flat board held sideways fetches it. The real fight is whether using a grave this way is forbidden benefit.
eruvin/31.question: If the priest's Shabbat residence is already fixed at twilight, why should wanting the bread still there in the morning turn the grave into a benefit?

judge.reachNote: Whether mere availability of food one may never need counts as deriving benefit from a place.

answer.quote: It is pleasing to him that the eiruv is safeguarded, for if he needs it the next day, he can eat it.
answer.explanation: The page states the Rabbis' reason exactly: because the priest still wants the food available for the next day, the grave is being used to preserve his meal, which is forbidden benefit.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 31a: "It is pleasing to him that the eiruv is safeguarded, for if he needs it the next day, he can eat it.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved in the very passage the summary is drawn from: the Rabbis answer that it is pleasing to him that the eiruv is safeguarded, so he uses the grave to preserve tomorrow's meal. Rewrite the question to ask something the page leaves open, for instance why Rava and Rav Yosef each need to recast the dispute rather than concede their principle is only one tanna's view, or what work "mitzvot were not given for benefit" does when the eiruv is voluntary. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

eruvin/32.summary: Rav Sheshet and Rav Naḥman argue over whether you may assume an agent did his job, testing it against the priests who offer the omer, the barley sacrifice that permits new grain, by midday. The proofs drift to figs picked from another man's tree and whether anyone tithed them. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says a meticulous man should risk a small transgression so a careless one avoids a large one; his father says the reverse.
eruvin/32.question: Is another person's large transgression your business, if stopping it costs you a small one of your own?

judge.reachNote: The question does reach the idea — how much of your own sin you may take on to spare another's — but the page names and answers that idea outright in both directions.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds: It is preferable to a ḥaver that he commit a minor transgression, namely separating tithes from produce that is not adjacent
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks "With regard to what principle do they disagree?" and answers it with both positions — Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepting the minor transgression to prevent another's major one, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel refusing — which is exactly what the question asks and what the summary's last sentence already reports.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 32b: "Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds: It is preferable to a ḥaver that he commit a minor transgression, namely separating tithes from produce that is not adjacent". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question just re-asks the dispute the page spells out and the summary already reports; the Gemara itself asks "With regard to what principle do they disagree?" and gives both answers. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi frames his view as only "appears to be more correct" rather than settled, or why the meticulous man is held responsible for what the am ha'aretz does with figs he gave away. Alternatively, build the question on the earlier agency thread, where Rav Naḥman keeps answering each proof by saying the court or the ḥaver, not an ordinary agent, is what we trust.

eruvin/33.summary: An eiruv, food set aside before Shabbat to fix where a person's Shabbat begins, is placed in a tree, and its height decides the case. Above ten handbreadths it fails; below ten it counts, but taking it down means using the tree, which is forbidden. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rescues it with a basket hung in the branches, the Rabbis answer that food one may not take is no eiruv, and Rabbi Yirmeya replies that a basket can be tilted.
eruvin/33.question: Why does tilting a basket count as being able to reach the food, while climbing the same tree to it does not?

judge.reachNote: What counts as 'able to take' the eiruv — physical reach, or reach by a permitted act — is the idea under the tilt-versus-climb contrast.

answer.quote: A basket is different, since one can tilt it and in that way bring it to within ten handbreadths of the ground.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yirmeya explains why the basket is reachable — it can be tilted so the eiruv comes down without carrying between domains — but the page never squares this against the separate prohibition of using the tree itself, so the contrast the question draws can still be pressed.

eruvin/34.summary: An eiruv here is food left before Shabbat at the spot a person wants to count as his base for the day. The page keeps testing whether he must be able to actually reach it: a cupboard he could tilt counts, one nailed to the wall does not, and a pit a hundred cubits deep still works. Then the cupboard is locked and the key is lost, and the eiruv holds anyway, on the claim that he could knock a hole in its brick side.
eruvin/34.question: If a cupboard nailed to the wall puts the eiruv out of reach, why does a locked cupboard with a lost key not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what counts as access — whether a barrier one may lawfully remove still separates a person from his eiruv — but the page states the resolution outright.

answer.quote: Here, we are dealing with a cupboard made of bricks, and the mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who said: One may create a breach
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks exactly the note's question about the locked cupboard and answers that the cupboard is of brick, which Rabbi Meir permits breaching, so the eiruv remains accessible unlike the nailed cupboard.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 34b: "Here, we are dealing with a cupboard made of bricks, and the mishna is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, who said: One may create a breach". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on the page: the locked cupboard is brick and Rabbi Meir permits breaching it, which the summary itself already reports. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance why the potential to tilt a cupboard counts as access while the potential to bring the eiruv to one's chosen spot does not, or why Rabbi Zeira's decree over a Festival after Shabbat governs every ordinary case. Keep the summary's accurate framing of accessibility but point the question at a tension the Gemara does not resolve.

eruvin/35.summary: An eiruv, a loaf placed before Shabbat to fix where your Shabbat rest begins, can be lost: rolled past the limit, buried under fallen stones, burnt, or made ritually impure if it was teruma, priestly produce. Ruined before dark it fails; after dark it holds; and when nobody knows which, Rabbi Meir makes the man both donkey driver and camel driver, hemmed in from both ends. Challenged that he is lenient about doubt elsewhere, the reply relocates the doubt into two sets of witnesses who contradict each other.
eruvin/35.question: If no one ever has to eat the eiruv, why should it matter whether the loaf burned an hour before nightfall or an hour after?

judge.reachNote: Whether the eiruv works by being consumed or merely by existing at the instant residence is fixed.

answer.quote: it is not a valid eiruv, since one did not have an eiruv at twilight, which is the time one's Shabbat residence is established
answer.explanation: The mishna states outright why the timing matters: the eiruv must exist at twilight, the moment when one's Shabbat residence is acquired, regardless of later eating.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 35a, mishna: "it is not a valid eiruv, since one did not have an eiruv at twilight, which is the time one's Shabbat residence is established". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The mishna already answers this question in plain words: the eiruv must be intact at twilight because that is when one's Shabbat residence is established. Pick something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why Rabbi Meir, who elsewhere is lenient with a doubtful corpse-impurity that is Torah law, is stringent here, or why the doubt has to be relocated into two contradicting sets of witnesses rather than left in the facts. Build the question on a line the page does not settle.

eruvin/36.summary: A loaf of teruma, the priest's portion of produce, is set out as an eiruv, food deposited to shift where a person's Shabbat walking limit begins, and then turns impure, with nobody sure whether that happened before dark. The page keeps settling such doubts by leaving a thing in whatever state it was already in. So a loaf declared unconsecrated today and holy tomorrow still works, while the reverse declaration fails, a difference Rav Naḥman explains only after a joke about eating salt.
eruvin/36.question: If a doubtful loaf can rest in its presumed state and still serve as an eiruv, why does the man holding two loaves, one of them certainly pure, end up with no eiruv at all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between presumptive-state leniency and the independent demand that eiruv food be edible before dark — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: we require that an eiruv consist of a meal that is fit to be eaten while it is still day, prior to the onset of Shabbat, and in this case there is none
answer.explanation: Rav Huna explicitly explains that the two-loaf eiruv fails not because of doubt-resolution but because neither loaf may be eaten before Shabbat, so there is no fit meal.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 36a: "we require that an eiruv consist of a meal that is fit to be eaten while it is still day, prior to the onset of Shabbat, and in this case there is none". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later by Rav Huna, who says both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei require a meal fit to be eaten while it is still day, and here there is none. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than ignoring it — for instance, ask why edibility before dark is a separate requirement that presumption cannot supply, or why the consecrated-loaf case (where the food is also unusable at twilight) is treated by presumption instead. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

eruvin/37.summary: A man with a hundred log of wine declares that the priest's portion he will set aside later counts from now, and drinks immediately. The page tests this backdating, called retroactive designation, and reaches an awkward move: to keep Rabbi Yosei consistent, the Gemara simply reverses the attributions in two sources. Rava asks about a man who places an eiruv, food set down to extend his Shabbat walking limit, for whichever of five people he later picks; Rav Nachman says nothing.
eruvin/37.question: If the leather flask bursts before any teruma is ever separated, was the wine already forbidden tevel while he was drinking it, or does that only become true once it bursts?
gate: the question uses "teruma", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a present permission may be undone by a future failure, but the page already resolves it.

answer.quote: perhaps the leather flask will burst before he manages to separate the teruma, and retroactively this person would have been drinking tevel
answer.explanation: The page states outright that if the flask bursts the wine is retroactively tevel, and closes by saying the tannaim dispute only the likelihood of bursting, not this principle.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 37b: "perhaps the leather flask will burst before he manages to separate the teruma, and retroactively this person would have been drinking tevel". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim at the end of 37b: the Rabbis say that if the flask bursts he was retroactively drinking tevel, and Rabbi Meir answers only that he is not presently worried about bursting. Write a question whose answer the page does not supply — for example, press on Rav Yosef's insistence that one who accepts retroactive designation accepts it for Torah law and rabbinic decrees alike, or on what justifies reversing two baraitot to protect a single mishna. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

eruvin/38.summary: When a Festival falls the day before or after Shabbat, Rabbi Eliezer says a person may set one eiruv, a meal left at a spot that makes it his Shabbat residence and shifts his two-thousand-cubit walking limit, to the east for one day and another to the west for the next. The Rabbis refuse: one direction, both days. The Gemara's admission is that they do not know whether the two days are one sanctity or two, so they rule strictly on both sides at once.
eruvin/38.question: If nobody can decide whether the Festival and the Shabbat beside it are one sanctity or two, is Rabbi Yehuda's man, prodded like a donkey and led like a camel, keeping the law or only keeping the doubt?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a ruling built only out of unresolved doubt is a substantive law or just a hedge against not knowing.

answer.quote: Rav said: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of these four Elders and in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer
answer.explanation: The page does not settle whether double stringency is law or mere doubt-keeping in principle, but it does report that Rav decided the halakha as two distinct sanctities, which bears directly on the question's premise that nobody can decide.

eruvin/39.summary: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the two days of Rosh HaShana are two doubtful days, so a person may place his eiruv, the food that fixes where he rests for Shabbat, to the east one day and the west the next. Rabbi Yosei answers that when witnesses to the new moon come late, both days are sanctified together as one long day, and one long day cannot be split. The argument ends with a deer, trapped by a gentile on the first Festival day and slaughtered on the second.
eruvin/39.question: Rav Sheshet finds the source that backs his refusal to eat the deer, then asks that it be kept from Rav Naḥman and Rav Ḥisda; why hide a proof you were right?
gate: the question brings in "Sheshet", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Naḥman", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the human idea of winning an argument versus embarrassing colleagues, but the page already supplies the stated motive.

answer.quote: do not tell them anything of what you just told me, lest they use this tannaitic source to embarrass me about my refusal to eat
answer.explanation: The page itself states Rav Sheshet's motive for suppressing the source — he does not want the baraita used to shame him over the dispute — so the note's 'why hide it' is answered in so many words.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Eruvin 39b: "do not tell them anything of what you just told me, lest they use this tannaitic source to embarrass me about my refusal to eat". eruvin/40.summary: Rabba asks whether to say the blessing "Who has given us life" on Rosh HaShana and Yom Kippur, days that are not pilgrim Festivals like Passover or Sukkot. Yom Kippur makes it awkward: the blessing calls for a cup of wine, but drinking accepts the fast, and leaving the cup untasted breaks the rule that the blesser must taste it. Nobody in the study houses answers, so the Sages send Rav Yeimar the Elder to watch what Rav Hisda actually does.
eruvin/40.question: Why does watching one man lift a cup on the eve of Rosh HaShana settle a question that Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda could not answer?
gate: the question brings in "Huna", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a sage's observed practice can decide a question that argument in the study house could not.

answer.quote: They brought him a cup of wine, and he recited kiddush and the blessing for time.
answer.explanation: The page reports that the observation of Rav Ḥisda's practice is followed by the ruling "The halakha is that one recites the blessing for time on Rosh HaShana and on Yom Kippur," so it shows the observation deciding the matter but never explains why a sage's deed carries that force.

eruvin/41.summary: A man whom gentiles carry past the Shabbat limit, or who wanders out while possessed by an evil spirit, may walk only four cubits from wherever he lands. Rav Pappa says produce carried out and brought back loses nothing, since it did not go out willingly, and the page argues over whether a person forced back counts the same way. When someone confined to four cubits needs to relieve himself, Rabba answers that human dignity overrides the boundary.
eruvin/41.question: If stepping past the boundary is permitted only because human dignity demands it, is the clever man from Neharde'a who walks back into his own limit and stays there using that permission or gaming it?
gate: the question brings in "Neharde'a", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a leniency granted for one narrow need (dignity) can be used to secure an unrelated lasting benefit (full Shabbat limit).

answer.quote: If this person is clever, he will enter into his original Shabbat limit, and since he was permitted to enter it, he entered, and may remain there.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the reasoning that legitimizes the clever man's move — the permitted entry establishes him in the limit — but it does not address whether leveraging a dignity-based leniency for a lasting gain is proper, so the question remains askable.
