Shmuel measures it against sin-offerings, which are sometimes shut away to die and sometimes left to graze, while Rabbi Yoḥanan sets the cutoff at the slaughter of the replacement. Rava adds that an animal missing at night, when it could not have been offered anyway, was never lost.
pesachim/97.question: If a lamb that vanishes before midday was never really lost, is being lost a fact about the animal or about the hour?
gate: gloss "peace-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether 'lost' describes the animal's condition or only its relation to the hour at which it could have been offered.

answer.quote: a Paschal lamb that is lost before midday is not considered lost because the time for slaughtering the Paschal lamb has not yet arrived
answer.explanation: The page ties lost status to whether the hour of fitness had arrived (midday, per Shmuel, versus the slaughter, per Rabbi Yoḥanan), which bears on the question without settling what lostness itself is.

pesachim/98.summary: A group sends one member to find their lost Paschal lamb, telling him to slaughter it for everyone; while he is gone they slaughter a replacement. The mishna sorts out who eats which animal, and when nobody knows which was slaughtered first, both are burned, yet no one owes an offering on the second Pesach. Two groups with mixed-up lambs swap a member each and declare conditions; two individuals must first each recruit a stranger from the marketplace.
pesachim/98.question: Why must a lamb never sit ownerless even for an instant, when the same people end up registered either way?

judge.reachNote: Registration is what constitutes the offering, so an offering that briefly has no registrants may cease to be an offering at all — the question reaches this.

answer.quote: to ensure that when each person withdraws from his original Paschal lamb and registers for the other, no Paschal lamb will be left ownerless
answer.explanation: The page states that the stranger is recruited precisely so that no lamb is momentarily ownerless, but it never says why an instant of ownerlessness would matter.

summaryProblems.claim: In the case where the group tells the agent to slaughter for them, if nobody knows which lamb was slaughtered first, both are burned.
summaryProblems.pageSays: he eats from his and they do not eat with him in case theirs was slaughtered first, and theirs must be taken out

judge.feedback: The summary says "In the case where the group tells the agent to slaughter for them, if nobody knows which lamb was slaughtered first, both are burned.", but the page says "he eats from his and they do not eat with him in case theirs was slaughtered first, and theirs must be taken out". Say what the page says. Keep the question; it reaches the real idea and the page only states the procedure's purpose, not its reason. Fix the burning detail: when the group authorized the agent and the order is unknown, he still eats his lamb and only the group's animal is burned; both lambs are burned only in the case where each side authorized the other. Make clear which case each ruling belongs to.

pesachim/99.summary: Two people whose Paschal lambs got mixed up fix the problem by swapping members between their groups, and the Gemara checks whether that works when no original owner stays registered to an animal. A second mishna bars eating from mid-afternoon on Passover eve so matza is eaten hungry, and gives even the poorest person, fed from the charity plate, four cups of wine. Rav Pappa splits Passover eve from Shabbat eve by a narrow margin of time; Mar Zutra doubts the wording it rests on.
pesachim/99.question: If a person is poor enough to be eating from the charity plate, what is gained by having charity buy him wine so he can recline like a free man?

judge.reachNote: Whether the seder obligates a person to enact freedom he does not possess, and whether the community must pay for that enactment.

answer.quote: should not eat the meal on Passover night until he reclines on his left side, as free and wealthy people recline when they eat
answer.explanation: The mishna states the purpose of the reclining — to eat as free and wealthy people do — but never explains why charity funds must underwrite wine for a man who eats from the plate, so the question survives the line that partly addresses it.

pesachim/100.summary: Three sages are reclining over a meal in Akko on a Friday afternoon when Shabbat arrives with the food still on the table. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel offers to break off out of deference to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds the meal must be interrupted for kiddush; Rabbi Yosei, who holds it need not be, takes the offer as an insult and quotes Esther. Shimon then drops it, afraid watching students would turn the gesture into law.
pesachim/100.question: If Rabban Shimon stopped short only because students were watching, was the halakha settled by the argument or by the audience?
gate: the question uses "halakha", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Law can be made by precedent and public perception as much as by argument — the sages' conduct itself becomes the ruling.

answer.quote: They did not move from there until they established the halakha in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yosei, that one need not interrupt one's meal
answer.explanation: The page reports that the halakha was formally fixed on the spot in Rabbi Yosei's favor, which bears on the question but does not say whether the deciding factor was the reasoning or the fear of what the students would infer.

pesachim/101.summary: Shmuel says kiddush, the blessing over wine that opens Shabbat, works only in the spot where the meal is eaten, and he acted on it: students saw him come down from the roof and say it again downstairs. Rav Huna's lamp went out after kiddush, so he carried his things to his son's house, said it again, and ate something. The argument then spreads: does walking to another room end a meal, or only walking out of the house?
pesachim/101.question: If a group leaves the table to greet a bride and leaves behind one elderly or sick person who cannot come, why does his sitting there keep their meal alive?

judge.reachNote: What holds a meal together across a break — the place, the eaters' intent to return, or a body left behind to hold the spot.

answer.quote: When they left there an elderly or a sick person who cannot go with them, and he remains in the place of the meal. In this case, the original meal is considered ongoing.
answer.explanation: The page states that the remaining person keeps the meal "ongoing" because he stays in the place of the meal, but it never explains why one person's presence anchors everyone else's meal, so the question survives.

pesachim/102.summary: A group is in the middle of a meal when Shabbat begins, and Rabbi Yehuda says to bring one cup of wine for kiddush, the blessing marking the day's holiness, and a second cup for Grace after Meals. Rabbi Yosei says they may keep eating until dark. Asked why two cups are needed, the Gemara answers that one does not perform mitzvot in bundles, then has to explain the single cup carrying a string of blessings when a Festival follows Shabbat.
pesachim/102.question: If pairing Grace after Meals with kiddush over one cup looks like rushing to be done, why does reciting wine, kiddush, candle, havdala and the blessing for time over one cup not look the same?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that bundling is only objectionable when the mitzvot joined are unrelated in subject, not merely numerous.

answer.quote: Havdala and kiddush are one matter, as they both mark and draw attention to the sanctity of certain days.
answer.explanation: The Gemara resolves exactly this difficulty by distinguishing blessings that share one subject (kiddush and havdala) from Grace after Meals and kiddush, which are "two entirely different matters."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 102b: "Havdala and kiddush are one matter, as they both mark and draw attention to the sanctity of certain days.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own difficulty, and the page answers it outright by ruling that havdala and kiddush are one matter while Grace after Meals and kiddush are two. Rewrite the question to start from that resolution and press on what it costs: e.g., why the number of blessings over a cup matters not at all so long as they share a subject, or why Grace after Meals — recited over that very cup — counts as a foreign matter. The summary should mention the one-matter/two-matters distinction so the question has somewhere to stand.

pesachim/103.summary: When a Festival begins the moment Shabbat ends, the sages argue over the order of five blessings, trading strings of initials: wine, kiddush (sanctifying the day), candle, havdala (marking Shabbat's departure), and the blessing over time. Rabbi Ḥanina compares it to escorting a departing king out of the city before greeting the incoming governor. Then a guest at Rava's table questions nearly every move he makes: spices before light, a repeated blessing over wine, a torch, a long havdala.
pesachim/103.question: If announcing that you are about to say Grace after Meals uproots your mind from drinking, why doesn't pausing for kiddush between the wine blessing and the cup count as the same kind of break?
gate: the question brings in "Grace", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Meals", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What counts as diverting one's attention — a declared intention to stop drinking versus a mere liturgical pause — and when a new blessing is therefore required.

answer.quote: There, when one is preparing himself to recite Grace after Meals, he has already uprooted his mind from drinking. Here, with regard to kiddush and havdala, he has not uprooted his mind
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this comparison (Rav Ashi's proof from Rav's yod-kuf-nun-heh order) and rejects it by distinguishing Grace after Meals, which uproots the mind from drinking, from kiddush and havdala, which do not.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 103b: "There, when one is preparing himself to recite Grace after Meals, he has already uprooted his mind from drinking. Here, with regard to kiddush and havdala, he has not uprooted his mind". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and 103b answers it outright by saying that preparing for Grace after Meals uproots the mind from drinking while kiddush and havdala do not; ask something that survives that line, such as why a declared intention counts more than an actual liturgical break. Also fix the summary: two different guests challenge Rava — Rav Huna bar Yehuda on spices before light, Rav Ya'akov bar Abba on the wine blessing, torch, and long havdala.

pesachim/104.summary: Havdala, the blessing said when Shabbat ends, lists separations: sacred from profane, light from darkness, Israel from the nations. Rabbi Elazar sets a floor of three distinctions and a ceiling of seven, and the Gemara then strains to make a list reach seven, dropping sea and dry land, then splitting priests from Levites to refill the gap. It closes with Rav Yehuda sending his son to watch how Ulla recites it.
pesachim/104.question: Rav Yehuda's son sent the young Abaye in his place and the ruling is now transmitted in Abaye's name, so why should it matter whose name carries a blessing that anyone can hear recited?
gate: the question brings in "Abaye", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Abaye's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that Torah is carried by named transmitters, so who witnessed and reported a practice is part of the teaching, not incidental to it.

answer.quote: The Master’s haughtiness and the Master’s pride caused the Master to act in a way that ensured that the halakha will not be said in his name.
answer.explanation: The page states that attribution was lost through pride and treats this as a rebuke, but it never explains why the name attached to a publicly audible formula should matter at all.

pesachim/105.summary: Students of Rav, eating as Shabbat falls, ask whether to clear the tables and restart the meal; Rav Hamnuna tells them Shabbat establishes itself. At the other end of the day one need not break off eating to say havdala, the blessing separating Shabbat from the week, though wine and beer must be set down. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak explains the asymmetry: welcome the day early, let it go slowly, so it looks like no burden.
pesachim/105.question: If havdala is delayed so that Shabbat will not seem like a burden, why does Rav Huna warn a man that a sip of water before it brings a fatal illness?
gate: the question brings in "Huna", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between treating Shabbat's departure as something to postpone lovingly and treating any taste before havdala as a capital danger.

answer.quote: the Sages of the school of Rav Ashi were not particular with regard to water. They refrained only from drinking more significant beverages before havdala.
answer.explanation: The page records that Rav Huna's stringency about water is disputed and not followed, which bears on the tension but does not explain how his warning squares with delaying havdala so Shabbat not seem a burden.

pesachim/106.summary: A cup someone has already sipped from is unfit for kiddush, the blessing over wine that opens Shabbat, and Rav Ashi says the reason is only that too little wine is left. Others went further: one sage refused a pitcher already drunk from, another a cup, and Mar bar Rav Ashi would open a fresh barrel. Asked in Meḥoza to recite the great kiddush, Rav Ashi stretched out the wine blessing until an elder drank, and knew it was over.
pesachim/106.question: Rav Ashi guessed his way through a local custom he did not know and then applied the verse about the wise man to himself, so was that alertness or bluff?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of how a visiting sage handles a local custom he does not know — improvised reading of the room versus claimed wisdom.

answer.quote: as he was alert enough to discern the expectations of the local residents
answer.explanation: The page itself glosses Rav Ashi's self-applied verse as alertness, though it does not address the suspicion of bluffing that the note raises.

pesachim/107.summary: Ameimar, offered beer instead of wine for havdala, refused it and passed the night fasting, since one may not eat before havdala is said. A year later, in the same house with the same beer, he declared that beer is the wine of the province and recited havdala over it. The page surrounds the story with harsher views: Rav barred beer for kiddush and havdala alike, Rava cursed whoever uses it, and Rav Huna caught Rav himself doing it.
pesachim/107.question: What changed between the two visits, the beer or Ameimar's sense of what that household could reasonably be asked to supply?

judge.reachNote: Whether fitness for havdala depends on the drink itself or on what counts as the standard beverage of a given place.

answer.quote: He said: If so, if it is so difficult to obtain wine in your place, beer is the wine of the province.
answer.explanation: The page states Ameimar's own reason for the reversal: recognizing that wine is genuinely unobtainable there, he ruled the local beer counts as the province's wine, so the change was in his assessment of the locality, not in the beer.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 107a: "He said: If so, if it is so difficult to obtain wine in your place, beer is the wine of the province.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim by Ameimar's stated reason — that wine is hard to obtain there, so beer is the wine of the province — so a reader reaching that line would find it already resolved. Rewrite so the question begins after that answer: e.g., press on why the first year's fast was warranted if local availability alone can upgrade beer, or on how 'wine of the province' squares with Rav and Shmuel barring beer for havdala outright and Rava's punishment for one who uses it. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

pesachim/108.summary: A person at the seder must recline, and the page works out how: not flat on the back, and not to the right, where food might slip into the windpipe. Rav Naḥman is quoted both ways on which cups of wine require reclining, the first two because freedom begins there, the last two because by then it has arrived; the Gemara requires all four. Abaye recalls students reclining on each other's knees for lack of room, until Rav Yosef said awe of a teacher exempts them.
pesachim/108.question: If reclining is the posture of a free person, what does it mean that a student sitting with his teacher is told he need not take it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that reclining enacts freedom, and asks what it means that a disciple's subjection to his teacher overrides that enactment — but the page states the reason outright.

answer.quote: the fear of your teacher is like the fear of Heaven. A student is subject to the authority of his teacher and may not display freedom in his presence.
answer.explanation: The page itself explains that the student is exempt precisely because he may not display the freedom reclining signifies before his teacher, whose fear is like the fear of Heaven.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 108a: "the fear of your teacher is like the fear of Heaven. A student is subject to the authority of his teacher and may not display freedom in his presence.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same lines the summary paraphrases: awe of the teacher is like awe of Heaven, so the student may not display freedom before him. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer — for example, ask why this one relationship can cancel a night whose whole point is acting free, when a son with his father must still recline, or why a craftsman's apprentice is obligated while a Torah student is not.

pesachim/109.summary: Rabbi Akiva handed roasted grains and nuts to children on Passover eve so they would stay awake and ask questions. Later the page raises a problem with the four cups of wine: four is an even number, and a baraita warns that drinking in pairs exposes a person to demons. Rav Nahman answers that Passover night is guarded; Rava instead counts the cup of blessing for Grace after Meals as joining the others for good but not for harm.
pesachim/109.question: If Passover night is already guarded from harmful spirits, what is left for Rava and Ravina to solve by recounting which cup counts and which does not?
gate: the question brings in "Ravina", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a danger is dissolved by divine protection or must still be answered on its own halakhic terms — hence why later Sages keep answering after Rav Naḥman.

pesachim/110.summary: Drinking an even number of cups of wine is treated here as a real danger, and the sages spend the page finding exits: leave the house and look at the marketplace between cups, count the ceiling beams, hold your two thumbs and tell the voice you are three. The clever move is arithmetic by verse, since words in the priestly blessing license four cups, then six, then eight. Then the page says people in Eretz Yisrael simply were not particular, and nothing happened to them.
pesachim/110.question: If demons only bother those who bother about them, why does Abaye's mother keep pressing two more cups into his hands?
gate: the question brings in "Abaye's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the danger of pairs is objective or exists only for those who credit it — and why the prominent are exempt from that leniency.

answer.quote: An important person is different. The demons focus their attention on him, and he must therefore be more careful than the average person.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the Abaye-and-his-mother report as an objection and answers that prominent people are singled out by demons, though it never reconciles this with the later rule that demons are particular only with those who are particular.

pesachim/111.summary: After a short dispute about whether water mixed with water counts toward the seder's cups, the page turns to demons and dangerous shadows. Reish Lakish lists four fatal habits, and the Gemara then whittles each one down with exceptions: four cubits of clearance, a public road, daylight, sixty passing footsteps. Then it concedes that where witchcraft is at work, every exception fails, and cites a man who rode a donkey in shoes and still shriveled.
pesachim/111.question: If the careful list of exemptions can be cancelled by witchcraft at any moment, what are the exemptions for?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that safeguards calibrated to impersonal hazard lose force against deliberate malice, and asks what such qualified rules are worth.

answer.quote: And all this applies only where there is no reason for concern for witchcraft, as no one is interested in harming him. However, where there is reason for concern
answer.explanation: The page distinguishes ordinary ambient danger, where the limiting conditions hold, from deliberate witchcraft, where they do not, which bears on the question without explaining what purpose the exemptions then serve.

pesachim/112.summary: A poor man living off the communal charity plate still drinks four cups of wine at the Passover seder, though Rabbi Akiva said to make your Shabbat like a weekday rather than depend on others; publicizing the miracle overrides him. Most of the page is advice given in prison or near death: don't drink water alone on Tuesday or Friday nights, stay fifty cubits from an ox. Ḥanina ben Dosa banishes the demon Agrat from inhabited places, then hands those two nights back.
pesachim/112.question: Ḥanina ben Dosa had the power to keep Agrat out of inhabited places entirely, so why did he grant her back the very two nights the page warns people not to drink water alone?

judge.reachNote: Why a sage with power to banish danger entirely leaves a residue of it in the world, and how that residue lines up with the nights the baraita warns about.

answer.quote: She said to him: I beg you, leave me a little space. He left for her Shabbat nights and Tuesday nights.
answer.explanation: The page states that Ḥanina conceded because Agrat begged for a little space, though it never says why those two particular nights were the space granted.

pesachim/113.summary: Rav gives his sons and students blunt advice: skin a carcass in the market rather than say the work is beneath a priest. Then the page turns sharp. Zigud testifies alone that Tuveya sinned, and Rav Pappa has Zigud lashed, since one witness only spreads a bad name; yet Rav holds that a man who saw such a thing may hate the sinner, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak calls that hatred required.
pesachim/113.question: If a lone witness's word counts for nothing in court and only blackens a name, why does the hatred he carries away from the same sight count for so much?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the gap between legal proof, which needs two witnesses, and private moral knowledge, which binds the one who saw.

answer.quote: Rather, is it not referring to a case like this, when he saw him perform a licentious matter? He is therefore permitted to hate him
answer.explanation: The page grounds the permitted hatred in the man's own eyewitness knowledge, which distinguishes him from others, but it never explains why that same sight is worthless in court yet sufficient for hatred.

pesachim/114.summary: Attendants pour the first cup of wine at the seder, and Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about which blessing comes first, the one over the day or the one over the wine. Beit Hillel gives two reasons, one being that a frequent blessing takes precedence over a rare one. Then the Gemara asks why anyone needed to rule for Beit Hillel at all, since a voice from Heaven already had.
pesachim/114.question: If the Tosefta still had to state that the halakha follows Beit Hillel, what work was the voice from Heaven doing?
gate: the question brings in "Tosefta", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "tosefta", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.
the question uses "halakha", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.
banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether heavenly proclamation settles halakha or rabbinic reasoning does — but the page answers it outright.

answer.quote: the Tosefta is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehoshua, who said that one disregards a Divine Voice when deciding halakha
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's question and gives two answers — either the Tosefta predates the Divine Voice, or it follows Rabbi Yehoshua, for whom the Voice carries no halakhic weight.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 114a: "the Tosefta is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehoshua, who said that one disregards a Divine Voice when deciding halakha". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later on the same daf: the Gemara answers that the Tosefta either predates the Divine Voice or follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who disregards such a Voice. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, press on what it means that the Gemara can offer 'one disregards a Divine Voice' as a routine solution, or on why Beit Hillel's two reasons are needed once a Voice has spoken. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

pesachim/115.summary: Hillel wrapped matza, unleavened bread, together with bitter herbs and ate them in one mouthful, citing the verse that the Paschal lamb be eaten with matzot and bitter herbs. Other sages read the same verse as permitting each to be eaten alone, and since neither side was ruled law, the seder does all three: matza, then lettuce, then both together. Rava then adds that matza swallowed whole counts, while bitter herbs swallowed whole do not.
pesachim/115.question: If matza swallowed without chewing still counts as eating, why does lettuce swallowed the same way fail?
gate: gloss "the Paschal lamb" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Underneath lies the idea that some mitzvot are discharged by ingestion alone while others require the experience of a taste.

answer.quote: if one swallowed bitter herbs without chewing them, he has not fulfilled his obligation, as he did not taste their bitterness
answer.explanation: Rava's own statement gives the reason for the difference—bitter herbs must be tasted as bitter, while matza need only be consumed.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 115b: "if one swallowed bitter herbs without chewing them, he has not fulfilled his obligation, as he did not taste their bitterness". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the summary paraphrases: Rava says bitter herbs swallowed whole fail "as he did not taste their bitterness." Ask something the page leaves open instead — for example, why the palm-net case voids even the matza when swallowing matza alone is fine, or why a mitzva of rabbinic standing (bitter herbs) can nullify a Torah-level one when combined. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

pesachim/116.summary: A son asks his father why this night is different, and a baraita keeps going: if the son cannot ask, the wife asks; if there is no wife, he asks himself; two scholars ask each other. Rav Naḥman asks his servant Daru what a freed slave says to a master who sends him off with gold and silver, hears "thank and praise," and begins: We were slaves. Later Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov exempts a blind person, since "because of this" means pointing at the matza.
pesachim/116.question: If the seder still works when a man sits alone asking himself the questions, why should it fail for a blind father who cannot point a finger at the matza in front of him?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Does the obligation of 'telling' require a physical demonstration of the matza, or only words that anyone, even alone or blind, can speak?

answer.quote: Consequently, there is no need to actually point with one’s finger in this instance, and therefore the blind are also obligated to recite the Haggadah.
answer.explanation: The Gemara's closing move rejects the pointing analogy outright and rules that the blind are obligated, so the note's question is resolved on the page itself.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 116b: "Consequently, there is no need to actually point with one’s finger in this instance, and therefore the blind are also obligated to recite the Haggadah.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page ends by dismantling the very difficulty the question raises: it says the verse could not have been phrased otherwise, so no finger-pointing is required and the blind are obligated. Rewrite the question so it starts from that resolution rather than stopping at Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov's exemption. For instance, ask why Rav Yosef's and Rav Sheshet's practice needed the separate 'rabbinic law' defense at all, or what it means that Rav Aḥa holds the Sages modeled their decrees on Torah law yet still exempts the blind.

pesachim/117.summary: Rav Ḥisda, Rav, and Rabba argue over whether halleluya is a single word or two, hallelu plus ya, a short name of God. Rav settles his view by citing a book of Psalms in his uncle Rabbi Ḥiyya's study hall where hallelu sat at the end of one line and ya at the start of the next. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi calls the ya a mere intensifier, then elsewhere ranks halleluya highest because it carries God's name.
pesachim/117.question: If the ya at the end of halleluya is only a way of saying "many praises," what makes it greater than the nine other words Psalms uses for praise?

judge.reachNote: Whether a word's praise is great because it contains the divine name or merely because it intensifies praise — the two halves of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's position.

answer.quote: The greatest of them all is halleluya, as it includes God’s name and praise at one time.
answer.explanation: The page states why halleluya ranks highest among the ten expressions, but only in the statement that treats ya as God's name, and it flags that this ruling "disagrees with another ruling that he himself issued" without resolving how greatness works on the intensifier reading.

pesachim/118.summary: The fourth cup of wine at the seder is paired with the great hallel, Psalm 136, called great because it says God "gives food to all flesh." From there the page stacks up claims that feeding a person is harder than childbirth, harder than redemption, as hard as splitting the Red Sea. Then the sea itself speaks, objecting that it was given the drowned Egyptians as a gift and asking who will guarantee God's promise of repayment.
pesachim/118.question: If the line the fish sing is that God's truth endures forever, why does the sea refuse to act until the Kishon River is named as co-signer?
gate: the question brings in "Kishon", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "River", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether trust in a divine promise needs collateral: the sea demands a guarantor for a word the fish later sing as eternally true.

answer.quote: He said to him: Master of the Universe, can a servant issue a claim against his master for a gift promised to him? Who will be my guarantor?
answer.explanation: The page states the sea's own stated reason — a servant has no enforceable claim against his master — and later places the fish's praise at the moment the promise was actually kept, but it never reconciles that praise with the sea's initial demand for security, so the question can still be asked.

pesachim/119.summary: Rav Avira describes a feast God will make for the righteous, ending with a cup of blessing that nobody will take. Abraham declines because Ishmael came from him, Isaac because of Esau, Jacob because he married two sisters, Moses because he never entered the land, Joshua because he had no son. David takes the cup, says it suits him, and quotes a psalm about lifting the cup of salvation.
pesachim/119.question: Every man before David names a disqualification and hands the cup on, while David names only a verse, so is he the one without a blemish or just the one willing to hold it?
gate: the question brings in "Every", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the right to bless belongs to the flawless or to the one who claims it, given that David too has a known past.

pesachim/120.summary: Rava holds that eating matza on the first night still applies by Torah law even with no Temple standing, while bitter herbs, tied to the Paschal lamb, are now only rabbinic. The mishna asks what happens when people at the seder fall asleep mid-meal, and Rabba, caught nodding off by Abaye, answers that dozing is not sleeping. Then Rava says matza eaten after midnight does not count, pulling it back onto the lamb's clock.
pesachim/120.question: If matza has its own verse and outlives the Paschal lamb, why should it still expire at the same midnight the lamb does?

judge.reachNote: Whether a mitzva given its own independent verse keeps the timing of the mitzva it was originally attached to.

answer.quote: Rava therefore teaches us that when the verse repeats the mitzva to eat matza on the first night, it restores this mitzva to its original status
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this difficulty — that the repeated verse might remove matza from the juxtaposition — and answers that the repetition restores matza to the Paschal lamb's timing.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Pesachim 120b: "Rava therefore teaches us that when the verse repeats the mitzva to eat matza on the first night, it restores this mitzva to its original status". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already states the answer: the Gemara asks why matza is not freed from the lamb's clock and replies that the repeated verse "restores this mitzva to its original status." Ask something that survives that answer — for instance, what it means that one verse can both create an independent obligation and re-bind it, or how Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov's rabbinic view would handle the midnight cutoff. The summary is accurate and can stay largely as is.

pesachim/121.summary: The Sages decreed that touching piggul, an offering spoiled by the wrong intent, or notar, sacrificial meat left past its time, makes a person impure; one Sage blames spiteful priests, the other lazy ones. The tractate then turns to blessings, with Rabbi Yishmael folding the Festival offering's blessing into the Paschal lamb's and Rabbi Akiva keeping each separate. At a firstborn son's redemption, Rabbi Simlai was asked who says sheheheyanu, the father or the priest who pockets the five silver sela.
pesachim/121.question: If sheheheyanu belongs to whoever benefits, what does the father gain by handing over five sela that the priest who takes them does not?
gate: gloss "the Paschal lamb's" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether sheheheyanu tracks material benefit or the performance of a commandment — and whether fulfilling an obligation is itself a gain.

answer.quote: Or, perhaps the father of the son recites sheheḥeyanu, as he is the one who performs the mitzva.
answer.explanation: The page resolves who recites the blessing by grounding it in performing the mitzva rather than in receiving benefit, but it never says what the father himself gains, so the note's question still stands.

shekalim/2.summary: Shekalim opens, in the Jerusalem Talmud, with a proclamation made on the first of Adar: bring your half-sheqel for the Temple treasury, and check your fields for kilaim, forbidden mixtures of seeds. The reason offered is scheduling, since the coins must be in hand so the new year's public offerings can be paid for from the first of Nisan. Then the discussion drifts to the givers, who once pulled gold rings from their ears for the calf and later gave gold for the Sanctuary.
shekalim/2.question: If the same readiness to hand over gold built both the calf and the Sanctuary, what in the giving itself tells them apart?

judge.reachNote: Whether an act of generosity carries its own moral valence, or only takes one from what it is given to.

answer.quote: may the gold of the cover come and atone for the gold of the calf
answer.explanation: The page relates the two acts of giving—the Sanctuary's gold atoning for the calf's—but never states what within the act of giving itself distinguishes them, and it even says "one cannot understand the character of this people."

shekalim/3.summary: Rabbi Yehuda recalls how the court once handled kilayim, forbidden mixed plantings: agents uprooted the offending crop and threw it down in front of the owner, who was delighted twice over, free weeding and free fodder. So they began throwing it on the roads instead, and owners were still pleased at having their fields weeded, until the court took to declaring the whole field ownerless. The Halakhah, the Jerusalem Talmud's discussion, grounds that power in Ezra's decree confiscating a no-show's property.
shekalim/3.question: The first two penalties failed because the offender came out ahead, so what keeps the third, losing the field to anyone who walks in, from turning into someone else's bargain?
gate: "Rabbi Yehuda" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a penalty only deters if the offender cannot profit from it, and asks whether hefker escapes that trap.

answer.quote: We understand that according to everybody, this is a fine. Following the House of Hillel, the poor give tithes and eat.
answer.explanation: The page's closing discussion of the gleanings-stack treats a penalty whose produce goes to others as a fine on the owner, which bears on the note's worry without squarely answering whether the ownerless field becomes a windfall for a taker.

shekalim/4.summary: The Talmud here is the Jerusalem one, and it works from the rule that no contribution to the Temple is accepted from a gentile or a Samaritan. Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish split over whether a gift earmarked for a specific object can be taken at all. Then a gap opens: a gentile echoes an Israelite's vowed offering, and the leftover money for wine libations ends up buying service vessels, allowed because his intent was for Heaven.
shekalim/4.question: If a gentile's money can end up in the Temple's service vessels once his intent was for Heaven, what is the refusal at the start of the page actually refusing?
gate: "Rabbi Yoḥanan" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.
"Rabbi Shimon" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea beneath the exclusion: is what is refused the gentile's money, or his claim to a share in the House?

answer.quote: Does this imply that one does not accept from them for an aqueduct, or the city walls, or its towers, because of you have no part, nor rightful claim
answer.explanation: The page does gesture at what the refusal protects — a gentile's share, claim or memorial in Jerusalem and in building God's House — but it never squares that with the service-vessels concession, so the question still stands honestly.

shekalim/5.summary: Half-shekel coins are heavy, so a town converts its collection into darics, gold coins, before sending them to Jerusalem. A pearl would travel lighter, but this Jerusalem Talmud passage rules it out, since the price could drop and the Temple treasury would lose. When the messengers are robbed, oaths decide who pays; behind that, Rebbi Joḥanan holds a man carries the risk on his shekel until a Temple trustee takes it, while Rebbi Simeon ben Laqish says it is Heaven's wherever it lies.
shekalim/5.question: If a shekel set aside for the Temple already belongs to Heaven wherever it happens to be, what is the man who lost it actually swearing about?
gate: gloss "the Temple treasury" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether an oath reports a real liability or is a rabbinic institution guarding Temple property — the page names this idea and settles it.

answer.quote: Still this is because of a regulation oath.
answer.where: Shekalim 5, HALAKHAH (on the lost sheqel dispute)
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this difficulty against Rebbi Simeon ben Laqish and resolves it by saying the oath is an instituted regulation rather than a claim of liability, adding that "Temple property cannot be released without an oath."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shekalim 5, HALAKHAH (on the lost sheqel dispute): "Still this is because of a regulation oath.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later: the Gemara answers the same objection with "Still this is because of a regulation oath" and "Temple property cannot be released without an oath." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating the difficulty — for instance, ask what work an oath does once everyone agrees to pay anyway, or press on the gap between Rebbi Joḥanan's "responsible until he delivers" and the instituted oath he uses to explain the Mishnah. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

shekalim/6.summary: Somebody sets aside a pile of coins and says, "these are for my sheqel," the yearly half-sheqel Temple tax, and ends up with extra. Shammai's students call the leftover a gift to the Temple; Hillel's call it ordinary money, and everyone agrees that "that I shall take from these" leaves the rest profane. This Jerusalem Talmud discussion turns on whether the unfixed price of a purification offering, unlike the fixed sheqel, makes leftovers sacred, and it ends with sages reading the half-sheqel as payment for selling Joseph.
shekalim/6.question: If a man sets aside two sheqalim believing he owes two and turns out to owe one, is the second coin a mistake that never became holy, or part of a pile he already handed over?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea beneath the case: does sanctity attach to the money because of the mistaken intent behind it, or because a designated pile was handed over as a whole?

shekalim/7.summary: The Mishnah asks where leftover charity money goes when more is collected than needed to ransom one particular kidnap victim or to bury one particular dead man. Rebbi Nathan would spend the surplus on a memorial at the grave, while Rabban Simeon ben Gamliel holds that no mausoleums are built for the just, since their words are their remembrance. The Jerusalem Talmud then turns to Rabbi Joḥanan, stung that Rabbi Eleazar taught his rulings without saying his name.
shekalim/7.question: If everyone in the study house already knows whose teaching it is, what is Rabbi Joḥanan still missing when his name goes unsaid?
gate: "Rabbi Joḥanan" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that being named is a form of survival after death, not mere credit — which is precisely the idea the page spells out.

answer.quote: If a Sage’s pronouncement in matters of practice is mentioned in this world, the latter’s lips whisper with him in the grave
answer.where: Shekalim 7 (the passage beginning "Why did Rebbi Joḥanan insist to require that traditions should be reported in his name?")
answer.explanation: The page itself poses the note's exact question and answers it: what is missing is the spoken name, which keeps the sage's lips moving in the grave, as David prayed that his words be mentioned in synagogues and houses of study.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shekalim 7 (the passage beginning "Why did Rebbi Joḥanan insist to require that traditions should be reported in his name?"): "If a Sage’s pronouncement in matters of practice is mentioned in this world, the latter’s lips whisper with him in the grave". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page asks this question in so many words ("Why did Rebbi Joḥanan insist to require that traditions should be reported in his name?") and answers it with David's prayer and the sleeping lips that whisper, so the note's question is already closed. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than reaching it: for instance, how the surviving name that Joḥanan wants sits against Rabban Simeon ben Gamliel's refusal to build memorials because "their words are their remembrance," or why Ben Idi's Joshua analogy did not satisfy Joḥanan. The summary is accurate and can stay.

shekalim/8.summary: The Jerusalem Talmud's mishnah has the collected Temple shekels scooped out of the lodge into three boxes of three seah each, marked alef, bet, gimel, or in Rebbi Ismael's version the Greek A, B, gamma. The man doing the scooping enters without pocketed trousers, shoes, sandals, phylacteries, or an amulet, anywhere a coin could hide. The stated worry is not theft but talk: if he later turns poor or rich, people will explain it by that room.
shekalim/8.question: If a man's later poverty or wealth will be read back into that room anyway, what do the missing shoes actually protect?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that visible precaution is about managing suspicion rather than preventing theft, and asks what such management can accomplish when suspicion is inevitable anyway.

answer.quote: for a person needs to be clean before people as he has to be clean before the Omnipresent
answer.explanation: The mishnah states the purpose of the precautions as the duty to appear blameless before people as well as before God, though it does not address the note's point that talk will follow the man regardless.

shekalim/9.summary: A man from Rabban Gamliel's household walks in with his half-sheqel between his fingers and throws it so the official scooping coins from the Temple chamber will take it. That official scoops three times, asking permission each time and hearing "disburse, disburse, disburse," and covers the first two scoops with cushions so the same money is not scooped twice. Since one heap would exempt the other anyway, the discussion asks why the source matters, and answers that people wanted their own coins used first.
shekalim/9.question: If every scoop is made in the name of all Israel, what did the man from Rabban Gamliel's household gain by getting his coin under the first cushion?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether a share in a communal offering can be personal at all when each scoop is made in the name of all Israel.

answer.quote: It gave them satisfaction that the sacrifice should be brought first from their money.
answer.explanation: The page states exactly what a donor gained by having his coin disbursed first — the satisfaction that the sacrifice come from his money — which is the gain the question asks about, and the summary itself repeats it.

summaryProblems.claim: The man walks in with his half-sheqel between his fingers.
summaryProblems.pageSays: A member of the household of Rabban Gamliel was entering with his sheqel between his fingers and threw it before the disburser.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shekalim 9, Halakhah: "It gave them satisfaction that the sacrifice should be brought first from their money.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The man walks in with his half-sheqel between his fingers.", but the page says "A member of the household of Rabban Gamliel was entering with his sheqel between his fingers and threw it before the disburser.". Say what the page says. The question is answered in the same lines the summary already paraphrases — "It gave them satisfaction that the sacrifice should be brought first from their money" — so it cannot stand as an open question. Build the new question from material the page leaves unexplained, such as why removing the covers makes everything "remainder," or Rebbi Meïr's claim that one commits me'ilah with the remainder because "perhaps one needs them at the end." Also keep the mishnah's wording: it says "his sheqel," not half-sheqel.

shekalim/10.summary: Returning exiles found no wood in the Temple's chamber, so certain families brought logs from home, and the prophets ruled that their wood burns first even when the chamber is full. This Jerusalem Talmud discussion then extends the principle: a woman who made a coat for her son has to surrender it to the public. A separate maneuver closes the page: harvesters and stonecutters are paid with coins from a money changer, which are then redeemed with Temple funds.
shekalim/10.question: If the wood donors keep the privilege of having their own logs burned first, why does the woman's coat for her son simply become public property?

judge.reachNote: What a donor retains after giving to the Temple public — honor of priority versus loss of ownership in the thing given.

answer.quote: Where do they disagree? About the body of the offering. But for enablers of the offering everybody agrees that a private offering can be turned into public offering.
answer.explanation: The page gives the rule under which the coat (an enabler of the offering) passes to the public, and elsewhere grounds the wood's priority in a prophetic stipulation, but it never directly contrasts the two donors' standing, so the question can still be asked.

shekalim/11.summary: Leftover incense at the end of the Temple year cannot simply be carried onto the new year's books, so the Mishnah has the Temple hand the incense to its artisans as wages and then buy it back with the new disbursement. The Jerusalem Talmud's discussion balks at the maneuver: how can Temple property redeem Temple property? Rebbi Simeon bar Carsana answers with a chain of coins and incense, and the argument drifts to leftover animals, where Samuel rules leniently.
shekalim/11.question: If incense only becomes new-year property by passing into the artisans' hands and straight back again, what about it has actually changed?

judge.reachNote: Whether sanctity/ownership is a matter of the object's substance or of which fund paid for it — a formal transfer that changes nothing tangible.

answer.quote: he brings coins and redeems them for the building; brings incense and redeems it for them, and gives it to the artisans as their wages
answer.explanation: Rebbi Simeon bar Carsana explains the mechanism by which the sanctity is moved onto coins and the incense reacquired, and Rebbi Joshua ben Levi's reason ("that it shall be brought from the disbursement from the lodge") points to the funding source as what changes, but the page never directly asks what has substantively changed in the incense itself.

shekalim/12.summary: A man dedicates all his property to the Temple, and among his goods are items usable for public offerings, which Rebbi Joḥanan identifies as incense; Rebbi Aqiba would simply hand it to the Temple artisans as their wages. Ben Azzai objects, and this Yerushalmi passage gives his reason: labor cannot take sacred property out of its sanctity, only coins can. The rest argues whether dedicated animals should be sold for cash or offered on the altar themselves.
shekalim/12.question: If the artisan walks away holding the incense under either method, what does routing it through his wages in coins actually change?

judge.reachNote: Whether the form of a transaction (coin-redemption) carries legal weight even when the end distribution of goods is identical.

answer.quote: What is Ben Azzai's reason? For Temple property cannot be redeemed by work, only by coins.
answer.explanation: The page states the principle that only money, not labor, effects redemption of consecrated property, which bears on the question but does not address what practically differs once the artisan ends up with the item.

shekalim/13.summary: A contractor who agrees to supply the Temple with fine flour loses either way: if the market price rises he still delivers at the low rate, and if it falls he delivers at the low rate too. The page then names the Temple's appointees, from the cymbal player to the man who locked the doors, and drifts into lament that earlier generations did everything and later ones can barely eat. It closes with a stolen she-ass who refused oats until demai, produce that may not have been tithed, was removed.
shekalim/13.question: If animal feed is exempt from demai anyway, is a donkey who starves for three days rather than eat it admirable, or simply mistaken?

judge.reachNote: The idea is piety beyond what the law demands — whether a stringency taken where one is exempt is holiness or error — which the page itself resolves in favor of the donkey.

answer.quote: Rebbi Mana said, at that moment they said, we are not even comparable to the she-ass of Rebbi Phineas ben Yair.
answer.where: Shekalim 13, Halakhah (after R. Abba bar Zemina)
answer.explanation: The story is introduced precisely as praise — the donkey's self-imposed stringency puts later generations to shame — and R. Phineas seals the valuation by saying "she is very restrictive for herself" and ordering the demai removed rather than correcting her.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shekalim 13, Halakhah (after R. Abba bar Zemina): "Rebbi Mana said, at that moment they said, we are not even comparable to the she-ass of Rebbi Phineas ben Yair.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: R. Mana frames the whole story with "we are not even comparable to the she-ass," and R. Phineas calls her "very restrictive for herself" and has the demai removed, so admirable is the page's own verdict. Ask instead about something left unsettled — for instance why the sages' answer to their own lament about lost generations is an animal's stringency rather than a scholar's learning, or what it means that the exemption for animal feed was written for the owner's convenience and the animal declines it.

shekalim/14.summary: The Garmu family baked the shewbread, the loaves set out in the Temple, and the Eutinos family compounded its incense, and neither would teach the craft. Alexandrian replacements made bread that went moldy and smoke that spread instead of rising, so the Sages brought the families back at double pay. The Jerusalem Talmud praises them for refusing white bread and perfume, then has Rebbi Yose tell a Eutinos child his family's honor shrank.
shekalim/14.question: If the families held back the recipes so no one would later burn that incense to other gods, why does Rebbi Yose tell their descendant they were hoarding prestige?

judge.reachNote: Whether a craft guild's stated pious motive for secrecy can also be read as self-interest — who gets to name a motive, the actors or the Sages.

answer.quote: In the past my family were humble, and transmitting this scroll one to the other. But now they are not trustworthy; here the scroll is yours
answer.explanation: The old man's confession, and Aqiba's tears with "from now on we do not have to mention them for shame," suggest the charge of prestige-seeking attaches to later untrustworthy generations rather than to the original protective motive, but the page never reconciles Yose's rebuke with the families' stated reason.

shekalim/15.summary: Two lodges stood in the Temple, one where sin-fearing people gave in silence and poor people from good families were supported in silence. The stories that follow prize hidden giving: a man everyone accused of taking charity he did not need turned out to be splitting it among others. Rebbi Jonah goes further and offers a ruined rich man a loan against an inheritance that does not exist, admitting it was a gift only once the money is taken.
shekalim/15.question: If the gift has to be disguised as a loan before it can be accepted, whose shame is actually being spared?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea beneath secret giving: whether concealment protects the poor man's dignity or the donor's own standing and merit.

answer.quote: it is not written, "hail to him who gives to the needy," but: hail to him who is considerate to the needy; this refers to him who fulfills this commandment intelligently
answer.explanation: The page grounds Jonah's loan-ruse in being "considerate to the needy," pointing toward the recipient's feelings, but it never says in so many words whose shame is spared, so the question can still be pressed.

shekalim/16.summary: Shekalim here is the Jerusalem Talmud, and its sages argue how the Ten Commandments sat on the two stone tablets: five per tablet, ten on each, twenty, or forty on all four sides. Ḥananiah, nephew of Rebbi Joshua, changes the question: between every two commandments stood the details and letters of the Torah, small waves between the sea's large ones. Then comes a dispute over whether the Torah scroll went inside the Ark or in a case beside it.
shekalim/16.question: If the details and letters of the whole Torah were already packed between the commandments on the tablets, what was left for the scroll placed by the Ark to hold?

judge.reachNote: If the tablets already contained the whole Torah's details and letters, the written scroll's distinct role becomes a question about what revelation is stored where.

shekalim/17.summary: The Mishnah counts thirteen prostrations in the Temple courtyard, one for each of thirteen gates, and names them: the Fuel Gate, the Firstborns' Gate, the Water Gate where the water for the Tabernacles libation came in, the gate Jehoiachin left through into exile. The Rabbis count only seven gates and match the bows instead to thirteen breaches the Greek kings made and were later sealed. Then Ezekiel's spring, thin near the golden altar, swells until no ship crosses it.
shekalim/17.question: If the bows answer thirteen breaches rather than thirteen gates, is a person bowing toward an entrance or toward a patched wound in a wall?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what an act of prostration is directed at — a place of entry and honor, or a scar of desecration remembered.

shekalim/18.summary: Thirteen horn-shaped collection boxes stood in the Temple, labeled new sheqalim, old sheqalim, bird pairs, wood, incense, gold, and six for voluntary gifts. Rebbi Jehudah, in the Jerusalem Talmud's discussion here, says there was no box for bird pairs at all, since money from someone who died before bringing a purification offering could be mixed in and may never be spent. Against him: a woman drops her bird money in and eats consecrated food without worry.
shekalim/18.question: If tossing two zuz, silver coins, into the river would clear the whole box, why can a choice made after the fact not do that work?
gate: the question uses "zuz", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a designation made after the fact can retroactively sort mixed consecrated money — but the page states the answer outright.

answer.quote: We could say, let us choose two zuz and throw them into the River, then the remainder should be permitted, but do we not say in general that Rebbi Jehudah does not accept retroactive choices?
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the river-toss solution and answers that it fails because Rebbi Jehudah rejects retroactive designation, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shekalim 18, Halakhah: "We could say, let us choose two zuz and throw them into the River, then the remainder should be permitted, but do we not say in general that Rebbi Jehudah does not accept retroactive choices?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates the page's own bracketed objection, which already answers it: Rebbi Jehudah does not accept retroactive choices. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for example, why the woman who drops her bird money in the horn may eat sancta without worry if Rebbi Jehudah's fear of mixed-in death-money is real, or how the Mishnah's thirteen horns stand against his claim that no nest-horn existed. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page well.

shekalim/19.summary: A coin found on the Temple floor between two collection horns, one for the half-shekel tax and one for voluntary gifts, belongs to whichever it lies nearer. Dead center, it goes to the stricter fund, and the discussion asks how the horns could have a middle at all: they stood in a spiral, like a snail. One voice compares a coin stranded in the middle to the shekel of a man who set it aside and then died.
shekalim/19.question: Why should a coin that landed equally between two boxes be treated like the shekel of a man who died before he could pay it?

judge.reachNote: Money whose owner or purpose can no longer be fixed defaults to the general gift fund, as with a donor who dies after designating his sheqel.

answer.quote: if somebody had set his sheqel apart and died? He told him, they shall fall to the gift account
answer.where: Shekalim 19, Halakhah on the first Mishnah
answer.explanation: The page supplies the point of the comparison — a dead man's set-aside sheqel goes to the gift account, which is exactly where a coin in the middle is assigned — though it never states why unassignable coins should be likened to a death, so the question can still be asked.

shekalim/20.summary: The mishnah, from the Jerusalem Talmud, lists seven standing rulings of the court. They cover who pays for the wine poured with a gentile's offering sent from overseas, and whether a dead High Priest's daily flour offering comes from his heirs or from public money. Rebbi Abbahu explains another: people were smearing the red cow's ashes on their wounds as a disinfectant, so taking them counted as larceny against sacred property, and later that was reversed.
shekalim/20.question: If the ruling on the cow's ashes flipped because people were treating their wounds with them, what would flip it back?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that sanctity rules can be set and unset in response to how people actually behave with holy matter — but the page already supplies the trigger.

answer.quote: When they were fenced in, they decided that one does not commit larceny with it.
answer.where: Shekalim 20, Halakhah (Rebbi Abbahu on the Cow's ashes)
answer.explanation: The page itself states the condition under which the ruling reverted — once people were restrained from the abusive use, misappropriation of the ashes no longer counted as larceny.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shekalim 20, Halakhah (Rebbi Abbahu on the Cow's ashes): "When they were fenced in, they decided that one does not commit larceny with it.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what would reverse the ruling, and Rebbi Abbahu's own line answers it directly: 'When they were fenced in, they decided that one does not commit larceny with it.' Rewrite so the question starts from that reversal rather than asking for it — for instance, why the court would attach sacred-property status to the ashes as a deterrent against a beneficial use in the first place, or what it means that a Torah-level larceny category is switched on and off by public conduct. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

shekalim/21.summary: Spittle found lying in the streets of Jerusalem is presumed pure, except on the Upper Market, according to Rebbi Meïr. Rebbi Yose sorts by place: most of the year the middle of the road is impure and the shoulders pure, but on a festival it flips, since the impure minority steps to the sides. The Jerusalem Talmud's discussion adds who has to speak up: on ordinary days the impure warn others off, on festivals the pure do.
shekalim/21.question: If the same stretch of road counts as impure down the middle on an ordinary day and pure down the middle on a festival, what has actually changed about the spit lying there?

judge.reachNote: Status here is assigned by the probable identity of the crowd that passed, not by anything in the object itself.

answer.quote: On holidays, those in the middle of the road are pure and those on the sides impure since the minority will remove themselves to the sides.
answer.explanation: The Mishnah gives the reason for the flip — the makeup of who walks where changes, not the spittle itself — but it never says outright that the ruling is a majority-presumption about an unchanged object, so the question can still be pressed.

shekalim/22.summary: The closing page of Shekalim, here in the Jerusalem Talmud, moves from where the limbs of the daily offering are laid on the altar ramp to what happens to gifts pledged after the Temple is gone. Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai cancelled the quarter-denar a convert brought for his pair of birds, because of the mishap. Yet if someone dedicates anyway, the cloth is burned, the animal shut in until it dies, and the coins thrown into the Dead Sea, so the dedication clearly took hold.
shekalim/22.question: If dedicating anything now is blocked because of the mishap, why does a pledge made in defiance still bind tightly enough that the money has to be drowned in the Dead Sea?
gate: "Rabban Yoḥanan" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.

judge.reachNote: A rabbinic cancellation can forbid the act without stripping the act of its power to consecrate — hence property that is holy and unusable at once.

answer.quote: in respect to other dedications, the proselyte’s nest does not have to be from new money; if he dedicated it is holy
answer.explanation: The page raises exactly this tension (Rebbi Yudan: "here you are saying it became sanctified, and there you are saying, it did not") and Rebbi Yose distinguishes the cases, but the reason a defiant dedication still binds despite the mishap is only gestured at, not spelled out.

yoma/2.summary: Seven days before Yom Kippur the High Priest was moved out of his house into the Chamber of Parhedrin, and a second priest was designated in case something disqualified him. Rabbi Yehuda would designate a second wife too, since the verse has him atone "for him and for his house," and house is read as wife; the Rabbis answer that such worry has no end. The Gemara then traces the seven days back to Aaron, and works to keep festivals out.
yoma/2.question: If a backup wife is rejected because the backup could die too, why does the same objection not sink the backup priest?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of where precaution against contingency legitimately stops, and why one substitute is reasonable while a substitute for the substitute is not.

yoma/3.summary: The High Priest is removed from his house seven days before Yom Kippur, and the page keeps asking why that same rule would not also apply before Shavuot or Rosh HaShana. Each answer narrows the comparison to the eighth day of the Tabernacle's inauguration: one bull and one ram, paid for out of the priest's own pocket, a service only he performs. Then Reish Lakish objects that the standby priest is never sequestered, and proposes Sinai instead: six days inside the cloud.
yoma/3.question: If the seven days are copied from the inauguration, where every written detail is indispensable, how can a substitute priest who never left his house step in and perform the Yom Kippur service?

judge.reachNote: Whether a law derived from a paradigm inherits the paradigm's strictness, i.e. how much of a source travels with the derivation.

answer.quote: Apparently, failure to sequester the priest does not invalidate the service.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the substitute-priest case and concludes from it that the inauguration's "all details invalidate" rule does not carry over to sequestering, which is exactly what the note asks.

summaryProblems.claim: Reish Lakish objects that the standby priest is never sequestered.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And if you say: Indeed, that is so; didn’t we learn in the mishna: And they would designate another priest in his stead

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 3b: "Apparently, failure to sequester the priest does not invalidate the service.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Reish Lakish objects that the standby priest is never sequestered.", but the page says "And if you say: Indeed, that is so; didn’t we learn in the mishna: And they would designate another priest in his stead". Say what the page says. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it outright: "Apparently, failure to sequester the priest does not invalidate the service." Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — e.g. why Rabbi Yoḥanan's inauguration derivation survives once its details are shown not to bind, or what Reish Lakish's Sinai source gains by trading the inauguration for six days in the cloud. Also fix the attribution: the standby-priest proof is raised against Reish Lakish's strict position, not by him.

yoma/4.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish argue about where the seven days of removing the High Priest from his home before Yom Kippur come from: Aaron's week-long inauguration, or Moses' six days in the cloud at Sinai. Yoḥanan presses a detail, that during those seven days the priest is sprinkled with water mixed with ashes of the red heifer, matching the sprinkling at the inauguration, which was with blood. Reish Lakish answers that the Sages simply raised the bar.
yoma/4.question: If the seven days of sprinkling are only a higher standard the Sages added, what work is Sinai still doing in Reish Lakish's account of the seven days?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Asks what a derivation is still supporting once its matching details are conceded to be later rabbinic additions.

answer.quote: Moses ascended in the cloud, and was covered in the cloud, and was sanctified in the cloud, in order to receive the Torah
answer.explanation: The Reish Lakish baraita shows Sinai supplying the model of withdrawal-and-sanctification before approaching God, i.e. the sequestering itself, while the sprinkling is only a rabbinic stringency, though the page never spells out how six cloud days yield seven.

yoma/5.summary: Rav Yosef, Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, Rav Pappa and Ravina each propose a test case for a dispute over the seven-day inauguration of Aaron and his sons as priests: does omitting any written detail void it, or only details that would void an ordinary offering? The proofs run through placing hands on an animal's head, waving a lamb, and anointing for seven days. One baraita concludes that skipping the hand-placing still atones, just not optimally.
yoma/5.question: If blood alone atones, what is actually missing from the atonement of someone who treated placing his hands on the animal as a detail and skipped it?

judge.reachNote: What a non-invalidating rite adds, if atonement is complete by blood alone — the gap between a valid offering and an optimal one.

answer.quote: the verse ascribes to him status as though he did not achieve optimal atonement; and nevertheless, the offering atones for his sins
answer.explanation: The page labels the deficiency as less-than-optimal atonement but never spells out what substantively remains lacking once the blood has atoned, so the question survives the line.

yoma/6.summary: The High Priest spends the week before Yom Kippur in a special chamber, and the Gemara wants to know why his wife cannot join him there. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira's concern is blood found on the sheets afterward, leaving him retroactively uncertain of impurity, and the wording is rephrased once the Gemara balks at the idea of a priest knowingly sinning. Then the sharper objection: corpses are worse, so why are visitors still allowed?
yoma/6.question: If corpse impurity is simply set aside for communal service, and the Gemara calls a sudden death in the chamber unlikely anyway, why does an uncertainty that may never arise justify seven days away from his wife?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of how likelihood versus severity of risk drives precautionary legislation — but the page itself resolves it.

yoma/7.summary: A priest holding the omer meal-offering, the barley offering brought after Passover, finds it has become impure, and he is told to say so and fetch another. If no other is available, the other priests tell him to be shrewd and keep silent. The argument turns on whether impurity in communal offerings is flatly permitted, as Rav Naḥman holds, or only pushed aside, as Rav Sheshet holds, in which case the plate on the High Priest's forehead is still needed to win acceptance.
yoma/7.question: If impurity really is permitted when the whole community's offering is at stake, why do the other priests coach the man to keep quiet rather than tell him it does not matter?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that behavior in the Temple (seeking a pure substitute) is read as evidence for whether a prohibition is annulled or merely pushed aside.

answer.quote: I concede that in a case where there are remnants of the offering designated for eating it must be performed in purity wherever possible
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman, the very authority who holds impurity is permitted for the public, explains that the omer's meal-offering is sought in purity because portions of it must be eaten in purity, which is why the priests prefer a pure substitute and only resort to 'be shrewd and keep silent' when none is available.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 7a: "I concede that in a case where there are remnants of the offering designated for eating it must be performed in purity wherever possible". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later by Rav Naḥman himself: the omer offering has remnants designated for eating, so purity is still sought even though sacrificial impurity is permitted. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer, for instance asking why the priests are told to keep silent rather than simply eat nothing, or press on the Tosefta's bulls and rams where Rav Naḥman must reinterpret each case. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

yoma/8.summary: For seven days before Yom Kippur the High Priest is kept apart, and water mixed with ashes of a red heifer is sprinkled on him in case he touched a corpse without knowing. Purification needs sprinkling on the third and seventh days, and Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, counts out the week to find that the fourth day of sequestering can be neither. Rava answers with a scheduling trick, starting the red heifer priest on Wednesday so the empty day falls on Shabbat, when sprinkling is barred anyway.
yoma/8.question: If the fourth day's sprinkling accomplishes nothing, why arrange the calendar to hide that day rather than simply drop it?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is whether an unnecessary ritual day should be openly dropped or absorbed into an already-lost day so the seven-day form stays intact.

answer.quote: sprinkling will not be performed only one day of the seven, as the day on which sprinkling is prohibited will coincide
answer.explanation: The page explains that the Wednesday start is arranged so the useless fourth day and the Shabbat on which sprinkling is forbidden fall together, costing only one day of the seven instead of two.
