answer.quote: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say: From the place that he interrupted that particular service, when the blood spilled, there he resumes performance
answer.explanation: The mishna states both sides of exactly this question — the anonymous ruling requires repeating the whole service from the beginning, while Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon hold that each sprinkling stands and he resumes where he stopped.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 60a (Mishna): "Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon say: From the place that he interrupted that particular service, when the blood spilled, there he resumes performance". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks the very thing the mishna answers, and the summary itself already reports both answers (restart the service vs. resume from the interruption), so it reads as a quiz rather than an opening. Build the new question on the pressure that remains after that dispute — for instance, why an act done outside the Sanctuary "for the purpose of it being taken inside" should or should not count as inside, given that the mishna makes him re-sprinkle blood but never makes him scoop the incense again. Keep it anchored to words actually on the daf.

yoma/61.summary: Blood spills from the High Priest's hand partway through the Yom Kippur sprinklings, and the argument is where he picks up again. Rabbi Meir has him bring new blood and restart that whole stage; Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon have him resume at the interruption. The same split is then run through the log of oil, a small measure, used to purify a leper, and ends with a baraita where "must" quietly means he has no remedy.
yoma/61.question: If each spilled bull forces a fresh pair of goats and a new lottery, what becomes of all the extra goats meant for the wilderness when only one may be sent?

judge.reachNote: Restarting a rite multiplies consecrated animals, raising what happens to sanctified surplus that the Torah's single-goat command cannot absorb.

answer.quote: He said to him: Does he send away his flock? In other words, the Torah said to send only one goat, not an entire flock.
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman answers that only one goat is sent, but the page breaks off ('Rava said to him:') before saying what becomes of the surplus goats, so the note's question remains largely live.

yoma/62.summary: The mishna asks that the two Yom Kippur goats, one slaughtered as an offering and one sent away to Azazel, be alike in color, height, and price, and bought at the same time. Then it says mismatched goats are valid anyway, and the Gemara gets both claims out of the word "two" appearing three times. If one goat dies after the lottery, a whole new pair is brought and drawn over, with a stipulation covering which one died.
yoma/62.question: If a pair of goats that differ in color, height, and price is valid anyway, what is the matching actually doing?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of a requirement that shapes the ideal performance without affecting validity — but the page names that category outright.

answer.quote: The Gemara answers that it teaches how the mitzva should be performed ab initio: One of the terms indicates that the goats should be identical in appearance
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks what the threefold "two" adds once mismatched goats are valid, and answers that matching is the ab initio manner of performing the mitzva (appearance, height, value).

summaryProblems.claim: the Gemara gets both claims out of the word "two" appearing three times
summaryProblems.pageSays: The verses state and repeat the word goat, goat (Leviticus 16:9–10) to amplify and indicate that the goats are valid even if they are not identical.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 62b: "The Gemara answers that it teaches how the mitzva should be performed ab initio: One of the terms indicates that the goats should be identical in appearance". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "the Gemara gets both claims out of the word "two" appearing three times", but the page says "The verses state and repeat the word goat, goat (Leviticus 16:9–10) to amplify and indicate that the goats are valid even if they are not identical.". Say what the page says. The question is answered flatly on the page: the Gemara asks why the threefold "two" is needed once mismatch is valid and replies that it prescribes the ab initio performance in appearance, height, and value. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance why the same amplification logic is refused for the daily offering, or why a lottery the High Priest performs outside the animal still leaves the goats "lacking an action." Also fix the derivation: validity of mismatched goats comes from the repeated "goat, goat," not from "two" appearing three times.

yoma/63.summary: A man who slaughters a Paschal lamb outside the Temple in the middle of the year is exempt, since no Paschal lamb belongs to that day; if he renames it a peace-offering, Rabbi Yirmeya says that renaming done outside does not stick. The same verses then split the two Yom Kippur goats: the one for Azazel is not "to the Lord," so killing it outside brings no penalty. Yet elsewhere the identical phrase pulls the scapegoat in, barring it if blemished or under eight days old.
yoma/63.question: Why must the goat sent to Azazel be unblemished and eight days old, when the page has just said it is not designated for God as an offering at all?
gate: gloss "the scapegoat" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the real idea — whether the scapegoat counts as an offering 'to the Lord' at all — but the page has already posed and answered that tension.

answer.quote: There the expression is understood in the context of the verse and here it is understood in the context of the verse.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises exactly this contradiction — does "to the Lord" exclude or include the scapegoat — and Rava resolves it by saying each verse's context determines the phrase's force, with the further note that the lottery requires both goats to be fit for God.mm

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 63b: "There the expression is understood in the context of the verse and here it is understood in the context of the verse.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question on 63b, and Rava answers it outright, so it cannot stand as written. Build a new question from something the page leaves unsettled — for instance, why the Gemara is not satisfied that the lottery alone forces both goats to be eight days old, and what Rav Yosef's and Ravina's search for a lottery-free case reveals about how the scapegoat acquires its status. The summary is accurate and can largely stay.

yoma/64.summary: Rava imagines a man who sold the Temple its two Yom Kippur goats, then slaughtered the scapegoat's mother to save a critically ill person, which matters because a mother animal and its young may not be killed on one day. That only works if shoving the scapegoat off a cliff counts as slaughter. The page then argues a harder case: one goat dies, a second pair is bought, and Rav and Rabbi Yohanan split over whether a disqualified animal can ever recover.
yoma/64.question: If a blemish that heals lets an animal be accepted again, why should the goat whose partner died stay rejected for the rest of its life?
gate: gloss "the scapegoat's" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real principle — whether disqualification is a passing condition or a permanent status — but the page states both the blemish analogy and its refutation.

answer.quote: The Merciful One limited this halakha by using the term: In them, which indicates that it is they, animals with temporary blemishes, that are accepted when their blemishes pass
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks how Rabbi Yoḥanan answers the temporary-blemish proof and answers that the word "in them" restricts recovery to blemished animals alone, so all others stay rejected.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 64a: "The Merciful One limited this halakha by using the term: In them, which indicates that it is they, animals with temporary blemishes, that are accepted when their blemishes pass". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question and it is answered a few lines later, both by the "in them" limitation and by the distinction that a lacking-time animal was never fit while this goat was fit and then fell away. Rewrite with a question that survives those answers — for example, why Rav needs the remaining goat of the first pair to be the one sacrificed rather than merely permitted, or what it means that Rava finds the mishna precise for Rav and the baraita precise for Rabbi Yoḥanan. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

yoma/65.summary: A goat set aside for the Yom Kippur lottery is lost, a replacement is bought, and then the first goat turns up. Rabbi Yehuda says the leftover animals are left to die; Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Shimon say they graze until unfit, are sold, and the money buys a gift-offering. Abaye presses for a reason, and four explanations are offered and knocked down by the same protest each time: a rabbinic worry cannot be enough to kill an animal.
yoma/65.question: If every proposed reason for killing the found bull and goat collapses under the same objection, why does the ruling itself stay standing?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether a mere rabbinic precaution can be weighty enough to condemn a consecrated animal rather than let it graze.

answer.quote: Rather, it is a rabbinic decree due to a concern that the goat will become a sin-offering whose year has passed.
answer.explanation: The page's final explanation is not rejected but defended ("This is not difficult, as it is possible that the goat will not be disqualified, in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi"), so the ruling stands on that surviving reason.

summaryProblems.claim: Four explanations are offered and knocked down by the same protest each time.
summaryProblems.pageSays: This is not difficult, as it is possible that the goat will not be disqualified, in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

summaryProblems.claim: No reason survives, so the ruling is left without support.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Nevertheless, it is disqualified by rabbinic decree due to a concern that other goats would be used in similar circumstances even if they were more than a year old.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 65b: "Rather, it is a rabbinic decree due to a concern that the goat will become a sin-offering whose year has passed.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Four explanations are offered and knocked down by the same protest each time.", but the page says "This is not difficult, as it is possible that the goat will not be disqualified, in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.". Say what the page says. The summary says "No reason survives, so the ruling is left without support.", but the page says "Nevertheless, it is disqualified by rabbinic decree due to a concern that other goats would be used in similar circumstances even if they were more than a year old.". Say what the page says. The rewrite must correct the count: only three explanations are dismissed by the "due to a rabbinic decree the offerings should be left to die" protest, and the fourth (sin-offering whose year has passed) is challenged differently and then upheld via Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's 365-day count. Since the page supplies a surviving reason, the question as posed is answered on the page and must be replaced. Ask instead about something that remains live, such as why the same protest that killed three decrees does not undo the decree that finally stands.

yoma/66.summary: Students ask Rabbi Eliezer what to do if the scapegoat, the goat driven to the wilderness bearing Israel's sins, falls ill on the road. He tells them the goat is strong enough to carry him and them, then bats away every follow-up with a proverb or a counter-question. The Gemara insists he was not dodging out of ignorance but because he never said anything he had not heard from his teacher; the Sages answer the questions plainly anyway.
yoma/66.question: If Rabbi Eliezer's evasions mark the edge of what he received from his teacher, what is his reply to the woman who asked why the calf's worshippers died three different deaths?

judge.reachNote: It reaches toward whether Eliezer's deflections are all of one kind — silence for lack of tradition — but asks only for a line the page already supplies.

answer.quote: He said to her: There is no wisdom in a woman except weaving with a spindle, and so it states: "And any woman who was wise-hearted spun with her hands"
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Eliezer's reply to the wise woman verbatim, which is exactly what the question asks for.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 66b: "He said to her: There is no wisdom in a woman except weaving with a spindle, and so it states: "And any woman who was wise-hearted spun with her hands"". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks for Rabbi Eliezer's reply to the wise woman, and the page gives that reply in so many words, so a reader gains nothing by asking. Rebuild it around what the page leaves unsettled: whether the dismissal of the woman is the same kind of silence as the halakhic deflections the Gemara explains as lack of tradition, given that Rav and Levi immediately supply answers to her question. Keep the question anchored in the page's own tension between "he never said anything that he did not hear from the mouth of his teacher" and the Sages who rule plainly.

yoma/67.summary: The goat sent to Azazel is pushed backward off a cliff outside Jerusalem, and a strip of crimson wool is cut in two, half tied to the rock and half tied between the goat's horns. The Sages taught that the crimson once hung at the Temple entrance for all to watch: if it turned white, sins were forgiven; if not, the crowd went home ashamed. So they moved it inside, then out to the cliff, where no one could read the answer until Yom Kippur ended.
yoma/67.question: If the crimson strip really reported whether the sins were forgiven, what was gained by putting the answer somewhere nobody could see it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a public sign of atonement can be withheld when the knowledge harms rather than helps the worshippers.

answer.quote: When the Sages saw that people were overly distressed on Yom Kippur, they established that they should tie the strip of crimson to the opening of the Entrance Hall on the inside
answer.explanation: The page explicitly states the gain: hiding the strip spared the people the distress and shame of seeing it fail to turn white on Yom Kippur itself, culminating in tying it to the rock and horns "so that the people would not know what happened to the strip until after the conclusion of Yom Kippur."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 67a: "When the Sages saw that people were overly distressed on Yom Kippur, they established that they should tie the strip of crimson to the opening of the Entrance Hall on the inside". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered flatly in the same baraita the summary paraphrases: the Sages hid the strip because people were "overly distressed" and so they would not know the outcome until Yom Kippur ended. Rewrite the question so it starts from that stated reason and asks what remains hard, for instance why a sign whose whole purpose is to report forgiveness may be deliberately kept unreadable, or how that squares with Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's report that the strip turned white when the goat reached the wilderness. Alternatively build the question on the untouched material on 67b, such as Rava's argument that the limbs must be permitted because the Torah would not send a mitzva out to cause mishap.

yoma/68.summary: After the goat is sent to the wilderness, the High Priest reads Torah, dressed either in the linen priestly garments or in a white robe of his own. Since reading is not a service, the Gemara asks whether this settles an old dilemma: may a priest get ordinary personal use out of consecrated clothes? It tries the rule that priests do not sleep in the vestments, infers that eating and walking in them are fine, and knocks both inferences down.
yoma/68.question: If a priest eating sacrificial meat still counts as serving because the owners gain atonement through it, what could he possibly do in those garments that would count as merely his own?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the category of 'service' keeps expanding to swallow apparently ordinary acts, leaving the benefit dilemma unresolvable.

answer.quote: One may infer that it is specifically sleep which is not permitted, but they may walk while wearing the sacred vestments even when not engaged in a service.
answer.explanation: The page floats walking as the candidate act that is purely the priest's own, but then rejects that inference, so the question of what counts as non-service benefit remains live.

yoma/69.summary: Moses called God "the great, the mighty, and the awesome." Jeremiah, watching foreign soldiers carouse in the sanctuary, dropped "awesome"; Daniel, watching God's children enslaved, dropped "mighty." The Sages of the Great Assembly, after the return from exile, put both words back by redefining might as restraint, the patience that holds off punishing the wicked, and Rabbi Elazar defends the prophets who cut them: they knew God hates a lie and would not say what they could not see.
yoma/69.question: If Jeremiah and Daniel were right to stop saying words they could not see borne out, what did the Great Assembly see that they did not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether praise must track what one can see, and whether the same facts can be reread as evidence of the attribute they seemed to deny — but the page spells that answer out.

answer.quote: that He conquers His inclination in that He exercises patience toward the wicked
answer.explanation: The page states exactly what the Great Assembly perceived that Jeremiah and Daniel did not — that God's restraint toward the wicked is itself His might, and that the survival of a lone hated people is His awesomeness.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 69b: "that He conquers His inclination in that He exercises patience toward the wicked". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: the Great Assembly saw God's restraint toward the wicked as might, and the survival of a lone hated nation as awesomeness. Since the summary already names the redefinition of might, ask something the page leaves standing — for instance how Rabbi Elazar's defense (that the prophets would not speak falsely) can coexist with the charge that they uprooted an ordinance of Moses, or why a perception-based prayer text may be edited at all. Keep the question at the level of the idea, not the story.

yoma/70.summary: The High Priest reads one Yom Kippur passage from memory instead of rolling the scroll forward to it, because making the congregation wait is a slight to them. A second scroll, pre-rolled, is rejected too: people would suspect the first was flawed, though nobody suspects anything when three men read from three scrolls on a Hanukkah Shabbat. Later, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar split the seven lambs in opposite proportions, one fearing exhaustion, the other fearing slackness.
yoma/70.question: Rabbi Yehuda keeps the High Priest's morning load light so he will not be too weak for the day's service, while Rabbi Elazar loads it heavy so he will not grow lax by afternoon; which failure is the likelier one?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that ritual law is calibrated to a predicted human weakness, and that sages differ over which weakness to legislate against.

yoma/71.summary: The High Priest is said to immerse five times and sanctify his hands and feet ten times on Yom Kippur, but reading Leviticus straight through yields only three immersions and six sanctifications. To make the count come out, the Sages declare one verse, about his reentry into the Holy of Holies, out of order, and Abaye and Rava each hunt for a proof. Later Rav Ashi asks how anything could be known before Ezekiel wrote it.
yoma/71.question: If a remembered count of five immersions is strong enough to shift a verse out of its place in Leviticus, what is holding the rest of the order in place?

judge.reachNote: What authority holds scriptural sequence binding when a remembered count can override it — tradition versus text.

answer.quote: The Gemara answers: Say that the intent of the baraita is that the verses are in order except for this verse and onward.
answer.explanation: The page shows the "in order" claim being trimmed again under pressure from the mishna, and elsewhere that a tradition can be held in place by verse-support ("they learned it as a tradition and then Ezekiel came and supported it with a verse"), which bears on but does not settle what secures the remaining order.

yoma/72.summary: A thread of the breastplate holds twenty-eight strands, since gold beaten into thin cords is spun into each of the four colored threads. Then Raḥava reports in Rav Yehuda's name that anyone who intentionally tears a priestly garment is flogged, learned from the robe's woven opening. Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov objects that the verse may merely explain why the hem is reinforced, and the rejection rests on three words the Torah did not write.
yoma/72.question: If a prohibition and a practical explanation are separated only by the absence of the words "in order that," how much weight can that silence carry?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the hermeneutical idea that a verse's silence about purpose ('in order that') is what converts a descriptive rationale into a floggable prohibition.

answer.quote: Is it written: In order that it not be torn? Clearly, the intention of the verse is to state a prohibition.
answer.explanation: The page asserts the very inference the question interrogates — and repeats it for the breastplate and staves — but never justifies how much weight the missing phrase can bear, so the question survives the reading.

yoma/73.summary: Consulting the Urim VeTummim, the lettered stones set in the High Priest's breastplate, requires the asker to enunciate his question without sound, the way Hannah prayed at Shiloh. One question at a time and in the right order: David asked two at once and got back only one answer. The claim that its words always come true runs into the defeats at Gibeah, and the answer given is that Israel only asked how to fight, never whether they would win.
yoma/73.question: If an oracle whose decree cannot be retracted still sends an army to two slaughters because nobody thought to ask whether they would win, what was actually being promised?

judge.reachNote: An infallible answer is only as wide as the question put to it; the guarantee attaches to the words spoken, not to the outcome hoped for.

answer.quote: The first two times they did not check with the Urim VeTummim whether they would be victorious or be defeated but only inquired how and whether they should go to battle.
answer.explanation: The page explains that the oracle's word held only over what was actually asked — permission to go to battle, not a guarantee of victory — which bears on but does not fully settle what the promise amounted to.

yoma/74.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish argue about eating half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat, less than the amount that carries a penalty. Reish Lakish says the Torah's word is "eat," and eating means an olive-bulk, so anything smaller is only a rabbinic matter. Rabbi Yoḥanan says the half is already forbidden by Torah law because it is fit to combine with a second half into a full measure that would be punishable.
yoma/74.question: If a person eats half an olive-bulk of fat and then stops, what was forbidden about a mouthful that never combined with anything?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition attaches to what an act could become (potential combination) or only to what it actually is.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan said it is prohibited by Torah law because it is fit to combine with another half-measure
answer.explanation: The page gives the fitness-to-combine rationale (and separately the derivation from "All fat" including a half-measure), but it never addresses the case of one who stops, so the challenge the question raises still stands.

yoma/75.summary: Manna, the bread that fell each morning in the desert, doubles as a courtroom on this page. Two men dispute a slave, one claiming theft, the other purchase; Moses says judgment comes in the morning, and whichever house receives the slave's portion of manna wins. The same test splits a husband and wife who each accuse the other, reading the landing place of her food as proof of who wronged whom.
yoma/75.question: If the morning's manna settles who stole the slave and who wronged whom in a marriage, what is left for either side to say once it lands?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a divine sign displaces human testimony and argument, leaving the court's deliberation with nothing to weigh.

yoma/76.summary: Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's students ask why manna, the food that fell in the desert, came daily rather than once a year; he answers with a king who gives his son an allowance every day so the son visits every day. Rabbi Elazar HaModa'i then measures the manna at sixty cubits, four times the Flood's fifteen, since the Flood came through windows and manna through doors, and a door is four windows. Rabbi Tarfon calls this baseless.
yoma/76.question: Rabbi Tarfon says the sixty-cubit calculation is words collected out of nothing, and the Gemara itself objects that forty days of rising floodwater cannot be compared to an hour of falling manna, so what makes the rescue by verbal analogy any better than the arithmetic it saves?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether a verbal analogy is a real derivation or a way of immunizing a homiletic calculation from the objection that its own logic invites.

answer.quote: He used a verbal analogy that teaches that the skies opened in both instances in the same way.
answer.explanation: The page answers the Gemara's own objection by invoking the verbal analogy of "opening"–"opening," but it never explains why that analogy carries more weight than the arithmetic comparison it replaces, which is what the question presses on.

yoma/77.summary: Gabriel is told to scatter burning coals over the city, and the coals cool as they pass from a cherub's hand to his, so a remnant survives. For deviating, and then for reporting the destruction plainly, he is driven out from behind the curtain where the inner angels sit and struck with sixty blows of fire. Later the page hunts proof that not bathing counts as affliction, then permits wading neck-deep across a river to reach a Yom Kippur lecture.
yoma/77.question: If the cooling of the coals is what left any remnant at all, what exactly was Gabriel being punished for?

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is whether an angel (or agent) may be faulted for a merciful deviation that turned out to save Israel.

answer.quote: if you did do it, why did you not do it according to what you were commanded but deviated from what you were instructed to do?
answer.explanation: The page states the charges against Gabriel outright — deviating from his instructions and then reporting the destruction in detail — which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 77a: "if you did do it, why did you not do it according to what you were commanded but deviated from what you were instructed to do?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what Gabriel was punished for, but the page says it in so many words — he deviated from his instructions and then gave a detailed report of destruction — and the summary itself already repeats this. Rewrite the question to press on what the page leaves unresolved, for instance why a deviation that alone preserved a remnant still counts as a fault, or why a messenger of destruction must only hint at his success. Keep it anchored to the Gabriel scene rather than restating the stated charge.

yoma/78.summary: Rav Yehuda went out on Yom Kippur in reed sandals, Abaye in sandals of palm fiber, and Rabba bar Rav Huna wrapped a scarf around his feet and walked out. The fast bars shoes, not comfort, so the argument turns on what counts as a shoe; Rava concludes a wooden prosthetic leg does, rejecting Abaye's claim that the rags padding it are the problem. Children may do everything else that day, but not wear shoes, since onlookers assume an adult dressed them.
yoma/78.question: If a scarf wound around the feet is fine and a wooden leg is not, is a shoe defined by what it does for the foot or by what it looks like to someone watching?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the definitional question underneath the case: is 'shoe' a category of function (protection/comfort for the foot) or of appearance and social recognition.

answer.quote: Rather, Rava said: Actually, according to everyone, a prosthetic leg is considered to be a shoe
answer.explanation: The page rules that the prosthetic leg counts as a shoe while cork, reed and palm-fiber sandals and a scarf do not, but it never states the criterion that separates them, so the note's question about what makes something a shoe can still honestly be asked.

yoma/79.summary: The measure of food that makes a person liable for eating on Yom Kippur is the bulk of a large date, and Rav Pappa asks whether that includes the pit. Rava, citing Rav Yehuda, says the date-bulk is larger than an egg-bulk, since less than that leaves a person's mind unsettled; the sukka stories of two dates and Rabbi Tzadok's small snack are pushed against him. Rav Zevid argues the reverse, from eating that satisfies.
yoma/79.question: If a date's pit can outweigh its flesh, why fix the line between affliction and relief at a fruit measured with its pit inside?

judge.reachNote: Whether a halakhic measure tracks the substance actually eaten and its effect on a person, or is simply a fixed volume standard borrowed from a familiar object.

answer.quote: Since it is stated in the mishna: Large, it means as large as possible, which must include the pit.
answer.explanation: The page explains that the word "large" forces the pit to be counted, but it does not explain why the threshold of affliction should be pegged to a fruit whose inedible pit can exceed its flesh.

yoma/80.summary: On Yom Kippur the food that makes a person liable is the bulk of a large date, the same amount for everyone, while the drink that makes him liable is his own cheekful, which differs from mouth to mouth. Rabbi Zeira presses the gap: why is one measure fixed and the other personal, and is Og, king of Bashan, really satisfied by a date? Abaye answers each time that the measure marks where a person's mind is settled.
yoma/80.question: If the measure is set by the point at which a person's mind is settled, why does a giant's own mouth decide how much he may drink but not how much he may eat?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether a legal threshold measures an objective quantity or a subjective state of relief — but the page already resolves it.

answer.quote: with regard to drinking, his mind is settled with the amount of his own cheekful, but his mind is not settled with the cheekful of his fellow who is smaller
answer.explanation: Abaye answers Rabbi Zeira's objection directly: drink is personal because satisfaction from drinking tracks one's own mouth, while the received tradition fixes the date-bulk as settling anyone's mind, even Og's, if only a little.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Yoma 80b: "with regard to drinking, his mind is settled with the amount of his own cheekful, but his mind is not settled with the cheekful of his fellow who is smaller". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Rabbi Zeira's own objection, which Abaye answers on the page: drinking satisfaction depends on one's own cheekful, while the tradition holds the date-bulk settles any person's mind, Og's only a little. Ask something that survives Abaye's answer — for instance, why a tradition may fix an absolute amount for food while conceding it barely relieves a giant, or press the parallel case of fatty meat versus grapevine shoots where the same measure yields unequal settling. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

yoma/81.summary: Reish Lakish asks why the Torah never simply forbids eating on Yom Kippur, and the Gemara tests one wording after another until Rav Ashi's suggestion sticks and the answer given is that the difficulty stands. Later, Rav Giddel bar Menashe announced in a public lecture that vinegar does not count as a drink, and the next year people mixed vinegar with water and drank it on the fast. He was furious, and added three limits nobody had heard him say.
yoma/81.question: When a crowd hears "not liable" and reaches for the cup, is the failure in their listening or in what Rav Giddel chose to say from the lectern?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of a teacher's responsibility for how a lenient ruling will be heard and used by a crowd.

answer.quote: He said: Say that I said one is not liable for drinking vinegar only after the fact; however, did I say it is permitted to drink it ab initio?
answer.explanation: Rav Giddel himself places the fault on the listeners' over-reading of his ruling, which bears on the question but does not settle whether his public wording was itself at fault.

yoma/82.summary: Children too young to fast are trained toward it in steps: a child used to eating at the second hour is fed at the third, and older children are habituated to a full day, though Rav Huna, Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree about which ages. A pregnant woman overcome by craving is fed, first gravy on a thin reed, then the forbidden food itself. Only idol worship, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed override saving a life.
yoma/82.question: If a man ordered to kill cannot claim his own blood is redder, why may the attacker of the betrothed woman be killed to save her?

judge.reachNote: When blood cannot be weighed against blood, the aggressor's own act is what removes his claim — the question reaches the asymmetry between an attacker and an innocent third party.

answer.quote: Just as with regard to the betrothed woman, permission is given to save her at the cost of the life of her attacker
answer.explanation: The page states that killing the attacker to save the betrothed woman is permitted, and derives the murder rule from it, but it never explains how this squares with Rava's 'whose blood is redder' reasoning, so the tension the question raises remains open.

yoma/83.summary: A sick person on Yom Kippur says he needs to eat, and the doctors say he does not, and Rabbi Yannai rules that the sick person is fed. Mar bar Rav Ashi pushes it further, so that even a hundred doctors who disagree are ignored, since the heart knows its own bitterness. But when the patient refuses food and a doctor says he needs it, the page says illness has confused him, and he is fed regardless.
yoma/83.question: If illness confuses a person enough that his refusal to eat cannot be trusted, why does that same illness leave him the one witness who outweighs a hundred doctors when he asks for food?

judge.reachNote: When is a person the authority on his own body, and when does the very condition that gives him that authority disqualify his judgment?

answer.quote: since it is a case of uncertainty concerning a life-threatening situation, and in all cases of uncertainty concerning a life-threatening situation, the halakha is lenient
answer.explanation: The page supplies the leniency principle that could explain why the ill person's word is followed only in the direction of eating, but it never addresses the asymmetry between trusting his request and distrusting his refusal, each of which gets its own separate reason ('The heart knows the bitterness of its soul' versus 'confusion [tunba] has taken hold').

yoma/84.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan had tzefidna, an ailment that starts in the gums and ends in the intestines, and a gentile woman known as a healer agreed to treat him only if he swore not to reveal her remedy. He swore, then taught it publicly. The Gemara rescues the oath by re-reading its wording, then worries the healer will think a great man broke his word, and answers that he warned her the moment she told him.
yoma/84.question: If Rabbi Yoḥanan really told the healer at the outset that he would publish her remedy anyway, what was she agreeing to when she made him swear?

judge.reachNote: Whether an oath kept by a hidden re-reading, disclosed after the fact, still counts as honoring a promise to an outsider.

summaryProblems.claim: The healer agreed to treat him only if he swore not to reveal her remedy.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Swear to me that you will not reveal the remedy; then I will tell you, and you can prepare it yourself should you need it.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The healer agreed to treat him only if he swore not to reveal her remedy.", but the page says "Swear to me that you will not reveal the remedy; then I will tell you, and you can prepare it yourself should you need it.". Say what the page says. Fix the sequence: the matron already prepared the medicine for him on Thursday and Friday without any oath, and the oath was the condition for her telling him the remedy so he could make it himself on Shabbat. The question is good and should stay; just make the summary state what the oath was actually the price of.

yoma/85.summary: A rockslide buries someone on Shabbat, and the debate is how far the diggers must go: to the nose, to check for breath, or down to the heart. Then five sages each offer a verse proving that saving a life overrides Shabbat, and Rava knocks every one of them down, since each proves only the case of certain danger, not doubt. Shmuel's verse, live by them and not die by them, is the one left standing.
yoma/85.question: If a foundling in a mostly gentile city may be fed non-kosher food on the strength of the majority, why does that same majority count for nothing when he is the one under the rubble?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that probability may settle status for food, property and damages, yet counts for nothing where a life hangs in the balance.

answer.quote: Shmuel said: But with regard to the matter of saving a life it is not so. Rather, one saves him based on the uncertainty.
answer.explanation: The page states flatly that the majority rule is not applied to saving a life and that one rescues on the strength of the doubt, but it never explains why the two domains differ, so the question still stands as a 'why'.

summaryProblems.claim: Five sages each offer a verse proving that saving a life overrides Shabbat.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Other tanna’im debated this same issue. Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says that it is stated: “But keep my Shabbatot” (Exodus 31:13).

judge.feedback: The summary says "Five sages each offer a verse proving that saving a life overrides Shabbat.", but the page says "Other tanna’im debated this same issue. Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, says that it is stated: “But keep my Shabbatot” (Exodus 31:13).". Say what the page says. Fix the count: six sages argue before Shmuel (Yishmael, Akiva, Elazar ben Azarya, Yosei b. Yehuda, Yonatan ben Yosef, Shimon ben Menasya), and Elazar ben Azarya argues from circumcision rather than a verse. Keep the question's idea, but sharpen it so it acknowledges Shmuel's own line that for saving a life we go by the uncertainty, and asks why that domain refuses the majority the other cases accept.

yoma/86.summary: Rabbi Yishmael's scheme sorts sins by what clears them: neglecting a positive commandment is forgiven at once, breaking a prohibition waits for Yom Kippur, and sins punishable by karet, being cut off, need suffering as well. Only desecration of God's name waits for death. The Gemara then asks what such desecration actually is, and Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan answer with themselves: meat taken from a butcher without paying on the spot, four cubits walked without phylacteries.
yoma/86.question: Why is the one offense that nothing but death can erase illustrated not by a crime but by how an unpaid butcher's bill looks to onlookers?

judge.reachNote: It reaches the idea that desecration is measured by the damage a public figure's appearance does to God's reputation rather than by the gravity of the act.

answer.quote: people are likely to think that I did not mean to pay at all. They would consider me a thief and learn from my behavior that one is permitted to steal
answer.explanation: Rav explains that the butcher case counts as desecration because of what onlookers conclude and imitate, which bears on the question but does not directly address why this outranks actual crimes.

yoma/87.summary: Yom Kippur atones for sins against God, the mishna says, but not for sins against another person until that person is appeased. Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina caps the asking at three tries, yet Rav went to Rabbi Ḥanina every Yom Kippur eve for thirteen years and was turned away. The refusal turns out to be strategy: Rabbi Ḥanina had dreamed of Rav hanging on a palm tree, a sign of a future head of a yeshiva, and wanted him in Babylonia.
yoma/87.question: If Rabbi Ḥanina withheld forgiveness to keep his own post, was Rav apologizing to anyone at all for thirteen years?

judge.reachNote: Appeasement is a two-sided act: the question asks whether an apology still counts as appeasement when the refuser has withdrawn from the exchange for reasons of his own.

answer.quote: Rav is different, since he was very pious and forced himself to act beyond the letter of the law.
answer.explanation: The page explains why Rav kept coming for thirteen years — supererogatory piety — which bears on the question but does not settle whether his appeasement had a genuine addressee once Rabbi Ḥanina's motive is known.

yoma/88.summary: Yoma ends by asking who may immerse in a ritual bath on Yom Kippur, a day when washing is otherwise banned. The argument turns on whether immersing at its appointed time is itself a commandment, tested by a man with God's name inked on his skin, who wraps it in a reed before going under. The tractate closes on a man who has a seminal emission on the fast: sins forgiven, or a sign of rejection.
yoma/88.question: If the emission is read as proof that his lust was subdued and his sins cleared away, why is he told to spend the whole year waiting to see whether he survives it?

judge.reachNote: Whether an involuntary bodily event on the fast is a verdict already delivered or an omen whose meaning only the coming year will disclose.

answer.quote: But if he survives the year, he can be assured that his good deeds protected him and ensured for him a share in the World-to-Come.
answer.explanation: The page states what surviving the year proves, and Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's "involuntary and not intentional" reasoning supports the favorable reading, but it never explains why the year of worry is imposed if the sins are already forgiven.

sukkah/2.summary: A sukka, the festival hut, is unfit if its roofing stands more than twenty cubits high, roughly ten meters, and the Gemara hunts for the reason. Rabba says the eye no longer catches the roofing; Rabbi Zeira says the shade then comes from the walls; Rava says nobody builds a flimsy temporary hut that tall. Abaye pokes at each, and Rabbi Yehuda points to Queen Helene of Lod, whose tall sukka the Elders walked in and out of without a word.
sukkah/2.question: If Helene's exemption as a woman drains the Elders' silence of meaning, what were her seven sons doing in that sukka?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the silence of sages can serve as halakhic evidence only if someone present was actually obligated — but the page spells this out.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda said to them in response: Didn’t she have seven sons and therefore require a fit sukka?
answer.explanation: The page states exactly why the sons matter — they were obligated in sukka (and at least one was past needing his mother), so the Elders' silence still counts as proof.

summaryProblems.claim: Abaye pokes at each of the three derivations (Rabba, Rabbi Zeira, Rava).
summaryProblems.pageSays: All of them, Rabbi Zeira and Rava, did not say that the fact that a sukka more than twenty cubits high is unfit is derived

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 2b: "Rabbi Yehuda said to them in response: Didn’t she have seven sons and therefore require a fit sukka?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Abaye pokes at each of the three derivations (Rabba, Rabbi Zeira, Rava).", but the page says "All of them, Rabbi Zeira and Rava, did not say that the fact that a sukka more than twenty cubits high is unfit is derived". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words on the daf: Rabbi Yehuda himself says the seven sons made a fit sukka necessary, and the Gemara explains that at least one was past needing his mother. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for instance whether the Elders' silence can prove anything when the obligation of a trained minor is only rabbinic, or why Rav Ḥanan bar Rabba's measure fits none of the three reasons. Also fix the summary: Abaye challenges only Rabbi Zeira and Rava; Rabba's derivation is rejected by those two sages on other grounds.

sukkah/3.summary: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak rules that a sukka, the festival hut, must be large enough to hold a person's head, most of his body, and his table. Rabbi Abba objects that this is Beit Shammai's view, and the law normally follows Beit Hillel; the reply is that here Beit Shammai is simply right. The Gemara then asks whether the two schools argue about the hut's minimum size at all, or about a man sitting inside with his table out in the house.
sukkah/3.question: If the rule is that Beit Hillel wins, what makes Rav Shmuel bar Yitzhak so certain that this is the case where a person should not budge from Beit Shammai?

judge.reachNote: When does a received ruling in a particular case override the general meta-rule that the halakha follows Beit Hillel?

answer.quote: Rather, in accordance with whose opinion should I rule? Yes, my ruling is in accordance with the opinion of Beit Shammai because in this case that is the halakha.
answer.explanation: The page records Rav Shmuel bar Yitzḥak's bare insistence that Beit Shammai's view is the settled halakha here, but never supplies a ground for that certainty, so the question can still honestly be asked.

sukkah/4.summary: Abaye argued that a pillar standing inside a sukka built too tall forms a fit sukka on its own, since a partition ten handbreadths high (about a hand's width times ten) is treated as rising upward without end. Rava refused, because the pillar's sides do not project above its surface, so nothing visible marks a wall. The same fight returns over four posts driven into the ground with roofing on top and no walls at all.
sukkah/4.question: If walls can be imagined rising from four bare posts stuck in the ground, why not from the four sides of a pillar a person can actually stand on?

judge.reachNote: When may a legal fiction like 'extend and raise' build a wall out of nothing — does the fiction need some visible thing to start from?

answer.quote: That is not so, since in order to have a fit sukka we require conspicuous partitions, and there are none, as the sides of the column do not actually project above the surface
answer.explanation: Rava states the standard that separates the two cases — partitions must be conspicuous — but the page never applies that standard to the four posts, which Rabbi Ya'akov permits and the Rabbis still reject, so the comparison the question presses remains open.

sukkah/5.summary: A sukka must be ten handbreadths high, a handbreadth being the width of four fingers, and the page hunts for where that number comes from. The chain runs through the Ark in the desert Tabernacle: nine handbreadths of box, plus a cover whose thickness the Torah never states, so it is measured against a table's border, a human face, a cherub's face like a child's. When Rabbi Yehuda's shorter cubit yields eleven and a half, the whole derivation is dropped for a tradition from Sinai.
sukkah/5.question: If the minimum height was received as a tradition from Sinai all along, what was the long chain of comparisons, from table border to cherub's face, actually doing?

judge.reachNote: What is scriptural derivation for, if the measure was already received as Oral Law — proof or presentation?

answer.quote: This calculation works out well according to Rabbi Meir, who said that all the cubits in the Tabernacle and the Temple were intermediate cubits
answer.explanation: The page limits the retreat to Sinai-tradition to Rabbi Yehuda's five-handbreadth cubit, implying the derivation still stands for Rabbi Meir, but it never says what the scriptural chain contributes once a received tradition is available.

sukkah/6.summary: The word basukkot, "in booths," appears three times in the Torah verses about dwelling in sukkot, twice spelled without the letter vav and once with it. The Rabbis count the spelling and derive three walls; Rabbi Shimon counts the pronunciation, plural every time, and derives four. Either way an oral tradition from Sinai shrinks the last wall to a single handbreadth, which sits oddly beside Rav Mattana's verse about shelter from storm and rain.
sukkah/6.question: Can two walls and a stub one handbreadth wide really be "refuge and cover from storm and from rain," or is that a shelter only on the page?

judge.reachNote: Whether a wall counted out of scriptural spelling and oral tradition must also function as a physical shelter, or whether halakhic structure suffices.

answer.quote: A sukka without three full-fledged walls does not provide shelter nor serve as refuge.
answer.explanation: Rav Mattana's derivation from Isaiah states that a sukka lacking three real walls gives no shelter, which speaks directly to the question, but it is offered as Rabbi Shimon's rationale and the Rabbis' minimal two-walls-plus-handbreadth sukka is never defended in those terms, so the question can still be honestly asked.

sukkah/7.summary: A sukka, the hut lived in during the festival of Sukkot, needs only two walls plus a third measuring one handbreadth, and the page argues over where that scrap of board goes and whether a pole overhead in the form of a doorway is also required. Rav Ashi finds Rav Kahana building both remedies at once, hedging between versions of Rava's ruling. Rava pushes further: a wall good enough for a sukka also makes a Shabbat partition, turning the flimsy structure into a private domain.
sukkah/7.question: If one handbreadth of board counts as a wall, what is left of the demand that a sukka be sturdy and roofed and cornered like a house someone actually lives in?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between symbolic, legally sufficient partitions and the substantive demand that a sukka be a dwelling.

answer.quote: Rabbi Shimon says: Three of the walls must be walls in the standard sense, and a fourth wall is required that measures even a handbreadth.
answer.explanation: The page presents the permanent-residence demand as the position of a named set of tannaim (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Rabbi Yoshiya, Rabbi Shimon, and others) who accordingly reject or tighten the two-walls-plus-a-handbreadth standard, which bears on the question without fully resolving how the lenient view squares with dwelling-like permanence.

sukkah/8.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan said a round sukka must measure twenty-four cubits around, a cubit being roughly a forearm, enough to seat twenty-four people. The Gemara's own geometry keeps landing near seventeen, so it says he was not precise, then limits that excuse to rounding that makes the requirement stricter rather than looser. The rest turns to potters' booths, where the inner one, lived in year-round, fails as a sukka while the outer sales booth passes.
sukkah/8.question: If a sage's number can be called imprecise only when the error runs toward strictness, is the extra seven cubits a measurement or a decision?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's stated measure reports geometry or legislates a margin — the page's own worry that imprecision is tolerated only toward stringency.

answer.quote: Actually, a man sits and occupies one cubit, and Rabbi Yoḥanan is not factoring the space that the men occupy in his calculation.
answer.explanation: Rav Asi's resolution recasts the twenty-four as the circle formed by the seated people rather than the sukka's own circumference, so the gap shrinks to a stringent rounding from sixteen and four-fifths to eighteen, though the note's larger question of whether the figure is measurement or ruling is still askable.

sukkah/9.summary: Beit Shammai hold that an old sukka, one built thirty days or more before the festival without anyone saying it was for the mitzva, cannot be used; Beit Hillel permit it. The Gemara hunts for a verse behind Beit Shammai's view, and each candidate turns out to be busy elsewhere: reserving the sukka's wood, allowing building on the intermediate days, excluding a stolen booth. The sharp move is the comparison to ritual fringes, where Shmuel demands the thread be spun with the mitzva in mind.
sukkah/9.question: If thread has to be spun for the sake of the mitzva before it is ever tied, why should a booth put up last year for shade be any different?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — when intention at the time of manufacture is constitutive of a mitzva object — but the Gemara asks and resolves it in so many words.

answer.quote: The Gemara answers that this term “for you” is required to exclude use of a stolen sukka; establish the sukka for you, and do not use a sukka belonging to another.
answer.explanation: The page raises the note's exact objection from tzitzit and answers it: in sukka the phrase "for you" is consumed by excluding a stolen booth, whereas tzitzit has a second verse ("for them") for theft, freeing "for you" to demand production for the sake of the mitzva.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 9a: "The Gemara answers that this term “for you” is required to exclude use of a stolen sukka; establish the sukka for you, and do not use a sukka belonging to another.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very objection the Gemara itself raises and answers on this page — that "for you" in the sukka verse is already spent excluding a stolen booth, while tzitzit has "for them" to do that job. Ask something that starts after that answer, for instance why a spare verse is what decides whether intent must be present from the moment of manufacture, or why Beit Hillel are content for the sukka to be sanctified without ever having been made for the Festival. Also correct the summary: the Gemara does settle on Deuteronomy 16:13 as Beit Shammai's source, and "for you" excluding a stolen sukka belongs to the tzitzit comparison, not to the search for Beit Shammai's verse.

sukkah/10.summary: A sukka, the festival hut roofed with cut plants, built beneath another sukka is unfit, and the Sages argue how much gap makes the upper one count: one handbreadth, four, or ten. Then sheets: one spread under the roofing to catch falling leaves ruins the sukka, while one hung to decorate it does not. Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna slept in a sukka they held unfit and said nothing, pleading exemption as travelers on a mitzva, a commanded errand.
sukkah/10.question: If they were genuinely exempt that night, why stay silent about a sukka they judged unfit rather than tell their host?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether a scholar's silence in another's house counts as concession, and when one must protest a practice one holds unfit.

answer.quote: We are on the path to perform a mitzva and, therefore, we are exempt from the mitzva of sukka. Therefore, it is permitted for us to sleep in this sukka.
answer.explanation: The page gives their stated reason for sleeping there and insists their ruling stood, which bears on the silence but does not directly explain why they withheld the ruling from Rav Naḥman until asked.

sukkah/11.summary: A live grapevine, gourd plant, or ivy trellised over a sukka and then covered with cut branches leaves the sukka unfit, since the verse "prepare for you the festival of Sukkot" is read as requiring that the roof be made, not found already made. Rav holds that cutting the vines is itself the act of making; Shmuel holds the branches must also be shifted. The same argument runs through ritual fringes threaded as loops and snipped only after tying.
sukkah/11.question: If Rav can say that pulling branches loose fails because the act of preparation is not conspicuous, does making something require that someone be able to see it was done?

judge.reachNote: Whether an act counts as 'preparing' depends on its being perceptible as an act, not merely on its effect.

answer.quote: Since, in that case, their active preparation is not conspicuous, it does not render the climbing plants fit roofing.
answer.explanation: The page states, for Rav's case of branches pulled loose, that inconspicuous preparation fails, which bears directly on the question without generalizing it into a rule about all making.

sukkah/12.summary: The Gemara hunts for a verse behind the rule that sukka roofing must be plant matter incapable of contracting ritual impurity, and lands on Deuteronomy's "from your threshing floor and from your winepress," read as the waste: stalks and vines. Rabbi Zeira argues you cannot roof with wine, until Rabbi Yirmeya raises congealed wine from Mount Hermon, solid as a cake of figs, and Zeira concedes the proof is wrecked. Rav Ashi rebuilds it out of the single word "from."
sukkah/12.question: If the rule about stalks and vines stood firm while its proof text was demolished and then patched from one preposition, what was the verse actually doing for it?

judge.reachNote: Asks what a proof text contributes when the halakha it supports never wavers while the derivation is demolished and rebuilt.

sukkah/13.summary: Bundled sticks are unfit for roofing a sukka, so the page works out what counts as a bundle. Palm offshoots that grew joined at the trunk pass, since a binding at the hand of Heaven is not considered a binding, and reeds from Sura tied by a seller pass too, because he tied them only to count them. A knot, it turns out, is measured by why someone tied it. Willow huts untied at the top pass as well.
sukkah/13.question: If a seller's knot is no knot because he was only counting, what would he have to be thinking when he ties the same string for it to spoil the roof?

judge.reachNote: Whether the legal status of a knot is fixed by the tier's purpose, and where the boundary of that intent lies.

answer.quote: any binding that is not destined to be moved is not considered a binding
answer.explanation: The page supplies a criterion adjacent to the question — permanence/portability of the tie rather than the tier's purpose — so it bears on but does not directly state what intent would render a binding disqualifying.

sukkah/14.summary: Rabbi Meir bars roofing a sukka with boards four handbreadths wide, roughly the width of four fingers-widths each, because a ceiling of planks blurs into the ceiling of a house. Rav and Shmuel split over whether that is the width the dispute covers or the width everyone already rejects, and each side finds a baraita to lean on. Rabbi Yehuda recalls roofing a porch with wide boards during a ban on sukkot; the Sages dismiss the memory as no proof.
sukkah/14.question: If the porch they sat under during the ban was not a valid sukka at all, what exactly were they risking their safety to do?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea of performing a mitzva-shaped act for remembrance when the mitzva itself is barred — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: It is possible that the sukka that they built on the porch was unfit, and they built it merely to commemorate the mitzva that they were unable to fulfill.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself explains that the porch roofing, even if unfit, was erected as a commemoration of a mitzva they could not properly perform, which is exactly what the question asks.

summaryProblems.claim: Four handbreadths is 'roughly the width of four fingers-widths each'
summaryProblems.pageSays: The dispute is with regard to boards that have four handbreadths in their width, the standard size for boards used in house ceilings

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 14b: "It is possible that the sukka that they built on the porch was unfit, and they built it merely to commemorate the mitzva that they were unable to fulfill.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Four handbreadths is 'roughly the width of four fingers-widths each'", but the page says "The dispute is with regard to boards that have four handbreadths in their width, the standard size for boards used in house ceilings". Say what the page says. The question is answered in the same baraita: the Gemara says the porch sukka may have been unfit and was built 'merely to commemorate the mitzva that they were unable to fulfill,' so ask something the page leaves open — for instance why a memory formed under duress is disqualified as halakhic evidence while still being recounted as precedent. Also drop the gloss equating four handbreadths with four fingers-widths; the page only calls four handbreadths the standard width of house-ceiling boards.

sukkah/15.summary: A house roof of bare boards four handbreadths wide, with no plaster on top, can be converted into a sukkah roof, and the fight is over how much work that takes. Beit Shammai want the boards lifted and one swapped out for proper roofing; Beit Hillel say either action alone suffices; Rabbi Meir says lifting them accomplishes nothing. The Gemara offers a reading in which even Beit Shammai treat the shifting as empty, leaving the same ceiling in place.
sukkah/15.question: If picking up a board and setting it back down makes it count as placed for the sake of the mitzva, what has actually changed about the roof?
gate: the question uses "mitzva", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether fitness comes from a physical change in the roofing or only from an act of intention-bearing handling — but the Gemara answers it in its opening lines.

answer.quote: If one moves the boards, he performs an action. Likewise, if he removes one of the boards from among them, he also performs an action.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that what changes is not the physical roof but that a human act of preparation has now been performed, satisfying "Prepare it, and not from that which has already been prepared," and later puts it as "the ceiling is thereby negated, by moving the boards."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 15a (Gemara on the first mishna): "If one moves the boards, he performs an action. Likewise, if he removes one of the boards from among them, he also performs an action.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the Gemara's first line, which says moving the boards is itself "an action" so the roofing counts as prepared, and later that "the ceiling is thereby negated, by moving the boards." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer and presses on what stays hard: for instance, why an act that changes nothing physical can undo a ceiling for Beit Hillel yet be called "inconsequential" once the concern is the decree of the roof. A question about the tension between preparation-by-handling and a decree aimed at how the sukka looks would stay open.

sukkah/16.summary: A sukka wall built up from the ground works at ten handbreadths even if it stops short of the roofing, but a wall lowered from above must come within three handbreadths of the ground, since animals could walk under it. Rabbi Yosei disagrees: ten handbreadths of hanging wall is a wall, period. The Gemara then shows Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda each accepting suspended partitions only in their own case, and refusing the other's.
sukkah/16.question: If a partition hanging in the air counts as a wall for a sukka but not for carrying on Shabbat, is it a wall at all, or only a wall when the stakes are low enough?

judge.reachNote: Whether a legal partition is a fact about space or a concession calibrated to the severity of what hangs on it — the idea is real, but the page names it explicitly.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yosei states his opinion that a suspended partition suffices only here, with regard to a sukka, which is a positive mitzva. However, in the case of carrying between courtyards on Shabbat, which is a prohibition that is punishable by stoning, no
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that the suspended partition works for the lighter case (a positive mitzva) and not for the severe one (a prohibition punishable by stoning), which is exactly the question's second horn.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 16b: "Rabbi Yosei states his opinion that a suspended partition suffices only here, with regard to a sukka, which is a positive mitzva. However, in the case of carrying between courtyards on Shabbat, which is a prohibition that is punishable by stoning, no". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks why a hanging partition counts for sukka but not for Shabbat carrying, and the page answers it in so many words — positive mitzva versus a prohibition punishable by stoning, Torah law versus rabbinic law. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer rather than requesting it. The Tzippori incident is good ground: sheets already spread were trusted as partitions for carrying a Torah scroll on Shabbat, a Torah-law severity, on the authority of a third tanna — ask what that leaves of the severity principle just established.

sukkah/17.summary: The mishna rules that a gap of three handbreadths between the roofing and the wall makes a sukka unfit, while up to four cubits of a breached house's old ceiling counts as a bent continuation of the wall. Rabba pressed the Sages of Rav's school with a sukka whose gap and whose unfit roofing are each too small to disqualify, then filled the gap with skewers and asked what happens. His position is that unequal measures do not combine.
sukkah/17.question: If empty air is the stricter problem, disqualifying at three handbreadths, how can filling that air with skewers make the sukka worse rather than better?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a disqualification is one of quantity of unfit covering or of distance separating roofing from wall, and whether stringency in one measure should carry over a fortiori to the other.

answer.quote: since their measures are not equal to each other, they do not combine to render the sukka unfit
answer.explanation: The note's question is Rabba's own objection, and the page gives his resolution: because the disqualifying measures of space and of unfit roofing are distinct and unequal halakhot they never combine, so on his view filling the gap with skewers does not turn a fit sukka unfit (while on the school of Rav's view the measure is one of distance from the wall, so space and unfit roofing are interchangeable).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 17b: "since their measures are not equal to each other, they do not combine to render the sukka unfit". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates Rabba's own challenge ("shouldn't space, which is more stringent... be as stringent as unfit roofing"), which the page answers a few lines later on 17b with the distinction between unequal measures that do not combine and a measure of distance from the wall — and the note's own last sentence already states that answer. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing: e.g. whether Rabba's reply to Abaye (that a small sukka is unfit for lack of minimum fit roofing, not for unfit roofing) quietly concedes that fit and unfit areas are measured against each other, or why in the zav case fabrics of unequal measures do combine once they share a single one-handbreadth use. Keep the summary as it is; it is accurate.

sukkah/18.summary: A gap smaller than three handbreadths in a sukka roof is treated as if it were closed, a rule called lavud. Rav Aha and Ravina split over whether lavud works in the middle of the roof or only along the side, and each brings a proof from elsewhere: a cross beam reaching across an alleyway, and a skylight in a house holding a corpse. Each then disqualifies the other's proof as a special case.
sukkah/18.question: If a gap narrower than three handbreadths counts as sealed at the edge, what makes the same gap in the middle of the roof a real hole?

judge.reachNote: Lavud may be a principle of joining to something (a wall) rather than of shrinking distance, so a gap with nothing beside it has nothing to be joined to.

answer.quote: Apparently, the principle of lavud is not applied in the center; if it were, all the objects in the house would become ritually impure regardless of the location
answer.explanation: The page supplies a scriptural-textual basis (the skylight mishna) for denying lavud in the center, but it never states what conceptually distinguishes an edge gap from a central one, so the question can still be honestly asked.

sukkah/19.summary: Abaye found his teacher Rav Yosef asleep inside a netted bridal canopy that stood inside a sukka, and objected that the sloping netting counts as a tent blocking the sukka's roofing. Rav Yosef answered that a baraita reverses the names: there Rabbi Eliezer permits and the Rabbis forbid. Abaye pressed him on preferring a baraita to the mishna, and Rav Yosef replied that the mishna's version is only Rabbi Natan's, while most Sages taught it the other way.
sukkah/19.question: Did Rav Yosef sleep under the canopy because the baraita convinced him, or did the baraita become authoritative because he was already sleeping there?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's ruling generates his practice or his practice is retroactively defended by selecting the authoritative text.

answer.quote: I have proof that the formulation of this particular baraita is precise, as the formulation of the mishna is an individual version of the dispute
answer.explanation: The page gives Rav Yosef's stated justification for following the baraita, but it does not settle whether his practice preceded and drove that justification, so the question can still honestly be asked.

sukkah/20.summary: A reed mat can roof a sukka only if it is not a vessel, so the argument turns on what the mat was made for. Size, weave, and even town of origin count: the soft mats of Usha are for lying on, the coarse mats of Tiberias for roofing and partitions, and mats from everywhere else are disputed. A single upturned edge settles it, since a rim makes the mat a receptacle.
sukkah/20.question: Should a mat be judged by what people usually do with it, or by the fact that someone, occasionally, sits down on it?

judge.reachNote: Whether an object's status follows typical, settled use or the bare possibility of occasional use.

answer.quote: Since there is no one who sits on these mats regularly, they are comparable to the mats of Tiberias and are pure. And one Sage, Rabbi Dosa, holds
answer.explanation: The page lays out exactly this fork as the dispute between the Rabbis (regular use) and Rabbi Dosa (occasional sitting), but does not decide between them, so the question can still be honestly asked.

sukkah/21.summary: Children raised in courtyards built over rock, kept from any contact with a grave, rode out on oxen to draw water for the ashes of the red heifer. Rabbi Yehuda says they brought no boards to sit on, only the broad-bellied oxen, since a confident child on a wide door might stick out a limb. That forces a question: an ox is no man-made tent, so why does its body block impurity from below?
sukkah/21.question: If an ox's hide and flesh count as a tent because they shelter its own innards, what keeps a person's own skin from doing the same?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the criterion behind 'tent': if sheltering-function makes flesh a tent, the definition threatens to swallow every living body, including the impure corpse itself.

sukkah/22.summary: A sukka can be roofed in two layers, with reeds above set over the gaps below, and the argument is when the two layers count as one roof. Abaye says they must be within three handbreadths, roughly a hand's width each; Rava says any gap works if the upper reeds are a handbreadth wide, since one imagines them lowered onto the lower layer. He proves it from ceiling boards and corpse impurity, and Rav Ashi pushes back with beams over an alleyway.
sukkah/22.question: If nothing actually moves, why should a handbreadth of width be what lets scattered reeds hanging high above be treated as lying on the layer below?

judge.reachNote: When may halakha imagine an object relocated — what makes a thing substantial enough to be treated as lying where it is not?

answer.quote: Apparently, when there is a handbreadth in the upper layer, we say lower and cast the upper sukka roofing down to the level
answer.explanation: Rava grounds the handbreadth requirement by derivation from the corpse-impurity mishna and its Tosefta, but the page supplies a source rather than a reason why width should license the fiction, so the note's 'why' can still be asked.

sukkah/23.summary: Rabbi Akiva built a sukka on the deck of a ship, and a wind uprooted it overnight, prompting Rabban Gamliel to ask where it went. Abaye reframes the quarrel as a question of measure: must a sukka withstand a typical sea wind, or only a typical land wind? The page then turns to using a live animal as a wall, worrying that it might die or run off, and settles on a tied elephant whose carcass would still stand ten handbreadths high.
sukkah/23.question: If Rabbi Meir assumes an absent husband is still alive so his wife keeps eating teruma, why should a tethered cow be too likely to die to serve as a wall?
gate: the question brings in "Meir", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "teruma", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether a tanna's estimate of how likely death is must stay consistent across teruma and partitions.

summaryProblems.claim: The page settles on a tied elephant whose carcass would still stand ten handbreadths high.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rather, this is the explanation: In the case where one established a wall with an elephant that is not tied, everyone agrees that the sukka is unfit lest it flee.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The page settles on a tied elephant whose carcass would still stand ten handbreadths high.", but the page says "Rather, this is the explanation: In the case where one established a wall with an elephant that is not tied, everyone agrees that the sukka is unfit lest it flee.". Say what the page says. The summary reports the rejected first explanation as the page's conclusion; the Gemara withdraws the tied-elephant resolution and ends up locating the dispute in a tied ordinary animal, with the untied elephant unfit for all. Rewrite that last sentence to follow the sugya's retraction, including the later refinements about filling the gaps between the legs and tying the animal from above. The question itself is good — it is the Gemara's own unanswered difficulty — and can stand.

sukkah/24.summary: Rabbi Meir rules that an animal tied in place cannot serve as a wall of a sukka, while Rabbi Yehuda allows it. The first explanation is fear the animal will die, until a case about a corpse covered by a living creature forces a rethinking: Rav A a bar Ya'akov says nothing held up by its own life force counts as a wall, or else nothing not set up by a person does. The test case separating the two is an inflated wineskin.
