sukkah/24.question: If Rabbi Meir's real objection is that a living animal holds itself up by nothing but its own life force, why was his reason first given as the worry that it might die?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the difference between a rabbinic worry about a contingency (it may die or run off) and an intrinsic disqualification of what can count as a wall at all.

answer.quote: Rather, Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov said, contrary to that which was stated above: Rabbi Meir holds that any partition that stands by means of air
answer.explanation: The page shows that the death/flight reason was an earlier assumption that the grave-covering objection forced the Gemara to retract, which bears on the question without explaining why that reason was advanced in the first place.

summaryProblems.claim: The animal in Rabbi Meir's case is tied in place.
summaryProblems.pageSays: If one utilized his animal as a wall for the sukka, Rabbi Meir deems it unfit and Rabbi Yehuda deems it fit.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The animal in Rabbi Meir's case is tied in place.", but the page says "If one utilized his animal as a wall for the sukka, Rabbi Meir deems it unfit and Rabbi Yehuda deems it fit.". Say what the page says.

sukkah/25.summary: The mishna exempts anyone traveling to perform a mitzva, plus the sick and those caring for them, from sitting in a sukka. The Gemara hunts for the source, landing on a groom who marries a virgin and is excused from reciting Shema because he is too preoccupied. Then it presses: a man whose ship just sank at sea is preoccupied too, and a mourner more so, yet both stay obligated. The line drawn is the source of the distraction, not its weight.
sukkah/25.question: If the man whose ship sank is just as distracted as the groom, what is the groom's exemption actually protecting?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "obligated: obligated to do what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether an exemption tracks subjective distraction or the halakhic status of what distracts you — engagement in a mitzva rather than intensity of worry.

answer.quote: Here, in the case of a groom, he is preoccupied with the preoccupation of a mitzva that he must perform; there, in the case of a ship lost at sea, he is preoccupied with the preoccupation of a voluntary act
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks the same comparison the note raises and resolves it by classifying the groom's distraction as mitzva-preoccupation, though it never says what value the exemption is meant to protect, which is what the note asks after conceding that distinction.

sukkah/26.summary: Watchmen who guard gardens and orchards are exempt from living in a sukka during the festival, and the page offers two reasons: a booth out in the field could never be furnished like a home, or, as Rava says, a booth would show thieves exactly where the guard is sitting. The talk then turns to sleep. A snack may be eaten outside the sukka, but not even a brief nap, since Rava holds sleep has no small size.
sukkah/26.question: If a few bites of bread outside the sukka count as casual, why can no amount of sleep ever be brief enough to count the same way?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether 'casual' is a measurable quantity for every act — but the page names Rava's answer and the summary restates it.

answer.quote: Taking a brief nap outside the sukka is prohibited because there is no concept of substantial duration with regard to sleep
answer.explanation: Rava states outright that sleep has no minimum measure, which is precisely the distinction the question asks about, and the note's own summary already repeats it.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 26a: "Taking a brief nap outside the sukka is prohibited because there is no concept of substantial duration with regard to sleep". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what Rava answers on the page, and the summary itself already supplies that answer ('sleep has no small size'), so it reads as self-answering. Build the question on what remains hard after Rava: for instance, what Rava's position costs when set against Rav Ashi's decree 'lest he fall into a deep sleep,' or how sleep can be unmeasurable here yet measured at a hundred cubits for phylacteries. Keep the summary; it is faithful.

sukkah/27.summary: Rabbi Eliezer counts fourteen meals in the sukka, one each day and one each night, while the Rabbis say a person eats when hungry and only the first night is fixed. He also holds that one sukka must serve all seven days, telling King Agrippas's steward that his two sukkot, one in Tiberias and one in Tzippori, will not do. The page ends with Eliezer twice dodging a question about a sheet over sun-hot roofing, then leaving the sukka rather than answer.
sukkah/27.question: If Rabbi Eliezer would repeat only what he had heard from his teacher, what was Yoḥanan supposed to do while the sun crept toward his guest's feet?
gate: the question brings in "Yoḥanan", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: A sage who will only transmit what he heard from his teacher leaves his student with an unanswerable practical moment — silence as a kind of ruling.

answer.quote: Yoḥanan took a sheet and spread it over the sukka. Rabbi Eliezer slung his cloak over his shoulder behind him and emerged from the sukka
answer.explanation: The page narrates what Yoḥanan in fact did in the face of his teacher's silence, and later infers Eliezer's own view — "he also prohibits adding to a temporary tent" — but it never says what the host ought to have done while waiting.

sukkah/28.summary: People in the Upper Galilee ask Rabbi Eliezer thirty questions about the sukka, the branch-roofed hut lived in during the festival, and he answers only the twelve he heard from his teachers. Asked whether he ever says anything on his own, he replies that they have forced him to, then lists his habits: first into the study hall, last out, no idle talk, never a word he had not heard. His one original statement is that he has none.
sukkah/28.question: Does Rabbi Eliezer's account of his own conduct break his rule about never saying what he did not hear, or does a man's description of himself simply not count as Torah?

judge.reachNote: Whether a report of one's own life is transmitted Torah or original speech — i.e., what counts as 'saying a matter' at all.

answer.quote: Now you forced me to say a matter that I did not hear from my teachers, as I must describe my character traits
answer.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer himself concedes that describing his own conduct is a matter he did not hear from his teachers, said only under their pressure, but the page never rules on whether such self-description counts as teaching Torah on one's own.

sukkah/29.summary: Rain heavy enough to spoil a congealed dish of pounded grain releases a person from the sukka. Wind blew splinters from the roofing onto Rav Yosef's food, well short of that measure, and he told Abaye to carry his vessels indoors because a delicate man counts it as spoiled. The page then reads rain on Sukkot as rebuke: a master throwing a jug of water in the face of the servant who came to pour his wine.
sukkah/29.question: If rain on the sukka is the master saying he wants no service, why may the one who went indoors to sleep stay there until dawn?

judge.reachNote: Rain is read as divine dismissal, yet the halakha still measures the obligation by human comfort and burden — the question puts those two readings against each other.

answer.quote: one does not burden him to ascend back to the sukka once the rain ceases; rather, he may sleep in the house until it becomes light
answer.explanation: The baraita states the leniency and grounds it in not burdening the person, but it never reconciles that indulgence with the parable of the master rejecting the servant's service, so the tension the question raises remains open.

sukkah/30.summary: A stolen lulav, the palm branch taken up on Sukkot, is unfit because it is a mitzva, a commandment, carried out through a transgression, just as a lame animal is unfit for the altar. Rabbi Yoḥanan cites a parable: a king pays the toll at his own customs house so that travelers will learn not to evade it. Rav Huna then tells merchants to let gentiles cut the myrtle branches, so that despair and the sale turn a possibly stolen branch into the buyer's own property.
sukkah/30.question: If God hates robbery in a burnt-offering so that people will keep their distance from robbery altogether, what is left of that once an owner's despair and a purchase make the stolen myrtle branch lawfully yours?
gate: the question uses "burnt offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether the disqualification of a stolen mitzva object expresses a moral revulsion at robbery or only a formal ownership requirement that acquisition rules can satisfy.

answer.quote: The combination of owner's despair and change of possession will render the myrtle branches the property of the merchants, and it will not be a mitzva fulfilled by means of a transgression.
answer.explanation: The page states the legal mechanism by which the taint is removed, which bears on the question, but it never addresses how that squares with the parable's deterrent rationale, so the tension can still be raised honestly.

sukkah/31.summary: Rabbi Eliezer rules that a sukka built on stolen ground is unfit, while the Rabbis hold that land cannot be stolen, so the robber has merely borrowed it and still fulfills his obligation. Stolen wood is treated differently: the original owner gets only its monetary value, not the beam back. Then an old woman comes before Rav Naḥman claiming the Exilarch's servants built his sukka from her wood, and he applies exactly that rule to her.
sukkah/31.question: Rav Naḥman's ruling about the wood may be correct, but does calling her a screamer answer anything she actually said?

judge.reachNote: Whether a technically correct monetary ruling answers a claimant's grievance, or merely silences the person making it.

sukkah/32.summary: A palm branch split down its spine like a fork is unfit, and so is one curved forward like a sickle, though Rava holds that a backward curve is simply how palms grow. When the Gemara asks why the four species could not include the oleander, Abaye answers from a verse: the Torah's ways are pleasant, and a plant whose leaves pierce the hand is out. Yet a lulav from the palms of the Iron Mountain, said to mark Gehenna's entrance, is fit.
sukkah/32.question: If a branch is rejected merely because it can wound the hand, why does a palm growing at the smoking entrance of Gehenna draw no objection at all?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that fitness is judged by the object in the worshipper's hand, not by the reputation of the place it grew — even though provenance does disqualify an asheira branch.

sukkah/33.summary: A myrtle branch whose top has snapped off is unfit for the bundle of four species taken on Sukkot, but Ulla bar Ḥinnana says a berry growing into the gap restores it. Rabbi Yirmeya asks what happens if the break came before the festival and the berry during it: once an object is disqualified, is it disqualified for good? The Gemara drags in blood that a wind covered and then uncovered, and notices the rule bends toward leniency in one case and stringency in the other.
sukkah/33.question: If wind-covered blood can become an obligation again once it is exposed, why should a myrtle branch not become fit again once its gap is filled?

judge.reachNote: Whether a single principle — that disqualification is not permanent for mitzvot — must apply symmetrically whether it eases or burdens the person obligated.

answer.quote: Or, perhaps the tanna was uncertain, and therefore, when that ruling leads to stringency, we say that there is no disqualification with regard to mitzvot.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the blood-versus-myrtle comparison and answers that the principle may be applied only where it produces stringency (re-covering the blood) and not where it produces leniency (restoring the myrtle), which is exactly what the note asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 33a: "Or, perhaps the tanna was uncertain, and therefore, when that ruling leads to stringency, we say that there is no disqualification with regard to mitzvot.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks the very thing the page answers a few lines later: the Gemara distinguishes blood from myrtle by saying the rule may hold only where it leads to stringency, not leniency. Rewrite the question to start from that distinction — for instance, why a principle about the nature of disqualification should bend according to whether it makes life easier or harder, or why the dilemma is left standing once the distinction is offered. The summary already notices the leniency/stringency split, so the question should push past it rather than back into it.

sukkah/34.summary: An early teaching tells a willow from a tzaftzafa, a mountain look-alike, by sight: red stem, long leaf, smooth edge, against white stem, round leaf, serrated edge. Then Rav Ḥisda says the names swapped after the Temple was destroyed, so the branch now called tzaftzafa is the one the verse wants; the same reversal hit shofar and trumpet, large and small tables, and the city of Babylon. The physical signs hold still while the words slide off them.
sukkah/34.question: If someone asks which instrument to sound on Rosh HaShana and is told to use a trumpet, what happens the next time the names trade places?
gate: the question brings in "Rosh", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "HaShana", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a halakha stated in words rather than in the object is hostage to language drift, so rulings keyed to current names may need re-keying.

sukkah/35.summary: The Sages read "fruit of a beautiful tree" as a tree whose wood tastes like its fruit, which points to the etrog. Peppers fit that description too, and lose only on practicality, since one pepper is too small to notice and the verse asks for one fruit, not three. Later the page asks whether an etrog must be yours, and Beit Hillel accepts produce that may not have been tithed, since its owner could always declare his property ownerless and become a pauper who may eat it.
sukkah/35.question: If an etrog counts as yours because you could have given everything away, what is ownership doing in the requirement at all?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what 'lakhem' demands — whether ownership is an actual legal fact or merely a potential availability to the taker.

answer.quote: According to the one who said: An etrog of orla is unfit because it has no monetary value, second tithe in Jerusalem is consecrated property of God and has no monetary value
answer.explanation: The page shows ownership still doing real work elsewhere — second tithe in Jerusalem is disqualified for R. Meir precisely because it is God's, not the owner's — but it never explains why a merely hypothetical renunciation suffices for demai while actual lack of ownership disqualifies, so the question survives.

sukkah/36.summary: An etrog, the citron held on Sukkot, is unfit if it is peeled all over, and Ulla bar Ḥanina rules that a hole going clear through ruins it at any size. Rava asks what happens when the fruit dissolves inside, the way a lung can liquefy and the animal still be kosher. The sharpest exchange comes later: Rabbi Ḥanina would dip his etrog and eat part of it, while Rav held that one gnawed by mice fails.
sukkah/36.question: If the same bite leaves an etrog beautiful when a sage takes it and repulsive when a mouse does, where exactly does the flaw live?

judge.reachNote: Whether hadar is a property of the fruit's remaining substance or of the associations attached to what damaged it.

answer.quote: Mice are different, as they are repulsive. When mice pierce an etrog, what remains is antithetical to beauty. When a person bites an etrog, what remains can still be considered beautiful.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the contrast between Rabbi Ḥanina's bitten etrog and Rav's mouse-pierced one and resolves it by locating the flaw in the repulsiveness of mice rather than in the hole itself.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 36b: "Mice are different, as they are repulsive. When mice pierce an etrog, what remains is antithetical to beauty. When a person bites an etrog, what remains can still be considered beautiful.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in so many words: Rav distinguishes mice because 'they are repulsive,' so what remains is antithetical to beauty while a person's bite is not. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what it leaves unsettled — for instance that the very next lines record Rav saying the opposite about mice, or that Rabbi Ḥanina's practice is defended only for the later days while Rav insists beauty is required all seven. Alternatively ask about hadar elsewhere on the page, such as why a Cushite etrog is unfit in Babylonia but fit in Eretz Yisrael.

sukkah/37.summary: Rabba tells the men who bind the four species for the house of the Exilarch to leave a bare handgrip, so nothing sits between the hand and the lulav. Rava answers that decoration never interposes, and that holding a thing through something else still counts as holding; he hunts for proof in the red heifer rite, where a hyssop stalk too short to reach the water is lengthened with a string. That proof is rejected, then patched with ashes poured from a tube.
sukkah/37.question: If a string tied to the hyssop counts as part of the hyssop, why can't a cloth wrapped around a hand count as part of the hand?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: When does an intermediary become an extension of the object itself rather than a barrier — the page answers it with attachment.

answer.quote: since he attached the string to the hyssop, its legal status is like that of the hyssop itself. However, the legal status of the cloth is not like that of the lulav, since it is not attached
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the string/cloth disparity and resolves it by attachment: the string becomes part of the hyssop, while the cloth is unattached to the lulav.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 37a: "since he attached the string to the hyssop, its legal status is like that of the hyssop itself. However, the legal status of the cloth is not like that of the lulav, since it is not attached". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very objection the Gemara raises and answers in the next line — the string is attached to the hyssop, the cloth is not attached to the lulav — so it reads as answered before the reader finishes the page. Rewrite around something the page leaves standing: for instance Rabba's demand for a "complete taking" against Rava's claim that taking through another object counts, or why beautifying additions are exempt from interposition while a plain cloth is not. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

sukkah/38.summary: A man who cannot say hallel himself, the psalms of praise recited on festivals, has a Canaanite slave, a woman, or a minor say it while he repeats every word after them. The mishna adds that a curse should come to him for being so ignorant that he needs this. Later the page holds that hearing counts as reciting, proved from King Josiah, who only heard Shaphan read the scroll aloud and is credited with reading it.
sukkah/38.question: If Josiah gets credit for words Shaphan read aloud to him, why does the man whose wife recites the blessing for him get a curse?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that halakhic validity and religious dignity can come apart — but the page itself already separates them.

answer.quote: a woman may recite a blessing on behalf of her husband, but the Sages said: May a curse come to a man who, due to his ignorance, requires his wife
answer.explanation: The baraita states both halves at once — the substitute recitation is valid, and the curse is for the man's ignorance, not for any failure to fulfill the obligation.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 38a (Gemara on the hallel mishna): "a woman may recite a blessing on behalf of her husband, but the Sages said: May a curse come to a man who, due to his ignorance, requires his wife". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: the same baraita grants that a wife's blessing works for her husband and curses him "due to his ignorance," and the mishna likewise ties the curse to ignorance rather than to invalidity. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, why the page grades hearing-as-reciting so differently depending on whether the reciter is an adult male or a slave, woman, or minor, given that Josiah is credited for merely hearing Shaphan. Keep the summary as it is; it is accurate.

sukkah/39.summary: During the Sabbatical Year, when produce carries sanctity and may not be traded as merchandise, the mishna has a buyer purchase the lulav and receive the etrog thrown in as a gift. If the seller refuses to give it, Rav Huna says to fold the etrog's cost into the lulav's price, and the Gemara asks bluntly why the artifice: sanctified coins should not reach an am ha'aretz, someone careless about these laws, beyond three meals' worth. A lulav is dated by when it grew, an etrog by when it was picked.
sukkah/39.question: If both sides know the inflated price of the lulav is really payment for the etrog, what has actually changed besides the words?

judge.reachNote: Reaches toward legal formalism — whether the form of a transaction can change its status when both parties know its real intent — but the page already resolves it.

answer.quote: That is necessary because one may not transfer money used to purchase Sabbatical-Year produce to an am ha’aretz, lest he make improper use of money that has sanctity
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection ("why employ artifice in the transaction?") and answers that what changes is the money's status: payment for a lulav carries no Sabbatical-Year sanctity, so no sanctified coins reach the am ha'aretz.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 39a: "That is necessary because one may not transfer money used to purchase Sabbatical-Year produce to an am ha’aretz, lest he make improper use of money that has sanctity". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question ("why employ artifice in the transaction?"), and the page answers it two lines later: the inflated lulav price is not Sabbatical-Year money, so no sanctified coins pass to the am ha'aretz. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer — for instance, ask why the same reasoning that permits paying for the lulav does not permit the three-meals allowance to be stretched, or press on the unresolved tension the page ends with: the Gemara says an etrog follows its picking, yet cites a mishna where Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Eliezer both date it by ripening for the Sabbatical Year. The summary is sound and can largely stand.

sukkah/40.summary: Seventh-year produce, grown when fields lie fallow and carrying a special sanctity, may be eaten, but the argument here is over soaking flax in it and laundering clothes with it. One view reads "for food" narrowly; Rabbi Yosei reads "for you" as covering all bodily needs, admitting laundering because everyone needs clean clothes and barring medicine because only the ill need it. Wood is excluded too, since its benefit arrives later, in the charcoal.
sukkah/40.question: Why should laundering count as a real need because everyone has it, while a remedy does not because only the sick person does?

judge.reachNote: Whether "for you" means what serves human beings generally or what any given person happens to need, i.e. how a universal standard defines permitted use.

answer.quote: I include laundering, which applies equally to every person, as everyone needs clean clothes, and I exclude a remedy, which does not apply equally to every person
answer.explanation: The page states the criterion Rabbi Yosei uses — universality of the need — but does not justify why commonality, rather than bodily benefit as such, should be the measure, so the question can still be pressed.

sukkah/41.summary: Four sages travel by ship on Sukkot and only Rabban Gamliel has a lulav, the palm branch taken on the festival, bought for a thousand zuz, silver coins. The verse says take "for yourselves," so each one receives it as an outright gift, uses it, and hands it on, until Rabbi Akiva returns it. The returning is the point: a gift conditioned on return still counts as full ownership, yet Rava says failure to return unravels it retroactively.
sukkah/41.question: If the etrog was fully his while he held it, why should failing to hand it back later mean he never owned it at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether ownership under a condition is real ownership now or only provisional pending fulfillment, i.e. how a condition can reach backward in time.

answer.quote: Since he did not fulfill the condition, retroactively he never acquired the gift at all.
answer.explanation: The page states the retroactive unraveling and grounds it in the unfulfilled condition, but it does not explain how that squares with the interim gift being "a full-fledged gift," so the tension the question names remains askable.

sukkah/42.summary: The Sages line up a child's obligations by what he can already do: wave a lulav, the palm branch taken on Sukkot, wrap himself in a garment for ritual fringes, keep phylacteries clean, speak his first verse of Torah. Further down, a child who knows how to slaughter an animal may slaughter, though Rav Huna adds that an adult must stand over him. Rabbi Yehuda wants more than appetite for the Paschal lamb: hand the child a pebble and a nut, and watch which one he keeps.
sukkah/42.question: If a child's slaughtering only counts while an adult stands over him, whose competence is actually being certified?
gate: gloss "the Paschal lamb" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: It reaches the idea behind the graded list of childhood obligations: whether a stage-based qualification certifies real capacity or only supervised practice.

sukkah/43.summary: Taking the lulav, the bundle of palm, myrtle, willow and citron, is blocked on Shabbat out of fear someone will carry it through the street to an expert to learn the waving. The Gemara asks why the willow branch set at the altar on the seventh day escapes that worry, and answers that court agents prepare it in advance. Rav Yosef guesses the willow rite was standing branches upright, and a story about Boethusians hiding branches under stones refutes him.
sukkah/43.question: If those branches reached the altar only because ignorant bystanders pulled them out from under stones nobody else would touch on Shabbat, was the mitzva performed or salvaged?
gate: the question uses "mitzva", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether a mitzva rescued by people acting in ignorance of the rules is a performance or merely a salvage — does the means of arrival affect the deed.

answer.quote: Apparently, based on the conclusion of the incident, the mitzva of the willow branch is fulfilled by taking it, as it is referring to waving the willow branch
answer.explanation: The page treats the incident as a valid demonstration of how the mitzva is performed, which bears on whether it counted, but it never addresses whether the ignoramuses' handling of set-aside stones compromised the fulfillment.

sukkah/44.summary: A willow branch carried around the altar on Sukkot gets three different pedigrees here, and Rabbi Yoḥanan is quoted for all of them: a law handed to Moses at Sinai, an ordinance of the prophets Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, and a rule the Babylonian Sages simply made up. Rabbi Zeira presses the contradiction, and the answer offered is that the exile erased the practice and prophets restored it. Meanwhile Rav takes a willow branch, waves it, and recites no blessing.
sukkah/44.question: If the willow rite goes back to Sinai, why does Rav wave the branch and say nothing over it?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that the authority behind a practice (Sinai, prophetic ordinance, or mere custom) determines whether a blessing is recited over it — but the page states this answer outright.

answer.quote: This indicates that he holds that the mitzva of the willow branch is a custom of the prophets and is therefore performed without a blessing.
answer.explanation: The page itself explains the wave-without-blessing: the one who does so holds the willow is a custom of the prophets rather than a Sinaitic or binding ordinance, and Rav is said to hold the same.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 44b: "This indicates that he holds that the mitzva of the willow branch is a custom of the prophets and is therefore performed without a blessing.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in the very line the summary cites: waving without a blessing is taken as proof that the sage holds the willow rite to be a custom of the prophets, not a Sinaitic law. Build the question on what remains hard after that answer — for instance, how Rabbi Yoḥanan can hold the Temple willow is from Sinai while the outlying-areas willow is prophetic, or why a forgotten-and-reinstituted Sinaitic law would be treated as mere custom for blessings. Keep the summary's three pedigrees; it is accurate.

sukkah/45.summary: Willow branches gathered at Motza, a village below Jerusalem, were stood against the altar so their tops leaned a cubit over it, which only works if they rested on the altar's base. Leaving at the festival's end, the people called out to the altar itself, and Rabbi Elazar reports the words as "To the Lord and to you, altar." A baraita says pairing God's name with another entity gets a person uprooted from the world, so the Gemara re-punctuates the sentence into two separate praises.
sukkah/45.question: If the same words can be split into two praises instead of one, what settles which way the people saying them meant it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a formula's meaning is fixed by its words, by the speaker's intent, or by the reading the halakha needs it to have.

answer.quote: To the Lord, we acknowledge that He is our God, and to you, the altar, we give praise
answer.explanation: The Gemara supplies the re-reading that separates the two praises, but it never states what fixes which meaning the speakers intended, so the note's question survives it.

sukkah/46.summary: A baraita has the man who puts up a sukka recite the blessing of time, "Who has given us life," and then a second blessing when he first sits inside. Whether such blessings repeat is disputed: Rav Mari reports that Rava ruled one blessing a day for phylacteries, yet blessed again each time he came back from the bathroom and put them on. Later the page argues over whose etrogim may be eaten on the seventh day, and children's are the easy case.
sukkah/46.question: If a child's etrog can be eaten freely because a child owes nothing by Torah law, why does Rabbi Zeira treat a promise made to that same child as binding?
gate: the question brings in "Zeira", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a child's exemption from obligation does not license adults to treat him casually, but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: because he thereby comes to teach him about lying, as it is stated: “They have taught their tongues to speak lies”
answer.explanation: The page itself supplies Rabbi Zeira's rationale: the duty is not about the child's own legal obligation but about not training him to break his word, which the page restates as "One must not accustom a child to fail to honor commitments."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 46b: "because he thereby comes to teach him about lying, as it is stated: “They have taught their tongues to speak lies”". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: the page says the promise matters because the adult "comes to teach him about lying," not because the child is obligated. Rewrite the question so it starts from that stated reason and asks what still presses, or pick a genuinely unresolved thread on the page, such as why a sukka stays forbidden into the eighth day through a doubtful twilight while a used etrog does not. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

sukkah/47.summary: Outside Eretz Yisrael, where the calendar was uncertain, the eighth day might actually be the seventh day of Sukkot, so does one sit in the sukka, and does one bless? The ruling is to sit and say nothing, and the proof offered is that Rav Huna bar Bizna and the great scholars, just in from herding flocks and sitting in a sukka for the first time that festival, still did not bless. Then the bulls: thirteen down to seven, then one.
sukkah/47.question: What is a person doing when he sits in the sukka on the eighth day but refuses to say the blessing for sitting in it?

judge.reachNote: Acting under calendrical doubt: one performs the mitzva in case it is owed, but withholds the declaration that would assert it is owed.

answer.quote: the halakha is that we reside in the sukka on the eighth day, with regard to which there is uncertainty that it might be the seventh day, but we do not recite the blessing
answer.explanation: The page states the ruling and its ground — the day's doubtful status — but never spells out what the split act of sitting without blessing amounts to, so a reader can still ask honestly.

sukkah/48.summary: A golden jug of water, drawn from the Siloam pool, was carried through the Water Gate and poured into one of two basins beside the altar. The wine basin had a broad hole and the water basin a thin one, so that two liquids of different thickness would finish draining at the same moment. When one Sadducee priest poured the water on his feet, the crowd pelted him with etrogim, chipping the altar's horn, which was then patched with a fistful of salt for appearance only.
sukkah/48.question: If the fistful of salt did nothing to make the altar fit again, who was the patch for?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that an act can serve honor and appearance rather than ritual fitness — but the page states that answer in so many words.

answer.quote: not because it rendered the altar fit for the Temple service, but in deference to the altar, so that the altar would not be seen in its damaged state
answer.explanation: The page states explicitly that the salt patch served the altar's dignity, so it would not appear damaged — which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 48b: "not because it rendered the altar fit for the Temple service, but in deference to the altar, so that the altar would not be seen in its damaged state". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim on the daf: the patch was made "in deference to the altar, so that the altar would not be seen in its damaged state." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer and asks what remains hard, for instance why the altar's honor is served by a covering everyone knows changes nothing about its fitness, or why deference here means hiding the damage rather than repairing it. Alternatively build the question on an unanswered thread on this page, such as why the lamp or the reduced roofing distinguishes the eighth day differently inside and outside Eretz Yisrael.

sukkah/49.summary: The altar has hidden drainpipes, the shittin, and Rabbi Yoḥanan says they were dug at Creation, running down to the depths to swallow the wine poured on the altar. Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok reports instead that the wine congealed in a gap beside the ramp, and young priests climbed down there once in seventy years to collect it. Reish Lakish has the pipes plugged so the wine pools, since the verse calls the libation strong drink.
sukkah/49.question: If matters of Torah are best kept concealed, like a thigh under clothes, how can Torah studied in order to teach it to others be the Torah of kindness?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between Torah as something concealed and modest and Torah as something given away to others.

sukkah/50.summary: Water drawn for the libation poured on the altar during Sukkot is disqualified if it was left uncovered overnight, and the Gemara asks why it cannot simply be strained. Rabbi Neḥemya says snake venom floats like a sponge and stays in the upper vessel, but the answer is that what a person may drink is not what one hands the governor. The mishna's flute at the water drawing celebration then splits the Sages: is the core of song the instruments or the mouth?
sukkah/50.question: If the water drawing is a significant mitzva going back to the six days of Creation, why is its music treated as mere rejoicing that yields to Shabbat?
gate: the question brings in "Creation", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "mitzva", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: What makes a practice override Shabbat is its status as Temple service, not its antiquity or its significance as a mitzva.

answer.quote: with regard to the song of the Drawing of the Water, everyone agrees that it is rejoicing and not a component of the Temple service; therefore it does not override Shabbat
answer.explanation: The page states the criterion — only what is a component of the Temple service overrides Shabbat — but never addresses why the celebration's ḥashuva status and Creation-era origin do not confer that standing, so the tension the question raises can still be asked.

sukkah/51.summary: At the close of the first festival day, priests and Levites went down to the Women's Courtyard, lit golden candelabra with wicks torn from worn-out priestly trousers, and the pious juggled flaming torches while Levites played lyres and harps. The mishna calls the arrangement a significant repair; the Gemara says it was a balcony, added so women sat above and men below after repeated mingling. Then it objects: the Temple's plans came in writing by divine inspiration, so how could sages alter the building?
sukkah/51.question: If the Temple's layout was handed down in writing from God's hand, what makes a crowd's behavior in the courtyard reason enough to build a balcony into it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a divinely dictated structure can be reshaped in response to human conduct — revealed plan versus the needs of the people inside it.

answer.quote: Rav said: They found a verse, and interpreted it homiletically and acted accordingly:
answer.explanation: The page signals that the Sages grounded the change in a homiletical reading of a verse, but the verse and its interpretation are not given here, so the question of what justifies altering a divinely written plan is only gestured at.

sukkah/52.summary: At the end of days, one view here says, God slaughters the evil inclination in front of everyone: the righteous see a mountain they somehow climbed, the wicked see a single hair they could not cross, and both weep. The same run of material sends Abaye trailing a man and a woman for three parasangs, roughly nine miles, through a marsh, certain they meant to sin; they parted innocently. He admits he could not have held out, and an Elder tells him greater people have greater inclinations.
sukkah/52.question: Is Abaye's discovery about himself really a mark of his greatness, as the Elder consoles him, or just an ordinary man startled by his own appetite?

judge.reachNote: Whether awareness of one's own susceptibility is evidence of spiritual stature or just ordinary appetite seen clearly for the first time.

answer.quote: Therefore, Abaye should not feel regret, as his realization is a consequence of his greatness.
answer.explanation: The Elder's teaching, as glossed on the page, explicitly says Abaye's self-discovery follows from his greatness, though the question presses on whether that consolation is true rather than merely comforting.

sukkah/53.summary: Hillel, rejoicing at the Temple's water-drawing celebration, says his feet carry him to the place he loves. Elsewhere he sees a skull floating on the water and tells it that it drowned others, was drowned, and its drowners will drown in turn. Then Solomon, finding the Angel of Death sad over two of his scribes, hides them in Luz, a town the angel cannot enter, and they die on arrival, exactly where he had been sent to collect them.
sukkah/53.question: If the scribes died only because Solomon shipped them off to Luz, was he rescuing them or delivering them?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a person's own evasive action is the very instrument of the decree — free will as the courier of fate.

answer.quote: In the place that they asked me to take them, there you sent them.
answer.explanation: The Angel of Death's reply, followed by Solomon's own exclamation that a person's feet lead him to where he is in demand, states outright that Solomon's attempted rescue was in fact the delivery.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 53a: "In the place that they asked me to take them, there you sent them.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: the Angel says "there you sent them" and Solomon himself concludes that a man's feet lead him to where he is in demand. Write a question that starts from that resolution rather than asking what the story already settles — for instance, why Solomon, who could command demons and interrogate the Angel of Death, still could not see that Luz was the destination, or what it means that the Gemara attaches this same maxim to Hillel's "to the place that I love, there my feet take me," where the walking is chosen rather than fated.

sukkah/54.summary: The mishna caps the Temple's trumpet blasts at forty-eight in one day, and the Gemara spends the page trying to break that ceiling. Passover eve with its three shifts of lamb slaughter, Rosh HaShana falling on Shabbat, each candidate is counted up and then trimmed back, sometimes by dropping the three blasts that merely signaled the opening of the gates. Rava swats one attempt aside as milling without watching what comes out.
sukkah/54.question: If the mishna picked Shabbat eve during Sukkot because that one case quietly settles two disputes about when the trumpets sounded, is forty-eight a tally or an argument in disguise?
gate: the question brings in "Sukkot", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a mishna's number is a record of practice or a vehicle chosen to decide disputes — the tanna's count as argument.

answer.quote: the tanna held that the case of Shabbat eve during the Festival is necessary in order to teach that the halakha is in accordance
answer.explanation: The page does state that the tanna chose Shabbat eve during Sukkot for its didactic value (and Rava adds "You would learn two matters from that case"), but it never settles whether forty-eight functions as a real maximum or as a polemical figure, and the counter-consideration "he is teaching matters that occur every year" pulls the other way.

sukkah/55.summary: A mishna counts out the Sukkot offerings bull by bull and parcels them among the twenty-four priestly watches, the groups of priests who rotate through Temple service, so that no watch handles bulls two days running. The total comes to seventy bulls across seven days, plus a single bull on the Eighth Day of Assembly. Rabbi Elazar reads the seventy as the seventy nations of the world, and Rabbi Yoḥanan mourns a loss the nations never noticed.
sukkah/55.question: If the nations never knew that seventy bulls were being offered on their behalf, what was the atonement doing for them while it lasted?

judge.reachNote: Whether atonement can be effective for those who neither know of nor request it — a benefit conferred on the unaware.

answer.quote: They correspond to the seventy nations of the world, and are brought to atone for their sins and to hasten world peace.
answer.explanation: The page states what the bulls accomplished for the nations — atonement for their sins and hastening world peace — but never addresses whether the nations' ignorance affected that, so the question can still be honestly asked.

sukkah/56.summary: Rav and Rabba bar bar Ḥana argue over which blessing comes first on the festival's opening night: the one for sitting in the sukka, or the one for reaching this season. The Gemara tests it against a priest handing out Temple bread on Shavuot, who names the ordinary shewbread before the day's own two loaves, and Abba Shaul reverses the order. The tractate ends with the watch of Bilga, penalized forever, either for Miriam kicking the altar or for arriving late.
sukkah/56.question: If Miriam learned her contempt for the altar at her parents' table, what did every other priest in the Bilga watch do to have his slaughtering ring nailed shut permanently?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of collective punishment — whether a household's private contempt can bind an entire priestly watch — but the Gemara asks and answers this very point.

answer.quote: And due to Miriam’s father and mother, do we penalize an entire watch? Abaye said: Woe unto the wicked, woe unto his neighbor.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the note's objection about punishing the whole watch and answers that proximity to the wicked itself brings woe, so no individual act by the other priests is required.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sukkah 56b: "And due to Miriam’s father and mother, do we penalize an entire watch? Abaye said: Woe unto the wicked, woe unto his neighbor.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, answered on the same page by Abaye's "Woe unto the wicked, woe unto his neighbor," so a reader reaching the end would find it already settled. Rewrite around something the page leaves open — for instance why two entirely different reasons for Bilga's penalty are preserved side by side, or why the frequent blessing loses to the day's blessing in the final ruling after the mishna's shewbread proof seemed conclusive against Rav. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

beitzah/2.summary: Beit Shammai say an egg laid on a Festival may be eaten that same day; Beit Hillel say it may not. Rav Naḥman reads the ban as muktze, the rule against handling things set aside before the day began, which forces him to explain why the same editor ruled leniently about bones on Shabbat and strictly about chopping wood on a Festival: the severe day needs no extra fence, the lighter one does. Rabba drops muktze and says the egg was already finished inside the hen yesterday.
beitzah/2.question: If a Festival gets the stricter ruling because people might treat it lightly, is the egg being judged, or the people?

beitzah/3.summary: An egg laid on a Festival is forbidden, and the sages keep proposing different reasons why. Rav Yosef likens it to fruit that drops from a tree, since both are food; Rabbi Yitzhak likens it to juice seeping from fruit, since an egg sits enclosed in a hen as juice sits enclosed in fruit. Later a baraita rules that one doubtful egg mixed into a thousand permitted eggs forbids them all.
beitzah/3.question: If the egg is off limits only because someone might climb a tree or squeeze a grape, why should one doubtful egg spoil a thousand good ones?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real tension between a merely rabbinic decree and stringent treatment of doubt, but the page states that tension and resolves it.

answer.quote: it is an object whose prohibition is temporary, as the egg will be permitted on the following day, and the principle is: Any object whose prohibition is temporary is not nullified
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely this objection — that on Rav Yosef's and Rabbi Yitzḥak's reasons the doubt is only rabbinic and should be lenient — and answers it, both by the rule that a temporary prohibition is never nullified and by reassigning the latter clause to an uncertain tereifa prohibited by Torah law.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 3b: "it is an object whose prohibition is temporary, as the egg will be permitted on the following day, and the principle is: Any object whose prohibition is temporary is not nullified". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection on 3b, and the page answers it twice — with the rule that a temporary prohibition is not nullified, and by rereading the clause as an uncertain tereifa. Write a question that starts after those answers: for instance, why a prohibition that will lapse tomorrow is treated as more unshakable than a permanent one, or what it means that an egg counts as 'significant' only if eggs are always sold by unit. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

beitzah/4.summary: Rav Adda bar Ahava's host had eggs laid on a Festival that fell on a Friday, and asked whether he could roast them that day to eat on Shabbat. Rav Adda says even the lenient view permits only swallowing such an egg raw the next day; on the day it was laid it may not even prop up a bed leg. Rav Pappa, asked a similar question, sent the man off until morning, because Festival wine kept sages from public rulings, and then admitted he would have ruled wrongly.
beitzah/4.question: If Rav Pappa's answer on the Festival would have been wrong and his answer the next morning right, what was the man supposed to do with his eggs overnight?

judge.reachNote: The cost of a sage's self-imposed silence falls on the questioner, whose eggs sit in limbo while the ruling waits for a clear head.

answer.quote: However, Rava said: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav with regard to these three issues
answer.explanation: The page eventually reveals that the correct ruling was that the eggs are prohibited, so the overnight delay cost the man nothing, though the page never addresses what he should do in the interim.

beitzah/5.summary: Rabba holds that once Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai restored all-day acceptance of witnesses for the new moon, an egg laid on the first day of Rosh HaShana may be eaten on the second. Rav Yosef answers that a ban fixed by a vote of the Sanhedrin needs another vote to lift it, even when its reason is gone, and points to a grapevine of Rabbi Eliezer whose fruit had to be carried to Jerusalem. Abaye objects that nobody ever voted on eggs.
beitzah/5.question: If the egg's status only ever trailed the rule about when witnesses could testify, what would a court even be voting to undo?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether a prohibition that is merely a by-product of another rule has any independent standing that a vote could attach to or release.

answer.quote: When they took a vote, it was with regard to testimony to determine the start of the month; they did not take a vote to annul the prohibition of an egg.
answer.explanation: The Gemara says the needed vote would be one specifically annulling the egg prohibition rather than the testimony ordinance, which bears on the question but does not resolve Abaye's point that the egg was never independently voted on — the Gemara instead concedes it and offers Rav Adda, Rav Shalman, and Rava's alternative reasons.

beitzah/6.summary: Rav rules that a chick which hatched on a Festival may not be eaten, since it was muktze, set aside and unusable when the day began. Shmuel counters that hatching is exactly what makes the chick fit to slaughter, so it is permitted. Pressed about a calf born to a tereifa, a cow doomed to die within a year, Rav went silent; Rabba answers for him that such a calf always counted as food for dogs.
beitzah/6.question: If a calf inside a doomed cow escapes being set aside because someone might throw it to dogs, whose mind was actually on that calf before the Festival began?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that muktze depends on whose intention rests on the item — but the page states that intention explicitly a few lines later.

answer.quote: something that is prepared for dogs is also considered fit and prepared for humans, as a person’s mind is on anything fit to be eaten by him
answer.explanation: Abaye's challenge is answered by exactly this point: the owner's own mind is on the calf, since food fit for dogs is still edible for him, and indeed "one has in mind the possibility that he might eat the calf of a cow that is a tereifa once it is born."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 6b: "something that is prepared for dogs is also considered fit and prepared for humans, as a person’s mind is on anything fit to be eaten by him". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered on the very next stretch of the page, where the Gemara says a person's mind is on anything fit for him to eat, so he has in mind eating the tereifa's calf once born. Build the new question on what remains hard after that answer — for instance, why an animal fit for humans that dies is not thereby prepared for dogs while the reverse holds, or what work "a person's mind" is doing when no actual owner thought about the unborn calf. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

beitzah/7.summary: Someone checks a hen's nest the day before a Festival, finds nothing, and finds an egg there the next morning; whether he may eat it depends on when it was laid. The workaround: eggs conceived with a rooster come by day, so the egg predates the Festival. Rav Mari searched sixty houses, found no rooster, and permitted the egg anyway, assuming one stood somewhere beyond. Hens cross bridges to roosters, though not ropes, usually.
beitzah/7.question: If Rav Mari was going to permit the egg whether or not he found a rooster, what was the search through sixty houses for?

judge.reachNote: When a presumption is strong enough to override an actual failed search, what work is the inquiry still doing?

answer.quote: where the hen can hear its voice by day, when sounds cannot be heard as easily as at night
answer.explanation: The page supplies the criterion of proximity that a search would be testing (a rooster within hearing range, with rivers and rope bridges as limits), but it never states why Rav Mari searched sixty houses and then permitted the egg despite finding nothing.

beitzah/8.summary: Slaughter a bird on a Festival and its blood must be covered with earth or ash prepared before the Festival began. The hard case is a koy, a kosher animal with traits of both domesticated and undomesticated kinds, where nobody knows whether covering is required at all. Rava draws the line by intention: earth brought in to cover a baby's excrement may later cover a bird's blood, but earth brought in for the bird may not cover excrement.
beitzah/8.question: If a man may be told on a weekday to go to the trouble of covering a koy's blood, why does giving him that same instruction on a Festival become the problem?

judge.reachNote: A ruling issued under uncertainty can itself be read as a ruling of certainty, and thus mislead about the fats.

answer.quote: On a Festival, however, if there is uncertainty, would the Sages say to him: Go and take the trouble and cover it?
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that instructing him on a Festival would indicate that a koy is definitely an undomesticated animal, whereas on a weekday the instruction carries no such implication.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 8b: "On a Festival, however, if there is uncertainty, would the Sages say to him: Go and take the trouble and cover it?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 8b, which says that a Festival instruction to cover would signal the koy is definitely undomesticated. Read to the end of the sugya and ask about something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why the dunghill and consulting-a-Sage objections do not equally undo the weekday leniency, or why Rami bar Rav Yeiva's appearance-based reason is offered at all after Rava's intention rule. Keep the summary as is.

beitzah/9.summary: Beit Shammai say a ladder used for reaching doves may not be carried from one dovecote to another on a Festival, while Beit Hillel permit it. The worry is not the carrying but the look of it, since a passerby may assume the man is off to plaster his roof. From there the argument widens to wet clothes spread in the sun, and to Rav's claim that an act forbidden for how it looks stays forbidden in the innermost chamber.
beitzah/9.question: If the whole concern is what a passerby might think, what is left of that concern in a room where no passerby can see?

judge.reachNote: Whether a decree grounded in how an act looks has any force where there is no one to look — i.e., whether such rules protect appearances or the actor himself.

answer.quote: Wherever the Sages prohibited an action due to the appearance of prohibition, even if one performs the act in his innermost chamber, where no one will see it, it is prohibited
answer.explanation: The page raises the note's very question and reports Rav's ruling that the prohibition survives in private, but it resolves the matter only by calling it a dispute between tanna'im and never explains what concern remains where nobody can see.

beitzah/10.summary: Doves in a dovecote may not be handled on a Festival unless they were prepared the day before, and Beit Hillel hold that standing there the previous evening and saying "I will take this one and that one" is enough. The mishna then tests those words against the next morning: black fledglings designated, white ones found; three designated, two found. Rava says the naming exists to keep a person from lifting and dropping one bird after another, handling birds he will not use.
beitzah/10.question: If the birds a person named the night before turn out thin in the morning, is he bound to them anyway, or free to leave them and go without the meal?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prior verbal designation binds a person to birds that disappoint him, weighing muktze against Festival joy.

answer.quote: Since he knows that he may not alter his decision on the Festival itself even if he does not like the ones he chose, he definitively decides
answer.explanation: The Gemara states explicitly that a person who designated birds the day before may not change his mind on the Festival even if the chosen birds displease him, and 10b adds the worry that if all turn out thin he will leave them and neglect the Festival rejoicing.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 10a: "Since he knows that he may not alter his decision on the Festival itself even if he does not like the ones he chose, he definitively decides". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words at the end of 10a and the top of 10b: he may not alter his decision even if he dislikes the birds, and the Gemara itself raises the case where all turn out thin and he abandons them, neglecting Festival joy. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than asking for it. For instance, press on why the fear of handling a muktze bird outweighs the risk that he skips the meal entirely, or why saying the words the night before is treated as more binding than handling the birds.

beitzah/11.summary: An animal slaughtered on a Festival leaves a hide and fats that will spoil, and the page argues over how much handling the day allows. Ulla collects three cases where the Sages permitted an unwanted result to encourage a wanted start: spreading a fresh hide for treaders, reopening shop shutters, a priest replacing his hand bandage after Temple service. Rav Mattana then refuses that same logic for airing out fats, since a man might reason himself into salting them.
beitzah/11.question: If the fear about airing out fats is that a man will talk himself step by step into salting them, what is Rav Adda bar Ahava doing when he salts one bone, says he prefers another, and works through all his meat?
gate: the question brings in "Adda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Ahava", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Why a man's chain of reasoning is feared as a slide into prohibited labor in one case yet deployed as a legitimate device in another.

beitzah/12.summary: Beit Shammai say a minor child, a lulav (the palm branch bundle taken on Sukkot), and a Torah scroll may not be carried into the street on a Festival, since none of them is food; Beit Hillel permit it. The Gemara reads Beit Hillel as holding that once carrying was allowed for cooking, it is allowed for anything people benefit from. Rav Yosef finds the limit: nobody argues about carrying stones.
beitzah/12.question: If the permission to carry food spills over onto a child and a Torah scroll, what exactly stops it before it reaches a stone?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the principle of 'since it was permitted for food, it is permitted generally' and asks where that permission's boundary lies.

answer.quote: from the fact that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel do not disagree with regard to stones but concerning objects that serve some sort of purpose
answer.explanation: Rav Yosef's objection contrasts stones with purposeful objects, and the earlier line limits the spillover to "any purpose that benefits people, whether directly or indirectly," which bears on the boundary but is offered as proof that carrying is prohibited on a Festival rather than as a stated rule of what halts the extension.

beitzah/13.summary: Someone peeling raw barley may eat the grains one at a time without tithing, but a handful gathered in the palm counts as a meal and owes tithes, the portions due priests and Levites. Rabbi Elazar applies the same line to threshing on Shabbat, yet Rav's wife peeled barley for him by the cupful. Rav Abba bar Memel objects that Shabbat should never be lighter than tithes; the reply is that Shabbat forbids only planned, constructive labor.
beitzah/13.question: If the same handful of peeled barley is a finished job when tithes are at stake and no job at all when Shabbat is, what counts as finishing something?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: Completion of a labor may be defined by the purpose of the law — readiness for a meal versus purposeful creative act — not by the physical act itself.

answer.quote: The Torah prohibited only planned, constructive labor on Shabbat, the type of work that involves the creation of something new
answer.explanation: The Gemara resolves the asymmetry by saying Shabbat measures creative intent rather than completion of processing, which bears directly on the question though it does not define 'finishing' for tithes.

beitzah/14.summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue over pounding salt and spices on a Festival, and the Gemara asks why salt always needs an unusual method. Two reasons compete: salt keeps overnight so you should have prepared it, or spices lose flavor and cannot be readied in advance, with saffron as the test case. Then detection: Rav Sheshet judges a pestle's clear sound as salt, and Rav Pappi refuses porridge because the husks looked freshly bright.
beitzah/14.question: If a small mortar is allowed in Babylonia only because there are no servants around to be lax with it, whose conduct is the restriction in Eretz Yisrael really governing?
gate: the question brings in "Babylonia", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Eretz", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yisrael", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: A householder's own permitted act can be forbidden because of how others in his household would abuse it.

answer.quote: Since servants might treat the prohibition lightly, by using a large mortar and pestle and claiming they had used only a small one, they are prohibited from pounding in all cases
answer.explanation: Rava's resolution states outright that the Eretz Yisrael restriction is aimed at servants' laxity, and the follow-up about Mar Shmuel adds that the householder must therefore ban all grinding in his house.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 14b: "Since servants might treat the prohibition lightly, by using a large mortar and pestle and claiming they had used only a small one, they are prohibited from pounding in all cases". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question just restates Rava's own answer, which names servants' laxity as the reason, so a reader who finished the passage would not still be asking it. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer and presses on what remains hard — for instance, why Mar Shmuel's guest refuses the porridge even though the household's own conduct was supposedly already restricted, or why suspicion of servants silences a permission rather than the servants themselves. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

beitzah/15.summary: When a Festival falls on a Friday, one may cook for the Festival itself but not with the aim of stocking the Shabbat that follows, unless a dish was set aside beforehand as an eiruv tavshilin, a joining of cooked foods. The page then turns to Rabbi Eliezer, who taught all Festival day and ranked each group that walked out by the size of the wine containers waiting at home, from huge jugs down to cups. Rabbi Yehoshua disagrees: split the day.
beitzah/15.question: If Rabbi Eliezer held that physical festival joy is merely optional, why did he send the students who stayed to the end home with "eat the fat and drink the sweet"?

judge.reachNote: Whether festival eating is a rival to Torah or its permitted complement once the day's study is done.

beitzah/16.summary: A cooked dish set aside before a Festival, an eiruv tavshilin, lets a person cook on the Festival for the Shabbat that follows. The Gemara shrinks it: lentils left at the bottom of a pot or fat scraped off a knife will count, so long as there is an olive-bulk, roughly the volume of an olive. One such portion covers a hundred people, and Shmuel's father made one for all of Neharde'a, but Mar Shmuel cut off a blind scholar who had forgotten two years running.
beitzah/16.question: If one cooked dish can cover a whole city of people who never asked for it, what makes the man who keeps forgetting the one person left out?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether an eiruv's reach depends on the maker's intent rather than the beneficiary's need, and whether repeated neglect forfeits communal generosity — but the page says this in so many words.

beitzah/17.summary: A man forgot to set aside an eiruv tavshilin, the dish prepared before a Festival that lets him cook on the Festival for the Shabbat that follows. The Gemara rules his flour is barred along with him, so he must hand it to neighbors who bake for him. Then it asks whether food he cooks anyway may be eaten, knocks down every proof offered, including cooking extra under pretense of guests, and leaves the question open.
beitzah/17.question: Why are the Sages harsher on the man who cooks a full pot and calls it guests than on the man who openly cooks for Shabbat with no eiruv at all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that concealed evasion of a rule corrodes the rule more than open violation — but the page states exactly this.

answer.quote: the Sages were more stringent with regard to one who employs artifice than with regard to one who intentionally cooks on a Festival for Shabbat
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi states the distinction and then gives the reason: the deliberate sinner knows he sinned and may repent, while the one using artifice thinks he acts permissibly and others will emulate him.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 17b: "the Sages were more stringent with regard to one who employs artifice than with regard to one who intentionally cooks on a Festival for Shabbat". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words by Rav Ashi on 17b, who says artifice is treated more stringently because the deliberate transgressor knows his sin and may repent while the schemer thinks himself permitted and will be copied. Write a question that starts after that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, why the Gemara still accepts an eiruv that is purely symbolic, or why the man who cooks extra 'for guests' is punished by having his food forbidden while the flour of the man with no eiruv can simply be transferred to neighbors. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

beitzah/18.summary: Rabba says a vessel may not be dipped in a ritual bath on Shabbat in case its owner carries it four cubits through the public domain, and Abaye spends the page hunting cases that break the decree: a menstruating woman with no clean clothes, a bucket drawn from a spring. Rav Yosef, Rav Beivai and Rava each offer a different reason instead. Rava's, that purifying a vessel looks like repairing it, forces the claim that a person in a murky pool just looks hot.
beitzah/18.question: If immersing a person is permitted only because onlookers might think he is cooling off, why does that permission survive on Yom Kippur, when no one bathes for pleasure and everyone can see exactly what he is doing?
gate: the question brings in "Yom", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Kippur", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — a permission built on how an act looks, once the look changes — but the page states and defends exactly that answer via the principle of 'since'.

answer.quote: Rather, since it is permitted on Shabbat, it is also permitted on Yom Kippur. The Sages did not issue decrees with regard to Yom Kippur that would make it more stringent than Shabbat.
answer.explanation: Rava explicitly answers the Yom Kippur objection with the principle of "since": what is permitted on Shabbat carries over to Yom Kippur even though the purifying intent is evident there.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 18b: "Rather, since it is permitted on Shabbat, it is also permitted on Yom Kippur. The Sages did not issue decrees with regard to Yom Kippur that would make it more stringent than Shabbat.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered outright a few lines later: Rava invokes the principle of "since" — permitted on Shabbat, therefore permitted on Yom Kippur — and the Gemara then tests whether Rava really holds that principle. Rewrite the question to start from that answer, for instance asking what it means that a leniency granted for how an act appears can be carried into a day where it plainly does not appear that way, or why the vinegar sugya makes the Gemara doubt Rava holds 'since' at all.

beitzah/19.summary: A man runs at twilight, an impure vessel in his hands, trying to reach the ritual bath before the Festival starts. The Sages of the school of Rav read his running as proof he knows the vessel stays impure until the stars come out; Rabbi Shimon Shezuri says he may simply be late from work and know nothing of the sort. Rava recasts the dispute around a man who asks whether a creeping animal smaller than a lentil defiles at all.
beitzah/19.question: If a man does not know that a creeping animal smaller than a lentil leaves his vessel clean, is that fair grounds to assume he also does not know the rule about waiting for sunset?

judge.reachNote: Whether ignorance of one obscure halakha licenses the presumption of ignorance about a basic, Torah-explicit one.

answer.quote: it is only this halakha with regard to the size of a creeping animal that he does not know, but the requirement of sunset he does know, as it is stated explicitly in the Torah
answer.explanation: The Gemara states the Rabbis' explicit rejection of exactly this inference — ignorance of the lentil-bulk rule does not imply ignorance of sunset, since sunset is written in the Torah — alongside Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's reason for drawing it.

summaryProblems.claim: The Sages of the school of Rav themselves read the running as proof the man knows the vessel requires sunset.
summaryProblems.pageSays: This Sage, i.e., the Rabbis, holds that the fact that he is running along indicates that he knows that the vessel requires sunset.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Beitzah 19a: "it is only this halakha with regard to the size of a creeping animal that he does not know, but the requirement of sunset he does know, as it is stated explicitly in the Torah". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The Sages of the school of Rav themselves read the running as proof the man knows the vessel requires sunset.", but the page says "This Sage, i.e., the Rabbis, holds that the fact that he is running along indicates that he knows that the vessel requires sunset.". Say what the page says. The question simply restates the two sides of a dispute the page already spells out, including the Rabbis' answer that sunset is known because it is written explicitly in the Torah. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer and presses on what it leaves unsettled — for instance why Rava rejects the school of Rav's framing in favor of testing what the man knows, or what it means to measure a person's knowledge by whether a rule appears in the verse. Also fix the attribution: the running case is the Rabbis' position as reported by the school of Rav, not the school of Rav's own view.

beitzah/20.summary: Hillel brought a burnt-offering into the Temple courtyard on a Festival so he could place his hands on its head, which Beit Shammai held was forbidden that day. Cornered by Shammai's students, he told them it was a female peace-offering and swung its tail so they could not check, and they left. The concealment nearly cost his school the ruling, until Bava ben Buta filled the courtyard with high-quality sheep from Kedar for anyone who wished to place hands.
beitzah/20.question: If Hillel's answer for the sake of peace is what nearly settled the halakha against his own school, who did that peace serve?
gate: gloss "burnt-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "peace-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question uses "halakha", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a concession made to avoid strife can itself distort the law it was meant to protect, so peace bought by concealment may serve no one.

beitzah/21.summary: Rav Avya asks Rav Huna whether an animal owned half by a gentile and half by a Jew may be slaughtered on a Festival; Rav Huna says yes, then dodges the follow-up question by pointing at a bird in the sky. The reason surfaces later: you cannot get an olive-bulk of meat without killing the whole animal, while dough can simply be divided before baking. The same logic then meets soldiers demanding bread.
beitzah/21.question: If a search party was about to pillage the whole city, what loss did Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava think outweighed what that slaughtered calf saved?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
