judge.reachNote: The idea is whether exemption tracks genuine compulsion or mere inability — but the page settles it in the final line the note's question asks about.

answer.quote: Rabban Gamliel did not exempt those in the city who do not come to the synagogue, as they are able to prepare their prayers and pray by themselves.
answer.explanation: The closing resolution states exactly why the field worker is covered and the townsman is not: the townsman could have prepared and prayed on his own, while the field worker was prevented by circumstances beyond his control.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Rosh Hashanah 35a: "Rabban Gamliel did not exempt those in the city who do not come to the synagogue, as they are able to prepare their prayers and pray by themselves.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim in the page's final resolution, which explains that field workers are exempted because they are prevented by work beyond their control while townspeople can prepare and pray themselves. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than asking for it. A live angle: the baraita about the Priestly Blessing says those behind the priests are excluded but those in the fields are included — so distance is forgiven while a small failure of effort is not; ask what that ranking of effort over proximity implies about who prayer is supposed to reach.

taanit/2.summary: Taanit opens with an argument about when to begin inserting the words "He makes the wind blow and rain fall" into the Amida, the standing prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua objects that rain during Sukkot is a curse, since it drives people out of their sukkot; Rabbi Eliezer answers that mentioning rain is not the same as requesting it, just as the resurrection of the dead is mentioned all year. Yehoshua's reply turns on timing: any day suits resurrection, but rain after Nisan ruins the wheat harvest.
taanit/2.question: If saying the words is not a request, what stops anyone from mentioning rain all through the dry summer, as Rabbi Eliezer says one may?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether uttering praise of rain is the same act as petitioning for it — but the page states the answer, and the note's own summary repeats it.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says: I say that when one ceases to request rain, one also ceases to mention it.
answer.explanation: The page directly addresses the question: Rabbi Eliezer indeed permits year-round mention ("if one seeks to mention rain throughout the year, he may mention it"), while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yehoshua supply the limit — mention ends when requesting ends, because not every season is rain's proper time.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 2b: "Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says: I say that when one ceases to request rain, one also ceases to mention it.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is settled on the page and even in the note's own summary: Rabbi Eliezer permits mention all year, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi limits it to the season of requesting, and the Gemara explains that unlike resurrection, not every day is rain's proper time. Rewrite the question to start from that answer rather than ask for it. A better angle would press on what remains odd — e.g., why praising God's might should be bounded by agricultural seasons at all, or why Rabbi Eliezer anchors the start in the lulav rather than the water libation.

taanit/3.summary: A baraita holds that the Sages never required mentioning dew and wind in the Amida, the standing prayer, since neither is ever withheld from the world. That runs into Elijah, who swore to Ahab there would be no dew or rain, so the Gemara narrows his oath to the dew of blessing that makes crops grow, and adds that God never announced dew's return because no one could tell the difference. The page closes by ranking weather: snow, wind, clouds, sunlight.
taanit/3.question: If the dew of blessing can be taken away and given back without anyone able to notice, what did Elijah's oath actually stop?

judge.reachNote: Whether a blessing that cannot be perceived as present or absent is nonetheless real in its effects.

answer.quote: Not only will there be no rainfall, but even the dew of blessing, which helps crops grow, will not come. This prediction was indeed fulfilled.
answer.explanation: The page says the oath withheld the crop-growing dew of blessing, which bears on the question, but it says the withdrawal and restoration are indistinguishable to people, so the tension the question raises is not resolved in so many words.

taanit/4.summary: Rabbi Yonatan lists three men who put open-ended requests to God: Eliezer, who promised Isaac whichever girl offered to water his camels, even if she turned out lame or blind; Saul, who offered his daughter to whoever killed Goliath, even a slave; and Jephthah, who vowed to burn whatever came out of his door. The first two got Rebecca and David. Jephthah got his daughter, and the page notes he could have sought to annul the vow.
taanit/4.question: If Eliezer and Saul made bets just as reckless and were handed Rebecca and David, what makes Jephthah the one answered in kind?

judge.reachNote: Whether recklessness in prayer is judged by the risk taken or by the content of what one pledged God would accept.

answer.quote: This verse alludes to the fact that had he sought a means to do so, Jephthah could have had his vow annulled.
answer.explanation: The page faults Jephthah for not seeking annulment and elsewhere groups his act with human sacrifice God "did not speak" of, which bears on his singular fate but never states why his entreaty itself drew an unfavorable answer while Eliezer's and Saul's did not.

taanit/5.summary: The mishna asks how long into the spring one keeps asking for rain in prayer, and Rabbi Meir says through the end of Nisan, citing Joel's line about rain in the first month. Rav Nahman objects that the first rain comes in Marheshvan, in autumn; the answer is that Joel described one locust-ruined year when rain held off until the first of Nisan. Told to sow their last seed, the people asked whether to eat it instead and live a while longer.
taanit/5.question: The prophet never answers the farmers' arithmetic, he only repeats "go out and sow", so what could have made that convincing before the hidden seeds turned up in the ant holes?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that obedience to a prophetic word is asked for before any evidence that it will pay off — trust against prudent calculation.

taanit/6.summary: A baraita pulls apart the name of the first rain, yoreh: it instructs people to plaster their roofs and bring in produce from the fields, and it must fall gently, since rain that washes trees away is no blessing. Later the Gemara asks why anyone needs to date the second rainfall, and answers with endings: from then anyone may gather forgotten olives, shortcut paths across fields close, and Sabbatical Year straw must go. Rav Abbahu measures that rainfall by mud thick enough to seal a barrel.
taanit/6.question: Why should a poor person's claim to the forgotten olives expire with a rainfall rather than on a fixed day of the month?

judge.reachNote: Deadlines for the poor's claims are set by facts on the ground (who has left the field, what a beast can still find) rather than by the calendar.

answer.quote: After the time of the second rainfall there is no longer any straw or hay in the fields.
answer.explanation: The page explains the rain-based cutoff in a parallel second-rainfall case (Sabbatical produce) as tracking what is actually still available in the field, but it never states why forgotten olives in particular end with a rainfall rather than a date.

taanit/7.summary: Rabbi Abbahu ranks a day of rain above the resurrection of the dead, since rain falls on the wicked as well as the righteous. Rava presses further with a rule about comparisons: the lesser thing is likened to the greater, so if Torah drops as the rain, rain outranks Torah. Then the same verse turns lethal, since the Hebrew for drop also means breaking a neck, so for an unworthy student the rain snaps it.
taanit/7.question: If a comparison always makes the lesser thing depend on the greater, where does that leave Torah once the page has likened it to rain, fire, a tree, water, and wine kept in clay?

judge.reachNote: Asks what a comparison does — rank two things, or teach about one — and whether Rava's ranking rule can survive the page's flood of Torah similes.

taanit/8.summary: Famine and plague strike together, and the Sages rule that prayer cannot address both at once, so they choose the plague and resolve to bear the hunger. Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani reverses them: pray about the famine, since food is given for the sake of the living, and the plague ends with it. Later, under a decree forbidding fasting, Rabbi Zeira tells people to accept a fast now and observe it whenever the decree lifts.
taanit/8.question: If Daniel's words were heard the moment he set his heart to fast, what does the fast itself add when it finally becomes possible?
gate: the question brings in "Daniel's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether the resolve of the heart exhausts the obligation or the physical act still carries its own weight.

taanit/9.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that rain can fall for the sake of one person, while sustenance comes only for many, and a baraita narrows rain further still, from a man to a single field to a single blade of grass. Rav Daniel bar Ketina walked his garden every day announcing which bed needed water, and the rain came only where he said. The manna, given in Moses' merit, is explained away: he asked on behalf of many, so he counted as many.
taanit/9.question: If rain can be aimed at one bed in one garden, what makes bread so different that it takes a crowd to draw it down?

judge.reachNote: Why divine provision of water can be individual and pinpointed while provision of food is treated as communal by nature.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan further proves that sustenance comes for the sake of many, as it is written: “Behold I will cause to rain bread from the heavens for you”
answer.explanation: The page grounds the rain/sustenance distinction only in the singular versus plural wording of the verses, and resolves the manna objection by saying "Moses is different, since he requested the manna for many," but never states why bread itself requires many.

taanit/10.summary: If the seventeenth of Marḥeshvan arrives and no rain has fallen, a mishna has certain individuals, not the whole community, begin three daytime fasts. Rav Huna says those individuals are the Sages, and a baraita defines one as anyone learned enough to be appointed leader and teacher over a community. Rabbi Meir says not everyone may make himself such an individual; Rabbi Yosei says he may, and is remembered for good, since the practice brings pain rather than praise.
taanit/10.question: If the line between self-appointed piety and self-display is whether the practice hurts or flatters, who is in a position to tell which one a person is after?

judge.reachNote: Whether piety is policed by the visible character of the practice (painful vs. flattering) or by an unreachable inner motive.

answer.quote: It is said with regard to a matter of praise, e.g., adorning oneself with the garments of a Torah scholar.
answer.explanation: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel supplies a test located in the act itself — garments of honor versus strictness that hurts — rather than naming anyone who judges the person's motive, so the question can still be asked.

taanit/11.summary: A baraita insists that when the community is suffering, no one should go home, eat, drink and say peace be upon you, my soul; Moses sat on a stone during the war with Amalek rather than a cushion. From there the page turns on fasting itself. Shmuel calls a faster a sinner, reading the nazirite, one who vows off wine, as harmed by his own abstinence; Rabbi Elazar reads the same verses and calls him sacred.
taanit/11.question: If Reish Lakish calls one who fasts pious, why does he also bar a Torah scholar from fasting at all?
gate: the question brings in "Reish", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Lakish", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea is that self-denial can be praiseworthy in itself yet forbidden when it costs a higher service — but the page supplies that reason in the very line it states the ruling.

answer.quote: A Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in observance of a fast, due to the fact that his fasting reduces his strength for the heavenly service
answer.explanation: The page states Reish Lakish's own reason for barring the Torah scholar — fasting drains the strength needed for Torah study and mitzvot — which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 11b: "A Torah scholar is not permitted to sit in observance of a fast, due to the fact that his fasting reduces his strength for the heavenly service". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same line it draws from: the page says the scholar may not fast because fasting reduces his strength for the heavenly service. Rewrite the question so it starts from that stated reason and presses on what remains hard — for example, why weakening one's body is pious for an ordinary person but a loss for a scholar, or how this sits with Rav Sheshet's image of the fasting student who has let a dog eat his portion. Keep the summary's thread on the sinner/sacred dispute if you like, but the question must not be one the page plainly answers.

taanit/12.summary: Rav Ḥisda holds that a fast the sun never sets on, where someone eats at midday, is no fast at all. Three counterexamples are brought and all three are waved off as mere self-inflicted distress, including Rabbi Yoḥanan's line that he was fasting until he got home, which was really a polite way to skip dinner at the Nasi's house. Shmuel adds that a fast not accepted the day before is not a fast either.
taanit/12.question: If a man eats nothing from dawn to dark but never declared a fast beforehand, what does the declaration add that the empty stomach does not?

judge.reachNote: Whether a fast is constituted by the bodily abstention or by the accepted intention that gives it status.

answer.quote: He is likened to a bellows that is full of air. His behavior does not constitute a fast, as he is merely a container full of air, without food.
answer.explanation: The page images the undeclared abstainer as empty air rather than a faster, which bears on the question but never states what the prior acceptance actually adds, so the question can still honestly be asked.

taanit/13.summary: A mourner and a person on a communal fast both stop bathing, and the argument here is whether that means hot water only or cold water too. Rav Ḥisda splits it by reason: what is forbidden as mourning covers both, what is forbidden as pleasure covers only hot. Every proof collapses, including the case of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina, who bathed in cold water through all seven days of mourning for his sons, and is explained away as grief upon grief.
taanit/13.question: When a grieving father actually bathed in cold water for seven days, should that count as evidence of what the law permits, or is the page right to set him aside as a man whose losses came too fast?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's actual practice under extreme circumstances is evidence of the law or an exception that proves nothing.

answer.quote: There it was a case where his mourning periods came one after the other, as his sons died in quick succession, and this leniency is as it is taught
answer.explanation: The page states its own reason for setting the incident aside, but does not address whether a sage's recorded conduct should count as legal evidence, which is what the question presses.

taanit/14.summary: When trouble struck in Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's time, he decreed thirteen fast days, got no answer, and wanted to keep going; Rabbi Ami stopped him, saying one does not trouble the community excessively. Rabbi Yoḥanan limits that cap to fasts for rain, since for other calamities the community fasts until it is answered. Later Rabbi Elazar rules that a prominent person may throw himself face-down in public prayer only if he is certain, like Joshua, of being answered.
taanit/14.question: If a leader may only pray face-down in public when he already knows the answer is coming, what is public prayer for everyone who does not know?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that public petition stakes the petitioner's (and God's) standing on being answered, and asks what prayer means when that guarantee is absent.

answer.quote: as if he is unanswered he will become an object of derision
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason for restricting the important person's public prostration — the risk of derision if unanswered — but never says what public prayer is for those who lack such certainty.

taanit/15.summary: On a public fast day the ark is carried out of the synagogue into the city square, ashes are put on it, and ashes go on the heads of the Nasi, his deputy, and everyone else. The elder's reproof points at Nineveh: God saw deeds, not sackcloth. The prayer leader chosen must have children and an empty house, poor enough that the community's hunger is his own, and he recites blessings recalling Abraham, Jonah, Elijah.
taanit/15.question: If going first with the ashes is an honor because the community is saying you are worthy of asking for mercy, why does someone else's hand have to place them on your head?

judge.reachNote: Being lowered by another's hand counts differently from lowering yourself — honor and humiliation depend on who performs the act.

answer.quote: Rabbi Abba of Caesarea said: This is done intentionally, as one who humiliates himself, in this case by placing ashes upon his own head, is not similar to
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact question and begins Rabbi Abba's answer — self-humiliation differs from being humiliated by another — but the sentence breaks off before the comparison is completed on this page.

taanit/16.summary: A community on a public fast moves its prayer out to the town square, carries out the ark that holds the Torah scrolls, wears sackcloth, puts burnt ash on their heads and on the ark, and walks to the cemetery. Each gesture gets two explanations, and each pair is tested by an edge case: plain earth instead of ashes, gentile graves instead of Jewish ones. Then the elder stands and says fasting and sackcloth atone for nothing.
taanit/16.question: If what God saw in Nineveh was deeds and not sackcloth, why does so much of the day turn on whether the ash is really ash and the graves are really Jewish?
gate: the question brings in "Nineveh", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that ritual precision and inward repentance pull against each other — why insist the symbols be exact if only deeds move God.

summaryProblems.claim: Each gesture gets two explanations.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And why do they cover themselves in sackcloth? Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said: This is as though to say: We are considered before You like animals

judge.feedback: The summary says "Each gesture gets two explanations.", but the page says "And why do they cover themselves in sackcloth? Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said: This is as though to say: We are considered before You like animals". Say what the page says. Drop or qualify the claim that every gesture receives two explanations: going out to the square, the ashes on the head, and the cemetery visit are disputed pairs, but removing the ark and donning sackcloth each get a single explanation, and only some pairs are tested by an edge case. Keep the question as is — it is strong and the page does not answer it. Also take care with the ash: the page puts burnt ashes on the ark and ashes on each person's head.

taanit/17.summary: A priest who still knows the week his family was scheduled to serve in the Temple is told not to drink wine that day, in case the Temple is suddenly rebuilt and he is called. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi extends that logic to every priest at all times, then abandons it: the long ruin makes the decree unsustainable, since his misfortune is his advantage. Long hair also kills a serving priest, but a haircut is quick, so no such decree stands.
taanit/17.question: If the Temple could be rebuilt on any given day, why should the sheer length of the wait be what finally lets priests drink?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rule grounded in a possibility that never expires can be undone by the practical weight of how long the wait has lasted.

answer.quote: what can I do, as his misfortune is his advantage? The unfortunate fact that so many years have passed since the destruction of the Temple
answer.explanation: The page states that the long ruin makes the decree unsustainable, but it asserts this rather than explaining why duration outweighs the daily possibility of rebuilding, so the question can still honestly be pressed.

taanit/18.summary: The twelfth of Adar was once Trajan's Day, one of the dates in Megillat Ta'anit, a list of days on which fasting and eulogizing were barred. Rav Nahman decreed a fast on it anyway, telling the Sages the day had been annulled because Shemaya and his brother Ahiya were killed on that date. Rav Ashi adds that once the day itself is void, nobody guards its eve, even though the thirteenth is Nicanor's Day.
taanit/18.question: If later killings on the same date can cancel a day of rescue, what holds Nicanor's Day, or any of the rest, in place?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a commemorative day's standing depends on continued good fortune on that date, so later grief can dissolve earlier joy.

answer.quote: Since if a calamitous event happened and they canceled the seven days commemorating the establishment of the daily offering, the eighth day itself will remain prohibited
answer.explanation: The page acknowledges that commemorative days can be canceled by a calamity and indicates that a date survives only when it rests on an independent reason of its own, but it never says what secures Nicanor's Day or the rest of the list.

taanit/19.summary: The mishna sorts calamities by how far the alarm spreads, from a patch of blight in Ashkelon the size of an oven's mouth to wolves that ate two children in Transjordan. Too much rain is the one trouble no one cries out about, since rain counts as a blessing, and that exception introduces Ḥoni HaMe'aggel, who draws a circle, swears he will not leave it, and then sends back both the drizzle and the downpour as wrong. Shimon ben Shetaḥ threatens ostracism and drops it.
taanit/19.question: If the rain fell exactly as Ḥoni specified, what was the ostracism going to be for?

judge.reachNote: Whether prayer that gets exactly what it demands can still be a punishable way of addressing God — conduct judged apart from outcome.

answer.quote: Were you not Ḥoni, I would have decreed that you be ostracized, but what can I do to you? You nag [mitḥatei] God and He
answer.explanation: The page names the nagging of God (and the oath-backed demand) as what made Ḥoni's conduct objectionable, yet it states only why Shimon ben Shetaḥ withheld the ostracism, never spelling out the charge itself.

taanit/20.summary: Rav and Shmuel spent thirteen years walking around a crumbling wall in Neharde'a, until the day Rav Adda bar Ahava joined them and Rav declared the detour unnecessary, since Rav Adda's merit would hold the wall up. Rav Huna later kept Rav Adda talking law inside a ramshackle house until all the wine was carried out. Rav Adda was angry, holding with Rabbi Yannai that a miracle is charged to the account of the one it saves.
taanit/20.question: If it is Rav Adda's merit propping up the wall, why is it his account that gets debited while Rav Huna keeps both his wine and his own merit intact?

judge.reachNote: Merit is treated as a finite, spendable account — so who pays when one man's righteousness is quietly borrowed to protect another man's property?

answer.quote: And if you say that a miracle will be performed for him, they will deduct it from his merits.
answer.explanation: The page states the principle that a miracle is deducted from the merits of the one endangered, but never addresses why Rav Adda bears that cost while Rav Huna, who engineered the situation and saved his wine, does not.

taanit/21.summary: Pestilence strikes Sura and spares only Rav's neighborhood, and a dream corrects the town: the merit belonged to a man who lent out his hoe and shovel for digging graves. Fire skips Rav Huna's street for the sake of a woman who heats her oven and lends it to neighbors. Abba the Bloodletter closes the page, greeted daily from the heavenly academy while Rava is greeted once a year, for a hidden fee box and a slit garment.
taanit/21.question: If the point of Abba's hidden fee box was that no one could tell who paid and who could not, what happens to that when Abaye sends two Sages to watch him?
gate: the question brings in "Abaye", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Concealed giving depends on no one watching, so testing a man's hidden righteousness may destroy the very thing it measures.

taanit/22.summary: A wild beast seen inside a town by day counts as an outbreak, and the court sounds the alarm with trumpets and a fast; the same beast in a field, or at night, does not. The baraita's oddest line: a beast that tore apart two people and ate one of them is an outbreak, but one that ate both is not, since hunger explains it. The sorting turns on whether the animal was behaving like an animal.
taanit/22.question: If the alarm goes up for a beast that killed two people and ate one, but not for a beast that ate both, is the emergency the harm done or the strangeness of it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real principle — an 'outbreak' is a sign read from unnatural conduct rather than a measure of damage — but the page already spells that principle out.

answer.quote: If it ate both of them, this is not an outbreak, as the animal was evidently hungry and acted in accordance with its nature.
answer.explanation: The baraita as glossed states the criterion outright — the alarm responds to behavior out of the animal's nature, not to the quantity of harm — and Rav Pappa reinforces it by excusing a marsh beast "Since it is in its own habitat, it is natural for a territorial beast to attack."

summaryProblems.claim: For a beast in a town by day the court sounds the alarm with trumpets and a fast.
summaryProblems.pageSays: If a dangerous beast is seen in the city, this is an outbreak. If it is seen in the field, where it is usually found, this is not an outbreak.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 22a: "If it ate both of them, this is not an outbreak, as the animal was evidently hungry and acted in accordance with its nature.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "For a beast in a town by day the court sounds the alarm with trumpets and a fast.", but the page says "If a dangerous beast is seen in the city, this is an outbreak. If it is seen in the field, where it is usually found, this is not an outbreak.". Say what the page says. The question is answered in the very line the summary quotes: the page says the beast that ate both was "evidently hungry and acted in accordance with its nature," so harm versus strangeness is already settled. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance why standing near a marsh counts as natural while standing away from one counts as fear-less and alarming, or what it means that a communal alarm is triggered by a sign rather than by danger. Also drop the added detail about trumpets and a fast, since this page mentions only sounding the alarm for dangerous beasts.

taanit/23.summary: Ḥoni HaMe'aggel draws a circle in the dust, stands inside it, and swears he will not move until rain falls. The rain arrives wrong twice, first in stingy drops, then in drops the size of a barrel's mouth, and he amends his request each time until it falls normally. Shimon ben Shetaḥ tells him that anyone else would have been ostracized for staking God's name on such an oath, then compares him to a child who nags his father into giving him nuts and pomegranates.
taanit/23.question: Is Ḥoni spared ostracism because his oath was defensible, or only because it happened to work?

judge.reachNote: Whether a bold act is licensed by its reasoning or by its results — i.e., whether intimacy with God excuses conduct that would otherwise be punishable.

answer.quote: However, what can I do to you, as you nag God and He does your bidding, like a son who nags his father and his father does his bidding.
answer.explanation: Shimon ben Shetaḥ states outright why Ḥoni escapes ostracism — not because the oath was defensible (he says it would have desecrated God's name in Elijah's years) but because of Ḥoni's privileged, son-like standing whose requests God grants.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 23a: "However, what can I do to you, as you nag God and He does your bidding, like a son who nags his father and his father does his bidding.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is settled on the page: Shimon ben Shetaḥ says the oath was indefensible in principle and that he can do nothing to Ḥoni because "you nag God and He does your bidding." Rewrite so the question starts from that stated reason and asks what is still hard — for instance, why the Sanhedrin then praises the same oath as a decree from below that Heaven fulfills, or what it means that Ḥoni's standing, not his reasoning, is what protects him. Keep the summary; it is faithful.

taanit/24.summary: Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat's son tells a fig tree to yield fruit early so his father's hungry laborers can eat, and his father tells him he will die young for forcing fruit out of season. Then come story after story of sages who decree fasts and get no rain: Rav Nahman asks to be thrown off a wall, Rav Pappa is mocked for eating porridge. In both cases rain falls only once the sage is upset or shamed.
taanit/24.question: If forcing a fig tree to fruit out of season costs a boy his life, and Rava's father warns him for pulling rain down in Tammuz, why does the page keep showing rain arriving the moment a sage is humiliated?
gate: the question brings in "Rava's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Tammuz", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: heaven punishes coercing nature out of its order, yet seems to yield to a righteous man's broken or humiliated state — what distinguishes the two.

taanit/25.summary: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's wife heats an empty oven so the neighbors will think she is baking, and when one knocks, the oven is full of bread. Later he prays about their poverty and a hand hands him one leg of a golden table, which his wife makes him pray away after she dreams the righteous eat at three-legged tables and she at a two-legged one. A baraita calls the second miracle the greater one, since Heaven gives but does not take back.
taanit/25.question: Why is undoing the gift counted the greater miracle, when it leaves the household exactly as hungry as it was before?

judge.reachNote: Whether a miracle is measured by the relief it brings now or by the standing it secures in the World-to-Come.

answer.quote: The last miracle was greater than the first, as it is learned as a tradition that Heaven gives but does not take back.
answer.explanation: The baraita supplies the stated rationale for calling the second miracle greater — reversing a heavenly gift runs against the rule that Heaven does not take back — but it says nothing about the household's restored hunger, which is the edge of the question.

taanit/26.summary:
Rav Pappa decreed a fast in Meu
aḥoza, rain fell before midday, and he had the people recite hallel on the spot instead of sending them home to eat first, because drunkenness was common in that town. The same worry drives the Gemara's question of why priests do not raise their hands for the Priestly Benediction at the afternoon prayer: a priest who drank at lunch may not bless. Rabbi Meir says a fast day removes the risk; Rabbi Yehuda keeps the rule anyway.
taanit/26.question: If the ban on blessing at the afternoon prayer exists only because of wine, why does Rabbi Yehuda hold it in force on a day when nobody has eaten or drunk?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rabbinic decree survives in cases where its underlying reason does not apply — the question reaches that idea, but the page answers it outright.

answer.quote: the Sages issued a decree that the Priestly Benediction should not be recited during them, despite the fact that intoxication is not a concern on a fast day
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yehuda's position exactly: the decree was enacted because drunkenness is common on ordinary days and stands even where the concern is absent, which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 26b: "the Sages issued a decree that the Priestly Benediction should not be recited during them, despite the fact that intoxication is not a concern on a fast day". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very lines the summary paraphrases: Rabbi Yehuda holds the blanket decree in force "despite the fact that intoxication is not a concern on a fast day." Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains, for instance why Rabbi Yosei's line about people confusing ne'ila with a weekday afternoon prayer treats the decree as guarding against confusion rather than against wine, or why the later halakha ends up permitting the benediction near sunset. Also fix the garbled spelling of Meḥoza in the summary.

taanit/27.summary: Twenty-four priestly watches rotated through the Temple, and each had a matching group of ordinary Israelites who stayed in their towns while the priests served. Those watches fasted Monday through Thursday, each day for a danger tied to what was created then: seafarers on Monday, when the sea was made; croup in children on Wednesday, when the lights, me'orot, were made, hinting at curses, me'erot. Then God tells Abraham that reading the order of offerings will count as bringing them.
taanit/27.question: If reading the offerings aloud counts as having sacrificed them, why does the page insist that priests, Levites and Israelites all be physically standing there for the daily offering?

judge.reachNote: Whether recited words can stand in for bodily presence at an offering — an idea the page raises and then bounds by time (Temple standing or not).

answer.quote: Master of the Universe, this works out well when the Temple is standing, but when the Temple is not standing, what will become of them?
answer.explanation: The page itself frames the reading of the offerings as the arrangement for when the Temple is not standing, so it does not compete with the requirement of physical presence while the Temple stands and the daily offering is actually sacrificed.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 27b: "Master of the Universe, this works out well when the Temple is standing, but when the Temple is not standing, what will become of them?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved by the page: Abraham's exchange explicitly sets the reading of the offerings as the substitute for when the Temple is not standing, so there is no conflict with the presence rules for the daily offering. Rewrite the question so it starts from that distinction rather than ignoring it — for example, ask why Rav Asi still ties the world's existence to the non-priestly watches and the Temple service if the reading alone earns credit as though the offerings were brought. Alternatively, build the question on the fasting days or on the Sunday exemption, which the summary also covers.

taanit/28.summary: On the fifteenth of Av, wood for the altar fire was brought by families remembered as those who deceived the guards with a pestle and those who packed dried figs. Under a Greek decree blocking wood and first fruits from Jerusalem, they hid baskets of first produce under figs and told the guards they were going to press fig cakes; others carried ladders and claimed to be fetching doves from a dovecote. The page names them by their cover stories.
taanit/28.question: Are these families remembered for the wood and first fruits they got to Jerusalem, or for the lies they told the guards to get them there?
gate: gloss "first fruits" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What a name commemorates: the offering delivered or the cunning deception that delivered it.

answer.quote: And about these families who provided these donations and others like them, the verse says: “The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing”
answer.explanation: The page ties their blessed memory to the donations they provided, though their very names on the page preserve the ruses, so the question can still be pressed.

taanit/29.summary: Two verses give two dates for the burning of the First Temple: the seventh of Av in II Kings, the tenth in Jeremiah. An early teaching splits them: gentiles entered the Sanctuary on the seventh, ate and defiled it two days, and set the fire near nightfall on the ninth, which burned on into the tenth. Rabbi Yoḥanan says he would have fixed the fast on the tenth, when most burned; the Sages marked the beginning.
taanit/29.question: Is a catastrophe dated from the hour it began or the hour it did most of its damage?

judge.reachNote: The question does name the underlying idea — whether a date commemorates onset or the bulk of the loss — but the page itself supplies both sides and the Sages' reason.

answer.quote: And the Sages, who established the fast on the ninth, how do they respond to that comment? They maintain that it is preferable to mark the beginning of the tragedy.
answer.explanation: The page poses exactly the choice the question asks — Rabbi Yoḥanan's tenth (most burned) versus the ninth — and states the Sages' resolution that the beginning of the tragedy is preferable.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Taanit 29a: "And the Sages, who established the fast on the ninth, how do they respond to that comment? They maintain that it is preferable to mark the beginning of the tragedy.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the summary paraphrases: the Sages hold "it is preferable to mark the beginning of the tragedy." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for example, ask what makes onset the preferable marker when Rabbi Yoḥanan can point to the day most of the Sanctuary actually burned, or press on the baraita's use of two conflicting verses to build one timeline. Keep the summary as it is; it is faithful to the page.

taanit/30.summary: Rava issues two rulings about the mourning that precedes the Ninth of Av, and the Gemara points out that both are leniencies. Other sages measure restraint rather than ban it: a man used to a liter of meat eats half a liter, ten cups of wine become five, ten dinner companions become five. Against that arithmetic sits Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi Ilai, eating stale bread and salt between the oven and the stove.
taanit/30.question: If the man who usually drinks ten cups of wine may still drink five before the fast, why is the man who never drinks wine forbidden even one?

judge.reachNote: Whether pre-fast mourning is measured relative to each person's habit or by an absolute standard of austerity.

answer.quote: And the Rabbis say: One must adjust and reduce his consumption of meat and wine.
answer.explanation: The page states the framing principle of reduction-from-one's-habit and states the rule that the abstainer is forbidden entirely, but it never gives a reason for that asymmetry, so the question can still honestly be asked.

taanit/31.summary: The fifteenth of Av collects reasons to celebrate, among them the day they stopped chopping wood for the altar's fire, called the breaking of the scythe. Then the borrowed clothes: a king's daughter borrows white garments from the High Priest's daughter, and so on down, so that no woman lacking her own is shamed. In the vineyards the unmarried women call out competing pitches to the watching men: beauty, distinguished family, or marry for Heaven's sake and buy us gold afterward.
taanit/31.question: If the white garments are all borrowed so no woman can be sorted by what she owns, what to make of the calls in the vineyard that sort the women by beauty, lineage, and the promise of jewelry?

judge.reachNote: Equalizing what can be borrowed while leaving unequal what cannot — the question asks what kind of equality the white garments were meant to secure.

megillah/2.summary: Megillah opens with five possible days for reading the scroll of Esther, the eleventh of Adar through the fifteenth. Cities walled since Joshua's day read on the fifteenth, unwalled towns on the fourteenth, and villagers may read early on a Monday or Thursday, when courts sit and they come to town anyway. The Gemara argues the extra days must be original, since no later court could overturn the Great Assembly, then hunts for the hint in a plural word.
megillah/2.question: If walled cities read on the fifteenth because that is when Shushan celebrated, why should the wall have to date from Joshua's time rather than from Ahasuerus's, when the rescue actually happened?
gate: the question brings in "Shushan", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Ahasuerus's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a city's Purim status follows the moment of the miracle or an older scriptural category of walled town.

answer.quote: Just as there, in Deuteronomy, the reference is to a city that was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua, son of Nun, so too here
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this dispute (Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's Ahasuerus standard versus the mishna's) and supplies the mishna's reason, the verbal analogy from Deuteronomy 3:5, with Rava adding that "Shushan is different since the miracle occurred in it on the fifteenth" so it does not set the rule for other cities.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 2b: "Just as there, in Deuteronomy, the reference is to a city that was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua, son of Nun, so too here". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already asks and answers this: the mishna's Joshua standard comes from the verbal analogy on "unwalled" with Deuteronomy 3:5, and Rava says Shushan is an exception because the miracle happened there on the fifteenth. A rewrite should start from that answer rather than ask for it, for instance pressing on why the same verse "every province and province" is read as a distinction by one tanna and as support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's adjacent-settlements rule by the other. Alternatively, work the earlier half of the page, such as how "their times" can yield exactly two extra days and no more.

megillah/3.summary: Priests at the altar, Levites singing on their platform, and Israelites at their watches all stop what they are doing to hear the Megilla read. From there a ladder gets built: an angel rebukes Joshua for neglecting Torah study rather than the skipped afternoon offering, and Rava ranks Megilla reading above both Temple service and study. Then he asks about a corpse with no one to bury it, and rules that human dignity outranks publicizing the miracle.
megillah/3.question: Why does a man on his way to circumcise his son turn aside for an unknown corpse, but not for his own sister?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that an obligation nobody else can discharge outweighs even a great mitzva — but the page states that reason outright.

answer.quote: he may not become impure for his sister, as someone else can attend to her burial, but he does become impure for a met mitzva
answer.explanation: The baraita states the exact reason: the sister has others to bury her, while the met mitzva has no one, so only the latter overrides the Paschal lamb or circumcision.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 3a (baraita on "or for his sister"): "he may not become impure for his sister, as someone else can attend to her burial, but he does become impure for a met mitzva". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim on the page: the sister has someone else to bury her, the met mitzva does not. Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for instance why Rava needed to resolve the Megilla-versus-met-mitzva dilemma by appeal to human dignity overriding a Torah prohibition, when publicizing the miracle had just outranked both Temple service and Torah study. The summary is accurate and can stay largely as is.

megillah/4.summary: Villagers were allowed to read the Megilla early, on a Monday or Thursday market day, and Rabbi \u1e24anina explains that this freed them to supply water and food to the cities on Purim itself. Three readings of the mishna dismantle that: if the arrangement served the cities, the timing rules would come out differently. The practice survives, but the reason is swapped, and the leniency turns out to be for the villagers, who came to town on those days anyway.
megillah/4.question: When the stated reason for a leniency collapses and a new reason is supplied to keep the same practice standing, how would anyone tell which reason came first?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a practice can outlive the reason given for it, and that a retrofitted rationale is indistinguishable from an original one.

megillah/5.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi planted a sapling on Purim, and much of the page tries to explain how he could. Tiberias, where he lived, counted as walled since Joshua's day, so its Purim fell on the fifteenth; both days forbid eulogies; and Rav once cursed a man planting flax on Purim so the crop never grew. The last answer given is that the people never accepted a ban on labor at all, only local custom.
megillah/5.question: If the prohibition on working on Purim was never actually accepted, what gave Rav's curse the power to keep that man's flax from growing?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that accepted local custom can bind where halakha does not — but the page states this answer outright.

answer.quote: It was a case of matters that are permitted by halakha, but others were accustomed to treat them as a prohibition, in which case one may not permit these actions
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's question — "If labor is permitted on Purim, what is the reason that Rav cursed that man who planted the flax?" — and answers that in that man's locale abstaining from labor was accepted custom, which one may not publicly violate.

summaryProblems.claim: The last answer given is that the people never accepted a ban on labor at all, only local custom.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And if you wish, say an alternative answer: Actually, it was the custom to abstain from labor on Purim in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s place, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi engaged in a joyful act of planting

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 5b: "It was a case of matters that are permitted by halakha, but others were accustomed to treat them as a prohibition, in which case one may not permit these actions". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The last answer given is that the people never accepted a ban on labor at all, only local custom.", but the page says "And if you wish, say an alternative answer: Actually, it was the custom to abstain from labor on Purim in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s place, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi engaged in a joyful act of planting". Say what the page says. The question is answered explicitly on the page: the Gemara asks why Rav cursed the flax planter if labor is permitted, and replies that in that place abstaining was accepted custom, which may not be publicly overridden. Write a question whose answer the page does not supply — for instance about why custom can bind where the nation's original acceptance did not, or why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's joyful planting counts differently from labor. Also fix the summary: the final answer offered is that his planting was joyful planting done for pleasure, not the non-acceptance of the labor ban.

megillah/6.summary: Rabbi Yitzḥak says not to provoke a wicked man whose hour is smiling on him, since provoking him only makes his ventures prosper and his court cases go his way. Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Dostai bar Matun say the opposite, and Dostai adds that whoever whispers otherwise is quieting his own guilty conscience. Three reconciliations follow, and the last one gives ground: when fortune favors the wicked man, even the completely righteous should stay out of it.
megillah/6.question: If holding back from a thriving wicked man is prudence because Heaven is helping him, how would anyone tell that prudence apart from the guilty silence Rabbi Dostai describes?

judge.reachNote: When is silence before a prospering wrongdoer piety and when is it self-interest dressed as piety — the page supplies distinctions but no test a person could apply to himself.

megillah/7.summary: Esther sends word to the Sages asking to be written down for future generations, and they refuse, since the verse allows Israel's war with Amalek only three mentions and hers would be a fourth. They relent once a reading of Exodus makes the two Torah passages count as one. Later sages each produce a verse proving the book was divinely inspired, and Rava knocks down every proof but Shmuel's, explaining that Mordecai simply understood the conspirators' language.
megillah/7.question: Can a book be inspired enough to be read aloud in public but not inspired enough to be written as sacred scripture?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that inspiration may attach to an act of public reading rather than to a text's status as scripture — but the page states that idea outright.

answer.quote: It was stated with the Divine Spirit that it is to be read in public; however, it was not stated that it is to be written.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself resolves the tension in Shmuel's position by distinguishing inspiration to be read publicly from inspiration to be written as a sacred scroll, which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 7a: "It was stated with the Divine Spirit that it is to be read in public; however, it was not stated that it is to be written.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on the page, where the Gemara resolves Shmuel's two statements by saying Esther was divinely inspired to be read but not to be written. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard: for instance, why reading in public should carry less sanctity than writing, or why a book whose contents the sages concede could only be known by divine spirit still fails to render the hands impure. Alternatively build a question from the Amalek counting or from Rava's willingness to refute proofs of inspiration one by one.

megillah/8.summary: A run of mishnayot here uses one formula: the only difference between two things. Vowing off all benefit from a neighbor differs from vowing off his food only in stepping on his land. Rav Pappa then notices that the same two words, "from his emission," exclude a zav, a man with an abnormal discharge, from bringing an offering in one verse and include him in counting seven clean days in another; Abaye answers that a verse meaning to exclude would have stayed silent.
megillah/8.question: If one phrase can add in one verse and subtract in another, what stops the reading from arriving wherever the reader already meant to go?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what disciplines midrashic reading when the same words can include or exclude — whether superfluity is a real check or a free hand.

answer.quote: let the verse remain silent and omit the term, as there would have been no basis to include a zav who experienced two emissions in that halakha
answer.explanation: Abaye supplies a constraint on the double reading — a term that merely excluded would be superfluous, so its presence must be inclusionary — which bears on the question without fully settling what limits such readings in general.

summaryProblems.claim: Vowing off all benefit from a neighbor differs from vowing off his food only in stepping on his land.
summaryProblems.pageSays: is only with regard to stepping foot on his property, and with regard to borrowing utensils from him that one does not use in the preparation of food

judge.feedback: The summary says "Vowing off all benefit from a neighbor differs from vowing off his food only in stepping on his land.", but the page says "is only with regard to stepping foot on his property, and with regard to borrowing utensils from him that one does not use in the preparation of food". Say what the page says. Fix the first mishna: the page names two differences, stepping on the property and borrowing utensils not used for food preparation, so "only in stepping on his land" misstates it. Keep the Rav Pappa–Abaye thread, which is reported accurately, and let the question press past Abaye's superfluity argument rather than restate the same worry it already answers.

megillah/9.summary: An argument over which languages sacred texts may be written in lands on a story about King Ptolemy, who shut seventy-two Elders in seventy-two separate rooms and ordered each to translate the Torah. All seventy-two produced the same text, and the same fifteen alterations to it. They wrote "God created in the beginning" to block a misreading, turned the slain man of Genesis 49 into an ox, and dropped the hare because Ptolemy's wife was named Arnevet.
megillah/9.question: If divine wisdom guided all seventy-two Elders alike, why did it guide them to write something other than what the Torah says?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a faithful translation may require unfaithful words, and asks what that says about the authority of the text itself.

answer.quote: They did so to negate those who believe in the preexistence of the world and those who maintain that there are two powers in the world
answer.explanation: The page supplies a protective motive for each alteration — blocking heretical or mocking misreadings — which bears on why the Elders departed from the literal text, though it never confronts the tension between divine guidance and fidelity to the words of the Torah.

megillah/10.summary: Rabbi Levi reports a tradition that the word vayhi, "and it came to pass," always signals grief, and proofs are lined up: Ahasuerus brought Haman, the days of the judges brought famine, Joshua met an angel with a drawn sword. Then the counterexamples arrive, including the dedication of the Tabernacle, Jacob seeing Rachel, and the first day of Creation. Rav Ashi saves the claim by shrinking it to vayhi bimei, "in the days of," five verses in all.
megillah/10.question: Once Rav Ashi narrows the rule until it covers only the handful of verses that suggested it, is it still a rule or just a list?

judge.reachNote: Asks when a hermeneutic principle stops being a principle and becomes a mere enumeration of its own supporting cases.

megillah/11.summary: Sage after sage opens the book of Esther with a verse from elsewhere in the Bible: fire and water, a hungry bear, a house whose roof leaks. Rav Yosef says the Persians are the bear because they eat and drink in quantity, grow their hair long, and never rest. Then comes arithmetic: Belshazzar of Babylonia counted out Jeremiah's seventy years of exile, concluded redemption would not come, and used the Temple vessels; Ahasuerus redid the sum and erred too.
megillah/11.question: If Ahasuerus had counted from the destruction of Jerusalem rather than the earlier exile, what would he have done with the Temple vessels then?

judge.reachNote: Under the arithmetic lies the idea that a man who thinks he has proven redemption will not come feels licensed to profane its vessels — the reckoning drives the sacrilege.

answer.quote: He too erred in his calculation, for he should have counted from the destruction of Jerusalem at the time of the exile of Zedekiah
answer.explanation: The page names the correct starting point and adds that eleven years were still lacking while he reigned fourteen, which bears on the counterfactual without ever saying what he would have done with the vessels.

megillah/12.summary: Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai's students ask him why the Jews of that generation deserved annihilation. Their own answer, that they ate at Ahasuerus's feast, he rejects: only the residents of Shushan attended, yet the decree covered Jews everywhere. His answer is that they bowed to the statue Nebuchadnezzar set up, and when the students press him on why a miracle rescued them anyway, he says the bowing was only for show, and so was God's anger.
megillah/12.question: If the idolatry was only for appearance and the anger only for appearance, what was the danger the miracle saved them from?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a punishment matched to a merely apparent sin may itself be merely apparent, and asks what is then actually at stake.

answer.quote: He too merely pretended to desire to destroy them, as all He did was issue a threat, but in the end the decree was annulled.
answer.explanation: The page states that God's anger amounted to a threat that was ultimately annulled, which bears on what the miracle averted without ever saying what real danger the Jews were in if the wrath was only for appearance.

megillah/13.summary: Mordecai is called Yehudi though the page places him in Benjamin, and Rabbi Yoḥanan says the word marks anyone who repudiates idols, including Pharaoh's daughter, who washed in the river to purify herself from her father's idols. The same method turns six names in one verse of Chronicles into Moses alone. Later the page rewards concealment: Rachel hands Leah the secret signs and stays silent, and her descendant Esther tells Ahasuerus nothing of her people.
megillah/13.question: If Rachel's silence about the signs earns her a line of kings, what does the page make of the fact that the person deceived that night was Jacob, who had just told her deception was only for swindlers?

judge.reachNote: When concealment is a virtue and when it is fraud — the page rewards Rachel's silence while Jacob has just bounded deception to the deceitful.

answer.quote: Rachel said to herself: Now my sister will be embarassed, for Jacob will ask her for the signs and she will not know them. So she gave them to her.
answer.explanation: The page supplies Rachel's motive (sparing Leah shame) and later credits her silence as modesty, but it never confronts the fact that the one deceived was Jacob, who had just limited permitted deception to swindlers, so the question still stands.

megillah/14.summary: Abigail rides out at night to stop David from killing her husband Nabal, and the Gemara turns her plea into a legal trap. She shows David a blood-stained cloth and asks whether it makes her ritually impure; he says blood cannot be examined by candlelight, and she answers that capital cases are not tried at night either. David shifts ground, calling Nabal a rebel who needs no trial, until Abigail replies that Saul is still king.
megillah/14.question: If Abigail's argument is only that tonight is the wrong night and David is not yet king enough, what stops him in the morning?

judge.reachNote: Procedural limits (no capital trial at night, no unrecognized king) are being used as substantive moral restraint — whether delay is itself a form of justice.

answer.quote: David accepted her words and said to her: "And blessed be your discretion and blessed be you who have kept me this day from coming to bloodguiltiness [damim]"
answer.explanation: The page reports that David accepted Abigail's argument and blessed her for preventing bloodshed, and later notes that Nabal died on his own and David married her, but it never explains what would have barred David from killing Nabal the next day, so the question still stands.

megillah/15.summary: Esther invites Haman to a private banquet with the king, and a long line of sages asks why. Rabbi Elazar says she hid a snare for him, Rabbi Yehoshua says she was feeding an enemy bread, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha says she wanted Ahasuerus to suspect an affair and have them both killed. Rabba bar Avuh puts the question to Elijah, who answers that every one of those reasons, from every sage, was hers.
megillah/15.question: If all of the motives the sages propose were Esther's at once, what were they disagreeing about?

judge.reachNote: If a dispute can be resolved by accepting every side at once, the disagreement must be about something other than fact — perhaps which motive is primary or which reading the verse compels.

megillah/16.summary: Haman is ordered to parade Mordecai on the king's horse, so he washes him in the bathhouse, trims his hair with scissors from his own house, and stoops down to be used as a mounting block, taking a kick on the way up. The retelling runs on through Esther's banquet, angels uprooting trees, and Haman's ten sons hanged on a single pole. Then the mood turns: the closing lines rank Torah study above saving lives, and demote Mordecai for public service.
megillah/16.question: If Mordecai's fasting and maneuvering are what saved the Jews of Shushan, why does the page count his move into communal affairs as a drop of one place in a list?
gate: the question brings in "Shushan", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the valuation question — whether communal salvation or Torah study is the higher good — but the page answers it in so many words.

answer.quote: Studying Torah is greater than saving lives, as initially, when listing the Jewish leaders who came to Eretz Yisrael, Mordecai was mentioned after four other people
answer.explanation: The page itself states the reason for the demotion — Rav Yosef's principle that Torah study outranks saving lives, so governmental involvement lowered Mordecai's stature one notch.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 16b: "Studying Torah is greater than saving lives, as initially, when listing the Jewish leaders who came to Eretz Yisrael, Mordecai was mentioned after four other people". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: Rav Yosef says Torah study is greater than saving lives, and that Mordecai's governmental involvement lowered his stature one notch. Rewrite so the question starts from that stated ranking and presses on what is still hard about it — for instance, that the same page credits the fasts with the miracle and reads the fast verses together with Esther's decree, or that the Sanhedrin's own parting is presented as their judgment rather than God's. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

megillah/17.summary: Ishmael's hundred and thirty-seven years are counted out in order to date the moment Isaac blessed Jacob, at sixty-three. Adding the years forward, Jacob should have been a hundred and sixteen when he reached Egypt, yet he tells Pharaoh he is a hundred and thirty. The resolution offered is that fourteen years spent hiding in Eber's study house simply do not count, while the eighteen months of building booths at Sukkot are charged against him.
megillah/17.question: Why do fourteen years away from his parents in Eber's study house leave no mark on Jacob's ledger, while the two years he lingered at Sukkot and Bethel are counted as absence?
gate: the question brings in "Bethel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether time spent learning Torah counts as culpable absence from one's parents, while mere lingering on the road does.

answer.quote: conclude from here that the fourteen years that he was in the house of Eber are not counted, as he was not punished for them
answer.explanation: The page asserts that the Eber years go uncounted because Jacob was not punished for them (derived from the baraita's twenty-two-year parallel), but it never explains why study exempts him while the Sukkot delay does not.

megillah/18.summary: The scroll of Esther has to be read aloud from writing, not recited from memory, and the Gemara then sorts out which languages count. A Greek speaker fulfills the obligation in Greek; a foreign speaker who hears it in Hebrew also fulfills it, since, as Ravina points out, even the Sages cannot say what ha'ahashteranim benei haramakhim means. Meanwhile the Sages learn four obscure biblical words by overhearing a maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's house talking about visitors, purslane, hair, and a broom.
megillah/18.question: If hearing words you cannot parse still counts as publicizing the miracle, what is the listener actually receiving?

judge.reachNote: What a recitation transmits when it transmits no meaning — whether the mitzva is comprehension or presence at the telling.

answer.quote: one who speaks a foreign language who hears the Megilla being read in Hebrew fulfills the mitzva of reading the Megilla and publicizing the Purim miracle
answer.explanation: The page rules that hearing the unparsed original still discharges the obligation and publicizes the miracle, but it never says what the uncomprehending listener actually receives, so the note's question survives.

summaryProblems.claim: The Sages learn four obscure biblical words from the maidservant
summaryProblems.pageSays: the Sages did not know what is meant by the word ḥalogelogot, which appears in various mishnayot and baraitot

judge.feedback: The summary says "The Sages learn four obscure biblical words from the maidservant", but the page says "the Sages did not know what is meant by the word ḥalogelogot, which appears in various mishnayot and baraitot". Say what the page says. Fix the description of the maidservant stories: only some of those words are biblical (salseleha, matatei), while seirugin and ḥalogelogot come from mishnayot and baraitot, so call them obscure words rather than biblical words. Everything else in the summary tracks the page. Keep the question as it stands — it reaches the real idea and the page's Ravina line only restates the ruling without answering it.

megillah/19.summary: Four sages disagree about where a person must begin reading the Megilla on Purim: from the very first verse, from the introduction of Mordecai, from the rise of Haman, or from the night the king could not sleep. Rabbi Yoḥanan says all four were reading one phrase in Esther, "acts of power," and each heard a different power in it: Ahasuerus, Mordecai, Haman, the miracle. Rav rules for reading all of it, and adds that even a partial reader needs a complete scroll.
megillah/19.question: If the scroll has to be written in full even for someone who starts reading at Mordecai, what is the difference between words that must exist and words that must be said out loud?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a sacred text's integrity as a written object may be a separate requirement from the obligation of what must be voiced.

megillah/20.summary: Rabbi Yehuda argues that a minor may read the Megilla and offers himself as evidence: as a boy he read it before Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders in Lod. The Sages dismiss him twice over, first because a minor's testimony cannot be cited, then because a man who permits a practice cannot prove it by doing it. Later the page hunts for when day begins; Rava reads Genesis, and his reading collapses once night is tested the same way.
megillah/20.question: If Rabbi Yehuda's own boyhood reading is disqualified because he was a minor then and biased now, what evidence could ever establish that minors read the Megilla?

judge.reachNote: Underneath: a precedent set by the one who permits the act cannot authenticate itself, so practice may be unable to serve as proof at all.

summaryProblems.claim: The Sages dismissed Rabbi Yehuda's own boyhood testimony twice over, both because he was a minor and because one who permits cannot prove by doing.
summaryProblems.pageSays: It is taught in a different baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: When I was a minor I read the Megilla before Rabbi Yehuda.

summaryProblems.claim: The 'one who permits it' objection was aimed at Rabbi Yehuda's report of reading before Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders.
summaryProblems.pageSays: They said to him: One cannot bring a proof that an act is permitted from the behavior of the very one who permits it.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The Sages dismissed Rabbi Yehuda's own boyhood testimony twice over, both because he was a minor and because one who permits cannot prove by doing.", but the page says "It is taught in a different baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: When I was a minor I read the Megilla before Rabbi Yehuda.". Say what the page says. The summary says "The 'one who permits it' objection was aimed at Rabbi Yehuda's report of reading before Rabbi Tarfon and the Elders.", but the page says "They said to him: One cannot bring a proof that an act is permitted from the behavior of the very one who permits it.". Say what the page says. The page contains two separate baraitot: Rabbi Yehuda testifying about himself before Rabbi Tarfon, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi testifying that he read before Rabbi Yehuda. Rewrite so the twofold rejection (minor's testimony plus the one-who-permits objection) is attached to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's report, where the Gemara places it. The question should then rest on that correct setup, and can still ask what evidence could ever establish the practice.

megillah/21.summary: A person may read the Megilla, the scroll of Esther, sitting or standing, but the Torah must be read standing, since receiving it is compared to Sinai, where the people stood. A baraita permits one Torah reader and one translator into Aramaic, but never two translators at once, because two voices cannot be heard simultaneously. Yet for the Megilla, ten may read and ten translate, since a cherished text keeps listeners straining to catch it.
megillah/21.question: If affection for a story is enough to make ten overlapping voices intelligible, what does it say about the Torah reading that it is assumed to need one voice and silence?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that attention, not acoustics, is what determines whether a text can be heard through competing voices.

answer.quote: as there is less of a need to ensure that everyone hears the precise translation, as the Prophets do not teach halakha
answer.explanation: The page bears on why Torah needs a single clear voice — its translation must be heard precisely because it teaches halakha — but it never directly states what the Torah's need for silence says about it, so the question survives.

megillah/22.summary: A Torah paragraph of five verses has to be split between two readers, and neither half reaches the required three verses. Rav has the second reader repeat the first reader's last verse; Shmuel has them cut the third verse in half, so that nobody entering or leaving the synagogue mid-reading can think a reader recited only two. Against Shmuel stands the rule that a verse Moses did not divide stays undivided, relaxed only for schoolchildren.
megillah/22.question: If a verse may be cut in half for children only because there is no other way to teach them, what makes two readers and five verses the same kind of no other way?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that necessity alone licenses breaking the rule against dividing a verse, and asks how far 'necessity' stretches.

answer.quote: Here, too, when a paragraph of five verses must be divided between two readers, it is not possible to divide them without dividing the middle verse.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself draws the schoolchildren comparison and states that the five-verse case is likewise a case where no other division is possible, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 22a: "Here, too, when a paragraph of five verses must be divided between two readers, it is not possible to divide them without dividing the middle verse.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The Gemara explicitly answers this comparison a few lines later, saying that here too it is not possible to divide the paragraph without splitting the middle verse, so the question is closed by the page. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing — for instance, why Shmuel treats the case as impossible when Rav's repetition plainly solves it, or why the enterers-and-leavers worry outweighs the ban on dividing what Moses did not divide. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

megillah/23.summary: Ten men are needed before the Torah is read in public, before the priests bless the people, and before mourners are blessed in the square by the cemetery. Rabbi Yoḥanan finds that number in the verse "And I shall be hallowed among the children of Israel," linking the word "among" to Korah's rebellious congregation, and that congregation in turn to the ten spies who slandered the land. The count that makes speech holy is borrowed from two groups the Torah condemns.
megillah/23.question: If ten is what turns a gathering into one that can say God's name aloud, why is that ten counted off from Korah's rebels and the ten slandering spies?

judge.reachNote: It asks why the minimum community capable of hallowing God's name is measured by assemblies the Torah condemns — whether a congregation's number is morally neutral.

megillah/24.summary: A priest whose hands are blemished, spotted, or bent may not lift them for the Priestly Benediction, since the congregation will stare. Then come the exceptions: Rav Huna's neighbor with constantly running eyes blessed anyway, and Rabbi Yoḥanan's one-eyed neighbor did too, because each was a familiar figure in his town. A dyer's stained hands are fine if most of the town dyes. The defect moves from the body to the crowd's attention.
megillah/24.question: If a priest with running eyes may bless once his neighbors are used to him, was the problem ever in his eyes?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether the disqualification lies in the priest's body or in the onlookers' distraction — but the page already says so in as many words.

answer.quote: That priest was a familiar figure in his town. Since the other residents were accustomed to seeing him, he would not draw their attention
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the disqualification tracks the congregation's attention rather than the defect itself, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Megillah 24b: "That priest was a familiar figure in his town. Since the other residents were accustomed to seeing him, he would not draw their attention". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question directly: the one-eyed priest is barred "because people will gaze at him," and the familiar-figure exception says the concern is attention, not the defect. The summary's own last line already concedes the answer, so the question adds nothing. Ask instead something the page leaves unsettled — e.g. why familiarity alone excuses running eyes and blindness in one eye, while Rabbi Yehuda's dyed hands are excused only when most of the town dyes, or why the baraita limits disqualifying blemishes to face, hands, and feet.

megillah/25.summary: A prayer leader who tells God that the mercy shown to a mother bird sent away from her nest should extend to the congregation is silenced. One sage says he makes God look like He favors one creature; another says he turns the King's decrees into sentiment. The page then sorts Scripture into what is read and translated and what is read only, with Reuben's night with Bilhah left untranslated and the translator told to stop mid-verse.
megillah/25.question: Why is the Golden Calf itself broadcast so that public shame brings atonement, while Aaron's excuse for it is read but kept from the translator?
