Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer, for instance asking why publicity and risk of punishment should count as two rival ways of establishing status, or why the Nehemiah precedent is said not to settle it. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

ketubot/25.summary: A man comes to Rabbi Ami and says another man is a priest, because he saw him called up to the Torah first in the synagogue. Reish Lakish wants harder evidence, a share of teruma (the produce portion given to priests) at the threshing floor; Rabbi Yoḥanan asks whether priesthood ceases where there is no threshing floor. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then splits a father's word in half: believed to feed his son teruma, not believed to marry him off.
ketubot/25.question: If a father's word is enough to put teruma in his son's mouth, what makes it too weak to find that son a wife?

judge.reachNote: The idea is that credibility is bounded by control — one is trusted only about what one could have effected anyway.

answer.quote: I deem him credible to enable his son to partake of teruma, as it is within his purview to feed his son teruma
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi explicitly explains the split: a man is believed about what lies within his own power (feeding teruma) but not about marrying off his son, which is not within his purview.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 25b: "I deem him credible to enable his son to partake of teruma, as it is within his purview to feed his son teruma". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the father is believed about teruma because feeding his son teruma is within his purview, and not believed about marriage because it is not. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, why Rabbi Ḥiyya refuses the split and insists on all-or-nothing, or why the relative-disqualification objection raised at the end applies to a brother but not obviously to a son. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

ketubot/26.summary: A man mentions in passing that as a child he was taken out of school, immersed, and fed teruma, the produce portion reserved for priests, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi elevates him to priesthood on that offhand memory. The Gemara then tracks a man demoted, restored, demoted, and restored again as witnesses trickle in one at a time. Rabbi Eliezer would leave him down, worried about contempt for the court; Rav Ashi says the real argument is whether separate witnesses merge.
ketubot/26.question: If two witnesses who came in separately say exactly what two witnesses arriving together would say, is a court that refuses to reverse itself again guarding the truth or its own dignity?

judge.reachNote: Whether a court's reluctance to reverse itself serves the integrity of its rulings or merely its public standing — the page itself sets 'contempt for the court' against 'the matter be determined based on the relevant testimonies.'

answer.quote: Rather, Rav Ashi said: It is with regard to whether two single witnesses join together and constitute two witnesses for the purpose of testimony that they disagree
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi rejects the contempt-of-court reading and relocates the dispute to the evidentiary question of whether separately arriving witnesses merge, which bears directly on the note's either/or but does not settle whether a court's refusal is truth-guarding or dignity-guarding.

ketubot/27.summary: A besieged city falls, and every woman married to a priest inside is forbidden to her husband unless a witness, even a slave or maidservant, says she was not raped. The Gemara then presses on doubt, asking whether one hiding place that holds a single woman can clear all of them. Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav swears his wife's hand never left his while the gentiles were in Jerusalem; the Sages reject his word, and he keeps her in a house in his courtyard, never alone with her.
ketubot/27.question: If the Sages will not accept Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav's oath about his own wife, what is he doing when he keeps her in his courtyard behind a screen of sons?

judge.reachNote: The gap between a man's certain private knowledge and the legal status the Sages impose on him: he obeys a ruling founded on a suspicion he knows to be false.

answer.quote: because with regard to a captive woman the Sages ruled leniently, since the prohibition is based on suspicion and not certainty
answer.where: Ketubot 27b (Gemara on Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav's mishna, Abaye's dilemma)
answer.explanation: Abaye's dilemma supplies a reason why this arrangement was tolerated for Rabbi Zekharya — the captive-woman prohibition rests on suspicion, not certainty — but the page never states what Zekharya himself intends by the arrangement, so the question can still be honestly asked.

ketubot/28.summary: A man who watched his father write as a small boy may testify years later that a signature is his father's hand. The same credit covers a teacher's writing, a wedding he remembers, a field where a grave was plowed up, but never a neighbor's disputed footpath, since a child's memory cannot move land. At the end comes ketzatza: relatives smash a barrel of fruit in the public square so that children will remember which marriage was unsuitable.
ketubot/28.question: If the barrel is broken in public precisely so that children will carry the memory into adulthood, what is being handed down, a record of lineage or a family's shame?

judge.reachNote: Asks what a publicized ritual actually transmits: a usable record of lineage, or a lasting stigma attached to a family.

ketubot/29.summary: The mishna lists young women whose rapist still owes the fine to their father: a mamzeret, born of a forbidden union, a Samaritan woman, his own sister, a menstruating woman. The Gemara objects that the verse says she shall be as a wife to him, which ought to limit the fine to women he could lawfully marry. Reish Lakish and Rav Pappa answer by counting the six times "young woman" and "virgin" appear in the two passages, assigning each word its own job.
ketubot/29.question: If the fifty-shekel fine belongs to the father in the first place, why does Abaye read the verse to mean that her death before the trial wipes the payment out?
gate: the question brings in "Abaye", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the fine is the father's property right or a payment that exists only through the living daughter's loss.

answer.quote: From the fact that the verse does not simply say: To her father, it is inferred: To the father of the young woman and not to the father of a dead woman.
answer.explanation: The page supplies Abaye's textual reason for the reading — the verse's phrasing "the father of the young woman" rather than "her father" — but it never addresses why the father's own claim to the fine should lapse with the daughter's death, so the tension the question raises remains live.

ketubot/30.summary: Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana held that someone liable to death at the hand of Heaven pays no damages, just as a person executed by a court pays nothing. Rav Ḥisda's objection bites: a thief who eats another's forbidden fat owns it the moment he lifts it, so the debt lands before the sin does. To save the rule, the Gemara builds a case where a non-priest has teruma, the priestly portion of produce, pushed straight down his throat.
ketubot/30.question: Is a rule still being tested when the only case left standing is food someone else shoved into another man's pharynx, retrievable only with great effort?

judge.reachNote: When a principle survives only in an artificially engineered case, is it still being tested or merely protected?

answer.quote: Rav Ashi said: It is referring to a non-priest who partook of his own teruma, e.g., if the non-priest inherited teruma from a priest, or acquired ownership from a priest.
answer.explanation: The page's closing answers (Rav Pappa's teruma liquids and Rav Ashi's inherited teruma) show the contrived pharynx case is not the only one left standing, so the Abaye–Rava dispute retains a plausible application, though the note's broader worry about testing a rule through forced cases still stands.

ketubot/31.summary: An arrow flies four cubits across a public domain on Shabbat, a capital act of carrying, and rips someone's silk in flight; Rabbi Avin says the shooter owes nothing, since the lifting and the landing are one deed. Rav Hisda answers that a thief who eats stolen forbidden fat still pays, because he could have bent down and eaten without picking it up. Two tests emerge, and a man walking with a knife separates them.
ketubot/31.question: If the thief who pauses to rest pays for the purse while the one who pauses only to shift it on his shoulder does not, what is that pause really dividing?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — when do lifting and placement count as one deed and when as two — but the page names that answer explicitly.

answer.quote: the initial lifting is exclusively theft and not the start of a prohibited labor, as by stopping, he separated the lifting from the carrying out
answer.explanation: The page states outright what the pause divides — it severs the act of lifting from the act of carrying out, so the lifting counts only as theft — and adds that adjusting the load is 'the typical manner of proceeding and would not be considered an interruption.'

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Ḥisda's reason for the fat-eater paying is that he could have bent down and eaten without picking the fat up.
summaryProblems.pageSays: he is obligated to pay for the fat, as he is already liable for theft before he comes to violate the prohibition against eating forbidden fat

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 31a: "the initial lifting is exclusively theft and not the start of a prohibited labor, as by stopping, he separated the lifting from the carrying out". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rav Ḥisda's reason for the fat-eater paying is that he could have bent down and eaten without picking the fat up.", but the page says "he is obligated to pay for the fat, as he is already liable for theft before he comes to violate the prohibition against eating forbidden fat". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words on 31a: stopping separates the lifting from the carrying out, so the lifting is theft alone, while shifting a load on the shoulder is the normal way of walking and no interruption at all. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — e.g. why the Gemara abandons the 'stopped' answer for ben Azzai's claim that every step is a pause, which would dissolve almost all carrying into separate acts. Also fix the attribution: Rav Ḥisda's own reason is that the theft is complete before the eating; the bending-down argument is the Gemara's later refutation of the arrow comparison.

ketubot/32.summary: Two mishnayot collide over a man who forces relations with his sister: one has him pay the fifty-shekel fine, the other has him flogged. Ulla narrows the flogging case down to a grown, seduced, or orphaned woman who is owed nothing, then argues that money always displaces lashes, and the Gemara demolishes each proof until only a shared word, tahat, "for," props it up. Rabbi Yohanan instead makes it turn on forewarning: warned by witnesses, he is flogged; unwarned, he pays.
ketubot/32.question: Why should a warning shouted by bystanders moments beforehand decide whether the woman's family collects fifty shekels or the man's back is struck instead?

judge.reachNote: A procedural precondition for corporal punishment ends up deciding whether the victim's family is compensated at all.

answer.quote: Since no lashes are administered without forewarning, the rapist pays the fine.
answer.explanation: The page explains the mechanism — lashes are legally impossible without forewarning, and the verse teaches "you cannot render him liable for two acts of wickedness," so lashes take precedence when available — but it never addresses why the woman's compensation should hinge on that procedural fact.

ketubot/33.summary: A man who injures another pays damages rather than receiving lashes, and the page hunts for a verse that proves it. One attempt reads the case of two men quarreling who strike a pregnant woman: if they were warned against killing, they were warned against injuring, and still the Torah says he pays. Rav Ashi breaks the chain by asking how anyone knows execution is the more severe punishment, citing Rav's claim that flogging would have broken three famous martyrs.
ketubot/33.question: If a whipping might have induced the three men who chose a fiery furnace over bowing to a statue to bow after all, which punishment is really the harsher one?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of how the law ranks the severity of punishments, but the page itself resolves it with the limited/unlimited flogging distinction.

answer.quote: And is there no difference to you between flogging that has a limit, e.g., forty lashes by Torah law, which is a less severe punishment
answer.explanation: Rav Samma answers Rav Ashi's severity comparison directly by distinguishing limited Torah lashes (less severe than death) from unlimited coercive flogging (more severe), which is what the Hananiah case involved.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 33b: "And is there no difference to you between flogging that has a limit, e.g., forty lashes by Torah law, which is a less severe punishment". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks which punishment is truly harsher, and the page answers it twice: Rav Samma distinguishes limited forty-lash flogging from unlimited coercive flogging. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for instance, why an argument about the relative severity of death and lashes should govern whether a forewarning for murder carries over to injury, or what it means that the Gemara measures severity by what would break a person's resolve rather than by what ends his life.

ketubot/34.summary: A thief who slaughters a stolen animal on Shabbat raises a prior problem: is meat produced by deliberate desecration of Shabbat even edible? Rabbi Ḥiyya reads the verse "it is sacred to you" to treat such food like consecrated Temple property, off limits to eat but not to benefit from. Rabba then moves the argument to timing: steal the kid first and slaughter it on Shabbat and the fine stands, but steal and slaughter in one act and the death penalty swallows the payment.
ketubot/34.question: Why should a thief owe the owner five times the animal when he stole it last week, and owe nothing when the theft and the slaughter happen in the same breath?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that liability must attach at a moment untouched by capital exposure — a fine can survive execution only if it was already incurred.

answer.quote: if there is no payment for theft, due to his liability to receive the death penalty for desecrating Shabbat
answer.explanation: Rabba himself explains the distinction the question asks about: prior theft means "he was already liable for stealing before he came to violate the prohibition" of Shabbat, whereas simultaneous theft carries no payment because of the capital liability, and without the theft payment the slaughter fine collapses.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 34b: "if there is no payment for theft, due to his liability to receive the death penalty for desecrating Shabbat". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim by Rabba's own reasoning on 34b ("he was already liable for stealing before he came to violate the prohibition" and "if there is no payment for theft... there is no liability for slaughter"), so it cannot stand as written. Rewrite it to press on what remains hard after that answer — for instance why Rabba needed to say it twice, for Shabbat and for burglary, given the Gemara's claim that eternal versus transitory punishment and forewarning make the two cases non-obvious, or why a fine is said to survive execution at all if the death penalty otherwise cancels payment. Keep the summary's thread about timing; only the question needs replacing.

ketubot/35.summary: A verse pairs two blows, one who smites an animal and one who smites a person, and the Gemara reads the pairing to mean that a man who kills owes no money at all, whether or not a court ever executes him. Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish then argue about a lesser penalty, lashes, meaning a court flogging: does liability for lashes also cancel a payment? Reish Lakish's proof needs an odd case, a man who strikes another and tears his silk in the same motion.
ketubot/35.question: If a man liable to lashes owes nothing even when no court ever flogs him, what is left for the person he injured?

judge.reachNote: Whether a punishment owed to the court can wipe out a debt owed to the victim — who bears the loss when two liabilities collide.

answer.quote: Therefore, in the case of one who is liable to receive lashes, unless one is actually flogged, he is obligated to pay for the damage he inflicted.
answer.explanation: The page gives Rabbi Yoḥanan's contrary position, which preserves payment when no flogging occurs, but it never says what recourse the injured party has under Reish Lakish's blanket exemption, so the question can still be asked.

ketubot/36.summary: Sumakhos, in Rabbi Meir's name, says a husband cannot claim his blind wife came to the marriage without her hymen intact: girls who fall and bleed show their mothers, and she never saw the blood. Much of the page runs on presumptions like that, about minors, a woman who never develops signs of puberty, and a woman ransomed from captivity. At the close, a man who pays her ransom and says she was untouched may marry her; a man who only testifies may not.
ketubot/36.question: Why does a man's ransom money count as proof of what he says, when the same man's sworn word alone does not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that costly action is treated as better evidence of belief than words, since words can be shaped by self-interest.

answer.quote: as a person does not throw away money for nothing. If he paid the ransom to redeem her, he must be certain
answer.where: Ketubot 36b (the Rabbis' explanation at the end)
answer.explanation: The page explicitly gives the reason the ransom payment is credited and mere testimony is not — the payer would not waste money, while a witness alone may be lying because "he had his eye on her."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 36b (the Rabbis' explanation at the end): "as a person does not throw away money for nothing. If he paid the ransom to redeem her, he must be certain". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: a person does not throw away money for nothing, while a mere witness is suspected of having his eye on her. Write a question that starts after that answer — for example, why the Rabbis trust a man's financial stake here when elsewhere on this page the halakha leans on presumptions about the woman's body rather than on anyone's word, or why Rabbi Yehuda's concern that a sinner not profit does not equally govern the captive's fine and her teruma.

ketubot/37.summary: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel catches Rabbi Yehuda holding two positions about how long a woman freed from captivity must wait before marrying, and Rav Yosef falls silent. The rest of the page hunts for separate work for each verse that forbids paying money in place of execution, including one that likens murderers to the heifer beheaded in a riverbed when a corpse is found between two towns. That likeness nearly imports the cleaver and the nape, until "love your neighbor" is read as choosing an agreeable death.
ketubot/37.question: If the likeness to the beheaded calf is strong enough to fix the neck as the place of execution, what makes it too weak to fix the cleaver as the tool?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is how far an analogy carries: which features of a compared case transfer and which are blocked by a competing value.

answer.quote: the verse says: "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18), from which it is derived: Choose for him an agreeable death.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection — that the likeness should import the cleaver and the nape — and answers that the command to love one's neighbor requires an agreeable death, so only the neck is derived and not the cleaver.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 37b: "the verse says: "And you shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18), from which it is derived: Choose for him an agreeable death.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a line later on the page — "choose for him an agreeable death" is precisely why the cleaver does not transfer, and the summary itself already names that answer. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and asks what remains hard, for example why an ethical reading of "love your neighbor" can trim one detail out of a derivation while leaving the rest of it standing. Alternatively, build the question from the untouched first half of the page, such as whether a captive's presumed self-protection is a claim about her piety or a legal convenience.

ketubot/38.summary: A man who blinds another and then kills him with a second blow pays nothing for the eye, since he gives his life instead. The mishna turns to a young woman betrothed, divorced, and then raped: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says no fine is owed at all, Rabbi Akiva says fifty silver pieces are owed, and the Gemara finds two Rabbi Akivas disagreeing over who collects. Rava closes by asking whether a girl who died can still reach adulthood in the grave.
ketubot/38.question: If being betrothed and divorced leaves her body unchanged, why should it change whose money the fine becomes?
gate: "Rabbi Akivas" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea: whether entitlement follows bodily change or legal status, but the page already states that status, not body, governs who collects.

answer.quote: her fine is paid to herself, not her father, as since she was betrothed and divorced she is no longer subject to her father's authority
answer.explanation: The page explicitly gives the reason the money changes hands — betrothal and divorce removed her from her father's authority — even though her body is unchanged.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 38a, Mishna: "her fine is paid to herself, not her father, as since she was betrothed and divorced she is no longer subject to her father's authority". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the mishna itself, which says the fine goes to her because betrothal and divorce removed her from her father's authority. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer, e.g. ask why the Gemara then needs the "her body did not change" reasoning, or why the same divorce that frees her from her father's authority leaves her still readable as "a young woman who is a virgin." Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

ketubot/39.summary: A rapist pays the father four things and a seducer three, the extra being payment for pain. The Gemara argues over what that pain is: Shmuel's father says it is being slammed to the ground, and Rabbi Zeira objects by asking what happens if he slammed her onto silk. Abaye, Rava and Rav Pappa each answer by reporting what a woman in their own household told them about the pain of first intercourse.
ketubot/39.question: If a rapist is bound by Torah law to marry his victim and never divorce her, yet Rabbi Yosei says he can torment her until she asks to leave, what is that forced marriage actually holding in place?
gate: the question brings in "Yosei", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Asks what a Torah obligation actually secures when the obligated party can engineer its dissolution — the gap between a legal bond and its protective purpose.

answer.quote: he can torment her until she says: I do not want you. When she initiates the divorce, he can divorce her. Therefore, the Sages instituted that she receives the marriage contract
answer.explanation: The page states that the forced marriage is in fact escapable through tormenting her into initiating divorce, and that the ketubah of a non-virgin was instituted precisely to deter this, which bears on but does not fully settle what the compelled marriage secures.

ketubot/40.summary: The fine for rape is fifty sela, a fixed weight of silver, the same whether the victim is a king's daughter or a commoner's. Rabbi Zeira argues the flat sum cannot cover everything, since humiliation and degradation obviously vary; Abaye answers that the Torah also fixes thirty sela for a slave gored by an ox, pearl-piercer and tailor alike. The extra payments are then derived from verses, and they go to the father.
ketubot/40.question: If the father collects for her humiliation because he could have humiliated her himself by marrying her off to a man afflicted with boils, whose injury is actually being paid for?

judge.reachNote: Whether compensation for shame tracks the person shamed or the person who holds authority over her standing.

answer.quote: it is reasonable that the payments of humiliation and degradation are paid to her father, as if he wished to do so he could give her hand in marriage to a repulsive man
answer.explanation: The page explains why the father receives the payment — her humiliation is under his control — but never says whose injury the money compensates, which is what the question presses on after granting that reasoning.

ketubot/41.summary: A man admits he seduced someone's daughter, and the mishna has him pay for humiliation and degradation but not the fine, since a confession never triggers a fine. Rav Pappa presses Abaye: what if the woman agrees to his account, and her father, and the whole family? Abaye keeps moving the line, ending with a relative overseas who would object. Later the Gemara conclusively refutes Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, on half damage for a goring ox, then rules like him anyway.
ketubot/41.question: If some relative abroad can always be presumed to object, is Abaye guarding a family's name or building a rule that nothing could ever satisfy?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rule whose conditions can never in practice be met is a protection of interests or simply an absolute prohibition in disguise.

answer.quote: as it is not within his power to tarnish the reputation of the daughter of so-and-so based merely on his confession
answer.explanation: The baraita gives the underlying rationale — a confession simply has no power to tarnish another's reputation — which suggests the exemption is categorical, but the page never says whether Abaye's chain of ever-receding consents is meant as protection or as an unsatisfiable condition.

ketubot/42.summary: A man who rapes or seduces an unmarried young woman owes her father fifty shekels of silver, a fixed penalty set by the Torah rather than payment for actual loss. The argument asks whether a court verdict converts that penalty into ordinary debt, collectible and inheritable by the father's sons. Rav Yosef, after twenty-two years stuck on it, read the wording "shall give" in Deuteronomy to mean the father owns the money only once it is handed over; if he dies first, the daughter takes it.
ketubot/42.question: If the father's right to the fifty shekels begins only when the coins are actually handed over, what did the court award him when it ruled in his favor?

judge.reachNote: What a court judgment actually creates — a vested, ownable claim or merely standing to collect — is the idea the question reaches.

answer.quote: The Torah entitled the father to this money only from the time of giving. Consequently, if the father dies before receiving the money, he does not bequeath
answer.explanation: The page states that the verdict leaves the father without a transmissible right, and that the daughter then takes his place as plaintiff, but it never says what the ruling in his favor did confer, so the question survives.

ketubot/43.summary: An orphan girl is fed from her dead father's estate, and the argument is over who keeps the money she earns. Rav Sheshet says the brothers step into the father's place; Rav says the wages are hers, reading a verse about bequeathing slaves to mean a man does not bequeath rights over his daughter to his sons. Along the way the Gemara weighs whose comfort a dead man would have wanted more, his daughter's or his widow's.
ketubot/43.question: If a dead father is assumed to want his daughter living in comfort, why is she the one sent begging at people's doors when the estate cannot feed both her and his widow?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a dead man's presumed wishes are the measure, and that those wishes can rank comfort and shame differently.

ketubot/44.summary: A husband writes his wife a second marriage contract for a larger sum, and Rav Huna lets her collect from either one. That pulls in Rav Nahman's rule that when two deeds cover the same field, the later one cancels the earlier, unless the writer threw in something extra, even a single palm tree. Rafram and Rav Aha split over the reason: one says the first deed was forged, the other that the buyer merely waived its earlier date.
ketubot/44.question: Rafram's explanation quietly makes the witnesses who signed the first deed suspect in every other document they ever signed, so is a guess about why someone rewrote a contract enough to stain two men who were never asked?

judge.reachNote: An inference drawn to explain a second deed silently convicts absent third parties, raising whether legal reconstructions may carry reputational costs for people never heard.

ketubot/45.summary: A young woman who committed adultery while betrothed is stoned at the entrance to her father's house, and the page asks what happens if she has grown into an adult before the witnesses arrive. Rabbi Ile'a reads the verse as fixing her status at the moment of the deed, so stoning stands. Rabbi Ḥanina presses back: then a husband who falsely defamed her should still owe the hundred sela, a heavy silver fine, and the two trade prayers to be spared each other's view.
ketubot/45.question: Is the distinction between a deed and a spoken accusation really enough to date her guilt to the adultery and his to the day he opened his mouth?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of when liability crystallizes — at the moment of the forbidden act or at the moment the accusation is uttered — and whether that timing principle is coherent across the two parties.

ketubot/46.summary: A husband comes to court and announces that he found no proof of his bride's virginity, and if the accusation is shown to be false he is flogged and pays her father a hundred sela, a large sum in silver. Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov reads the verses plainly: the couple had intercourse, and the father spreads an actual stained cloth before the Elders. The Rabbis read the same cloth as witnesses being cross-examined until the matter is clear.
ketubot/46.question: If "go in unto her" can mean words and the spread garment can mean cross-examined witnesses, what in the passage would the Rabbis still be obliged to read literally?

judge.reachNote: Where a school's figurative reading of verses must stop, i.e. what anchors a non-literal midrash so the law still has a case attached to it.

ketubot/47.summary: A father may not eat the produce of land his daughter owns, though a husband may eat his wife's, and the Gemara asks what the difference is. The answer is a trade: the Sages granted the husband that produce in exchange for his duty to ransom her from captivity, assuming that unpaid, he might not bother. Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, extends the same suspicion to fathers; the first tanna refuses to.
ketubot/47.question: If a father really will not turn a blind eye to his own flesh and blood, why does Rabbi Yosei think he would leave a captive daughter to pay her own ransom?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether natural paternal love can be relied on as a legal presumption, but the page already supplies Rabbi Yosei's counter-reasoning verbatim.

answer.quote: a father will also refrain from redeeming her, as he will reason: A pouch of money is held in her hand for a time of need, so let her go and redeem herself.
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yosei's exact reasoning for why a father might leave his captive daughter to ransom herself — she has her own funds available.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 47a: "a father will also refrain from redeeming her, as he will reason: A pouch of money is held in her hand for a time of need, so let her go and redeem herself.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very lines the summary paraphrases: the page says the father reasons that a pouch of money is in her hand, so let her redeem herself. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance, why the Sages let the husband consume the produce now rather than reserve it for ransom, or why Abaye's pairing of common obligation with common right should govern which right is exchanged for which duty. Keep the summary; only the question needs replacing.

ketubot/48.summary: A father hands his daughter to her husband's messengers for the trip to the wedding canopy, and the page asks what that handover actually transfers. Rav says everything except teruma, the food set aside for priests that only their households may eat; Shmuel says only inheritance; Reish Lakish adds her marriage contract. The Tosefta, an early collection of teachings parallel to the Mishna, refutes them all on teruma, yet a separate teaching treats her adultery as a married woman's.
ketubot/48.question: If handing her to the messengers is not enough to let her eat teruma, why is it enough to change the death she would face for adultery?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a change of domain may be partial — a woman can count as married for one body of law and unmarried for another.

answer.quote: “To play the whore in her father’s house” (Deuteronomy 22:21), which excludes a case when the father has delivered her to the husband’s messengers
answer.explanation: The page supplies a scriptural derivation for why the handover changes her adultery status, but never reconciles that with the Tosefta's ruling that teruma waits for the wedding canopy, so the tension the question names remains open.

ketubot/49.summary: A mishna rules that a father is not legally obligated to feed his daughter; only after his death do daughters draw sustenance from his estate. The Gemara then reports an Usha enactment that a man must support his young sons and daughters, and asks whether courts enforce it. The answer comes from what judges actually did: Rav Yehuda invoked the jackal that feeds its young, Rav Hisda made the father stand on an overturned mortar and shame himself publicly, Rava asked if charity suited him.
ketubot/49.question: If a court can stand a man on a mortar in the marketplace until he supports his children, in what sense is it declining to compel him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of moral suasion versus legal compulsion, but the page names that distinction outright.

answer.quote: although these Sages stated forcefully that it is proper for a father to support his children, they did not force him to do so by the authority of the court
answer.explanation: The page itself draws the very line the question asks about: the sages' shaming was forceful moral pressure, not compulsion by court authority, and it adds that only a wealthy father is actually coerced.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 49b: "although these Sages stated forcefully that it is proper for a father to support his children, they did not force him to do so by the authority of the court". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words, saying the Sages spoke forcefully but "did not force him to do so by the authority of the court," so the question as written is already resolved. Build the new question on what the page leaves unsettled, for instance why wealth changes the picture ("if he is wealthy we coerce him against his will"), or why the Usha enactment can be instituted yet not be the halakha. The summary is accurate but should mention the wealth distinction so the question has something to stand on.

ketubot/50.summary: Orphaned daughters are sustained from their dead father's estate, and the argument here is whether that support can come from movable goods or only from land. Rav Nahman tells judges who collected from movable property to reverse themselves or he will seize their own houses, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim stops Rabbi Elazar from ruling for the daughters, telling him he is moved by pity rather than law. Rav Yosef awards a daughter dates, then insists he meant dates still hanging on the tree.
ketubot/50.question: If everyone agrees the daughters need feeding, why is the fear that students will copy a merciful ruling enough to stop it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the tension between compassion in a single case and the law-making force of a judge's precedent.

ketubot/51.summary: A marriage contract binds a husband to ransom his wife from captivity even if he never wrote that clause, since the court imposes it. Shmuel's father reads the danger differently: a woman who was raped may have acquiesced partway through, so she becomes forbidden to her Israelite husband. Rav objects from the ransom clause itself, Shmuel's father answers nothing, and Rava holds that even a woman who ends willingly acted under compulsion and stays permitted.
ketubot/51.question: If Rava says the evil inclination seized her and she is permitted, why does the same page still sort captive women by whether they carried bread to their captors or whether their captor was grand enough never to marry them?

judge.reachNote: When is compulsion presumed as a doctrine, and when must it still be proved from the woman's conduct and her captor's standing?

answer.quote: those stolen by bandits are not considered to be like captives, as there is a concern that they might have consented to their captors, thinking that they will marry them
answer.explanation: The page indicates the sorting concerns whether there was genuine duress or consent motivated by hope of marriage, which is a different matter from Rava's case of an act that begins as rape, but the page never states this reconciliation with Rava explicitly, so the question can still be asked.

ketubot/52.summary: A husband's marriage contract promises, "And I will restore you to me as a wife," and that clause is what obligates him to ransom her if she is taken captive. The page tests what happens when a vow barring her from benefiting from him makes the promise impossible; Sumakhos reasons the exemption can only apply if the vow came first, or a husband could simply vow his way out of paying. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then caps ransom at a captive's ordinary price, since overpaying invites more kidnapping.
ketubot/52.question: If a husband who vows after his wife is captured is suspected of trickery, while one who vowed beforehand is simply exempt, what has changed for the woman still in the captors' hands?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The rule tracks the husband's obligation, timing and motive rather than the captive's actual plight, which is identical either way.

answer.quote: If he wants to release himself from the duty to ransom his wife after she is captured, he can simply vow that she may not derive benefit from him
answer.explanation: The page explains that the distinction turns entirely on preventing the husband's manipulation, which bears on the question but never addresses what differs from the captive woman's side, so it can still honestly be asked.

ketubot/53.summary: Rav Pappa pushes Yehuda bar Mareimar to enter the house of Abba of Sura, who is marrying off his daughter; Yehuda resists, because a guest of his standing will shame the father into enlarging the dowry. Forced inside, he sits without a word, and Abba reads the silence as anger and writes over everything he owns. Yehuda then says the gift is not to his liking, but refuses to let Abba retract, since a man should not become one who takes back his word.
ketubot/53.question: If Yehuda bar Mareimar knew his mere presence would empty the man's estate, does holding him to the signed dowry repair the pressure or complete it?

judge.reachNote: Whether keeping a man to a promise extracted by honor and awe restores his dignity or merely locks in the coercion.

answer.quote: I did not speak so that you should turn yourself into the kind of person who retracts once he gives his word.
answer.explanation: The page gives Yehuda's stated reason for barring retraction — protecting Abba from becoming a man who breaks his word — but does not settle whether that repairs or seals the pressure Yehuda's presence created.

ketubot/54.summary: A widow who stays in her late husband's house keeps eating from his estate, and the page hunts for the moment that right ends. Rav Hisda says licentious relations end it; Rav Yosef says painted eyes and dyed hair do, since sex may be mere appetite while dye is a plan. The accepted ruling rejects both and picks suing in court for her marriage contract payment; then the court appraises the clothes on her back and deducts them.
ketubot/54.question: Why should demanding in court the money she is owed count as cutting ties with her dead husband, when dyeing her hair for suitors apparently does not?

judge.reachNote: What counts as a widow severing her bond with the dead husband: a formal legal act asserting her claim, versus behavior that merely signals readiness to remarry.

answer.quote: One who claims the payment specified in her marriage contract in court does not have the right to continue receiving sustenance, as she has thereby demonstrated her desire to sever her ties
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason for the accepted rule about suing in court, but never explains why dyeing and painting fall short of that same severing, so the comparison the question asks about remains open.

ketubot/55.summary: A dying man gives away property and, though his word alone would suffice on a deathbed, also performs a formal act of acquisition. Rav's school says the gift now rides on two horses: valid even if he recovers, and strong enough to hand over a debt owed to him by speech alone. Shmuel says he does not know, since the extra act may show the man meant to wait for a bill of sale, which death voids.
ketubot/55.question: When a man reaches for a second safeguard, does that make his gift twice as firm, or show he never thought the first one finished the job?

judge.reachNote: Whether belt-and-suspenders drafting compounds a transaction's force or betrays that the giver did not rely on the simpler mode at all.

answer.quote: Perhaps his performance of an act of acquisition indicates that he resolved to transfer it to him only with a bill of sale.
answer.explanation: The page voices both halves of the note's dilemma — Rav's "two horses" strengthening and Shmuel's suspicion that the extra act shows the transfer was meant to await a deed — but leaves the matter undecided, Shmuel still saying he does not know.

ketubot/56.summary: Rabbi Yehuda lets a husband write a marriage contract, the document promising his wife a set sum if he dies or divorces her, for the full two hundred dinars, and then have her write a receipt for a hundred she never received. Rabbi Meir says any reduction below two hundred makes the marriage licentious intercourse. The page holds that the same waiver spoken aloud is worthless, since the Sages reinforced their own rules harder than Torah law.
ketubot/56.question: If the receipt records coins that never changed hands, why does the written fiction hold where the identical words said out loud do not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that form, not substance, can carry legal force when the Sages fortify their own decrees.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda holds: The marriage contract is a rabbinic law, and the Sages reinforced their pronouncements with greater force than Torah law.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly answers why the waiver must be written rather than spoken — the Sages reinforced their own rabbinic ordinance, so her declaration "has no force unless it is written down" — and Abaye separately explains why the fictional receipt is tolerated ("if he did not save it, it is he himself who will lose").

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 56a: "Rabbi Yehuda holds: The marriage contract is a rabbinic law, and the Sages reinforced their pronouncements with greater force than Torah law.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the page answers, and worse, the summary's own last sentence already gives that answer (rabbinic rules reinforced harder than Torah law), so the note answers itself. Rewrite the question to press on what stays difficult after that answer — for instance that the Gemara immediately undercuts the reinforcement principle with the produce case and the donkey drivers, forcing Abaye to invent the common/uncommon and certain/uncertain distinctions. Or ask about Rabbi Meir's move of calling the ketubba Torah law in order to void the stipulation.

ketubot/57.summary: Rav Dimi and Ravin each carried the same tradition from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, about when a wife can give up part of her marriage contract by word alone, and reported it backwards from each other. Rabbi Abbahu breaks the tie by citing a private conversation: Rabbi Yoḥanan told him that he and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi never disagreed at all. Rav Pappa says he would have read the sources the opposite way, since sages more plausibly differ in reasoning than in memory.
ketubot/57.question: Is it really easier to believe that two sages reasoned their way to opposite conclusions than that one of them carried the message home wrong?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a received tradition's chain of memory is treated as more reliable than a sage's independent reasoning, and asks why that ranking should hold.

answer.quote: it is more plausible to say that there is a dispute about logical reasoning than that there is a dispute about the correct transmission of a halakhic tradition
answer.explanation: The Gemara states the preference the question challenges, asserting that a dispute in reasoning is more plausible than a dispute in transmission, but it gives no grounds for that assertion, so the question can still be pressed.

ketubot/58.summary: A husband who consecrates his wife's earnings to the Temple finds the consecration ineffective; she goes on spinning wool and feeding herself from what she makes. Rav Huna says she may refuse the whole arrangement, taking no support from him and keeping her earnings, because the Sages instituted her sustenance first and her earnings only as his compensation. A baraita states the exchange in the opposite order, so the Gemara emends the baraita's wording to fit.
ketubot/58.question: If the wording of the baraita had to be flipped to survive, on what strength does Rav Huna's ruling still stand?

judge.reachNote: What authority an amoraic ruling retains once the tannaitic text cited against it has to be rewritten to agree with it.

ketubot/59.summary: A wife declares her hands consecrated to the One Who made them, the sanctity to take effect only once she is divorced. The Gemara hunts for a matching case in real estate: a field sold and bought back, a field already sold, a field mortgaged, a field mortgaged for ten years. Each analogy breaks at the same seam, until Rav Ashi points out that a redemption date always arrives, while divorce never lies in her hands.
ketubot/59.question: If her hands have always been her own, why does the whole argument hang on a divorce she cannot bring about herself?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — owning the limb versus controlling its output — but the page already answers it with subjugation/lien and then discards the 'in her power' criterion.

answer.quote: The Sages reinforced the husband's lien in order that it not become consecrated now.
answer.explanation: The page states why the consecration must wait for divorce despite her owning her hands — her earnings are under the husband's lien, which the Sages reinforced against present sanctity — and Rav Ashi's konam resolution explicitly abandons the whole 'is it in her power' line of analogies.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 59b: "The Sages reinforced the husband's lien in order that it not become consecrated now.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered twice over on the page: first by "She is subjugated to her husband with regard to her earnings" and the divorce-deferral answer, and finally by Rav Ashi's ruling that konamot are different and only the Sages' reinforcement of the husband's lien delays the sanctity. Write a question that starts from that resolution rather than asking what it already explains — for instance, why a sanctity powerful enough to abrogate a lien on mortgaged property is held back here by rabbinic reinforcement alone, or what it means that the Gemara keeps testing her case against fields while Rav Pappa insists her body is not property at all. Keep the summary; it tracks the page accurately.

ketubot/60.summary: A widow with a nursing baby is told to wait twenty-four months before remarrying, so the child does not lose its food; Rabbi Yehuda says eighteen. Abaye's tenant farmer asks whether he may betroth such a woman at fifteen months, and Abaye stacks four authorities to say yes. Then his teacher Rav Yosef cites Rav and Shmuel: twenty-four, even for betrothal, and Abaye ran three parasangs, several miles, after the man without catching him.
ketubot/60.question: If each of Abaye's four reasons was sound, what exactly went wrong, the ruling or the room he was standing in?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a ruling's correctness may depend on where the ruler stands rather than on the strength of his reasons — but the page states that very answer.

answer.quote: rather because he will not be successful in saying the matter correctly. An illustration of this principle is what just happened, since I had learned this halakha
answer.explanation: The page has Abaye himself draw the lesson: the fault lay in ruling in his teacher's vicinity, which caused him to state the halakha wrongly despite knowing it.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 60b: "rather because he will not be successful in saying the matter correctly. An illustration of this principle is what just happened, since I had learned this halakha". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Abaye explicitly says the failure was not disrespect but that one "will not be successful in saying the matter correctly" near one's teacher. Build the question on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why four converging authorities (Beit Hillel, Rabbi Yehuda, Ulla, Rav Ḥanina's own practice) still lose to Rav and Shmuel, or why betrothal alone was treated as a lighter step and then wasn't. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

ketubot/61.summary: A wife who brings one maidservant into the marriage stops grinding, baking, and washing clothes, and the Gemara tries to push the count high enough that she does nothing at all. Each time the husband answers that a bigger household draws more guests and wayfarers, until four maidservants can cover everything between them. Even then Rav Huna keeps three tasks for her: pouring his cup, making his bed, washing his face, hands and feet, because those count as affection rather than chores.
ketubot/61.question: If pouring his cup is affection and not labor, why is it enough for Shmuel's wife, while menstruating, to pour with her left hand?
gate: the question brings in "Shmuel's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that an act of affection can be neutralized by a token change rather than by abstention, but the page already states that rationale.

answer.quote: since if she made some change in the manner of pouring, this would serve as a reminder of her status and mitigate the concern that it might lead to intimacy
answer.explanation: The page itself explains that the left-handed pouring works because any deviation flags her status and defuses the risk of intimacy, which is exactly what the question asks.

summaryProblems.claim: Each time the husband answers that a bigger household draws more guests and wayfarers.
summaryProblems.pageSays: This maidservant toils for me and for herself like any other woman, but who will toil for you?

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 61a: "since if she made some change in the manner of pouring, this would serve as a reminder of her status and mitigate the concern that it might lead to intimacy". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Each time the husband answers that a bigger household draws more guests and wayfarers.", but the page says "This maidservant toils for me and for herself like any other woman, but who will toil for you?". Say what the page says. The question is answered verbatim on the page, which says the change in pouring "would serve as a reminder of her status and mitigate the concern that it might lead to intimacy" — ask something the page leaves open instead, such as why Rava permits bed-making out of sight while pouring requires only a token variation. Also fix the summary: the husband's first rebuttal is that the maidservant works for him and herself and no one works for the wife; only the later rebuttals invoke guests and wayfarers.

ketubot/62.summary: Rav allows a husband a month in the study hall for each month at home; Rabbi Yoḥanan allows one month away for every two at home. Between that and the stories of men gone twelve years sits a smaller ruling: a donkey driver may not switch to camel driving for better pay, because a woman prefers a kav, a small measure of grain, with her husband present over ten without him. Yet the Rabbis let students leave for two or three years without asking her.
ketubot/62.question: If a wife's preference settles whether her husband may change jobs, on what grounds do the Rabbis let a student leave for years without asking her at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether a wife's preference is a binding claim or a consideration that Torah study can override.

answer.quote: with regard to Torah study, which cannot be performed by others, he is given permission to spend a month here and a month there
answer.explanation: The page grants Torah study a special exemption because it cannot be delegated, which bears on why students get latitude, but it never states the grounds for the Rabbis' two-to-three-year leave without permission — indeed Rava notes those who relied on it met fatal results.

ketubot/63.summary: A wife who rebels against her husband has her marriage contract, the sum owed her if he divorces her, cut by seven dinars, silver coins, every week. The Gemara argues over what she is refusing: marital relations, says Rav Huna, or the household tasks she owes him, says Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina. Ameimar holds that a woman who says she is disgusted with her husband is not forced to stay; Mar Zutra forced one, and the page credits the good that followed to heaven.
ketubot/63.question: If nothing good ordinarily comes of a marriage the wife is compelled into, why does the page preserve the name of the child born from the one Mar Zutra compelled?

judge.reachNote: Whether a tradition's own counterexample, once explained away as heavenly exception, still carries weight as memory of a blessing from coercion.

answer.quote: That case should not serve as a precedent, as there the positive outcome was due to heavenly assistance. Ordinarily, nothing good results from conjugal relations that the wife does not desire.
answer.explanation: The page explains why the story of Rabbi Ḥanina of Sura is reported and then neutralized as exceptional, which bears on why it is preserved, but it never addresses why the child's name is kept on record once the precedent is rejected.

ketubot/64.summary: A court can write a letter of rebellion, an order docking value from a wife's marriage contract, and the page asks whether one can be written against a widow who refuses the brother-in-law waiting to marry or release her. Every proposed distinction collapses under the next question, until the split is pinned on two versions of an older mishna. Then the Gemara tries to stretch a husband's weekly ration of two kav of wheat into fourteen meals.
ketubot/64.question: Should the smallest allowance a person is owed still contain a portion for a guest who has not arrived?

judge.reachNote: Whether a minimum entitlement is measured by bare personal need or must include the capacity to host another.

answer.quote: the husband cannot give his wife the absolute minimum amount she requires for herself and no more. He must give her enough to provide for the occasional visitor.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly states that the minimum ration must include extra for guests and wayfarers, which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 64b: "the husband cannot give his wife the absolute minimum amount she requires for herself and no more. He must give her enough to provide for the occasional visitor.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and answered outright on 64b, where the Gemara removes a meal "for guests and wayfarers" and says the husband cannot give only the bare minimum she needs for herself. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and presses on what remains hard — for instance why the same generosity is not built into the rebellious wife's daily deductions, or why guest-portions are used to reconcile every conflicting opinion at once. Alternatively, take up an unresolved thread from 64a, such as why the yavam's claim that "they will not give me another wife" counts for ḥalitza but not for levirate marriage.

ketubot/65.summary: The Sages argue over whether a wife is allotted wine at all, reading Hannah at Shiloh, who ate but did not drink, as proof that she is not. Then Ḥoma, Abaye's widow, comes to court claiming support from his heirs and asks Rava for wine too, gesturing to show the size of the cups Abaye poured her; her arm uncovers. Rava's wife then chases Ḥoma out of Meḥoza with the lock of a chest.
ketubot/65.question: The page never says whether Ḥoma got her wine, so did the uncovered arm prove her claim or wreck it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a litigant's own body and manner can serve as evidence for her claim, and what it costs her when it does.

answer.quote: Since you were not accustomed to drinking wine during your husband's lifetime, you are not entitled to it after his death.
answer.explanation: The page states the criterion Rava applies and narrates that Ḥoma was driven from Meḥoza, but it never says whether her wine claim was granted, so only part of the question is met.

ketubot/66.summary: The mishna gives a woman the payment for her own humiliation, while Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira gives her husband a share of it. Rava bar Rav Ḥanan tests that: does a man who humiliates someone's horse pay the owner? The test sharpens to spit landing on a person's clothing, which an earlier ruling treats as costing nothing, and Rav Ashi answers that a humiliated relative's shame is not yours, but a wife's is.
ketubot/66.question: If a wife's humiliation really is the husband's own humiliation, why does Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira hand him only a portion of the payment instead of all of it?

judge.reachNote: If a wife counts as the husband's own self for shame, ownership of the compensation should be whole, not fractional — the question presses on how far that identification goes.

ketubot/67.summary: A baraita reads the verse "sufficient for his deficiency" to mean a poor person gets what he personally lacks, which can stretch to a horse to ride and a servant running ahead of him. Hillel, unable to find a servant for one impoverished nobleman, ran in front of the horse himself for three mil. When a beggar told Rabbi Neḥemya that he usually dined on fatty meat and aged wine, Neḥemya fed him lentils instead, and the man died.
ketubot/67.question: If a man raised on fattened hen and aged wine dies of Rabbi Neḥemya's lentils, why does the argument end up faulting him for pampering himself rather than the man who served the lentils?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of who bears responsibility when a standard of living becomes a physical need, but the page states its resolution outright.

answer.quote: Rather, Rabbi Neḥemya meant that it was he, the pauper, who should not have pampered himself so much. The poor man was to blame for his own death.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the objection that Neḥemya should have blamed himself, and resolves it by saying the pauper's own self-indulgence caused his death.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 67b: "Rather, Rabbi Neḥemya meant that it was he, the pauper, who should not have pampered himself so much. The poor man was to blame for his own death.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it in the next line by saying the pauper should not have pampered himself and was to blame for his own death. Write a question that starts from that resolution instead, for example how the same baraita can both obligate the community to fund a horse and servant for a man accustomed to them and then fault a man for being accustomed to fatty meat. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

ketubot/68.summary: Rabbi Ḥanina reports that Rabbi Elazar said to appreciate the swindlers who collect charity they do not need, since without them, failing the truly poor would be a sin every day. A baraita right after sets a harsher line: whoever fakes a blind eye, a bloated stomach or a crushed leg will not leave the world before he really suffers it. Then the threshold, two hundred dinars, and an argument over whether a poor man must trade silver cups for copper.
ketubot/68.question: Is Rabbi Elazar offering a real excuse for giving less, or naming, dryly, the excuse people already reach for?

judge.reachNote: Whether a statement about sin can function as a genuine legal-moral exemption or only as a mirror held up to the excuse people already use.

answer.quote: Because the swindlers take our money in the name of charity, we have an excuse of sorts for failing to fully meet the needs of the truly poor.
answer.explanation: The page glosses Rabbi Elazar's saying as providing "an excuse of sorts," which leans toward the excuse being real but hedged, so a reader can still honestly ask whether the remark is sincere exemption or dry irony.

ketubot/69.summary: Rav tucks a question to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi between the lines of a letter, choosing the vague word "mortgaged" so that either reply will cover both sold and merely pledged land. Later another letter goes badly, as Rav Anan opens "Huna, our friend" and asks Rav Huna to give a woman one-tenth of her father's estate as her dowry, and Rav Huna answers with a jeer about the word marzeiḥa, a mourner. Rav Sheshet must relay the insult word for word.
ketubot/69.question: A woman was standing there with Rav Anan's letter asking for her tenth of her father's estate, so did she ever get it while the sages argued about who may call whom "friend"?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: a live claimant's support depends on sages whose exchange turns into a quarrel over honor and epistolary etiquette — does the human claim get lost in the scholarly duel?

answer.quote: Rava said: The halakha is that one may collect from the inheritors from real estate and not from movable property, whether for sustenance, whether for the marriage contract
answer.explanation: The page never says whether the particular woman holding Rav Anan's letter was paid, but it does report the conclusion of that exchange — Rav Huna's taunting question about real estate versus movable property is settled in favor of collecting the tenth from real estate — so the underlying claim is resolved even though her case is not tracked.

ketubot/70.summary: A husband vows that his wife may not benefit from him or his property; the mishna gives him thirty days with a parnas, a trustee who supports her, before he must divorce her and pay her marriage contract. The Gemara first asks how a vow can cancel a debt he already owes her, then hits a sharper snag: if the trustee acts as his agent, the benefit still comes from him. Rav Huna's fix is wording. The husband announces to nobody in particular that whoever feeds her will be reimbursed.
ketubot/70.question: If a man trapped in a pit who calls out for someone to write his wife a bill of divorce has made agents of whoever hears him, why has the vowing husband not made an agent of whoever feeds his wife?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — what turns speech into the appointment of an agent — but the page states the command/general-statement distinction outright.

answer.quote: Here, however, does he say that anyone should sustain his wife? He merely says: Whoever sustains her will not lose out
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this comparison and answers that the pit case is a command that creates agency, while "whoever sustains her will not lose out" is a mere general statement.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 70b: "Here, however, does he say that anyone should sustain his wife? He merely says: Whoever sustains her will not lose out". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it a line later: a command creates agency, a general offer of reimbursement does not. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, why the Sages' permission in the fire case is then needed at all, or why familiarity with the storekeeper nearly makes him an agent when a broadcast statement does not. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

ketubot/71.summary: A wife vows off some food or a perfume, her husband hears and stays silent instead of nullifying it, and the argument is over who made the vow stick. Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar get sorted into pairs, then resorted, then resorted again, because every arrangement contradicts something one of them says elsewhere. Both sides use the same image: a finger placed between teeth, so that it gets bitten.
ketubot/71.question: If the pairs can be reversed three times to keep each sage consistent, what would it take for a reshuffling to fail?

judge.reachNote: Asks what constrains the Gemara's harmonizing emendations — whether reversal of attributions can ever be refuted rather than endlessly adjusted.

answer.quote: And if you say the opinions of the tanna’im listed in the baraita are taught in pairs, and therefore it cannot be that three of them share the same opinion
answer.explanation: The page supplies one explicit constraint on reshuffling — the baraita's pair structure blocks any arrangement that puts three sages on one side — and each rejected arrangement fails by clashing with a sage's ruling elsewhere, but it never states the general limits of the device, so the question can still be asked.

ketubot/72.summary: A mishna lists wives divorced without the payment of their marriage contract, among them one who serves her husband untithed food or skips ḥalla, the dough portion given to a priest. The Gemara presses each case: if he knew, he should not eat; if he did not know, how does he ever find out? Each answer needs a lie about a named third party, and when Rabbi Meir suggests the husband simply police her, the Sages answer that no one lives in a basket with a snake.
ketubot/72.question: If the grounds only appear when he checks with the kneader and catches her out, is she losing her marriage contract for the missing ḥalla or for the lie?

judge.reachNote: What is actually being penalized: the ritual transgression itself, or the deception that makes it discoverable.

answer.quote: In this case, she was known by her neighbors to be a menstruating woman, but she had not told her husband. She then engaged in sexual intercourse with him
answer.explanation: In the parallel niddah case the Gemara offers a second resolution in which no lie is told at all, which suggests the lie serves only to establish how the husband finds out rather than being the ground of divorce, but the page never says this about the ḥalla case itself, so the question remains askable.

ketubot/73.summary: A man betroths a woman on condition that no vows bind her, then marries her without repeating the condition, and vows turn up. Rav says she still needs a bill of divorce, reasoning that a person does not knowingly have licentious intercourse, so the act of marriage itself served as a fresh, unconditional betrothal; Shmuel disagrees. Rava reads the mishna as sheer uncertainty: stringent about adultery, lenient about money, so she stays bound and collects nothing.
ketubot/73.question: If the status of the betrothal is genuinely in doubt, why does the doubt break against her on both counts, leaving her tied to him and without the payment her marriage contract promised?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that one doubt is resolved by two different default rules — but the page already names both defaults.

ketubot/74.summary: A man betroths a woman on a condition, then sleeps with her without mentioning the condition again, and the Sages argue whether the act cancels the stipulation or leans on the failed betrothal. The rules for conditions are traced to Moses' bargain with the tribes of Gad and Reuben, yielding an odd test: a condition holds only where an agent could carry out the deed. At the end, a dissolved vow is uprooted retroactively, while a blemish a doctor cures is not.
ketubot/74.question: When the Sages could not tell whether the betrothal had taken hold and forced the man to write a bill of divorce anyway, were they ruling on the case or admitting they could not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of a court ruling out of unresolved doubt rather than on the merits, but the page already says this in so many words.

answer.quote: the Sages did not have the power to allow her to leave her husband without a bill of divorce, since they could not definitively rule
answer.explanation: The page itself states that the get was imposed precisely because the Sages could not decide whether the betrothal was valid, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 74a: "the Sages did not have the power to allow her to leave her husband without a bill of divorce, since they could not definitively rule". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim by the page's own explanation that the Sages imposed the get because they could not definitively rule the betrothal invalid. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for example, why intercourse gets an exception to the Gad-and-Reuben agency test through the juxtaposition of betrothal methods, or why Rabbi Ami thinks a man errs about a condition but not about a peruta. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

ketubot/75.summary: The Gemara lists blemishes that could void a betrothal, among them sweat that will not wash off, bad breath, a mole hidden under a woman's cap, a scar from a dog bite, and a deep voice. A priest with a foul mouth can hold pepper and serve; a woman, the argument runs, cannot keep that up. Then it turns to who must prove when a blemish appeared, and to two presumptions that pull against each other.
ketubot/75.question: If a man is presumed to inspect before he betroths, how can he also be presumed never to have accepted what he saw?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that presumptions about the same person's conduct can point in opposite directions and must be weighed rather than simply applied.

answer.quote: his claim of a mistaken betrothal is not accepted because there are two presumptions opposing it
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the clash between the inspection presumption and the presumption that a man is not appeased by blemishes, and begins to resolve it by weighing two presumptions against one, but the resolution is cut off mid-sentence ("Even so, it is"), so the tension can still honestly be asked.

ketubot/76.summary: A husband who finds blemishes on his wife and her father argue over who must prove when the blemishes appeared, and a woman with an extra toe makes the case sharp, since no proof can show a toe grew later, only that the husband saw it before betrothal and was appeased. Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel applying the same burden to a cow traded for a donkey that died mid-deal. Then Rami bar Yehezkel arrives and tells everyone to ignore his brother's version.
ketubot/76.question: Rav Yehuda and Rami bar Yeḥezkel both point to the same mishna about a bride to support opposite rules about who must bring proof, so what was that mishna actually saying?
gate: the question brings in "Yeḥezkel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: does the burden of proof follow possession of the disputed money/object, or the domain in which the uncertainty arose?

answer.quote: And the tanna of the mishna also taught along similar lines with regard to a bride. If the bride was in her father's domain he must provide proof; if she was living with her husband the burden of proof is upon him.
answer.explanation: Rami bar Yeḥezkel restates the mishna's bride rule as assigning proof by whose domain the doubt arose, though the page never adjudicates between his reading and Rav Yehuda's, so the question can still be asked.

ketubot/77.summary: A mishna lists what forces a husband to divorce his wife: boils, a polyp (a foul smell from the nose or the mouth), and trades that leave a stench, gathering dog excrement for tanning, hewing copper, tanning hides. Rabbi Meir holds she can back out even if she agreed to the smell in advance, saying she misjudged what she could live with. The talk of disease slides into ra'atan, which most sages fled, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sat with the afflicted and studied Torah.
ketubot/77.question: If Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's Torah kept him safe among those afflicted with ra'atan, what were Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Elazar doing when they stayed upwind and out of the tent?
gate: the question brings in "Zeira", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Elazar", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the protection Torah study affords is something one may rely on in the face of real danger, or a merit only the rare individual may presume upon.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan would announce: Be careful of the flies found on those afflicted with ra’atan, as they are carriers of the disease.
answer.explanation: The page gives a reason for the sages' avoidance (the disease is genuinely transmissible) and later treats Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's conduct as exceptional — "But did you attach yourself to those afflicted with ra’atan and study Torah, as he did?" — but it never states why the others declined to rely on Torah's protection.

ketubot/78.summary: A woman inherits property, is then betrothed, then married, and the question is whether she can still sell it or give it away. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree she may sell what she owned before betrothal, and split over property that arrives after; Beit Hillel say she may not sell, though a completed sale holds. Rabban Gamliel answers the Sages that he is already ashamed of the rule for property inherited after marriage, and refuses to extend it backward.
ketubot/78.question: If Rabban Gamliel is ashamed of the restriction he already enforces, what keeps him from discarding it instead of just declining to widen it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a sage may concede a rule is indefensible yet still enforce it, treating an inherited ruling as binding while refusing to expand it.
