answer.quote: if you said that the sale is void with regard to a married woman, concerning whom the husband has many rights, as her husband is entitled to items she has found
answer.explanation: Rabbi Ḥanina ben Akavya's version supplies a substantive ground for the married-woman restriction (the husband's many rights), which bears on why it stands, but it is presented as an alternative to the shame reply rather than as an explanation of why Rabban Gamliel keeps a rule he is ashamed of.

ketubot/79.summary: A mother wrote a document handing her property to her daughter, and Rav Nau0125man tore it up, ruling it was only a maneuver to keep the property away from her husband. The rest of the page sorts a wife's property into principal, which stays hers, and produce, which her husband consumes: land over houses, palm trees over other trees, and any plant whose trunk regrows counts as produce. A stolen calf counts as produce, the Rabbis say, because even a dead cow leaves a hide.
ketubot/79.question: How can one document be real enough to keep a husband's hands off the property and fake enough for a judge to tear it up?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — a deed can be void toward the recipient yet still effective in stripping the husband's claim — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: Abaye said: The Sages rendered this property given as a gift like property that is unknown to the husband
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's difficulty — if the recipient does not acquire, the husband should — and Abaye resolves it by giving the property the status of property unknown to the husband, so the void document still blocks him.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 79a: "Abaye said: The Sages rendered this property given as a gift like property that is unknown to the husband". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 79a: the Gemara asks exactly this (if the purchaser does not acquire, the husband should) and Abaye says the Sages treat the property as unknown to the husband. Write a question that starts after that answer, or move to a thread the page leaves open — for instance why Rabbi Zeira makes all-versus-part the dividing line for a document of evasion, or why double payment counts as 'produce of the produce' and goes to the wife while the calf itself goes to the husband.

ketubot/80.summary: The Sages gave a husband the use of his wife's land, and the page asks whether he can sell those rights to a buyer who works the land for its produce. Abaye worries the buyer will let the land rot; Rava says the arrangement existed for the gain of the house, and a sale brings the house nothing. A woman brought two maidservants into her marriage, her husband married a second wife and handed one of them over, and Rava ignored her tears.
ketubot/80.question: If a husband holds his wife's property only for the gain of the house, whose house is it when one of her two maidservants is moved to serve his second wife?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether 'gain of the house' means the household as a unit or the wife who brought the property — but the page states its own answer.

answer.quote: the Sages instituted the ordinance that a husband owns the rights to the produce of his wife's property for the gain of the house, and here the house does gain
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself explains Rava's silence by ruling that the maidservant moved to the second wife still works for the house, so the household gain persists and the first wife has no complaint.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 80b: "the Sages instituted the ordinance that a husband owns the rights to the produce of his wife's property for the gain of the house, and here the house does gain". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: it says the house does gain because the maidservant also performs work for the house, which is why Rava took no notice of the first wife. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance, why Abaye's worry about the land deteriorating and Rava's 'no gain of the house' should split over land near the town or a husband who trades the produce money, or what work 'the house' is doing as a legal unit once a second wife lives in it.

ketubot/81.summary: Rava lets the brother of a childless dead man argue that he inherits the estate but owes the widow no burial; Abaye says the claims come at him from two sides, take the duties with the rights or hand over her marriage contract. In Pumbedita a man buys his brother's consent to marry that widow with a promise of half the property, then gives him nothing. Rav Yosef voids the promise: the estate is mortgaged to her marriage contract, so it was never his to give.
ketubot/81.question: If the Pumbedita brother's promise is void because the property was never his to hand over, does the ruling leave the man who broke his word holding exactly what he schemed for?

judge.reachNote: Whether a protection enacted for the widow's marriage contract can be pocketed by a brother who used it to cheat his co-heir.

answer.quote: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Abaye, but if Rav Yosef states a different reason for it, send his reasoning to me
answer.explanation: The page never weighs the schemer's gain, but it does undercut the question's premise by ruling, after Abaye's objection, that the sale (and so the promise) is not voided.

ketubot/82.summary: Rav Yehuda tells how the marriage contract, two hundred silver dinars for a virgin and one hundred for a widow, was once cash a husband had to set aside, so men grew old and did not marry. The Sages moved the money to her father's house, then to her husband's, where rich wives shaped it into silver baskets and poor ones into a urine vessel. An angry husband could still say: go to your marriage contract, until Shimon ben Shataḥ spread the debt across all his property.
ketubot/82.question: If the ordinance works by making divorce expensive, what has a woman gained when her hundred dinars stop being a vessel in her own house and become a claim on property she may never see?

judge.reachNote: Whether a wife's security is better served by tangible property in hand or by a lien that raises the cost of divorce.

answer.quote: he would need to sell some of his property if he wished to divorce her, and would therefore think carefully before undertaking such a drastic course of action
answer.explanation: The page states the ordinance's purpose as deterring hasty divorce, which the question already concedes, and elsewhere calls the property a "guarantee and security for her marriage contract," but it never addresses what she gains if she never collects.

ketubot/83.summary: A husband who writes to his wife that he has no dealings with her property still eats its produce and still inherits from her; all the document does is let her sell it. The Gemara then stacks the waivers, producing a chain of produce, produce of the produce, and forever. Abaye reads the vague wording as narrowly as possible, assuming a man clings to what he eats now, a cucumber in hand over a future gourd.
ketubot/83.question: If the husband's right to inherit from his wife is only a rabbinic ordinance, as Rav holds, why is it harder to waive than the produce he gives up with a sentence?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a rabbinic right can be less waivable than a Torah one because the Sages fortified their own decrees.

answer.quote: as the Sages reinforced their pronouncements with greater severity than those of Torah law and decreed that the inheritance of a husband cannot be canceled in any manner
answer.explanation: The closing lines state exactly why, on Rav's view that a husband's inheritance is rabbinic, the stipulation against it is nonetheless void, unlike waivable rights to produce.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 83b: "as the Sages reinforced their pronouncements with greater severity than those of Torah law and decreed that the inheritance of a husband cannot be canceled in any manner". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the page's last line, which says the Sages reinforced their pronouncements with greater severity and decreed the husband's inheritance can never be canceled. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it: press on what remains strange, e.g. why a right the Sages themselves created for the husband is locked shut while the wife may opt out of her own rabbinic arrangement, or why produce instituted by the Sages is freely waivable and inheritance is not.

ketubot/84.summary: A man dies owing his wife her marriage contract and a creditor his debt, and some of his money sits with a third party as a loan or a deposit. Rabbi Tarfon says it goes to the weakest claimant; Rabbi Akiva answers that one is not merciful in judgment and gives it to the heirs, who collect without swearing an oath. The rest of the page watches judges fumble this, including Rabbi Yoḥanan ruling for his own relatives over a seized cow.
ketubot/84.question: Why is it currying favor when Rabbi Abbahu approves the prince's household seizing a maidservant, but not when Rabbi Yoḥanan tells his own relatives the cow is theirs?
gate: the question brings in "Abbahu", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When a judge rules for people close to him, what separates a genuine legal position from currying favor — and does precedent bind the judge who rejects it?

answer.quote: One Sage, Rabbi Yoḥanan, holds that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Akiva in his disputes with his colleague, but not in his disputes with his teacher
answer.explanation: The page supplies Rabbi Yoḥanan's principled legal ground for ruling like Rabbi Tarfon (his teacher), which distinguishes his ruling from mere favoritism, but it never states this contrast or defends him against Rabbi Abba's charge.

ketubot/85.summary: Rava's wife, the daughter of Rav Ḥisda, told him that a woman due to swear in his court was suspected of false oaths, and Rava shifted the oath to her opponent. Later Rav Pappa testified alone that a loan document had already been paid, and Rava refused him. Rav Adda bar Mattana pressed the obvious point: a woman cannot testify, yet she was believed. Rava's answer is not a rule but a measure of his own certainty.
ketubot/85.question: If Rava can act on private certainty about one person's honesty, what keeps a judge's confidence from quietly replacing the witnesses the court demands?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea beneath the case: whether formal rules of admissible testimony can be displaced by a judge's personal knowledge of a person's truthfulness.

answer.quote: How can it enter your mind that the court can tear a document based on the word of a single witness? Rather, the statement should be that I can weaken the document
answer.explanation: The Gemara does impose one limit on acting from private certainty — such a claim can only weaken a document, not tear it — but it never explains what bounds a judge's confidence generally, so the question survives.

ketubot/86.summary: A daughter inherited her mother's marriage contract, the document recording what her father owed, and Rav Naḥman advised her to forgive that debt, wiping out the men who had bought the document from her mother. He later regretted it: an important person should not look like he is coaching his own relatives, even though Isaiah says not to hide from your own flesh. The rule itself stands, so a cautious buyer is told to jangle coins at the debtor until he writes a fresh note.
ketubot/86.question: Was Rav Naḥman's advice wrong, or only wrong coming from him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real tension between a judge's duty to kin and the appearance of favoritism, but the page resolves that tension in so many words.

answer.quote: in the case of an important person who must be very careful to avoid any impression of having favored his family in judgment
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly explains that Rav Naḥman first relied on "you should not hide yourself from your own flesh" and only regretted it because an important person is judged by a stricter standard, i.e. the advice was faulty coming from him, not in itself — and Shmuel's underlying ruling stands unchallenged.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 86a: "in the case of an important person who must be very careful to avoid any impression of having favored his family in judgment". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara already answers: it distinguishes "do not hide yourself from your own flesh" from the stricter standard for "an important person," and Shmuel's ruling is left intact, so the advice was sound but unbecoming from him. Write a question that starts after that resolution — for instance why forgiveness is even possible against a purchaser who paid for the document, or what Ameimar's indirect-damage remedy says about whether the sale transferred anything real. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

ketubot/87.summary: A widow who admits she already received part of her marriage contract, the sum owed her from her husband's estate, can collect the rest only by swearing. Rami bar Ḥama calls that oath a Torah obligation; Rava refutes him twice, since Torah oaths exempt a person from paying rather than let her collect, and lands on rabbinic law: the payer remembers precisely, the one paid does not. Then a woman itemizes every sum received, down to less than a peruta, the smallest copper coin.
ketubot/87.question: If she can account for every payment down to a fraction of a coin, is that precision a sign she is telling the truth or a sign she prepared the story?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that excessive precision is ambiguous evidence — it can mark honesty or a rehearsed fabrication — though it is a restatement of the Gemara's own unresolved teiku.

summaryProblems.claim: The one who vitiates her marriage contract is a widow collecting from her husband's estate.
summaryProblems.pageSays: and her husband said to her: You already received your marriage contract, and she says: I received only one hundred dinars

judge.feedback: The summary says "The one who vitiates her marriage contract is a widow collecting from her husband's estate.", but the page says "and her husband said to her: You already received your marriage contract, and she says: I received only one hundred dinars". Say what the page says. Fix the opening: the vitiating case on this page is a woman whose living husband claims he already paid her, not a widow collecting from the estate — collection from orphans is a separate clause of the mishna. Keep the Rami bar Ḥama/Rava thread, which is accurate. Consider giving the question its own angle rather than repeating the Gemara's teiku verbatim, e.g. why the Sages left precision unresolved when Rava's rationale was that the payee is imprecise.

ketubot/88.summary: A husband who paid his wife's marriage contract, the sum owed her on divorce or his death, with only one witness present is coached on how to get her under a Torah oath: pay the whole sum again before two witnesses, then call the first payment a loan and sue for it. Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, and then Rav Ashi patch the holes, including her comeback that she held two separate marriage contracts. Later the page chases what Rabbi Shimon was disputing through four rival readings.
ketubot/88.question: Why does the discussion spend itself on making the husband's staged loan airtight, and never on whether he should be setting the trap at all?

judge.reachNote: It reaches the idea that the sugya treats a contrived legal maneuver purely as a technical problem, asking whether halakhic discourse ever weighs the legitimacy of the device itself.

ketubot/89.summary: A divorced woman comes to court holding her bill of divorce and asks for the sum promised in her marriage contract. The worry running through the argument is double collection: nothing stops her from carrying the same document to a second court and collecting again. Rav Huna's fix is physical. Tear the bill of divorce, then write on its back that it was torn for payment, not because the divorce was flawed.
ketubot/89.question: The discussion ends without finding any source that a woman widowed after betrothal was ever promised a marriage contract, so what were the courts paying out all along?

judge.reachNote: Whether payment rests on a rabbinic entitlement that exists whether or not a document was written, or only on a document the husband chose to write.

answer.quote: Perhaps the mishna is referring to a case where he wrote a marriage contract for her on his own accord.
answer.explanation: The page's repeated suggestion is that betrothed women collected on documents their husbands wrote voluntarily rather than on a Sages' enactment, which bears on what the courts were paying, though the page still closes without establishing a source for an enactment.

ketubot/90.summary: A boy married off by his father writes his wife a marriage contract, and the mishna says it holds after he comes of age, since he kept her as his wife on those terms. Rav Huna limits her to the fixed sum the Sages set, one hundred or two hundred dinars, while Rav Yehuda says she also gets the extra the boy promised. A baraita refutes Rav Yehuda, and the Gemara says the mishna's wording misled him.
ketubot/90.question: If a document written by a minor carries no legal weight, why does his wife collect anything at all, and if it does carry weight, why not the extra sum he wrote into it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the real idea — the split between what a document creates and what the Sages' enactment creates — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: She receives the main sum only as a result of an ordinance instituted by the Sages.
answer.explanation: Rav Huna's statement explicitly explains both halves of the question: the document is void so the extra sum is lost, and the main sum is collected only by rabbinic ordinance.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 90a: "She receives the main sum only as a result of an ordinance instituted by the Sages.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered in the very lines the summary paraphrases: Rav Huna says the document is not binding and the main sum comes only from a rabbinic ordinance. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for example, why the Sages' enactment attaches to a marriage the boy's father arranged, or why the husband's continuing to keep her as his wife validates the fixed sum but not the sum he himself wrote. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

ketubot/91.summary: A man married two women, both died, then he died, and the sons of each wife want the sum promised in their own mother's marriage contract. The mishna lets them collect only if the estate exceeds both contracts by one dinar, a silver coin, and sons who offer to overvalue their father's land to manufacture that surplus are refused. When the thin estate of bar Tzartzur later appreciated, Rav Naḥman froze everyone's rights at the value on the day the father died.
ketubot/91.question: If rights are fixed by the estate's worth on the day the father died, why did Rav Amram first push the better-off sons to appease their brothers and threaten them with excommunication when they refused?
gate: the question brings in "Amram", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the tension between a judge pressing compromise or equity on the parties and the strict rule that fixes inheritance rights at the moment of death.

ketubot/92.summary: Three men named Reuven, Shimon, and Levi keep selling each other the same field, sometimes with a guarantee against repossession and sometimes without, while creditors circle. Rava limits the guarantee: a seller answers for old debts on the land, not for the buyer's own creditors. The sharpest move is practical advice: when Reuven's orphans hold only cash owed by Shimon, which no creditor can seize, Rava says a clever Shimon should pay them in land instead, then take that land back.
ketubot/92.question: Why does Rava, having stated the rule that shields orphans' movable property from their father's creditors, immediately explain how a debtor can maneuver around it?

judge.reachNote: The orphans' immunity is formal, attached to the type of asset rather than to the orphans themselves, so a change of asset dissolves it.

answer.quote: When orphans collect real estate for a debt owed to their father from one person, their father's creditor can come and seize this land from them.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the legal basis for the workaround — the shield attaches only to the category 'movable property,' so once the debt is paid in land the creditor's lien revives — but it never says why Rava volunteers the maneuver rather than letting the protection stand.

ketubot/93.summary: A man dies leaving three widows whose marriage contracts are for one hundred, two hundred, and three hundred dinars, and the estate holds only two hundred. The mishna splits it fifty, seventy-five, seventy-five, and the Gemara presses: why does the first wife get fifty rather than a third of the hundred all three claim? Shmuel supplies an unmentioned waiver document, Ravina has the money arriving in two installments, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi just disagrees.
ketubot/93.question: If the mishna's numbers only work once you invent a waiver nobody mentioned or payments nobody described, is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's blunt "divide the estate equally" the more honest reading?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the interpretive question of whether a mishna should be saved by supplying unstated facts or simply read as a disputed opinion.

ketubot/94.summary: Two deeds for the same field bear the same date, and Rav would split the property between the buyers while Shmuel hands the choice to the judges' discretion. The mother of Rami bar Ḥama did just that, deeding her property to one son in the morning and to another son that evening, and two sages ruled for opposite brothers. Rav Naḥman defended his ruling as discretion, then told Rav Sheshet that his discretion did not count.
ketubot/94.question: If discretion means ruling as the case seems to a judge, what makes Rav Naḥman's sense of what the mother wanted worth more than Rav Sheshet's?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea of what authorizes discretion — whether a good instinct or an office makes a ruling binding — but the page answers it in so many words.

answer.quote: One response to your point is that I am a judge, and the Master is not a judge, as Rav Sheshet did not serve in the official capacity of a judge.
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman states explicitly why his discretion counts and Rav Sheshet's does not — official judicial standing — and adds that Rav Sheshet's ruling originally rested on the dating theory, not on discretion at all.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 94b: "One response to your point is that I am a judge, and the Master is not a judge, as Rav Sheshet did not serve in the official capacity of a judge.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered on the page: Rav Naḥman says outright that he is a judge and Rav Sheshet is not, and that Rav Sheshet's ruling rested on the dating theory rather than on discretion. Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for example, why a doubt in monetary law should be settled by a judge's feel for what the mother wanted rather than by dividing, as Rav would, or what it means that the same instinct produces opposite rulings. Keep the summary as it is; it is faithful.

ketubot/95.summary: A man married to two wives sells a field, and the first wife writes to the purchaser that she has no legal dealings with him. The second wife then takes the field for her marriage contract, the first takes it from her, the purchaser takes it back from the first, and the cycle runs until they compromise. The sharp move is that a wife who signed away her rights can claim she only meant to please her husband, a claim Rav Ashi limits to a single sale.
ketubot/95.question: If a wife's signature on her husband's sale can be waved away as keeping peace at home, what did the purchaser think he was buying when he asked for it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a consent given under domestic pressure may be legally worthless, and asks what value a formal waiver has if the signer can always disown it.

answer.quote: If it is true that you acted only in order to please your husband, you should have done so with regard to the first purchaser
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi explains when a wife's ratification actually binds her — where a prior unsigned sale exists, the "to please my husband" excuse collapses — which bears on what the purchaser gains by obtaining her signature, though in the single-sale case the signature is still conceded to be disavowable, so the question can honestly persist.

ketubot/96.summary: A wife's lost-and-found objects belong to her husband, and the stated reason is to spare him resentment over money he cannot account for; the heirs who sustain a widow get no such protection. The answer is blunt: let them have enmity toward the widow. The same friction returns when Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seized a saddlebag of coins for her food and the Sages could not take it back, though Ravina would take it back had she seized it for her marriage contract.
ketubot/96.question: If a widow's grab at a saddlebag of coins stands when she calls it food, why should the identical grab fail when she calls it payment of her marriage contract?

judge.reachNote: Whether the label a claimant puts on a self-help seizure — daily bread versus an old debt — can change whether the grab holds.

answer.quote: If it is that a marriage contract is paid only from real estate and not from movable property, there is a rabbinic enactment that sustenance is also
answer.explanation: Mar bar Rav Ashi raises the note's very question and names the only candidate reason (ketuba is collected from land alone), but then refutes it since sustenance too is enacted to come from land, so no accepted reason for Ravina's distinction is given.

ketubot/97.summary: A man sold land to Rav Pappa to raise money for oxen, then found he did not need the oxen, and Rav Pappa handed the land back. The Gemara refuses to treat that as precedent, calling it conduct beyond the letter of the law. Harder is Neharde'a, where a drought drove everyone to sell their mansions for wheat money; when a wheat ship arrived and prices dropped, Rav Naḥman ordered the houses returned, and Rami bar Shmuel warned that no one would buy land again.
ketubot/97.question: If a sale made under pressure can be undone once the pressure lifts, what stops Rami bar Shmuel's worry that nobody will risk buying anything?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real tension between undoing sales made in error and keeping the land market reliable for buyers.

answer.quote: Is that to say that it is so common, that there is a drought every day? I said that the properties are returned only in these specific circumstances.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises Rami bar Shmuel's exact worry about deterring buyers and has Rav Naḥman answer it by limiting reversal to rare, drought-like circumstances.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 97a: "Is that to say that it is so common, that there is a drought every day? I said that the properties are returned only in these specific circumstances.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Rav Naḥman replies that drought is not an everyday event, so reversal applies only in these specific circumstances. The rewrite should start after that answer — note that Rami bar Shmuel counters "Yes, in Neharde'a drought is a frequent occurrence" and that the halakha still concludes the sale is reversed, and ask what is left of the rarity limit once the exception is admitted to be common. Alternatively ask about the distinction the Gemara actually leans on, between an error present at the time of sale (the ship already in the bays) and circumstances that change afterward.

ketubot/98.summary: A widow sells her dead husband's land to collect what his estate owes her under her marriage contract. A man holding orphans' coral priced it himself at four hundred dinars, took it, and watched it rise to six hundred; Rabbi Ammi asked who assessed it for him and gave the profit to the orphans. The mishna makes the widow eat the loss when she sells too cheaply, and hand the heirs the gain when she sells well.
ketubot/98.question: If a widow who undersells the land absorbs that loss alone, what makes the profit from a good sale belong to the orphans rather than to her?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the asymmetry of risk and reward for one who sells another's property — which the page resolves by treating her as an agent whose gains belong to the owner of the money.

answer.quote: it can be learned from this mishna that it is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s opinion that everything belongs to the owner of the money
answer.explanation: The Gemara on 98a raises exactly the note's objection (why can she not say "I profited... I am entitled to another one hundred dinars") and answers on 98b that the widow acts as an agent, and profit belongs to the owner of the money.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 98b: "it can be learned from this mishna that it is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s opinion that everything belongs to the owner of the money". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question on 98a, and it is answered a few lines later on 98b: the widow is like an agent, and "everything belongs to the owner of the money." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating the difficulty it resolves — for instance, press on why the agent-and-owner dispute (Rabbi Yehuda vs. Rabbi Yosei, fixed price vs. no fixed price) does not give the widow a share of the surplus. Alternatively, build the question on the coral case or on the "who assessed this for you" requirement and whether an assessment can ever make her a true purchaser.

ketubot/99.summary: An owner tells his agent to sell a kor, a large measure of grain, and the agent sells only half; the page asks whether that is helpful restraint or plain disobedience. One objection raised is social rather than financial: more sales mean more deeds, and a man with many documents looks heavily mortgaged. Rav Naḥman allows an agent to sell to a hundred buyers, yet says that if the agent misprices the land, the agency collapses.
ketubot/99.question: If a man who undersells his own field has no claim of fraud, why does the identical underselling by his agent undo the sale entirely?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that an agent's authority is bounded by the principal's benefit, while an owner may freely act against his own interest — but the page states exactly this answer.

answer.quote: the homeowner can say to the agent: I sent you to act for my benefit and not to my detriment
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman explicitly distinguishes the owner's own error, which cannot be undone for fraud, from the agent's error, which voids the agency because the agent was sent only for the owner's benefit.

summaryProblems.claim: The kor the agent is told to sell is 'a large measure of grain'.
summaryProblems.pageSays: small tracts of land that are geographically separated and do not form one land mass that can be sold as a single unit

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 99b: "the homeowner can say to the agent: I sent you to act for my benefit and not to my detriment". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The kor the agent is told to sell is 'a large measure of grain'.", but the page says "small tracts of land that are geographically separated and do not form one land mass that can be sold as a single unit". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words on 99b, where Rav Naḥman says the owner may tell the agent "I sent you to act for my benefit and not to my detriment"; ask something the page leaves standing instead. A better line might probe why an agent's mispricing voids the agency outright while a court's appraisal survives an error of one-sixth, or press on the teruma comparison. Also drop the gloss calling the kor a measure of grain, since the surrounding discussion treats the sale as land.

ketubot/100.summary: A court that sells an orphan's inherited land is supposed to announce the sale publicly, morning and evening, for thirty days; selling without the announcement counts as an error that undoes the deal. Then Rav Naḥman reports that Neharde'a never made such announcements at all, and the reason given is not that its judges were expert appraisers but that buyers at announced sales got a bad name, so decent people stopped coming. Elsewhere Rav Kahana holds an orphan's beer until the Festival, accepting some souring for a better cash price.
ketubot/100.question: If the public announcement exists to draw buyers and protect orphans, does dropping it in Neharde'a protect the orphans or only the reputations of the people who would have bid?

judge.reachNote: A protective procedure can defeat its own purpose when the stigma it creates drives away exactly the buyers it was meant to attract.

answer.quote: Since decent, honest people did not wish to buy property whose sale had been announced, they stopped making announcements.
answer.explanation: The page gives the stated rationale — announced sales repelled respectable buyers — which bears directly on whether dropping the announcement helped or hurt the orphans, though it never says whose interest was thereby served.

ketubot/101.summary: The mishna lists women who leave a marriage with no payment of their marriage contract: a girl married off as a minor who ends it by refusal, and an ailonit, a woman who cannot bear children. Shmuel limits the loss to the fixed sum the Sages set, one or two hundred dinars, since any extra amount a husband wrote in himself counts as a gift she keeps. When a tanna recites that an unfaithful wife forfeits even her worn clothes, Rav Nahman makes him teach the opposite.
ketubot/101.question: Why should the penalty fall on the money the Sages promised her and leave untouched the money her husband promised on his own?

judge.reachNote: The Sages can cancel what they themselves instituted but not what a husband undertook of his own will — the limits of a rabbinic penalty.

answer.quote: the additional sum listed in the marriage contract, which their husband specified for them of his own accord, is considered a gift and they are entitled to it
answer.explanation: The page gives a reason for the untouched half of the distinction — the extra sum is a voluntary gift rather than a Sages' enactment — but never says why the Sages' own instituted sum is the thing forfeited, so the question survives in part.

ketubot/102.summary: Two families haggling over a marriage settlement ask each other how much they will give the son and how much the daughter, and Rav Giddel says that once the couple is betrothed those spoken promises bind with no further act of acquisition. Rava objects that the bride's father at least gains the betrothal money, while the groom's father gains nothing but the match itself. Ravina then asks whether such spoken deals may later be put into a contract, and Rav Ashi says no.
ketubot/102.question: Why should the bare satisfaction of seeing the two married be enough to bind the groom's father, when the page also entertains that a man who writes "I owe you one hundred dinars" may owe nothing at all?
gate: the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: What makes a self-imposed obligation binding: does it need a countervailing benefit or exchange, or can a bare declaration of debt suffice?

answer.quote: Rather, it must be explained that in exchange for that benefit, i.e., that the groom and bride marry each other, the fathers fully transfer the rights to the respective payments to each other.
answer.explanation: Rava supplies a reason — the obligation binds because each father receives the reciprocal transfer, not bare satisfaction — but the page never reconciles this with ben Nannas's view that a written "I owe you one hundred dinars" creates no debt, so the question can still be honestly pressed.

ketubot/103.summary: A widow who stays in her late husband's house keeps the use of everything she had while he lived: the maidservants, the pillows, the silver utensils. But Abaye holds that if those living quarters collapse, the heirs need not rebuild, and an early teaching adds that even if she offers to rebuild at her own expense, they may refuse her. Abaye then asks what the law is if she merely repairs the house, and the question is left unresolved.
ketubot/103.question: Why should the heirs be able to refuse a widow who offers to rebuild the collapsed house with her own money, when rebuilding costs them nothing?

judge.reachNote: Whether the widow's right is a claim on one particular house or a claim on housing, and whether an owner may refuse a benefit that costs him nothing.

answer.quote: since they are obligated to maintain her in the residence that was mortgaged to her and are not required to provide her with a place to live
answer.explanation: The page explains why the heirs need not rebuild — her lien is on that specific residence — but never says why they may also block her from rebuilding at her own expense, so the question still stands.

ketubot/104.summary: A widow who never sues for the money her marriage contract promises her from her husband's estate is presumed, after twenty-five years, to have waived it. Rabbi Meir says she forfeits while living among her husband's heirs; the Rabbis say living there is exactly why she was too embarrassed to ask. Then Rav Ḥiyya Arikha, who carried his widowed sister-in-law's food to her father's house for twenty-five years, is ordered to pay, because his kindness is what kept her quiet.
ketubot/104.question: If treating a widow generously is the very thing that proves she never gave up her claim, what does an heir gain by carrying her food on his own shoulders?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the law reads kindness as the cause of a widow's silence, so generosity preserves rather than extinguishes her claim — raising whether the ruling penalizes decency.

ketubot/105.summary: A judge named Karna charged an istera, a small coin, from each side before hearing a case, and the Gemara strains to explain why that is a wage rather than a bribe. The talk then slides from money to favors: a hand offered off a ferry, a feather lifted from Ameimar's head, spittle covered over, each one enough to disqualify the judge. Rabbi Yishmael refused his sharecropper's basket of fruit, fruit legally his own, and still caught himself building the man's case.
ketubot/105.question: If refusing fruit that already belonged to him left Rabbi Yishmael silently arguing the man's side, what does handing the case to two scholars in his own house actually fix?

judge.reachNote: Bias works below intention, so the question asks whether stepping aside actually removes the tilt or only hides it.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yishmael seated a pair of rabbinic scholars and they judged the sharecropper’s case.
answer.explanation: The page reports that the verdict was removed from Rabbi Yishmael's hands and given to other judges, which bears on what recusal accomplishes, but it never says what that cures given his admitted lingering partiality.

ketubot/106.summary: Inspectors who checked animals for blemishes before they could be offered drew their wages from the Temple chamber, the fund built from the public collection of shekels. So did the proofreaders of Jerusalem's Torah scrolls, the women who wove the curtains, and the women who raised children in lifelong purity so they could draw water for the red heifer. Then the argument turns to leftovers, and Rabbi Akiva bars trading with them: the Temple is too rich to haggle, the poor fund too urgent to tie up.
ketubot/106.question: When does a fund become wealthy enough that earning a little more is beneath it, and who gets to decide that?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether a fund's dignity or purpose can forbid it from prudent gain, and who has standing to declare a treasury rich enough.

answer.quote: It is because there is no poverty in a place of wealth, i.e., the Temple must always be run in a lavish manner.
answer.explanation: The page gives the principle behind Rabbi Akiva's ban on profiting from consecrated funds, but it does not say where the threshold of such wealth lies or who sets it, so the question survives in part.

ketubot/107.summary: A husband sails overseas leaving his wife with nothing, and Rav says the court takes money from his property to feed her while Shmuel says it does not. Shmuel's doubts are concrete: maybe the husband slipped her a bundle of money before leaving, or told her to live on her own earnings. Every source brought against him gets re-read as a case where word came back that he died, and Rabbi Yohanan is openly astonished at the stretch.
ketubot/107.question: Does the mere possibility that a husband left a bundle of money behind justify making his wife wait to eat until someone proves he did not?

judge.reachNote: Whether an unproven possibility of provision may override a present, daily need — burden of doubt versus burden of hunger.

answer.quote: And the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav, and therefore one apportions sustenance for a married woman whose husband went overseas.
answer.explanation: The Gemara's concluding ruling decides exactly this: the suspicion of a bundle of money does not justify withholding sustenance, and the court feeds her.

summaryProblems.claim: Every source brought against Shmuel gets re-read as a case where word came back that he died.
summaryProblems.pageSays: If the concern is due to the possibility that he gave her a bundle of money before his departure, the mind of the yavam is not that close to this woman

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 107b: "And the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav, and therefore one apportions sustenance for a married woman whose husband went overseas.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Every source brought against Shmuel gets re-read as a case where word came back that he died.", but the page says "If the concern is due to the possibility that he gave her a bundle of money before his departure, the mind of the yavam is not that close to this woman". Say what the page says. The page settles this question outright — "the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav" — so the question as posed is closed before the daf ends. Ask instead about something the ruling leaves unresolved, such as why Shmuel's own concession about the first three months ("a person does not leave his house empty") does not simply extend forever, or why the two suspicions of Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa fail against a minor or a yevama. Also fix the summary: not every objection is deflected by the rumor-of-death reading; the yevama and the refusing minor are answered by saying the two suspicions do not apply.

ketubot/108.summary: A man has vowed not to derive benefit from another, and the mishna still permits that other to donate his half-shekel to the Temple, return his lost object, and pay off his debt. Paying the debt looks like straight gain, so Rav Oshaya and Rava each narrow it to a loan the borrower was never really obliged to repay. Rav Oshaya then presses back: even an open-ended loan leaves the borrower ashamed before his lender, and relief from shame is benefit.
ketubot/108.question: If being spared embarrassment counts as a benefit received, what can anyone still do for a person forbidden to benefit from him?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether intangible relief (freedom from embarrassment) counts as 'benefit,' and if so how any assistance escapes the vow.

answer.quote: Granted, he may contribute his shekel for him, as he thereby performs a mitzva.
answer.explanation: The page shows that acts which are mitzvot and confer no direct gain (the half-shekel, returning a lost object) remain permitted, which bears on what may still be done, but it never addresses how the shame standard would reshape that boundary.

ketubot/109.summary: A man sails overseas and comes back to find the path to his field swallowed by a neighbor's land, its exact line now unknown. Admon says he walks the shortest route; the Rabbis say he must buy one at whatever price, even a hundred dinars, a steep sum, or fly through the air. Rava explains the Rabbis: a neighbor who bought all four surrounding fields from four different owners can threaten to hand each deed back, leaving the claimant no one to press.
ketubot/109.question: If everyone agrees the man once had a path somewhere inside that land, is the neighbor's threat to return the deeds an argument about who owns what, or only a way to force a settlement?

judge.reachNote: Whether a litigant's procedural leverage counts as a legal claim about title or merely as bargaining pressure that the law tolerates.

answer.quote: If you will stay silent, then stay silent and we will compromise; and if not, I will return the document of each field
answer.explanation: The Rabbis' own words frame the deed-return as leverage toward a compromise rather than as a denial of the claimant's underlying right, though the page never says outright that it is not an ownership argument.

ketubot/110.summary: A man who marries in Judea cannot make his wife move to the Galilee, and even within one region he cannot move her from a town to a city or a city to a town. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel goes further: not even from a bad house to a nice one, since Shmuel says a change of diet or dwelling starts intestinal disease. Yet a few lines later anyone may force his household to ascend to Eretz Yisrael, pleasant home to noxious one included.
ketubot/110.question: If moving even to a better house can make a person sick, why does that worry stop counting the moment the destination is Eretz Yisrael?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a person's bodily welfare and settled habits are protected against a husband's will, yet yield when the destination itself carries religious weight.

answer.quote: but you may not take the slave abroad with you, due to the mitzva of settling Eretz Yisrael
answer.explanation: The page supplies a countervailing value — the mitzva of settling the land, reinforced by the teaching that living outside it is like idol worship — which bears on why comfort concerns are overridden, but it never addresses Shmuel's health worry directly.

ketubot/111.summary: Rabbi Elazar says the dead buried outside the Land of Israel will not be resurrected, reading a verse about glory set in the land of the living. Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects from another verse, and the compromise offered is that the righteous elsewhere roll underground to the land, which one sage calls an ordeal, so Abaye supplies tunnels. Then Karna notes that Jacob, who knew he was completely righteous, still made Joseph carry him out of Egypt.
ketubot/111.question: If tunnels are prepared for the righteous, what did Jacob think he was missing when he made his sons haul his body out of Egypt?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that even one who knows himself completely righteous cannot count on a promised concession like the tunnels — but the page states this outright.

answer.quote: why did he trouble his sons to bring him to Eretz Yisrael? The reason is that he was concerned lest he not merit the tunnels.
answer.explanation: The page asks the note's exact question about Jacob and answers it in the same line: he feared he might not merit the tunnels.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Ketubot 111a: "why did he trouble his sons to bring him to Eretz Yisrael? The reason is that he was concerned lest he not merit the tunnels.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question and Karna answers it on the same line: Jacob feared he might not merit the tunnels. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than repeating it — for example, why a man certain of his own righteousness still doubts he will receive the concession, or what it means that the tunnels are a merit rather than a guarantee. The summary itself is accurate and can stand.

ketubot/112.summary: Three traveling sages are handed a peach as large as a stewpot from Kefar Hino, a pot holding five se'a, roughly forty liters; they eat a third, give a third to their animals, and declare the rest ownerless. A year later the peach fits in one hand. In between, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sees grape clusters the size of calves and tells the earth to stop yielding fruit for the gentiles ruling over Israel, and the clusters shrink to goats.
ketubot/112.question: Rabbi Hanina filled in potholes so travelers would have nothing bad to say about the land, while Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi told that same land to hold back its fruit, so which of them was loving it?
gate: the question brings in "Hanina", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether love of the land means guarding its good name or refusing to let its blessing serve its conquerors.

answer.quote: For whom do you produce your fruit? For these gentiles who stand over us in our sins? It would be preferable if you did not produce such large fruit.
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's motive — grief that Israel's bounty feeds its oppressors — which bears on whether his curse was love, but it never weighs his act against Rabbi Ḥanina's pothole-filling or says which expresses love of the land.

summaryProblems.claim: The grape-cluster episode happened 'in between' the two peach years.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Once Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi happened to come to Gavla, in the Golan, and he saw those clusters of vines that were standing as large as calves.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The grape-cluster episode happened 'in between' the two peach years.", but the page says "Once Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi happened to come to Gavla, in the Golan, and he saw those clusters of vines that were standing as large as calves.". Say what the page says.

nedarim/2.summary: Nedarim opens with a man who makes something forbidden to himself by speaking, saying an object is to him like an offering. Garbled versions count too: konam for korban, ḥerekh for ḥerem, nazik for nazir. Half-sentences count as well, so "I am avowed from you" binds, though when a man says "I am ostracized from you" Rabbi Akiva could not decide, and leaned strict. The Gemara then spends the rest of the page on why the mishna explains its clauses out of order.
nedarim/2.question: If a mispronounced word like konam still binds a person, what is missing from "I am ostracized from you" that left even Rabbi Akiva unsure?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the criterion that makes speech binding: not correct wording but whether something is clearly declared forbidden.

answer.quote: However, if he says: I am ostracized from you, which does not clearly declare any matter to be prohibited, Rabbi Akiva was uncertain about this halakha
answer.explanation: The mishna itself states what is lacking in the ostracism formula — it declares no matter prohibited — which is precisely what the question asks for.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nedarim 2a: "However, if he says: I am ostracized from you, which does not clearly declare any matter to be prohibited, Rabbi Akiva was uncertain about this halakha". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the mishna's own words, which say that "I am ostracized from you" "does not clearly declare any matter to be prohibited." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for example, press on why the fragmentary "I am avowed from you" is treated as declaring something prohibited while ostracism language is not, or why Rabbi Akiva leans stringent while still in doubt. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

nedarim/3.summary: A nazirite, someone who vows off wine and grapes, becomes one the instant he says so, which makes it hard to see how he could ever be guilty of delaying his vow. Rava finds a case in a man who says he will not depart the world until he becomes a nazirite; he is bound from that moment, since he could die at any second. The same reasoning bars a priest's wife from teruma, the priestly food portion, the moment he dates her divorce to an hour before his death.
nedarim/3.question: If we really say at every moment that perhaps he is already dead, why does that suspicion bind only the nazirite and the divorced wife and nothing else a person does?

judge.reachNote: When does a possibility that can never be ruled out (that one may already be dead) count as legally binding rather than merely doubtful?

nedarim/4.summary: A man vows to become a nazirite, one who swears off wine, haircuts, and contact with corpses, while standing in a cemetery, where a nazirite may not be. The sages hunt for exactly how the prohibition "you shall not delay" bites on such a vow: the postponed purification, the unshaved hair, the offerings not yet brought. The sharpest move comes when they define what makes the nazirite strange, since his sin-offering atones for nothing and permits nothing.
nedarim/4.question: If the nazirite's sin-offering neither wipes away a sin nor unlocks anything the way a new mother's offering lets her eat consecrated food, what is he bringing it for?
gate: gloss "sin-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question uses "sin offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Asks what an offering is for when it is neither atonement nor a permitting rite — the underlying question of what a sacrifice does.

nedarim/5.summary: A man tells another, "I am avowed from you," and the argument is whether that bars one of them from benefiting from the other, or both. Shmuel's position is restated three times before it survives, ending with the claim that such loose words mean only that the speaker will not talk to him, or do business, or stand near. From there the dispute turns on whether half-stated wording binds at all, with divorce documents as the test case.
nedarim/5.question: If everyone listening knows exactly what the speaker meant, why should the missing words "of yours" be enough to unmake the vow?

judge.reachNote: Whether a vow is made by the words said or by the intent everyone can see behind them — the idea is real, but the page states its own answer.

answer.quote: just as accepting naziriteship must be expressed with a distinct articulation, so too, intimations of naziriteship must be expressed with a distinct articulation as opposed to ambiguous intimations
answer.explanation: The page asks exactly why obvious wording is required when the context makes the intent plain, and answers with Rabbi Idi's derivation from "nazir lehazir" that intimations need distinct articulation, after Rava had already concluded from the mishna's "of yours" that "the intent of the individual taking the vow must be indicated by his verbal statement and not merely by the context of his statement."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nedarim 5b: "just as accepting naziriteship must be expressed with a distinct articulation, so too, intimations of naziriteship must be expressed with a distinct articulation as opposed to ambiguous intimations". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the one the page itself raises and settles: Rava's proof from "nazir lehazir" is precisely why context is not enough and the words "of yours" matter. Ask instead about what the page leaves unresolved — for instance why Rabbi Yehuda demands clear wording only for a bill of divorce, where "we require full severance of the relationship," and not for vows, or what Abaye gains by letting unclear words still bind. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

nedarim/6.summary: A man points at an object and says "it is upon me," and it becomes forbidden to him like an offering, but if he says only "it is hereby," the words might mean ownerless property, charity, or consecrated to the Temple. Abaye, who had held that such half-statements still bind, retracts. Rav Pappa then asks whether saying "and you" to a second woman betroths her, and whether a furrow joins pe'a, the field corner left for the poor.
nedarim/6.question: If "and you" leaves the second woman unable to tell whether she has just been betrothed, whose reading of those two words settles her status?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether legal status is fixed by the speaker's intent or by what the hearer could reasonably understand.

summaryProblems.claim: Abaye, who had held that such half-statements still bind, retracts (i.e., gives up his position that ambiguous intimations are valid).
summaryProblems.pageSays: He retracted this statement and admitted that Rabbi Yehuda holds that ambiguous intimations are not valid intimations.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Abaye, who had held that such half-statements still bind, retracts (i.e., gives up his position that ambiguous intimations are valid).", but the page says "He retracted this statement and admitted that Rabbi Yehuda holds that ambiguous intimations are not valid intimations.". Say what the page says. Correct the account of Abaye's retraction: he did not abandon his own view that ambiguous intimations bind, he only conceded that Rabbi Yehuda does not hold that way, and Rava then insists his own view stands even according to the Rabbis. Keep the "upon me" / "it is hereby" distinction and the Rav Pappa dilemmas, which the page supports. The question may stay, since the page poses the "and you" dilemma without resolving it.

nedarim/7.summary: A man says that one dinar, a small silver coin, is for charity, then points to a second and says only: and this. The Gemara asks whether half a sentence binds him, and runs the same puzzle through renouncing property to whoever wants it and through declaring a spot a bathroom, where sacred items may not be brought. Later the page turns to bans: Rav Huna excommunicated a woman for saying God's name in vain and released her on the spot.
nedarim/7.question: If Rav Huna's ban on the woman began and ended in the same moment, what had she actually undergone?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a ban may work as a marking or declaration rather than as a duration of suffering, just as 'and this' may bind without being completed.

answer.quote: learn from this that there is nothing, i.e., no minimum time that must pass, between ostracism and nullification of the ostracism
answer.explanation: The page licenses an instantaneous ban by ruling that no interval is required, but it never says what the woman thereby underwent, so the question survives.

nedarim/8.summary: Rav Yosef holds that a man ostracized in a dream needs ten people to release him, and they must have studied halakha, not merely recited Mishna. If ten scholars cannot be found, he sits at a crossroads greeting passersby until some happen along. Rav Ashi then rules that the figure who banned him in the dream cannot lift the ban, and that a dreamed release proves nothing, since dreams, like grain, never come without straw.
nedarim/8.question: If a dream is unreliable enough that its dissolution means nothing, why is its excommunication binding enough to need ten scholars?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that dream-authority is treated asymmetrically: stringent when it binds, worthless when it frees.

answer.quote: It is possible that the excommunication was real and the dissolution was not real, and he must have the ostracism dissolved by ten people.
answer.explanation: The page states the asymmetry the question probes — the ban may be genuine while the dreamed release is the dream's idle matter — but it does not explain why the reverse possibility (an unreal ban) is not equally entertained, so the question survives in part.

summaryProblems.claim: If ten scholars cannot be found, he sits at a crossroads greeting passersby until some happen along.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And if there are not even ten people who have studied Mishna, let him go and sit at the crossroads and extend a greeting of shalom

summaryProblems.claim: They must have studied halakha, not merely recited Mishna.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And if there are not ten people who have studied halakha, then even those who have recited Mishna and have not studied halakha are fit

judge.feedback: The summary says "If ten scholars cannot be found, he sits at a crossroads greeting passersby until some happen along.", but the page says "And if there are not even ten people who have studied Mishna, let him go and sit at the crossroads and extend a greeting of shalom". Say what the page says. The summary says "They must have studied halakha, not merely recited Mishna.", but the page says "And if there are not ten people who have studied halakha, then even those who have recited Mishna and have not studied halakha are fit". Say what the page says. Keep the question — it names a real asymmetry the page only partly resolves. Fix the summary's tiering: the page allows Mishna-reciters when ten halakha scholars are unavailable, and only when even ten Mishna-reciters are lacking does he go to the crossroads. Consider also noting Rav Ashi's stated reason, that the dreamed ban may be real while the dreamed release is not, so the question builds on it rather than ignoring it.

nedarim/9.summary: The mishna says a person who declares himself bound "like the vows of the wicked" has vowed, while "like the vows of the virtuous" binds him to nothing, since the virtuous are said not to vow. The virtuous do bring gift offerings, animals volunteered rather than promised in advance, so Rabbi Meir's objection to vows has to be narrowed. Hillel's answer was timing: he brought his animal to the Temple courtyard unconsecrated, consecrated it there, laid his hand on its head, and slaughtered it at once.
nedarim/9.question: Shimon HaTzaddik kissed a shepherd who vowed to shave his curls on the spot after glimpsing his reflection in a spring, yet the page defends the vows of pure nazirites on the grounds that such a man coolly assessed what he could keep, so which of the two is the safe vow?
gate: the question brings in "Shimon", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "HaTzaddik", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).
the question uses "nazirite", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: What makes a vow safe: sincere motive seized in a moment, or sober measurement of what one can actually carry out.

answer.quote: In the case of a pure nazirite there is no concern because he assessed himself and realized that he was able to vow and to keep his vow
answer.explanation: The page states why a pure nazirite's vow is trusted (self-assessment), and separately praises the shepherd's vow as made "with entirely pure intentions rather than as a rash statement," but never sets the two standards against each other, so the tension the question raises survives.

nedarim/10.summary: A mishna lists konam, konaḥ and konas, garbled near-misses of korban, "offering," and rules that a vow made with any of them holds, forbidding the item to the speaker as if it were Temple property. Reish Lakish says the Sages invented these words so that nobody would open with "To the Lord," change his mind, and leave God's name hanging in the air. Then the substitutes breed substitutes, and the questions pile up.
nedarim/10.question: If a man says kina and may simply have meant a chicken coop, has he bound himself, and who gets to decide that?

judge.reachNote: When a word's sense is ambiguous, does the vow ride on the sound of the word or on what the speaker meant by it?

answer.quote: or perhaps it is a term for konam and expresses a vow? With regard to these cases, the Gemara says: The dilemma remains unresolved.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the kina case and leaves it undecided, so it names the difficulty but never says whether the man is bound or who decides.

nedarim/11.summary: A man says his food shall be laḥullin, one letter away from the word for non-sacred, and the page asks whether that added lamed means "not non-sacred," that is, consecrated. Rabbi Meir will not read a positive out of a negative, since he demands conditions spelled out both ways, as Moses did with the tribes of Gad and Reuben. Then Rami bar Ḥama points at peace-offering meat, forbidden before its blood is sprinkled and permitted after, and asks which state a vow attaches to.
nedarim/11.question: When someone points at a piece of meat and says "this is like that," is he pointing at what the meat is now or at what it used to be?
gate: gloss "peace-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Does a verbal association attach to the item's present status or to the forbidden status it once carried?

answer.quote: To resolve this question, Rava said: Come and hear a proof from the mishna: If he said the food shall be considered an offering that has become notar or piggul
answer.explanation: The page brings Rava's proof from the mishna's notar/piggul case toward resolving the dilemma, but stops before stating the conclusion, so the question can still honestly be asked.

nedarim/12.summary: A person can forbid food to himself by calling it like something already forbidden, and the page keeps asking which moment he means: an offering's meat before its blood is sprinkled on the altar, when nobody may eat it, or after, when priests may. Proofs come from a man who swears off meat and wine like the day his father died, and from teruma, the priests' share of the thanks-offering loaves. The page turns each proof aside.
nedarim/12.question: When a man vows to abstain like the day his father died, is he pointing at that one Sunday long ago or at every anniversary since?
gate: the question brings in "Sunday", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the page's real issue — whether a vow points at an item's original forbidden status or its present one — but the page settles this very case.

answer.quote: Shmuel said: And this is if he was continuously obligated by a vow from that day forward to abstain from meat and wine on the anniversary of his father’s death.
answer.explanation: The Gemara first suggests he means the original Sunday, then resolves that because he was under a continuing vow every year, his words refer to the day's current status, so the proof collapses.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nedarim 12a: "Shmuel said: And this is if he was continuously obligated by a vow from that day forward to abstain from meat and wine on the anniversary of his father’s death.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later on 12a, where Shmuel's statement is reread to mean the man was continuously bound by a vow each year, so he refers to the day's current status. Rewrite the question so it starts from that resolution rather than asking what the page already settles — for instance, why a reworded report of Shmuel can dissolve a proof, or what the firstborn-meat dispute at the end still leaves undecided about original versus current status.

nedarim/13.summary: To make food forbidden, a person can compare it to something already off limits, but the comparison works only if that something was itself banned by someone's vow. A sin-offering, the animal a person sets aside to atone for a wrong, counts, since he chose it; a firstborn animal, holy from the moment it is born, does not. Yet one view notes its owner is still commanded to consecrate it, which would make even the firstborn a creature of words.
nedarim/13.question: If a firstborn animal is already holy from birth no matter what its owner says, what work is left for the owner's words when he is commanded to consecrate it?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Whether a human declaration adds anything to a status the Torah has already imposed — do words do work when the outcome is fixed?

answer.quote: its owner is still commanded to declare it consecrated, and it is therefore considered an item forbidden by means of a vow
answer.explanation: The baraita cited in the name of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the owner's declaration gives the firstborn the status of a vow-forbidden item, but the opposing view immediately answers that it is consecrated anyway, so the question remains live.

nedarim/14.summary: A man who tells his wife she is to him like his mother's flesh, or calls his food pig meat, has created no vow, since those things are already forbidden and a vow must borrow its force from something a person forbade himself. Abaye still sends him to a sage by rabbinic law; Rava sends only the ignoramus, since a scholar knows nothing happened. With a Torah scroll lying on the ground, Rav Naḥman assumes the man pictures blank parchment.
nedarim/14.question: If the vow never took effect at all, what is the sage dissolving when the ignoramus comes to ask?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a request for dissolution can be required as a rabbinic educational measure even where there is legally nothing to dissolve.

answer.quote: This mishna, on the other hand, is referring to an ignoramus, with regard to whom a rabbinic ordinance is necessary lest they take vows lightly.
answer.explanation: Rava gives the purpose of the rabbinic requirement — deterring the unlearned from treating vows lightly — which bears on why a sage is approached, but the page never says what the sage actually dissolves when nothing took effect.

nedarim/15.summary: A man vows that sleeping will be forbidden to his eyes today if he sleeps tomorrow, and the question is whether he may sleep today at all. Rav Yehuda says no, since tomorrow's sleep would make today's nap a violation retroactively; Rav Naḥman permits it. One by one, the mishnayot brought to refute Rav Yehuda get the same answer: the text described what happens once someone has already acted, not what he may do in advance.
nedarim/15.question: If every source that seems to permit an act in advance can be reread as merely describing what was already done, what evidence could ever have refuted Rav Yehuda?

judge.reachNote: Whether an inference from how a text phrases a case ('he ate' vs. 'he may eat') can ever be probative, or whether such readings make a position unfalsifiable.

answer.quote: the latter clause also teaches the halakha in the case where he went, and does not teach that he may go, to maintain a uniform style
answer.explanation: The Gemara concedes that the wording-based inference proves nothing because a uniform style explains it, and closes with "neither opinion is refuted" — which bears on the note's question about what could count as evidence, without stating what evidence would ever settle it.

nedarim/16.summary: Guests keep pressing a man to eat, and he answers with the words "an oath that I will eat." Abaye says those same three words point two ways depending on what came before: if he has been saying "I will eat," the oath commits him to eating, and if he has been refusing, the oath locks in the refusal. Rav Ashi rejects context entirely and rewrites the mishna's wording to "that I will not eat," so the words mean what they say.
nedarim/16.question: If a man's oath means the opposite of its words whenever he has been refusing long enough, who gets to decide how many refusals it takes?

judge.reachNote: Whether the meaning of a binding formula comes from the words themselves or from the conversation surrounding them — and who fixes the point at which context overrides the plain words.

answer.quote: Rather, the tanna in tractate Shevuot clearly established a principle: That I will eat, indicates that I will eat, and: That I will not eat, indicates I will not eat.
answer.explanation: The page does not set a threshold of refusals, but it does state Rav Ashi's resolution: a fixed tannaitic principle governs the wording rather than a count of prior statements, so the question can still be pressed against Abaye but is partly met.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Ashi rejects context entirely.
summaryProblems.pageSays: he held that the phrase: That I will not eat, also indicates two expressions, depending on the context

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Ashi rejects context entirely.", but the page says "he held that the phrase: That I will not eat, also indicates two expressions, depending on the context". Say what the page says. Fix the description of Rav Ashi: the page has him accepting that context flips meaning even more widely — "That I will not eat" can itself mean "I will eat" — and concluding from that overreach that the mishna's wording must be emended and the tanna's fixed principle followed. Then let the question push against Abaye knowing the page already answers with a fixed principle, e.g. ask what is lost when meaning is pinned to words rather than to the speaker's evident intent.

nedarim/17.summary: A man says he is hereby a nazirite, someone bound by a vow to a thirty-day stretch of abstinence, then says it again, and the mishna counts two full terms. Say the same oath about not eating figs twice and he owes only one offering for breaking it. Rav Huna restricts the doubling to today plus tomorrow, Shmuel lets two identical terms stack, and one objection is brushed aside because Rabba was Rav Huna's student.
nedarim/17.question: If saying the same nazirite vow twice binds a person twice over, why does repeating the very same oath about figs bind him only once?

judge.reachNote: Why repetition creates a fresh obligation for a vow but adds nothing to an oath — what the mishna's vow/oath distinction rests on.

answer.quote: even if he said: I am hereby a nazirite today, I am hereby a nazirite today, a second vow of naziriteship takes effect with regard to him, as one can apply two obligations of naziriteship to himself one after the other
answer.explanation: Shmuel gives a reason why repeated naziriteship can double — the two terms can be observed consecutively — which bears on the contrast with a repeated oath, but the page never states why an oath cannot take effect upon an oath, and Rav Huna in fact denies that identical vows double at all.

nedarim/18.summary: A man says an item is forbidden to him like salted meat, and never says which salted meat. If he meant the meat of an offering, the vow binds; if he meant meat sacrificed to an idol, it does not, because a vow holds only when the thing it is compared to was itself made forbidden by a vow. Rabbi Yehuda makes it local: in Galilee, unspecified teruma, the priests' share of the harvest, binds nothing.
nedarim/18.question: If the force of a vow depends on what the speaker's neighbors happen to mean by a word, what binds a Judean who says "like teruma" while standing in the Galilee?
gate: the question brings in "Judean", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a vow's binding force is fixed by the speaker's own intent or by the conventional meaning of words in his community.

nedarim/19.summary: A man says he is a nazirite, abstaining from wine and haircuts, if a certain heap of grain holds a hundred kor, a large dry measure, and then the heap is stolen before anyone can measure it. Rabbi Yehuda frees him, Rabbi Shimon binds him. Rava explains Yehuda by noting that doubt here is harsher than certainty: an uncertain nazirite can never shave or bring the offerings that end the term.
nedarim/19.question: Rava waves off the nazirite like Samson as something the Sages never taught, then gives way the instant a baraita is quoted at him, so was his rule ever about the law or only about what he had heard?
gate: the question brings in "Samson", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's denial that a category exists is a legal claim about what can be vowed or merely a report of what he has received in tradition.
