Abaye rereads the mishna so that the speaker also added a second clause, that he will be a nazirite even if it is not that man, and it is the second clause that binds. If the walker turns back unidentified, nobody is a nazirite; the page then runs out, its second side filled with later commentary rather than Gemara.
nazir/33.question: If the approaching man really was so-and-so, why should his turning back before anyone can identify him undo a vow that was already true?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether a conditional vow takes effect on the underlying fact or only on a fact that becomes known.

answer.quote: The reason is only because he turned back, from which it may be inferred that if that person comes before us and is identified, the one who said he would be a nazirite if it is so-and-so is considered to be a nazirite
answer.explanation: The Gemara states that the turning back itself is the operative reason and that identification is what activates the vow, which bears on the question without explaining why an objectively true condition fails absent verification.

nazir/34.summary: Six people look at a koy, a kosher animal with traits of both domesticated and wild kinds, and each vows naziriteship on a different guess about what it is. Three more vow on whether those six are nazirites, and the mishna rules all of them nazirites; Rav Sheshet pictures one man taking all nine terms on himself. Later, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei flatly reverse which word, ḥartzannim or zaggim, means grape skin and which means seed.
nazir/34.question: If liability can rest on eating at least two ḥartzannim and one zag, and two sages hold opposite views about which word is the skin and which the seed, who is counting what?

judge.reachNote: A measured threshold of liability depends on which object each disputed word names, so the same rule counts different things for different sages.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yosei says: The opposite is the case and this is the mnemonic so that you should not err: It is like a bell [zog] worn by an animal
answer.explanation: The page records the dispute and Rabbi Yosei's mnemonic argument for which term is the skin, but never says how the two-ḥartzannim-and-one-zag count is applied under either naming, so the question still stands.

nazir/35.summary: A nazirite, who has vowed off wine and grapes, is bound by the verse "from pits to grape skin," and the page argues over how lists in verses should be read. Rabbi Abbahu points to a man given a neighbor's donkey, ox, sheep, or any animal "to guard": details around a general word limit it to things that can be guarded. Two rival methods then yield nearly the same result, differing only over how much resemblance counts.
nazir/35.question: If two ways of reading the same list can both be defended, what actually decides that a grapevine's tendrils are forbidden to a nazirite while its leaves are not?

judge.reachNote: Asks what authorizes the choice between competing exegetical methods when each is internally defensible and they yield different prohibitions.

answer.quote: with the method of restriction and amplification one includes less, as tendrils, yes, they are included in the prohibition, whereas leaves, no
answer.explanation: The page states that the tendrils-yes/leaves-no outcome follows from the restriction-and-amplification method rather than detail-and-generalization, but it never says what settles which method governs the nazirite verse.

nazir/36.summary: Rabbi Yochanan held that a permitted food combines with a forbidden one only for a nazirite, and Abaye spends the page trying to break that rule. He points to a pot of ordinary soup flavored with teruma, the priestly portion, where a non-priest is flogged for eating an olive-bulk. Rav Dimi answers that the measure is time-based: enough teruma swallowed in the span it takes to eat half a loaf.
nazir/36.question: Rav Dimi waves off the mixed-up spice mortars because spice teruma is only rabbinic, but when Abaye comes back with two baskets of actual grain, the page gives no answer, so why does the same benefit of the doubt still hold?

judge.reachNote: Whether a statistical 'I say' assumption can be relied on when the mistake would create a Torah-level prohibition rather than only a rabbinic one.

nazir/37.summary: A nazirite, a person under a vow barring wine and grapes, soaks his bread in wine and eats it, and the sages argue over what the word "soaked" in the verse is there to prove. One reading makes it the source for the rule that a forbidden food's taste counts as the food itself; others try to get that rule instead from meat cooked in milk, or from the Midianite pots purged in fire. Both alternatives are thrown out as too strange to generalize from.
nazir/37.question: If a rule drawn from an unusual case cannot be extended, what makes a nazirite's wine-soaked bread ordinary enough to govern every prohibition in the Torah?

judge.reachNote: Which cases are fit to found a general rule — the lenient-and-typical versus the anomalous — is exactly the idea the page argues about.

answer.quote: all other prohibitions in the Torah are more severe than the case of a nazirite in one of these aspects
answer.where: Nazir 37a (the baraita's a fortiori derivation from "soaked")
answer.explanation: The baraita explicitly explains why the nazirite can ground a universal rule: his prohibition is temporary, permits benefit, and can be dissolved, so every other prohibition is more stringent in at least one respect and follows a fortiori.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 37a (the baraita's a fortiori derivation from "soaked"): "all other prohibitions in the Torah are more severe than the case of a nazirite in one of these aspects". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered outright by the baraita's a fortiori argument: the nazirite's prohibition is temporary, permits benefit, and can be dissolved, so every other prohibition is more severe in at least one respect. Ask instead about what remains contested — why the Rabbis and Rabbi Akiva can look at the same case (meat in milk, or a pot used that day) and disagree over whether it is a "novelty," i.e. what makes a case anomalous rather than exemplary. Also correct the summary: the gentile vessels derivation is not thrown out for Rabbi Akiva, since Rav Huna son of Ḥiyya defends it by limiting it to a pot used that day.

nazir/38.summary: Rabbi Elazar counts ten places in the law where a quarter-log, roughly a cupful, is the deciding measure, and Rav Kahana holds a mnemonic for them: five red, five white. The red ones cover wine and blood, including the wine a nazirite (a person under a vow to avoid grapes, corpses, and haircuts) may not drink, and the four cups at the Passover seder. Each time someone offers an eleventh case, the answer is that disputed rulings do not make the list.
nazir/38.question: If a case drops off the list because the Sages argue about it, why does the annulled rule about immersing tiny vessels in a quarter-log of rainwater get excluded on completely different grounds?

judge.reachNote: What qualifies a rule as settled law worth counting: a live dispute and a repealed ruling are both 'not law', but for different reasons.

answer.quote: His list excludes that case, as the Sages annulled that halakha by ruling that one must use a standard ritual bath of forty se’a
answer.explanation: The page states the ground for excluding the small-vessel immersion case (the halakha was annulled), but it never explains why this criterion differs from the 'subject to a dispute' criterion used for the other challenges.

summaryProblems.claim: Each time someone offers an eleventh case, the answer is that disputed rulings do not make the list.
summaryProblems.pageSays: His list excludes that case, as the Sages annulled that halakha by ruling that one must use a standard ritual bath of forty se’a

judge.feedback: The summary says "Each time someone offers an eleventh case, the answer is that disputed rulings do not make the list.", but the page says "His list excludes that case, as the Sages annulled that halakha by ruling that one must use a standard ritual bath of forty se’a". Say what the page says. Fix the overstated claim: only three of the four proposed extra cases are dismissed as disputed, while the small-vessel immersion case is dismissed because the Sages annulled the ruling. Let the summary say that plainly, so the question builds on an accurate account. The question itself is worth keeping, but it should acknowledge that the page does give a reason (annulment) and press on why the two grounds of exclusion differ.

nazir/39.summary: A nazirite, someone who vows to let his hair grow long and keep away from wine, loses thirty days of his count if bandits shave him against his will. That sends the Sages into a question about hair itself: does it grow from the root or from the tip? They test it on a live louse at the scalp, a dead one stuck at the tip, braided hair, dyed sheep, and old men whose dyed beards come in white at the roots.
nazir/39.question: If the hair a nazirite vowed over is steadily being pushed up and away from his scalp, when does what is on his head stop being the hair he sanctified?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the identity question under the case: what makes a strand of hair the very hair that was vowed over, once growth constantly replaces what is at the scalp.

answer.quote: he has removed the hair of the naziriteship, which is the hair he vowed not to shave
answer.explanation: The Gemara's dilemma and its conclusion that hair grows from the bottom bear directly on which hair on the head is still the sanctified hair, but the page frames this as a question about shaving and negated days rather than stating when sanctified hair ceases to be sanctified as it is pushed outward.

nazir/40.summary: A nazirite, someone under a vow to avoid wine and let his hair grow, must shave with a razor when the term ends, and Rav Ḥisda sorts the thresholds: one hair for flogging, two hairs left over to invalidate the final shaving, most of the head to cancel days already counted. Three people shave as a commandment: a nazirite, a leper being purified, and the Levites at their sanctification. The leper's razor turns out to have the shakiest source of the three.
nazir/40.question: If a poor leper may bring turtledoves instead of sheep, why assume the tool in his hand is held to the stricter standard?

judge.reachNote: Does leniency in one part of a ritual (a poor man's cheaper offering) license leniency in another part (the shaving implement)?

answer.quote: They derive the halakha of a leper's shaving from the prohibition against destroying one's beard.
answer.explanation: The note's question repeats Rava of Barnish's refutation, and a few lines later the Gemara asks "What, then, is the source for the halakha that a leper must use a razor?" and answers that the Rabbis get it not from analogy but from the beard-destruction verses.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 40b: "They derive the halakha of a leper's shaving from the prohibition against destroying one's beard.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Rava of Barnish's objection, and the page answers it outright on 40b: the Rabbis never needed the analogy, since they learn the leper's razor from the prohibition against destroying the beard. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than stopping at the objection — for instance, ask what is left unsettled once the razor comes from a priest's beard rather than from a nazirite or the Levites, or press on the closing kal vaḥomer that a leper's shaving, being a mitzva, should be easier than a nazirite's transgression.

nazir/41.summary: A person recovering from tzara'at, a skin affliction, must shave off all his hair to become pure, and the argument here is about which tool. Reish Lakish's rule drives it: when a positive command collides with a prohibition, do both if you can, and only if you cannot does the command override. Since tweezers or a plane could remove hair without destroying the beard, the verse's permission to use a razor is read as proof that nothing but a razor counts.
nazir/41.question: If a permission written in the verse is read as proof that the gentler method would not have counted, what stops that reasoning from turning every allowance into a requirement?

judge.reachNote: Whether a verse that licenses an otherwise forbidden act tells us the act is permitted or that it is the only valid way to perform the mitzva.

answer.quote: That is to say that he is permitted to shave even with a razor. As, it might enter your mind to say that since with regard to a nazirite
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself floats the reading that the verse grants mere permission rather than mandating a razor, but then rejects it on Reish Lakish's grounds, so the note's worry about permissions hardening into requirements is engaged but not settled.

nazir/42.summary: A nazirite, someone under a vow not to cut his hair or go near a corpse, shaves when the term ends, and if he leaves two hairs the mishna says he has done nothing at all. Abaye asks what happens when that hair grows back and he shaves only those two. Rava asks about one hair shaved and one that falls out on its own; Ravina rules there is still no shaving.
nazir/42.question: If a head with nothing left on it can still count as unshaved, what is the act of shaving actually being measured against?

judge.reachNote: Whether a mitzva of shaving is measured by the resulting state of the head or by the completeness of the act itself.

answer.quote: Even though there is no hair here, as only one hair remains, nevertheless there is no fulfillment of the mitzva of shaving here, as he failed to shave it all
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's puzzle ("If there is no hair here, then there is shaving here") and answers it: shaving is measured by the act removing the whole at once, not by the resulting bare head.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 42a: "Even though there is no hair here, as only one hair remains, nevertheless there is no fulfillment of the mitzva of shaving here, as he failed to shave it all". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and Ravina's reply on 42a states the answer outright: the act failed because it did not remove everything at once and the second pass was less than the required amount. Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for example Abaye's dilemma about shaving the two regrown hairs, which is never resolved, or the Eretz Yisrael derivation that lets the impure nazirite's stringency travel back to the pure one. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

nazir/43.summary: A nazirite, under a vow that bars contact with corpses, is liable twice for entering a house with a corpse in it, once for contracting impurity and once for entering the enclosure, but only if both happen in the same instant. The Gemara cannot stage that instant: a hand goes in first, then a nose, then toes, until Rav Pappa has him carried in inside a sealed chest that someone else opens. Later Rav Ḥisda says a priest may not bury a father whose head was severed.
nazir/43.question: If a father lying headless on the road counts as a corpse with nobody to bury him while his own son stands right there, what would it take for a person to count as having people?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that 'having people' is about practical availability of burial help, not the mere presence of a relative — but the page states that test outright.

answer.quote: If the corpse is in a place where if he would call, others would answer him, that is not considered a met mitzva.
answer.explanation: The baraita quoted on the page states exactly the test for when a corpse counts as having people to bury it — whether calling out would bring others — and the Gemara then explains that a man on the road counts as having no one precisely because that test fails.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 43b: "If the corpse is in a place where if he would call, others would answer him, that is not considered a met mitzva.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same page: the baraita defines a met mitzva as one who has no one else, and says a corpse is not a met mitzva if calling out would bring others, with the Gemara adding that a traveler on the road counts as having no one. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it. A better angle would probe the tension the page leaves standing — that a son who is right there does not count as 'people,' so the category is about who will actually do the burying rather than who is present — or press on why Rav Ḥisda's whole-body requirement yields to the met mitzva obligation.

nazir/44.summary: Word reaches Rabbi Yitzhak, a priest, three years after his father died in Ginzak, and the Elders rule he may not handle the remains, since "for his father" means a whole body, not bones. The mishna then ranks the three things forbidden to a nazirite, a person who vows for a term to avoid corpses, haircuts, and wine. The Gemara tries deriving each rule from the others, and a verse knocks down every inference in turn.
nazir/44.question: If a priest may become impure for a close relative because that burial falls to him, why does the duty lapse once his father is only bones?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a burial duty may track the whole person rather than surviving remains — but the page already answers it from the verse.

answer.quote: “For his father” (Leviticus 21:2), which indicates a priest may become impure only when his father is whole, and not when he is lacking.
answer.explanation: The page states outright why the permission lapses once only bones remain — the verse limits it to a whole body — and it also frames the dependency-based derivation as Rabbi Yehuda's competing opinion, with Rav following the tanna of the Ginzak incident.

summaryProblems.claim: a verse knocks down every inference in turn
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara answers: We require hair growth, and there is none at that point.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 44a: "“For his father” (Leviticus 21:2), which indicates a priest may become impure only when his father is whole, and not when he is lacking.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "a verse knocks down every inference in turn", but the page says "The Gemara answers: We require hair growth, and there is none at that point.". Say what the page says. The question is answered in plain words on the page: the Elders' reason is the verse "for his father" — whole, not lacking — and the page further explains the conflict as a dispute between tannaim. Ask something the page leaves standing, for instance why impurity, the most severe of the three nazirite prohibitions, is the one that yields to a met mitzva while wine never yields, or what Rabbi Akiva's "his purification depends on his days" versus the leper's "depends on his shaving" says about what makes a person pure. Also drop "a verse knocks down every inference": at least one inference is answered by the practical need for hair growth, not a verse.

nazir/45.summary: A nazirite, someone who vowed off wine and haircuts for a fixed term, closes the term by shaving and bringing three animals. The verse says he shaves "at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting," and the Sages refuse the literal reading, since shaving at the Sanctuary door would be degrading. Others take the phrase as a time (only while the doors stand open) or as a limit to men, since a female nazirite paints her eyes and might arouse the young priests.
nazir/45.question: If uncovered hair is the risk, why is the woman suspected of adultery stood before those same young priests while the female nazirite is kept away?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the concern is adornment rather than exposure as such — but the page states exactly that distinction a line later.

nazir/46.summary: A nazirite, a person under a vow to avoid wine, corpses, and haircuts, ends the term with offerings and a shaving of the head. Rabbi Eliezer holds that wine is permitted only after every step, including waving the offering before the altar; the Rabbis say one action suffices. The argument sharpens on a completely bald nazirite, where Beit Hillel have him pass a razor over his head anyway, and on Rabbi Eliezer's leper with no thumb, who can never become pure.
nazir/46.question: Why should a bald man finish his vow by dragging a razor across nothing, while a man born without a thumb is told there is no remedy at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether a commanded act can be discharged symbolically when its object is absent, or whether the body's lack simply bars the ritual forever.

answer.quote: Beit Shammai and Rabbi Eliezer said the same thing, i.e., they follow the same principle.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Pedat's statement dissolves part of the tension by showing that the bald man's razor is Beit Hillel's remedy while Rabbi Eliezer stands with Beit Shammai, who grant no remedy, yet the page never explains why a token razor stroke counts where a missing thumb cannot.

nazir/47.summary: A High Priest and a nazirite, a person under a vow barring wine, haircuts, and contact with the dead, walk along a road and find a corpse nobody else will bury. One of them must do it: Rabbi Eliezer says the priest, since he owes no offering for impurity, and the Rabbis say the nazirite, since his holiness ends when his vow does. The Gemara then ranks pairs of priests by who is still useful tomorrow.
nazir/47.question: If the priest anointed for war is the one to ransom first from captivity, why is he the one sent to handle the corpse?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that precedence in one respect (saving a life) need not mean precedence in another (staying fit for service), which is exactly Mar Zutra's stated distinction.

answer.quote: With regard to preserving his life and rescuing him from captivity or from a dangerous situation, it is preferable to preserve the one anointed for war.
answer.explanation: Mar Zutra explicitly resolves the tension the question raises: the war priest takes precedence for rescue because the public depends on him in war, but for impurity the deputy stays pure since he can serve in the High Priest's stead.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 47b: "With regard to preserving his life and rescuing him from captivity or from a dangerous situation, it is preferable to preserve the one anointed for war.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very contradiction the page raises between the two baraitot, and Mar Zutra answers it in so many words by splitting rescue from impurity. Write a question that starts after that answer, for example asking why fitness for Temple service outweighs fitness for war when deciding who may be defiled, or why the deputy's standby role counts more than the war priest's actual duty.

nazir/48.summary: A nazirite, who vows off wine and contact with the dead, may not become impure even to bury his own father, and the page mines each word of the list (father, mother, brother, sister) for something extra. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi reads "when they die" narrowly: the nazirite may still tend a parent's leprosy or discharge. The word "sister" yields the sharpest result, that a man heading off to slaughter his Paschal offering or circumcise his son stops to bury an abandoned corpse.
nazir/48.question: If the verse lists his own father, mother, brother and sister, why does it end up granting precedence to a corpse that nobody claims?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that naming one's closest kin as forbidden is exactly what carves out a duty to the corpse with no kin — but the page states this derivation outright.

answer.quote: It emphasizes that it is to bury his father and to bury his mother that he may not become impure; however, he may become impure to bury a met mitzva.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself asks what the listed relatives teach and answers that the specification is exclusionary — only for them is impurity barred, leaving the met mitzva permitted, a point repeated for "brother" and "sister" throughout the page.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 48b: "It emphasizes that it is to bury his father and to bury his mother that he may not become impure; however, he may become impure to bury a met mitzva.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very question the baraita asks and answers ("what is the meaning when the verse states: 'For his father, or for his mother'?" — it teaches that he may become impure for a met mitzva), so it needs replacing. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing: why the met mitzva overrides even the Paschal offering and circumcision, whose neglect carries karet, or why the nazirite's bringing an offering for his impurity was thought to block the a fortiori from the High Priest. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

nazir/49.summary: A nazirite, bound by vow to avoid wine, haircuts, and corpses, may not become impure even to bury a parent, and the Gemara asks why the verse names both father and mother. The answer is oddly asymmetrical: fatherhood is only a presumption, while a mother is known to have given birth, yet lineage follows the father. Then a mishna lists what impurities force a nazirite to shave, and Rabbi Yehuda bars Rabbi Meir's students from his study hall.
nazir/49.question: Sumakhos quoted a list that begins with a whole corpse and then an olive-bulk of one, and the mishna's own wording says the same thing, so was he being vexatious or accurate?
gate: the question brings in "Sumakhos", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether faithfully repeating a received text can itself be a provocation — the tension between transmitting a master's wording and editing out its redundancies.

answer.quote: The clause: For a corpse, is unnecessary, as, if a nazirite must shave for impurity imparted by an olive-bulk from a corpse
answer.explanation: The page gives Rabbi Yehuda's stated reason for calling the citation vexatious — the whole-corpse clause is redundant by a fortiori reasoning — but it never addresses the note's point that the mishna's own wording contains the same clause, so the question survives.

nazir/50.summary: A nazirite, bound by a vow that bars contact with the dead, must shave and begin the term again for an olive-bulk of corpse and also for an olive-bulk of fluid. Fluid turns out to mean flesh that liquefied and then congealed, and Rabbi Yirmeya makes hardening the test: what sets came from the corpse, what stays runny may be only phlegm and spittle. The discussion then asks whether a poured stream links two vessels, and ends with the size of a ladle of dust unresolved.
nazir/50.question: If the substance is already known to have come from the body, why should its power to defile wait on whether it hardens in the pan?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a physical test can settle what a substance is when origin alone does not determine impurity — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: referring to an unspecified substance that is definitely from the corpse but is not necessarily a substance that imparts impurity
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely this objection and Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the substance's corpse origin is known but its identity is not, so congealing serves to distinguish impure corpse fluid from harmless phlegm and spittle.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 50a: "referring to an unspecified substance that is definitely from the corpse but is not necessarily a substance that imparts impurity". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and Rabbi Yirmeya answers it two lines later in the summary's own words, so it cannot stand as an open question. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for example the unresolved animal-fluid dilemma, or why the Rabbis reject Beit Shammai's 'returns backward' criterion while accepting viscosity, or why the ladle-of-dust measure is left standing. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

nazir/51.summary: A nazirite, a person under a vow that bars wine, haircutting and contact with the dead, must shave if touched by a full ladle of dust from a decayed corpse. The Sages limit that dust to a body buried naked in a marble coffin or on a stone floor, since wood, cloth or brick crumbs would mix in and spoil it. The questions then multiply: hair, an unborn child, excrement, skin, phlegm, spittle, a corpse ground up before it decayed.
nazir/51.question: If the only corpse that yields qualifying dust is one dosed with palm water, rubbed bald and boiled in the hot springs of Tiberias, what is the rule actually about?
gate: the question brings in "Tiberias", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a purity category may be defined so narrowly that its content is conceptual rather than practical.

nazir/52.summary: A nazirite, bound by a vow to keep away from wine and from corpses, must shave and start over for certain remains, among them "a spine and a skull." Whether that means both bones together or either one alone is never settled, though four proofs are tried: a spine stripped of its ribs, a box of bones inspected in the blacksmiths' synagogue by Todos the doctor, Rabbi Akiva's list of six impure items that actually names seven, and Shammai's stringency.
nazir/52.question: When four different Sages each name a different item as the one that does not belong in a list of six that contains seven, has the count been explained or only rescued?

judge.reachNote: Whether a chain of 'if you wish, say' alternatives constitutes an explanation of a text or only a series of rescues of it.

answer.quote: No proof can be brought from here, as when the tanna teaches this tally he lists seven items. However, only six are fully relevant here
answer.explanation: The page does give a general account of why the tally says six while listing seven, but it never weighs whether the four competing candidates for the excluded item explain the count or merely each save it.

nazir/53.summary: Earlier Elders disagreed over whether a quarter-kav of bones or a quarter-log of blood, roughly half a cup, spreads impurity to everything under one roof. A later court split it: that quantity invalidates teruma, the priest's portion, and offerings, but does not force a nazirite, someone under a vow to avoid corpses and wine, to shave and start over. The Gemara objects that a third opinion inventing new distinctions decides nothing; Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi answers that it came from the last prophets.
nazir/53.question: If that ruling really came down intact from Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, what were the earlier Elders arguing about?
gate: the question brings in "Haggai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Zechariah", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Malachi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: If a ruling is ancient prophetic tradition, how can earlier authorities have been in dispute about it — what is the relation between received tradition and argument?

nazir/54.summary: A nazirite, who has vowed not to cut his hair or come near a corpse, walks under a tree overhanging a body: he does not shave and does not lose the days already counted. The same list includes land outside Eretz Yisrael, which the Sages decreed impure, and the Gemara asks whether that impurity sits in its air or its earth. Then it notices the mishna's sprinkling on the third and seventh days cannot cover every item it just listed.
nazir/54.question: If the line about sprinkling comes right after a list of ten sources of impurity, what in the mishna itself tells a reader which ones it actually means?

judge.reachNote: It reaches for how the scope of a blanket clause appended to a list is fixed, but the mishna's wording and the Gemara's vessels argument both settle it on the page.

answer.quote: And in those cases listed that involve ritual impurity from a corpse, one sprinkles the purification water upon him on the third and on the seventh days
answer.explanation: The mishna's own qualifying phrase limits the sprinkling clause to the corpse-impurity items, and the Gemara then spells out which ones: "it is referring to the other items listed in the mishna, e.g., the grave cover, the grave walls, and a quarter-log of blood."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 54a (end of mishna): "And in those cases listed that involve ritual impurity from a corpse, one sprinkles the purification water upon him on the third and on the seventh days". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered twice over on this page: the mishna itself restricts the sprinkling to "those cases listed that involve ritual impurity from a corpse," and the Gemara names the grave cover, grave walls, and quarter-log of blood. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing, for example why the Gemara ends up preferring that the land of the nations was decreed impure on account of its air even though nothing there was touched or overlaid, or why these uncertain and decreed impurities cost the nazirite nothing in counted days while the corpse impurities of the earlier mishna cost him everything.

nazir/55.summary: A man is carried into gentile land shut inside a chest, a box, or a cabinet, and the question is whether the rabbinic impurity on foreign soil reaches him. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says he is impure, Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says pure, and the Gemara tries three readings of why: air or earth, whether a moving container counts as a tent, and whether the Sages bothered to decree about a rare way of traveling. A wagon or boat makes him impure, since people actually ride in those.
nazir/55.question: If a chest protects a traveler only because riding in a chest is unusual, what happens to that protection once the unusual becomes ordinary?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rabbinic decree's scope is fixed by the custom of travel at the time it was made, or tracks whatever becomes usual.

answer.quote: he is ritually impure. The difference is that the latter vessels are commonly used to convey people
answer.explanation: The page shows that once a mode of conveyance is commonly used for people the decree does apply, which bears on the question without directly addressing a change in custom for chests.

nazir/56.summary: Rabbi Eliezer reports a ruling about which corpse impurities oblige a nazirite, a person under a vow against wine and haircuts, to shave, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya. A baraita shows he actually heard it from Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel, who heard it from ben Hananya, and the Gemara draws a rule from this: in a chain of three, keep the first and last names and drop the middle. Rabbi Akiva's inference about a barley-sized bone gets called flawless and is rejected anyway.
nazir/56.question: If Rabbi Yehoshua bar Memel can be dropped from the chain simply for standing in the middle, what is the chain of names doing?

judge.reachNote: Asks what an attribution chain is for — authentication of a line back to a source versus credit to each transmitter — given that middle links are droppable.

nazir/57.summary: A stranger tells two nazirites, men under a vow that bars haircuts, that one of them became impure but cannot say which. Both shave and bring offerings, trading claims on each other's sacrifices; but whichever one is pure shaves for nothing and seems to break the ban on rounding the corners of the head. Shmuel reads the case as women or minor boys, which sends the Gemara to Rav Huna, whose wife Ḥova cut their sons' hair, and to Rav Adda's curse, which the page says killed the children.
nazir/57.question: Rav Huna and Rav Adda agree that shaving a whole head counts as rounding it, so what makes their narrow disagreement about who holds the scissors worth a curse the page reports as coming true?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: how much moral weight a narrow exegetical difference over who bears a prohibition can carry, up to a curse the page treats as effective.

answer.quote: Whoever has the prohibition of the destruction of the beard also has the prohibition of rounding
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks with regard to what Rav Huna and Rav Adda disagree and supplies each one's derivation, but it never explains why the dispute drew a fatal curse.

nazir/58.summary: A person healed of the skin affliction the Torah calls leprosy must shave off all his hair. The page asks what happens when he is also a nazirite, vowed to let no razor touch his head, or a priest forbidden to shave the corners of his beard. The argument hangs on two spare words in the verse, "his head" and "his beard," and on Reish Lakish's rule that a prohibition yields only when there is no way to keep both.
nazir/58.question: If the priest's case can be brushed aside because priestly rules do not bind everyone, and the nazirite's because a vow can be dissolved by a halakhic authority, what is still holding up the rule that a positive command overrides a prohibition?

judge.reachNote: What a general halakhic principle rests on once each of its proof-texts is shown to be a special case.

answer.quote: the juxtaposed verse: "You shall make for you fringes" (Deuteronomy 22:12), teaches that one may prepare ritual fringes even from diverse kinds of wool and linen
answer.explanation: The page states that the simple principle that a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition rests on the fringes/diverse-kinds juxtaposition (and on "his head" for the leper), while the two refutations the note cites are explicitly limited to generalizing the compound case: "we cannot derive from these two cases that a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition and a positive mitzva."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Nazir 58a: "the juxtaposed verse: "You shall make for you fringes" (Deuteronomy 22:12), teaches that one may prepare ritual fringes even from diverse kinds of wool and linen". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered by the page: the priest/nazirite refutations only block generalizing the stronger rule (that a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition plus a positive mitzva), and the page says the plain rule still stands on "his head" for the leper and on the fringes/diverse-kinds juxtaposition. Rewrite so the question does not ask for something the page supplies. A better line of attack: why the Gemara is content to split one verse's two general terms between priest and nazirite as "equally balanced," or Rav's permission to remove body hair against the baraita's flogging for women's practice.

nazir/59.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that a man who removes his armpit or pubic hair is flogged, reading the verse barring a man from putting on a woman's garment as covering grooming too. An earlier teaching spends that verse differently: on a man dressing as a woman to sit among women, and on a woman not going out to war with weapons. Then a man condemned to lashes is stripped, Rabbi Ami sees unshaved armpit hair, and calls off the flogging.
nazir/59.question: Should one unshaved armpit, a stringency most people ignore, be enough to cancel the lashes a man has already been found liable to receive?

judge.reachNote: Whether one visible stringency can be read as evidence of a whole character, and whether character evidence can undo a judgment already rendered.

answer.quote: Leave him; this is one of those who are meticulous in observance of mitzvot
answer.explanation: Rabbi Ami states his reasoning — the unshaved armpit marks the man as scrupulous about prohibitions ordinary people ignore — but the page never defends why that inference should outweigh an established liability for lashes.

nazir/60.summary: A man who vowed to be a nazirite, avoiding wine and letting his hair grow until a final shaving, may also be an uncertain leper and uncertain corpse-impure; the page counts out four shavings and, for a year-long vow, four years before he may drink wine. Then Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's students press him: why can't one haircut serve both obligations? Each time he answers with a difference: growing hair versus removing it, before or after the sprinkling of blood, before or after immersion.
nazir/60.question: Is Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai uncovering real differences between the two shavings, or producing a fresh one each time his students close off the last?

judge.reachNote: Whether a chain of distinctions each raised only when the previous one is closed off reflects a real principle or is argumentative improvisation.

nazir/61.summary: The mishna says gentiles cannot take on naziriteship, the vow to avoid wine, haircuts, and contact with the dead, while women and Canaanite slaves can. A master may force his slave to drink wine or shave his hair, so the slave's vow bends under his owner. To keep gentiles out, the Gemara argues a gentile has no father in the relevant sense, and finally that a gentile cannot become ritually impure at all, even touching a corpse.
nazir/61.question: If a master can march his slave to wine and a razor, in what sense is that slave a nazirite at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether a vow can bind someone whose body and will belong to another — the meaning of a self-imposed prohibition under coercion.

answer.quote: The aforementioned verse teaches us that a slave can in fact take a vow of naziriteship.
answer.where: Nazir 61a (Gemara on the mishna about gentiles, women, and slaves)
answer.explanation: The page affirms that the slave's vow is valid despite his soul not being in his own possession, but it never explains what the vow amounts to once the master overrides it, so the question can still be asked.

nazir/62.summary: A slave takes a vow of naziriteship, which bars him from wine and grapes, and his master can simply force him to break it. The Gemara works hard to explain why a master can override that vow but not an ordinary vow to skip a single cluster of grapes, and lands on the master's loss: a hungry slave is a weakened asset. Then a slave runs away, and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei argue over his wine.
nazir/62.question: Rabbi Meir forbids the runaway wine and Rabbi Yosei permits it, but both reason from what serves the master, so whose vow is it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a slave's vow is ever truly his own, or is always measured by the master's interest in his body.

answer.quote: the Torah is referring only to one whose soul is in his possession, i.e., who is not owned by another; this excludes a slave, whose soul is not in his possession
answer.explanation: The page supplies a principle bearing on whose vow it is — a slave's soul is not his own — but it never resolves the runaway dispute in those terms, so the question survives.

nazir/63.summary: A nazirite, someone under a vow to avoid wine and corpses for a set term, shaves at the end and only then learns he was near a corpse. A body floating at the mouth of the cave he immersed in counts as known impurity and wipes out the term; one sunk in the ground does not. Two verses are offered as the source, then dropped: the rule holds that a corpse anyone anywhere knows of is not hidden.
nazir/63.question: Why should a nazirite's completed term collapse because one stranger at the end of the earth once saw the corpse he never knew he walked over?

judge.reachNote: Whether impurity is defined by what this person knew or by whether the fact was knowable to anyone in the world.

answer.quote: Granted, according to the one who says that this halakha is derived from the verse that states that ritual impurity is like a road, it is fine
answer.explanation: The page voices the note's exact objection against the "beside him" derivation and offers Reish Lakish's "like a road" standard (impurity must be open to the world) plus the fallback that the rule is a received tradition, so it bears on the question without fully justifying why a stranger's knowledge binds the nazirite.

nazir/64.summary: A dead creeping animal floating in water does not render a person impure through uncertain contact, while the same carcass lying on the ground does. Rami bar  f8ama presses on what counts as resting: a corpse inside a floating vessel, a corpse on a floating creeping animal, one creeping animal atop another, a creeping animal on a carcass that has dissolved into liquid, then on semen, then on purification water. Every one of these is left standing unanswered.
nazir/64.question: At what point does a carcass stop being a solid thing something rests on and start being a liquid something floats on?

judge.reachNote: What makes a surface a resting place rather than a floating medium — solidity, or the substance's classification as food versus drink.

answer.quote: Or, perhaps this carcass is still considered food, rather than a liquid, and the creeping animal is on a solid surface.
answer.explanation: The page raises exactly this boundary question and names the axis (food versus liquid, and viscosity in the case of semen and purification waters), but it closes with "the dilemmas shall stand unresolved," so no criterion is settled.

nazir/65.summary: Three corpses buried together in one spot turn a field into a graveyard, so the page works at ruling corpses out: one buried sitting, one with his head between his thighs, two lying head to foot. When three are found anyway and nothing turns up for twenty cubits more, Reish Lakish says flatly that the Sages found a pretext to keep Eretz Yisrael pure. Later the logic reverses: once a man is twice confirmed as a zav, no one asks whether he merely jumped or overate.
nazir/65.question: If the Sages were openly looking for a pretext to declare the land pure, does the reasoning attached to that pretext still carry any weight?

judge.reachNote: Whether a ruling openly driven by a desired outcome (keeping the land pure) can still function as binding legal reasoning.

answer.quote: The Sages wished to avoid uncertain impurity because people were careful to observe the halakhot of ritual purity in Eretz Yisrael
answer.explanation: The page supplies the motive behind the pretext — easing an impossible burden of doubtful impurity in Eretz Yisrael — but it never says whether the halakhic reasoning built on that pretext retains independent force, so the question can still be asked.

nazir/66.summary: A tractate of vows closes by arguing over one word in Hannah's prayer for a son: "And no mora shall come upon his head." Rabbi Nehorai reads mora as razor, matching the verse about Samson, whom scripture calls a nazirite, and concludes Samuel was one too. Rabbi Yosei says mora means fear of flesh and blood, and Nehorai refutes him by citing Samuel's terror of Saul, years after the vow was made.
nazir/66.question: Does Nehorai's proof hold, given that Hannah's vow covered her unborn son's head while Samuel's fear of Saul came a lifetime later?

judge.reachNote: Whether a fact from later in a person's life can settle the meaning of a word spoken in a vow before he was born.

sotah/2.summary: Sotah opens with a husband warning his wife not to seclude herself with a particular man, and a dispute over how many witnesses that warning and the seclusion require. Rabbi Eliezer accepts the husband's own word about the seclusion; Rabbi Yehoshua demands two witnesses for both. The Gemara reads the mishna's phrasing as conceding that such a warning works after the fact but should never be issued at all, and the Rabbis object that a lying husband leaves no end to the matter.
sotah/2.question: If the warning is something a husband ideally should never issue, why does the page spend so much effort fixing exactly how many witnesses make it stick?

judge.reachNote: Why law gives precise machinery to an act it says should never be performed — the gap between what is permitted after the fact and what is advisable ab initio.

answer.quote: all the halakhot concerning a sota are for one who issued a warning when not obligated to do so
answer.explanation: The page acknowledges that the sota laws are framed around a warning given when one was not obligated to give it, which bears on why the rules are elaborated despite the act being discouraged, but it never explains why the witness count is worked out in such detail.

sotah/3.summary: The verse says a spirit of jealousy came upon the husband before he warned his wife not to seclude herself with a particular man. The Rabbis read that spirit as impurity, since in their view a husband should not warn at all; Rav Ashi reads it as purity, proof he will not tolerate what he sees. That reading decides a larger fight: Rabbi Yishmael calls the warning optional, Rabbi Akiva mandatory, and the same split runs through a priest burying his sister and keeping a Canaanite slave.
sotah/3.question: If the same jealousy can be a spirit of impurity or a spirit of purity, what tells a husband which one has entered him?

judge.reachNote: The same jealous impulse can be a defiling suspicion or a righteous refusal to tolerate promiscuity; the question reaches for how motive is discerned.

answer.quote: And it stands to reason like the one who says that Rabbi Yishmael was speaking of a spirit of purity
answer.explanation: The Gemara resolves which spirit the verse means — purity, since the Torah would not make introducing impurity optional or mandatory — but it never supplies a test by which a husband could tell which spirit has entered him.

summaryProblems.claim: The purity/impurity reading of the spirit 'decides a larger fight' over whether the warning is optional or mandatory.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And it stands to reason like the one who says that Rabbi Yishmael was speaking of a spirit of purity, as it is taught in a baraita

judge.feedback: The summary says "The purity/impurity reading of the spirit 'decides a larger fight' over whether the warning is optional or mandatory.", but the page says "And it stands to reason like the one who says that Rabbi Yishmael was speaking of a spirit of purity, as it is taught in a baraita". Say what the page says. Reverse the direction of the argument: the Gemara uses the tannaitic dispute over whether warning is optional or mandatory as evidence that Rabbi Yishmael meant a spirit of purity, not the other way round. Keep the Rabbis' and Rav Ashi's readings, but say plainly that the page leans to purity because the Torah would not make introducing impurity into oneself optional or mandatory. Then let the question ask what remains: how a husband tells a pure jealousy from an impure one.

sotah/4.summary: A woman's seclusion with another man counts only if it lasted long enough for intercourse, and the Sages measure that span in kitchen terms: circling a palm tree, mixing a cup of wine with water, roasting an egg. Rav Ashi presses the loaf-from-a-basket measure hard: hot loaf or cold, wheat or barley, new basket or old, and every one of those questions is left standing. Rabbi Yoḥanan says each Sage estimated from himself, which leaves ben Azzai, who never married.
sotah/4.question: If each of these measures came from a Sage's own body, what happens to an accusation that falls between the barley loaf and the wheat one?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a legal threshold built from each Sage's private bodily experience gives no fixed line, so cases between two men's estimates have no determined verdict.

sotah/5.summary: God passed over every tall mountain to rest the Divine Presence on low Mount Sinai, and passed over the fine trees for a bush. A long run of sayings follows: the arrogant man's dust will not stir at the resurrection, and God says of him that the two of them cannot share a world. Then Rav sets a dosage, one-eighth of one-eighth of arrogance for a Torah scholar, and Rava would excommunicate a scholar who has none.
sotah/5.question: If a scholar with no arrogance at all deserves excommunication, what is that eighth of an eighth actually doing for him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a teacher needs some measure of self-regard to carry authority, but the page already answers it.

answer.quote: And this minute measure of arrogance crowns him as the awn of bristle-like growth on the top of the husk.
answer.explanation: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, states directly what the eighth of an eighth does for the scholar: it crowns him, like the awn atop the husk.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 5a: "And this minute measure of arrogance crowns him as the awn of bristle-like growth on the top of the husk.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, says the minute measure of arrogance crowns the scholar like the awn on the husk. Write a question that starts after that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, why Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak rejects even that eighth of an eighth given the same verse-heavy case against pride, or what it means that the very image of the withering husk-top used to condemn the arrogant becomes the scholar's crown. The summary is accurate and can stand.

sotah/6.summary: Rav Sheshet argues that the bitter water given to a wife suspected of adultery, a sota, tests nothing if witnesses who saw the act happen to be living overseas. Rav Yosef counters that the water still works, and that a guilty woman may survive because her own merit delays the punishment. Rabbi Shimon objects that once merit can postpone death, every innocent woman who drinks and lives is left under a cloud.
sotah/6.question: If distant witnesses, a woman's own merit, and even gossip among weavers spinning in the moonlight can all leave a guilty woman standing, what has an innocent woman who drinks and survives actually proved?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the evidentiary worth of the ordeal: if survival has several innocent-looking causes, what does surviving prove?

answer.quote: only one who survived the drinking of the bitter water due to her fidelity will conceive a child, but this will not happen in a case
answer.explanation: The baraita's reading of "utehora hee" supplies a distinguishing sign — conception — for the woman spared by genuine innocence rather than by merit, distant witnesses, or public gossip, though the page itself closes by pressing Rabbi Shimon's worry that such exclusions still discredit the rite.

sotah/7.summary: A husband bringing his wife, suspected of adultery, to the Temple to drink the bitter water is assigned two Torah scholars as escorts, lest he have intercourse with her on the road and spoil the ordeal. Rabbi Yehuda says the escorts are unnecessary: a man is already trusted alone with a menstruating wife, where the penalty is heavier. The Rabbis run the same comparison backwards, since a menstruating wife becomes permitted again, and stolen water tastes sweeter.
sotah/7.question: Which way does that comparison really run: is a man more likely to break a rule whose end he can see, or one that may never end?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether temptation tracks the severity of a prohibition or its permanence — but the page already decides it.

sotah/8.summary: A priest pulls open the clothing of a sota, a woman suspected by her husband of adultery and brought to the Temple to drink bitter water, and unbraids her hair while anyone who wishes looks on. Rabbi Yehuda would spare a woman whose body or hair is attractive, yet he also has a condemned woman stoned nearly bare; the Rabbis hold the reverse on both counts. Rava sorts it out: exposure is the public warning, and stoning already warns enough.
sotah/8.question: Why does "love your neighbor as yourself" spare a woman on her way to be stoned from humiliation, but not the sota who may walk out of the courtyard proven innocent?

judge.reachNote: When a public deterrent is at stake, does the dignity owed a person (even a possibly innocent one) yield to it?

answer.quote: Here, with regard to a sota, what is the reason that her hair and body are uncovered? Because of what is stated in the verse,
answer.explanation: The page gives the ground of the distinction — the sota's exposure serves the Ezekiel warning to other women, whereas stoning itself already chastens, so only there does "select a good death" bar added humiliation — but it never applies "love your neighbor" to the sota herself, so the tension the question raises remains open to ask.

sotah/9.summary: The mishna matches a suspected wife's punishment to her adornments, so the eyes she painted for her lover bulge, and the hair she braided a priest pulls loose. The same accounting runs through Samson, who wanted a Philistine woman because she was pleasant in his eyes and later had those eyes gouged out in Gaza. But Judges says the match came from God; the Gemara answers that Samson still went after his own inclination.
sotah/9.question: If Samson's Philistine marriage was God's plan for striking the Philistines, what is left in it for his eyes to pay for?
gate: the question brings in "Philistines", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether an act that serves God's plan can still be charged to the one who did it out of desire.

answer.quote: Although God did plan the punishment of the Philistines, in any event when he went, he followed his inclination and did not act for the sake of Heaven.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the objection that Samson's Philistine marriage was a Divine mission and answers that he was nonetheless driven by his own lust, which is what his eyes paid for.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 9b: "Although God did plan the punishment of the Philistines, in any event when he went, he followed his inclination and did not act for the sake of Heaven.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara asks and answers on 9b, and the summary even repeats the answer ('Samson still went after his own inclination'), so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite the question to push past that answer — for instance, why the measure-for-measure tally singles out the eyes, or why Gaza counts as the first wrongdoing when Timnah came earlier and the Gemara admits he at least married there. Keep the summary's thread of adornment-matched punishment, but let the question land on something the page leaves unresolved.

sotah/10.summary: A baraita lists five people created with a feature that mirrored something on high, and each was struck by that very feature: Samson's strength, Saul's neck, Absalom's hair, Zedekiah's eyes, Asa's feet. Asa, who conscripted Torah scholars to haul stones and exempted no one, not even a bridegroom, was given gout, which Rav Na f1dman describes as a needle in living flesh. Absalom, hung by his hair in a tree, reached for a sword to cut himself loose and stopped.
sotah/10.question: If David's seven cries of "my son" could raise Absalom out of the seven chambers of Gehenna, what exactly was he seeing when the gates opened under the tree and he let the sword drop?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempted: exempt from what?" Name the object.
the question brings in "Gehenna", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a glimpse of Gehenna is a final sentence or something a father's prayer can still undo.

answer.quote: At that moment, the gates of the netherworld opened beneath him and he was afraid to fall into it, so he did not cut his hair
answer.explanation: The page states that what opened beneath Absalom was the gates of the netherworld and that fear of falling in stopped him, though it says nothing about how that vision squares with David's later cries pulling him out of Gehenna's seven chambers.

sotah/11.summary: Miriam waited an hour by the Nile to see what would happen to the baby Moses, and later the whole nation waited seven days in the desert for her. Abaye says the match is uneven, so good is not repaid precisely; Rava insists the manner matches while the measure of good runs larger. Pharaoh's advisors then pick drowning, reasoning that God swore off floods, and miss that one nation can still drown in a sea.
sotah/11.question: If the measure of good always runs greater than the measure of punishment, why does Job's silence at Pharaoh's council cost him a life of suffering?
gate: the question brings in "Job's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The asymmetry between reward and punishment, and whether silent non-protest counts as a deed to be measured at all.

sotah/12.summary: Amram, called the great man of his generation, hears Pharaoh's order to drown every newborn boy and divorces his wife so that no children will be born, and every other man copies him. His daughter Miriam argues that his decree is worse than Pharaoh's, since it ends girls as well as boys, and since a righteous man's word, unlike a king's, is certain to take effect. He remarries Jochebed with a palanquin, dancing, and angels singing.
sotah/12.question: Does Miriam's argument honor her father or corner him, by telling him that his righteousness is exactly what makes his despair so dangerous?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a person's acknowledged righteousness can be turned into a weapon against him: praise and pressure in one argument.

sotah/13.summary: Esau arrives at the Cave of Machpelah and blocks Jacob's burial, arguing the last plot is his; the brothers answer that he sold it, and Esau demands the deed. While Naphtali runs to Egypt to fetch it, Hushim son of Dan, who is hard of hearing, asks why his grandfather should lie in degradation and clubs Esau. From there the discussion turns to credit: Moses raised Joseph's coffin from the Nile, but the verse credits those who finished the burial.
sotah/13.question: If Joseph's descendants gained honor by leaving his burial to Moses and the many, why is Judah demoted for starting his rescue and leaving it to others?
gate: the question brings in "Judah", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When is stepping aside from a mitzva deference that honors, and when is it abandonment that costs you your standing?

answer.quote: Rabbi Elazar says with regard to one who initiates performance of a mitzva but does not complete it when capable of doing so: He is also demoted
answer.explanation: The qualifier "when capable of doing so" bears directly on the tension, since Joseph's descendants deferred for the sake of greater honor rather than abandoning a mitzva they could have finished, but the page never spells out this distinction.

sotah/14.summary: Soldiers from the garrison at Beth Peor are sent to find where Moses is buried, and the grave keeps appearing on whichever side of the mountain they are not standing on. From there the page asks how a person can follow a God described as a devouring fire, and answers with acts: clothing the naked, visiting the sick, burying the dead. Then the mishna puts a palm-branch basket of barley flour into a suspected wife's hands until she tires, and Abba Ḥanin calls that mercy.
sotah/14.question: If making her hold the basket until she is worn out is meant to save her life, why does Rabban Gamliel explain her barley flour as animal feed?
gate: the question brings in "Gamliel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The same ritual is defended as protecting her life and explained as marking her as animal-like, so degradation and mercy are built into one act.

sotah/15.summary: The priest fills an earthenware cup with water from the Temple basin and mixes in dust from under a marble tablet in the Sanctuary floor, for a wife accused by her husband of adultery to drink. Rava says the cup must not be blackened from use, since the water has to look clear and the vessel unchanged; then he asks what happens if a blackened cup is fired white again. A baraita adds that if no loose dust lies there, dust from elsewhere is placed and picked up.
sotah/15.question: If dust can be carried in from outside, set down on the Sanctuary floor, and then lifted, what is left of the requirement that it be dust of the floor of the Tabernacle?
gate: the question brings in "Tabernacle", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When a ritual requirement of provenance can be satisfied by staging the material in place, does the requirement describe origin or only the state of things at the moment of taking?

answer.quote: Therefore, the verse states: “And of the dust that is on the floor of the Tabernacle,” indicating that the dust must be lying there loosely.
answer.explanation: The baraita explains that the residual force of the phrase is that the dust must be lying loose on the Sanctuary floor rather than dug up, which bears on the question but does not directly explain why importing dust and setting it down satisfies "of the Tabernacle."

sotah/16.summary: A sota, a woman suspected by her husband of adultery, drinks water mixed with dust from the Tabernacle floor, and the Sages ask what to do when no dust is there. To rule out ashes, the Gemara cites Rabbi Yishmael's list of three cases where received law overrides the plain verse and notes that ashes are missing. The answer is that the list was never complete. Rav ends up allowing decomposed vegetable matter, which will become dust, while ashes never will.
sotah/16.question: If Rabbi Yishmael's list of three was only a sample all along, why was its silence about ashes ever treated as an argument?

judge.reachNote: When does omission from a Sage's list count as evidence, and what does it take to dismiss a list as merely illustrative?

answer.quote: What else did he omit that he omitted this? It is not reasonable that he would provide a list lacking only one item.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection to the "not exhaustive" answer and explains why silence counts as an argument — a list missing only one item is implausible — and then supplies the leper as the additional omission.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 16a: "What else did he omit that he omitted this? It is not reasonable that he would provide a list lacking only one item.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same page: the Gemara presses "What else did he omit that he omitted this?" and produces the leper case, showing that silence is only an argument if no other omissions exist. Read to the end of that exchange and ask something that survives it — for instance, about Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's and Rav Pappa's competing tests for what belongs on such a list, or about why decomposed matter that "will become dust" counts while ashes never will.

sotah/17.summary: The priest writing the scroll for a woman accused of adultery copies only part of the Torah's passage, and the Mishna argues over where he starts and stops. Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda all read the same phrase, "these curses," and pull different lists out of its definite articles and the extra word et. Rabbi Meir needs the verse promising innocence to carry a curse, so hinnaki, you shall be free, is read as you shall choke.
sotah/17.question: If the one sentence that promises an innocent woman she will go free has to be heard as "you shall choke," what is left in the passage for her to hope for?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rite built entirely of curses can hold any promise for the woman who is innocent.

answer.quote: if she merits to be proven faithful after drinking the water of the sota, a child like our Patriarch Abraham will emerge from her
answer.explanation: Rava's teaching on the dust supplies a positive prospect for the innocent woman — a child like Abraham — though it is not offered as a reply to the hinnaki/ḥinnaki reading, so the question can still be honestly asked.

sotah/18.summary: Rava asks about a priest who writes curse scrolls for two women suspected of adultery and erases the ink of both into one cup. He pushes further: erase them in separate cups, mix the water, then split it again into two, and ask whether each woman drinks her own. All three versions stand unresolved, and the page moves on to fitting the oath and its curse into a single sentence.
sotah/18.question: If the mixed water is divided back into two cups, is each woman drinking her own water again, or has it stopped being anyone's?

judge.reachNote: Whether a later act of separation can retroactively fix identity — can water that was designated, merged, and re-divided still be 'hers'?

sotah/19.summary: The priest lifts a suspected wife's meal-offering out of an Egyptian basket of woven palm leaves, sets it on her hand, slides his own hand underneath, and waves it with her. Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis then split over the order of what follows: burn the handful of flour first, or make her drink the bitter water first, each reading one of three nearly identical verses. Later Rabbi Yehuda has an iron hook forced into her mouth if she refuses; Rabbi Akiva says refusal is already the answer.
sotah/19.question: If refusing the water can count either as an admission of guilt or as plain fear, who decides which one a given woman's refusal is?
gate: gloss "meal-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: An ambiguous act (refusal) can be read as confession or as terror, and someone must decide which — the question reaches the problem of who reads the defendant's silence.

answer.quote: this case, where she is forced to drink, is referring to a situation where she retracts her decision to drink due to fear
answer.explanation: The Gemara supplies the criterion that sorts the two readings of refusal — fear versus "a state of good health" — but never says who judges which state a particular woman is in, so the question survives in part.

sotah/20.summary: Rabbi Meir, who wrote Torah scrolls, says he mixed iron sulfate into his ink so that a fly landing on a dalet could not rub it into a reish. Rabbi Yishmael objects: the curses written for a sota, a woman suspected by her husband of adultery, are blotted into the water she drinks, so that ink must come off. The Gemara then catches Rabbi Meir contradicting himself about which teacher banned the additive, and quits: difficult.
sotah/20.question: If the scroll need not be written for this particular woman and only the erasing must be done for her sake, at what moment do those words become hers?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of lishmah — when a generic written text becomes bound to one particular person — but the page names that moment itself.

answer.quote: What is the performance referred to in the verse? It is referring to the erasure, whereas the writing need not be done for the sake of a specific woman.
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that the designation for this woman attaches at the erasure, not the writing, which is exactly the moment the question asks for.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 20b: "What is the performance referred to in the verse? It is referring to the erasure, whereas the writing need not be done for the sake of a specific woman.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same sugya it draws on: the Gemara says the "performance" required for her sake is the erasure, so the words become hers when they are blotted. Build a new question on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance the tension in Rabbi Meir's own craft, where ink that must survive a fly's rubbing is the same ink the sota passage must surrender to water, or the unresolved clash over whether Akiva or Yishmael banned the additive. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

sotah/21.summary: The mishna says some merit can delay a suspected adulteress's punishment for up to three years, and the Gemara asks which merit is strong enough to do it. A baraita compares a mitzva, a commanded good deed, to a lamp carried in the hand, and Torah study to daylight: the lamp reveals the pits, the dawn clears off the bandits, and only a crossroads tells a person the way. Rabba objects that Doeg and Ahithophel studied Torah and still hunted David.
sotah/21.question: If Torah study protects a person in the grave and after the resurrection, what exactly did it fail to do for Doeg and Ahithophel while they were still studying it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the distinction between being shielded from harm and being rescued from one's own evil inclination — which is exactly what Rava states on the page.

answer.quote: at the time when one is not engaged in it, it protects one from misfortune but it does not save one from the evil inclination
answer.explanation: Rava's statement is given precisely as the resolution of Rabba's Doeg and Ahithophel objection: Torah study protects and saves while one is engaged in it, but only protects when one is not.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 21a: "at the time when one is not engaged in it, it protects one from misfortune but it does not save one from the evil inclination". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: Rava resolves the Doeg and Ahithophel problem by saying Torah saves from the evil inclination only while one is actually engaged in it. Read to the end of the sugya and ask something the page leaves standing — for instance Ravina's claim that a woman earns merit through her sons' and husband's study, or why merit that only delays the sota's death is worth teaching her Torah for at all.

sotah/22.summary: A man who has read Scripture and memorized the Mishna but never served under Torah scholars, learning the reasoning behind the rulings, is called an ignoramus, a boor, a Samaritan, and finally a sorcerer chanting words he does not understand. The same suspicion of surfaces produces a list of seven false pious men: one dragging his feet to look humble, one walking with eyes shut until he bangs his head bloody. Abaye and Rava order the reciter to strike two entries from that list.
sotah/22.question: If Rabbi Yoḥanan could hear a maiden pray and learn fear of sin from her, yet Yoḥani bat Retivi prayed constantly and was secretly a sorceress, what good is a list of frauds sorted by how a person walks?
gate: the question brings in "Yoḥanan", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yoḥani", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Retivi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether visible behavior can ever diagnose inner sincerity, when the same constant prayer yields a saint in one woman and a sorceress in another.

answer.quote: That which is hidden is hidden, and that which is revealed is revealed, but in Heaven everything is known
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak, followed by King Yannai's warning about hypocrites who merely 'appear like Pharisees,' concedes that outward signs cannot finally identify the fraudulent and leaves that judgment to Heaven, which bears on the question without fully answering why a gait-based list is taught at all.

sotah/23.summary: A woman suspected of adultery brings a flour offering, and if she is married to a priest it is never eaten; a handful goes to the altar and the rest is scattered on the place of the ashes. The mishna then runs two lists of differences, priest against priest's daughter and man against woman, and the Gemara pins nearly every one to a single word in a verse. Twice Rabbi Yoḥanan finds no verse and says the rule came orally from Sinai.
sotah/23.question: When the word "him" could have meant that a woman is not stoned at all, and instead is made to mean only that she is not stripped first, what decides which reading survives?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — what constrains a midrashic reading of a pronoun — but the page states the constraint outright: another explicit verse blocks the wider reading.

answer.quote: If we say this means that they stone him but not her, i.e., that a woman is not stoned at all, but isn’t it written:
