answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the alternative reading of "him" and rejects it because Deuteronomy 17:5 explicitly says "that man or that woman… you shall stone them," leaving only the reading that excludes her garment.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 23b: "If we say this means that they stone him but not her, i.e., that a woman is not stoned at all, but isn’t it written:". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same passage it quotes: the Gemara rejects "a woman is not stoned at all" because Deuteronomy 17:5 explicitly commands stoning "that man or that woman." Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance why the same exclusionary "him" yields modesty for the stoned woman but total exemption from hanging and from being sold for theft, or what work is left for Rabbi Yoḥanan's oral halakha from Sinai on a page that otherwise anchors every distinction in a verse.

sotah/24.summary: The mishna lists women who neither drink the bitter water nor collect their marriage contract, among them one who confesses, one who simply refuses to drink, and one whose marriage was forbidden from the start. At the end of the list the court steps into the husband's place, warning his wife when he has become a deaf-mute, lost his reason, or been jailed. The Sages say this warning only costs her the contract; Rabbi Yosei says he makes her drink once released.
sotah/24.question: When the husband is locked up or cannot speak, and the court issues the warning for him, whose suspicion is the woman answering?

judge.reachNote: Whether the sota warning is the expression of one husband's personal jealousy or a public legal instrument the court can wield for him.

answer.quote: And these are the women to whom the court issues a warning in place of their husbands: One whose husband became a deaf-mute or became an imbecile, or was incarcerated in prison.
answer.explanation: The mishna frames the court as warning "in place of their husbands" (and the Gemara adds "whom the court warns on behalf of the husband"), so the suspicion is formally the husband's, though the page never explains how a jealousy he did not voice can be attributed to him.

sotah/25.summary: A husband who warns his wife not to seclude herself with a particular man sets the bitter water ordeal in motion, and the Sages ask whether he can take that warning back. Ze'eira of Jerusalem reported three rulings: a warning can be retracted, a court may forgive a rebellious Elder, and parents may forgive a stubborn and rebellious son. His colleagues in the South accepted two of the three and refused to let the Elder off, so that discord would not spread.
sotah/25.question: If a father and mother can call off the case against their stubborn and rebellious son, why can a court not call off its case against a rebellious Elder?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — whether an offense against the public can be waived by those it directly injures — but the page already supplies the answer.

answer.quote: They held that a rebellious Elder cannot be forgiven, in order that discord not proliferate among the Jewish people.
answer.explanation: The page states outright why the Elder alone cannot be forgiven — to prevent discord spreading among the Jewish people — which is exactly what the question asks.

summaryProblems.claim: Ze'eira's colleagues in the South accepted two of the three rulings.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And when I came to my colleagues in the South and told them these rulings, they agreed with me with regard to two of them

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 25a: "They held that a rebellious Elder cannot be forgiven, in order that discord not proliferate among the Jewish people.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Ze'eira's colleagues in the South accepted two of the three rulings.", but the page says "And when I came to my colleagues in the South and told them these rulings, they agreed with me with regard to two of them". Say what the page says. The question is answered in the very next line of the page, which says the Elder cannot be forgiven so that discord not proliferate among the Jewish people; pick something the page leaves open instead. The retraction thread offers better material — for instance why the Rabbis' answer to Rabbi Yosei about a menstruating woman's ability to become permitted settles whether a warning can be withdrawn after seclusion. Also make clear that it was Rabbi Yoshiya, not Ze'eira, who brought the rulings to the colleagues in the South.

sotah/26.summary: A baraita sorts which suspected wives drink the bitter water, the ordeal for a wife warned by her husband and then seen secluding herself with another man. Rabbi Akiva reads "And she shall be cleared, and shall conceive seed" as a promise: a barren woman who drinks and is cleared will finally conceive. Rabbi Yishmael objects that barren women would then seclude themselves deliberately, and the one who keeps away from other men gets nothing at all.
sotah/26.question: If being cleared by the bitter water earns a barren woman a child, what does the woman who never gave her husband cause to warn her receive?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a reward attached to surviving suspicion leaves virtue unrewarded, and asks what scripture owes the woman who never came under suspicion.

sotah/27.summary: A wife suspected of adultery drinks bitter water, and the argument here keeps shrinking the set of couples the ritual can touch. Since the verse puts the meal offering in her hands and has her answer "Amen, Amen," a woman who cannot stand, has no hands, or cannot speak does not drink. Then a spare phrase comparing a man to a woman sends every one of those disqualifications back at the husband: blind, lame, handless, or mute, he cannot make her drink.
sotah/27.question: Why should a husband's missing hand or silent mouth cancel an ordeal that the verses describe happening in his wife's body?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the ordeal tests a marriage, not just a woman's body, so the husband's capacity conditions it.

answer.quote: is superfluous, and serves to compare a man to a woman and a woman to a man
answer.explanation: The page supplies the textual mechanism (a superfluous verse equating husband and wife) that transfers disqualifications to the husband, but never states why his body should matter to a rite performed on hers.

sotah/28.summary: A woman suspected of adultery drinks the bitter water, and the argument here is whether the man accused with her is evaluated by it too. Rabbi Akiva squeezes this from one letter, the vav prefixed to "and the water shall enter," counted three times to yield six clauses, half for her and half for him. Then a baraita swings wider, making the uncertain adulteress the model for every doubt about ritual impurity: doubt in a private domain defiles, doubt in the street does not.
sotah/28.question: If doubtful impurity sticks only where there is someone who could be asked, why is the model case a woman whose answer nobody is willing to accept?

judge.reachNote: What 'capable of being asked' really does in the doubt rules — whether it means a source of reliable testimony or merely the presence of a knowing subject.

answer.quote: just as a sota is an entity that has awareness in order for her to be asked whether she actually committed adultery, so too, contact with a creeping animal
answer.explanation: The page states the criterion that the sota is 'an entity that has awareness in order for her to be asked,' which bears on the question but never addresses the tension that her own testimony is precisely what is not trusted.

sotah/29.summary: Rabbi Akiva read the words "shall be impure," written about an earthen vessel, to mean that a loaf with second-degree impurity can pass a third degree of impurity to whatever it touches. Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai held the same, while admitting no verse says so, and predicted a later generation would declare such a loaf pure. The Gemara reconstructs his reasoning from a person who immersed that day and waits for nightfall, watches each step get refuted, and lands back at the start.
sotah/29.question: If Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai knew his loaf rested on an argument with no verse behind it, and could name the generation that would undo it, on what strength did he rule at all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of ruling by reasoning alone when no verse backs it, and knowing the reasoning is vulnerable.

answer.quote: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai maintained that although it has no explicit basis from a verse in the Torah, it has proof for its impurity through an a fortiori inference
answer.explanation: The page states outright the strength on which he ruled — an a fortiori inference — and 29b completes it with the common denominator argument he refused to have refuted.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 29a: "Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai maintained that although it has no explicit basis from a verse in the Torah, it has proof for its impurity through an a fortiori inference". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question directly: Rav Yehuda in Rav's name says he ruled on the strength of an a fortiori inference, and 29b explains he rejected the refutation because he would not overturn a two-source inference on the grounds that each source has its own stringency. Rewrite the question to ask about something the page leaves open — for instance why a common denominator built from two cases each with its own unique stringency counts as proof at all, or what it means that the predicted later generation refutes precisely on that ground. The summary is accurate and can largely stand, but it should not present the derivation as simply collapsing, since the page goes on to rebuild it.

sotah/30.summary: Much of the page counts degrees of ritual impurity, arguing whether ordinary non-sacred food can carry impurity past a second remove, with a lump of pure dough set between an impure batch and a clean one as the test case. Then the subject turns to how Israel sang after crossing the sea: Rabbi Akiva has Moses lead and the people answer only the refrain, while Rabbi Eliezer, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, has them repeat every word, as listeners repeat after a child.
sotah/30.question: If the people could only echo Moses word for word, the way a congregation repeats after a minor whose recitation counts for nobody, whose song was it?

judge.reachNote: Whether repeating words after a leader makes the song your own, or merely makes you an audience with moving lips.

answer.quote: Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song unto the Lord, and said, saying
answer.explanation: The verse the sages are parsing already ascribes the song jointly to Moses and the people, which bears on whose song it was, but the page never addresses the difficulty that an echo which "is insufficient for fulfilling one's obligation" raises about the people's own singing.

sotah/31.summary: A husband who warned his wife against secluding herself with a particular man may act, Rabbi Eliezer says, even if he heard of the seclusion from a flying bird. The mishna then argues by degrees in both directions and gets blocked both times: verses fix two witnesses for the seclusion but only one for the defilement itself, the charge that ends the marriage for good. Ulla then asks how a second witness can contradict the first, if the Torah already treats that one witness as two.
sotah/31.question: Why should the lighter matter of seclusion require two witnesses when the ruinous charge of adultery can rest on one?

judge.reachNote: Evidentiary thresholds here track the text rather than the gravity of the charge, so severity and proof come apart.

answer.quote: With regard to it, that in this matter of defilement one witness suffices, but not with regard to the warning. With regard to it, but not with regard to the seclusion.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the scriptural derivation (the word "bah") that limits the single-witness allowance to defilement alone, but it gives no rationale for why the lighter matter should demand more witnesses, so the question can still be asked honestly.

sotah/32.summary: The mishna sorts recitations by language, allowing the sota oath, Shema, and Grace after Meals in any tongue, while first fruits, halitza, and the Priestly Benediction stay in Hebrew. From a stray word the Gemara reaches Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai on volume, then reverses him: the Amida is whispered so confessing transgressors are not shamed, and sin-offerings are slaughtered where burnt-offerings are, so onlookers cannot tell. The female goat brought for idol worship ruins the disguise, and the answer is that shame atones.
sotah/32.question: If the altar is arranged so that no one can tell who is bringing a sin-offering, why is the idol worshipper's exposure suddenly part of his atonement?
gate: gloss "sin-offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "burnt-offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question uses "sin offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is whether public shame is something the law shields a sinner from or a component of atonement itself, varying with the gravity of the sin.

answer.quote: There, due to the severity of the sin, let him go and be embarrassed, so that his sin will be atoned for through his embarrassment as well.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly states that for the severe sin of idol worship the shame is allowed to stand and itself contributes to atonement, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 32b: "There, due to the severity of the sin, let him go and be embarrassed, so that his sin will be atoned for through his embarrassment as well.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim at the end of the page ('due to the severity of the sin, let him go and be embarrassed'), and the summary itself already reports that answer. Write a question that starts from that resolution rather than asking for it, for example probing how a system that hides the sin-offering's identity to spare embarrassment can also treat embarrassment as atoning, or what that says about whispered prayer versus the leper who must cry out.

sotah/33.summary: The mishna's rule that the Amida, the standing prayer, may be said in any language runs into Rav Yehuda's warning that a person should never ask for his needs in Aramaic, since the ministering angels do not understand it. The Gemara splits the case: an individual needs the angels' support, a community does not. Then a Divine Voice from the Holy of Holies announcing Caligula's death turns out to have spoken Aramaic, and the answer shifts to Gabriel, who knows every language.
sotah/33.question: If prayer is a request for divine mercy, why should it matter at all whether the angels can follow the words?

judge.reachNote: If prayer is a direct appeal to God's mercy, why is it routed through intermediaries who must understand the language?

answer.quote: referring to the prayer of an individual, who needs the support of the angels, whereas this statement of the mishna is referring to communal prayer
answer.explanation: The Gemara says an individual's prayer depends on angelic support while communal prayer does not, which explains when the angels' comprehension matters but not why a request for mercy should depend on them at all.

sotah/34.summary: When the priests' feet touch the Jordan, the river stops and piles up. Rabbi Yehuda says the water stood twelve mil high, a mil being roughly a kilometer, matching the width of the camp; Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, objects that water moves faster than people and would have drowned them, so it heaped over three hundred mil. Later the arithmetic runs backward, from riverbed stones of forty se'a to the spies' grape cluster.
sotah/34.question: Caleb had to throw himself on the graves at Hebron to be saved from the spies' plan, while Moses' prayer covered Joshua before he ever set out, so is a rescue that must be begged for worth more than one arranged in advance?
gate: the question brings in "Caleb", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Hebron", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Joshua", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether protection earned by one's own pleading outranks protection granted in advance by another's merit.

answer.quote: which implies that Caleb changed his mind over time. Joshua, however, was opposed to the intentions of the other spies from the outset.
answer.explanation: The page distinguishes the two rescues — Caleb wavered and had to plead, Joshua was firm and pre-covered by Moses' prayer — which bears on the comparison without ruling which is worth more.

sotah/35.summary: Uzzah puts out a hand to steady the Ark of the Covenant when the oxen hauling it stumble, and God strikes him dead. The Ark, the Gemara says, had once carried its own bearers through the air across the Jordan, so it needed no help; Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar split over whether Uzzah died for forgetting that or for relieving himself in front of it. Then Rava says the death was David's punishment, for calling words of Torah songs.
sotah/35.question: If Uzzah's death was David's punishment for calling Torah songs, and Uzzah himself entered the World-to-Come, what was that death to Uzzah?
gate: the question brings in "World", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Come", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: One death can be a message aimed at David and still be a reckoning, or even a reward, for the man who dies in it.

answer.quote: And over this matter Uzzah was punished for not taking proper care of the Ark
answer.explanation: The page does say the death was Uzzah's own punishment for his mishandling of the Ark (glossed further as forgetfulness or relieving himself before it), which bears on what the death meant to him, though it never reconciles that with Rava's claim that it was David's punishment or with Uzzah's entry into the World-to-Come.

sotah/36.summary: Twelve tribal names were engraved on two precious stones set on the shoulders of the High Priest's ephod, and the page argues over how they were divided. The letters come to forty-nine, not fifty, so Rabbi Yitzhak adds a heh to Joseph's name; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak objects that Joseph was not called Yehosef at birth, and points instead to a second yod in Benjamin. That same heh reappears when Gabriel teaches Joseph seventy languages, and Joseph later uses Hebrew to corner Pharaoh over an oath.
sotah/36.question: When Joseph reminds Pharaoh that his own secret oath could be dissolved too, is he keeping that promise or spending it?

judge.reachNote: An oath held in reserve as leverage: whether fidelity to a secret can be kept while being used as a threat.

sotah/37.summary: Two tellings compete over who entered the Red Sea first. Rabbi Meir says the tribe of Benjamin plunged in and the princes of Judah stoned them for going out of turn; Rabbi Yehuda says every tribe hung back until Nahshon ben Amminadab of Judah waded in and prayed as the mire gave way. In both versions the one who jumped wins something lasting, the Temple site or kingship, and God cuts Moses's prayer short mid-crisis.
sotah/37.question: If going in first was the right thing, why are the princes of Judah stoning Benjamin for doing it?

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is whether zeal that breaks rank is merit or trespass — but the page settles it in the same clause the question quotes.

answer.quote: And the princes of the tribe of Judah were stoning them [rogmim otam] for plunging in first and not in the proper order
answer.explanation: The page states outright why Judah's princes stoned Benjamin: the plunge was taken out of the proper tribal order, so the very words the question asks about carry their own reason.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 37a: "And the princes of the tribe of Judah were stoning them [rogmim otam] for plunging in first and not in the proper order". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered by the same sentence it paraphrases: Judah stoned Benjamin "for plunging in first and not in the proper order." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — e.g., press on why the tribe that broke rank still hosts the Divine Presence while the tribe that kept order gains kingship, or on why Rabbi Yehuda rejects the whole account. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

sotah/38.summary: The Sages derive from two words, "So you shall bless," that the priests bless in Hebrew, standing, with hands raised, out loud, and facing the congregation. Rabbi Yonatan finds this hard: if it all comes from Aaron blessing at the Tabernacle's dedication, why not also limit it to a High Priest, on the New Moon, during a communal offering? Later, farmhands stuck in the fields are covered by the blessing, an iron wall does not block it, but people standing behind the priests are left out.
sotah/38.question: If even an iron partition cannot keep the blessing from reaching someone, what exactly is it about standing behind the priests that does?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a blessing travels by relationship and orientation toward the blesser rather than by physical line of sight, so walls cannot block it but turning away can.

answer.quote: people who are not compelled to be away but still do not stand face-to-face with the priests. Consequently, they are not included in the benediction
answer.explanation: The page indicates the disqualifying factor is voluntarily failing to stand face-to-face (as the baraita on 38a requires, "like a person who is talking to another"), not physical obstruction, though it never directly contrasts this with the iron partition ruling.

sotah/39.summary: Rava bar Rav Huna says that once a Torah scroll is opened, talking is forbidden, even talk of halakha, learned from Ezra reading to a crowd that stood in silence. From there the page builds a chain of waiting: the caller waits for the congregation's amen, the priests wait for the caller to finish the word, the translator waits for the reader's verse. Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua credits his long life to small restraints, like never cutting through a synagogue as a shortcut.
sotah/39.question: If a congregation may slip out the second door while the Torah scroll leaves by the first, is the respect in walking behind it or only in not being seen to walk ahead?

judge.reachNote: Whether reverence is a real act of deference (following the scroll) or only the avoidance of a visible affront (not being seen ahead of it).

answer.quote: this halakha is derived from the verse: “After the Lord your God you shall walk” (Deuteronomy 13:5), meaning that one must walk after the Torah scroll and not in front of it
answer.explanation: Rava's derivation states the operative rule — not walking in front of the scroll — which bears directly on the question, yet the page never settles whether the two-exit leniency means respect is substantive following or merely avoiding the appearance of precedence.

sotah/40.summary: The Gemara asks what a congregation says while the priests bless them, and whether speaking at all is like a servant talking through his own blessing. Rabbi Abbahu concluded he was not humble after seeing Rabbi Abba of Akko unbothered when his interpreter offered a different explanation than his own. Stories follow proving Abbahu humble, ending with his parable about selling cheap trinkets rather than precious stones, which leaves Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, whose audience had walked out on his law lecture, still offended.
sotah/40.question: Was telling Rabbi Ḥiyya that crowds swarm the trinket seller a comfort, or one more reminder that they had left him?

judge.reachNote: Consolation that explains away a slight can restate the slight; humility offered downward may land as condescension.

answer.quote: On that day, Rabbi Abbahu escorted Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba to his lodging place, and even so, Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba’s mind was not at ease
answer.explanation: The page states that the parable (offered "to appease him") failed to settle Rabbi Ḥiyya's mind, which bears on the question's outcome without settling whether the words themselves consoled or stung.

sotah/41.summary: At the assembly held in the year after the Sabbatical Year, the king reads aloud from Deuteronomy, and King Agrippa, a descendant of Herod, wept when he reached the verse barring a foreigner from the throne. The whole nation called back that he was their brother, and Rabbi Natan says that for this flattery they were sentenced to destruction. Yet Reish Lakish holds flattery of the wicked is permitted, citing Jacob telling Esau his face was like an angel's.
sotah/41.question: If Jacob could safely compare Esau's face to an angel's, what made the crowd's comfort to a weeping Agrippa the kind of flattery that doomed them?

judge.reachNote: When does soothing speech become the kind of falsehood that corrupts judgment, and does the character of the person flattered decide it?

sotah/42.summary: A priest appointed specifically for war addresses the troops in Hebrew before battle, and the Gemara works out who that priest is: not the High Priest, who has no one above him in his own line of work, and not the deputy, since Rabbi Ḥanina says the deputy exists only to step in if the High Priest is disqualified. Much of the rest reads Goliath's name apart, closing with Rabbi Elazar's rule against reciting a wicked man's praise.
sotah/42.question: If relating the praise of the wicked is off limits, what is the page doing when it measures Goliath's spear and counts out his forty days?

judge.reachNote: The question does reach a real idea — when describing an enemy's greatness serves a permitted purpose — but the page states that idea and resolves it explicitly.

answer.quote: It was necessary in this case in order to relate the praise of David, who defeated Goliath.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very objection the note asks — that the verse should not praise Goliath at all — and answers that his greatness is recounted only to magnify David's victory.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 42b: "It was necessary in this case in order to relate the praise of David, who defeated Goliath.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same passage it draws on: the Gemara objects that the verse should not praise Goliath and replies that it is needed to relate David's praise. Write a question that starts after that answer, or take up a thread the page leaves unresolved — for example why an appointed office is required for the war priest while the deputy High Priest, always ready to serve, is said not to count as appointed. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

sotah/43.summary: A man who built a shed for wood goes home from the battle lines; a man who built a gateway or a balcony does not. The mishna sorts new houses, new vineyards, and new betrothals into those that release a soldier and those that do not, and the Gemara presses the edges: grafted trees, layered vines, a vineyard owned by two partners. Sharpest is Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's case of a stolen house whose thief repaid the owners and still marches.
sotah/43.question: If the thief repaid the owners in full and now holds the house as a legal purchaser, what is left of the theft that keeps him in the ranks?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a thing's status attaches at the moment of acquisition and survives later legitimation, but the page already states that answer.

answer.quote: Since initially it entered his possession with the status of stolen property, he does not return.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection—that after repayment he is a legal purchaser—and answers that the house's origin as stolen property permanently bars his return.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 43b: "Since initially it entered his possession with the status of stolen property, he does not return.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim a line later: the Gemara itself asks why the repaid thief isn't a purchaser and replies that the house first entered his possession as stolen property. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, why an origin-taint should govern military exemption when the man has repented and paid, or how this squares with the partners' vineyard, where a real share in a young tree still does not send anyone home. Aim at the principle the page leaves unexplained, not at a line it supplies.

sotah/44.summary: The officers' speech before battle sends home the man who built a house, planted a vineyard, or betrothed a wife he has not yet married. Rabbi Akiva hears "fearful and fainthearted" as plain terror, a man who cannot stand the sight of a drawn sword; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili hears fear of one's own sins, small enough to include talking between binding the arm phylactery and the head one. Behind the ranks stand guards with iron rods, licensed to break the legs of anyone who runs.
sotah/44.question: If the long list of exemptions exists so a frightened or guilty man can walk home without naming his reason, at what moment does he stop being exempt and become the man the guards are allowed to beat?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: an army that invites the fearful and the guilty to leave with dignity must still fix a point past which leaving becomes desertion.

answer.quote: And it shall be, when the officers conclude speaking to the people, that captains of legions shall be appointed at the head of the people
answer.explanation: The mishna marks the transition — once the officers finish the speech of exemptions, the captains and guards with rods are posted, and anyone who then turns back may be beaten — but it never states the cutoff as an answer to when exemption lapses, so the question survives.

sotah/45.summary: A corpse found in an open field triggers the heifer ritual, so the Gemara asks what counts as an open field: not a body hidden in a pile of stones, hanging on a tree, or floating on water. To settle whether a body lying on another body is hidden or floating, the Sages reach for the law of forgotten sheaves, where a sheaf dropped on another sheaf raises the same question. The mishna closes with elders washing their hands and swearing they sent no traveler off without food.
sotah/45.question: If a body under a pile of stones cancels the ritual entirely, what happens to the elders' claim that they fed and escorted every traveler who passed through?

judge.reachNote: The question presses on why textual exclusions (concealed, hanging, floating) should silence the ritual's moral reckoning about hospitality and responsibility for the traveler.

sotah/46.summary: A corpse is found outside a town with no known killer, and the elders break a heifer's neck by a hard-flowing stream and declare that their hands did not spill this blood. The Gemara takes that declaration as a confession of something else: they did not send the man off without food, and did not let him leave unaccompanied. Rabbi Meir presses it, holding that whoever refuses to escort a traveler is himself like a spiller of blood.
sotah/46.question: If the people of Jericho had walked Elisha to the edge of town, would the forty-two children still have been torn by bears, and whose hands would the blood be on?
gate: the question brings in "Jericho", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Elisha", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is liability for omission — that failing to escort a traveler makes one responsible for what befalls him.

answer.quote: had the inhabitants of Jericho accompanied Elisha, he would not have incited the bears to attack the children
answer.explanation: The page states outright that escorting Elisha would have prevented the bears' attack, and the same passage assigns the blood-guilt to those who fail to accompany.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sotah 46b: "had the inhabitants of Jericho accompanied Elisha, he would not have incited the bears to attack the children". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question's counterfactual is spelled out on the page itself, which says that had Jericho's inhabitants accompanied Elisha he would not have incited the bears, and that one who does not accompany another is like a spiller of blood. Ask instead about what the passage leaves unresolved — for example why the youths, not the negligent townsmen, bear the consequence, or how Rabbi Meir's coercion of escort squares with the elders' declaration that their hands did not spill this blood. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

sotah/47.summary: Elisha fell ill three times, and one illness is counted as punishment for shoving his servant Gehazi away with both hands instead of leaving him a way back. The same charge lands on Yehoshua ben Perahya, who excommunicated his student Jesus the Nazarene and then, while reciting the Shema prayer, raised a hand meaning wait that was read as never. Both students quote their teachers' own rule back at them: whoever causes the masses to sin is not given the chance to repent.
sotah/47.question: If both teachers are faulted for pushing with both hands, why does the refusal to return stand on a rule those same teachers taught?

judge.reachNote: Whether a teacher's own transmitted ruling can be turned against him, and how blame for the push coexists with the finality it produced.

answer.quote: With regard to the evil inclination, to a child, and to a woman, the left hand should reject and the right hand should welcome. If one pushes too forcefully, the damage might be irreversible.
answer.explanation: The closing baraita explains why a two-handed push is blameworthy — the damage becomes irreversible — which bears on the question but does not state why the teachers' own rule about causing the masses to sin remains binding against them.

sotah/48.summary: A mishna says that when the Sanhedrin, the high court, ceased, singing at wine feasts ended too, and the Gemara pushes the ban further. Rav Huna allows the work songs of men hauling ships and driving herds, since the rhythm helps, but forbids weavers, who sing for pleasure; then he bans song altogether and grain and ducks turn cheap. Rav Ḥisda belittles the ban, people sing again, and a single duck cannot be found for a dinar, a silver coin.
sotah/48.question: If the proof that silencing song was right is the price of wheat and ducks, was the ban ever really about mourning a destroyed Temple?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition's real ground is the grief it expresses or the material blessing it is said to produce.

answer.quote: Rav said: The ear that hears song should be uprooted, as it is prohibited to listen to music after the destruction of the Temple.
answer.explanation: The page does supply a mourning-based rationale for banning song, but it never addresses why the ban's vindication is then narrated in market prices, so the question can still be asked honestly.

sotah/49.summary: Rava reads a verse from Deuteronomy to mean that each day is more cursed than the one before, and the page piles up lists of what ended when a sage died: parables with Rabbi Meir, wondrous deeds with Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, humility with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. The mishna bans bridegrooms' crowns after one war and brides' gold crowns after the next. Then Rav Yosef tells the man who recites the mishna to strike humility from the list, since he is still here.
sotah/49.question: If humility ended with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, what exactly is Rav Yosef doing when he asks that the line be deleted on his own account?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the paradox of a sage asserting his own humility to correct a mishna's obituary of virtues — whether the claim refutes the list or performs it.

gittin/2.summary: Gittin opens with a courier who carries a bill of divorce, a get, from overseas to a wife in Eretz Yisrael, and must announce that the document was written and signed in front of him. Rabba explains that distant scribes may not know a get must be written for this particular woman's sake; Rava says the worry is simply that no witnesses are nearby to confirm the signatures. The two reasons split apart in odd cases, like two couriers instead of one.
gittin/2.question: If most scribes already know a get must be written for her sake, and the Sages added the declaration only as a precaution, what is the courier's sentence actually proving?

judge.reachNote: What is the content of a testimony that the Sages require as a precaution rather than to resolve a genuine doubt?

answer.quote: he is testifying that the writing and the signing of the bill of divorce were performed for the sake of the man and woman in question
answer.explanation: The page states what the courier's declaration attests to, but it does not resolve what that attestation accomplishes once it concedes that most scribes are expert and the Sages imposed the testimony only as an extra precaution — the passage breaks off mid-sentence at "And here, with regard to this testimony,".

gittin/3.summary: An agent bringing a bill of divorce from overseas must say that it was written in his presence and signed in his presence, one witness where two are usually required. The Gemara objects twice that this helps no one: with two witnesses the husband could never contest the document, while with one he can. Rabba defends the short formula by arguing that adding "for her sake" would make three terms, and an agent drops one word of three but not one of two.
gittin/3.question: If a single agent's word leaves the husband free to come back and challenge the document, in what sense is accepting one witness a leniency for the woman?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the leniency/stringency tension in trusting a single agent, but the page states and resolves that tension explicitly.

answer.quote: Therefore, at the outset the agent is careful to clarify the matter fully, and he will not act to his own detriment by bringing an invalid bill of divorce.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection that the one-witness rule is a stringency and answers it twice: because the agent must hand over the document before two or three people, he verifies it fully in advance, so the husband's ability to contest is not a real disadvantage.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 3a: "Therefore, at the outset the agent is careful to clarify the matter fully, and he will not act to his own detriment by bringing an invalid bill of divorce.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it twice with the agent's caution before two or three witnesses, so it cannot stand as written. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and ask what remains hard, e.g. why the agent's self-interest is trusted to substitute for two witnesses, or why the dispute over two versus three witnesses at delivery matters. The summary itself is accurate and can largely stay.

gittin/4.summary: An agent who carries a bill of divorce from overseas must declare that it was written and signed in his presence, and the page keeps asking why. Rabba says people abroad do not know the document must be written for that particular woman's sake; Rava says witnesses to confirm the signatures are not nearby. Each clause of the mishna is read as proof for one side, then reread to fit the other, until Rabba adopts Rava's reason and adds his own.
gittin/4.question: If Rabba ends up holding both reasons at once, what is left of the disagreement besides the two thin cases the Gemara scrapes together at the end?

judge.reachNote: When one side absorbs the other's reason, is there still a dispute, or only a pair of residual edge cases where the extra reason does work?

gittin/5.summary: An agent who carries a bill of divorce from overseas must announce that it was written and signed in his presence, and the page tests that rule against odd cases: an agent who goes deaf and mute before speaking, two agents instead of one, a woman carrying her own divorce document. Rare situations usually escape rabbinic decrees, yet the woman must recite anyway, so that agents are not sorted into types. The husband who delivers it himself is excused; he could just tear it up.
gittin/5.question: If the whole point of making the woman recite the formula is that agents should not be sorted into types, what makes the husband a type worth excusing?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is when a blanket uniformity decree yields to the vanishing of the decree's underlying purpose—but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: The reason for the decree is that perhaps the husband will come to contest and invalidate the bill of divorce. However, here the husband himself now holds the document in his hand
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the note's objection—that the husband too should recite since agents are not distinguished—and answers that the decree's whole rationale (fear the husband will contest) is absent when he himself delivers the document, since he could simply tear it up.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 5a: "The reason for the decree is that perhaps the husband will come to contest and invalidate the bill of divorce. However, here the husband himself now holds the document in his hand". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The Gemara itself asks why the husband is not included in the uniformity rule and answers it plainly: the decree exists lest the husband contest the document, and a husband holding it in his own hand could simply tear it up. Do not ask a question the page resolves a line later. Push instead into something left unsettled—e.g. why the uniformity concern overrides rarity for the woman but the 'return to its corrupt state' decree is waived once she has remarried, or what it means that Rabba must lean on Rava's reason to keep the rule standing.

gittin/6.summary: A messenger carrying a bill of divorce from abroad must declare that it was written and signed in his presence, and the page keeps shrinking what counts as abroad. Rav Ḥisda demanded the declaration for documents going from Akteisfon to Bei Ardeshir but not the reverse, since the Bei Ardeshir traders go to the Akteisfon market and their signatures are known there. Rava required it inside a single cluster of houses in Meḥoza, where people never stay put.
gittin/6.question: If the witnesses in Meḥoza can go missing from one house to the next, what is left of the difference between a bill of divorce from overseas and one from next door?

judge.reachNote: Whether "overseas" is a real legal category or merely a rough proxy for the availability of witnesses to ratify the document.

answer.quote: Rava issued this decree only with regard to his city of Meḥoza. The reason is that the residents of Meḥoza are different, as they are constantly mobile
answer.explanation: The page limits Rava's stringency to a single anomalous city, which bears on how much of the overseas/local distinction survives, but it never asks or resolves whether the geographic category has collapsed into a test of witness availability.

gittin/7.summary: A bill of divorce is written on a boat, and two teachings disagree about whether that boat counts as inside Eretz Yisrael, which decides whether the agent delivering it must announce that it was written and signed in his presence. Rabbi Yehuda's test, borrowed from a case of foreign soil carried by ship, is whether the hull scrapes the sea floor. Rabbi Zeira stretches that to a flowerpot with a hole in it standing on pegs; Rava pushes back.
gittin/7.question: What makes a patch of earth belong to a country, the place it floats above or the ground it actually touches?

judge.reachNote: Whether territorial belonging is a matter of physical attachment to the land or of location within its bounds.

gittin/8.summary: The Rabbis fix the western edge of Eretz Yisrael by imagining a string pulled taut from Turei Amnon in Syria south to the River of Egypt, with islands east of it inside the land. Syria comes out half and half: obligated in tithes and the Sabbatical Year like the land, but foreign for its impure soil and for bills of divorce. Still, one may enter it inside a chest and stay pure, and have a gentile write a deed of sale there on Shabbat.
gittin/8.question: If Syria counts as outside the land when a slave is sold there or a divorce document is written there, why is buying a field in it worth suspending the rule against telling a gentile to work on Shabbat?
gate: gloss "the Sabbatical Year" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The idea is that a land's partial sanctity can still carry the full weight of the mitzva of settling it, enough to lift a rabbinic Shabbat fence.

answer.quote: here the Sages did not impose this decree, due to the mitzva of settling Eretz Yisrael
answer.explanation: The Gemara states explicitly that the decree against telling a gentile to work on Shabbat is waived for a Syrian land purchase because of the mitzva of settling Eretz Yisrael, and it earlier grounds Syria's partial sanctity in David's conquest being 'called a conquest.'

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 8b: "here the Sages did not impose this decree, due to the mitzva of settling Eretz Yisrael". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 8b: the decree is waived "due to the mitzva of settling Eretz Yisrael," with Syria's sanctity traced to David's individual conquest. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what it leaves open — e.g., why the mitzva of settlement reaches Syria while tithes need a separate conquest argument, or why the same land is foreign for slaves and divorce documents yet holy enough to override a rabbinic Shabbat fence. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

gittin/9.summary: A baraita counts three ways a bill of divorce and a bill of manumission, the document freeing a slave, are alike; Rabbi Meir counts four. The number four, the Gemara decides, excludes a rule for witnesses who cannot write: a stencil is torn from blank paper and they fill in their names with ink, which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits for bills of divorce alone. The Gemara asks why other shared rules are missing and answers that the list counts only rabbinic invalidations, not Torah ones.
gittin/9.question: If a witness who cannot write his name inks in letters through a stencil someone else cut for him, whose signature is on the document?

judge.reachNote: What makes marks on a document count as a person's signature — the hand that forms the letters or the will that inks them.

answer.quote: It is said with regard to bills of divorce. However, with regard to bills of manumission and all other documents, if the witnesses know how to read and sign, they sign
answer.explanation: The page limits the stencil device to bills of divorce, implying that such a traced signature is a deficient one tolerated only there, but it never says whose signature the document bears.

gittin/10.summary: A mishna rules that any document with a Samaritan witness signed on it is invalid, except bills of divorce and bills of manumission, and it reports that Rabban Gamliel approved such a bill in the village of Otnai. The Gemara hunts for whose view this fits, citing a dispute over whether a Samaritan's matza works on Passover, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says Samaritans keep accepted commandments more strictly than Jews. When the Otnai story mentions two Samaritan witnesses, Abaye rereads the word as singular.
gittin/10.question: Is Abaye changing "its witnesses" to "its witness" because the story requires it, or because two Samaritan signatures would wreck the rule he already holds?

judge.reachNote: Whether a received text gets reread to fit an established rule, or the rule bends to the text.

answer.quote: Rava said: Actually, you do not need to say that the case was concerning one Samaritan witness, as it indeed is referring to two Samaritans witnesses
answer.explanation: Rava's counter-reading shows the incident itself does not compel Abaye's singular emendation, implying Abaye reads it that way to preserve Rabbi Elazar's rule that only one Samaritan witness is valid, though the page never states Abaye's motive outright.

gittin/11.summary: A man tells an agent to hand a bill of divorce to his wife, or a bill of manumission to his slave, and then wants to take it back. The Rabbis let him retract the divorce but not the freedom: a benefit can be acquired for someone in his absence, and a wife is owed sustenance while a slave is not. Rabbi Meir presses back that a priest's freed slave loses teruma, the produce set aside for priests.
gittin/11.question: The page decides that freedom is in the slave's interest and divorce is against the wife's, so who gets asked, and who does not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of when another may act for you without asking — but the mishna states that rule explicitly in the very lines the summary paraphrases.

answer.quote: therefore an agent cannot receive it for her without her consent
answer.explanation: The mishna states outright that a benefit may be acquired in a person's absence — so the slave is never asked — while a detriment requires presence, so the wife's consent is required.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 11b, Mishna: "therefore an agent cannot receive it for her without her consent". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered in the mishna the summary paraphrases: benefit may be conferred in a person's absence, detriment only in his presence, so the slave is not asked and the wife is. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance Rabbi Meir's objection that a priest's slave loses teruma and the Rabbis' reply that he ate only as his master's acquisition, or Rabbi Yirmeya's rule that "give to so-and-so" is like "acquire for so-and-so" yet seizing for a creditor to others' detriment acquires nothing. The first half of the daf (gentile-signed documents, Persian deeds collecting only from non-liened property) is also untouched.

gittin/12.summary: A slave who killed someone unintentionally is exiled to a city of refuge, and even there his earnings belong to his master, who owes him no food. The Gemara uses this case and others to test one question: may a master say, work for me but I will not sustain you? Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel has the slave demand in famine years to be fed or freed, so strangers will pity him; the Rabbis answer that pity reaches slaves too.
gittin/12.question: If mercy finds a slave as readily as a free man, why is the starving slave asking for his freedom at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether legal status changes who draws other people's compassion — the slave's freedom as a means to be seen and pitied.

answer.quote: the slave can say to his master: Either sustain me or emancipate me, so that people will see me in my helpless state, and they will have mercy on me
answer.explanation: The page states outright why the starving slave seeks emancipation — visible helplessness as a free man will draw charity — which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 12a: "the slave can say to his master: Either sustain me or emancipate me, so that people will see me in my helpless state, and they will have mercy on me". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already gives the slave's motive in so many words — he wants to be freed so that people will see his helpless state and have mercy on him — so the question is answered before a reader finishes the passage. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved, such as why the Rabbis think a master may keep ownership of a slave he cannot feed at all, or why Rav's two rulings force the conclusion that the master's hold on the slave's labor depends on feeding him. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

gittin/13.summary: A man tells messengers to hand a bill of divorce to his wife, then dies, and the errand dies with him; but if he told them to give someone a hundred dinars, the money is still handed over. Rav attaches a condition: only if the coins were piled in a corner when he spoke, since otherwise he may have meant a buried hundred that no one can locate. Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa then split over whether the speaker was healthy or dying.
gittin/13.question: Why should a man's death cancel his instruction to deliver a divorce document but leave his instruction to hand over a hundred dinars standing?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a get requires the husband's personal act, so agency dies with him, while money can pass by other acts of acquisition — but the page says this outright.

answer.quote: bills of divorce and manumission must be transferred by the husband or the master. Once he has died the document can no longer be given, and the agency he appointed for this purpose is likewise canceled
answer.explanation: The mishna's own explanatory clause states exactly why the divorce errand lapses at death while a monetary gift does not depend on the husband's own act of transfer.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 13a (Mishna): "bills of divorce and manumission must be transferred by the husband or the master. Once he has died the document can no longer be given, and the agency he appointed for this purpose is likewise canceled". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates the mishna's own reason, which the page gives verbatim, so it is answered before the Gemara even begins. Build the question instead on something the page leaves unsettled: for instance why Rav insists the coins be piled in a corner when a deathbed statement is treated "as though it were written and delivered," or what Rav Zevid and Rav Pappa each gain by reading the speaker as healthy versus dying. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

gittin/14.summary: Two agents sent to Neharde'a to fetch Rabbi Ahai's silver vessel are handed it, then asked to accept responsibility for it on the road. Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar refuses, and also refuses to give the vessel back; the men beat him while his colleague Rabbi Dostai tells them, "You are acting well; hit him." Rabbi Ahai accepts the excuse only after hearing the men had government ties, servants and horses, which sits oddly beside the page's cool debate over when a sender can still retract.
gittin/14.question: Did Rabbi Ahai excuse the words "hit him," or only the failure to help?

judge.reachNote: How far duress excuses not merely passivity but actively egging on violence against a colleague.

answer.quote: If so, you acted well, as the situation was entirely out of your control.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Aḥai blanketly approves Rabbi Dostai's conduct once he learns of the men's power, but the page never separates the failure to help from the words "hit him," so the distinction the question draws remains open.

gittin/15.summary: An agent bringing a bill of divorce from overseas must say it was written and signed in his presence; witnessing only one of the two signatures voids it. Rav Ḥisda holds that outside witnesses cannot patch the gap, since one document cannot be validated by two kinds of credibility, and the page tracks that idea into ledges, fences and hands washed half at a time. Rava objects that if the agent's word alone sufficed, extra testimony should not make the divorce worse.
gittin/15.question: If the agent's single declaration would have made the document valid, why does adding a second witness to the same signature ruin it?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a document must stand wholly on one mode of credibility, so adding a second kind of proof can weaken rather than strengthen it.

answer.quote: Perhaps people will come to confuse it with the typical case of ratification of legal documents, and will rely on one witness who testifies about his own signature
answer.explanation: Rava himself raises the note's objection and then supplies the reason extra testimony still spoils the document — the fear that mixed testimony will be copied over to ordinary document ratification and extract money on one witness.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 15b: "Perhaps people will come to confuse it with the typical case of ratification of legal documents, and will rely on one witness who testifies about his own signature". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very objection Rava raises on the page, and the page answers it twice: Rava's fear that people will confuse this with ordinary ratification and extract money on one witness, and Rav Ashi's rule that a bill of divorce cannot be validated by two types of credibility. Ask something that survives those answers — for instance why the Shabbat partition case, built on the same all-or-nothing principle, is decided the other way ('the halakha is that they join together'), or what the 'not only this but also that' reply costs Rav Ḥisda's reading of the mishna. Keep the summary, which is faithful, and hang the new question on a tension the page leaves standing.

gittin/16.summary: Ilfa asks whether the wetness left on one half of a washed hand counts as joined to the water poured over the other half. Rabbi Yehuda holds that water dripping off a man leaving a ritual bath of exactly forty se'a, a volume measure, still connects to the bath, yet two dilemmas about a body purified half by immersion and half by pouring are dropped unresolved. The same arithmetic of halves then hits testimony: one agent saw the bill of divorce written, another saw it signed.
gittin/16.question: If two men saying "she was divorced in our presence" would simply be believed, why should it matter that one of them watched only the writing and the other only the signing?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the gap between a witness being believed and a document being formally valid, which the page resolves by naming the decree against confusion with ratification.

answer.quote: The Sages decree that it is invalid lest people will come to confuse this case with the typical situation of ratification of legal documents.
answer.explanation: The page explains that split testimony is disqualified not because the agents are disbelieved but because of a rabbinic decree lest people think documents can be ratified by a single witness.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 16b: "The Sages decree that it is invalid lest people will come to confuse this case with the typical situation of ratification of legal documents.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered flatly on the page: the split declaration is invalid because of the decree lest it be confused with ratification of documents by one witness, not because the agents are disbelieved. Rewrite so the question starts from that decree and asks what still pinches, for instance why Rabbi Yehuda drops the worry about the halakha being forgotten yet keeps the worry about confusion with ordinary documents. Alternatively press on the two competing reasons for the declaration (lack of expertise in writing for her sake versus absence of witnesses to ratify) and what each implies about what the agent's words are doing.

gittin/17.summary: A bill of divorce has to carry a date, and the Gemara asks why, since such a document is never used to collect money. Rabbi Yoḥanan says the date stops a man from backdating a divorce to shield a wife who is also his sister's daughter from punishment for adultery; Reish Lakish says it fixes the moment her fields' produce stops belonging to him. Abaye then presses Rav Yosef until the date shrinks to a seven-year span.
gittin/17.question: If a get with no date at all still divorces after the fact, and a date naming only a seven-year stretch is acceptable from the start, what is the date actually stopping?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether a rabbinic ordinance is justified by partial rather than complete protection — but the Gemara itself raises and settles it.

answer.quote: It helps for the seven-year period before it and the seven-year period after it.
answer.explanation: Abaye asks precisely the note's question — what the dating ordinance accomplishes given these leniencies — and Rav Yosef answers that even a vague date fixes liability for the periods before and after it, just as a day's date works for the day before and after, while the undated get is limited in that 'she may not marry ab initio.'

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 17b: "It helps for the seven-year period before it and the seven-year period after it.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question, and Rav Yosef answers it on 17b: a loose date still fixes the periods before and after it, and an undated get is barred ab initio. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating it — for instance, press on why Rav Yosef's day-before/day-after analogy should license stretching the same logic across seven years, or on what a date that cannot fix the hour is worth to Rabbi Yoḥanan's adultery concern. The summary itself is faithful and can stay largely as is.

gittin/18.summary: A divorced woman waits three months before remarrying, so that no child's paternity falls into doubt, and Rav and Shmuel split over when that clock starts: when the bill of divorce is written, or when it reaches her hand. Rav Natan bar Hoshaya objects with two women in one courtyard who receive their documents in the same moment, one free to remarry, one not, because one document was drafted earlier. Abaye answers that each woman's written date settles her own case.
gittin/18.question: If two women are handed their bills of divorce in the same hour, can ink dated months apart really make one of them free to remarry and the other not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward whether a document's written date creates the legal reality or merely records an event, but the page resolves it outright with Abaye's reply.

answer.quote: With regard to this woman, the date of her bill of divorce proves concerning her that she may not remarry yet; and with regard to that woman
answer.explanation: Abaye answers precisely the question the note asks — each woman's written date is the proof that governs her own status — and the note's own summary already reports this answer.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 18a: "With regard to this woman, the date of her bill of divorce proves concerning her that she may not remarry yet; and with regard to that woman". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is simply Rav Natan bar Hoshaya's objection, which Abaye answers on the page and which the summary itself reports, so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to probe something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why the halakha finally follows counting from the writing when a baraita and several sages counted from the giving, or what work the dating ordinance does once overseas bills of divorce are admittedly not counted from their date. Keep the summary's accurate account of the three-month dispute as the setup.

gittin/19.summary: A mishna lists what a bill of divorce may be written with: ink, arsenic, red dye, tree resin, iron sulfate, anything permanent, even a cow's horn, valid if he hands over the cow. The Gemara then worries about witnesses who cannot sign, and Rav Pappa has a name written in saliva for Pappa the ox herder to trace in ink. The leniency stops at divorce documents; a man who let witnesses trace names on ordinary documents was flogged.
gittin/19.question: If a traced signature really shows the witness stood there, why does it hold a marriage apart and get a man flogged over a loan?

judge.reachNote: Whether a signature's validity can depend on the stakes of the document rather than on the act of signing itself.

answer.quote: He holds that there is reason to be lenient with bills of divorce, so that the daughters of Israel should not be deserted.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Elazar states outright why tracing is permitted for a bill of divorce but not for loan documents, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 19b: "He holds that there is reason to be lenient with bills of divorce, so that the daughters of Israel should not be deserted.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on the page: Rav Pappa's leniency is limited to gittin "as there is a concern that witnesses will not be found, and the woman will be unable to remarry," and Rabbi Elazar gives the same reason for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. Write a question that starts after that reason instead of asking for it. For instance, press on Rabbi Yoḥanan's refusal to carry the Shabbat ruling on writing-over-writing into gittin, or on why the same desertion worry does not extend to bills of manumission.

gittin/20.summary: Rav Ḥisda claims he could invalidate every bill of divorce in the world, since the wife usually pays the scribe and the writing surface is worth nothing; the answer is that a document written on material forbidden for any benefit still works. The discussion then presses on what the husband actually hands over: a gold plate, paper he keeps for himself, letters without the blank space between them. Rami bar Ḥama asks about a divorce tattooed on a slave who turns up in the wife's possession.
gittin/20.question: If the slave with the writing on his hand walked over to the wife on his own because he prefers her as an owner, has the husband given her anything at all?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that giving requires an act by the giver, not merely the object ending up in the recipient's hands.

answer.quote: the slave, and by extension the bill of divorce, was given to her, and consequently the woman is not divorced
answer.explanation: After laying out both sides of Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma, the Gemara brings Reish Lakish's rule that livestock (and so a slave) carry no presumption of ownership from mere possession, concluding that without witnesses to the transfer she is not divorced.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 20b: "the slave, and by extension the bill of divorce, was given to her, and consequently the woman is not divorced". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later: the Gemara imports Reish Lakish's rule that possession of livestock (or a slave) proves nothing, and concludes she is not divorced. Rewrite so the question starts from that resolution — for example, why a tattooed slave who cannot be forged still fails as a delivered document, or what the slave's own preference for the wife implies about a document that can walk. Alternatively, build the question on an untouched thread, such as Rav Pappa's unresolved case of keeping the blank space between the letters, or the husband keeping the paper while giving the writing.

gittin/21.summary: Rava says a husband can divorce his wife by placing the bill of divorce in his slave's hand and then deeding her the slave, or by leaving it in a courtyard he gives her. The objection: a slave walks around, and a moving courtyard acquires nothing, so the answer is that the slave was tied up. Abaye presses harder, since her hand takes things against her will, while a gift needs her consent.
gittin/21.question: If a courtyard counts as an extension of her hand, how can it ever deliver a divorce she does not want, when she has to agree to accept the courtyard first?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: whether a mode of acquisition derived from 'her hand' must share the hand's power to acquire against the woman's will, and whether a consensual gift can carry that power.

gittin/22.summary: A pot with a hole in its bottom straddles the border of Eretz Yisrael, the hole over land inside and the branches hanging outside, and Abaye and Rava argue whether tithing obligations follow the hole or the leaves. To test this, the Gemara brings two stacked terrace gardens with vegetables growing out of the wall between them. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda each award the vegetables to the gardener who could wipe them out, by carting off his soil or burying them in earth.
gittin/22.question: Why should the power to ruin a thing count as proof that it is yours?

judge.reachNote: Whether ownership is constituted by control over a thing's very existence rather than by location or origin of growth.

answer.quote: rather, they disagree with regard to who has control over the continued existence of these plants
answer.explanation: The page recasts the dispute as being about control over the plants' continued existence, and twice asserts that ability to destroy "is an indication that he is the owner," but it never explains why destructive power should establish ownership, so the question can still be honestly asked.

gittin/23.summary: The mishna lists who may not carry a bill of divorce to a woman: a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a minor, a blind person, and a gentile. Rav Sheshet says the blind man cannot tell who handed him the document, and Rav Yosef objects that a blind husband, or any husband in the dark, knows his wife by her voice. So the reason shifts: outside Eretz Yisrael the agent must declare he watched the writing and signing.
gittin/23.question: If an ear is trusted to identify a man's own wife in the dark, what is it that an eye does here that an ear cannot?

judge.reachNote: The idea is that recognizing a person and attesting to an act are different kinds of knowledge, but the page already states this resolution and the summary repeats it.

answer.quote: a blind man cannot say this because he is unable to see it being written or signed
answer.explanation: Rav Yosef's own resolution states exactly what sight does that hearing cannot — witness the writing and signing so the agent can make the required declaration.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 23a: "a blind man cannot say this because he is unable to see it being written or signed". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the eye does that the ear cannot, and the page answers it in the very line the summary already paraphrases: the agent must testify it was written and signed in his presence, which requires sight. Write a question that starts after that answer — for example, press on Abaye's challenge that someone who saw the writing and later went blind should still qualify, or on why the mishna's wording forced the Gemara to say sight is needed only at the start. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

gittin/24.summary: A man walking through the marketplace hears scribes drilling their students on a divorce document and recognizes both names, his own and his wife's; he cannot use it. The mishna then escalates: not a neighbor's abandoned bill, not one written for the older of two wives who share a name, not even one written for whichever wife the husband later picks. That last case is the sharp one, since choosing afterward does not make the earlier writing hers.
gittin/24.question: If the husband eventually hands the document to one of his two identically named wives, why doesn't that choice count as having written it for her?

judge.reachNote: Whether a later act of designation can retroactively supply the intent a document required at the moment of writing.

answer.quote: there is no retroactive clarification, i.e., that one does not say that since he gave the bill of divorce to this wife, it is clarified retroactively
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks why the last clause is needed and answers that the final choice does not retroactively establish that the document was written for that wife's sake.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 24b: "there is no retroactive clarification, i.e., that one does not say that since he gave the bill of divorce to this wife, it is clarified retroactively". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered word for word on 24b: the Gemara says the last clause teaches that there is no retroactive clarification, so writing must be for her sake from the outset. Build the new question on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance Rav and Shmuel's dispute over whether a scribe's practice document still disqualifies the woman from the priesthood, or why Abaye's answer needs witnesses of transmission and Rabbi Elazar's view to save the older wife's bill. Keep the summary; it tracks the mishna accurately.

gittin/25.summary: A husband tells a scribe to write a bill of divorce for whichever of his wives walks out the door first, and the argument is whether a later event can settle, in hindsight, who the document was written for. Rav Hoshaya presses the point with a father who slaughters the Paschal lamb for whichever child reaches Jerusalem first. Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that the father had already included all of them and staged the race only to hurry them along.
gittin/25.question: If the father had already registered every child for the offering before announcing the race, what were the children actually running for?
gate: gloss "the Paschal lamb" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a contest can be staged for the sake of cultivating alacrity rather than for any legal outcome — but the page already says this outright.

answer.quote: He created this competition only in order to galvanize them, so that they would be expeditious in their fulfillment of mitzvot.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly states that the race had no stake in the offering itself and existed solely to train the children in zeal for mitzvot, which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 25a: "He created this competition only in order to galvanize them, so that they would be expeditious in their fulfillment of mitzvot.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what Rabbi Yoḥanan answers in the line the summary itself paraphrases: the race was staged to galvanize the children toward zeal in mitzvot, and the baraita about the daughters confirms the stake was praise, not a portion. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance, why Rav Yehuda thought a case depending on someone else's action (who exits first, who arrives first) could be settled by a mishna about the husband's own choice, the very move Abaye challenges and Rava defends.

gittin/26.summary: A scribe who prepares bills of divorce in advance must leave blank the husband's name, the wife's name, and the date. Rabbi Yehuda invalidates such pre-written forms entirely; Rabbi Elazar invalidates only bills of divorce, since the Torah says the husband writes it for her sake. The Gemara then offers rival reasons for the blanks: sparing scribes hurried work, stopping a wife who overhears her name from starting a quarrel, and slowing an angry husband down.
gittin/26.question: If the missing lines are meant to delay a furious husband, how can the same blanks also be defended as a way to speed a bill of divorce to a woman whose husband is about to sail away?
