judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that one ordinance can be justified by opposite practical fears; the page already resolves it by assigning each fear to a different view of what effects the divorce.

answer.quote: Some say that he explained the mishna in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, and some say that he explained it in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Elazar.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself separates the two "remedy for deserted wives" explanations as rival versions resting on opposite tannaitic premises — under Rabbi Meir the ordinance forbids pre-writing the essential part (to delay the angry husband), under Rabbi Elazar it permits pre-writing the standard part (to speed the departing husband's get) — so they are not two functions of the same blanks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 26b: "Some say that he explained the mishna in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir, and some say that he explained it in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Elazar.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question assumes the delaying rationale and the hastening rationale describe the same blank spaces, but the page distinguishes them: under Rabbi Meir the ordinance bars pre-writing the essential part, under Rabbi Elazar it licenses pre-writing the standard part, and the Gemara flags them as two versions of Avimi's teaching. Write a question that starts after that distinction — for instance, why the Sages would let the identity of the effective witnesses determine whether an ordinance slows divorce down or speeds it up. Keep the summary as it is; it is accurate.

gittin/27.summary: An agent carrying a bill of divorce drops it and then finds one lying there; if he picks it up immediately it is valid, otherwise it may belong to a different man with the same name. Rabba sorts the cases by whether caravans pass through the place, and Rav Ashi wants a precise mark, a hole beside a particular letter. Then Rabba bar bar Hana loses one himself and offers the court both a mark and his own recognition.
gittin/27.question: If Rabba bar bar Hana could not tell whether the document came back because of the hole he described or because of who he was, what would an ordinary man have walked out with?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that identification can rest either on an objective mark or on the credibility of the person claiming it — but the page already says which one the ordinary man loses.

answer.quote: it is specifically Torah scholars [tzurva miderabbanan] like me who are relied upon when they say that they recognize an item, but an ordinary man would not be relied upon
answer.explanation: The page states outright that an ordinary man's claim of visual recognition would not be accepted, leaving him only the distinguishing-mark route that the preceding lines describe.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 27b: "it is specifically Torah scholars [tzurva miderabbanan] like me who are relied upon when they say that they recognize an item, but an ordinary man would not be relied upon". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the note is paraphrasing: the page says an ordinary man would not be relied upon for recognition, only a Torah scholar. Ask instead about what stays unresolved — why a scholar's bare say-so counts as identification at all where another's does not, or what Rav Ashi's uncertainty about whether distinguishing marks are Torah law leaves undecided for the ordinary finder who gives only a vague mark.

gittin/28.summary: An agent carrying a bill of divorce left the husband elderly or sick, and the mishna lets him deliver it on the assumption the man is still alive. Rava tries capping that assumption at age eighty, until Abaye produces a baraita about a hundred-year-old husband and the limit collapses. What survives is a narrower rule: nobody worries the man has already died, while worrying that he will die is left as an old dispute, unresolved.
gittin/28.question: If the page refuses to worry that the husband already died yesterday, what makes the same death, a day later, worth worrying about?

judge.reachNote: The asymmetry between a presumption that holds the past steady and a concern that opens toward a certain but undated future.

answer.quote: he rendered her forbidden to himself one hour prior to his death, meaning that she will definitely be prohibited from partaking of teruma at some point
answer.explanation: Rav Adda son of Rav Yitzḥak explains why the future death is worried about — the prohibition is certain to arrive, making it an uncertainty from the outset — but Rav Pappa objects and Rava ultimately leaves the future-death concern as an unexplained tannaitic dispute, so the question can still be honestly asked.

gittin/29.summary: An agent carrying a bill of divorce falls ill partway, and the mishna lets him pass the document to a second agent, though not if the husband also asked him to collect a deposit from the wife. The Gemara tests whether the husband's exact wording, "deliver" or "you deliver," changes the answer. Then two courtroom stories, in which Rav Safra corrects three ordained sages who blush, and Rava rules, is embarrassed, and is later rescued by a fact nobody knew.
gittin/29.question: If Rava's ruling only turns out defensible because the woman was discovered to be betrothed rather than married, was he right when he gave it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a ruling's correctness lies in the reasoning available when it is given or in facts that surface afterward.

answer.quote: Rava said: If they said that there is a concern with regard to a married woman that perhaps he was mollified, would they say the same with regard to a betrothed woman
answer.explanation: Rava himself claims vindication — since she was only betrothed, the mollification concern never applied and he concludes "my ruling was correct" — but the page never addresses whether the ruling was justified at the moment he gave it, before that fact emerged.

gittin/30.summary: A man leaves a bill of divorce with agents, to take effect if he does not come back within thirty days, and on day thirty the ferry is on the wrong bank. He shouts across the water that he has arrived, and Shmuel rules that shouting is not arriving. A second man conditions the divorce on appeasing his wife, tries, and fails, and two versions of Rav Yosef split over whether the attempt counts as fulfilling the condition.
gittin/30.question: If the wife simply would not be appeased, no matter what he offered, did the husband break his condition or keep it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a condition is judged by the husband's effort or by the result, i.e., whether forces outside his control excuse performance.

answer.quote: This second version, in which the bill of divorce does not take effect, is according to the one who says: Circumstances beyond one's control have legal standing
answer.explanation: The page frames the two versions of Rav Yosef as turning on whether circumstances beyond one's control have standing in divorce, but it does not settle which view governs, so the question can still be asked.

gittin/31.summary: Someone sets aside a jug of wine to serve as teruma, the priest's portion, for produce he will harvest later. The mishna lets him rely on the jug being intact; if he finds it lost or turned to vinegar, his earlier tithing is suspect "from the time until the same time," and the Gemara splits over which day that names. A ritual bath found short of its forty se'a, by contrast, voids immersions back to the last measuring.
gittin/31.question: If wine can sour unseen at any moment, why does either reading stop at twenty-four hours instead of doubting everything back to the last check, the way the deficient ritual bath does?

judge.reachNote: How far back a failed presumption should undo what was done on its strength — a fixed day's doubt versus doubt reaching to the last verification.

answer.quote: The amora Rabbi Elazar says: Rabbi Elazar's colleagues disagree with him
answer.explanation: The page presents the mikveh rule as the position of sages who reject Rabbi Elazar's twenty-four-hour window, but it never explains why his window is capped at a day rather than running back to the last check.

gittin/32.summary: A husband who sent a bill of divorce with an agent can cancel it before it reaches his wife, and even running into the agent by chance counts. The Gemara then weighs exact wording: saying it is void works, saying it is invalid does nothing, since a husband can nullify a document but cannot describe one into uselessness. Rav Nahman and Rav Sheshet split over whether a canceled document can be handed over again later.
gittin/32.question: If speech can undo the agent's errand but not the parchment he carries, what exactly did the husband cancel when he said the words?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether a declaration acts on a mission or on a physical object — but the page states that answer explicitly.

answer.quote: even though it is true that the husband rendered void the agency of the agent, does he also render void the bill of divorce itself?
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that the husband's speech nullified the agency and not the document, since a tangible object cannot be voided by speech, and the halakha follows Rav Naḥman accordingly.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 32b: "even though it is true that the husband rendered void the agency of the agent, does he also render void the bill of divorce itself?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: it says the husband voided the agency but not the scroll, because a tangible object cannot be made void by speech, and it rules with Rav Naḥman that the document can be reused. Build the question on something the page leaves unsettled instead — for example Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's unresolved dilemma about "this bill of divorce is void" without the pause, or why the retraction-within-thirty-days comparison to betrothal is rejected as speech-against-speech. Keep the summary as is; it holds up.

gittin/33.summary: Rabban Gamliel the Elder ruled that a husband may not cancel a bill of divorce in some far-off court, and the Gemara asks what harm that prevents: Rabbi Yoḥanan worries about a wife who remarries never knowing, Reish Lakish about a wife too frightened to remarry at all. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel goes further, saying a cancellation made anyway simply fails. To hold that up, the Sages retroactively strip the betrothal money, or relabel betrothal by intercourse as licentious.
gittin/33.question: If the Sages can reach back and undo a betrothal so that a husband cannot outmaneuver the court, what was holding that marriage in place to begin with?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what grounds a marriage's validity — private act or rabbinic sanction — but the page names that ground explicitly.

gittin/34.summary: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent his wife a bill of divorce, the document that ends a marriage, and when the agent returned without delivering it Giddul blessed God for good news. Abaye and Rava then split over whether such a display, short of the words of cancellation, voids the document. Abaye points to Rav Yehuda, who told witnesses to plug their ears with gourd so a reluctant husband's shouted cancellation could not reach them.
gittin/34.question: If the witnesses can see the husband running after them while their ears are stopped with gourd, what is left of the difference between saying what you want and showing it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether demonstrated intent carries the force of spoken cancellation — but the page's Rava already supplies the distinguishing line.

answer.quote: Since they cannot hear him, his intent is not disclosed; this, that he is running after them, does not prove that he wishes to render the bill of divorce void
answer.explanation: Rava answers precisely this objection: visible pursuit is ambiguous (he might be urging haste), so showing only counts as disclosure when unequivocal, which is what distinguishes it from saying.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 34a: "Since they cannot hear him, his intent is not disclosed; this, that he is running after them, does not prove that he wishes to render the bill of divorce void". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Abaye's own proof, and Rava answers it a few lines later by saying that running after unhearing witnesses proves nothing since he might be urging haste. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating the objection — for example, ask why an ambiguous gesture counts as no disclosure at all, or press on why the halakha finally sides with Abaye and disregards disclosure of intent even in clear cases like Giddul's blessing. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

gittin/35.summary: During a famine a man deposits a gold dinar with a widow; she hides it in a jug of flour, bakes it into a loaf, and gives the loaf to a poor man. She swears she took no benefit from it, and a child dies, since the coin took up space and spared her a bit of flour. From that case the Sages stop administering oaths to widows, and Rav then refuses to collect their marriage contracts at all.
gittin/35.question: If her oath was true as far as she knew, why should the safeguard built from her case fall on every widow who comes to court after her?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of legislating a blanket rule from a single frightening incident, and whether a rule may burden the innocent to prevent the guilty.

answer.quote: A widow is different, as she continues to live in the house with the orphans and performs many services for them in the running of the home.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains why the ordinance is limited to widows and not divorcées — because a widow, benefiting the orphans, may rationalize a false oath — which bears on why the safeguard covers widows as a class, though it does not address the justice of building it from one inadvertently false oath.

gittin/36.summary: Hillel saw people refusing to lend as the Sabbatical Year drew near, when debts are wiped out, so he instituted the prosbol, a document assigning the loan to a court so it can still be collected. Abaye defuses the problem: nowadays the cancellation is only a rabbinic reminder, so Hillel overrode the Sages, not the Torah. Shmuel calls the prosbol an ulbena of the judges and says he would abolish it if he grew strong enough.
gittin/36.question: If Shmuel thinks the prosbol is insolence and would scrap it given the power, why does he go on telling people which courts may write one?
gate: gloss "the Sabbatical Year" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: A judge who disapproves of an ordinance still administers and refines it, because dissent is not authority to repeal.

answer.quote: It can be explained that this is what he said: If my strength increases so that I become greater than Hillel, then I will nullify the prosbol.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains that Shmuel is bound by the rule that a court may only nullify an earlier court's ordinance if it is greater, so until then he must work within the prosbol — though the page never directly addresses why he restricts it to Sura and Neharde'a, and it leaves open whether ulbena even means insolence.

gittin/37.summary: The Sabbatical Year wipes out debts, and a prosbol, a document handing a loan over to the court, keeps a creditor's claim alive. The page lowers the land the debtor must own to almost nothing: a patch big enough for one cabbage stalk, a perforated pot resting on stakes, a palm stump still rooted. Then Rabba tells a debtor "I abrogate this debt," the man walks off with his money, and Rabba sits sad until Abaye coaches him back with the right words.
gittin/37.question: When Abaye teaches Abba bar Marta the sentence that lets Rabba take the money, has the debt been released or only rerouted?
gate: the question brings in "Marta", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a legally abrogated debt that is then paid anyway has actually been cancelled or merely re-described as a gift.

answer.quote: he should not say to him: I give this to you in payment of my debt; rather, he should say to him: This is my money and I give it to you as a gift
answer.explanation: The baraita Abaye cites treats the debt as genuinely released, so that any money handed over afterward must be framed as a voluntary gift rather than repayment, though the page does not directly address whether coaching the debtor hollows that release out.

gittin/38.summary: Shmuel's maidservant was taken captive, redeemed by strangers, and sent back to him; he treated her as free and did not even give her a bill of manumission, the document that releases a slave. Against that, Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel himself: freeing a slave breaks a positive commandment to hold them forever. Then a baraita reports that Rabbi Eliezer, who held that obligation binding, freed his slave anyway to make ten men for prayer.
gittin/38.question: If a missing tenth man for prayer justifies freeing a slave, why is the maidservant of Pumbedita, whom her master cannot protect from men, told that marrying another slave would do?
gate: the question brings in "Pumbedita", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of when the mitzva to keep slaves forever yields — for a communal mitzva but not for preventing sin when another remedy exists.

answer.quote: Here, in the case of the maidservant, it is possible for the master to assign her to marry his slave, and that slave will guard her
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains why emancipation is unnecessary for the Pumbedita maidservant — an alternative remedy exists — though it never directly weighs this against freeing a slave to complete a quorum.

gittin/39.summary: A man on his deathbed hears his maidservant crying that her servitude will never end, so he throws her his hat and tells her to acquire it and thereby acquire herself. Rav Naḥman rules that he did nothing, since a transfer of this kind works only with an item belonging to the one receiving, not the one giving. Earlier the page argues over whether a slave's hair, ready to be cut, already counts as separate from him.
gittin/39.question: If everyone could see what the dying man meant when he threw his hat, why should the ownership of the hat decide whether she goes free?

judge.reachNote: Whether emancipation turns on the transferor's evident intent or on the formal correctness of the mode of acquisition.

answer.quote: this mode of acquisition takes effect only when the one who transfers ownership acquires an item belonging to the one to whom the ownership is being transferred
answer.explanation: The page states the formal reason the hat's ownership voids the act, but it never addresses why that formality should override the master's plainly visible intent, which is what the question presses on.

gittin/40.summary: A slave who dons phylacteries, the boxes worn at prayer, before his master, or reads three verses of Torah in synagogue, does what only freemen do, and a baraita says none of it frees him. Only the master's own hand placing the phylacteries counts as proof. Later a man whose partner freed half their shared slave deeds his half to his minor son, and Rav Pappa's fix is to have the slave jingle coins before the boy until he wants the money.
gittin/40.question: If the father earned the verdict that his dealing returns upon his own head, is it fair that the trap is actually sprung on a child who simply likes coins?

judge.reachNote: Whether a court may reach a fraudulent adult through the appetites of a minor who bears no guilt, and whose interest the guardian then represents.

answer.quote: since the master acted deceitfully to circumvent the ruling of the Sages, one should deal with him deceitfully. We know that a child is attracted to money.
answer.explanation: The page justifies the ruse as deceit repaid to the scheming father and notes the child's attraction to money as the practical lever, but it never addresses whether using the minor this way is fair to him.

gittin/41.summary: A man owned by two partners, one of whom freed his share, serves his master one day and himself the next, according to Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai objects that this fixes nothing for the man: he may marry neither a maidservant nor a free woman, and the world was formed to be inhabited. Beit Hillel retracts, and the remaining owner is forced to free him, with the freed man writing a note owing half his own value.
gittin/41.question: If the argument for freeing him turns on his being unable to marry anyone, why does he walk out carrying a debt for half his own price?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that 'betterment of the world' overrides the master's control but not his property claim, so freedom arrives as a debt.

answer.quote: the slave writes a promissory note for his value to be paid to his original master, who was forced to emancipate his slave without receiving compensation
answer.explanation: In the parallel case of the liened slave the page states that the note compensates a master compelled to free a slave for nothing, which bears on why the half-slave leaves owing half his value, though the page never says this about the half-slave mishna itself.

gittin/42.summary: A man who is half slave and half free works for his master one day and for himself the next, and the Gemara asks who collects the damages when an ox gores him. If the goring falls on the master's day the master is paid; if it falls on the man's own day, the payment is his. Why he cannot then marry a maidservant on his master's day and a free woman on his own gets a flat answer: the daily alternation does not apply to prohibitions.
gittin/42.question: If his days can be split finely enough to decide who pockets the damages, why can they not be split finely enough to decide whom he may marry?

judge.reachNote: Monetary entitlements can be split by the day, but personal status and prohibitions are all-or-nothing — the question reaches exactly that asymmetry.

answer.quote: We are not saying that he is viewed as entering and leaving a state of slavery each day with regard to prohibitions.
answer.explanation: The Gemara states the distinction — the daily alternation governs monetary claims but not prohibitions — yet gives no reason for it, so a reader can still ask why status is divisible for money and not for marriage.

gittin/43.summary: A man who is half slave and half freeman betroths a free woman, and the Sages cannot decide whether the betrothal counts. The same puzzle runs the other way for a woman who is half maidservant and half free; Rabba bar Rav Huna taught in public that her betrothal fails, then put an interpreter before the crowd to announce he had been wrong. Later a court forces one such woman's master to free her, because men were taking liberties with her.
gittin/43.question: Why is freeing the woman the court's remedy for men taking liberties with her, rather than anything directed at the men?

judge.reachNote: The remedy attacks the legal condition that made her vulnerable rather than the wrongdoers, treating her half-status itself as the injury.

answer.quote: the reason that he was forced to emancipate her was because she was unable to marry, and other men took liberties with her
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak explains that her unmarriageable status is what exposed her, so emancipation removing that bar is the remedy, though the page never weighs this against acting against the men.

gittin/44.summary: If a Jew sells his slave to a gentile, the Sages free the slave as a penalty, and Rav applies this even when a government official forced the sale, on the grounds that the owner could have bought the man off some other way. Rabbi Yirmeya keeps testing the edges: a sale for thirty days, a sale that excludes the slave's labor, a sale that excludes his Shabbatot. Then comes a harder question: does the penalty die with the seller, or stick to his property?
gittin/44.question: If a man whose slave is seized by a violent Sicarius goes unpenalized, why is the man squeezed by a government official assumed to have had a bribe that would have worked?
gate: the question brings in "Sicarius", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is when coercion excuses a forbidden sale — whether a penalty presumes the coerced party still had a workable alternative.

answer.quote: There, the owner should have appeased the official in some other way so that he would not take the slave, and he did not appease him, therefore it is appropriate to penalize him.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the comparison ("There too, he neither desired nor profited from the sale") and answers that the official, unlike a Sicarius, could have been appeased, which is why the seller is penalized.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 44a: "There, the owner should have appeased the official in some other way so that he would not take the slave, and he did not appease him, therefore it is appropriate to penalize him.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question and it is answered twice on the page with the "he should have appeased the official in some other way" line, so it cannot stand as written. Build a new question on ground the page leaves unsettled — for example the tension in the later penalty discussion, where selling a slave is called an uncommon matter the Sages did not decree about, even though the same seller is penalized up to a hundredfold. Or press on the house-versus-slave distinction, where a person can live without a slave but not without a house.

gittin/45.summary: A mishna rules that captives are not ransomed for more than they are worth, and that no one should help a captive escape. The Gemara asks which harm the cap prevents: draining community funds, or making Jews unprofitable to kidnap. Levi bar Darga paid thirteen thousand gold dinars for his captive daughter, which looks like proof that a private person may overpay, until Abaye says he may simply have acted against the wishes of the Sages.
gittin/45.question: If the page never settles whether Levi bar Darga was within his rights, what stops any parent with money from setting the ransom price for everyone else?

judge.reachNote: Whether a ransom cap protects communal funds or the whole market, i.e. whether one rich person's private generosity prices everyone else's freedom.

answer.quote: Or perhaps it is because the result of this will be that they will not seize and bring additional captives, as they will see that it is not worthwhile
answer.explanation: The page names the market-inflation concern as one horn of the dilemma — which, if correct, would bar even a private overpayment — but the dilemma is left unresolved after Abaye deflects the proof from Levi bar Darga.

gittin/46.summary: A man who divorces his wife because of a vow she took may not remarry her, and two reasons compete on the page: keeping him from later claiming the divorce was a sham, which would taint her future children, or warning women off loose vows. Rabbi Yehuda limits the rule to vows made in public, citing Israel's oath to the Gibeonites, who lied about coming from a distant country. The Rabbis answer that the oath never took hold at all.
gittin/46.question: If the oath to the Gibeonites was void from the start, why would breaking it still desecrate God's name?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — that public honor of God's name can bind where legal obligation does not — but the page states that idea outright.

answer.quote: If they would have killed them, they would have desecrated God's name by not fulfilling their word, although this vow did not take effect.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the very tension the question poses and answers it: the desecration lies in visibly breaking one's given word, independent of whether the oath legally took hold.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 46a: "If they would have killed them, they would have desecrated God's name by not fulfilling their word, although this vow did not take effect.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates something the page already says in so many words: killing the Gibeonites would have desecrated God's name "by not fulfilling their word, although this vow did not take effect." Find a tension the page leaves standing — for instance, why Rav Naḥman's three and Rabbi Yitzḥak's ten are both read out of the same public-vow rule, or why Rav Huna treats habitual borrowers as if they had already sold themselves three times. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

gittin/47.summary: A Jew who sells his field to a gentile must still buy first fruits, the season's first ripe produce brought to the Temple, and bring them from the field he no longer owns. Rav Ashi explains this as two reversals: the Sages first cancelled the obligation so that selling would cost something, then reimposed it as a penalty to push sellers into buying the land back. The same duty, pointed in opposite directions, for the same purpose.
gittin/47.question: If an obligation can be cancelled to discourage selling and then restored to discourage selling, what is it besides pressure?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a mitzva can be deployed as a policy lever, and asks what content the obligation retains once its direction is set by social consequence.

answer.quote: For the betterment of the world, yes, he must bring the first fruits; however, by Torah law, no, he is not required.
answer.explanation: The page does say that this bringing of first fruits is a rabbinic institution rather than a Torah requirement, which bears on the question of what the obligation is, but it never addresses what such a reversible duty amounts to, and Rav Ashi in fact concludes that nothing can be proven from the mishna.

gittin/48.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish argue about a man who buys a field that will revert to its original owner in the Jubilee Year, the fiftieth-year reset of land sales. Yoḥanan says he brings his first fruits to the Temple and recites the verse calling it the land God gave him; Reish Lakish says he brings the fruits and says nothing. Rav Yosef presses the cost of the strict view: only an only child of an only child, back to Joshua son of Nun, could ever recite.
gittin/48.question: Does buying fifty years of harvests make a field yours enough to stand there and call it the land God gave you?
gate: gloss "first fruits" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether owning the yield of a thing is owning the thing — the identity of produce-rights with title, and what ownership must be to let a person say 'the land You gave me.'

answer.quote: the acquisition of an item for its produce is considered to be like the acquisition of the item itself. Consequently, the one bringing the fruits can truthfully recite
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan's stated reason answers the question in the affirmative, but the page leaves it contested, since Reish Lakish holds the opposite and Rava brings a verse and a baraita supporting him.

gittin/49.summary: A man whose ox ate someone's field pays from his best land, a creditor collects from middling land, and a woman's marriage contract is paid out of the worst. Rabbi Shimon supplies motives: a robber should fear losing his finest field, and if lenders could reach only poor land, no one would lend at all. For the marriage contract the reasoning shifts from economics to desire, since a woman is said to want marriage more.
gittin/49.question: If a creditor gets middling land so that lending stays possible, what is kept possible by paying a woman's marriage contract from the worst land?

judge.reachNote: The graded land rules are read as incentive design — each grade protects some transaction from drying up — and the question asks what the ketubah rule is protecting.

answer.quote: It is because more than a man wants to marry a woman, a woman wants to become married to a man.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Shimon gives a reason for collecting the marriage contract from inferior land — the asymmetry of desire means women will marry anyway — but he does not name an interest that this grade of land protects, as the "locking the door" answer does for loans, so the note's question remains honestly askable.

gittin/50.summary: By Torah law, Ulla says, a creditor collects only from a debtor's worst land, since the pledge handed out the door is the least valuable vessel; the Sages upgraded that to middling land so lenders would not stop lending. When a debtor dies and his children inherit, the Sages leave the Torah's rule standing, and the creditor takes the worst land. Rava presses back: if the promissory note itself stipulated superior land, why should orphans escape that?
gittin/50.question: Does someone lending money really never consider that the borrower might die first, as the argument for leaving orphans with the harsher rule assumes?

judge.reachNote: The question probes whether a rule can rest on an assumption about what lenders actually have in mind — legal fiction versus real commercial calculation.

answer.quote: it does not enter the mind of the creditor that he should not lend money as perhaps the borrower will die and his property will fall to the orphans
answer.explanation: The page states this assumption as one side of Rav Aḥadevoi's dilemma, and the concluding halakha on 50b (orphans means adults and all the more so minors) effectively adopts it, but the page never defends the assumption's realism against the challenge the question raises.

gittin/51.summary: A man says the finder picked up two of his money pouches tied together; the finder admits to one. Because pouches do not come untied on their own, Rabbi Yitzḥak has him swear, while two oxen, which do wander apart, bring no oath. Behind the oath sits Rabba's claim that nobody is brazen enough to deny a debt to a creditor's face, which the Rabbis say fails once the creditor is dead and his son is asking.
gittin/51.question: If shame is what stops a debtor from denying the whole loan, why would the same man look the creditor's son in the eye and deny it all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the partial-admission oath rests on shame before someone who knows you are lying, not on shame as such.

answer.quote: There is a presumption that a person would not be so brazen as to stand before his creditor and deny his debt when his creditor knows that he is lying.
answer.explanation: Rabba's presumption hinges on the creditor's own knowledge of the truth, and the page elsewhere notes the son "does not know with certainty how much money the borrower repaid," which bears on the question without spelling out the Rabbis' reasoning for brazenness toward the son.

gittin/52.summary: A steward may sell orphans' cattle, houses and vineyards to feed them today, but not to put the proceeds aside for later. He buys them a lulav, a shofar, a Torah scroll, anything with a fixed cost, but may not give charity or redeem captives with their money. Then Shmuel's rule that orphans' property is acquired only when money changes hands is tested against prices that rise and fall, and each time the students apply it, Rav Sheisha shows it would leave the orphans poorer.
gittin/52.question: If the rule that orphans' sales close only when money changes hands is dropped every time it would cost them, is it a rule about acquisition or just a thumb on the scale?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether "orphans' property is like consecrated property" states how ownership transfers or is merely a one-way protective device applied only when it profits the orphans.

answer.quote: This would be bad for the orphans were they treated in this manner, as they might at times need produce and nobody will give it to them
answer.explanation: Rav Sheisha's repeated objection, together with the maxim that "the power of orphans should not be less than that of other people," shows the rule is bounded by the orphans' welfare, but the page never says outright whether it is therefore a rule of acquisition or only a protective policy, so the question survives.

gittin/53.summary: Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan argue over damage nobody can see: food made ritually impure, wine poured before an idol, teruma (produce reserved for priests) mixed into someone's ordinary grain. Ḥizkiyya holds such loss is real damage under Torah law, and says the Sages excused the accidental offender only so he would come forward and warn the owner. Rav Pappa refutes him with a robber who hands back a coin the government has since voided and owes nothing further.
gittin/53.question: Why should the man who ruined your food on purpose be counted on to tell you, while the one who did it by accident needs an exemption to make him talk?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a penalty is set where silence is likely, and malice itself guarantees disclosure — but the page states this answer outright.

answer.quote: Now, since it was his intention to cause him damage, will he not inform him? If he does not tell him, the other person will never know that he suffered damage.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact question — why not exempt the intentional offender too so he will inform — and answers that a malicious damager will certainly tell his victim, since otherwise the victim never learns he was harmed.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 53a: "Now, since it was his intention to cause him damage, will he not inform him? If he does not tell him, the other person will never know that he suffered damage.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is asked and answered verbatim on the page: the Gemara proposes exempting the intentional offender too, and replies that one who meant to harm will certainly boast of it. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, why Ḥizkiyya's Torah-law liability survives at all once the Sages have rearranged exemption and liability purely for disclosure, or what it means that Rabbi Yoḥanan builds the mirror-image rule from the opposite premise. Keep the summary; it is faithful.

gittin/54.summary: A scribe comes to Rabbi Ami and says that in the Torah scroll he wrote for a customer he did not write the mentions of God's name with the required intention. Rabbi Ami believes him enough to cost him his wage, the entire wage, but not enough to invalidate the scroll, which is now in the buyer's hands; inking over every divine name would leave the parchment speckled. A second scribe tells Rabbi Abbahu the same kind of thing about the parchment, and is believed for both.
gittin/54.question: If a man's word against himself is good enough to cost him his whole fee, why is it not good enough to say what the scroll actually is?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a self-incriminating admission binds the speaker's own claim but may not determine the status of a thing now belonging to someone else.

answer.quote: This Torah scroll is currently in whose possession? The scribe said to him: It is now in the buyer's possession.
answer.explanation: The page flags that the scroll has passed to the buyer, which bears on why the scribe's admission cannot reach it, but it never states the reason for splitting credibility, and Rabbi Abbahu rules the opposite way from the same premise.

gittin/55.summary: A beam stolen and built into a building is repaid in money rather than pried out, so a robber who wants to repent need not demolish the house. The same testimony holds that a stolen animal brought as a sin-offering still atones for the robber, provided nobody knows it was stolen. Ulla says the rule spares the priests, who eat that meat, from distress; Rav Yehuda says it keeps people from saying the altar consumes stolen goods.
gittin/55.question: If the atonement holds only while the theft stays secret, is the robber actually forgiven, or is everyone else simply being spared the sight of it?
gate: gloss "sin-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether the rabbinic atonement is genuine expiation or a social fiction protecting priests and the altar's reputation — exactly the axis Ulla and Rav Yehuda argue.

answer.quote: It is so that the priests not be distraught about having sacrificed an animal unfit for the altar.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself asks why a secretly stolen sin-offering atones and gives Ulla's answer that by Torah law it does not atone at all and the rule exists only to spare the priests, while Rav Yehuda's counter-answer is that despair does transfer ownership so atonement is real and only publicity blocks it for the altar's honor.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 55a: "It is so that the priests not be distraught about having sacrificed an animal unfit for the altar.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very question Ulla and Rav Yehuda answer on this page: Ulla says there is no real atonement and the rule exists only so priests not be distraught, while Rav Yehuda says despair transfers ownership so the atonement is genuine. Since the summary already reports both reasons, the question must push past them. Try asking something that remains hard after the dispute, for example why Rava concludes the Sages gave the thief the animal only from the moment of consecration, or why a rule about the priests' feelings is stated in the mishna as being 'for the benefit of the altar.'

gittin/56.summary: A man named bar Kamtza, humiliated and thrown out of a feast while the Sages sat by in silence, tells the emperor the Jews have rebelled, then nicks the lip of the calf the emperor sends as a test offering. Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas blocks both available fixes, sacrificing the blemished animal and silencing the informer, and Rabbi Yoḥanan blames his scruples for the destruction. The same charge of excessive caution later lands twice on Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, who asks Vespasian only for Yavne.
gittin/56.question: If Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai asked small because he calculated that a larger request would be refused outright, on what grounds does the page still call him a wise man turned backward?

judge.reachNote: Whether a reasoned, realistic estimate of what can be won still counts as a failure of wisdom when more might have been asked.

answer.quote: as he should have said to him to leave the Jews alone this time
answer.explanation: The page states the grounds of the rebuke — that he should have asked Vespasian to spare the Jews entirely — while immediately afterward offering his prudential calculation as the reason he did not, leaving the tension the question raises unresolved.

gittin/57.summary: Roman soldiers seize the rooster and hen carried before a bride and groom in the King's Mountain, the townspeople beat them, and a war follows. Later Nebuzaradan finds the blood of the prophet Zechariah, murdered generations earlier, still bubbling up from the Temple floor, and kills judges, young men, and schoolchildren beside it, trying to make it stop. It settles only when he asks whether destroying everyone would please Zechariah, and that is when he begins thinking about repentance.
gittin/57.question: Why does Zechariah's blood finally go quiet at the offer to kill them all, and why is that the moment Nebuzaradan turns toward repentance?

judge.reachNote: What the unsettled blood is demanding — appeasement by more killing versus the moment the killer sees himself as accountable.

answer.quote: At that moment Nebuzaradan contemplated the idea of repentance and said to himself: If, for the death of one soul, that of Zechariah, God punishes
answer.explanation: The page states Nebuzaradan's own reasoning for turning to repentance (an a fortiori fear of punishment for the countless souls he killed), but it never explains why the blood settles precisely at the offer to destroy everyone.

gittin/58.summary: Rabbi Yannai counts three large baskets of phylactery boxes taken from the heads of the dead at Beitar, and the atrocities keep coming, including a captive brother and sister sold to different masters who decide to breed them for beautiful children. The argument then turns dry, to fields seized by a Sicarius, an armed extortionist, and later bought a second time from the original owner. Rav says a bill of sale settles it; Shmuel wants a written guarantee against repossession.
gittin/58.question: If a man signs over his field only because a Sicarius already took it from him, what does a written guarantee prove that a bill of sale does not?

judge.reachNote: What counts as evidence that a coerced seller's transfer was genuinely willing — a document of sale, or an undertaking that costs him something.

answer.quote: unless the woman writes him a guarantee. This supports Shmuel’s opinion that only when the prior owner writes the buyer a guarantee is it assumed that he sold him the field wholeheartedly.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the guarantee shows the seller sold wholeheartedly (and on 58a, "as by writing this guarantee he demonstrates that this is a true sale"), which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 58b: "unless the woman writes him a guarantee. This supports Shmuel’s opinion that only when the prior owner writes the buyer a guarantee is it assumed that he sold him the field wholeheartedly.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and answered on the page: Shmuel's guarantee is said to show the seller "sold him the field wholeheartedly" / that "this is a true sale." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer, for instance pressing on Rav's reply that the baraita's "guarantee" is itself just a bill of sale, or on why a guarantee against a creditor's repossession should tell us anything about willingness. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

gittin/59.summary: A deaf-mute can buy and sell by gestures, and a child of six or seven can make a binding purchase, the reason given being that he may have no other way to eat. The mishna then lists rules made for the ways of peace: a priest reads from the Torah first, the pit nearest the irrigation channel is filled first. Abaye objects that all of Torah is peace, and lands on a narrower point: in the synagogue a priest may not yield his turn.
gittin/59.question: If the rule forbids yielding because congregants quarrel over who is greatest, how can it be set aside for Rav Huna on the grounds that nobody disputed he was greatest?
gate: the question brings in "Huna", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: A blanket rule made to forestall disputes over rank is suspended by a judgment about rank—when does a preventive enactment yield to the facts it was meant to ignore?

answer.quote: Rav Huna is different, as even Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, the most important priests in Eretz Yisrael, were subject to his jurisdiction.
answer.explanation: The Gemara does explain the exception—no quarrel was possible because Rav Huna's supremacy was universally accepted—but it does not address the note's sharper point, that the rule exists precisely because rank in the synagogue is contestable.

gittin/60.summary: Rav and Shmuel disagree about who irrigates first when farmers dam a river into channels: Rav says the owners of the lowest fields, Shmuel says the highest. Since neither view was accepted as law, Rav Huna bar Tahalifa concludes that whoever is stronger prevails. Rav Shimi bar Ashi, angling for study time with Abaye, quoted Rav to the upper farmers and Shmuel to the lower ones, dammed the river while they argued, and Abaye then refused that year's produce.
gittin/60.question: If the court has already stepped back and let the stronger party win the water, what exactly made Rav Shimi's win unlawful enough that Abaye would not eat the crop?

judge.reachNote: Whether a court's refusal to decide ('whoever is stronger prevails') licenses any means of prevailing, or only actual strength and not manipulation of the undecided law.

answer.quote: You have acted for me in accordance with two opposing opinions. And Abaye would not even taste the produce of that year
answer.explanation: The page gives Abaye's own stated grievance — that Rav Shimi won by invoking two mutually contradictory rulings — but it does not explain why that deceit is unlawful once the court has already abandoned the case to whoever is stronger.

gittin/61.summary: Rav Kahana gathered dates that a man had knocked off a palm tree with sticks and ate them, then heard the man claim they were already his. The mishna permits lending a winnow, sieve, mill or oven to a neighbor suspected of eating Sabbatical-Year produce past its permitted time, but not sorting or grinding alongside her. The wife of a ḥaver, meticulous about purity, may grind with the wife of an am ha'aretz, who is not, until water touches the flour.
gittin/61.question: If shame explains why a mother-in-law swaps her son-in-law's food and resentment explains the innkeeper, what keeps everyone else from being suspected of the same swap?

judge.reachNote: Suspicion of wrongdoing attaches only where a specific motive exists; absent motive, people are presumed honest.

answer.quote: There, the innkeeper rules for herself that it is permitted for her to do this and says: Why should this student of Torah eat hot food while I will eat cold food?
answer.explanation: The page explains each suspect case by a particular motive (shame, self-justification), implying ordinary people lack such motive, but it never states a general rule of trust and immediately presses the challenge again with the baraita about the ḥaver's wife grinding, which is left unresolved at the daf's end.

gittin/62.summary: A woman tells a messenger to bring her bill of divorce to her, and he reports to her husband that she said to receive it on her behalf. The mishna holds that a husband can cancel a delivery agent until the document reaches his wife's hand, while an agent she appointed to receive it ends the marriage the instant he takes it. Rav says the misquote ruins it: even when the document reaches her, she is not divorced.
gittin/62.question: If the document ends up in her hand exactly as she asked for, why should a messenger's wrong wording leave her married?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that agency is defined by the terms under which the document was handed over, not by where the document ultimately lands — but the page states that reasoning outright.

answer.quote: the husband relies on the agent’s statement as to what his status is, and hands him the bill of divorce as an agent for receipt
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains directly why the misreport voids the divorce: the husband gave the document in reliance on the agent's claim to be an agent of receipt, a status neither the wife conferred nor the husband may confer, so no agency exists.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 62b: "the husband relies on the agent’s statement as to what his status is, and hands him the bill of divorce as an agent for receipt". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara answers two lines later: the husband relied on the agent's words, making him an agent of receipt he had no power to appoint, so no agency existed and her later possession is irrelevant. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard — for instance, why the husband's reliance on a false report should defeat the wife's own valid appointment for delivery, or why Rav Ashi immediately objects that the cases cannot be compared. Keep the summary; it is accurate.

gittin/63.summary: Much of the argument turns on which word a husband used when handing over a bill of divorce: deliver, acquire, or here you are, and whether that makes the carrier his courier or already the wife's agent for receipt. Then a courier finds a woman kneading; she says her hands are covered with dough and tells him to hold the document. Rav Naḥman and Rava send the case up, and Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba answers that it is equally uncertain to him.
gittin/63.question: If her hands really were only full of dough, should an offhand remark count as appointing an agent and cancelling her husband's?

judge.reachNote: Whether words said for practical convenience carry the legal force of appointing an agent, and whether a new agency can displace one still in progress.

answer.quote: By designating him as her agent before he completed the agency on behalf of the husband, the wife nullified the agency of the husband.
answer.explanation: Rava treats her dough-handed remark as a genuine appointment that nullified the husband's agency, and Rabbi Ami agrees the divorce does not take effect, yet Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba leaves the matter uncertain and the page rules stringently out of doubt, so the question can still honestly be pressed.

gittin/64.summary: A husband hands a bill of divorce to a middleman and later says it was given only for safekeeping, while the middleman says it was given to divorce her. Rav Huna believes the husband, since he could have handed the document straight to his wife; Rav Ḥisda believes the middleman, since the husband trusted him with it. The Gemara then narrows the middleman's standing: he is believed only while the document is still in his hands.
gittin/64.question: Why does the wife's claim that she was divorced become weaker, not stronger, once her husband and the middleman both agree a bill of divorce was sent?

judge.reachNote: Corroboration can undercut rather than strengthen a claim, because the presumption of credibility rests on the boldness required to lie without support.

gittin/65.summary: A woman tells her agent to receive her bill of divorce for her in a named place, and he takes it from the husband somewhere else instead. One tanna voids the divorce; Rabbi Elazar upholds it, because a husband divorcing of his own will insists on his terms, while a wife, divorced even against her will, is only naming a place. The same problem of the deviating agent returns with an eiruv, food set aside to extend Shabbat travel: dates ordered, dried figs used.
gittin/65.question: If a wife's named place counts as a mere suggestion because she can be divorced against her will, what is she actually doing when she appoints an agent?

judge.reachNote: Whether a party who cannot withhold consent can nonetheless attach binding terms to the agency she creates — the gap between appointing an agent and instructing one.

answer.quote: Since the divorce takes effect when the husband hands the bill of divorce to the agent, the concern is that the agent encountered the husband nearby.
answer.explanation: The page shows that her appointment of an agent for receipt does have real legal force — the divorce takes effect at the handover to him — even though her named place is treated as mere indication, so the question is addressed in part but not squarely answered.

gittin/66.summary: A man thrown into a pit calls out that whoever hears him should write a bill of divorce for his wife, and he supplies his name, hers, and the details; the mishna says the listeners write it and deliver it, though they never see him. The Gemara then worries the voice belongs to a demon, and tests for human form, then a shadow, then the shadow of a shadow. The worry that it is a jealous rival wife faking the voice gets no test at all.
gittin/66.question: Why does the possibility of a demon get a three-step verification while the far more likely fraud, a rival wife imitating a husband's voice, is answered only by saying the situation is dangerous?

judge.reachNote: Why some doubts must be tested empirically while others are simply waived by the exigency of the moment — a question about when halakha stops investigating.

answer.quote: one writes and gives the bill of divorce, as there is no possibility of properly clarifying the issue
answer.explanation: The Gemara does supply a reason for waiving the rival-wife concern — the danger situation admits no clarification — but it never explains why that reasoning does not equally excuse the demon inquiry, so the asymmetry the note asks about remains live.

gittin/67.summary: A man tells ten people to write a bill of divorce for his wife, and one writes while two sign. But if he says "all of you write," every one of them must take part, so Rav Yehuda composed a long formula covering both options. Rava objects that the formula is itself a trap, since a husband may truncate it, say "all of you," and leave the document void.
gittin/67.question: If a safeguard can be undone by a husband who trails off halfway through the sentence, is the woman's divorce resting on the law or on his phrasing?

judge.reachNote: Whether a woman's marital status rests on substantive law or on the precise words her husband happens to utter.

answer.quote: Rather, Rava said that he must say: Each of you may write it, every two of you may sign it, each one of you may deliver it.
answer.explanation: Rava supplies a revised formula that removes the truncation trap, which bears on the note's worry but does not address whether the woman's status ultimately hangs on the husband's exact wording.

gittin/68.summary: Solomon needs the shamir, a creature that splits stone without iron, so that the Temple can be built without hammer or axe. Benayahu captures Ashmedai, king of the demons, by draining his pit and refilling it with wine, and Ashmedai points to a hoopoe entrusted with the shamir by oath. Solomon's servant startles the bird off it, takes the shamir, and the bird kills itself over an oath it was tricked out of keeping.
gittin/68.question: The bird dies for a broken oath while the man who engineered the breaking walks off with the shamir and builds the Temple with it, so who does the story consider the oath-breaker?

judge.reachNote: Who bears the guilt of a broken oath when another party's trickery made keeping it impossible.

answer.quote: the wild rooster went and strangled itself over the fact that it had not kept its oath, by not returning the shamir
answer.explanation: The page assigns the failed oath to the bird itself and gives the bird's own fatal verdict, but never weighs the culpability of Solomon's servant who engineered the loss, so the question still stands.

gittin/69.summary: A remedy for eye disease calls for a seven-colored scorpion, dried in the shade and ground with a black eye powder called stibium. Most cures here run in chains, each step followed by "and if he is not able to do this": white dog feces, a louse, the hand of someone who died on Shabbat. The only real argument comes when Rav Ami presses Rav Ashi on why blood traced to the liver is hopeless while lung blood is treatable.
gittin/69.question: If nearly every cure on the page comes with another fallback for the person who cannot manage it, why does blood that fails to stick to the straw of wheat get none?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the boundary between illness that medicine can chain after and a condition declared beyond remedy.

answer.quote: Since the blood comes out from this person's mouth, one must say that the liver has dissolved and he will not survive.
answer.explanation: The page explains that liver-sourced mouth blood means the liver has already dissolved and the patient is doomed, which is why no remedy or fallback is offered.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 69a: "Since the blood comes out from this person's mouth, one must say that the liver has dissolved and he will not survive.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered where Rav Ashi says the liver has dissolved and the patient will not survive, so there is nothing left to ask about the missing fallback. Rewrite the question to start from that answer, for instance asking what makes a sage willing to declare a case hopeless when every other ailment on the page gets step after step of substitute cures, or why the objection needed a mishna about tereifa animals to settle a human prognosis. Also drop the unsupported gloss that stibium is a black powder, since the page only names it.

gittin/70.summary: A man who swallowed a hornet is given sharp vinegar to drink, not to save him but to buy time to instruct his household before he dies. The same holds for a man whose throat has been slit: Shmuel says he is alive enough to order a bill of divorce for his wife, and dead enough for witnesses to report his death. And the one who cut him, by accident, is not exiled.
gittin/70.question: If the man with the slit throat is alive enough to divorce his wife and dead enough to be testified about, who is it that killed him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of divided causation and the legal status of a man who is both alive and already counted dead — but the page names that idea itself.

gittin/71.summary: Rav Kahana rules that a man who can neither hear nor speak may have a court write a bill of divorce for his wife based on what he writes down. The page first sorts the terms: someone who talks but cannot hear is deaf, someone who hears but cannot talk is mute, and both are treated as competent. Then writing hits a wall at testimony, which the verse ties to the witnesses' mouths and not their hands.
gittin/71.question: If a man's wordless gestures were enough to make the marriage, why should the same gestures not be enough to end it?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is symmetry: the mode of expression that suffices to create a bond should suffice to dissolve it — but the page already resolves it by distinguishing rabbinic from Torah-level bonds.

answer.quote: If the baraita is referring to his wife, indeed this would be the case and he could divorce her through intimations
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's question — "just as he marries her with intimation… so too, he divorces her with intimation" — and answers that for his own wife this is indeed so, the restriction applying only to a yevama whose levirate bond is by Torah law.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 71a: "If the baraita is referring to his wife, indeed this would be the case and he could divorce her through intimations". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is asked and answered in so many words on 71a, where the Gemara replies that for his own wife intimation does suffice, since that marriage is only rabbinic, and the restriction concerns a yevama bound by Torah law. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance about why a rabbinically instituted marriage is dissolvable by gestures while a Torah-level bond is not, or about the confusion-based decree the Gemara proposes and then rejects on 71b. The summary is faithful and can largely stand, but it should touch the part of the page the new question grows from.

gittin/72.summary: A man tells his wife, this is your bill of divorce if I die, and the mishna treats the words as empty, since the document cannot take effect after his death. Add two words, from today, and it works backward from the moment he spoke. Rav Huna links such a divorce to a deathbed gift: if the man recovers, both collapse, which forces the Gemara to read "he arose and walked in the market" as a man leaning on a staff.
gittin/72.question: Can "he arose and walked in the market" honestly mean a man shuffling along with a staff, or is the phrase being bent to protect the rule that recovery cancels what a dying man handed over?

judge.reachNote: Whether a plain phrase in the mishna may be narrowed to save a principle (recovery voids a deathbed act), i.e., how far reading serves doctrine.

answer.quote: This means that he walked with his staff for support, meaning that he was not fully recovered from his illness
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very objection the note raises and supplies the staff reading, but it only asserts the reinterpretation rather than defending it against the charge of being forced, so the note's challenge can still be pressed.

gittin/73.summary: A man sold land and accepted responsibility for any unavoidable accident; then the government dug a canal through it. Ravina told him to pay, Rava said a diverted river is too uncommon to fall under such a condition, and when Ravina cited a conflicting teaching about a divorce condition and a snakebite, Rava dismissed the teaching as self-contradictory and never really taught. When two sages pressed sailors to hire donkeys after the Malka River was dammed, Rava called them white geese who strip men of their cloaks.
gittin/73.question: If a source can be set aside as corrupted because its two halves point opposite ways, what protects any inconvenient teaching from the same treatment?

judge.reachNote: When a received text argues against itself, does authority pass from the text to reasoning, and who decides?

answer.quote: Since there is a difficulty presented by the contradiction between the first clause of the baraita and the latter clause, this baraita was never stated in the study hall
answer.explanation: Ravina states the condition for discarding a source — its own two clauses yield opposite inferences, so neither can prove anything and one must follow reason — but the page never sets a limit protecting other teachings, and Rav Aḥa of Difti's protest that a contradiction should not silence an objection is simply overruled.

gittin/74.summary: A man hands his wife a bill of divorce on the condition that she give him two hundred dinars, and the argument is over when the divorce takes effect: the moment the document reaches her hand, or only when she pays. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel recalls a case in Tzaidan where the condition was a coat the wife then lost, and the Rabbis accepted its cash value instead. Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that if the husband waives the payment outright, she stays married.
gittin/74.question: If the two hundred dinars were only ever a way to vex her, why does paying them free her while the husband's waiving them leaves her bound?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a condition's fulfillment is measured by the stipulator's underlying purpose — vexation versus profit — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: There, in the case of a bill of divorce, he intends to vex her, and until she pays him he did not vex her.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains that the payment itself is the vexation the husband intended, so handing over the money fulfills his purpose while waiving it leaves that purpose unfulfilled and the divorce inoperative.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 74b: "There, in the case of a bill of divorce, he intends to vex her, and until she pays him he did not vex her.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim on 74b, where the Gemara says the husband intends to vex her and until she pays he has not vexed her, so waiving leaves his intent unfulfilled. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance why the sharecropper who was spared the fourth watering still collects a third, if intent-not-fulfilled governs the divorce case, or why the same 'vex' logic lets the Rabbis accept the coat's value but not a waiver. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

gittin/75.summary: Shmuel fixed the wording for a bill of divorce written by a man on his deathbed: if I do not die, it is not valid; if I die, it is. The Gemara asks why the gloomy clause comes first, and answers that a man does not want to name his own death at the head of the sentence. Rava objects that every condition copies Moses's deal with Gad and Reuben, and builds a three-clause formula that satisfies both pressures.
gittin/75.question: If the shape of every condition is fixed by Moses's words to the children of Gad and Reuben, what makes a dying man's reluctance to say "if I die" strong enough to bend that order?

judge.reachNote: Why a human sensibility (not naming one's own death) is given weight against a formal structure derived from Scripture.

answer.quote: The husband first says: If I do not die this will not be a bill of divorce, because a person does not hasten a calamity upon himself.
answer.explanation: The page shows the reluctance is accommodated by a prefatory clause rather than by overriding the Gad-and-Reuben order, but it never explains why that psychological concern has legal standing in the first place.

gittin/76.summary: A man leaving Judea for the Galilee tells his wife that her bill of divorce takes effect if he does not return within thirty days. He reaches Antipatris and turns back, so nothing happens, though a baraita puts Antipatris in Judea, not the Galilee; Abaye reads the husband as having stated two conditions at once. Later the document's validity hangs on the wife's word that he was never secluded with her, and only because he said in advance that he believes her.
gittin/76.question: If her word is what settles whether the two of them were ever secluded, why does it count only because the husband declared in advance that he trusts her?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a fact only she can know is established not by her reliability but by the other party's prior waiver of suspicion.

answer.quote: Since the husband states explicitly that he believes her about this, if she said that he was not secluded with her then the bill of divorce remains valid.
answer.explanation: The page states that the wife's word works because of the husband's explicit declaration of trust, and elsewhere notes that where he died there is no such concern, but it never explains why her word alone would be insufficient.

gittin/77.summary: A man throws a bill of divorce to his wife while she stands in her own courtyard, and the mishna counts that as if he had placed it in her hand. The trouble is that whatever a married woman acquires belongs to her husband, so the courtyard is his. Rava's answer is that the document and the courtyard reach her in the same instant, since the divorce itself ends the husband's claim on her property.
gittin/77.question: If the courtyard only becomes hers at the very instant the divorce document lands in it, what is it in the instant before?

judge.reachNote: Whether an act can create the very legal conditions that make it valid, i.e. whether simultaneity is a real moment or a legal fiction.

answer.quote: her bill of divorce and her courtyard enter her possession simultaneously, as her husband's rights to her property are terminated at the time of divorce
answer.explanation: The page asserts the simultaneity and implies the courtyard is under the husband's rights until the divorce takes effect, but it never addresses what the courtyard's status is in the instant before, so the question can still be asked honestly.

gittin/78.summary: A husband throws a bill of divorce to his wife standing in the public domain, and the page argues over how close it has to land. Rav measures four cubits; Rabbi Yoḥanan asks instead who could guard the document if a dog ran off with it. Shmuel then warns Rav Yehuda not to let her remarry until it actually reaches her hand, and one woman whose lost bill was closer to her still needed ḥalitza, the release from marrying her late husband's brother.
gittin/78.question: If a bill of divorce landing nearer the wife already divorces her, why did the court treat that woman as still bound to her husband's brother?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether a divorce takes effect at the legal moment of proximity or only upon actual physical receipt — but the page answers it in the very line the note paraphrases.

answer.quote: They did not rely on the bill of divorce that was given to the woman, since it never actually reached her hand.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the court disregarded the proximate bill because it never physically reached her hand, which is exactly what the question asks.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Yoḥanan asks instead who could guard the document if a dog ran off with it.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Eliezer says: With regard to any bill of divorce that is closer to her than it is to him, and a dog came and took it

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 78b: "They did not rely on the bill of divorce that was given to the woman, since it never actually reached her hand.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rabbi Yoḥanan asks instead who could guard the document if a dog ran off with it.", but the page says "Rabbi Eliezer says: With regard to any bill of divorce that is closer to her than it is to him, and a dog came and took it". Say what the page says. The question is answered in the same passage the summary retells: the court required ḥalitza because the bill never reached her hand, and Shmuel had already warned not to permit remarriage before that. Rewrite the question to probe what remains hard after that answer — for instance, why the mishna's proximity rule settles divorce and debt in theory yet practice demands the document in hand. Also keep the dog case with Rabbi Eliezer's baraita rather than attributing it to Rabbi Yoḥanan's guarding criterion.

gittin/79.summary: A husband standing below throws a bill of divorce to his wife on a roof, and the mishna rules she is divorced the moment it enters the roof's airspace, even if the writing is erased or the document burns before landing. The Gemara asks how open air can hold anything, and answers with security: a parapet, or lower walls that jut out past the upper ones. Rav Nahman then splits the arc: erased on the descent, divorced; erased on the ascent, not.
gittin/79.question: If the erasure happens while the document is still rising, nothing about where it will land has changed, so why does the top of the arc turn it into hers?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of when a thing in motion counts as already delivered — destiny of landing versus present position — but the page answers it in the next line.

answer.quote: Because initially, before it began its descent, the bill of divorce is not destined to land in her domain, since it could be blown elsewhere.
answer.explanation: The Gemara states the reason for Rav Naḥman's distinction outright: on the ascent the document is not yet destined to land in her domain, so it cannot be treated as resting there.

summaryProblems.claim: In the case where the husband is below and the wife is on the roof, she is divorced once it enters the airspace even if the writing is erased or the document burns before landing.
summaryProblems.pageSays: If he was above on the roof and she was below, and he threw it to her, once it leaves the area of the roof

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Gittin 79a: "Because initially, before it began its descent, the bill of divorce is not destined to land in her domain, since it could be blown elsewhere.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "In the case where the husband is below and the wife is on the roof, she is divorced once it enters the airspace even if the writing is erased or the document burns before landing.", but the page says "If he was above on the roof and she was below, and he threw it to her, once it leaves the area of the roof". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few lines later: the Gemara says that on the ascent the bill is "not destined to land in her domain, since it could be blown elsewhere." Rewrite so the question starts from that reason and presses on what is still hard — for instance why a document that is secured within the partitions on the way down counts as hers while the same partitions do not secure it on the way up. Also fix the summary: the erased/burned clause belongs to the mishna's second case, where he is on the roof and she is below.

gittin/80.summary: A bill of divorce dated by the wrong kingdom is invalid, and the mishna rules that a woman who remarried on the strength of it must leave both husbands. Ulla says the dating rule exists only to keep peaceful relations with the ruling government, which provokes the obvious objection: for a courtesy like that, the child of the second marriage is called a mamzer, barred from marrying most Jews? The answer given is yes, following Rabbi Meir.
gittin/80.question: If the date is there only so the local ruler stays content, why should a scribe in Babylonia writing Rome's years, on a document no Roman will ever read, cost a woman both husbands?
gate: the question brings in "Babylonia", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Rome's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
