judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 47a: "the matter is embarrassing for her, preventing her from claiming the final dinar from him, since he has given her almost the entire sum". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: the Sages say that ninety-nine dinars given embarrasses her "since he has given her almost the entire sum," while one dinar given does not. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, why the law should let a woman's reluctance to press a claim decide whether the man has fulfilled his stated terms, or how that squares with Rabbi Elazar's ruling that a single dinar already betroths. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

kiddushin/48.summary: A woman hands a goldsmith gold and tells him to make her bracelets, earrings and rings, and says she will be betrothed to him as his wage. The trouble is that a wage owed is a debt, and a debt already owed cannot buy a betrothal. One way out: the wage comes into being only when he hands back the finished work. Another: he quietly adds a nofekh, a jewel of his own, to the pile.
kiddushin/48.question: When a man offers a debt she already owes plus one peruta, the smallest copper coin, whose mind decides which of the two the betrothal rests on?

judge.reachNote: Whose intent constitutes the act of acquisition — the giver's designation or the receiver's understanding of what she is accepting.

answer.quote: Rabbi Meir, holds that if a man betroths a woman with a loan and one peruta, his mind is focused on the peruta. And one Sage, i.e., the Rabbis, holds that his mind is focused on the loan
answer.explanation: The page states the dispute in terms of the man's mind, yet immediately reframes the same case as "whether her intention is to become betrothed with the payment for the work... or with the jewel," so whose mind governs is touched on but never settled.

kiddushin/49.summary: A man betroths a woman on condition that he is literate in Torah, and reading three verses in the synagogue settles it, though calling himself a reader raises the bar to Prophets and Writings. The page keeps deflating boasts: strong means people fear him, wealthy means his town honors him, a student means he can answer one question. Then it rules that a wicked man who claims to be righteous has betrothed her, since he may have thought of repenting.
kiddushin/49.question: If a silent thought of repentance is enough to make the betrothal hold, why does the seller's silent plan to move to Eretz Yisrael count for nothing?
gate: the question brings in "Eretz", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yisrael", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When does an unspoken state of mind carry legal weight — the idea that a stated condition can be satisfied by a hidden thought while an unstated intention cannot bind at all.

answer.quote: Since he did not explicitly state that he was selling his property on the condition that he ascend to Eretz Yisrael, that is an unspoken matter that remained in the heart
answer.explanation: The page gives the rule for the seller (nothing was stated aloud) but never sets that beside the righteous-man ruling, where the condition was spoken and only the inner change of heart was silent, so the tension the question names still stands.

kiddushin/50.summary: A man who owes a burnt-offering and refuses to bring it is coerced until he says he wants to. The Gemara asks what a forced "I want" is worth, and answers that unspoken matters in the heart carry no weight, then hunts for a clean proof of that rule. Candidate after candidate is rejected until one holds: an agent sent to fetch an item from a window ledge that turned out to be consecrated property.
kiddushin/50.question: If the court can credit a beaten man with secretly wanting atonement or wanting to obey the Sages, why is the owner of the consecrated item not believed about which shelf he meant?
gate: gloss "burnt-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "consecrated property" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: When does a person's unstated intent override his words — only where we independently know what he really wants.

answer.quote: But perhaps there it is different, since it is clear to us that it is satisfactory for him to achieve atonement
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself explains the asymmetry: in the coercion cases there is an independent presumption about the man's true desire (atonement, or the mitzva of obeying the Sages), while in the consecrated-item case nothing overrides the rule that unspoken matters in the heart are not significant.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 50a: "But perhaps there it is different, since it is clear to us that it is satisfactory for him to achieve atonement". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already states the distinction the question asks about: the coerced man is credited because "it is clear to us that it is satisfactory for him to achieve atonement" and because "it is a mitzva to listen to the statements of the Sages," while the consecrated-item owner has no such presumption. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance, why the Gemara keeps rejecting proofs on the grounds that each case has its own special reason, yet finally accepts the misuse case once the suspicion of self-exemption is cleared. Or press on Rava's two opposite rulings about the man who sold his property to ascend to Eretz Yisrael, where an explicitly stated intention still yields contradictory outcomes.

kiddushin/51.summary: A man separates two-tenths of his grain as tithe instead of one-tenth, and Rabba argues the crop is still properly tithed because half of every single grain can carry tithe status. The page tests that logic against animal tithe, against eighty loaves brought with a thanks-offering, and then against Rava's rule that a betrothal which could never lead to permitted intercourse is no betrothal. Each challenge from a mishna gets rescued the same way: he once knew which sister, and forgot.
kiddushin/51.question: If a man who forgot which sister he betrothed leaves both bound until they receive bills of divorce, while a man who never specified leaves both free, is the difference in the women's situation or only in his memory?

judge.reachNote: Does validity of a betrothal depend on the objective state of the act at the moment it took effect, or only on what the man can now identify?

answer.quote: It is when they were identified and later intermingled. The actual betrothal was given to consummation, so the sisters are betrothed due to the uncertainty.
answer.explanation: The Gemara does say why the forgetful case differs — the betrothal was determinate and consummable when it took effect — but whether that difference is anything more than the man's knowledge (the page even leans on 'he does not know' versus 'it is not known') can still be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Each challenge from a mishna gets rescued the same way: he once knew which sister, and forgot.
summaryProblems.pageSays: With what are we dealing here? It is when there is only one adult daughter and one minor daughter.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Each challenge from a mishna gets rescued the same way: he once knew which sister, and forgot.", but the page says "With what are we dealing here? It is when there is only one adult daughter and one minor daughter.". Say what the page says. Drop the claim that every mishna challenge is answered by "he once knew and forgot" — the daughters-betrothed-without-specification case (64b) is rescued instead by positing one adult and one minor daughter, and then by agency and "a person does not set aside a mitzva that is incumbent upon him." Say that the intermingling answer covers the closing run of challenges, not all of them. The question can stand as it is.

kiddushin/52.summary: A sharecropper took a handful of onions from the field he worked and betrothed a woman with them, and Rava asked who had given him the right to them. A brewer used sediment from someone else's date beer; when the owner found him and said to take the sharper sediment instead, the question was whether that counted as consent. Rava says such a hint works only for teruma, the crop share owners must set aside anyway; otherwise the owner is just too embarrassed to object.
kiddushin/52.question: When an owner finds a man helping himself to his onions or his beer and says take the better one, what tells anybody whether he means it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of how one reads consent from words that may be sarcasm or embarrassed silence, but the page states the test.

kiddushin/53.summary: Rabbi Ya'akov recalls two rulings he heard from Rabbi Yoḥanan about betrothal that fails: one using second tithe, produce that may be eaten only in Jerusalem, and one using property consecrated to the Temple treasury. One fails because the woman does not want such a gift, the other because neither she nor the man wants it, and he cannot remember which case goes with which reason. Rabbi Yirmeya reconstructs the pairing by logic, and Rabbi Ya'akov shows the opposite pairing works just as well.
kiddushin/53.question: If both cases can be explained equally well by opposite reasons, what is left of what Rabbi Ya'akov actually learned?
gate: gloss "the Temple treasury" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What survives of a received tradition when its transmitted reasons are lost and reconstruction by logic cuts both ways.

answer.quote: Therefore, the reasons for Rabbi Yoḥanan's statement cannot be determined by logic alone.
answer.explanation: The page concedes that reasoning cannot settle which reason belongs to which case, which bears on the question but leaves open what force the transmitted teaching still has.

kiddushin/54.summary: A priest betroths a woman with a Temple tunic still fit for service, and Rabbi Meir rules she is not betrothed if he acted unwittingly, since such garments never fully leave sacred status. The reason given is that priests were always meant to benefit from them, because a person cannot wear clothes only at the instant of service. The Gemara then presses the same logic on Jerusalem's walls, built from leftover Temple shekels, whose shade no passerby can avoid.
kiddushin/54.question: If every source that contradicts Rabbi Meir can simply be reassigned to Rabbi Yehuda, what would ever count as evidence against him?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When a school's position can absorb every counter-source by reattribution, what constrains attribution itself and makes the position falsifiable?

answer.quote: If it is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yehuda, is Jerusalem consecrated at all?
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself tests the reassignment-to-Rabbi-Yehuda move and finds it costly, which bears on the question without stating any general criterion for what would refute Rabbi Meir.

kiddushin/55.summary: A stray animal found anywhere within the distance from Jerusalem to Migdal Eder is presumed to have come from the city, where most animals were offerings. Rabbi Oshaya has the finder redeem it by consecrating its value, leaning on Rabbi Meir's view that deliberate misuse strips sanctity; Rabbi Yoḥanan refuses, since that amounts to telling a person to sin and profit. His alternative: wait until the animal develops a blemish, then bring substitute animals with conditions attached.
kiddushin/55.question: If redeeming an unblemished offering outright counts as sinning for gain, what makes it cleaner to sit and wait for the animal to become blemished?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea of engineering a permitted route rather than licensing a transgression, but the page already supplies the distinction it asks for.

answer.quote: waits for it until it develops a blemish. At that point it would no longer have inherent sanctity but merely sanctity that inheres in its value, so the animal may be redeemed
answer.explanation: The page states outright why waiting is licit: once blemished the animal has only value-sanctity, so redeeming it is not misuse at all and no sin is involved.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 55b: "waits for it until it develops a blemish. At that point it would no longer have inherent sanctity but merely sanctity that inheres in its value, so the animal may be redeemed". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the summary paraphrases: waiting for a blemish leaves only value-sanctity, so redemption is lawful and no sin occurs. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance, why the Gemara is content to let common possibilities (thanks-offering, firstborn) be covered by stipulations and extra animals while rare ones (lepers, nazirites, an overage sin-offering) are simply dismissed. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

kiddushin/56.summary: Second-tithe money, set aside from a harvest and meant to be spent on food eaten in Jerusalem, gets used to buy a slave, a field, or a non-kosher animal. The purchase does not strip the money of its holiness, so one party absorbs the loss, and the Gemara puts it on the seller, who is holding the coins. Then it asks what the hole accomplishes without a mouse, and answers that the penalty falls wherever the money sits.
kiddushin/56.question: If buyer and seller both made the forbidden sale happen, why should the penalty follow the money rather than the fault?
gate: gloss "Second-tithe" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether a penalty tracks culpability or mere possession of the forbidden proceeds.

answer.quote: It stands to reason that anywhere that the forbidden item is, i.e., anywhere that the money is, and in this case it is with the seller, there we should penalize.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection ("if not for the mouse, what has the hole done?") and answers that the penalty attaches to wherever the forbidden money is located.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 56b: "It stands to reason that anywhere that the forbidden item is, i.e., anywhere that the money is, and in this case it is with the seller, there we should penalize.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it explicitly — and the summary even reports that answer before the question asks it. Rewrite so the question starts from the page's ruling that the penalty follows the money, and probes what remains hard: e.g. why fleeing with the coins should shift the loss, or why the buyer who initiated the desacralization walks free. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

kiddushin/57.summary: The purification of a leper uses two birds: one is slaughtered, the other set free into an open field. Rabbi Yoḥanan says benefit from them is forbidden only from the slaughter; Reish Lakish says from the moment they are taken, reasoning from the heifer whose neck is broken over an unsolved murder. Then the question flips: why not forbid the freed bird instead? Rava answers that the Torah would not release a forbidden bird into the world.
kiddushin/57.question: Is the released bird permitted because the verse says so, or because a bird loose over a field could never be kept forbidden in practice?

judge.reachNote: Whether a permission rests on a scriptural derivation or on the impossibility of enforcing a prohibition once the animal is loose in the world.

kiddushin/58.summary: An Israelite cannot eat teruma, the portion of produce set aside for priests, yet the mishna says he can betroth a woman with it. Ulla says the only thing such a man holds, the right to choose which priest receives the gift, is worth no money, so he rereads the case as produce inherited from a priestly grandfather. Rav Huna reads the mishna straight, and his reply to Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Avin sounds so much like an insult that the man is embarrassed.
kiddushin/58.question: Is the right to decide who receives something you may never use yourself worth actual money?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether a bare power of allocation over something you may never consume is itself property — but this is the page's own stated question, not one left open by it.

answer.quote: No, everyone agrees that the benefit of discretion does not have monetary value, and here the case is with an Israelite who came into possession of untithed produce
answer.explanation: The page itself poses the note's question — "Does the benefit of discretion have monetary value, or does it not have monetary value?" — and answers it, first with Rav Huna's "This indicates that the benefit of discretion has monetary value" and then repeatedly with the Gemara's settled "everyone agrees that the benefit of discretion does not have monetary value."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 58b: "No, everyone agrees that the benefit of discretion does not have monetary value, and here the case is with an Israelite who came into possession of untithed produce". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates the Gemara's own inquiry, which the page asks in those words and then answers twice over — Rav Huna says the benefit of discretion has monetary value, and the later rounds conclude that everyone agrees it does not. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer: for instance, why three of the four resolutions must reread the case as inherited priestly produce or as a rabbinic penalty rather than simply letting the mishna mean what Rav Huna says it means, or why Abaye's split between filling the vessel and sprinkling rescues the mishna. Keep the summary, which the page supports, but let the question press on what remains unsettled once discretion is said to be worthless.

kiddushin/59.summary: Ravin the Pious was sent to betroth a woman for his son and betrothed her to himself; Rav, handed money to buy land for Rabba bar bar Ḥana, bought the field for himself. The Gemara excuses both, since the woman's family would accept only the father and the violent neighbors respected only Rav, and any delay would lose the deal. Then Rav Giddel loses a plot to Rabbi Abba, who concedes he acted like a man snatching a pauper's loaf.
kiddushin/59.question: If Rabbi Abba agreed that taking the pauper's loaf makes a man wicked, why does the story end with a field that neither he nor Rav Giddel would set foot on?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a claim short of legal title (prior negotiation) can bind a pious person's conscience even when the law lets him keep the land.

answer.quote: Rav Giddel did not descend to claim this plot of land, as it is written: “But he who hates gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27)
answer.explanation: The page states both reasons the field was abandoned — Rav Giddel refused a gift, and Rabbi Abba stayed off because Rav Giddel had been negotiating first — so the question is answered in so many words.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Abba concedes he acted like a man snatching a pauper's loaf.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Abba said to him: I did not know that Rav Giddel was trying to acquire the land.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 59a: "Rav Giddel did not descend to claim this plot of land, as it is written: “But he who hates gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27)". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rabbi Abba concedes he acted like a man snatching a pauper's loaf.", but the page says "Rabbi Abba said to him: I did not know that Rav Giddel was trying to acquire the land.". Say what the page says. The question is plainly answered on the daf: it says Rav Giddel refused it because "he who hates gifts shall live" and Rabbi Abba stayed off because Rav Giddel had negotiated first. Ask instead about something the page leaves open — for example why Ravin and Rav are excused for taking what was entrusted to them while Rabbi Abba, who acted in ignorance, ends up unable to use his land. Also correct the summary: Rabbi Abba answers the pauper hypothetical in the abstract and then pleads that he did not know of Rav Giddel's offer, rather than conceding he acted wickedly.

kiddushin/60.summary: A man betroths a woman with the words "from now and after ten days," and no one can tell whether that sets a condition or takes back what he just said. Rabbi Yoḥanan says a hundred men could betroth her this way, each like a brick in a row leaving a gap for the next. Rav Ḥanina objects that the same phrase in a bill of divorce, the document ending a marriage, would leave part of the bond intact.
kiddushin/60.question: If these words leave a gap wide enough for a hundred other betrothals, why should a bill of divorce written the same way leave no gap at all?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is whether an act of creating a bond can take effect in stages while an act of dissolving one must be total.

answer.quote: It is not because the bill of divorce is in any way valid. Rather, it is a rabbinic decree due to the case
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises Rav Ḥanina's objection and resolves it: according to Rabbi Yoḥanan the get with this phrase really does leave a remnant and is worthless, and the only reason she performs ḥalitza is a rabbinic decree modeled on "from today if I die" (with Rava's earlier answer that death completes the severance also on offer).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 60a: "It is not because the bill of divorce is in any way valid. Rather, it is a rabbinic decree due to the case". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the page's own objection, and the page answers it twice: Rava says death completes whatever the get left over, and Abaye replies that under Rabbi Yoḥanan the get is not valid at all and the ḥalitza is only a rabbinic decree. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating the objection. For instance, ask why the Sages decreed ḥalitza for "from today and after my death" but refused to decree it for "from today if I die," or press on Abaye's own distinction that a get removes her from the yavam while death delivers her to him.

kiddushin/61.summary: Moses told the tribes of Gad and Reuben both halves of a deal, that crossing the Jordan armed would win them Gilead and refusing would leave them a portion in Canaan. Rabbi Meir reads that doubling as the rule for every condition, so one stated only positively counts for nothing. Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel says the verse had its own reason to spell out both sides, and the argument then moves to God's warning to Cain and Abraham's oath to Eliezer.
kiddushin/61.question: Is it convincing to say that Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel's mishna and his parable disagree only because Rabbi Meir spoke in between?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's two apparently clashing statements can be reconciled by dating them to before and after his opponent's objection — i.e. how far a tradition may be read as a record of a developing argument.

answer.quote: This is not difficult, as this case, referring to Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel's ruling in the mishna, was stated before Rabbi Meir said to him
answer.explanation: The Gemara does give exactly the chronological resolution the question names, but it asserts it without defending its plausibility, which is what the question presses on.

kiddushin/62.summary: Rav Asi asks whether a farmer can declare produce still attached to the ground to be teruma, the portion set aside for priests, so that it takes effect once the produce is cut. Rabbi Yoḥanan says yes: whatever a person could do right now does not count as missing. The mishna's list of failed betrothals is then pushed against that rule, since a man could convert, could free his maidservant, could divorce his wife.
kiddushin/62.question: If a freed maidservant is treated as so changed that the earlier words cannot reach her, why is the man who converts treated as the same man who spoke them?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether a change of legal status makes someone a new legal person, and why that test is applied to the maidservant but not to the convert.

answer.quote: There, the Canaanite maidservant initially had the legal status of an animal, i.e., she is not subject to betrothal at all, whereas now she has an independent mind.
answer.explanation: The page explains why the maidservant counts as a changed person, but it rejects the convert case only on the ground that three judges may not be available, never addressing whether the convert is the same man who spoke, so the question survives.

kiddushin/63.summary: A father says he betrothed his minor daughter to someone but cannot remember to whom, and a man steps forward claiming it was him. Rav believes that man only enough to hand her a bill of divorce, since nobody lies for nothing; Rav Asi believes him enough to marry her, since he would not dare lie to the girl's father's face. Then the stakes rise: does the father's word also make her liable to stoning for adultery?
kiddushin/63.question: If a woman's own statement that she is betrothed is strong enough to forbid her to every man alive, why is it too weak to convict her?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — credibility that suffices to create a prohibition need not suffice to impose death — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: as far as punishment is concerned her claim is treated by a court in accordance with the regular rules of evidence
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly resolves Rav Asi's own version of this difficulty: a woman can render herself forbidden, but the Torah granted her no special credibility for capital matters.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 63b: "as far as punishment is concerned her claim is treated by a court in accordance with the regular rules of evidence". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very difficulty Rav Asi calls his "roof breakers," and the Gemara answers it a few lines later by distinguishing a woman's power to forbid herself from credibility for punishment. Write a question that starts after that answer rather than restating it. Good ground: why the father's word is trusted even to kill while Rav limits it to prohibition, or why Rav Ḥisda withholds capital credibility from the father too despite the Torah's grant.

kiddushin/64.summary: A father states that he betrothed his daughter years ago, while she was still a minor, and the court takes his word and bars her from marrying any other man. The Gemara first explains this by saying he could betroth her even now, so he is believed about the past; Rav Ashi objects that he cannot divorce her and cannot force a groom to agree. He grounds the credibility in a verse instead.
kiddushin/64.question: If a father's bare word can shut his daughter out of marriage to every man alive, why does the same word count for nothing when he says she was taken captive?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that credibility tracks the scope of a father's lawful power over his daughter — but the page names that idea and then replaces it with scriptural grant.

answer.quote: The Merciful One deems the father credible with regard to marriage, whereas He does not deem him credible with regard to a captive.
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi states outright that the Torah's grant of credibility covers the father's claim of betrothal but not his claim that she was captured, and the earlier answer adds that disqualifying her by handing her to a gentile was never in his power.

summaryProblems.claim: The believed case is a father saying he betrothed her years ago while she was a minor, i.e. she is now grown.
summaryProblems.pageSays: and she is an adult woman at the time of his declaration, his statement is not deemed credible

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 64a (Rav Ashi's resolution): "The Merciful One deems the father credible with regard to marriage, whereas He does not deem him credible with regard to a captive.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The believed case is a father saying he betrothed her years ago while she was a minor, i.e. she is now grown.", but the page says "and she is an adult woman at the time of his declaration, his statement is not deemed credible". Say what the page says. The question is answered flat out by Rav Ashi: the Torah believes the father about marriage and not about captivity, and the earlier answer already says disqualifying her via a gentile was never in his power. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance what Rav Ashi's verse-based credibility means once he has shown that the father can neither divorce her nor compel a groom. Also fix the opening: the father is believed only while the daughter is still a minor at the moment he speaks; once she is an adult he is not believed.

kiddushin/65.summary: A man says to a woman, I betrothed you, and she says he did not; the page keeps him forbidden to marry her relatives while she stays free to marry his. From there the argument moves to a betrothal done in front of a single witness, which several sages say need not be treated as binding even when both sides admit it happened. Rav Ashi presses: in money a person's own admission counts like a hundred witnesses, so why not here?
kiddushin/65.question: If witnesses exist only to catch liars, why can two people who both admit they were betrothed still be told that nothing happened?

judge.reachNote: Whether witnesses merely prove a fact or constitute it, and why self-admission can create liability in money but not in personal status.

answer.quote: he does not act to the detriment of another, whereas here, he acts to the detriment of another, as their confessions render them forbidden
answer.explanation: Rav Kahana answers Rav Ashi's exact challenge: a monetary admission harms only the admitter, while a joint admission of betrothal imposes prohibitions on other people, so admission cannot substitute for witnesses here.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 65b: "he does not act to the detriment of another, whereas here, he acts to the detriment of another, as their confessions render them forbidden". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very challenge Rav Ashi raises and Rav Kahana answers on 65b, that a betrothal admission harms others while a monetary admission does not, so as written it is closed. Rewrite so it starts from that answer and asks what still presses, for example why the couple's own admission should be silenced for the sake of relatives who are not party to it, or how that squares with Rav Ashi telling Mar Zutra that witnesses were created only for liars. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

kiddushin/66.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day, and the messenger sent to fetch him came back saying he had seen the man's wife with another man. Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her only if he trusted the messenger, which Abaye reads as proof that one witness suffices here and Rava reads as meaning trusted like two. The same question runs through silence: if the accused says nothing, is that agreement?
kiddushin/66.question: Why does Mar Shmuel turn the decision over to the blind man's own sense of whether the messenger is honest, rather than answering the question of law that was put to him?

judge.reachNote: Whether a person's private confidence in a speaker can do the work that formal testimony does in forbidden-relations cases.

answer.quote: And Rava explains that Mar Shmuel meant: If he is trusted by you like two witnesses, go and divorce her, but if not, do not divorce her.
answer.explanation: The page debates what Mar Shmuel's appeal to personal trust amounts to — Abaye reads it as ordinary single-witness credibility, Rava as a stand-in for two witnesses — which bears on why he framed it subjectively without ever stating his reason for doing so.

kiddushin/67.summary: A convert who marries a mamzeret, a woman barred from marrying most Jews because of her parents' forbidden union, produces a child who is a mamzer too, and the Gemara hunts for where that case fits the mishna's rules about which parent a child follows. The engine here is the assumption that a mishna wastes no words: "any case" pulls extra situations in, "in which case is this applicable" pushes them out. Then both readings concede one phrase is repeated merely for style.
kiddushin/67.question: If every spare phrase in a mishna must include or exclude something, what happens to the whole method once one phrase is allowed to be there just for symmetry?

judge.reachNote: Asks about the standing of the exegetical premise itself: if parallelism can license an empty phrase, when is a superfluous word evidence at all?

answer.quote: Since the mishna taught its first clause using the phrase: In which case is this applicable, it also taught its latter clause using the phrase: In which case is this applicable, merely for the sake of stylistic consistency.
answer.explanation: The page states the stylistic-consistency concession the question is built on, but it never addresses what that concession does to the no-wasted-words method itself, so the question remains honestly askable.

kiddushin/68.summary: Rav Pappa reads a verse about a man with two wives, "the one beloved and the one hated," and asks whether God could hate a wife; rather, "hated" means her marriage was forbidden and yet still counts as a marriage. Rabbi Akiva holds that where any prohibition applies betrothal never takes hold at all, so he must squeeze that verse into rare cases, a widow or a non-virgin married to a High Priest. The Gemara admits the reading is forced.
kiddushin/68.question: If a verse about any man with two wives has to be bent into a case only a High Priest could ever be in, what stops a forced reading from simply being a wrong one?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the interpretive principle at stake: when a position forces a verse into an implausible case, whether that counts as reading the verse or overriding it.

answer.quote: You are forced to leave this verse aside, as it establishes itself as dealing with a difficult case.
answer.explanation: The Gemara concedes the difficulty and defends the forced reading only on the grounds that Rabbi Akiva has no alternative, which bears on the question without settling when a forced reading is simply wrong.

kiddushin/69.summary: Rabbi Tarfon proposes that a mamzer, a child of certain forbidden unions barred from marrying most Jews, marry a Canaanite maidservant, a non-Jewish slave woman, so their son is born a slave and, once freed by his master, emerges a free Jew with no taint. Rabbi Eliezer rejects the scheme; the other Sages note that it purifies sons and leaves daughters exactly where they were. The argument rests on treating a maidservant's unborn child as if it were an animal's.
kiddushin/69.question: If a mamzer's son can be turned into a free Jew by first being born a slave, what is left for the mamzer's daughter, whose child follows her whomever she marries?

judge.reachNote: The asymmetry of lineage: a child's flaw can be laundered through the mother's slave status but never through the father's, since a slave has no lineage at all.

answer.quote: A slave has no lineage. Even if she were to marry a slave, their child would not be considered his, but would be a Jewish mamzer like her.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly explains that the daughter's child stays a mamzer like her because a slave father confers no lineage, so Rabbi Tarfon's device cannot work for her — exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 69a: "A slave has no lineage. Even if she were to marry a slave, their child would not be considered his, but would be a Jewish mamzer like her.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on the page: the Sages raise the daughters' case themselves and the Gemara replies that a slave has no lineage, so her child is a mamzer like her. Rewrite the question to start from that answer rather than ask for it — for instance, press on why the mother's status can launder a child's flaw while the father's cannot, or on what it means that Rabbi Tarfon's response likens a maidservant's womb to an animal's. Keep the summary; it is faithful to the page.

kiddushin/70.summary: A man walks into a butcher shop in Pumbedita, is told to wait until Rav Yehuda's servant takes his meat, and insults Rav Yehuda; Rav Yehuda excommunicates him and, told he habitually calls others slaves, proclaims him a slave, a status that bars marriage into unflawed families. Summoned to court, Rav Yehuda spends the visit correcting Rav Nahman's word choices, then wins the case. In Neharde'a marriage contracts are torn up and a crowd gathers to stone him.
kiddushin/70.question: If the sign of flawed lineage is calling other people flawed, what is Rav Yehuda's public proclamation about the man?

judge.reachNote: A rule that diagnoses flawed lineage in whoever accuses others turns back on the sage who applies it publicly.

answer.quote: You can say that Shmuel said this halakha only to the degree that one should suspect him of being of flawed lineage. But did he actually say this
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman presses exactly the difficulty the note asks about — that the sign may warrant suspicion but not a public proclamation — and the page never resolves whether Rav Yehuda's own proclaiming implicates him, instead sustaining the ruling on the separate Hasmonean tradition.

kiddushin/71.summary: Rabbi Pineḥas told his servants to wait with a stretcher, floated a surprising claim about slaughtering birds to occupy the study hall, then announced that Babylonian ancestry was purer than that of Eretz Yisrael and was carried off at a run. Rabbi Yoḥanan swears he could name a family of flawed descent but will not, since the generation's greatest have married into it. Such names pass to students once every seven years, the same rate as God's name.
kiddushin/71.question: If a family that has quietly blended in can never be named again, not even by Elijah, what is the point of whispering the other names to one's children every seven years?
gate: the question brings in "Elijah", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — why lineage knowledge is preserved in some cases and buried in others — but the page draws exactly that line (known families vs. assimilated ones) and states the whisper's purpose.

answer.quote: once every seven years, and some say twice every seven years, to prevent them from marrying into their family
answer.explanation: The baraita states the purpose of the septennial whisper outright — to keep the Sages' own children and students from marrying into that family — and Abaye's gloss distinguishes such known families from one that "has already become assimilated," whose flaw nobody publicizes.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 71a: "once every seven years, and some say twice every seven years, to prevent them from marrying into their family". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: the baraita says the names are transmitted "to prevent them from marrying into their family," and Abaye distinguishes families "whose status we know" from one that "has already become assimilated." Rewrite the question so it starts from that distinction rather than asking for it — for instance, why a private warning that protects only the Sages' own households counts as righteousness toward everyone else, or why Rav Naḥman prefers the rarer transmission when rarer telling means more people marry in unwarned.

kiddushin/72.summary: The Sages sort Babylonian towns by lineage, naming Shunya, Guvya and Tzitzora the finest of all, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi on his deathbed names towns where the children are mamzerim, born of forbidden unions. Abaye tells people to disregard Rav Ika bar Avin's ruling that Ḥillazon Nihavnad is unflawed, since a childless widow from there awaited him in levirate marriage and he wanted her; Rav Ḥananel confirms the ruling anyway. Later, Rav Yosef is relieved that mamzerim will someday be purified.
kiddushin/72.question: If Rav Yosef welcomes the ruling because it keeps Elijah from dragging off family after family, is that a claim about what is true or a decision about what is bearable?
gate: gloss "levirate marriage" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Elijah", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a halakhic ruling about the future status of mamzerim is adopted because it is true or because the alternative is unlivable for the community.

kiddushin/73.summary: Rabbi Zeira told a crowd in Meḥoza that a convert may marry a mamzeret, a woman born of a forbidden union and barred from marrying most Jews, and the converts present pelted him with their etrogim, the citrons used on Sukkot. Rava taught the same ruling in the opposite order and was carried on silk. Rava also argues that a foundling, a baby abandoned in the marketplace, is fit by Torah law, and that the ban rests on no halakhic fear at all.
kiddushin/73.question: If the worry about a foundling accidentally marrying his own sister is dismissed as unlikely, what is the raised standard of lineage actually guarding against?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a rabbinic prohibition can survive the collapse of the specific danger it was said to prevent, resting instead on a standard of communal lineage.

answer.quote: it is prohibited for a foundling to marry a Jew with unflawed lineage not due to any halakhic concern. Rather, the Sages established a higher standard with regard to lineage
answer.explanation: The page states that the prohibition rests on no halakhic fear but on a raised standard of lineage barring people of unknown background, which names the rationale without spelling out what harm it guards against.

kiddushin/74.summary: A judge is believed when he says which litigant won the money case, but only while the two are still standing in front of him. Why rely on his word when the winner holds the written verdict? Because the writs were torn up, and the original ruling rested on the judges' own sense of who deserved to win, so a second hearing might go differently. Then credibility shifts to births: a midwife immediately, a mother for seven days, a father forever.
kiddushin/74.question: If a father's word alone can name his firstborn forever, why do the Rabbis refuse to let a priest's word mark his son as the child of a divorced woman?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that credibility granted by a verse for one declaration may not extend to a declaration that disqualifies one's own child.

answer.quote: Expounding the verse: “But he shall acknowledge the firstborn” (Deuteronomy 21:17), the Sages said: The father shall acknowledge him to others.
answer.explanation: The page grounds the father's credibility in a verse that speaks only of the firstborn, which bears on why the Rabbis cap it there, but it never states their reason for rejecting the divorced-woman claim.

kiddushin/75.summary: Three tanna'im build their rulings on a single case, a High Priest who has intercourse with a widow and so bars her from ever marrying a priest. The first tanna says the operative detail is the transgression itself; Rabbi Yosei says it is that the children of such a union are unfit for the priesthood; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says even the daughters must be unfit. One case, read three ways, produces three different lists of men who disqualify a woman.
kiddushin/75.question: When the High Priest and the widow can be read for the transgression, for the unfit sons, or for the unfit daughters, what settles which detail is doing the work?
gate: banned phrase: "doing the work".

judge.reachNote: When one case serves as a model for analogy, which of its features is the operative one — and what, if anything, constrains that choice.

kiddushin/76.summary: A priest who wants to marry the daughter of another priest is told to investigate four mothers, which works out to eight women in her family tree. The Gemara asks why her male ancestors go unchecked, and answers that men insult each other over lineage, so any flaw on that side would already be public knowledge. The same logic exempts charity collectors, who seize collateral even on Friday afternoon and so accumulate enemies who would have said something.
kiddushin/76.question: If a family's flaws surface only when someone picks a fight about them, what becomes of a family nobody has ever bothered to quarrel with?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that lineage is known only through hostile publicity, so silence must either prove fitness or leave it unknown — but the page settles it with ḥezkat kashrut.

answer.quote: if no objection was registered, everyone agrees that the family retains its presumptive status of fitness
answer.explanation: The Gemara states directly that where no objection has been raised about a family, it keeps its presumption of fitness and needs no investigation, which is exactly what becomes of a family nobody has quarreled with.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 76b: "if no objection was registered, everyone agrees that the family retains its presumptive status of fitness". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 76b, where Rav rules that families retain a presumptive status of fitness unless an objection has been registered. Read through to that exchange and build the question on what remains hard after it — for instance, why a presumption of fitness suffices for a silent family while the mishna still demands eight generations of investigation, or what the dispute between Rav's two reported statements leaves unresolved. Keep the summary; it is accurate.

kiddushin/77.summary: A ḥalal, the child of a priest's forbidden marriage, passes that disqualification to his daughters forever, while an Israelite who marries a ḥalala has daughters fit for priests. Later the page counts lashes for a High Priest with one woman who became, in order, a widow, a divorcée, a ḥalala, then a zona: he is flogged for each. Reverse the sequence and it is a single set, since Rava counts a prohibition only when it widens the circle of men barred to her.
kiddushin/77.question: Why should the very same act carry four punishments or one, depending only on the order in which her disqualifications happened to pile up?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether overlapping prohibitions can stack, and why sequence determines liability — but that is precisely Rava's issur mosif answer, quoted in the summary itself.

answer.quote: Rava said: In general, this tanna does not accept the principle that a prohibition takes effect where another prohibition already exists
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the order problem and Rava resolves it with the principle of an expanded prohibition (issur mosif), which only operates when each new status adds to the previous one.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 77b: "Rava said: In general, this tanna does not accept the principle that a prohibition takes effect where another prohibition already exists". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara asks and Rava answers on the same page, and the summary even states that answer, so it reads as self-answering. Rewrite so the question begins after Rava — for instance pressing on Rav Ḥana bar Rav Ketina's move of counting the zona's disqualification to an Israelite husband as an 'expansion' of a priestly prohibition, or on what it means that becoming barred from teruma widens a ban on the High Priest. Alternatively, build a question from the page's other thread, such as why a woman who sinned becomes profaned while the priest who sinned does not.

kiddushin/78.summary: A man announces that his son is a mamzer, a child of a forbidden union barred from marrying most Jews, and the mishna rules that nobody has to believe him, even when the mother agrees. Rabbi Yehuda disagrees, working from a verse about a father acknowledging which son is his firstborn: if he is trusted to name the heir, he is trusted to name the disqualified one. The Rabbis split the two, trusting him only about inheritance.
kiddushin/78.question: If a father's bare word can hand one son a double share of the estate, why is the same word worthless when he says that son is a mamzer?

judge.reachNote: A father's word is authoritative over what he owns and can give, but not over a child's standing in the community, which is not his to bestow.

answer.quote: he could have made a more advantageous claim [miggo]: If he desired to give him a double portion as a gift while he was alive
answer.explanation: The Gemara's miggo argument explains that the father's word about the firstborn's double portion is obvious because the money is his to give away anyway, which bears on why his word carries weight there and not about lineage, though it never states that contrast directly.

kiddushin/79.summary: A father betroths his daughter to one man while he is away traveling, and that same day she betroths herself to another man back in the city; she is now a grown woman, past her father's authority. Rav says her present adulthood reaches backward, so the father's betrothal never took hold, while Shmuel says both betrothals must be treated as possibly valid. The Gemara tests this against a ritual bath later found short of water and a barrel of wine later found to be vinegar.
kiddushin/79.question: Is a flash of Shmuel's temper at a colleague's ruling really enough evidence to prove that he and Rav disagreed at all?

judge.reachNote: What counts as evidence that two sages actually disagreed — can a recorded emotional reaction do the work of a stated legal position?

answer.quote: Now, if it enters your mind that they did not disagree at all, why did Shmuel take offense?
answer.explanation: The page itself rests the proof of a genuine dispute on Shmuel's offense, and defends it by ruling out the reading that Rav Yosef acted in a denial case, but it never justifies treating a sage's annoyance as probative in principle.

kiddushin/80.summary: A woman came to Jerusalem with a child riding on her shoulders, raised him, and years later the court stoned them both for incest, with no testimony that she was his mother beyond the fact that he clung to her. Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that presumption like this can carry a death sentence, yet refuses to burn teruma, food set aside for priests, on a comparable assumption. The argument then turns to impure dough, a child's grabbing hands, and pecking chickens.
kiddushin/80.question: Why should a presumption strong enough to stone a mother and her son be too weak to condemn a loaf of priestly dough?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the evidentiary threshold for acting on presumption may vary with what is at stake, and that a counter-presumption (the dough's purity) can block destruction where nothing blocks execution.

answer.quote: and the dough itself retains a presumptive status of purity, since its impurity has not been definitively determined
answer.explanation: The page hints at the asymmetry — the teruma has its own countervailing presumption of purity, so Rabbi Yoḥanan leaves it in suspension — but it never states this as the reason capital presumption is stronger than teruma-burning presumption.

kiddushin/81.summary: Rav says a court may flog a man for merely being secluded with a woman, since nothing can be proven either way. The page then piles up sages who mocked temptation and were caught halfway: Rav Amram hauling a ladder ten men could not lift, Rabbi Akiva climbing a palm tree after an apparition, Peleimu hosting a revolting pauper on Yom Kippur eve. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ashi sleeps with a prostitute who turns out to be his wife, and fasts the rest of his life for the intention.
kiddushin/81.question: If the woman was his own wife, what exactly was Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Ashi fasting for until he died?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that intent alone incurs guilt even when the act turns out permitted — but the page says this in so many words and then proves it from Numbers 30:13 and Leviticus 5:17.

answer.quote: All the days of that righteous man he would fast for the transgression he intended to commit, until he died by that death in his misery.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that he fasted for the transgression he intended, and has him say "I, in any event, intended to transgress," after which it brings Rabbi Akiva's verses on culpability for intent.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav permits flogging for seclusion "since nothing can be proven either way"
summaryProblems.pageSays: not prohibited from marrying a priest due to being secluded, as it cannot be stated definitively that the secluded pair engaged in sexual intercourse

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Kiddushin 81b: "All the days of that righteous man he would fast for the transgression he intended to commit, until he died by that death in his misery.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rav permits flogging for seclusion "since nothing can be proven either way"", but the page says "not prohibited from marrying a priest due to being secluded, as it cannot be stated definitively that the secluded pair engaged in sexual intercourse". Say what the page says. The question is answered explicitly on the page — the text says he fasted "for the transgression he intended to commit" and he tells his wife "I, in any event, intended to transgress." Ask something the page leaves standing instead, e.g. why Rabbi Akiva's verses treat unknowing sin and deliberate intent as requiring the same atonement, or why the wife's test is narrated without any blame attached to her. Also fix the summary's reasoning: the page uses the impossibility of proof to explain why the wife is not forbidden to her husband, not as the ground for flogging.

kiddushin/82.summary: Kiddushin's final page opens with a rule that an unmarried man may not teach children, and the Gemara asks what exactly anyone is worried about. Not the students, it answers, since Jews are not suspected of that; the risk is the mothers who come by the school. From there the tractate slides into ranking trades: donkey drivers mostly wicked, sailors mostly pious, the best doctors bound for Gehenna, and Rabbi Nehorai teaching his son Torah alone.
kiddushin/82.question: If the world cannot exist without tanners, why does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi pity the tanner instead of thanking him?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "HaNasi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the gap between a trade's necessity to the world and the esteem it earns its practitioner.

answer.quote: woe is he whose trade is as a tanner, who works with materials that have a foul smell
answer.explanation: The page supplies a reason for the pity — the foul-smelling materials — but never reconciles that pity with its own statement that the world cannot exist without tanners, so the question can still be asked.

bava-kamma/2.summary: The mishna lists four primary categories of damage, among them an ox, a pit left open in a public place, and a fire. The Gemara asks whether subcategories carry the same liability as the parent category, comparing Shabbat labors, where they do, with ritual impurity, where a secondary case contaminates food but not people or vessels. Then the sorting turns strange: an ox's bite counts under Goring rather than Eating, because the animal takes no pleasure in it.
bava-kamma/2.question: If a bite belongs to Goring only when the ox gets no pleasure from it, who is in a position to say whether the animal enjoyed itself?

judge.reachNote: Whether liability categories can rest on the animal's inner experience (benefit) rather than on an observable act.

answer.quote: In this case of damage caused by biting, there is no intrinsic pleasure for the animal in the course of the damage that it causes
answer.explanation: The page supplies the operative test — whether the exclusive objective of the act is to cause damage — but never says who determines the animal's pleasure, so the question survives in part.

bava-kamma/3.summary: Rav Pappa said that some primary categories of damage have subcategories that behave differently, and the page hunts for a single example. One by one the candidates collapse: an ox rubbing a wall for its own pleasure, a bell that damages while the animal walks, a pit nine handbreadths deep, a stone left in the street. What survives is pebbles kicked up by a walking hoof, where the owner pays only half, filed under Trampling anyway.
bava-kamma/3.question: If pebbles flung by a hoof differ from Trampling in how much is paid and what it is paid from, is calling them a subcategory a description of what they are or a decision about where the owner goes free?

judge.reachNote: Whether a legal category names a shared essence or is a device for attaching a desired exemption — the page resolves this for Rava and for Rav Pappa separately.

answer.quote: It is classified as a subcategory of Trampling in order to exempt from liability pebbles that cause damage in the public domain, just as damage in the category of Trampling is exempt
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that, for Rava, the label "subcategory of Trampling" is assigned precisely to produce the public-domain exemption, which is the very alternative the question poses.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 3b: "It is classified as a subcategory of Trampling in order to exempt from liability pebbles that cause damage in the public domain, just as damage in the category of Trampling is exempt". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: for Rava the pebbles are filed under Trampling "in order to exempt from liability" in the public domain, and for Rav Pappa because they share the payment-from-best-property aspect. Write a question that starts from those two stated reasons rather than asking what the page has already settled. One live opening is why Rav Pappa needs a substantive shared trait at all if a classification can be justified purely by the exemption it produces.

bava-kamma/4.summary: Rav reads the mishna's obscure word Maveh as Man, meaning damage a person does with his own body. The Gemara objects that the listed categories all share a typical manner of causing damage, and people do not usually damage things; the answer offered is sleep, since a sleeper contracts and extends his limbs onto whatever lies beside him. Then the mishna's phrase about safeguarding does not fit a person, so Rabbi Abbahu has the reciter reword it.
bava-kamma/4.question: When a phrase in the mishna refuses to fit Rav's reading, is rewording the phrase a fair repair, or does the wording get a vote on what Maveh means?

judge.reachNote: Whether the mishna's exact phrasing is evidence for the meaning of a term or merely loose language that may be corrected to fit a reading.

bava-kamma/5.summary: Rabbi Ḥiyya lists twenty-four primary categories of damage, and the Gemara asks why an informer, who tips off the authorities to seize someone's property, is left out. The answer is that he ruins a man by talking, and pure speech does not count. But the husband who falsely defames his bride is on the list, so speech that comes with an act qualifies, and conspiring witnesses stay on because a verse calls their testimony something they did.
bava-kamma/5.question: If a verse can declare that false witnesses performed an action, what keeps the informer's words from being an action too?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of when words are treated as deeds — whether the Torah's designation of testimony as an act is a one-off decree or a principle about speech that causes loss.

answer.quote: There, although it involves no action, the Merciful One characterizes it as an action, as it is written: "And you shall do to him as he conspired to do unto his brother"
answer.explanation: The page explains that conspiring witnesses are treated as having acted only because a verse so designates them, and separately that the informer is excluded because "the damage is caused through speech," but it never states why that scriptural designation cannot be extended to the informer.

bava-kamma/6.summary: A stone, a knife, or a load left on a roof is blown off by an ordinary wind, and someone trips over it where it lands. Abaye, Rava, Rav Adda bar Ahava, and Ravina each offer such an in-between case to explain what the mishna's "common denominator" adds; Rav Adda's is household sewage drained into the street in the rainy season, when the Sages permit it. Each time the argument swings between Pit, Fire, and Ox, neither settles it, and liability falls out of what the two share.
bava-kamma/6.question: If the Sages permitted draining the sewage into the street, what is that permission worth to the man who pays for the slip anyway?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the gap between being permitted to act and being answerable for what the act does.

answer.quote: What is notable about the primary category of Pit? It is notable in that the pit was dug in the public domain without permission.
answer.explanation: The page shows that the permission does real work — it blocks the direct derivation from Pit and forces the case onto the common denominator — but it never says what that permission is worth to the man who still pays, and indeed the baraita insists "although all these people perform their actions with permission, if they cause damage they are liable to pay for it."

bava-kamma/7.summary: One verse says a person who causes damage pays from "the best of his field," while another verse is read to allow payment in anything worth money, even bran, the husks left from milled grain. Rava first splits the cases: best land when the court forces him, any goods when he pays on his own. The page lands somewhere else entirely, that all movable goods count as best quality, since what will not sell here sells in another city.
bava-kamma/7.question: If a sack of bran counts as best-quality because it can always be sold somewhere, why does the man whose fields no one will buy in Tishrei still get fed from the poor man's tithe?
gate: the question brings in "Tishrei", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "poor man's tithe", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that 'best quality' means liquidity rather than intrinsic worth, and tests whether that measure holds across sugyot.

bava-kamma/8.summary: A debtor owes damages, a loan, and the payment written in his wife's marriage contract, and he sells his superior, intermediate, and inferior fields to a single buyer, one after another. Ulla says Torah law lets a creditor collect only from the worst land, and the Sages upgraded him to intermediate land so lenders would keep lending. The sharpest move is Rava's: a buyer can refuse a protection the Sages built for him, and hand each creditor the field originally liened to him.
bava-kamma/8.question: If the rule shielding a buyer exists only for his benefit, and he waives it, what happens to the injured party who was promised the best land?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a rule enacted for one party's benefit can be waived by him, and asks who bears the consequence — but the page answers it: each lien snaps back to its original plot.

answer.quote: I would prefer for the lien of each creditor to remain in effect with regard to the land it had been on initially
answer.explanation: The page states that when the buyer declines the Sages' ordinance, each creditor — including the injured party — collects from the land originally liened to him, which for damages is the superior-quality land, as the Tosefta itself rules.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 8b: "I would prefer for the lien of each creditor to remain in effect with regard to the land it had been on initially". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same passage the summary cites: the buyer says he prefers each lien to rest on the land it was on initially and gives each creditor that land, so damages come from the superior-quality field. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance, why the earlier threat-based explanation fails for the injured party specifically, or why an ordinance made for the buyer's benefit is also relied on by a later buyer who never consented. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

bava-kamma/9.summary: Someone hands over an ox, a pit, or a glowing ember to a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor, people the baraita treats as unable to guard them. For the ox and the pit he pays; for the ember he does not, and the distinction offered is what each thing does when nobody touches it. An ox works loose, a pit's cover slips, but an ember left alone dims until someone fans it.
bava-kamma/9.question: Is the man who hands over an ember excused because an ember is harmless, or because someone else chose to blow on it?

judge.reachNote: Whether liability turns on the object's inherent danger or on the intervening choice of another actor breaking the chain of causation.

answer.quote: with regard to an ember, as long as he leaves it alone it progressively dims, and the only way in which it will cause damage is if someone else actively fans it
answer.explanation: The page gives the exemption's rationale but states both grounds together — the ember's self-extinguishing nature and the need for another's act — and later reframes it as the incompetent person's handling (tzevata), so the question of which ground is operative can still be asked.

bava-kamma/10.summary: Five people sit on a bench and it holds; a sixth, as heavy as Pappa bar Abba, sits down and it breaks, and he pays for all of it. The Gemara keeps trying to file such cases under the mishna's rule about facilitating part of a damage, and keeps failing: either the last person caused everything, which is obvious, or the break was coming anyway, so what did he do? The rule survives only where he leaned on the other five and the bench broke at that instant.
bava-kamma/10.question: If every shared case collapses into either all his fault or none of it, what is the mishna's rule about facilitating part of the damage actually describing?

judge.reachNote: What it means to 'facilitate part' of a damage when causation is shared — the idea the page settles by restricting the rule to the deepened pit.

answer.quote: How so? In the case of one who digs a pit to a depth of nine handbreadths, and another person comes along and completes the digging to a depth of ten handbreadths
answer.explanation: The baraita states outright which case the mishna's rule describes — the second digger who deepens a pit from nine to ten handbreadths, with Rav Pappa narrowing it to liability for death so that it is the sole unanimous case.

summaryProblems.claim: The mishna's rule survives only in the case where he leaned on the other five and the bench broke at that instant.
summaryProblems.pageSays: It is apparent, then, that the mishna is not referring to this case.

summaryProblems.claim: The leaning-at-that-instant case is the residue of the mishna's rule.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Therefore, the baraita teaches us that causing damage with one's direct force is equivalent to causing damage with one's body.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 10a: "How so? In the case of one who digs a pit to a depth of nine handbreadths, and another person comes along and completes the digging to a depth of ten handbreadths". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The mishna's rule survives only in the case where he leaned on the other five and the bench broke at that instant.", but the page says "It is apparent, then, that the mishna is not referring to this case.". Say what the page says. The summary says "The leaning-at-that-instant case is the residue of the mishna's rule.", but the page says "Therefore, the baraita teaches us that causing damage with one's direct force is equivalent to causing damage with one's body.". Say what the page says. The page answers the question directly: the baraita says the mishna's rule describes the digger who deepens a pit from nine to ten handbreadths, and Rav Pappa limits it to liability for death so no dispute remains — ask something the page leaves open instead. Also fix the summary: the Gemara concludes the mishna is not referring to the bench case at all, and the leaning-at-that-instant resolution serves the bench baraita's own necessity, teaching that one's direct force is equivalent to one's body. A rewrite could press on why the objectors' cases (five watchmen, added bundle, sixth sitter) all dissolve into all-or-nothing while the pit does not.

bava-kamma/11.summary: An ox falls into a pit and dies, and the argument turns to who must haul the carcass out to be appraised. Abaye objects that a digger who profits by lifting it needs no verse to make him do it; Rava supplies the case where the carcass is worth one dinar in the pit and one dinar at the edge. Later Rav tells a man who broke a borrowed ax to pay for a whole one, then goes silent when two sages challenge him.
bava-kamma/11.question: If Rav's silence counts as conceding that the borrower overpaid, how would anyone tell a concession from a refusal to keep arguing?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the evidentiary idea of treating a sage's silence as legal assent rather than as an unwillingness to continue the dispute.

answer.quote: And the halakha is that the court does not appraise value either for a thief or for a robber; but it appraises value for a borrower
answer.explanation: The page's closing ruling endorses Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's position, which supports reading Rav's silence as concession, but it never explains how silence in general is to be distinguished from mere withdrawal from argument.

bava-kamma/12.summary: Ulla waits until Rav Naḥman leaves the study hall before telling the other sages the rest of Rabbi Elazar's view, that a creditor may collect a dead debtor's slaves from his orphans, because slaves count as land. Rav Naḥman, who holds slaves are movable property, orders judges who did so to return the slaves or pay from their own mansions. The argument drifts to a slave tied up so he cannot walk, who then counts as an immobile courtyard and acquires whatever is placed on him.
bava-kamma/12.question: If a slave becomes land only once he is bound and cannot walk, what exactly is being sorted here, the man or the ground he stands on?

judge.reachNote: Asks what the legal category actually tracks — the person's status or the immovability of the thing acquired.

answer.quote: an entity legally classified as land that moves around, such as a slave, is different from land that does not move around
answer.explanation: The page states that what is being sorted is mobility rather than the slave's underlying classification, since a slave can be classified as land yet still fail the requirement of not moving around, but it does not directly address the note's framing of the bound slave as thereby becoming land.

bava-kamma/13.summary: An ox that its owner had consecrated as a peace-offering gores another animal, and Rabbi Abba says the injured party collects from the meat the owners would have eaten, not from the portions burned on the altar. Rava applies this to a thanks-offering, where the victim eats meat worth his damages while the owner still brings the forty accompanying loaves. The page lets the owner object out loud, then rules the bread is his obligation anyway.
bava-kamma/13.question: If the entire animal did the goring, on what grounds does the injured man's claim shrink to the size of the portion its owner would have eaten?
gate: gloss "peace-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: when a damaging body is partly God's and partly a man's, does liability follow the whole body or only the owner's share?

answer.quote: Rabbi Abba is teaching that when assessing the damage to determine the amount to be paid, one deems the owner responsible only according to his share of the animal
answer.explanation: The Gemara states the ground explicitly — liability is assessed by the owner's proportional share (the meat) in the animal as a whole — and 13b reinforces it: "Since the entire animal caused the damage, he does not collect the full cost of the damage from the meat portions."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 13a: "Rabbi Abba is teaching that when assessing the damage to determine the amount to be paid, one deems the owner responsible only according to his share of the animal". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in so many words: Rabbi Abba deems the owner responsible "only according to his share of the animal," and 13b adds that since the whole animal gored, the victim cannot load the full sum onto the meat. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and pushes somewhere the page leaves open — for instance, why the consecrating owner's own act of dedication should reduce what his victim can recover, or how this squares with the rule that the whole body of an innocuous ox stands as security for the damage.

bava-kamma/14.summary: Two partners share a courtyard, and one partner's ox eats the other's produce there. Two baraitot clash over liability, and the Gemara splits them by what the partners agreed the yard was for: if oxen are allowed in, no payment; if only produce is kept there, the owner pays. Rabbi Zeira objects that a jointly owned yard can never be the "field of another" the verse requires, and Abaye answers that excluding oxen is enough to make it another's field.
bava-kamma/14.question: If both partners own the courtyard outright, can a private arrangement about what may be kept there turn one partner's ground into "a field of another"?

judge.reachNote: What makes ground count as "another's" — formal ownership or the use the owners agreed to permit there.

answer.quote: Since it is not designated for them to keep oxen there, that is sufficient for it to be termed “a field of another.”
answer.explanation: Abaye answers exactly what the question asks: the partners' arrangement excluding oxen suffices to make the jointly owned courtyard "a field of another."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 14a: "Since it is not designated for them to keep oxen there, that is sufficient for it to be termed “a field of another.”". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks the very thing Abaye answers, and the summary itself already reports that answer, so it reads as settled rather than open. Rewrite so the question starts where the page ends: Ravina says Rav Ḥisda and Rabbi Elazar may disagree precisely over whether to accept Rabbi Zeira's difficulty or Abaye's resolution, so ask what is still unresolved about designated use standing in for ownership. Alternatively build the question on Rabbi Tarfon versus the Rabbis, where the same yard counts as the injured party's for Eating but as public domain for Goring.

bava-kamma/15.summary: An ox that has never gored before gores, and its owner pays half the cost of the damage. Rav Pappa says that half is real restitution: oxen can always turn belligerent, full liability was the default, and the Torah took pity on an owner who had no warning.
