the question brings in "Pappa", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a fixed measure of foreseeability has a sharp edge, or whether the tannaim's counting direction shows the number is only a rough marker.

answer.quote: There is no dispute between the tanna of the mishna and the tanna of the baraita; there is merely a difference of how they stated their rulings.
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa's resolution bears directly on the question by saying the two rulings are only phrased from opposite directions, yet the page still says of the mishna "a minimum of four cubits high, where the one who kindled the fire is still exempt" and of the baraita "a maximum of four cubits high, where the one who kindled the fire is still liable," so the exact four-cubit case remains unresolved in the text.

bava-kamma/62.summary: A man kicks another man's safe into the river, and the owner comes to court claiming what was inside it. Since the safe is gone, the argument turns to when such a claim is believed: coins, yes, because people keep coins in a safe, but a pearl is left unresolved. Rav Ashi's test for a silver goblet lost in a house fire examines the claimant rather than the claim, asking whether he is wealthy or known as trustworthy.
bava-kamma/62.question: If belief turns on whether a man looks rich enough to have owned a pearl, what happens to the poor man whose pearl really was in the safe?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that proof by plausibility of the person, not of the claim, must fail the atypical claimant whose loss was real.

answer.quote: But if he is not such a person, it is not in his power to be believed in such a claim.
answer.explanation: The page states the outcome for a claimant who does not fit the profile — he simply is not believed — but says nothing about a true loss wrongly disbelieved, so the question still stands.

bava-kamma/63.summary: A caught thief repays double, and the verse lists ox, donkey, sheep and garment; the Gemara asks whether a stolen bird counts. Read as a list of samples, the rule would cover only animals like those named, but the word kol, any, is taken as an expansion that admits even non-kosher birds. Then a bailee, holding another's deposit, swears it was stolen when he ate it himself: he pays double, while claiming it was lost costs only the principal.
bava-kamma/63.question: Why should a guard who lies and says "stolen" owe double, while the one who lies and says "lost" owes only what the deposit was worth?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a false claim of theft is itself a kind of theft ("passive theft") while a false claim of loss is merely a lie, so only the former carries the thief's penalty.

answer.quote: Both verses are necessary because one verse serves to exclude from double payment the case of one who falsely states the claim that the item has been lost.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the scriptural source for the distinction (a surplus verse, and alternatively the definite article in "hagannav"), but it never gives a reason why the Torah treats the "lost" lie more leniently, so the question survives.

bava-kamma/64.summary: A verse about a thief lists ox, donkey, sheep, and "alive," and the page asks why each of those words is needed to fix what double payment covers. Each added word blocks a narrower reading, until the method breaks: slot the details between the doubled verb himmatze timmatze and "sheep" has nothing left to exclude, so the approach is dropped for another. That same doubled verb then does other work: a thief who admits liability before any witnesses testify pays no fine.
bava-kamma/64.question: If the words of the verse can be sorted one way until "sheep" is left with nothing to do, and then sorted an entirely different way, what decides which sorting was right?

judge.reachNote: What makes an exegetical sorting of a verse correct, when the same words can be arranged under rival hermeneutical rules.

answer.quote: This is not expounded as a generalization, and a detail, and a generalization, because the detail does not appear between the generalizations.
answer.explanation: The page gives one criterion for choosing the method — the position of the details relative to the two generalizations, together with the demand that no word ("sheep") be left idle — but it does not settle why Ravina's license to relocate the detail yields to that criterion, so the question survives.

bava-kamma/65.summary: Rav rules that a thief pays the principal, the plain value of the stolen thing, as of the day he stole it, while the penalty of double payment is figured by its worth at the time of trial. Two baraitot push back, one about a lean animal the thief fattened, one about a fat animal he starved, and both are explained away. The page then turns to a stolen lamb that grew into a ram in the thief's keeping.
bava-kamma/65.question: If the lamb has become a ram while in the thief's pen, has he changed it enough to own it, or did it simply get older on its own?

judge.reachNote: Whether natural growth counts as the kind of transformation that turns a stolen animal into the thief's own property, or is merely the same animal older.

bava-kamma/66.summary: Stolen wood that a thief turns into vessels stays his, and he pays only what the wood was worth when he took it. Rabba pushes further and asks whether an owner's despair of ever recovering the item also hands it over, by Torah law or only as a rabbinic ordinance. After twenty-two years of Rabba's question, Rav Yosef answers that a change of name works like a change of substance: yesterday a hide, today a leather table top.
bava-kamma/66.question: If renaming a hide a table top is enough to make it the thief's, why does a stolen beam, now a joist inside someone's house, stay the owner's until an ordinance for penitents releases it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a change of name is a real acquisition-effecting change, or whether the beam case shows name-change alone never transfers ownership and only the penitents' ordinance does the work.

bava-kamma/67.summary: A stolen beam built into a house is the test case for whether altering a stolen item makes it the thief's. Rav Yosef says no real change has happened, since a beam keeps its name once it is in the wall, and Rabbi Zeira says a change that can be undone does not count. Then comes the hollowed-out log that becomes a water duct, a new name that never goes back.
bava-kamma/67.question: If hollowing a log into a water duct counts as a real change of name, why doesn't sinking a stolen beam into a wall?

judge.reachNote: What makes a change in an object real enough to transfer ownership — irreversibility of the new identity.

answer.quote: drawn water may not be used for a ritual bath is different, as it applies by rabbinic law, and consequently the Sages were lenient
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the duct objection against the reversion criterion and answers that the mikveh rule is only rabbinic, so its leniency proves nothing about change of name — and Rabbi Zeira's stated rule (a change that can revert is no change) already distinguishes the removable beam from the hollowed log.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 67a: "drawn water may not be used for a ritual bath is different, as it applies by rabbinic law, and consequently the Sages were lenient". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it twice — by Rabbi Zeira's reversion rule (which the summary itself quotes) and by saying the mikveh rule is merely rabbinic, hence lenient. Ask something that survives those answers, for instance why Rav Yosef and Rabbi Zeira need two different grounds for the same beam, or why a change in name works for teruma and consecration where nothing physical happened at all.

bava-kamma/68.summary: A thief who steals a sheep and then slaughters or sells it pays four or five times its value, but only if the animal still belonged to someone else when he sold it. The argument keeps testing whether an owner's giving up hope of recovery hands ownership to the thief, and at one point Rava declares a baraita's clauses scrambled and swaps them. Rabbi Yoḥanan answers with kidnapping: a sold captive never despairs of freedom, yet the seller is liable.
bava-kamma/68.question: If a kidnapped man never gives up on his own freedom, what makes the sale of him real enough to be punished at all?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether guilt tracks the legal effectiveness of an act or the doing of it — the sale that transfers nothing yet condemns the seller.

summaryProblems.claim: A thief pays four or five times the value only if the animal still belonged to someone else when he sold it.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: He is liable, as the thief's liability applies whether the animal is sold before the owner's despair or after his despair.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Yoḥanan answers (i.e., resolves the problem) with the kidnapping case.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Yoḥanan said to Rabbi Elazar: The case of stealing a human being, i.e., kidnapping, proves that your reasoning is incorrect.

judge.feedback: The summary says "A thief pays four or five times the value only if the animal still belonged to someone else when he sold it.", but the page says "Rabbi Yoḥanan says: He is liable, as the thief's liability applies whether the animal is sold before the owner's despair or after his despair.". Say what the page says. The summary says "Rabbi Yoḥanan answers (i.e., resolves the problem) with the kidnapping case.", but the page says "Rabbi Yoḥanan said to Rabbi Elazar: The case of stealing a human being, i.e., kidnapping, proves that your reasoning is incorrect.". Say what the page says. The opening sentence states as settled law a point the page presents as a live dispute: Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yoḥanan hold the thief liable whether the sale came before or after the owner's despair, while Rav Sheshet and Reish Lakish hold the opposite. Rewrite it as a disagreement rather than a rule. Also note that Rabbi Yoḥanan brings kidnapping as an objection against Rabbi Elazar's reasoning, not as a resolution, and the question should acknowledge that Rava and Rav Naḥman already offer the "the act itself is the sin" reply.

bava-kamma/69.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that a stolen object hangs in a gap: the thief cannot dedicate it to the Temple, since it is not his, and the owner cannot either, since it is no longer in his hands. Against him stands a mishna about vineyards marked with clods of earth and potsherds, where pious owners set coins aside so that grapes a passerby steals are redeemed anyway. The Gemara reshuffles who said what, then has Rabbi Yoḥanan prefer a rival unattributed mishna backed by a verse.
bava-kamma/69.question: When two unattributed mishnayot flatly contradict each other, does the verse Rabbi Yoḥanan produces actually decide between them, or only dress up a choice he had already made?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what makes a derashah decisive: whether a supporting verse genuinely resolves a clash of equally weighted anonymous mishnayot or merely licenses a ruling already held.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan followed the mishna that discusses the double payment because there is a verse that supports it: "And when a man shall sanctify his house to be holy to the Lord"
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's first half — on what basis one anonymous mishna was chosen over the other — and answers that the double-payment mishna has scriptural support, but it says nothing about whether the verse is the real ground or a later justification.

bava-kamma/70.summary: Two witnesses testify that a man stole an ox, and two others testify that he then slaughtered it, which would make him liable for the fourfold or fivefold penalty paid by a thief who kills or sells what he took. Rabbi Akiva holds that witnesses must testify to an entire matter and not part of one, so each pair here appears to have seen only half a crime. Abaye answers that the theft witnesses stand alone while the slaughter witnesses cannot, and on that asymmetry both count as whole.
bava-kamma/70.question: If the pair who saw the slaughter proves nothing without the pair who saw the theft, why should their half count as a complete matter?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what makes a testimony 'whole' — self-sufficiency rather than covering the full liability — but the page states that answer outright, and the summary even repeats it.

answer.quote: since the witnesses testifying about the theft do not require the testimony of the witnesses who testify about the slaughter, as their testimony alone establishes that person as a thief
answer.explanation: Abaye's stated reason is exactly that the one-directional dependence suffices, so each pair is called a complete matter — which is the question the note asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 70b: "since the witnesses testifying about the theft do not require the testimony of the witnesses who testify about the slaughter, as their testimony alone establishes that person as a thief". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks for the very reason Abaye gives and the summary already restates, so it is answered on the page. Rewrite it to press past Abaye: for instance, ask why one-directional dependence should satisfy Rabbi Akiva, or compare the betrothal-and-intercourse analogy with the two-hairs case the Rabbis exclude, where each pair also testifies to something real yet the testimonies do not combine. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

bava-kamma/71.summary: A thief who steals an animal and slaughters or sells it pays four or five times its value, but not when the same act carries execution. To rescue a baraita that charges the thief anyway, the Sages read it as a case where he sent someone else to do the slaughtering, on Shabbat or for idol worship. Mar Zutra objects that an agent cannot create liability his sender would not have; Rav Ashi answers that the thief was always liable, just excused.
bava-kamma/71.question: If a thief who slaughters a stolen ox on Shabbat pays nothing because the death penalty swallows the fine, why should handing the knife to someone else cost him five oxen?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether an exemption from payment reflects absence of liability or merely absorption by a greater penalty — but the page names and resolves it.

bava-kamma/72.summary: A thief who steals an ox and slaughters it owes the owner five times its value, and the Gemara argues over whether the slaughter counts from the first cut or only the last. Then the mishna turns to witnesses exposed as conspirators: they pay the accused thief everything they tried to make him pay. Rava calls that rule a novelty, since two witnesses against two ought to leave a deadlock and no one punished.
bava-kamma/72.question: When two pairs of witnesses contradict each other, what makes the second pair believable rather than simply the later to speak?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the credibility of the second pair rests on decree rather than reason — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: Yet the Torah teaches that the second set of witnesses is always deemed credible and the first set is subjected to punishment as conspiring witnesses.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's question ("What did you see that causes you to listen to the second set of witnesses") and answers that nothing logical does — it is a Torah-decreed novelty, which is why Rava limits the disqualification going forward.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 72b: "Yet the Torah teaches that the second set of witnesses is always deemed credible and the first set is subjected to punishment as conspiring witnesses.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very question Rava asks and the page answers it in the same breath: the Torah simply deems the second set credible, which is why the rule is a "novelty." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating it — for example, ask why a rule admitted to be counterintuitive should therefore apply only from the moment of exposure, or what it means that Rava can accept the logic of retroactive disqualification and still refuse to apply it. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-kamma/73.summary: Two witnesses testify that a man stole an ox and then slaughtered it, and later a third pair proves they were nowhere near the scene. Abaye holds their disqualification reaches back to the moment they spoke; Rava holds it begins only when they are exposed. Whether the theft testimony falls along with the slaughter testimony ends up hanging on the length of a pause, measured against two greetings: a student's long one to a teacher, and a teacher's short one back.
bava-kamma/73.question: Why should a man's liability for a stolen ox turn on whether the witnesses paused long enough for a student to greet his teacher?

judge.reachNote: What makes two statements one act of testimony, and why a formal unit of speech should decide a monetary fine.

answer.quote: the legal status of a pause or retraction within the time required for speaking a short phrase is like that of continuous speech
answer.explanation: The page supplies the mechanism — a short enough pause fuses the two statements into one testimony, so that invalidating part invalidates the whole — but never justifies why so fine a temporal measure should govern liability.

bava-kamma/74.summary: A master who knocks out his Canaanite slave's tooth and later blinds his eye owes the slave freedom and payment for the eye, and the page picks apart what happens when the witnesses to that order are shown to have been elsewhere. Abaye and Rava argue whether testimony already contradicted by a second pair can still be punished as false. Then Rabban Gamliel blinds his slave Tavi's eye and is delighted, since it frees him.
bava-kamma/74.question: If Rabban Gamliel had long wanted Tavi free and was glad when he blinded him, why should his own account count for nothing while two strangers' would count for everything?

judge.reachNote: Why a person's own word, however sincere, cannot generate a fine, while two outsiders' words can — the difference between confession and proof.

answer.quote: The principle is that one does not pay a fine based on his own admission. One pays a fine only based on the testimony of witnesses.
answer.explanation: The page states the governing rule that an admission cannot create liability for a fine, but it never explains why a fine uniquely requires witnesses, so the question's 'why' still stands.

bava-kamma/75.summary: A thief who confesses before witnesses arrive pays back what he stole but escapes the Torah's fines: double payment, or fourfold for a slaughtered sheep and fivefold for a slaughtered ox. Rav holds that witnesses arriving afterward cannot revive those fines; Shmuel holds that they can. Rav Hamnuna sharpens the rule so that the confession shields him only when it costs him something, since admitting the theft obligates him to repay the animal's value.
bava-kamma/75.question: If an admission only exempts a thief from the fine when it also obligates him to pay the principal, is it his honesty buying the exemption or his money?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: What gives a confession its legal force — the truthfulness of the speaker, or the self-imposed financial liability it creates.

answer.quote: In order for an admission to exempt the perpetrator from a fine, it must include an admission that he is liable to pay some payment.
answer.explanation: The page states Rav Hamnuna's rule that the admission must carry a self-imposed obligation to pay, which bears on the question but does not settle whether the exemption rests on candor or on the financial cost the confession imposes.

bava-kamma/76.summary: A thief steals an ox, consecrates it as an offering, then slaughters or sells it, and the mishna gives him only the double payment, not the fourfold or fivefold penalty that slaughtering a stolen animal usually brings. The Gemara presses hard: selling to a person transfers ownership, so why not selling to Heaven? The answer is that consecration moves nothing, since before it was Reuven's ox and after it is still Reuven's ox, while the slaughter now belongs to the Temple.
bava-kamma/76.question: If consecrating the stolen ox makes the later slaughter Temple business rather than the owner's, how is that same ox still Reuven's ox when the question is whether consecration counts as a sale?

judge.reachNote: What ownership transfer actually means: whether consecration shifts a domain for one purpose (slaughter) while leaving title untouched for another (sale).

bava-kamma/77.summary: A thief who steals an ox or a sheep and then slaughters or sells it pays four or five times its value. Rabbi Shimon holds that slaughter which leaves meat forbidden is no slaughter at all, and the page asks whether the same applies to selling a stolen animal with a fatal wound: Rabbi Yohanan says the seller still pays, Reish Lakish says he does not. A baraita about a sheep-goat hybrid is dragged in, and its lopsided wording decides nothing cleanly.
bava-kamma/77.question: If slaughtering a mortally wounded stolen animal is not really slaughter because the meat may not be eaten, what makes selling that same animal a real sale?

judge.reachNote: Whether selling and slaughtering are one legal category because the verse pairs them, or two acts whose validity is judged by different standards — effectiveness of transfer versus fitness of the meat.

answer.quote: as its meat may not be eaten, nevertheless, it is applicable for its sale
answer.explanation: The page records Rabbi Yoḥanan's position that sale of a tereifa incurs liability even though its slaughter does not, but it asserts this distinction rather than explaining what makes the sale valid, so the note's question can still honestly be asked.

bava-kamma/78.summary: A thief who steals an ox or a sheep and then slaughters or sells it pays four or five times its value, but the mishna says that holding back one hundredth of the animal from the sale drops him to the ordinary double payment. The dispute is over which hundredth counts: a foreleg, a horn, the fleece that would have been sheared anyway. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar is quoted saying both opposite things, and the Gemara blames two reporters.
bava-kamma/78.question: If the buyer walks off with the whole beast and the thief keeps only wool that was going to be cut off regardless, in what sense has the animal not been sold?

judge.reachNote: What makes a transfer complete — the letter of total conveyance versus the practical insignificance of a part that was destined to leave the animal anyway.

answer.quote: the term "or sells it" teaches that we require him to sell all of it, not leaving any portion at all for himself, even the fleece
answer.explanation: The Gemara's analysis of the tanna'im states outright that the first tanna reads the verse as demanding a total sale, so retaining even fleece makes the sale incomplete, while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's counter-view (fleece "meant to be cut off in the animal's lifetime, is not considered a significant withholding") is also given.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 78b: "the term "or sells it" teaches that we require him to sell all of it, not leaving any portion at all for himself, even the fleece". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question twice over: it says the first tanna derives from "or sells it" that the whole animal must be sold, even the fleece, and it says Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds fleece destined to be sheared is no significant withholding. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for example Rabbi Yirmeya's unresolved dilemmas about selling except for thirty days, except for the animal's work, or except for the fetus, where the page itself concludes the matter stands unresolved. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

bava-kamma/79.summary: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai's students ask why the Torah fines a thief double, fourfold or fivefold while a robber, who grabs in the open, pays only the value. His answer: the sneak fears people but not God, treating the servant's honor as greater than the Master's. Rabbi Meir then pairs this with a second oddity, that stealing an ox costs five and a sheep only four, and offers two rival reasons.
bava-kamma/79.question: If the thief is penalized precisely for minding what people think of him, why does the page then shave his payment down to fourfold because carrying a sheep on his shoulder embarrassed him?

judge.reachNote: It asks whether concern for how one appears to others is a vice (fearing people over God) or a dignity the law protects, and how one page can hold both.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Meir offers two rival reasons for the ox-five/sheep-four difference.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said: Come and see how great human dignity is.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rabbi Meir offers two rival reasons for the ox-five/sheep-four difference.", but the page says "Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said: Come and see how great human dignity is.". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: Rabbi Meir gives only the reason about the greatness of labor, while the human-dignity explanation of the sheep's fourfold payment belongs to Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai. That correction actually sharpens the question, since it is the same sage who condemned the thief for fearing people who then credits his embarrassment. Keep the question as it stands and let the summary set up that pairing accurately.

bava-kamma/80.summary: Physicians tell a sick man to suckle warm milk every morning, so a she-goat is tied to the leg of his bed. His visiting friends see it, turn back, and call it an armed bandit, since small animals graze on other people's crops; dying, the man names that goat as his only sin. Later three sages stall in a doorway over who should enter last, and while they stall a cat severs a newborn's hand.
bava-kamma/80.question: Does the page notice that the contest over who should defer to whom is what left the baby alone with the cat?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that competitive humility about honor can itself be a costly neglect of what is urgent.

answer.quote: In the meantime, while all this was going on, a cat [shunara] came and severed the hand of the baby.
answer.explanation: The page marks the timing — the cat struck while the sages were still sorting out precedence — but never states that their deference contest caused or is blamed for the injury, so the question remains askable.

bava-kamma/81.summary: Joshua apportioned the land of Israel, a baraita says, on ten conditions: public rights carved out of private property, from grazing sheep in forests to relieving oneself behind a fence in a field of saffron. Walking with Rabbi Ḥiyya, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi veers off the road onto private land and notices a man taking broad steps to avoid doing so; he calls it showing off. Counted up, the conditions come to eleven, so one gets handed to King Solomon.
bava-kamma/81.question: Why should a man who declines a permission and keeps to the road be threatened with iron shears rather than admired for it?

judge.reachNote: Extra stringency can be arrogance rather than piety — the page also softens it with Rabbi Ḥiyya's 'all of his actions are undertaken for the sake of Heaven.'

answer.quote: Who is this man who is showing off his supposed greatness in our presence? By acting more stringently than required by halakha, he is displaying insolence.
answer.explanation: The page itself supplies Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reason: refusing a permission in front of one's teachers is a display of insolence, not piety.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 81b: "Who is this man who is showing off his supposed greatness in our presence? By acting more stringently than required by halakha, he is displaying insolence.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers why he was threatened — acting more stringently than required in the presence of the Sages is insolence — so the question as written is closed by the next line. Rewrite it to press on what remains hard: Rabbi Ḥiyya's defense that all Yehuda ben Kanosa's acts are for the sake of Heaven, and how one tells sincere stringency from showing off. Alternatively ask what it means that a permission Joshua granted becomes something one may not visibly decline.

bava-kamma/82.summary: A baraita credits Ezra the Scribe with ten ordinances: Torah reading on Monday and Thursday, laundry on Thursday, garlic on Shabbat eve, peddlers of cosmetics circulating through every town so wives stay appealing to their husbands. Twice the Gemara protests that an item is already Torah law, combing the hair before immersion and immersion after a seminal emission, and twice the answer is that Ezra pushed an existing duty past its minimum. Jerusalem then gets its own list of ten.
bava-kamma/82.question: If Torah law already demands that water reach every hair, what is Ezra adding by requiring a comb through hair known to be clean and unknotted?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what a rabbinic ordinance adds to a duty the Torah already imposes — but the page states that answer outright, and the summary itself repeats it.

answer.quote: And Ezra came and added to the Torah's minimal obligation. He instituted the requirement of combing the hair even when it is known that it is not knotted
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection, answers that Torah law requires only inspection for knots or repulsive substances, and states that Ezra added combing even when the hair is known to be clean.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 82b: "And Ezra came and added to the Torah's minimal obligation. He instituted the requirement of combing the hair even when it is known that it is not knotted". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 82b, and the summary already gives the answer ('Ezra pushed an existing duty past its minimum'), so the reader has nothing to chew on. Build the question on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why the Gemara is content to say a prohibition is 'a tradition; there is no known explanation for it' about leaving a corpse overnight while giving reasons for the other nine Jerusalem halakhot, or why so many Jerusalem exemptions all hang on the claim that the city 'was not apportioned to any one of the tribes.' Keep the summary's shape but let the question point past what the page settles.

bava-kamma/83.summary: A person may not raise a dog unless it is chained, though a town on the border may release it at night. A woman baking in a building is barked at, and when the owner says the dog's teeth were removed, she answers that the baby has already moved in her womb. The rest turns to five payments for injury, and to the long argument that "an eye for an eye" means money rather than an eye.
bava-kamma/83.question: If the eye cannot be taken literally because one man's eye is larger than another's and the law must be equal for all, why is payment for pain and humiliation set by the particular sufferer and the particular insulter?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the tension between a uniform standard of law and valuations that depend on who this particular sufferer or insulter is.

bava-kamma/84.summary: One sage after another tries to prove that "an eye for an eye" means money, and the Sages dismantle each proof, including Rav Ashi's comparison to an ox that gored an ox, which he retracts. The payment turns out to require pricing a human being on the slave market. Then a donkey severs a child's hand, and the father refuses to let his son be appraised that way, saying he will compensate the boy himself when he grows up.
bava-kamma/84.question: If the only way to put a number on a child's severed hand is to price him as a slave, was the father protecting his son or costing him?

judge.reachNote: Whether a person's dignity can be traded against the only valuation the law has for his body — the slave market price.

answer.quote: But you are acting to the detriment of the child, as he will not receive compensation for his injury.
answer.explanation: The court officers raise exactly this objection and the father answers it by promising to appease the boy with his own money, so the page frames both sides of the tension without resolving which choice was right.

bava-kamma/85.summary: Assessing payment for pain means asking what a person would accept in order to suffer it, and the Gemara cannot find a clean case. It tries a hand already severed, then a hand the government has condemned to be cut off, until the question flips: how much would a man pay to have it removed by a painless drug rather than by a sword? That sum, collected from the one who injured him, is the price of pain.
bava-kamma/85.question: If the figure comes from what a man would pay to escape pain, is that the same as what his pain is worth?

judge.reachNote: Whether pain can be priced at all, and whether the price of avoiding suffering is the same quantity as the value of suffering undergone.

answer.quote: the court evaluates how much this one, the injured party, will take from that one, i.e., the one who caused the injury
answer.explanation: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, explains that the sum a man would have paid the government to avoid the sword is what the injured party collects, which bears on but does not settle whether avoidance-price equals the worth of pain.

bava-kamma/86.summary: Rabbi Abba bar Memel asks about a man humiliated in his sleep who dies before waking and never learns of it. The dilemma splits the payment two ways: is it for the sting the victim feels, or for the disgrace done to his standing, or to his family's name? The test cases are a deaf-mute, a minor, and an imbecile, and the answers wobble, since a minor collects only once he is old enough to feel shame.
bava-kamma/86.question: If humiliation is paid for as disgrace in other people's eyes, why does the imbecile, of whom the Sages say no one could be brought lower, collect nothing?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea—whether humiliation compensates a felt sting or an objective loss of standing—but it asks the very objection the Gemara states and resolves.

answer.quote: With regard to an imbecile, you can have no greater humiliation than this. It is impossible to degrade him further.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection—on the disgrace theory the imbecile should collect—and answers that he is already maximally degraded, so no further disgrace can be inflicted on him.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 86b: "With regard to an imbecile, you can have no greater humiliation than this. It is impossible to degrade him further.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it in the next line: an imbecile can have no greater humiliation, so nothing further can be taken from him. Rewrite the question to start after that answer rather than to ask for it. For instance, probe what it means that the imbecile is treated as already at the floor of honor while the minor's claim depends on his own capacity to feel shame, or press on why the family's humiliation does not carry the imbecile's claim.

bava-kamma/87.summary: Rabbi Elazar asks Rav who collects the money when someone injures another man's minor daughter. Her father takes her betrothal gifts, but Rav answers that the Torah granted him only the profits of her youth; the line drawn is that a father may marry her off to a man afflicted with boils, yet may not lay a hand on her. The rest sorts out which fathers are grasping, and what to buy a child with damages: a Torah scroll, or a date palm.
bava-kamma/87.question: If a father may hand his daughter to a man with boils but may not bruise her, what is it he actually owns?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a father's right is in his daughter's earning and marital value, not in her person — but the page already names that right and its limit.

answer.quote: The Torah granted the father only the profits of her youth and nothing else. Therefore, compensation for the injury goes to the daughter.
answer.explanation: Rav states exactly what the father holds — the profits of her youth alone — with Abaye adding that loss of livelihood is his because her earnings are his, so the question's "what does he actually own" is answered in so many words.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 87b: "The Torah granted the father only the profits of her youth and nothing else. Therefore, compensation for the injury goes to the daughter.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the father owns, but the page answers it directly — and the summary itself already quotes that answer, that the Torah granted him only the profits of her youth. Rewrite the question to press on something the page leaves unsettled: for instance why the father's claim on compensation should turn on whether he is a "captious man" or whether his children eat at his table, rather than on a fixed rule of ownership. Or ask why physical pain suffered in obtaining money should decide whose money it is.

bava-kamma/88.summary: Rabbi Yehuda says a Canaanite slave, a non-Jewish slave owned by a Jew, gets no payment for humiliation, since the verse about two men fighting says "a man and his brother." The Sages answer that a slave is a brother in the matter of mitzvot, which forces the page to explain why that brother may not be king or testify. Each attempt to reason him out of the witness box collapses, until a missing word in a verse about fathers and children does the work.
bava-kamma/88.question: If every logical argument for disqualifying a slave's testimony fails and only the absence of the word "their" in one verse settles it, what is he actually being disqualified for?
gate: banned phrase: "does the work".

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — what quality in a person makes him a fit witness — but the page names it outright as lack of common lineage.

answer.quote: with regard to a slave, who has no common lineage with those above him or those below him, he is the one who is disqualified
answer.explanation: The page states the substantive ground of the slave's disqualification: he has no ḥayis, no common lineage with either his parents or his children, unlike a convert who has lineage with those below him.

summaryProblems.claim: Each attempt to reason him out of the witness box collapses, until the verse does the work.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rather, derive the halakha from a robber and from one of these other two, either a woman or a minor. Their common denominator is that they do not observe all the mitzvot

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 88a: "with regard to a slave, who has no common lineage with those above him or those below him, he is the one who is disqualified". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Each attempt to reason him out of the witness box collapses, until the verse does the work.", but the page says "Rather, derive the halakha from a robber and from one of these other two, either a woman or a minor. Their common denominator is that they do not observe all the mitzvot". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few lines later: Mar son of Ravina's reading of "Fathers shall not be put to death for children" supplies the substantive ground — the slave has no common lineage with parents or children, which is exactly what he is disqualified for. Rewrite the question to start from that answer, for instance asking why lineage rather than obligation in mitzvot should be the test of a witness, given that the slave keeps most mitzvot and the convert keeps them all yet only one is fit. Also fix the summary's claim that every logical derivation collapses: the combined derivation from a robber together with a woman or minor is offered and not refuted.

bava-kamma/89.summary: A married woman who injures someone is treated as having no money to pay, and the Gemara asks why she cannot sell the speculative value of her marriage contract, what a buyer would pay for the chance that she is widowed or divorced and collects. One answer after another fails, until Shmuel's rule lands: she could later waive the whole debt to her husband, leaving the buyer holding nothing. So the court declines to arrange a sale it expects to collapse.
bava-kamma/89.question: If the Sages are certain she will forgive the debt the moment it benefits her husband, in what sense is the marriage contract her property at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether a right whose exercise is predictably surrendered to another's benefit can still count as the holder's own property.

answer.quote: Rava said: The halakha is that the money received for selling the financial advantage of the marriage contract is given only to the wife
answer.explanation: The page affirms that the proceeds of the marriage contract's financial advantage belong to the wife alone, and even the profits of those profits are hers, which bears on the question of her ownership without settling why the Sages nonetheless treat her waiver as certain.

bava-kamma/90.summary: A slap on the cheek costs two hundred dinars, silver coins worth roughly a day's wage each, and uncovering a woman's head in the marketplace costs four hundred. A man ordered to pay that sum broke a jug of oil worth an issar, a small copper coin, by her door, then watched her uncover her own head to use the oil. Rabbi Akiva rejected the argument: one who injures himself pays nothing, but others who injure him pay.
bava-kamma/90.question: If she will bare her head herself for a jug's worth of spilled oil, what exactly were the four hundred dinars paying for?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that humiliation payment measures an objective, conferred dignity rather than the victim's own sense of shame.

answer.quote: This is the principle of assessing payment for humiliation caused to another: It is all evaluated in accordance with the honor of the one who was humiliated
answer.explanation: The page states that the payment measures the humiliated party's honor — and Rabbi Akiva adds that even the poor are treated as impoverished freemen, children of Abraham — which bears on what the four hundred dinars compensate, but it does not directly resolve why the sum stands once she uncovers her own head for an issar of oil beyond the self-injury/other-injury distinction the note already cites.

bava-kamma/91.summary: A man pulled the head covering off a woman in the marketplace, and Rabbi Akiva fined him four hundred dinars, then granted him time to pay. The man spent that time waiting outside her courtyard until he got her to uncover her own head, arguing that she cheapens her own dignity. Akiva still holds him liable, which pushes the Gemara into a longer fight over whether a person is permitted to injure or shame himself at all.
bava-kamma/91.question: If Rabbi Akiva had refused the man's request for time to pay, as the court does with injuries, would the woman ever have been ambushed at her own doorway?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that treating humiliation as a lesser, non-monetary loss gives the offender room to humiliate again.

answer.quote: But with regard to humiliation, where he did not cause him a monetary loss, we do give him time to pay compensation.
answer.explanation: The page explains why the court grants time for humiliation but not injury, which bears on the question's premise, yet it never addresses the counterfactual of what would have happened had the request been refused.

bava-kamma/92.summary: A mishna rules that an assailant who has paid every coin of the damages is still not forgiven in the heavenly court until he asks the victim himself, and a victim who refuses is called cruel. Permission cuts oddly: tell someone to break your jug and owe nothing, and he is exempt, but tell him to blind your eye on the same terms, and he pays. The rest is Rava asking Rabba bar Mari for the scriptural roots of common sayings.
bava-kamma/92.question: If forgiveness is what finishes the payment, why can a person waive a smashed jug in advance but not his own eye?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: How far a person's consent reaches over his own body as against his property, and whether money can ever close a bodily injury.

bava-kamma/93.summary: Someone tells a neighbor to blind his eye and promises not to sue; the neighbor does it and still pays. Rava explains that a person does not really sign away his eyes, hands or feet, so the promise was never sincere, but Rav Asi bar Ḥama counters with a case where a man asks to be struck and wounded and collects nothing, and Rava has no answer. Rav Sheshet suggests a lost limb shames the whole family, not only the man.
bava-kamma/93.question: If a spoken yes can be reread as a no whenever a man seems to be giving away too much, what can he ever actually waive?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — the limits of consent, i.e. which injuries a person is competent to sign away — but the page names those limits outright.

answer.quote: He is not in a position to forgive the assailant for the harm caused to his family, but he may forgo compensation for his own pain.
answer.explanation: The page draws exactly the line the question asks for: a person may effectively waive payment for his own pain (and, per the mishna, for property), but not for loss of a limb, since that harms his family.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 93a: "He is not in a position to forgive the assailant for the harm caused to his family, but he may forgo compensation for his own pain.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question: Rav Sheshet's family-flaw reason states that a man may forgo payment for his own pain but not for a lost limb, and the baraita's "no that is like a yes" lets him waive damage to a garment. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and presses on something still hard — for instance why the family's stake, which no one asked, overrides the injured man's own explicit word, or why a torn garment involves no such third party. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page closely.

bava-kamma/94.summary: A robber grinds stolen wheat, bakes it, and separates the priest's portion with a blessing over it; Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov says that man is not blessing but blaspheming. Much of the argument tests whether grinding, dyeing, or carving changes a stolen item enough to make it the robber's. Then a thief's wife tells him that repenting means giving back even his belt, and the Sages respond by ruling that victims should not accept what robbers return.
bava-kamma/94.question: If the people a thief robbed are told not to take their property back, whose repentance is the ordinance protecting, and what happens to them?

judge.reachNote: Repentance is made affordable for the thief by shifting the loss permanently onto the person he robbed.

answer.quote: And with regard to one who does accept it from them, the Sages are displeased with him, since by doing so he discourages those who wish to repent.
answer.explanation: The page states plainly that the ordinance shields the would-be penitent robber, but it never says what becomes of the victims who are told to refuse their property, beyond Rav Naḥman's limit to items no longer in their initial form.

bava-kamma/95.summary: A robber takes a pregnant cow and it calves in his hands; another takes a wool-laden ewe and shears it. Rabbi Meir says he returns the animal together with the calf or the wool, and the Gemara asks why: because the animal never left its owner's ownership, or because the calf is legally the robber's and the handover is a penalty. A mishna about a dyer told to dye wool red who dyed it black decides it is a penalty.
bava-kamma/95.question: The dyer chose black over red deliberately, yet the page counts him among those who act unintentionally and lets him keep the added value, so where does violating instructions stop and robbery begin?

judge.reachNote: What makes a taking culpable enough to forfeit the enhancement: knowing the goods are not yours, or merely acting deliberately against instructions.

answer.quote: No, it is speaking of a purchaser who is a Torah scholar, and he knew that the robber had no right to sell this land. The purchaser is therefore penalized
answer.explanation: The field case shows that for Rabbi Meir's penalty "intentional" means knowing the item was not yours to take, which bears on why a deliberate but authorized handler like the dyer escapes the penalty, though the page never says this of the dyer himself.

bava-kamma/96.summary: Rav Pappa and Rava sort out which alterations to a stolen object make it the robber's own: a palm frond stripped into leaves counts, a broom twisted into rope does not, since it can be unraveled back into a broom. Crushing a stolen brick into earth counts, because any brick rebuilt from it would be a different brick. Then a man who stole a pair of oxen, plowed and sowed with them, and returned them is charged half the field's enhancement.
bava-kamma/96.question: Rav Naḥman concedes the robber owes nothing beyond the oxen themselves and charges him anyway because he is a habitual thief, so what separates that from simply deciding as he pleases?
gate: the question brings in "Naḥman", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of a judge's power to impose a penalty the law does not require, and what distinguishes penalty from caprice.

answer.quote: as our friend Huna has said about me, that King Shapur and I are brothers with regard to monetary laws
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman's only defense of the penalty beyond 'he is an experienced robber' is an assertion of his own authority in monetary law, which bears on the question without settling what limits such discretion.

bava-kamma/97.summary: Rav holds that a man who seizes another's Canaanite slave and puts him to work owes the owner nothing, since the owner lost no money. The comparison offered is a squatter in an empty courtyard: an inhabited house stays in repair, so the owner is not out of pocket. Rav Yosef bar Hama applied this to the slaves of people who owed him money, until his son pointed out that free labor from a debtor looks like interest.
bava-kamma/97.question: Rav Yosef bar Hama kept seizing his debtors' slaves after being told their labor was worth more than their board, and retracted only once it was called the appearance of interest, so why did the second objection move him and the first did not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a benefit which is otherwise free becomes forbidden once a debt relationship makes it look like interest — but the page already narrates why each objection landed as it did.

answer.quote: This statement of Rav Daniel applies when the one who seizes the slave is not owed money by the owner of the slave. But since the Master is owed money
answer.explanation: The page shows Rav Yosef bar Ḥama had a legal fallback against the first objection — "I hold in accordance with the opinion of Rav Daniel" — while Rabba's second objection removed exactly that fallback for a creditor, after which he retracted.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 97a: "This statement of Rav Daniel applies when the one who seizes the slave is not owed money by the owner of the slave. But since the Master is owed money". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page itself answers this: the first objection only knocked out Rav Naḥman's "not worth the bread in his stomach," and Rav Yosef bar Ḥama simply fell back on Rav Daniel's exemption, whereas Rabba's second objection showed Rav Daniel's rule does not apply when the seizer is the owner's creditor. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance, why the appearance of interest matters when, on Rav Daniel's own logic, the owner suffered no loss at all, or why "satisfactory to the owner" can justify free labor for a stranger but not for a creditor.

bava-kamma/98.summary: Rabba holds that throwing another person's coin into the Great Sea costs nothing, since the owner can see it resting there and go in after it. The same reasoning exempts flattening a coin's image with a hammer, slitting a cow's ear so it can no longer be brought as an offering, and burning a creditor's promissory note, which is only paper. Then Rafram makes Rav Ashi, who burned a document in his youth, pay the entire debt.
bava-kamma/98.question: If a burned note is nothing but burned paper, on what grounds did Rafram collect the full value of the debt from Rav Ashi?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether a thing whose worth is only evidentiary or potential (a note, an ear, a coin's stamp) can be damaged at all — but the page already resolves it via the garmi dispute.

answer.quote: Ameimar said: The one who rules that there is liability for damage caused by indirect action collects, in this case, the value of a proper promissory note
answer.explanation: The Gemara supplies the grounds for Rafram's collection immediately before recounting the incident: Rafram is one who holds there is liability for indirect damage (garmi), against Rabba, and therefore collects the debt's full value.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 98b: "Ameimar said: The one who rules that there is liability for damage caused by indirect action collects, in this case, the value of a proper promissory note". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a line before the Rafram story: Ameimar states that one who holds there is liability for indirect damage collects the full value of the note, which is exactly Rafram's grounds. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, press on why Rabba's "only your paper" reasoning works for a note but the Gemara still needs Rabbi Shimon's "item that causes financial loss" dispute, or on what makes a deafening blow a real change while a hammered coin is not. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-kamma/99.summary: An expert butcher cuts in the wrong spot and turns the animal into a carcass no one may eat, and Shmuel rules he pays the owner even if he worked for free. When two people press him with a source exempting unpaid experts, he tells the first his mind should be muddled, then explains he was speaking for Rabbi Meir, who counts a stumble as negligence. Rabbi Zeira adds a trick: advance the butcher a dinar, a silver coin, and he becomes liable.
bava-kamma/99.question: If a coin handed over in advance is what makes a butcher answerable for ruining your animal, what is that coin actually paying for?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether a wage buys labor or buys accountability — a nominal coin converting a favor into a guaranteed undertaking.

answer.quote: should advance him a dinar, so that he is paid for his services, and he is consequently liable to pay damages
answer.explanation: The page states the mechanism — the coin makes him a paid worker (paid bailee), which raises his liability — but it does not probe what such a token payment is really purchasing, so the question survives.

bava-kamma/100.summary: Reish Lakish hands Rabbi Elazar a dinar, a coin, to appraise, and Elazar pronounces it good. When Reish Lakish adds that he is relying on that word, Elazar asks whether an appraiser who merely spoke, and touched nothing, really owes a replacement if the coin turns out bad. The hunt for a supporting ruling of Rabbi Meir ends at a vineyard fence: the owner who never repairs the breach does nothing, and pays for the neighbor's ruined wheat.
bava-kamma/100.question: Does saying out loud that you are relying on someone's word change what that word costs them if it is wrong?

judge.reachNote: Whether announcing reliance converts free advice into an obligation, i.e. when words alone become actionable damage.

answer.quote: No, I intended to say that this is the opinion of Rabbi Meir, and we do hold in accordance with his opinion.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Elazar himself asks what the declaration of reliance accomplishes, and Reish Lakish answers that liability for such indirect harm is the accepted ruling, though the page never states outright that the spoken reliance is what creates the charge.

bava-kamma/101.summary: A carpenter is handed wood for a chair and builds a bench instead; Rabbi Meir says the change makes the furniture his and he pays for the wood, while Rabbi Yehuda gives him only the smaller of his costs or the value he added. The page then chases a harder question: once dye soaks into wool, is it still a separate thing? Ravina finds the clean test case, where a monkey dyes one man's wool with another man's dye.
bava-kamma/101.question: If the dye is visibly there but can never be handed back, is it the dye owner's property or only his loss?

judge.reachNote: Whether an enhancement absorbed into another's object is a thing one owns or only a value one can claim for.

answer.quote: Let the owner say to him: Give me my dyes that you have caused to be lost.
answer.explanation: The Gemara says that even if the dye is not substantive the owner is still entitled to monetary compensation, and it rules out literal return ("With what should he take the dyes, with soap?"), but it never resolves whether the dye remains the owner's property, which is exactly what decides Ravina's monkey case.

bava-kamma/102.summary: A man gives his agent money to buy wheat and the agent comes back with barley. Two baraitot clash: one hands the agent both the loss and the profit, the other leaves the loss with the agent but splits the profit with the investor. Then the Sages in Eretz Yisrael laugh at the whole reconciliation, asking who told the grain seller to hand his wheat to a buyer he never dealt with.
bava-kamma/102.question: If a seller has no idea he is selling to anyone but the person standing in front of him, what makes the grain belong to the man whose money it was?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of how agency transfers ownership when the seller never knew a principal existed — but the page names that idea ('like an extension of his wife's hand') and answers it.

answer.quote: the agent is performing his assignment and, as such, he is like the customer, i.e., the one who appointed him, and it is as though the latter has purchased the grain himself
answer.explanation: Rav Shmuel bar Sasrati raises exactly the note's objection, and Rabbi Abbahu answers it: an agent who performs his assignment is an extension of the principal's hand, so the grain is acquired by the one whose money it was.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 102b: "the agent is performing his assignment and, as such, he is like the customer, i.e., the one who appointed him, and it is as though the latter has purchased the grain himself". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same daf: Rav Shmuel bar Sasrati raises the identical objection and Rabbi Abbahu resolves it by treating the obedient agent as an extension of the principal's hand, proved from the wife's dyed clothing in Arakhin. Rewrite the question to start from that answer — e.g., why the 'extension of the hand' logic fails the moment the agent deviates, or why Rabbi Abba rejects Abbahu's proof and substitutes a prior transfer of the wife's clothing. Keep the summary, which tracks the page, and let it set up whichever of those tensions the new question takes.

bava-kamma/103.summary: A robber who denies the theft under oath and later repents must carry the stolen money, plus a fifth, to the victim, even as far as Media. The Gemara asks who holds this, since Rabbi Tarfon lets a man who robbed one of five people drop the money among them and walk away, while Rabbi Akiva makes him pay all five. Rava's objection is sharp: the pious man in the story never swore at all.
bava-kamma/103.question: If the Sages excused a robber from chasing his victim when the travel costs more than the theft, why is the man who cannot remember which of five people he robbed made to pay every one of them?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a leniency meant to spare expense only holds where the money actually reaches its owner — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: Rabbi Akiva holds that when the Sages instituted the ordinance, they did so only for cases where the robber knows whom he robbed
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks exactly this and answers that the Sages' leniency of paying the court applies only where the robber knows his victim, not in the case of five possible victims where the money would not reach its owner.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 103b: "Rabbi Akiva holds that when the Sages instituted the ordinance, they did so only for cases where the robber knows whom he robbed". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 103b, where the Gemara says the Sages instituted the ordinance only where the robber knows whom he robbed, since otherwise the money never reaches the owner. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for example why Rabbi Akiva penalizes even the buyer who took no oath, or why the verse about "the day of his being guilty" is read as limiting the duty to one who swore falsely. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

bava-kamma/104.summary: A robber returning what he stole may not hand it to the victim's son or to the victim's agent. Rav Ḥisda says an agent named before witnesses is a real agent, so the debtor is clear once he hands the money over; Rabba says the creditor is only vouching for a courier, and the risk of the road stays with the debtor. Rava adds that even a signed receipt fails if the creditor dies en route, so Rabbi Abba sells the debt outright.
bava-kamma/104.question: If the creditor picked the courier himself and troubled to name him before witnesses, why should the loss fall on the debtor when the money disappears on the road?

judge.reachNote: Whether naming an agent before witnesses transfers the risk of loss along with the errand, or only certifies the courier's reliability.

answer.quote: Rabba said that he is not an agent because this is what the creditor is assumed to be saying to the debtor: This individual is a trustworthy person.
answer.explanation: The page states Rabba's reason directly: appointing before witnesses is read as mere vouching for a trustworthy courier, an offer the debtor may accept at his own risk, so the risk stays with him.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Abba sells the debt outright.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rava replied: Go, and Rabbi Abba will transfer to you the rights to the money owed to him by means of acquisition of land from him

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 104a: "Rabba said that he is not an agent because this is what the creditor is assumed to be saying to the debtor: This individual is a trustworthy person.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rabbi Abba sells the debt outright.", but the page says "Rava replied: Go, and Rabbi Abba will transfer to you the rights to the money owed to him by means of acquisition of land from him". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few lines below the dispute it cites: the Gemara spells out Rabba's reasoning, that the creditor is only telling the debtor the man is trustworthy and he may rely on him if he wishes. Build the question on what remains hard after that reason is given — for instance why Rav Ḥisda's 'he took the trouble to appoint before witnesses' does not settle it, or how the court's agent escapes the problem for both sides. Also drop or correct the claim that Rabbi Abba sold the debt; the page reports Rava's advice that the rights be transferred by acquisition of land, and shows the actual transfer only in Rav Pappa's case.

bava-kamma/105.summary: Rava asks about a man who stole two bundles worth one peruta together, the smallest copper coin, and then handed back only one of them. His own answer sounds like a contradiction: nothing stolen remains in his hands, yet the mitzva of returning a stolen item was never performed. The same shape recurs twice, with a nazirite, a person under a vow not to cut his hair, who shaves all but two hairs, and with a cracked barrel whose hole is only half sealed.
bava-kamma/105.question: If the bundle left behind is too small to count as stolen property, what exactly is it that the robber still has not done?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that an obligation can lapse as a debt while the positive act of restoration still goes unperformed — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: Even though the robber is exempt from returning the second bundle, as there is no stolen item here, there is nevertheless no fulfillment of the mitzva of returning a stolen item here
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly unpacks Rava's paradoxical formulation and states that what remains undone is the mitzva of returning a stolen item, because the bundle he did hand back was itself worth less than a peruta.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 105a: "Even though the robber is exempt from returning the second bundle, as there is no stolen item here, there is nevertheless no fulfillment of the mitzva of returning a stolen item here". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara answers in so many words, and the summary itself already supplies the answer ("the mitzva of returning a stolen item was never performed"), so it is circular. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing — for instance why the barrel dilemma stays unresolved while the bundles and the nazirite hairs both get Rava's "no X here, no doing of X here" resolution, or what makes a vine-plug different from a half-seal. Keep the summary's clear framing of the three parallel dilemmas.

bava-kamma/106.summary: Rav rules that if a man swears in court that he holds none of another's hundred dinars, a dinar being a silver coin, and witnesses later prove the oath false, he pays nothing: the oath itself closes the account. Objections pile up from cases of bailees, people entrusted with someone else's property, who swore falsely and still paid. Rava rescues Rav by shrinking the ruling to one narrow case: he swore the deposit was lost, never confessed, and witnesses showed he took it.
bava-kamma/106.question: If witnesses can prove the oath was a lie, what is left in that oath that still cancels the debt?

judge.reachNote: Whether an oath settles a claim as a procedural event regardless of its truth, or only because it is believed.

answer.quote: teaching that once the owner received an oath, the one who took the oath no longer pays monetary restitution
answer.explanation: The page grounds Rav's exemption in the owner's acceptance of the oath under Exodus 22:10, which bears on what the oath accomplishes, but it does not explain why a proven lie leaves that closure intact, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-kamma/107.summary: A man admits owing part of a debt and denies the rest, and the Torah puts him under oath. Rabba explains why: no one is brazen enough to lie outright to the creditor who did him the favor of a loan, so the partial denier is really stalling, hoping to pay once he has money. That reasoning collapses for a deposit, an item left with a neighbor for safekeeping, where the owner did the keeper no favor at all.
bava-kamma/107.question: If the oath exists because a stalling debtor still has enough shame to admit part of the claim, what stops that same man from swearing falsely and stalling a little longer?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the psychological premise behind oaths: whether fear of a false oath is a stronger restraint than the shame that already stops outright denial.

answer.quote: Therefore, the Merciful One imposes an oath on him, in order to ensure that he will admit to him with regard to all of the debt.
answer.explanation: The page states the oath's purpose is to press the evader into full admission, which presumes an oath deters him, but it never explains why the same shame-lacking-but-stalling man would not simply swear falsely and stall further.

bava-kamma/108.summary: A man leaves an ox with a friend, it is stolen, and the friend swears it was taken rather than paying. Later the thief is caught, and the argument is over who collects the thief's double payment: the owner, or the bailee who paid out of his own pocket. Rava sorts it by the oath itself, since a bailee who swore truthfully is still someone the owner would trust to chase the thief, while a liar is not.
bava-kamma/108.question: If a bailee stands up to swear falsely and the owner stops him before he opens his mouth, has he already lost the standing that an honest oath would have kept?

judge.reachNote: Whether a man's standing as a trusted bailee turns on the act of lying or on the intention to lie that never reached his lips.

summaryProblems.claim: Rava resolves the who-collects-the-double-payment dispute by the truth or falsity of the bailee's oath.
summaryProblems.pageSays: once he paid, the owner grants acquisition of the double payment to the bailee

summaryProblems.claim: The oath's truthfulness is Rava's criterion in the dispute with Abaye over who collects the double payment.
summaryProblems.pageSays: since the bailee troubled him by taking an oath instead of paying immediately, the owner is not willing to grant acquisition of the double payment to the bailee

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rava resolves the who-collects-the-double-payment dispute by the truth or falsity of the bailee's oath.", but the page says "once he paid, the owner grants acquisition of the double payment to the bailee". Say what the page says. The summary says "The oath's truthfulness is Rava's criterion in the dispute with Abaye over who collects the double payment.", but the page says "since the bailee troubled him by taking an oath instead of paying immediately, the owner is not willing to grant acquisition of the double payment to the bailee". Say what the page says. Separate the two sugyot the summary has fused: in the Abaye–Rava dispute over who collects double payment, Rava's criterion is that the bailee paid (the owner then grants him acquisition), while it is Abaye who cares that the bailee took an oath. Rava's true-oath/false-oath test belongs to a later, different case about whether the thief's admission to the bailee exempts him from double payment. Rewrite the summary so the case it describes and the reason it attributes to Rava come from the same passage, and keep the question tied to that passage.

bava-kamma/109.summary: A man robs his father, the father dies, and the son is the sole heir, yet the mishna says he still cannot keep the money. The Gemara asks why he cannot simply forgive the debt to himself, and tests it against the case of someone who robbed a convert with no heirs, whose payment goes to the priests on duty. Rabbi Akiva holds the robber has no relief until the stolen item leaves his hands.
bava-kamma/109.question: If a priest on the week's watch already owns a share of whatever a robber pays, why does money already sitting in his hands become less his rather than more?

judge.reachNote: Whether physical possession strengthens a claim or is irrelevant when others hold an equal prior share — the page states the answer outright.

answer.quote: so too, other priests on that watch have a portion in it. Rather, the halakha is that the item he stole is removed
answer.explanation: The baraita explicitly rejects the priest-robber's a fortiori argument by noting that the other priests of the watch share a portion in the payment, unlike teruma, so it is taken from him and divided among all of them.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 109b: "so too, other priests on that watch have a portion in it. Rather, the halakha is that the item he stole is removed". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered flatly on the page: the baraita rejects the priest's kal vaḥomer because his fellow priests of the watch also have a portion, so the money is taken from him and split. Write a question from something the page leaves unsettled — for example why the Gemara abandons the impure-priest answer and reaches for the verbal analogy from the ancestral field, or why a robber can forgive a debt to others but not to himself. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

bava-kamma/110.summary: A man robs a convert, swears falsely that he did not, and then the convert dies leaving no heirs, so the principal plus a fifth goes to the priests instead. Rava asks whether those priests hold the money as the convert's heirs or as people receiving a gift, and tests it with stolen bread that sat through Passover until it was worth nothing. A baraita listing twenty-four priestly gifts settles the question: gift.
bava-kamma/110.question: If the stolen loaf has turned into worthless dust by the time it reaches the priests, has the robber handed over anything at all?
gate: gloss "priestly gifts" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward whether 'giving' requires transferring value or only transferring the very object the Torah assigned to the priests.

bava-kamma/111.summary: A man robs food, feeds it to his children, and dies, and the mishna exempts the children from paying the victim. Rami bar Ḥama reads that as meaning an heir is like a buyer, with the stolen item fully changing hands; Rava says inheritance is no sale, and the exemption applies only once the children have eaten it. Against Rava stands the ruling that even a stolen cow the father plowed with must go back, for his honor.
bava-kamma/111.question: Why should a stolen cow be returned as a matter of honoring the dead father rather than as a debt owed to the man it was taken from?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the difference between a legally enforceable debt and a duty of filial honor that restores what law no longer demands.

answer.quote: Since the owner has despaired of retrieving the item and the item has changed domains, it is entirely the property of the new owner, and he is exempt from payment.
answer.explanation: The page explains why no monetary debt binds the heirs (change of domain after despair), which bears on why the cow's return is framed as honor rather than debt, but it never states why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi chose honor as the ground.

bava-kamma/112.summary: A man robs his neighbor of food, feeds it to his children, and dies; the children owe nothing for what they ate, but early teachings disagree about stolen goods still sitting in the house when the heirs are minors. Rabbi Yirmeya's young brother-in-law shut the doors of a disputed house against him, and Rabbi Avin refused to hear witnesses, because a minor's presence is not legally recognized. Rabbi Yirmeya's retort, that the world adopted Sumakhos just to seize what is his, gets no answer.
bava-kamma/112.question: If a minor's presence in court does not count, how can a court order that same minor to hand back the stolen goods his father left him?

judge.reachNote: Whether a minor can be a legal party at all — liable to return property yet unable to be tried — is the idea, but the page asks and settles this exchange itself.

answer.quote: Sumakhos's dispute is at your side, i.e., Sumakhos disagrees with this ruling and holds that the minors are exempt from paying.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yirmeya raises precisely the note's objection from the baraita obligating minor heirs, and Rabbi Avin answers it by invoking Sumakhos, who exempts minors, so no court ever obligates a minor.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Yirmeya's retort about Sumakhos gets no answer.
summaryProblems.pageSays: In the meantime, the matter circulated and eventually came before Rabbi Abbahu, who said: Did you not hear that which Rav Yosef bar Ḥama says
