judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Kamma 112b: "Sumakhos's dispute is at your side, i.e., Sumakhos disagrees with this ruling and holds that the minors are exempt from paying.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rabbi Yirmeya's retort about Sumakhos gets no answer.", but the page says "In the meantime, the matter circulated and eventually came before Rabbi Abbahu, who said: Did you not hear that which Rav Yosef bar Ḥama says". Say what the page says. The question is the very objection Rabbi Yirmeya raises on 112b, and Rabbi Avin answers it on the spot by saying that ruling is Sumakhos's disputant and that Sumakhos exempts minors. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing — for instance why a presumption of ownership inherited from a father protects a minor when a minor holding slaves in another's field is dispossessed at once. Also drop or correct the claim that Rabbi Yirmeya's retort goes unanswered, since the case then travels to Rabbi Abbahu, who rules for him before the Gemara rejects the comparison.

bava-kamma/113.summary: A man who ignores a court summons gets three dates, Monday, Thursday, Monday, before a document of ostracism is written about him; Rav Kahana wrote one against a woman after a single missed evening, since she is always in town. The page then sets Shmuel's rule that the law of the kingdom is the law against a mishna barring changing coins from a tax collector's trunk. The answer: that collector has no limit set on him, or appointed himself.
bava-kamma/113.question: Why does Rabbi Akiva block a judge from steering a case circuitously toward the Jew only because God's name would be desecrated, rather than because the steering is crooked?
gate: the question brings in "Akiva", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether honesty in judgment is owed intrinsically or only because God's reputation is at stake.

answer.quote: if there is no consideration of the sanctification of God’s name, the court does approach the case circuitously. Apparently, it is permitted to deceive a gentile.
answer.explanation: The Gemara's own inference explains that the crookedness itself is not the bar — deceiving a gentile is otherwise permitted (later narrowed by Rava to abrogating a loan rather than actual robbery) — so only desecration of God's name restrains the judge, though why that should be so morally is not spelled out.

bava-kamma/114.summary: A customs collector takes a man's donkey and gives him a donkey seized from some other Jew, and he may keep it, since the first owner had already given up hope. Rav Ashi says such despair is assumed only when the bandit is a gentile; Rav Yosef reverses him, because gentile courts seize property by force while Jewish courts can only pronounce a verdict. Much of the argument then turns on whether a sneak thief or a brazen robber is harder to catch.
bava-kamma/114.question: If a victim gives up hope only because his own court cannot enforce its rulings, has the thief acquired the donkey, or has the court handed it to him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that despair-based acquisition may rest on the court's inability to enforce rather than on any real act of the owner's will.

answer.quote: where it is known that the owners despaired, all agree that their despair effects legal acquisition
answer.where: Bava Kamma 114a (Ulla's statement on the dispute)
answer.explanation: The page states that known despair does effect acquisition (Ulla), and Rabba's counter that there is no true despair, but it never addresses the question's second horn — whether the transfer is really the court's doing rather than the owner's relinquishment.

bava-kamma/115.summary: A thief steals a cloak and sells it, and then he is identified; the argument is whether the owner can reclaim the cloak from the buyer, and whether he must repay what the buyer paid. The Sages' provision ensuring the integrity of the marketplace reimburses the innocent buyer, but not everyone qualifies, and Rava withholds it when the seller is a well-known thief whom a buyer should have suspected. Ḥanan the Wicked was famous, the page says, for villainy rather than theft.
bava-kamma/115.question: If a buyer knows a man is called the Wicked, how finely is he expected to sort the crimes that man is known for from the ones he might commit?

judge.reachNote: What knowledge a buyer is charged with: does a seller's general bad reputation put him on notice, or only notoriety for the specific crime of theft?

answer.quote: Although he was well known for villainy, he was not well known for theft.
answer.explanation: The page draws exactly the distinction the question probes — notoriety must be for theft specifically — but it never states how a buyer is expected to make that discrimination, so the question survives.

bava-kamma/116.summary: A man fleeing prison offers a ferryman an entire dinar, a silver coin worth far more than the crossing, and then claims he was only fooling. The distinction drawn is wording: say "take this dinar as your wage" and the full sum is owed, and Rami bar Hama imagines the ferryman as a fisherman losing a dinar of fish. Rav then rules that a man who let his own donkey go to save another's still collects, even when his donkey climbs out by itself.
bava-kamma/116.question: If the rescuer keeps his payment when his own donkey surfaces alive, why does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi give him only a wage when he dives in and the other donkey drowns?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "HaNasi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward whether compensation rests on the rescuer's loss or on his accomplishment of the task, but the page spells that distinction out.

bava-kamma/117.summary: A man holding someone else's silver cup in trust hands it over when thieves break into his house, and Rabba exempts him from paying. Abaye objects three times with the same line: the man is saving himself with another's property. Rabba answers differently each time, calling the owner of a donkey that nearly sank a crowded ferry a pursuer, while Rav Ashi settles the cup case by how rich the man holding it looked to the thieves.
bava-kamma/117.question: If liability for the handed-over cup turns on whether the thieves were likely after the rich man rather than the cup, what is the man actually being judged for?

judge.reachNote: Whether liability for handing over a deposit rests on the act itself or on whose interest the handover actually served.

answer.quote: If the bailee is a wealthy man, the thieves came with the intent to steal his property, and he is therefore liable to pay, as he saved himself from financial loss
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi states the basis of judgment — whether the bailee used another's property to spare his own loss — though the question can still be pressed as to why presumed thief intent decides that.

bava-kamma/118.summary: A thief slips a stolen lamb back into the flock without saying a word, and later it dies or is stolen again. Rav, Shmuel, Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rav Ḥisda split four ways over whether the owner's routine count of his sheep ends the thief's liability, and whether it matters that the owner ever knew of the theft. Rava adds a wrinkle: the lamb has learned to wander off, so it now needs closer watching than its owner knows to give.
bava-kamma/118.question: If the returned lamb has picked up a habit of straying, can an owner who counted his flock and found it whole really be said to have gotten his animal back?

judge.reachNote: What counts as restoration: is an object returned when its condition or habits have made it riskier to guard than what was taken?

answer.quote: Since the thief taught the lamb to take steps outside, i.e., to leave the owners’ property, it will now require greater supervision, which the owners can provide only if they are aware
answer.explanation: Rava's explanation of Rav Ḥisda bears directly on the question — a strayed-trained lamb needs awareness, not just a count — but only for the case where the owners never knew of the theft, so the question of whether counting itself restores the animal remains live.

bava-kamma/119.summary: Rava buys grapevine branches from a sharecropper, and Abaye objects that a sharecropper, like a hired produce watchman, does not own what he sells. From there the page reaches Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says robbing another of a peruta, the smallest copper coin, is like taking his life, and stacks four verses to block every escape from that claim. Then it turns to who owns a launderer's loose threads, a carpenter's sawdust, and weeds nobody planted.
bava-kamma/119.question: If taking a peruta is counted as taking a life, why does ownership of the shavings and the weeds depend on whether the owner happens to be particular about them?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that theft's gravity depends first on what counts as owned, and ownership can hinge on what an owner cares about.

answer.quote: Dodder [keshut] and green grain [veḥaziz], are not subject to the prohibition against robbery, as they grow on their own and no one tends to them.
answer.explanation: The page explains that items nobody tends to or cares about are simply not within the category of robbery, which bears on the tension but does not directly address why severity of theft coexists with owner-dependent ownership.

bava-metzia/2.summary: Two people walk into court holding one garment, each claiming he found it and all of it is his. The mishna splits it, but only after each swears he owns no less than half. The Gemara worries about the doubled wording: why say both "I found it" and "all of it is mine"? One answer is that seeing a lost item first is not acquiring it. Another reads the second clause as a disputed sale, where the seller took money from both buyers.
bava-metzia/2.question: If ben Nannas refuses an oath when one party is certainly lying, does the court's escape here, that maybe both men really lifted the garment at once, work as a truth or just as a convenience?
gate: the question brings in "Nannas", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a merely conceivable scenario can license an oath, or whether law here leans on a fiction to get a workable outcome.

answer.quote: Say that they are both taking an oath truthfully, as they lifted the item together, and therefore each of them owns half of it.
answer.explanation: The Gemara does state the escape route the question asks about — that the two oaths can both be true if the pair lifted the garment simultaneously — but it never addresses whether this possibility is a real account or a convenient device, so the question survives.

bava-metzia/3.summary: Two men come to court each holding a garment and each saying he found it, and the page asks which sages could agree that they swear and split it. Rabbi Yosei would lock away a disputed deposit entirely, since one of two depositors is certainly a swindler; the garment case differs because both may have lifted it at once. Then Rabba explains why a debtor who admits owing half must swear: a person hesitates to lie to his creditor's face.
bava-metzia/3.question: If Rabba is right that a person shrinks from denying a debt to his creditor's face, why would that same person be willing to swear falsely about the rest?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the psychology behind the oath of partial admission — why reluctance to lie to a creditor's face coexists with a false denial.

answer.quote: This rationalization enables one to falsely deny part of a claim. And therefore, the Merciful One states: Impose an oath on him, in order to ensure that he will admit
answer.explanation: The page itself resolves the tension: the debtor only rationalizes a temporary partial denial (intending to pay later), and the imposed oath is precisely what is expected to make him admit the whole debt rather than swear falsely.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 3b: "This rationalization enables one to falsely deny part of a claim. And therefore, the Merciful One states: Impose an oath on him, in order to ensure that he will admit". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: the debtor's partial denial is a rationalized delay ("I will continue doing so until I have money"), and the oath is imposed "in order to ensure that he will admit to him with regard to all of the debt." Ask something that survives that answer — for instance, why Rabba's insolence logic cannot extend to a defendant convicted by witnesses, whose oath the Gemara calls worthless, yet the baraita still imposes one on him.

bava-metzia/4.summary: A creditor claims a hundred dinars, silver coins; the debtor says he owes only fifty and hands them over on the spot. Rabbi Ḥiyya holds he must still swear he owes nothing more, while Rav Sheshet says money already handed over is not an admission to part of a claim, so no oath. Testing this against a promissory note written for unspecified dinars, the Gemara worries that a debtor might admit to three coins rather than two purely to escape swearing.
bava-metzia/4.question: If admitting to more than you have to can free you from an oath, is the court rewarding honesty or rewarding calculation?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that an oath rule can create incentives, so the law must be shaped so a defendant cannot profit by confessing more than he owes.

answer.quote: Perhaps this debtor is employing artifice, thinking: If I say that I owe two, I will be required to take an oath. Therefore, I will say that I owe three
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this worry about calculation and uses it to conclude that one who admits to two is also exempt, so no advantage is gained by overstating, though it never frames the choice as rewarding honesty.

summaryProblems.claim: The hundred dinars claimed are described as silver coins.
summaryProblems.pageSays: I have one hundred dinars in your possession, and the other says in response: You have only fifty dinars in my possession

judge.feedback: The summary says "The hundred dinars claimed are described as silver coins.", but the page says "I have one hundred dinars in your possession, and the other says in response: You have only fifty dinars in my possession". Say what the page says.

bava-metzia/5.summary: A shepherd who was handed animals each day, once without witnesses, denied receiving them, and witnesses testified he had eaten two of them. Later the Gemara asks why two men each gripping half a garment must swear at all, since each walks away with what he holds; Rabbi Yoḥanan says the oath exists so people will not grab garments and claim them. A man suspected of stealing is still trusted to swear, because a false oath is assumed to frighten him more than theft does.
bava-metzia/5.question: If a man will seize another's garment and claim it in court, why assume a false oath is the line he will not cross?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that transgressions are graded in a person's own conscience, so dishonesty about money does not presume dishonesty under oath — but the page states that idea outright.

answer.quote: we do not say that since one is suspect with regard to financial dishonesty he is suspect with regard to taking an oath. This is because even one who steals property is presumed to consider taking a false oath more severe.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection and answers that a thief is still presumed to regard a false oath as the graver transgression, a distinction it then supports with Rabba's 'buying time' explanation and Rav Ḥisda's ruling on loans versus deposits.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 5b: "we do not say that since one is suspect with regard to financial dishonesty he is suspect with regard to taking an oath. This is because even one who steals property is presumed to consider taking a false oath more severe.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the summary already paraphrases: the Gemara asks whether one suspect about money is suspect about oaths and replies that even a thief holds a false oath to be more severe. Build the new question on what the page leaves unsettled after that answer — for instance why denying a deposit disqualifies a witness while denying a loan does not, or why the bailee's rationalization ('I gave him money for the item') is enough to keep his oath credible. Keep the summary, which is accurate.

bava-metzia/6.summary: If a court already suspects a man of holding money that is not his, it is strange that it then trusts him with an oath. Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, answers that people will grab property they are unsure about but hesitate to swear about it, since property can be handed back and a false oath cannot be undone. Rabbi Zeira then asks about a man whose garment was seized in front of the judges, who said nothing and only shouted later.
bava-metzia/6.question: Is staying quiet while judges watch your garment being grabbed an admission that it was never yours, or the reasonable thought that the judges saw it and would say something?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether silence before a court counts as consent, or is excused when the court itself witnessed the taking.

bava-metzia/7.summary: Two men hold one garment, and an early teaching has each take the cloth as far as his hand reaches, dividing only the middle. Rav Pappa keeps the Mishna's even split by having both grip the fringes, and Rava rules that gold thread lying nearer one of them is still halved, since the other can demand a widthwise cut. Ravina finally says such divisions are of value, not fabric, though the page still allows that the two actually cut the garment.
bava-metzia/7.question: If splitting a disputed item is really a splitting of its worth, why does the discussion end by conceding that the two men might in fact cut the garment in half and wreck it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what 'dividing' a disputed item means — apportioning worth or severing substance — and whether the garment case proves it.

answer.quote: The Gemara rejects this proof: This is not difficult, as it is possible to explain that they actually cut the garment in two.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the concession itself as a rejection of the proof from the garment, but it never explains why cutting a garment in two would be acceptable, so the question can still be honestly asked.

bava-metzia/8.summary: Two people grip one garment, each claiming all of it, and the Gemara asks whether dividing it means tearing the cloth in half. A non-kosher animal settles the point: slaughtering it would leave a worthless carcass, so what gets split is value, not substance. Then Rami bar Ḥama argues that lifting a found object on another's behalf wins it for that person, and Rava counters with thieves, since a partner who lifts stolen goods acquires a share for his partner.
bava-metzia/8.question: If the Sages gave two deaf-mutes what they lifted together so they would not quarrel with anyone who grabbed it, why is it so certain that a deaf-mute lifting alongside a competent person would quietly let go?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a rabbinic enactment is calibrated to the likelihood of a quarrel rather than to acquisition capacity, but the page already spells that calibration out.

answer.quote: the deaf-mute says to himself: If even the mentally competent person does not acquire the item, can I acquire it? Therefore, in that case, he will not quarrel
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this contrast with the two-deaf-mutes ordinance and states the reason the deaf-mute will not quarrel in the mixed case.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 8a: "the deaf-mute says to himself: If even the mentally competent person does not acquire the item, can I acquire it? Therefore, in that case, he will not quarrel". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words a few lines later, where the deaf-mute reasons that if even the competent person acquires nothing, he cannot, and so will not quarrel. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than asking for it. A better target is the oddity that two incapable people acquire by ordinance while one incapable person paired with a capable one acquires nothing, or that Rava's miggo is quietly replaced mid-passage by a different miggo.

bava-metzia/9.summary: A man sits on a donkey while another holds the reins, and the Gemara spends several rounds deciding who owns what, down to the strip of rope between them. Rava then says a walking animal cannot acquire the vessels on its back, since a courtyard acquires for its owner only if it stays put. Asked about fish jumping into a moving boat and a bill of divorce dropped into a walking woman's basket, he answers that boat and basket sit idle; the water, and the woman, do the moving.
bava-metzia/9.question: If a basket sits idle while the woman walks beneath it, why doesn't a pack of vessels sit idle while the donkey walks beneath them?

judge.reachNote: What disqualifies a mobile courtyard: that the receptacle is in motion, or that the receptacle is itself the thing doing the moving?

answer.quote: Her basket is not considered a mobile courtyard, as it sits idle, and it is she who walks beneath it.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the criterion the question leans on — the receptacle itself being idle while something else moves it — but never applies it to the vessels resting on a self-propelled donkey, so the question survives the answer.

bava-metzia/10.summary: A man sees a found object in the street and throws himself on top of it; another comes along, picks it up, and the second man owns it. Reish Lakish says the four cubits around a person work like his courtyard and acquire ownerless things for him, an ordinance made to prevent quarrels. The answer offered here is that by falling on the object he showed he preferred that method, and so forfeited the one that would have worked.
bava-metzia/10.question: If the four-cubit rule was instituted to stop fights over found objects, why should a man's clumsy lunge at the object cancel the very protection that would have kept him from losing it?

judge.reachNote: Can a rule enacted for the public good (preventing quarrels) be forfeited by the private, half-formed intention of the person it protects?

answer.quote: Since he fell upon it, he revealed his intention that it is satisfactory for him to acquire the item by falling on it, and it is not satisfactory
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains that falling constitutes a deliberate forgoing of the four-cubit ordinance, but it never addresses why an ordinance instituted for public peace should be waivable by an individual's fumbling act, which is the note's pressure point.

bava-metzia/11.summary: The mishna pictures someone watching a crowd chase a deer with a broken leg, or fledgling pigeons too young to fly, who says: my field has acquired it for me. Shmuel adds a condition, that the field only works if the owner is standing beside it, and the page hunts for proof in a sheaf forgotten by a farmer who is back in town. Rabbi Abba objects with Rabban Gamliel assigning tithes while at sea, and Ulla simply refuses to engage.
bava-metzia/11.question: Why should a bill of divorce, which can be given to a wife against her will, require her to stand beside her courtyard, while a gift she must actively want can reach her anywhere?

judge.reachNote: Whether a courtyard needs its owner's presence depends on whether consent or another person's mind is driving the transfer.

answer.quote: A bill of divorce is different, as it is possible to give it to one's wife even against her will.
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa offers exactly this distinction, but the page immediately has Rav Sheshet refute it with the a fortiori the note's question voices, and Rav Ashi's replacement answer is cut off at the end of the daf.

bava-metzia/12.summary: The mishna says an object found by a man's minor son belongs to the father, and Shmuel explains that a small child runs home with what he finds. But a baraita lets a sharecropper's son glean stalks left for the poor, which works only if the boy can own things. Abaye says the poor write off that field once they see the boy; Rav Adda bar Mattana asks whether one may keep a lion crouching there too.
bava-metzia/12.question: Rava's fix repays the poor with gleanings their own sons might collect years from now, so is that payment or only a promise?
gate: the question brings in "Rava's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a future reciprocal benefit can stand as present consideration for waiving a present entitlement.

answer.quote: This arrangement is satisfactory for the poor people themselves, so that when they are hired under similar terms themselves, their sons will be able to glean
answer.explanation: The page states Rava's rationale — the poor accept the ordinance because of the reciprocal future benefit to their own sons — but never addresses whether such a deferred, contingent benefit counts as real compensation or merely a promise, so the note's question survives the line it quotes.

bava-metzia/13.summary: Someone finds a promissory note, a written record of a loan, and the question is whether to hand it back to the creditor. If it carries a property guarantee, the creditor can seize land the debtor sold years ago, so the finder keeps it. Abaye and Rav Asi argue over when the creditor's claim on that land begins; in Shmuel's version the note ends up worth only its paper, good for covering the opening of a flask.
bava-metzia/13.question: When the creditor and the debtor both say the debt is real, what makes their agreement grounds for suspicion rather than proof?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a debt admitted by both parties can still be a fiction because the loser is an absent third party, the purchaser of the land.

answer.quote: Although the debtor admits his debt, he is suspected to be lying, as after he repaid the debt he might have colluded with the creditor to repossess land that he sold
answer.explanation: The page explicitly states why the two parties' mutual agreement is grounds for suspicion: they may be colluding after repayment to repossess land from purchasers and split the proceeds.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 13a: "Although the debtor admits his debt, he is suspected to be lying, as after he repaid the debt he might have colluded with the creditor to repossess land that he sold". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered flatly on the daf: Abaye explains the mishna by saying the tanna suspects "repayment and collusion," with the debtor and creditor splitting money squeezed from purchasers. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard, for example that Rabbi Elazar and Shmuel refuse to suspect collusion at all while the baraita suspects it even under Rabbi Meir, or that the debtor who denies the loan is denied even the paper. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-metzia/14.summary: Avuh bar Ihi bought a loft from his sister, her creditor seized it, and Shmuel told him there was no guarantee clause in the deed: go to peace. Shmuel treats a missing guarantee in a loan document as a scribal slip, but in a land sale as a real choice, since a person may buy land for a single day. Then the page asks whether a buyer whose field is repossessed collects for improvements he made, or whether that payment looks like interest.
bava-metzia/14.question: If paying a buyer for the improvements he made to a field that was never the seller's to sell looks like interest, why does the same payment look clean when it is the seller's own creditor who takes the field?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that whether a payment counts as interest depends on whether the underlying sale was ever a real sale or a disguised loan.

bava-metzia/15.summary: A man buys a field knowing the seller robbed it, and when the true owner takes it back, the money he paid is left stranded. Rav says he meant it as a deposit; Shmuel says a gift, and each side explains why the buyer never said so aloud: the seller would have refused it, or been embarrassed. The same split is then run through a man who hands betrothal money to his own sister, where the betrothal cannot take effect.
bava-metzia/15.question: What in a wordless handing over of money decides whether it was a deposit to be returned or a gift to be kept?

judge.reachNote: How law reconstructs unspoken intent when a payment's stated purpose collapses — deposit or gift is read off the relationship and social plausibility, not off words.

answer.quote: as people do not tend to give gifts to non-relatives, and therefore it is clear that the purchaser intended for the money to be a deposit
answer.explanation: The Gemara's discussion of why both cases are needed names the relationship between the parties as the consideration that tips a silent transfer toward deposit or gift, but the underlying dispute between Rav and Shmuel is left standing, so the question can still be asked.

bava-metzia/16.summary: A man sells land he stole, then buys it from the rightful owner, and Rav says the buyer keeps it. The Gemara hunts for a case that separates two motives, not wanting to be called a robber and wanting to keep a reputation for reliability, and lands on land handed over as a gift, where the recipient lost nothing. Then it asks how long the motive lasts: until trial, until the seizure order, until the days of announcement.
bava-metzia/16.question: If the sale holds only because the buyer relied on the robber to make it good, why does the clock run on the robber's reputation rather than on the moment the buyer stopped trusting him?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the real idea — whether the sale is held together by the seller's concern for his name or by the buyer's reliance — but the page already fuses the two in explaining the deadline.

answer.quote: Once the purchaser takes the robber to court, it is too late for the robber to protect his reputation, as the purchaser has demonstrated that he does not consider the robber to be trustworthy.
answer.explanation: The page explains Rav Huna's deadline precisely as the moment the buyer shows he no longer trusts the robber, so the reputation clock is the trust clock.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 16a: "Once the purchaser takes the robber to court, it is too late for the robber to protect his reputation, as the purchaser has demonstrated that he does not consider the robber to be trustworthy.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Rav Huna's cutoff at trial is explained by the purchaser having "demonstrated that he does not consider the robber to be trustworthy," so the reputation clock and the trust clock are the same clock. Rewrite the question to start from that and press on what is still hard — for instance why Ḥiyya bar Rav and Rav Pappa push the deadline past the trial to the seizure document or the days of announcement, when the buyer's distrust was already on record. Or ask what Rava's reliance answer to Rami bar Ḥama adds if reliance is only the mirror of the seller's fear of being called a robber.

bava-metzia/17.summary: Shabbtai, son of Rabbi Marinus, pledged a cloak of fine wool in his daughter-in-law's marriage contract, then denied ever writing it; witnesses said he had, so he switched to claiming he already handed it over. Rabbi Ḥiyya ruled he had become a known denier of debts and could not clear himself even by oath. But a debtor who stalls before the court finalizes its verdict is treated as merely evading, not lying, and keeps his oath.
bava-metzia/17.question: Why does one caught denying a debt outright lose the oath forever, while one who stalls until the verdict is final is credited with simply hoping the judges would rule his way?

judge.reachNote: When does a false statement destroy a litigant's credibility, and when is it read as permitted tactical delay within an unfinished proceeding?

answer.quote: It is because before the court verdict was finalized, the debtor was merely trying to evade the creditor, thinking to himself: Since the court has not yet finalized the verdict
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself asks why the pre-verdict staller is not presumed a liar and answers that he was only evading until the verdict became binding, though it never states why outright denial forfeits the oath permanently.

bava-metzia/18.summary: The mishna says a finder may not hand over bills of divorce, wills, receipts, or deeds of gift, since the writer may have written them and then changed his mind. But if the writer says to deliver it, the finder must, and that collides with a rule elsewhere that a lost bill of divorce counts only if found immediately. Rabba splits the cases by whether caravans pass through the place and whether two men in town share a name.
bava-metzia/18.question: Rabba ruled that a bill of divorce found in a flax house in Pumbedita should be returned, yet the report splits over whether it was the place flax is sold or the place flax is soaked, two facts that lead to opposite reasons; what is left of a ruling when nobody can say where it happened?
gate: the question brings in "Pumbedita", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: A ruling's force lies in the principle it applies, not in the contested facts of the incident — precedent survives even when the reported setting is disputed.

answer.quote: Rabba performed an action, i.e., issued a practical ruling, with regard to a certain bill of divorce that was found in a flax house in the city of Pumbedita, in accordance with his halakha
answer.explanation: The page reports that the ruling was made 'in accordance with his halakha' and then shows that each version of the location supplies a reason consistent with that same principle, which bears on the question without directly addressing what survives when the setting is unknown.

bava-metzia/19.summary: A found bill of divorce can be handed to the wife when the husband admits he wrote it, but a found promissory note with a property guarantee cannot be handed back to the lender. Both raise the same fear: a document written in Nisan, delivered only in Tishrei, used to claw back property sold in between. The distinction turns on what a buyer will assume about why the court released the paper, not on the paper itself.
bava-metzia/19.question: Should a document's fate depend on what a third party will guess about the court's reasoning?

judge.reachNote: Whether a court's procedural act becomes a public representation of validity that third parties may rely on.

answer.quote: here, with regard to a promissory note, the purchaser will not come and demand proof, because he will infer from the fact that the Sages returned the promissory note
answer.explanation: The page states that the outcome does hinge on the purchaser's inference about the court's act, but it never addresses whether it ought to, so the note's normative question survives.

bava-metzia/20.summary: A simpon is a note saying a debt has been paid, and Rav rules that one found in the creditor's hands is void even in the creditor's own handwriting. His reason: the creditor may have written it in advance, in case the debtor shows up with the money at twilight on the eve of Shabbat. Three separate mishnayot appear to treat such a receipt as binding, and each time the answer is the same, that it turned up among torn documents.
bava-metzia/20.question: If a creditor's own handwriting proves nothing but the scrap heap he tossed it into proves everything, what is actually being trusted here?

judge.reachNote: What gives a document credibility: its content and script, or the circumstances and conduct surrounding it.

answer.quote: had the debt not been repaid, the creditor would not have put the simpon note among torn documents
answer.explanation: The page states outright what is being trusted in the torn-documents case: not the writing, but the creditor's act of discarding the note, which he would only do after repayment.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 20b: "had the debt not been repaid, the creditor would not have put the simpon note among torn documents". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question: the writing proves nothing because the creditor may have prepared it in advance, while the torn-document pile proves payment because he would not have discarded it otherwise. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and presses on what still troubles a reader, for example why a creditor's deliberate signed writing counts for less than where a note happened to be lying, or what a rule like this assumes about how people handle their own papers.

bava-metzia/21.summary: A mishna lists found items a finder may keep because nothing marks them as anyone's: scattered coins, baker's loaves, strings of fish, bundles of flax. Rabbi Yitzhak sets a threshold for scattered wheat, one kav, a dry measure of a few quarts, spread over four by four cubits, and Rabbi Yirmeya's questions about sesame, dates and pomegranates all end unresolved. Then Abaye and Rava split over whether a man who does not yet know he dropped something has already given up on it.
bava-metzia/21.question: Can an owner lose his claim through a despair he has not felt yet, simply because everyone agrees he would feel it once he checked his pocket?

judge.reachNote: Whether a legal status (relinquishment of ownership) can attach on the basis of what a person would feel rather than what he does feel.

answer.quote: Rava said: Despair that is not conscious is considered despair, as when he discovers that it fell from him, he will despair of its recovery
answer.explanation: The page names exactly this dispute and gives Rava's affirmative reasoning, but Abaye holds the opposite and the long chain of proofs is each time rejected, so no resolution is reached.

bava-metzia/22.summary: Three Sages stop at Mari bar Isak's orchard, and his sharecropper sets dates and pomegranates before them. The owner arrives and scolds the sharecropper for not serving better fruit; Ameimar and Rav Ashi keep eating, but Mar Zutra refuses, saying the same sentence that counts as consent when someone separates teruma, the priest's portion of a crop, is here only embarrassment. The larger argument, whether an owner who does not yet know his property is gone can have given up on it, ends with Rava refuted.
bava-metzia/22.question: If the same words signal real consent over teruma but only shame over a bowl of dates, how would anyone at that table know which one Mari bar Isak meant?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is how to tell sincere consent from polite embarrassment in identical words — but the page supplies the mitzva/shame test outright.

answer.quote: indicates consent of the owner only with regard to the matter of teruma, due to the fact that it is a mitzva
answer.explanation: Mar Zutra, citing Rava, states the very criterion the question asks for: the words count as consent only where a mitzva is at stake, and otherwise are said out of shame.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 22a: "indicates consent of the owner only with regard to the matter of teruma, due to the fact that it is a mitzva". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in the very line the summary paraphrases: Rava's rule that the phrase signals consent only for teruma, because the owner is amenable to a mitzva being fulfilled. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what it leaves unsettled — for instance, why presumed goodwill toward a mitzva is treated as real knowledge, when the surrounding sugya is fighting over whether despair a person has not yet felt counts at all. Alternatively, build the question on another thread of the page, such as the dates blown off the tree or the trampled distinguishing mark.

bava-metzia/23.summary: A finder picks up bundles of grain in a busy street, and the question is whether anything about them still identifies their owner after feet have trampled and kicked them. The discussion runs through candidates for an identifying mark: the fisherman's knot everyone ties the same way, the number of fish on a string, the weight of a cut of meat, Rabba bar Rav Huna's habit of cutting meat into triangles. Location fails the test, since someone else could just as easily have left something in that spot.
bava-metzia/23.question: If a Torah scholar gets a lost vessel back on his word that he recognizes it, how does that square with the same passage listing three subjects on which Sages may say something untrue?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: Why a scholar's bare recognition counts as legal proof at all, and what trust in a Sage's word is worth once the page concedes he sometimes deviates from the truth.

answer.quote: With regard to these three matters alone, it is normal for Sages to amend their statements and deviate from the truth
answer.explanation: The page cites the three-matters teaching as the very support for returning items to a scholar, implying that outside those three limited subjects a Sage's word is reliable, though it never spells out that resolution.

bava-metzia/24.summary: Mar Zutra Ḥasida found the thief of his host's silver goblet by noticing a student who dried his hands on another man's cloak. Most of the daf asks whether a purse dropped in a crowded market belongs to the finder, on the theory that the owner has despaired of it. Shmuel says it is legally the finder's but returns such things anyway, beyond the letter of the law; Rav Naḥman tells the still-shouting owner he is shouting about a sunken ship.
bava-metzia/24.question: If the man who lost the purse is standing there screaming for it, on what basis is he said to have given up hope?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of presumed (objective) despair versus the owner's actual, voiced refusal to give up hope.

answer.quote: He becomes as one who screams to no avail about his house that collapsed or about his ship that sank in the sea.
answer.explanation: Rava raises exactly the note's objection — the owner is standing and screaming — and Rav Naḥman answers that such screaming is futile, since the loss in a public place already took effect like a collapsed house or sunken ship.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 24b: "He becomes as one who screams to no avail about his house that collapsed or about his ship that sank in the sea.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection on 24b, and Rav Naḥman answers it with the collapsed-house/sunken-ship line that the summary itself already quotes. Ask something that starts after that answer — for instance, why a loss the owner never accepted is treated as irreversible, or why Shmuel and Rav Naḥman split on returning to an owner who can identify the purse. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful to the page.

bava-metzia/25.summary: A finder who comes upon three coins stacked one atop another must announce the find, and the Gemara works out why: a wide coin, a middling one, and a small one piled up looks placed rather than dropped. Rav Naḥman offers a physical test, whether a wood chip slid underneath would lift the whole pile at once. Then a man claims a lost sela, a silver coin, saying his own name is written on it, and gets nothing.
bava-metzia/25.question: If a name written on a silver coin proves nothing, because the owner may simply have spent it, why should the tidy stacking of three coins prove that someone put them there on purpose?

judge.reachNote: What makes a mark on fungible property count: identification by the owner versus evidence that the object was set down on purpose.

answer.quote: It is when the bottom coin is broadest, and the intermediate-sized coin is atop it and the smallest coin is atop the intermediate one, as we say: They were placed there
answer.explanation: The page explains that the graduated stack shows the coins were deliberately placed and thus not lost at all, while the sela ruling rests on a coin's circulating from hand to hand, so the two reasons are given separately but never explicitly weighed against each other.

bava-metzia/26.summary: A sela, a silver coin, falls from one of two men walking together, and Rav Naḥman says the finder must return it, since the loser will confront the only other person there. Make it three men and the loser gives up hope, so the coin stays with the finder. Rava then rules that whoever snatches such a coin before that despair remains a robber, and handing it back later counts only as a present.
bava-metzia/26.question: If despair is what hands the coin to the finder, and that despair grows from the loser's guess that the men beside him mean to rob him, does his suspicion of their character decide who owns the coin?

judge.reachNote: Ownership here turns on the loser's own subjective state of mind, so the question asks whether his reading of his companions' honesty is what transfers title.

answer.quote: Since he cannot make a definitive claim, he despairs of recovering his coin.
answer.explanation: The page grounds the despair in the loser's inability to lodge a definite claim against any one of the three rather than in a judgment about their honesty, which bears on the question without settling it, since Rav Naḥman's inn case does speak of 'their intention to rob me.'

bava-metzia/27.summary: A messenger loses the bill of divorce he was carrying to a woman, and whether he can reclaim it by describing its markings turns on whether identification by distinguishing marks is Torah law or only rabbinic. The page tests this against a donkey claimed by its saddle, a dead man identified by a mole, and a lost pouch. Rava says finders accept marks so their own losses come back; Rav Safra objects that the finder is spending property that is not his.
bava-metzia/27.question: If the whole system rests on an owner's confidence that nobody else knows the marks on his lost thing, what happens the day a stranger names them first?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the epistemic premise beneath simanim: the whole return mechanism rests on an owner's presumed monopoly of knowledge about his own object.

answer.quote: Scrutinize him [darshehu] to determine whether the claimant is a swindler or whether he is not a swindler. Only then may you return the lost item to him.
answer.explanation: The page requires the finder to vet the claimant for fraud (and in its rejection says the vetting is done through witnesses), which bears on the danger of a stranger naming the marks, but it never resolves what happens once an impostor successfully describes them.

bava-metzia/28.summary: Rava ranks the ways a claimant proves a found item is his: the length of a garment counts for more than its width, its weight for more than both, and a wife claiming a found bill of divorce must name a perforation beside a particular letter. Once swindlers grew common, marks alone no longer sufficed and claimants had to bring witnesses vouching that they were honest. Rav Pappa's father brought witnesses who answered yes when asked if he was a swindler.
bava-metzia/28.question: Rabba bar Rav Huna read the witnesses' yes as a no because nobody volunteers witnesses against himself, but how far can a court rewrite what a witness actually said?
gate: the question brings in "Rabba", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Huna", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When a court may read a witness's words against their plain sense on the strength of a presumption about human behavior.

answer.quote: The witnesses said to him: We were saying that you are not a swindler.
answer.explanation: The page shows the witnesses themselves clarifying their intent, and gives Rabba bar Rav Huna's stated ground for accepting that reading, but it never sets a limit on how far a court may reinterpret testimony.

bava-metzia/29.summary: A found scroll has to be read once every thirty days so it does not mold, and a finder who cannot read rolls and unrolls it instead. Found silver and copper are used just enough to keep off tarnish, while gold and glass, which neglect does not ruin, stay untouched until Elijah comes and identifies the owner. The upkeep is measured from both ends: a found garment gets shaken monthly, but may not be hung out for the finder's own prestige.
bava-metzia/29.question: If a bailee who reads the scroll while airing it is permitted, and one who opened it for his own sake is not, what is different about the two acts besides why he did it?

judge.reachNote: Whether permission turns on the physical act or only on the intention behind an identical act.

answer.quote: If, when he is rolling the Torah scroll to ventilate it, he opens it and reads it, it is permitted. If it is for himself that he opened it, it is prohibited.
answer.explanation: The Gemara's resolution of the baraita's apparent contradiction rests the whole distinction on the purpose of the opening, which bears on the question but never says whether anything beyond motive separates the two acts.

bava-metzia/30.summary: A found garment may be spread out to air it but not draped on a bed to impress visiting guests, and the Gemara cannot settle whether spreading it for both reasons at once is allowed. The page then exempts an elderly man from retrieving a lost item beneath his dignity, and Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, twice pays half a dinar, a silver coin, to avoid lifting a stranger's firewood. It ends by blaming Jerusalem's destruction on courts that ruled strictly by law.
bava-metzia/30.question: If the law itself excuses a dignified elder from lifting the wood, why does the same page say a city fell for ruling by the law and nothing more?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the law's exemptions are a floor and piety lies in going beyond them — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: he conducted himself beyond the letter of the law, and he could have simply refused the request for help
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the tension between the elder's dignity exemption and Rabbi Yishmael's conduct, and resolves it by the category of acting beyond the letter of the law, which it then derives from Exodus 18:20 and links to Jerusalem's destruction.

summaryProblems.claim: The page ends by blaming Jerusalem's destruction on courts that ruled strictly by law.
summaryProblems.pageSays: MISHNA: Which is the item that is considered lost property? If one found a donkey or a cow grazing on the path, that is not lost property

summaryProblems.claim: He pays half a dinar, 'a silver coin'.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The man said to him: A half-dinar. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, gave him a half-dinar, took possession of the wood

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 30b: "he conducted himself beyond the letter of the law, and he could have simply refused the request for help". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The page ends by blaming Jerusalem's destruction on courts that ruled strictly by law.", but the page says "MISHNA: Which is the item that is considered lost property? If one found a donkey or a cow grazing on the path, that is not lost property". Say what the page says. The summary says "He pays half a dinar, 'a silver coin'.", but the page says "The man said to him: A half-dinar. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, gave him a half-dinar, took possession of the wood". Say what the page says. The question's tension is exactly what the Gemara raises and answers: it says Rabbi Yishmael acted beyond the letter of the law, and that Jerusalem fell for stopping at the letter. Ask instead about something left unresolved, such as why burial and visiting the ill need separate derivations to override dignity while returning a lost item does not, or the unresolved dilemma about field versus city. Also drop the claim that the page ends with the Jerusalem statement and the unsupported description of the half-dinar as a silver coin.

bava-metzia/31.summary: A sage asks Rava whether the doubled verb in "you shall return them" means a finder must chase a runaway ox back only twice. Rava answers that the first word obliges return even a hundred times, while the second teaches something extra, and the same move runs through dispatching a mother bird from her nest, rebuke, and returning a poor man's blanket each night. Where a sage rejects the derived law, the identical doubling becomes mere idiom, since the Torah speaks in the language of people.
bava-metzia/31.question: What decides whether a doubled verb hides a second law or is only the way people happen to talk?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the hermeneutic principle itself: whether the doubled verb is a signal carrying law or plain human idiom, and what settles which.

answer.quote: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya holds there is nothing extraordinary about it and therefore, nothing may be derived from it.
answer.explanation: The page shows that a sage who rejects the substantive derived law treats the doubling as ordinary speech, but it never states a general rule for deciding when a doubled verb yields a second halakha, so the question survives.

bava-metzia/32.summary: The mishna has a donkey collapsed under its load, and a passerby who must unload it again and again, four or five times over. It also splits the work: unloading is done for free, loading for pay. Rava reads that split as proof that preventing an animal's suffering is a Torah obligation, and the Gemara hunts for support, rejecting proof after proof, including the odd rule that if the owner sits down and refuses to help, the passerby may walk on.
bava-metzia/32.question: If the donkey's pain is what the Torah is commanding about, why does the owner sitting down and refusing to lift a finger let the next person keep walking?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether the command is about the animal's pain or about the owner's claim on a neighbor's help — but the page already resolves it.

answer.quote: Perhaps it means that the passerby is exempt from unloading the burden for free, but is obligated to do so for remuneration
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the note's objection — that the animal suffers whether or not the owner helps — and resolves it by reading the mishna's "exempt" as exempt only from unpaid labor.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 32b: "Perhaps it means that the passerby is exempt from unloading the burden for free, but is obligated to do so for remuneration". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 32b: the passerby is exempt only from unloading for free, not from unloading altogether, so the animal's suffering is still addressed. Rewrite so the question either starts from that resolution and asks what remains hard, or picks an unresolved thread — for instance why loading an enemy's animal to subdue one's evil inclination outranks relieving a friend's animal's actual pain. Keep the summary's shape; it is faithful to the page.

bava-metzia/33.summary: A mishna ranks whose lost item you pick up first: your own before your father's, and your teacher's before your father's, unless your father is himself a Torah scholar. Rav grounds the own-first rule in a verse, "Only so that there shall be no needy among you," and then warns that whoever insists on that right will end up needy. The page then argues over who counts as a teacher; Rabbi Yosei says even someone who explained the meaning of a single line.
bava-metzia/33.question: If the law plainly permits a person to rescue his own property first, why does the one who always exercises that permission end up poor?

judge.reachNote: The gap between what the halakha permits and what it commends: a right one may exercise yet should not insist upon.

answer.quote: anyone who fastidiously fulfills this principle with regard to his property at the expense of others’ property ultimately comes to experience that fate
answer.explanation: The page states the outcome and hints at its mechanism — others will likewise prioritize themselves at his expense — but never explains why a permitted act carries this penalty.

bava-metzia/34.summary: A cow left with a bailee is stolen, and the bailee chooses to pay the owner rather than swear an oath; when the thief is caught and pays double, the extra money goes to the bailee. Rava explains this as a silent condition at the moment of deposit, transferring the cow to the bailee retroactively, and Rabbi Zeira trims it: not the fleece and offspring, which any owner expects. Then come a dozen cases about heirs, halves and partners, all left unresolved.
bava-metzia/34.question: If the double payment moves to the bailee because he pleased the owner by paying, why should the bailee's sons, handing over the identical money, please him any less?

judge.reachNote: Is the transfer of the double payment a personal favor to the man who pleased the owner, or a term of a transaction triggered by payment itself?

answer.quote: Or perhaps this case is no different, and the owner transfers rights to the double payment provided that he receives payment
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises this exact dilemma and states the side the question presses, but resolves nothing, concluding: "All of these dilemmas shall stand unresolved [teiku]."

bava-metzia/35.summary: A man deposited jewels with a friend, and when he asked for them back the friend said he did not know where he had put them. Rav Nahman ruled that not knowing where you put a deposit is itself negligence, and had the bailee's palace sold to pay. Then the jewels turned up, worth more than before, and Rav Nahman unwound the whole thing: jewels to the owner, palace back to the bailee, because the court's appraisal had rested on a mistake.
bava-metzia/35.question: If the jewels were sitting in the bailee's house the entire time, what exactly was the wrong that made him liable for them?

judge.reachNote: The idea is that failing to account for a deposit counts as negligence even when the item was never actually lost — but the page says this in so many words.

answer.quote: Every circumstance where a bailee claims: I do not know where I placed them, is in and of itself negligence. Go pay him for the jewels.
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman states the wrong explicitly: a bailee's inability to account for where he put the deposit is itself negligence, which is what generated the liability.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 35a: "Every circumstance where a bailee claims: I do not know where I placed them, is in and of itself negligence. Go pay him for the jewels.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what wrong made the bailee liable, and the page answers it in the very line the summary paraphrases: "I do not know where I placed them, is in and of itself negligence." Ask instead about what remains puzzling after that ruling — for instance, why the later discovery of the jewels makes the appraisal "erroneous" and reversible, when Rava insists the bailee still does not gain the increase because he dragged the owner to court. That would push on the tension between negligence that was real and a repossession that is treated as a mistake.

bava-metzia/36.summary: A man entrusted with someone else's property hands it on to a second person to watch, and the amoraim split over whether that alone makes him liable. Rava's reason for liability is the owner's voice: you are trustworthy to me under oath, that other man is not. Then a careless keeper lets an animal into a marsh where it dies of natural causes; Abaye says the marsh air killed it, Rava says the Angel of Death does not care where it stood.
bava-metzia/36.question: If the cow would have dropped dead wherever it was standing, is the careless keeper who drove it into the marsh still the reason it died?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of causation — whether negligence that only changed the animal's location counts as the cause of a natural death — but the page already answers it as a stated dispute.

answer.quote: It is because we say with regard to the Angel of Death, who causes death by natural causes: What difference is there to me if the animal was here
answer.explanation: The page states both sides of exactly this question in so many words — Rava holds the keeper is not the cause and is exempt, while Abaye holds "The air of the marsh killed the animal" and he is liable.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 36b: "It is because we say with regard to the Angel of Death, who causes death by natural causes: What difference is there to me if the animal was here". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question only restates the Abaye–Rava dispute that the summary itself has already spelled out, so the page answers it two lines later. Write a question that starts from that dispute and presses on what stays hard, for instance why Abaye concedes when the animal walks home and Rava concedes when it dies in the thief's house, or why Rava's "that person is not trustworthy to me when he takes an oath" reason lets him escape Abaye's objection about the rented cow. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-metzia/37.summary: Two men leave money with one bailee, a person holding it for safekeeping: one deposits a hundred dinars, the other two hundred, and later each claims the two hundred. The Rabbis say he hands each a hundred and the disputed hundred waits until Elijah comes; Rabbi Yosei objects that the liar loses nothing, so the whole deposit is held. Elsewhere the page says a robber who cannot recall which of two men he robbed pays both in full, but only to settle his debt to Heaven.
bava-metzia/37.question: Rabbi Yosei's rule also freezes the honest depositor's own hundred dinars, so is it fair to hold his money hostage in the hope that the liar cracks?

judge.reachNote: Whether a court may impose a certain loss on an innocent party in order to pressure an unidentified liar into confessing.

answer.quote: As his fraud will cause him to lose even the one hundred dinars that he deposited, perhaps he will be discouraged from making a fraudulent claim.
answer.explanation: The page gives Rabbi Yosei's deterrence rationale, which bears on the question, but it never addresses the cost imposed on the honest depositor whose hundred is also frozen.

bava-metzia/38.summary: A person leaves produce with a neighbor for safekeeping and it begins to rot or is eaten by vermin; the first opinion in the mishna says the bailee may not touch it, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he sells it in court, like one returning a lost item. Rav Kahana explains the refusal by preference: people want their own. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak explains it by risk: the owner may already have designated that produce as teruma, the priestly portion, for grain stored elsewhere.
bava-metzia/38.question: If a person really would rather have one measure of his own produce than nine of someone else's, who decides the point at which that preference stops counting and the rot is simply loss?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — how far a bailee must honour an owner's sentimental preference before rot is simply destruction — but the page names the threshold outright.

answer.quote: This expression is merely an exaggeration, and actually one prefers his own produce only when its rate of deterioration is standard.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself sets the cut-off for Rav Kahana's preference — it holds only at the standard rate of deterioration, and Rabbi Yoḥanan adds that beyond that rate "everyone agrees that the bailee sells it before the court."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 38a: "This expression is merely an exaggeration, and actually one prefers his own produce only when its rate of deterioration is standard.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: the nine-kav line is called an exaggeration, and the preference is said to hold only at the standard rate of deterioration, beyond which all agree the bailee sells. Build the question on what the page leaves unsettled instead — for instance why Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's teruma worry is not solved by simply selling to priests at teruma prices, or why Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis split over whether an "insignificant loss" like the ruined barrels counts at all. Keep the summary as it stands; it tracks the page.

bava-metzia/39.summary: The court will not let a minor manage the field of a man taken captive, and will not let a relative manage a minor's field, lest the relative later be taken for its owner. Then a stranger from Bei Hozai tells Mari bar Isak, a rich and violent man, that he is his brother and wants half their father's estate. Mari says the claimant must prove his case; Rav Hisda tells Mari to bring the witnesses instead.
bava-metzia/39.question: If the standing rule is that the claimant brings proof, what keeps a judge who reverses it for a violent man from reversing it whenever he dislikes the defendant?

judge.reachNote: When intimidation makes the ordinary burden of proof unusable, may a judge shift it, and what keeps that discretion from swallowing the rule?

answer.quote: This is the way I judge you and all of your fellow violent people.
answer.explanation: Rav Ḥisda limits the reversal to a class — violent men whose witnesses are afraid to testify, as the brother had said — but the page never states what restrains a judge from extending it, so the question survives.

bava-metzia/40.summary: A mishna sets how much stored grain a guardian may keep back for shrinkage: nine half-kav per kor of wheat, a kor being 180 kav, a kav roughly six pints. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri objects that mice eat the same amount whether the pile is large or small, so the deduction should be flat; the Sages answer that grain is also lost and scattered. The oil debate turns on whether a seller may stir sediment back in.
bava-metzia/40.question: If Abaye and Rav Pappa can each read Rabbi Yehuda's sediment deduction as proof that mixing sediment is permitted and as proof that it is forbidden, what is either reading actually resting on?
gate: the question brings in "Abaye", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Pappa", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yehuda's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a fixed deduction can be justified by opposite premises depending on whether silence counts as waiver.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda conforms to his standard line of reasoning, as he is not of the opinion that one can presume renunciation
answer.explanation: The Gemara spells out what each reading rests on — whether renunciation can be presumed, plus the merchant maxim for Rav Pappa's side — so the question's demand for the underlying basis is met in the text.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 40b: "Rabbi Yehuda conforms to his standard line of reasoning, as he is not of the opinion that one can presume renunciation". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already states what each reading rests on: Abaye's turns on Rabbi Yehuda not presuming renunciation, and Rav Pappa's turns on presumed renunciation plus the maxim that one who buys and sells at the same price is no merchant. Ask something the page leaves standing after that — for example, why silence about sediment should count as a waiver at all, or why the same custom-based deduction can survive both premises. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

bava-metzia/41.summary: A bailee moves a barrel left in his keeping and it breaks, and the mishna splits: exempt in one clause, liable in the other, depending on whether the owner had assigned the barrel a spot. Rabbi Yoḥanan offers to carry the garments of anyone who can read both clauses as one sage's view. Rav Sheshet tries, saying the bailee only climbed on the barrel to reach fledglings in a nest. Then the argument turns to whether misusing a deposit requires actual damage.
bava-metzia/41.question: If Rav Sheshet did reconcile the two clauses under a single tanna, why does Rabbi Yoḥanan get to keep his own garments?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is what counts as 'returning' a deposit — whether replacing an item anywhere ends the bailee's liability — but the page settles the dispute the question raises.

answer.quote: He holds that the term: He placed it, indicates that he replaced it in its designated place. Therefore, the latter clause cannot be explained in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks why Rabbi Yoḥanan does not accept Rav Sheshet's unified reading and answers that Yoḥanan reads 'he placed it' as a return to the designated spot, so the contradiction stands for him.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 41a: "He holds that the term: He placed it, indicates that he replaced it in its designated place. Therefore, the latter clause cannot be explained in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Yishmael". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: the Gemara itself asks why Rabbi Yoḥanan doesn't accept Rav Sheshet's reading and answers that Yoḥanan reads 'he placed it' as meaning the designated place, so no reconciliation was achieved. Rewrite the question to start from that answer, for instance probing why a single word like 'placed it' should decide whether an item counts as returned, or what is at stake in whether misappropriation needs actual loss.

bava-metzia/42.summary: A bailee who ties deposited coins in a cloth and slings the bundle behind his back is liable if they are stolen. Shmuel says money is safe only buried in the ground, and the thieves keep adapting: diggers, beam-dismantlers, wall-tappers, so the hiding place climbs to the handbreadth nearest the floor or the ceiling. Then come chains of blame where everyone has an answer: the bailee handed the deposit to his mother, she put it in a chest, both swear, neither pays.
bava-metzia/42.question: If a bailee who cannot say where he put the money is negligent on the spot, why does the man who passed it to his mother, who lost it from a chest, walk away paying nothing?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.
no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is what counts as negligence: forgetting the money's location versus entrusting it to a household member who hid it imperfectly.

answer.quote: anyone who deposits an item with another, it is with the awareness that at times, the bailee's wife and his children will safeguard the item
answer.explanation: The page explicitly states why the bailee who handed the deposit to his mother is within his rights, and Rava then rules that he and his mother each take an oath and the bailee is exempt.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 42b: "anyone who deposits an item with another, it is with the awareness that at times, the bailee's wife and his children will safeguard the item". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: depositors are presumed to accept that a bailee's wife and children may safeguard the item, and Rava resolves the case with oaths and exemption. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved, for example why the mother's failure to bury the money (the stated optimal safeguarding, per Shmuel) costs no one anything, or why the bailee's admitted concealment of the money's ownership from her improves rather than worsens his position.

bava-metzia/43.summary: Money left with a money changer is sorted by how it is tied; bound coins he may not touch, and he owes nothing if they vanish, while loose coins he may trade with, and he pays if they are lost. Then a stolen barrel of wine, worth one dinar, a silver coin, when taken and four dinars later. The Gemara tries and discards two readings of Beit Hillel's "time of removal" before settling on sheared fleece and newborn lambs.
bava-metzia/43.question: If the same quarter-log of wine is drunk and the same barrel breaks, why should lifting it rather than tilting it leave the bailee owing the whole barrel?

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is that a formal act of acquisition, not the physical damage, fixes the scope of liability — but the mishna already says this.

answer.quote: If he lifted the barrel and took from it a quarter-log of wine, and the barrel broke, since he acquired the barrel by lifting it, he pays the value of the entire barrel.
answer.explanation: The mishna states the reason outright: lifting is an act of acquisition, so the whole barrel becomes his, while tilting acquires only the quarter-log he took.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 43b (final MISHNA): "If he lifted the barrel and took from it a quarter-log of wine, and the barrel broke, since he acquired the barrel by lifting it, he pays the value of the entire barrel.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line it is drawn from: the mishna says he pays for the whole barrel "since he acquired the barrel by lifting it." Rewrite so the question starts from that reason rather than asking for it — for instance, press on why a formal act of acquisition should govern liability when the wine drunk and the breakage are identical, or connect it to the Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel dispute over whether misappropriation requires loss. Also consider tightening the muddled middle sentence of the summary about the barrel's value.

bava-metzia/44.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches his son Shimon that in a swap of gold for silver, pulling the gold closes the deal, because gold is the goods and silver is the money; his son answers that in his youth he taught the reverse. The youthful ruling made gold the money because it is worth more; the older one makes silver the money because merchants everywhere accept it. Rav Ashi argues the early version fits the rest of the mishna better, and the Gemara knocks his proof down.
bava-metzia/44.question: If gold counts as money against produce but as merchandise against silver, what is left of the line between money and goods?

judge.reachNote: Whether 'money' is an intrinsic property of a coin or only a role it plays relative to whatever it is traded against.

answer.quote: Although gold coins are a commodity relative to silver coins, relative to produce they are currency. Therefore, one may desacralize produce with gold dinars.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly states that currency/commodity status is relational rather than fixed, which bears directly on the question, but it never says what principle preserves the distinction once it is made relative, so the question can still honestly be asked.

bava-metzia/45.summary: Borrowing a gold dinar and repaying with a gold dinar is barred as interest, since gold rises and falls like merchandise instead of holding still like money. The same gold coin, though, may still redeem second tithe, the produce a farmer must carry to Jerusalem or convert into cash. Beit Shammai fear a man will hoard silver until it adds up to a whole gold dinar and delay the trip; Rav Pappa says a coin's worth is only its stamp.
