bava-metzia/45.question: If a coin counts as money only because of the form stamped on it, and rulers can cancel that form at will, what makes it solid enough to buy anything with?

judge.reachNote: Whether a coin's worth lies in its metal or in a sovereign's stamp, and what that leaves it able to do in a transaction.

answer.quote: this means only that money does not effect a transaction of exchange; but he concedes that money is acquired by means of a transaction of exchange
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa narrows the doubt about a coin's substance — the cancellable stamp only disqualifies money from being the instrument of exchange, not from being acquired — but the page never says what positively makes a stamped coin solid enough to buy with.

bava-metzia/46.summary: The argument is whether a coin can serve as the instrument in a barter swap, the kind where handing over one object closes the deal on the other. The Gemara presses Rav Pappa until it produces his own conduct: sending an agent to collect twelve thousand dinars, silver coins, lent out in Bei Ḥozai, he transferred the money by granting the agent acquisition of his doorstep instead. Coins a king or a province has pulled from circulation, though, count as goods.
bava-metzia/46.question: If what disqualifies a coin from barter is that it is money rather than a thing, why does a banned coin become a thing again the moment people stop honoring it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that money's disqualification from barter rests on a conventional status (acceptance, apparent value) rather than on the metal itself.

answer.quote: I would have said it is not a coin due to the fact that it does not circulate at all, as the king banned its use.
answer.explanation: The page ties coin-status to circulation — an invalidated coin may not count as a coin at all — which bears directly on the question, though it never spells out why circulation rather than substance is the criterion for exchange.

summaryProblems.claim: The twelve thousand dinars are described as silver coins.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Pappa had twelve thousand dinars that he lent to another in Bei Ḥozai.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The twelve thousand dinars are described as silver coins.", but the page says "Rav Pappa had twelve thousand dinars that he lent to another in Bei Ḥozai.". Say what the page says.

bava-metzia/47.summary: A buyer hands over coins for wheat, and by Torah law the wheat is already his; the Sages ruled that ownership passes only when the buyer pulls the produce. Rabbi Yoḥanan gives the reason: a seller whose upper story catches fire will not exert himself to rescue grain that belongs to someone else. The Gemara presses back, notes that an arsonist pays damages anyway, and narrows the worry to a fire nobody set.
bava-metzia/47.question: Is it fair to build a rule of acquisition on the assumption that a paid seller will stand and watch another man's wheat burn?

judge.reachNote: Whether a legal rule of acquisition may rest on a presumption about how self-interested people behave in a crisis.

answer.quote: But if you do not establish the purchase item in the possession of the seller, he will not expend great effort, exert himself, and rescue the item.
answer.explanation: The page states the behavioral assumption behind the decree — not malice but a failure to exert effort for property no longer his — which bears on the question without settling whether such an assumption may found a rule.

bava-metzia/48.summary: A buyer pays for goods, the seller backs out, and the Sages have a formula for him: He Who exacted payment from the generation of the flood will exact payment from whoever does not stand by his statement. Abaye says the court merely reads it to him as a warning; Rava says the court curses him, since the ban on cursing covers only someone acting as your people do. The salt seller Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef then complicates both readings.
bava-metzia/48.question: If the formula is a real curse, and it is permitted only because a man who reneges has stepped outside "your people," what is his standing the moment he relents and delivers the salt?

judge.reachNote: Whether exclusion from "your people" is a permanent moral verdict on the man or a status that lasts only as long as the act.

answer.quote: Go and give them the salt, and if not, accept upon yourself: He Who exacted payment.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan's either/or implies the curse attaches only while the seller persists in reneging, which bears on the question but never states what the reneger's standing is once he relents and delivers.

bava-metzia/49.summary: Buyers gave Rav Kahana money for linen, the price rose, and Rav told him to hand over only as much linen as the money had already covered. Behind that ruling sits a dispute: Rav says backing out of a bare verbal commitment, with no formal act of acquisition, is not bad faith, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says it is. Then Rav Tavot, said never to deviate from truth for anything, tells a story about stolen coins and, when pressed, says it never happened.
bava-metzia/49.question: If Rav Tavot would not shade the truth for the whole world, what is he doing when a challenge to his story is answered by declaring the story never took place?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that truthfulness in speech may mean refusing to let a false report stand rather than defending one's own account — the same concern as Abaye's 'one matter with his mouth and one other in his heart.'

bava-metzia/50.summary: An item worth six ma'a, small silver coins, sold for five is off by exactly one sixth, and that fraction decides everything: below it the sale stands, above it either side can walk away, at it the overcharge is refunded. The Gemara keeps circling the clock, arguing whether a buyer's window lasts only as long as it takes to show the goods to a merchant or a relative. The merchants of Lod cheered Rabbi Tarfon's wider standard, then asked him to drop it.
bava-metzia/50.question: If Rabbi Tarfon's threshold let the merchants of Lod keep bigger markups, why was a full day of buyer's regret worse for them than the few minutes the Rabbis allowed?

judge.reachNote: The idea is that a merchant prefers a short, certain window of buyer revocation over a wider margin he may keep but all day risk losing.

answer.quote: When he said to them that the exploited person can renege on the transaction for the entire day, they reverted
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself states that the merchants rejoiced at Tarfon's wider exploitation threshold but reverted precisely because his day-long window for reneging outweighed that gain, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 50b: "When he said to them that the exploited person can renege on the transaction for the entire day, they reverted". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered twice on the page: the Gemara explains that the merchants rejoiced at Tarfon's threshold and reverted once they heard the whole-day renege window, and later adds that "Nullification of the transaction is uncommon" in their calculation. Rewrite so the question starts from that trade-off rather than asking for it, for instance pressing on why a long window to cancel a whole sale should worry a merchant more than refunding overcharges, or on what the page's admission that nullification is uncommon does to its own proof. Keep the summary; it is faithful.

bava-metzia/51.summary: A man with silk strips to sell announced six ma'a, a small silver coin, though the strips were worth five, and he would have settled for five and a half. A buyer deliberately paid the full six, reasoning that a discount would count as a waiver but an overpayment would let him later sue to recover the excess as exploitation. Rava dismissed the claim, but on other grounds: the overcharging rules cover buying from a merchant, not from a homeowner selling his own goods.
bava-metzia/51.question: If the silk had come from a merchant rather than a homeowner, would the buyer's plan have worked, given that nobody on the page faults him for overpaying on purpose?

judge.reachNote: Whether the exploitation rules protect against an honest mistake in pricing or can be weaponized by a buyer who knowingly overpays to manufacture a claim.

answer.quote: The Sages taught this halakha of exploitation only with regard to one who buys merchandise from a merchant, but one who buys merchandise from a regular homeowner does not
answer.explanation: Rava's and Rav Ḥisda's rulings imply the exploitation claim would stand against a merchant (and the mishna says exploitation applies to a merchant), but the page never addresses whether the buyer's deliberate overpayment would spoil the claim.

bava-metzia/52.summary: A silver sela wears down with use, and the sages argue over how much erosion turns spending it at full value into exploitation: four issar, four pundeyon, or eight pundeyon. Once a coin is too worn to pass, it may not be sold to a merchant or a violent man who would push it on others; instead it gets a hole and hangs on a child's neck. Another baraita bans exactly that, and the fix is where the hole goes.
bava-metzia/52.question: If refusing a slightly worn coin makes a person a miserly soul, why does the page also say no one can be forced to take one back?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the gap between moral censure of fussiness and what the law can actually force a party to accept — but the page closes that gap explicitly.

answer.quote: One cannot compel the person from whom he received the coin to accept it in return, as although the coin maintains its value, not everyone is willing to conduct business
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself states why there is no compulsion despite the coin's validity, and elsewhere limits the "miserly soul" label to coins that "still circulate" and frames the acceptance as "an attribute of piety."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 52b: "One cannot compel the person from whom he received the coin to accept it in return, as although the coin maintains its value, not everyone is willing to conduct business". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved on the page: Rav Ḥisda calls the acceptance an attribute of piety, the miserly-soul label is limited to coins that still circulate, and the Gemara states outright that one cannot compel acceptance because not everyone will do business with a coin of questionable value. Write a question the page leaves open — for example, why perforating in the middle removes the fear of deceit while perforating from the side does not, or why a dinar worn down from a shekel may be kept while one worn down from a sela may not. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

bava-metzia/53.summary: A sliver of second tithe, produce that must be eaten in Jerusalem or exchanged for money, is worth less than a peruta, the smallest copper coin, and so may be too small to redeem. The Gemara offers workaround after workaround: pair it with another half-peruta, buy it out with an issar worth eight perutot, and knocks each one down. The reason keeps being what someone might do wrong next time, not what is wrong now.
bava-metzia/53.question: If the Sages decreed that a city's walls gather in tithe produce, and then applied that decree even to walls that have fallen down, what work is the wall still doing?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: When a decree is grounded in a physical boundary, what remains of the boundary's role once the Sages apply the decree in its absence.

answer.quote: The halakha that a partition enables one to eat second-tithe produce is by Torah law, and the halakha with regard to the capability of partitions of the city to gather second-tithe produce into the city is by rabbinic law
answer.explanation: Rava's distinction shows the wall still does Torah-level work (permitting eating inside) while only the rabbinic 'gathering' function was extended past its collapse, but the page's stated reason for the extension is simply that "the Sages did not distinguish between cases where there are intact partitions and cases where there are not intact partitions," so the question can still be honestly pressed.

bava-metzia/54.summary: Someone who redeems second tithe, produce that must be eaten in Jerusalem or exchanged for money taken there, pays its value plus an added fifth. The page asks whether skipping that fifth blocks eating the food: Rabbi Eliezer says one may eat it, Rabbi Yehoshua says one may not, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi splits it by the calendar, siding with Eliezer for Shabbat. Rav Pappa recasts the whole fight as worry that the payer will simply never get around to paying.
bava-metzia/54.question: If the missing fifth either invalidates the redemption or it doesn't, how can the day of the week decide which?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether an unpaid fifth is a defect in the redemption itself or only a precaution against non-payment — which is exactly what the page resolves.

answer.quote: the Sages deemed it permitted for one to eat without the additional payment, in deference to Shabbat
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the Shabbat leniency is a rabbinic dispensation in honor of Shabbat, and Rav Pappa then explains that the dispute is not about intrinsic invalidation at all but about whether we fear negligence, so the day can indeed decide.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 54a: "the Sages deemed it permitted for one to eat without the additional payment, in deference to Shabbat". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered twice on the page: the split is explained as a leniency "in deference to Shabbat," and Rav Pappa says all agree the missing fifth does not invalidate, the dispute being only about fear of negligence. Since the summary already reports Rav Pappa's recasting, the question cannot then ask how the day of the week could decide. Ask instead something the page leaves open, e.g. why negligence is feared for second tithe but not for consecrated property, where "the Temple treasurers demand payment from him in the marketplace."

bava-metzia/55.summary: A mishna collects five laws that turn on a peruta, the smallest copper coin: admitting to part of a claim, betrothing a woman, misusing Temple property, announcing a lost object, and robbery. Rav Kahana reads the list as proof that overcharging below a peruta is not exploitation at all; Levi taught a rival list that includes it. Rav Ketina's claim that courts hear suits worth less than a peruta gets rewritten into something narrower.
bava-metzia/55.question: If the Temple treasury is repaid for a misuse worth less than a peruta, why should an ordinary person's loss of the same amount be too small for a court to hear?
gate: the question uses "the Temple treasury", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Why a de minimis floor governs claims between people but not obligations to the sacred — whether the threshold measures the loss or the standing of the claimant.

answer.quote: To the Temple treasury, yes, one must return that which he took; but to an ordinary person [hedyot], no, one need not pay restitution for theft of less than one peruta
answer.explanation: The page asserts the distinction (grounded in the verse about restitution "in the sacred matter") but never explains why sub-peruta losses matter to the Temple and not to a person, so the question can still be asked.

bava-metzia/56.summary: A mishna lists four things exempt from the laws of exploitation, where a price off by a sixth undoes a sale: slaves, documents, land, and consecrated property. Old documents sold to a perfumer for wrapping his wares do count, since there the paper itself is the goods, which rejects Rav Kahana's view that sums of mere perutot, small copper coins, cannot be exploited. Rava then asks about wheat kernels a laborer has sown into a field.
bava-metzia/56.question: At what moment do scattered wheat kernels stop being goods a buyer can be cheated over and become part of the ground?
gate: gloss "consecrated property" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: When does movable property become subordinated to the land, losing the protections that attach to goods that can be handled and measured?

bava-metzia/57.summary: Land, slaves, documents, and property consecrated to the Temple are exempt from the rules of exploitation, the claim brought when a sale price is off by a sixth or more. The question raised is whether that exemption also shields a wildly lopsided sale from being cancelled outright, and Shmuel pushes hardest: a hundred dinars of consecrated goods redeemed onto one peruta, the smallest copper coin, is redeemed. Rav Ḥisda flips the exemption into a stringency instead.
bava-metzia/57.question: If a hundred dinars of Temple property really is redeemed once someone hands over a single peruta, what keeps the rule that he should not have done it from being empty?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — how a transaction can be valid after the fact yet forbidden in advance — but the page states the answer.

answer.quote: is desacralized after the fact, but ab initio, no, one may not do so. Therefore, one must nevertheless pay the difference to the Temple treasury by Torah law.
answer.explanation: The Gemara's second resolution states exactly what keeps the ab initio prohibition from being toothless: a Torah-level obligation to pay the shortfall to the Temple treasury.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 57a: "is desacralized after the fact, but ab initio, no, one may not do so. Therefore, one must nevertheless pay the difference to the Temple treasury by Torah law.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 57a, where Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the redemption works only after the fact and therefore the difference must still be paid by Torah law. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than asking for it, for example probing why Reish Lakish is willing to let Shmuel's rule operate even ab initio, or why the payment is rabbinic for one sage and Torah law for the other. The summary itself is accurate and can stay largely as is.

bava-metzia/58.summary: The mishna stretches ona'a, the ban on cheating someone on price, to cover words, like asking a seller his price with no intention of buying, or telling a man burying his children that he must have sinned. Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani ranks verbal mistreatment worse than monetary because money can be paid back. The list of three who descend to Gehenna and never rise includes one who calls another a derogatory name, even once the target no longer minds it.
bava-metzia/58.question: If the man has grown used to the nickname and is no longer stung by it, what is still being done to him?

judge.reachNote: Whether the wrong of verbal mistreatment lies in the injury actually felt by the victim or in the speaker's intent, once the sting is gone.

answer.quote: Although the victim grew accustomed to being called that name in place of his name, and he is no longer humiliated by being called that name, since the intent was to insult him, the perpetrator’s punishment is severe.
answer.explanation: The page raises the same difficulty and answers by relocating the offense in the speaker's insulting intent, but it never says what is still done to the desensitized victim, so the question can still be honestly asked.

bava-metzia/59.summary: An earthenware oven, cut into rings and reassembled with sand between the segments, splits Rabbi Eliezer from the other Sages over whether it can still become ritually impure. He summons a carob tree that uproots itself, a stream that reverses, leaning walls, and finally a voice from Heaven, and Rabbi Yehoshua answers that the Torah is not in heaven. Then the page counts the cost: Rabbi Eliezer is ostracized, his tears blight the crops, and a wave rises against Rabban Gamliel.
bava-metzia/59.question: If Rabban Gamliel was right to ostracize Rabbi Eliezer, why does his own sister spend the rest of his life keeping her husband from lowering his head in prayer?

judge.reachNote: Being right in the ruling does not cancel liability for the pain inflicted; the victim's tears are heard even when the court acted for Heaven's sake.

answer.quote: All the gates of Heaven are apt to be locked, except for the gates of prayer for victims of verbal mistreatment.
answer.explanation: Imma Shalom states the tradition she acted on — a mistreated person's prayer always reaches Heaven — and the page also says plainly that "She feared that were her husband to bemoan his fate and pray at that moment, her brother would be punished," though it never reconciles this with Rabban Gamliel's claim that the ostracism was justified for God's honor.

bava-metzia/60.summary: Mixing strong wine with weak wine is allowed because it improves the wine, while mixing water in and staying quiet is not. A storekeeper who hands out toasted grain and nuts to children draws a dispute, and the Rabbis shrug: his competitors can hand out jujubes. The same line runs through adornment, where new garments may be tapered and decorated but old ones may not, since there the polish is hiding flaws.
bava-metzia/60.question: When the elderly slave dyed his hair black to get himself bought and then washed the dye out to avoid fetching water, was he a seller deceiving a buyer or goods refusing to be sold?

judge.reachNote: A slave is at once person and property, so his self-adornment collapses the roles of deceiving seller and deceptive goods.

answer.quote: Adornment of a person, what is it? The Gemara relates: It is as in that incident involving a certain elderly slave who went and dyed
answer.explanation: The Gemara introduces the story as its illustration of the mishna's ban on adorning a person for sale, which implies the slave was doing the forbidden embellishing, but it never says whether he stands as seller or as merchandise, and Rav Pappa's verse comments only on Rava's escape.

bava-metzia/61.summary: Rava asks why the Torah forbids interest, robbery, and overcharging separately, when each is just taking money that isn't yours. The answers turn on consent and awareness, and the Sages end up calling the robbery verse superfluous, reassigning it to an employer who holds back a hired laborer's wages overnight. Later, Rabbi Yoḥanan holds that even fixed interest cannot be pried back by a court, since Ezekiel sets the lender beside a murderer, and murderers do not repay.
bava-metzia/61.question: If the lender is grave enough to be placed beside someone who sheds blood, why does that comparison end with him keeping the interest?

judge.reachNote: Severity of a sin and its enforceability in court are separate axes: the graver the framing, the more the sanction moves to Heaven and out of the judges' hands.

answer.quote: It can be inferred that one who takes interest is subject to death at the hand of Heaven but not to repayment
answer.explanation: The page supplies the mechanism — the interest-taker's liability is to Heaven, not to the court, and Rava's reading of the juxtaposition is precisely about non-repayment — but it never addresses why such gravity yields no restitution, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-metzia/62.summary: Two men are walking a desolate path with one jug of water, enough to keep only one of them alive. Ben Petora says both should drink and die rather than watch the other die; Rabbi Akiva reads "and your brother shall live with you" to mean your own life comes first. The same verse elsewhere forces a lender to hand back interest so the borrower can live, and the page then argues over whether collected interest must really be returned.
bava-metzia/62.question: If "and your brother shall live with you" puts your own jug of water first, why does the same phrase pry interest out of a lender's hands?

judge.reachNote: One verse grounds both the priority of your own survival and an obligation to restore another's livelihood — when does 'your brother shall live' limit and when does it oblige?

bava-metzia/63.summary: A man owed a hundred dinars, silver coins, stands at his debtor's granary and agrees to take wheat instead of cash, then wine instead of the wheat, then oil instead of the wine. The baraita permits each swap only if the debtor actually owns that wine and oil; otherwise a rise in price is interest paid for waiting. Rava pushes further, arguing that since a buyer could go purchase produce whenever he liked, owning it now hardly matters.
bava-metzia/63.question: If buying produce at the going market rate really does the buyer no favor at all, why is he handing over his money early?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between the legal fiction that the buyer gains nothing ('your favor is taken and thrown on the thorns') and the real economic motive that makes him pay in advance.

answer.quote: One who gives money in advance to purchase produce at the advance price gives it to two or three different sellers, in order to ensure that he will collect a profit.
answer.explanation: The page elsewhere says the advance buyer pays early precisely to lock in profit across several sellers, which bears on the question but concerns the advance-price case rather than the market-rate case where the buyer claims no benefit at all, so the question can still honestly be asked.

bava-metzia/64.summary: The mishna rules that a lender may not live rent-free in the borrower's courtyard, since free housing is interest on the loan. Rav Naḥman pushes further, holding that even a courtyard nobody would rent out, used by a man who would otherwise sleep elsewhere, still requires rent, to avoid the look of interest. Then Rava's father is found seizing his debtors' slaves and working them, on the grounds that a slave eats more than his labor is worth.
bava-metzia/64.question: If a lender may not sleep for free in a borrower's courtyard, how is seizing that borrower's slaves and putting them to work any different?

judge.reachNote: When does a lender's free benefit from a borrower count as interest — does it turn on actual loss to the borrower or on the appearance of a return on the loan?

answer.quote: A slave is not worth even the bread in his stomach. When the slaves work for me and eat in my home, I am not causing the owners any monetary loss.
answer.explanation: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama gives a reason distinguishing the slave case — no monetary loss to the owner — but the page has just ruled that even a loss-free courtyard requires rent to avoid the appearance of interest, so the tension the question raises remains open.

bava-metzia/65.summary: The mishna lets a landlord charge less for a year's rent paid in advance than for the same year paid month by month, but forbids a seller from raising a field's price from a thousand dinars, silver coins, to twelve hundred if the buyer pays at harvest. Rav Naḥman permits the higher price so long as the seller never says it is for waiting. Rav Pappa defends his own liquor sales that way, and when Rav Sheshet presses him, he says nothing.
bava-metzia/65.question: If Rav Pappa's customers would have bought at the cheap price had they had cash in hand, does it help them that Rav Pappa lost nothing by waiting?

judge.reachNote: Whose vantage point defines interest — the seller who loses nothing by waiting, or the buyer who pays more because he lacks cash.

answer.quote: if they had money available they would buy liquor at the current price, but now that they have no money available they buy it in accordance with the future, more expensive rate
answer.explanation: Rav Sheshet already makes exactly the note's point — the customers' side makes it interest regardless of Rav Pappa's lack of loss — and Rav Pappa's silence lets the objection stand.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 65a: "if they had money available they would buy liquor at the current price, but now that they have no money available they buy it in accordance with the future, more expensive rate". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question just restates Rav Sheshet's challenge, which the page spells out and Rav Pappa answers with silence. Write a question that starts from that silence rather than reaching it — for instance, why the page's own halakhic summary endorses Rav Ḥama's tarsha and says nothing about Rav Pappa's, or what makes Rav Ḥama's arrangement survive the same two-perspective test. The summary is accurate and can stay largely as is.

bava-metzia/66.summary: A lender holds a borrower's field as security and says that if the debt is unpaid after three years the field is his. Rav Naḥman first ruled such a promise binding, watched Rav Yehuda tear up the resulting deed, and eventually reversed himself: a promise made under pressure, an asmakhta, transfers nothing. The rest of the page hunts for a test of sincerity, and each test, beer in hand, fussiness about price, gets picked apart.
bava-metzia/66.question: If every sign that a borrower was at ease can be re-read as a man drinking to calm his nerves or bluffing about prices, what evidence could ever show he meant to hand over his field?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether a person's inner willingness can ever be read off outward behavior — but the page supplies the answer it asks for.

answer.quote: If he is particular about any other land he owns and does not want to sell it even at its market rate, he is clearly not suffering from financial problems
answer.explanation: After the beer and the price-fussiness tests are picked apart, Rav Pappa supplies a surviving test of sincerity — unwillingness to sell unrelated land at market rate — and the page also offers the 'from now' formal act of acquisition as a way to make the commitment stick.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Naḥman watched Rav Yehuda tear up the resulting deed.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Exilarch said to Rav Naḥman: Rav Yehuda tore up your document, i.e., he overruled your decision.

summaryProblems.claim: Each test of sincerity gets picked apart.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rather, Rav Pappa said that there is a different distinction: If he is particular about any other land he owns

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 66b: "If he is particular about any other land he owns and does not want to sell it even at its market rate, he is clearly not suffering from financial problems". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rav Naḥman watched Rav Yehuda tear up the resulting deed.", but the page says "The Exilarch said to Rav Naḥman: Rav Yehuda tore up your document, i.e., he overruled your decision.". Say what the page says. The summary says "Each test of sincerity gets picked apart.", but the page says "Rather, Rav Pappa said that there is a different distinction: If he is particular about any other land he owns". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few lines later: Rav Pappa's final test — a borrower who won't sell his other land even at market rate — survives Rav Aḥa's objections, and the 'from now' act of acquisition also saves the transaction. Fix the summary, which claims every test gets picked apart and has Rav Naḥman witnessing the tearing when the Exilarch reports it to him. Then ask something that begins after Rav Pappa's surviving criterion, for instance why the law lets an outward sign of financial ease stand in for what the borrower actually intended.

bava-metzia/67.summary: A lender holds a borrower's field as security and eats its crops for years, and the page asks whether those crops count as forbidden interest. Rava says it is only a hint of interest, banned by the rabbis but too faint for a court to claw back, since no sum was fixed in advance. Then a wrinkle: grown owners are assumed to forgive the surplus, minor orphans cannot forgive, so it is taken back from the lender, until Rav Ashi declines to do so.
bava-metzia/67.question: If the crops the lender ate are too faint a form of interest for any court to recover, why do Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi refuse to eat them at all?
gate: the question brings in "Kahana", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Pappa", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: It reaches the real idea — that what a court cannot recover may still be forbidden to a pious person — but the page says this in so many words.

answer.quote: Rav Kahana, and Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi would not consume the produce of mortgaged fields even with a deduction in the amount of the loan, as they were concerned about the possible violation of the prohibition of interest.
answer.explanation: The page states outright why these sages abstained — fear of transgressing the interest prohibition — and earlier gives the same principle in general form, that a tzurva miderabbanan "must be especially careful with regard to his conduct" and may not consume even with a deduction.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 67b: "Rav Kahana, and Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi would not consume the produce of mortgaged fields even with a deduction in the amount of the loan, as they were concerned about the possible violation of the prohibition of interest.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered flatly on the page: the sages abstained "as they were concerned about the possible violation of the prohibition of interest," and the page already says a Torah scholar may not consume even with a deduction. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why Rav Ashi treats minor orphans "as though they were adults" when the stated reason for collecting from a lender was precisely that orphans are too young to forgive. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

bava-metzia/68.summary: A storekeeper who sells another man's produce for half the profits is half borrower and half employee, and the mishna bars the deal unless he is paid a wage, since free labor for a lender looks like interest. The argument then shrinks that wage: Rabbi Yehuda says one dried fig eaten together is enough, Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai demands full pay. The same test is run on whey, plucked wool, unfertilized eggs, and a calf's dung.
bava-metzia/68.question: If one shared fig can turn a disguised loan into an honest partnership, what is the payment actually doing?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether the wage is real compensation for labor or a formal marker that converts a loan-plus-free-service into a paid arrangement.

answer.quote: holds in accordance with the opinion of his father, who says that even if he only immersed his bread in brine with him, or only ate one dried fig
answer.explanation: The page states, in explaining Rabbi Yehuda's position, that "there is no demand that his wages be commensurate with his toil," which indicates the payment functions as a token that makes the deal a hire rather than a compensation for labor, yet it never spells out why any token suffices to remove the appearance of interest.

bava-metzia/69.summary: Two Samaritans went into business together, and one of them split the cash on his own; Rav Pappa let it stand, since money counts as already divided. The next year the other split their jointly bought wine alone, and Rav Pappa ruled against him, which looked to the loser like the judge hounding him. So Rav Pappa explained himself: a coin is a coin, but some wine is sweet and some is not, so barrels cannot be halved by counting.
bava-metzia/69.question: Does a judge owe his reasoning to every litigant, or only to the one who suspects him of playing favorites?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of when judicial transparency is owed — but the page states that rule explicitly in its opening line.

answer.quote: Although a judge is not always obligated to explain the reasons for his decision to the litigants, in a case like this, where there is room for suspicion, he must.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that a judge need not normally explain himself but must do so where suspicion of favoritism has arisen, which is exactly the question's alternative.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 69b: "Although a judge is not always obligated to explain the reasons for his decision to the litigants, in a case like this, where there is room for suspicion, he must.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim in the first line of 69b, so it cannot stand as posed. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why the appearance of being hounded, rather than the litigant's actual right, is what triggers the duty to explain, or what it means that Rav Pappa's two opposite rulings both rested on Rav Naḥman's principle that money is already divided. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

bava-metzia/70.summary: Rav Anan reports that Shmuel permitted lending orphans' money at interest, and Rav Naḥman snaps back that feeding orphans forbidden things will send them after their dead father. The proof turns out to be a copper kettle belonging to Mar Ukva's minor children, weighed out and weighed back, rented for a fee and charged for lost metal. Rabba and Rav Ashi then argue over where to park such money so the inheritance is not slowly eaten away.
bava-metzia/70.question: If an investor who arranges terms close to profit and far from loss is called a wicked person, what does it mean that this is exactly the arrangement chosen for orphans?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a standard of piety for an ordinary investor can be suspended when the party being protected cannot protect itself.

answer.quote: the relevant prohibition is a matter of rabbinic law, and the Sages rendered it permitted in the case of minor orphans, in order that their inheritance be preserved for them
answer.explanation: The page explicitly explains that the 'close to profit, far from loss' arrangement is only a rabbinic-level hint of interest, which the Sages waived for orphans so their estate would survive.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 70a: "the relevant prohibition is a matter of rabbinic law, and the Sages rendered it permitted in the case of minor orphans, in order that their inheritance be preserved for them". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: the 'wicked' label attaches to a rabbinic-level hint of interest, which the Sages permitted for orphans so their inheritance would be preserved. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and presses on what remains hard — e.g. why the same terms are piety-failing for an adult investor yet the preferred vehicle for orphans, or what Rav Ashi's willingness to drop the gold-scraps precaution says about how much risk of a loss the halakha will trade for purity. Alternatively ask about the kettle case, where Rav Naḥman insists the practice was never an orphans' leniency at all.

bava-metzia/71.summary: An early teaching ranks who gets your loan first: a Jew before a gentile, a poor borrower before a rich one, your relative before another poor person in your city. Rav Naḥman sharpens it, saying the Jew comes first even when the alternative is a profitable interest loan to a gentile and the loan to the Jew earns nothing. Rabbi Yosei then pictures the interest lender hiring witnesses, a scribe, pen and ink to sign a document declaring that he denies God.
bava-metzia/71.question: If honest people who lose everything are said to collapse and later rise, and a fully righteous person is never swallowed at all, what ruin could ever count as evidence against the rule?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a moral claim that reinterprets every apparent counterexample can still be tested at all.

answer.quote: Those who do not lend money with interest collapse but then ultimately rise, but these, who lend with interest, collapse and do not rise again.
answer.explanation: The page raises the counterexample of honest people whose property collapses and answers it with Rabbi Elazar's rise/no-rise distinction, which bears on the question but does not address what ruin could ever refute the rule.

bava-metzia/72.summary: A lender holds a man's orchard as security for a loan and eats its fruit for three years, then threatens to hide the mortgage document and claim he had bought the land outright. The borrower deeds the field to his minor son, sells it to the lender anyway, and then demands the sale be annulled. The Gemara asks only whether the buyer can recover his money from property the seller has since sold, and Rava says the deed is one that may not be written at all.
bava-metzia/72.question: If the sale is worthless because the seller was forced into it, why does the threat that forced him cost the lender nothing?

judge.reachNote: Coercion voids the transaction but the law here only unwinds it; whether the coercer himself bears any loss is the idea the question reaches.

answer.quote: Consequently, this document is completely invalid and cannot be used to collect from liened property.
answer.explanation: The page does impose one cost on the coercing lender-buyer — his deed is void so he cannot recover his money from liened property — but it never addresses why the extortionate threat itself draws no penalty, so the question remains askable.

bava-metzia/73.summary: Donkey drivers carrying goods between towns may charge the cheap town's price, and the Gemara argues whether the discount buys them a new market or cheaper stock at home. Rav, buying wheat in Kafri at six se'a for a sela, took only five, because an important person guards against even the look of interest. Then the Rabbis accuse Rava himself: others take four kor of grain, a large dry measure, in Nisan; he waits until Iyar and takes six.
bava-metzia/73.question: Rav takes less than the law allows him because of how it looks, and Rava takes more than his neighbors and calls it the sharecropper's gain, so who gets to decide which of the two is the appearance and which is the thing?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the gap between the appearance of interest and interest itself, and who is entitled to judge on which side a transaction falls.

answer.quote: On the contrary, you are the ones who are acting unlawfully, as in truth all of the land is liened to the sharecropper until he finishes working it
answer.explanation: Rava defends his own practice by pointing to the sharecropper's real gain, which bears on the question but does not say who decides when something is mere appearance versus substance, so the question survives.

bava-metzia/74.summary: Merchants used to label goods already sold with a marker, situmta, even while the crates still sat in the seller's warehouse and no money had changed hands. Rav Ḥaviva said that mark transfers ownership outright; the Rabbis said it only means that whoever backs out accepts the curse of He Who exacted payment. The conclusion keeps the curse everywhere and grants full acquisition only where local custom already treats the mark that way.
bava-metzia/74.question: If custom alone can turn a chalk mark into a binding purchase, what is a court doing when it declines to enforce the sale and pronounces a curse on the one who walks away instead?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a court may register an obligation it refuses to enforce, and that local practice can upgrade a moral bond into ownership.

answer.quote: The court does not force the parties to complete the transaction but applies the curse to the one who withdraws for his lack of integrity.
answer.explanation: The page states that the court withholds enforcement and instead attaches the curse to the retracting party's lack of integrity, which bears on the question but does not explain why custom can make full acquisition while the default remedy stays moral rather than coercive.

bava-metzia/75.summary: Hillel holds that a woman may not lend a neighbor a loaf of bread unless she first fixes its value in money, since wheat might rise before the loaf comes back. Shmuel, meanwhile, asks Avuh bar Ihi for a hundred peppers and offers 120 in return, saying scholars know the rule and the extra twenty is simply a gift. Rabbi Shimon pushes the other way, ruling that even a greeting the borrower never used to offer counts as interest.
bava-metzia/75.question: If twenty extra peppers can be called a gift because both men know better, why can a borrower's hello not be called mere politeness?

judge.reachNote: Whether awareness and intent can turn an extra payment into a gift, and why the same reasoning does not rescue a well-timed hello.

answer.quote: Since his intention is to provide a benefit to the lender, he has effectively paid him an extra sum for the money he lent him, which constitutes interest.
answer.where: Bava Metzia 75b (mishna, Rabbi Shimon on verbal interest)
answer.explanation: The page explains why a greeting is not mere politeness — it is aimed at benefiting the lender — but it never sets this against the scholars' pepper leniency, so the contrast the question draws still stands.

bava-metzia/76.summary: An employer sends a middleman to hire laborers, and the middleman names a wage the employer never authorized. The Gemara asks what the workers actually lost, since they accepted the terms they heard: maybe a better job elsewhere, maybe the extra effort they put into digging a ditch now filled with water, where good work cannot be seen. Later, laborers show up to a field too wet to till, and the question becomes who absorbs the wasted day.
bava-metzia/76.question: Why should laborers who walked out to a rained-out field swallow the loss just because the owner happened to look at his land the night before?

judge.reachNote: Who bears a loss when neither side is at fault — diligence as the dividing line for absorbing an accident.

answer.quote: It is their misfortune that something occurred in the meantime to prevent them from carrying out the task.
answer.explanation: The page states the reason directly: an owner who surveyed his field the night before did all he could, so the mishap falls on the laborers, while one who did not check "must bear the responsibility."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 76b: "It is their misfortune that something occurred in the meantime to prevent them from carrying out the task.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: the owner who surveyed his land did all he could, so the rained-out day is the laborers' misfortune, while the owner who failed to check bears responsibility. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for instance, asking why mere looking at the field counts as doing all one could, or why Rabbi Ḥiyya would pay nothing where the baraita pays idle-laborer wages. Alternatively, build the question off the middleman thread the summary opens with, which the page leaves with three competing explanations.

bava-metzia/77.summary: Rava sorts out who absorbs the loss when hired laborers show up and the work disappears. If rain falls and the field no longer needs watering, the laborers eat it; if the river itself rises and irrigates the field, the employer pays wages for idling, since he should have considered the possibility. When a river is prone to stopping midday, the split runs on knowledge: workers who live in that city lose the day, outsiders get paid.
bava-metzia/77.question: Why should knowing the local river's habits cost a laborer his wages, when the employer beside that same river pays nothing for the same knowledge?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the principle that risk follows the party who could have anticipated it, and presses on the asymmetry in how that knowledge is charged to each side.

answer.quote: if the river comes up and irrigates the field, this is the employer's loss, as he should have taken this possibility into consideration
answer.explanation: The page grounds loss-allocation in whose foreseeability was at fault, which bears on the note's question but never explains why the employer's own local knowledge of the river does not count against him.

bava-metzia/78.summary: A renter takes a hired donkey through the valley instead of over the mountain, ten mil either way, and the animal dies; the mishna holds him liable even when the route made no difference. Rabbi Yoḥanan ties this to Rabbi Meir, who calls anyone who departs from the employer's terms a robber, and a robber pays even for accidents. The Gemara then hunts for where Rabbi Meir said it, discarding the dyer and the Purim charity money along the way.
bava-metzia/78.question: If a snake bites the donkey on a road exactly as long and no more dangerous than the agreed one, is the renter really a robber, or only someone who broke his word?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether breaking the terms of a hire is merely breach of word or converts possession into theft, with liability for pure accident.

answer.quote: Conclude from it that he is called a robber because he changed and departed from the terms of the agreement
answer.explanation: The Gemara's own conclusion is that departing from the agreed terms is itself what makes one a robber, and 78b's opening adds that "A robber is liable for any damage that occurs, even due to circumstances beyond his control," which covers the snake-bite case directly.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 78b: "Conclude from it that he is called a robber because he changed and departed from the terms of the agreement". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the page concludes: Rabbi Meir holds that departing from the agreement is itself robbery, and a robber pays even for accidents. Rewrite so the question starts from that conclusion instead of requesting it — for instance, press on the fact that Rabba explains the snake bite without any robber logic (equally likely on either road), while Rabbi Yoḥanan needs Rabbi Meir to reach the same ruling, and ask what is at stake in choosing between them. Alternatively, ask why the Gemara insists on the words "diverges from the intent of the homeowner" rather than accepting the suspicion explanation.

bava-metzia/79.summary: A rented donkey dies halfway along the road, and the renter pays for the distance covered and is left with nothing but a grievance against the owner. The argument then narrows to the carcass: Rav says the money from selling it may buy a replacement donkey but not merely hire one, since hiring would use up the owner's principal, while Shmuel permits hiring. The same rule is tested against a tree pledged for a loan that dried up.
bava-metzia/79.question: If the carcass is worth only enough to hire a replacement, why should protecting the owner's principal matter more than the renter stuck where no donkey can be hired?

judge.reachNote: Whose loss the law prefers to absorb: the owner's remaining capital or the renter's frustrated journey.

answer.quote: as the carcass now constitutes the principal value of the donkey, one may not use the proceeds of its sale to pay rental fees
answer.explanation: The page states Rav's rationale — the carcass is all that remains of the owner's capital, so it cannot be spent on rent — but it never weighs that against the stranded renter's loss, which it leaves as a mere grievance.

bava-metzia/80.summary: One who rents a cow and plow for mountain ground and plows the valley instead is exempt when the plowshare, the blade at the base of the plow, breaks, since the mountain was the harder job. The page then turns to a seller who warns that his cow gores, bites, kicks, and lies down habitually, when in fact it does only one of these. The sale is void, because the buyer discounted the whole list. Rava says a cow with every listed fault stays sold.
bava-metzia/80.question: Where exactly is the line between a seller who buries his cow's one real fault in a pile of inventions and a seller who simply tells the whole ugly truth and is not believed?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether disclosure is judged by the seller's honesty or by what the buyer reasonably took in — but the page states Rava's line already.

answer.quote: If the animal had all of these defects, it is not a mistaken transaction, as he was forthright. The seller is not at fault
answer.explanation: The page draws the line explicitly: a list containing invented defects voids the sale, while a list that is entirely true (or that says 'this defect and other defects') does not.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 80a: "If the animal had all of these defects, it is not a mistaken transaction, as he was forthright. The seller is not at fault". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks for the line the page itself draws, since Rava's ruling that a fully truthful list 'is not a mistaken transaction, as he was forthright' states it outright. Ask instead about what remains unsettled: why the buyer's disbelief protects him when one item is invented but not when the seller says 'this defect and other defects' without naming them. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-metzia/81.summary: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for each other, and one of them handed his cloak to the others for safekeeping before heading to the oven; it was stolen through their carelessness. Rav Pappa held them liable, and the Sages objected that a watchman goes free when the owner is working for him at the time of the loss. The ruling survived only because it later emerged that the cloak's owner had been drinking beer, not baking.
bava-metzia/81.question: Was Rav Pappa right when he ruled, or only once someone found out where the cloak's owner had actually been standing?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether a verdict is judged by the judge's reasoning at the time or by facts that surface afterward — being right versus being lucky.

answer.quote: Since he was not doing work for them, this was not a case of safeguarding with the owner, and therefore Rav Pappa’s ruling was vindicated.
answer.explanation: The page states that the ruling was vindicated by the later discovery about the beer, and that Rav Pappa had been "embarrassed over his apparent mistake" before it, but it never says whether his original reasoning was sound, so the question can still be asked.

bava-metzia/82.summary: A porter carries another man's barrel from one place to another, breaks it, and the mishna lets him off if he swears he was not careless, whether he was guarding it for free or for a fee. Rabbi Eliezer repeats that ruling from his teachers and then says he wonders how either man can swear it. The Gemara presses the same way: a paid guardian owes for theft and loss anyway, and a man who stumbles looks negligent.
bava-metzia/82.question: If Rabbi Eliezer cannot see how the oath saves either carrier, what keeps him repeating the ruling instead of dropping it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between faithfully transmitting a received ruling and being able to justify it — but the page names that resolution explicitly.

answer.quote: this is the halakha that I heard from my teachers, but I do not understand their ruling
answer.explanation: The page states outright that Rabbi Eliezer keeps transmitting the ruling because it is a received tradition from his teachers even though he cannot account for it, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 82b (mishna): "this is the halakha that I heard from my teachers, but I do not understand their ruling". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the summary paraphrases: Rabbi Eliezer says he heard this from his teachers and repeats it though he does not understand it, and the Gemara restates that he received it as a tradition matching Rabbi Meir. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for example why a paid bailee's oath should help him at all when he is liable for theft and loss, or what a stumble has to be for it not to count as negligence.

bava-metzia/83.summary: Porters broke Rabba bar bar Ḥanan's barrel of wine; he seized their cloaks, and Rav made him return them and then pay their wages as well, quoting Proverbs rather than any rule about hired guards. The mishna then lets local custom set the workday and the workers' meal, bread and legumes or something sweeter. The page ends with Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, teaching an officer to spot thieves by who dozes in a tavern, and then becoming that officer.
bava-metzia/83.question: When Rabbi Elazar's belly fat refuses to rot in the summer sun, has he answered Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's charge, or only outlived it?
gate: the question brings in "Yehoshua", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Korḥa's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "kor", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether being right about who is wicked answers the charge that handing Jews to a gentile court is not yours to do.

answer.quote: In this manner, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, received proof that his decisions were correct and that he was a wholly righteous individual.
answer.explanation: The page treats the unputrefied fat as proof that his judgments were accurate and he was righteous, but it never has Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's objection — that it is not his place to eradicate God's thorns — met or withdrawn, so the question can still be honestly asked.

bava-metzia/84.summary: Rabbi Yohanan, bathing in the Jordan, is chased by Reish Lakish, then the leader of a band of marauders, and offers him his sister in marriage if he turns to Torah. Years later the two dispute when a sword or dagger becomes susceptible to ritual impurity, and Rabbi Yohanan tells him a bandit knows weapons because he once was one. Reish Lakish sickens and dies; the scholar sent to comfort Rabbi Yohanan only agrees with him, which is no comfort.
bava-metzia/84.question: If Rabbi Yohanan prized a partner who raised twenty-four objections, why did one accurate remark about where Reish Lakish learned about knives destroy them both?

judge.reachNote: The difference between opposition that builds a halakha and a true word aimed at who a person used to be.

answer.quote: What benefit did you provide me by bringing me close to Torah? There, among the bandits, they called me: Leader of the bandits, and here, too
answer.explanation: The page shows why the remark wounded — it told Reish Lakish his transformation counted for nothing — and adds that "Rabbi Yoḥanan was offended, which in turn affected Reish Lakish, who fell ill," but never explains why this exchange, unlike their usual twenty-four objections, proved fatal.

bava-metzia/85.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, hearing that another sage's greatness grew out of suffering, accepts thirteen years of kidney stones and scurvy; his stableman times the cattle's feeding so their lowing will cover the screams from the latrine. Then the page explains the pain a second way: a calf being led to slaughter hid its head in his cloak and wept, and he sent it off. Relief came only when he stopped a maidservant from sweeping out young weasels.
bava-metzia/85.question: If he asked for the afflictions himself, why does the page insist they came because of a calf he brushed aside?

judge.reachNote: Whether suffering that is asked for counts the same as suffering that is deserved — the page's 'out of love' versus 'due to an incident' distinction.

bava-metzia/86.summary: Rabba bar Naḥmani, accused before the king of keeping twelve thousand Jews from the head tax, flees from town to town and hides in a swamp. There he is summoned to settle a dispute in the heavenly academy over a leprous spot: God says the man is pure, every other member says impure. The Angel of Death cannot approach while Rabba studies aloud, so it takes wind in the branches, mistaken for soldiers, to make him say: let me die.
bava-metzia/86.question: Why does it take a gust of wind and Rabba's own fear of capture to bring him to the heavenly academy that had summoned him?

judge.reachNote: The question gestures at the idea that even a heavenly summons cannot override a man's own Torah and his own will to live, but the page spells that mechanism out.

answer.quote: the Angel of Death was unable to approach Rabba bar Naḥmani, as his mouth did not cease from his Torah study
answer.explanation: The page states outright that Torah study shielded him from the Angel of Death, and that only when the wind made him say "Let that man die" was "The Angel of Death... therefore able to take his soul."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 86a: "the Angel of Death was unable to approach Rabba bar Naḥmani, as his mouth did not cease from his Torah study". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in so many words: Torah study kept the Angel of Death away, and the wind broke it by making Rabba wish for death. Build the new question on top of that answer rather than around it — for instance, why heaven, which wanted him for its own dispute, still needed his Torah to lapse and his own consent to die, or why his fear of the government rather than of death is what undid him.

bava-metzia/87.summary: Abraham promises his three visitors a morsel of bread and then runs to fetch a calf, which Rabbi Elazar reads as the way of the righteous, who say little and do much. The verse-by-verse reading reaches Sarah laughing inside the tent, and God repeats her words to Abraham with her remark about her husband's age quietly dropped, which the school of Rabbi Yishmael calls truth altered for peace. The second half asks which produce a hired laborer may eat while working.
bava-metzia/87.question: If peace was worth editing Sarah's words, why was Abraham told about the laugh at all?

judge.reachNote: If peace justifies editing a report, what makes the report itself necessary — the question probes the limits of altering truth for peace.

bava-metzia/88.summary: Produce becomes liable for tithes, the portions set aside for priests, Levites and the poor, only once its processing is finished, and Rabbi Yannai says that moment comes when it enters the house while Rabbi Yoḥanan says a secured courtyard suffices. A fig tree rooted outside a courtyard with branches leaning in tests the line. Later the page sets a hired laborer beside a threshing ox, and the ox comes out with the stronger protection.
bava-metzia/88.question: If an employer who starves his worker breaks no muzzling prohibition while one who muzzles his ox does, what exactly is the ox getting that the worker is not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the asymmetry of legal protection: the ox is shielded by an enforceable prohibition while the worker's right to eat rests on a different footing (the mitzva to sustain a brother).

answer.quote: What is notable about an ox? It is notable in that you are commanded concerning its muzzling. Can you say that a similar halakha should apply to a person
answer.explanation: The page names the ox's unique feature (a command concerning muzzling) and, in the reverse inference, notes the person's unique feature (a command to sustain him), but it grounds the laborer's exclusion only in the word "kenafshekha" rather than explaining what the ox substantively gains.

bava-metzia/89.summary: The ox that may not be muzzled while it threshes sets the terms for what a hired laborer may eat, and the Sages read the word threshing narrowly: only produce grown from the ground, and only when its work is finished. Then the discussion stalls on a smaller question: may a worker roast figs in fire to sweeten them first? Salt is out, since salt is an added ingredient, but fire adds nothing, and the question is left open.
bava-metzia/89.question: If an employer may hand out wine so workers eat fewer grapes, and workers may dip bread in brine so they eat more, why should sweetening the grape itself sit on the other side of the line?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the line between making the eater readier to eat and making the food better to eat — but the page draws that line itself.

bava-metzia/90.summary: A cow treading grain on the threshing floor may not be muzzled, and the Sages press on what muzzling actually means. Rav Sheshet settles one question: the point of the law is that the food does the animal good, which he learns from Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai's vetches. Then come harder cases, none resolved: a thorn that settled in her mouth, a lion crouching nearby, her calf set outside, a leather blanket spread over the grain.
bava-metzia/90.question: If a lion crouches beside the threshing cow and the owner simply declines to chase it off, has he muzzled her or only left her frightened?

judge.reachNote: Whether muzzling is defined by the physical device on the mouth or by any act — or omission — that keeps the animal from eating the food it sees.

bava-metzia/91.summary: A man who muzzles his cow while it threshes is flogged and also owes the owner four kav of grain, roughly what the animal would have eaten, which breaks the rule that one offense brings one punishment. Rav Pappa then recalls two questions put to him, kneading dough with milk and penning a male and female of different species together; he forbade both, and reports that only one of those answers was right. Rav Ashi admits his own strict ruling was wrong too.
bava-metzia/91.question: If Rav Ashi's worry that slaves would crossbreed the animals and claim it happened on its own was a real one, why is the ruling he built on it recorded as the wrong answer?

judge.reachNote: Whether a plausible suspicion about how people will behave can by itself generate a prohibition, when the act itself carries no liability.

answer.quote: he is liable only if witnesses attest that he inserted the male organ into the female like a brush into a tube
answer.explanation: Shmuel's rule that crossbreeding liability requires manual insertion is the page's stated ground for holding that merely penning animals together is not prohibited, which bears on why the pen rulings are not halakha, though the page never says why Rav Ashi's slave-immorality reasoning itself fails.

summaryProblems.claim: The man muzzles his own cow ('his cow') yet owes its owner payment.
summaryProblems.pageSays: he must pay the owner of the cow four kav for a cow, the usual amount it consumes while threshing

judge.feedback: The summary says "The man muzzles his own cow ('his cow') yet owes its owner payment.", but the page says "he must pay the owner of the cow four kav for a cow, the usual amount it consumes while threshing". Say what the page says. Fix the ownership detail: the offender muzzles a cow he rented from someone else, which is why he pays its owner ("from the time of his pulling of the cow to rent it"). Then sharpen the question so it engages Shmuel's rule that crossbreeding requires actual insertion, since that is the page's reason why the pen rulings were not halakha, and ask what remains difficult about Rav Ashi's suspicion-based reasoning after it.

bava-metzia/92.summary: A hired worker picking cucumbers may eat a dinar's worth of them even if his whole wage comes to a sixth of a dinar, and the Rabbis add only that a person should be taught not to be a glutton, since word spreads and hiring dries up. From there the Gemara presses a harder question: is that food the worker's own property, or something Heaven grants him personally? The test case is a worker asking that his wife and children eat instead.
bava-metzia/92.question: Why can a master bargain away his minor slave's right to eat from the vines while he cannot do the same to his own minor son standing beside them?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a father's power over his household ends where the child's own bodily distress begins, but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: The Merciful One does not entitle him to waive the suffering of his minor son and daughter.
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks precisely why a master may stipulate for a minor slave but not for minor children, and answers that one may not waive a young child's suffering.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 92b: "The Merciful One does not entitle him to waive the suffering of his minor son and daughter.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words at the end of the daf: minor slaves can be stipulated away but minor children cannot because "the Merciful One does not entitle him to waive the suffering of his minor son and daughter." Ask something the page leaves unresolved instead — for instance, why the Gemara is content to explain a laborer's inability to hand food to his wife and children by the nazirite's "go round, go round," rather than by the worker's rights, or what it means that Ravina must call the son's portion something that merely "looks like a sale." Keep the summary's thread about own property versus Heaven's property, which is accurate.

bava-metzia/93.summary: A shepherd herding animals on the bank of the Pappa River lost one when it slipped into the water and drowned, and Rabba exempted him, since he guarded the way people guard. Abaye pushes back: may that paid shepherd also walk into town when others do, and nap when others nap? Rabba says yes, while Rav Ḥisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna hold that the wage was paid for exactly that extra watching.
bava-metzia/93.question: If a hired shepherd may go to town and sleep whenever ordinary people do, what is the owner buying with the wage?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — what a wage actually purchases in a custodial relationship — but the page states Rabba's answer outright.

answer.quote: whereas a paid bailee is obligated to do so even for payment
answer.explanation: Rabba himself states what the wage buys within his own view: the paid shepherd, unlike an unpaid one, must hire other shepherds and sticks even at a cost (recoverable from the owner), so the question is answered on the page.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 93b: "whereas a paid bailee is obligated to do so even for payment". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 93b: Rabba says the paid bailee, unlike the unpaid one, must gather shepherds and sticks even for payment, which he then recovers from the owner. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer — for instance, if the owner reimburses the guard money anyway, press on Rav Pappa's difficulty about what the owner gains, or on why 'the way people guard' still counts as a paid standard. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

bava-metzia/94.summary: A man hands his wife a bill of divorce on the condition that she climb to the sky, or swallow a reed a hundred cubits long. One view holds the divorce takes effect only if she does it, which means never; Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima says a demand that impossible is only talk, so the condition falls away and the divorce stands. Elsewhere the page lets someone guarding another's property contract out of the liability the Torah assigns him, since money can be waived.
bava-metzia/94.question: Who gets to decide that a man demanding his wife cross the sea on foot was exaggerating rather than meaning every word?

judge.reachNote: When may a court read a person's plain words as bluster rather than binding intent?

bava-metzia/95.summary: A borrower is liable if the borrowed animal is injured or dies, and the page works out how he also becomes liable for theft and loss, reasoning from the paid bailee who is liable for theft though exempt for injury and death. Then the strange exemption: if the owner's own services were borrowed along with the cow, the borrower pays nothing. Rav Hamnuna narrows this to an owner doing the same work throughout, and two baraitot demolish him.
bava-metzia/95.question: Why should an owner working for the borrower for one moment at the handover cancel all liability, while an owner plowing right beside his animal as it dies leaves the borrower paying in full?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether the bailee's exemption attaches at the moment the arrangement is formed or at the moment the loss occurs.

answer.quote: If he was with him, i.e., working for him, at the time of borrowing, he does not need to be with him at the time when the animal is injured
answer.explanation: The page states the asymmetrical rule and derives it by reconciling the two verses, but it gives a scriptural mechanism rather than a reason why presence at the handover should be decisive.

bava-metzia/96.summary: A borrower is exempt from paying when the animal's owner was working for him at the time of the loan, and Rav Ashi finds that timing hidden in the wording of the verse. Rami bar Ḥama then pushes at the edges: borrowing an item only to be seen with it and look wealthy, or borrowing work worth less than a peruta, a small coin. Then a borrowed ax breaks; Rava wants witnesses of normal use, Rav orders full payment.
bava-metzia/96.question: If an animal that dies from the ordinary work it was borrowed for costs the borrower nothing, why does Rav tell the man whose ax broke to pay for a whole new one?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that an exemption a borrower is entitled to in principle may still depend on his ability to prove ordinary use.

answer.quote: The Gemara asks: And if there are no witnesses, what is the halakha? The Gemara provides a precedent: Come and hear a similar case
answer.explanation: The page frames Rav's full-payment ruling as the case where the borrower cannot produce witnesses that he used the ax normally, which bears on the question, though the page breaks off mid-challenge ('Rav Kahana and Rav Asi said to Rav:') before justifying that severity.

bava-metzia/97.summary: A man borrows a cat to hunt mice, the mice band together and kill it, and Rav Ashi asks whether that counts as death from ordinary labor. Rava then hands borrowers a loophole: ask the lender to pour you water at the moment of borrowing, since an item borrowed along with its owner's services carries no liability. His students try the rule on him, and he bristles that they are lent to him, not he to them.
bava-metzia/97.question: If Rava is lent to his students during the kalla gatherings of Elul and Adar, what exactly changes in the rest of the year that makes the same teaching in the same room his loan rather than theirs?
gate: the question brings in "Elul", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Adar", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of who is serving whom in teaching, but the page already names the criterion (who controls the subject matter).

answer.quote: the teacher is required to teach a specific subject, and therefore he is lent to them. During the rest of the days of the year
answer.explanation: The page states exactly what changes: during kalla the subject matter is dictated to the teacher, while the rest of the year he chooses it, so the students are lent to him.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 97a: "the teacher is required to teach a specific subject, and therefore he is lent to them. During the rest of the days of the year". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the page: during the kalla the teacher must teach an assigned subject, while the rest of the year he can deflect students from tractate to tractate, so they are lent to him. Rewrite the question so it pushes past that answer — for instance, why control over the subject matter should be what decides who is 'lent,' or why a teacher's service to students counts less than their service in sharpening his learning. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-metzia/98.summary: A cowherd's arithmetic runs through the first half of the page: the Gemara counts out two, three, then four cows so that a bailee's answer can be part admission, part denial, and part honest ignorance. The rule it keeps landing on is harsh.
