A bailee who says he does not know which cow died cannot swear, and so pays in full, yet when both owner and bailee plead ignorance, the mishna has them split the loss.
bava-metzia/98.question: Why should saying "I do not know" cost the bailee everything when he says it alone, and only half when the owner says it too?

judge.reachNote: Whether the cost of one's own ignorance depends on the other party's certainty: an owner's definite claim triggers an unswearable oath, while mutual doubt is merely divided property.

answer.quote: It is in accordance with the opinion of Sumakhos, who says: When there is property of uncertain ownership, the parties divide it equally between them.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the reason for the half-payment (Sumakhos on uncertain ownership) and, separately, the reason for full payment (a partial admission creates an oath the bailee cannot swear), but it never sets the two side by side to explain the asymmetry the question raises.

bava-metzia/99.summary: Shmuel prices a stolen cake of fifty pressed dates at forty-nine perutot, small copper coins, though sold one at a time they fetch fifty. A robber pays a private victim the lower, bundled price; one who robs a cake belonging to the Temple treasury pays the full fifty plus a fifth. Rav Beivai bar Abaye objects that the victim could have sold them singly, and the answer arrives from a trampled garden bed, appraised as part of a whole field.
bava-metzia/99.question: If the date thief owes only the block price because the cake is valued whole, why do the porters who smashed a barrel owe the five-dinar market-day price instead of the ordinary four?
gate: gloss "the Temple treasury" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Is loss measured by what the owner actually could have realized, or by the item's most favorable possible valuation?

answer.quote: only in a case in which the shopkeeper did not have other barrels of wine to sell on that market day and consequently lost out
answer.explanation: The page's qualification of Rava's ruling shows the porters pay five only where an actual sale was lost, which bears on the contrast with the cake but never states the comparison, so the question remains askable.

bava-metzia/100.summary: A cow is traded for a donkey and later found to have calved, and nobody can say whether the calf came before the deal closed or after. The Gemara reaches first for possession: the calf is standing in a marsh, the maidservant's newborn in an alley, so neither buyer nor seller holds it. Pressed further, it drops the ownership logic entirely and credits Sumakhos, who splits property of uncertain ownership down the middle.
bava-metzia/100.question: When Rava rescues the mishna by inserting "perhaps" into two claims that the text states flatly, is he reading the mishna or rewriting it?
gate: the question brings in "Rava", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When a sage 'emends' a tanna's words to save a ruling, is that interpretation of the text or substitution for it — the limits of amoraic authority over the mishna's language.

answer.quote: Granted, according to the opinion of Rava, from the fact that the last clause of the mishna is referring to a case where there is a conflict
answer.explanation: The Gemara supplies an internal textual warrant for Rava's emendation — the mishna's own final clause speaks of uncertain claims, so the first clause may be read that way — which bears on whether he is reading rather than rewriting, without settling the question of emendation as a method.

bava-metzia/101.summary: A man plants trees in another's field without asking, and Rav tells the owner to pay the planter the lesser of his expenses or the added value. The owner protests twice that he never wanted the trees, and Rav lets the matter drop. Later Rav sees that the owner has fenced the field and is guarding the trees, and rules that he now owes the greater of the two amounts.
bava-metzia/101.question: If putting up a fence counts as accepting the trees, what was the owner supposed to do with trees he never asked for and could not uproot?

judge.reachNote: Whether guarding a benefit you never asked for and cannot refuse counts as accepting it, and so creates a debt.

bava-metzia/102.summary: Manure dropped in a rented courtyard by oxen that wandered in from the street belongs to the landlord, and the Gemara reads that as support for Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, who holds that a person's courtyard acquires items for him even when he knows nothing about them. The rule frays quickly. An unsecured courtyard acquires nothing, unless news of a lost item spreads through town and people stop reaching for it, at which point it counts as secured.
bava-metzia/102.question: If an unsecured courtyard acquires a lost item only once everyone in town assumes the owner will collect it, is the acquisition being done by the courtyard or by the neighbors' restraint?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what makes a space legally 'acquiring' — the physical enclosure or the social fact that others defer to the owner.

answer.quote: people withdraw themselves from it, as they assume that the owner of the courtyard will take it. Therefore, no one will even try to take it and the courtyard will be like a secured courtyard
answer.explanation: The Gemara says the townspeople's withdrawal is what makes the courtyard count as secured, so that the courtyard itself then effects acquisition — but it does not settle which factor is the operative acquirer, so the question can still be pressed.

bava-metzia/103.summary: A man borrows a well to irrigate his fields, its walls fall in, and whether he may rebuild depends on whether he asked for this well or for a well. That small word runs through the whole page: a rented house that collapses, a hoe lent for one orchard or for orchards, a field leased with a spring that later dries up. Again and again the Gemara rules that whoever meant something narrower should have said so in advance.
bava-metzia/103.question: Why is a landlord's "a house like this" narrowed to mean only length and width, while a sharecropper's silence about why he weeded is read against him?

judge.reachNote: Who bears the cost of an unspoken intention: is a vague phrase read narrowly, or is silence charged to the one who stayed silent?

answer.quote: the mishna teaches us that the renter should have specified this intention explicitly to the landowner beforehand in order to exempt him from the requirement to plow
answer.explanation: The page states the shared principle — an unspoken narrower intent must be voiced in advance — which bears on both halves of the question, but it never sets the house-clause ruling beside the weeding ruling or explains the apparent asymmetry the question raises.

bava-metzia/104.summary: A sharecropper's standard contract says that if he leaves the field fallow he will pay the owner in best-quality produce, and Rabbi Meir treats that boilerplate line as binding. The Gemara then collects sages who read ordinary document wording the same way, including Hillel, who saved the children of Alexandrian women from being declared mamzerim by finding a clause that delayed the marriage until the wedding canopy. Later, dowry sums written at double or triple their real value are read down.
bava-metzia/104.question: If a marriage contract that says four hundred dinars is understood by everyone to mean two hundred, why is the clause Hillel found in one binding to the letter?

judge.reachNote: When is a document read by its literal words and when by the convention everyone knows stands behind the words?

bava-metzia/105.summary: A tenant farmer refuses to weed the field he rents, arguing the owner loses nothing since he will hand over the agreed produce either way. The Gemara supplies the owner with three sharp replies, about inferior wheat, about market wheat, about the field's reputation, and then throws all three out because the mishna gave only one reason: weed seeds already in the soil keep sprouting long after the tenant walks away. A second thread measures when a crop is big enough to bother harvesting.
bava-metzia/105.question: If the owner's other complaints, bad wheat and a bad name for his land, are all reasonable, why does the mishna's single stated reason force them off the table?

judge.reachNote: When a text gives one reason, does that reason silently exclude every other good reason that could have been given?

answer.quote: But didn't we learn in the mishna that the reason they do not listen to him is: Because it will grow weeds for me, indicating that these other claims are not accepted?
answer.where: Bava Metzia 105a (Gemara on the weeding mishna)
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection and acts on it by discarding the three replies in favor of 'the seed that fell has fallen,' but it asserts rather than explains why the mishna's single reason is exclusive.

bava-metzia/106.summary: A tenant told to plant wheat plants barley instead, the whole valley is wind blasted, and the fight is over whether the owner can claim that wheat would have brought him better fortune. The Gemara lets him claim it, and Shmuel goes further: a tenant who never planted at all still owes full rent, since the owner's merit might have spared the field. Rav Sheshet answers with a shepherd who left his flock, and the argument about miracles runs out.
bava-metzia/106.question: If the owner cannot demand the kind of great miracle that brought Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's goats home with bears on their horns, why can he not at least demand a small one?
gate: the question brings in "Dosa's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a litigant can charge another with the loss of divine favor he might have enjoyed, and how far such a claim can be pressed.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Sheshet answers Shmuel with the case of the shepherd who left his flock.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Sheshet raises an objection from a baraita: In the case of a shepherd who was herding the animals of others, and he left his flock

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Sheshet answers Shmuel with the case of the shepherd who left his flock.", but the page says "Rav Sheshet raises an objection from a baraita: In the case of a shepherd who was herding the animals of others, and he left his flock". Say what the page says. Fix the direction of the exchange: Rav Sheshet does not answer Shmuel, he raises an objection from the baraita of the shepherd against Shmuel's ruling. The question is fine and genuinely open, since the page ends with "this is difficult," but the summary should make clear that the miracle argument collapses under a challenge, not an answer.

bava-metzia/107.summary: Rav Yehuda and Ravin bar Rav Naḥman own neighboring fields whose trees lean across the line, and Rav Yehuda proposes that each takes the fruit of whatever tilts his way. Rav rules that way; Shmuel says the two owners split all the fruit, and a baraita supporting Shmuel is reread as a tree straddling the whole boundary. Later, Rabba bar Rav Huna refuses to clear his riverbank trees for the boat haulers until the Persian general's men clear theirs.
bava-metzia/107.question: If cutting his own trees alone would do nothing for the men hauling boats, is Rabba bar Rav Huna genuinely free of the rule that one acts first and advises others after, or only spared from looking foolish?

judge.reachNote: Does the duty to act before advising others depend on the act having practical effect, or is it about the adviser's own integrity?

answer.quote: If the workers of the Persian officer cut down, I will cut down as well, and if they do not cut down, why should I cut down for no purpose?
answer.explanation: The Gemara supplies Rabba bar Rav Huna's reason — futility, since the general's men would ignore a Jewish scholar — but does not address whether futility truly releases him from 'adorn yourself first' or merely excuses the appearance, so the question can still be asked.

bava-metzia/108.summary: Rabba bar Rav Naḥman ordered a riverside forest cut down to clear a path for men hauling boats; the owner, Rabba bar Rav Huna, was within his rights to refuse, and his curse killed the cutter's children. The page then gives a neighbor whose field borders a plot for sale the power to take it from the buyer, resting on a verse about doing right and good. Then come the exceptions: gifts, urgent sales for taxes or burial, sales to orphans.
bava-metzia/108.question: If "right and good" can pull a legally purchased field out of a buyer's hands, why does the curse of a man standing on his legal right to keep his trees still land?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: When does a bare legal right protect a person, and when does the demand to do 'right and good' override it?

answer.quote: Since he was within his rights not to cut down his trees, as explained above, he grew angry and pronounced a curse
answer.explanation: The page grounds the curse's force in the owner's legal right to leave his trees standing, but never reconciles that right with the later principle that 'right and good' can strip a legally entitled purchaser of his field.

bava-metzia/109.summary: A tenant who leases a field for fewer than seven years may not plant flax, which drains the soil, and may not cut a sycamore's branches for beams. Abaye and Rava then argue over whether a departing cultivator is paid for growth he never planted, and Rav Pappa, whose hay field sprouted palm trees, demands payment for them. He loses the argument: by admitting he wanted saffron there, he shows he meant to take his crop and go.
bava-metzia/109.question: Rav Pappa gets something because the palms crowded out his saffron, while Rav Beivai gets nothing because his trees came up along a fence he built, so is a cultivator ever paid for value he made rather than for value he was denied?
gate: the question brings in "Beivai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — compensation as reward for creation versus compensation for loss inflicted — but the page's planter cases already settle it.

answer.quote: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who said to him: Give the planter the value of his enhancement.
answer.explanation: The later half of the page deals with planters who are paid outright for the enhancement they produced — the departing planter who wishes to ascend to Eretz Yisrael is awarded a share of the enhancement itself, and Rav Minyumi sets the fractions — so the page does state that a cultivator can be paid for value he made rather than value he was denied.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 109b: "Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who said to him: Give the planter the value of his enhancement.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered later on the same page: the planter cases on 109b pay a departing worker for the enhancement he produced, with Rav Pappa bar Shmuel and Rav Minyumi arguing only over the fraction. Rewrite the question so it starts from that, for instance asking why the planter is credited for growth he created while the field-cultivator with a sycamore is not, or why the owner's own soil is treated as a co-producer that halves the planter's claim. The summary is accurate and can stay, though it may be worth noting that Rav Pappa is left with the wood value rather than nothing.

bava-metzia/110.summary: A creditor holding a field against a loan says the mortgage ran three years; the debtor says two, and while the case is still open the creditor goes and eats the third year's crop. Rav Kahana rules that the produce stays with whoever consumed it, since the witnesses who signed the document may yet reveal what it said. But land already pledged to a creditor counts as collected, so orphans claiming they improved the field must bring proof.
bava-metzia/110.question: If the one who ate the crop keeps it, what stops each side from racing into the field before the court rules?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a possession-based tiebreaker rewards self-help and may invite parties to seize facts on the ground before judgment.

answer.quote: Therefore, the produce should remain in the possession of the one who consumed it until the matter is resolved.
answer.explanation: The page indicates the consumer's hold is only provisional because the signing witnesses may yet reveal the document's terms, which bears on—but does not directly address—what deters a race to the field.

bava-metzia/111.summary: A middleman who hires laborers for someone else escapes the ban on paying late, since the work was not done for him. Yehuda bar Mareimar used that: he sent his attendant to hire with the words that the wages are the employer's obligation, and Mareimar and Mar Zutra hired workers for each other. Later the sages argue over what separates oppression from theft, until Rava says they are one act, split in two so the withholder breaks two prohibitions.
bava-metzia/111.question: If a man can step outside the prohibition by having someone else say the words for him, what is left of the worker's protection?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition framed around who owes the wage can be emptied by wording, and what the law of timely payment is actually protecting.

answer.quote: where the middleman said to them: The obligation to pay your wages is incumbent upon the employer, in which case they share responsibility for the payment and neither violates
answer.explanation: The page explains the mechanism of the evasion — responsibility is shared so neither party is the one who 'withholds' — but it never states what remains of the laborer's protection once the Torah prohibition is sidestepped.

bava-metzia/112.summary: A laborer climbs a tall ramp or hangs from a tree to earn his pay, and the verse "for he sets his soul upon it" is read two ways: withholding wages costs the withholder his own soul, or it takes the worker's. Later the page asks why the laborer, the one making the claim, swears and collects, when normally the defendant swears and pays nothing. The answer, that an employer juggling many workers forgot, then unravels into why an oath is needed at all.
bava-metzia/112.question: If the whole reason for flipping the oath is that a busy employer probably forgot paying, whose mind is the laborer's oath actually meant to settle?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that an oath can function as reassurance rather than proof, but the page already names that function outright.

answer.quote: The laborer takes an oath in order to alleviate the concerns of the employer, as, if he is not required to take an oath, the employer will feel that he has been cheated.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly states that the oath exists to settle the employer's mind, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 112b: "The laborer takes an oath in order to alleviate the concerns of the employer, as, if he is not required to take an oath, the employer will feel that he has been cheated.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words a few lines after the passage the summary paraphrases, so it cannot stand as written. Rewrite it to start from that answer and press on what remains hard, for instance why the Gemara first grounded the flipped oath in the laborer's livelihood and then abandoned that reason for the employer's forgetfulness, or why the presumption that employers do not delay wages outweighs the same preoccupation once the payment time has passed. Keep the summary; it is accurate.

bava-metzia/113.summary: A creditor whose loan is unpaid may not walk into the debtor's house to grab collateral; he stands outside while the debtor brings something out. Shmuel says even a court agent must stay outside, and the Gemara piles up baraitot on both sides before conceding the tannaim disagree. The agent who does enter must leave a bed, a second bed, and bedding, because Shmuel the doctor held that eating and sleeping in one spot sickens a man.
bava-metzia/113.question: If the debtor keeps two beds so he can walk a few steps after eating, why does the baraita leave nothing at all for his wife and children?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward whose upkeep a creditor must subsidize — the debtor's person or his household — but the page answers it outright.

answer.quote: as the Torah did not obligate the creditor to care for the debtor's family
answer.explanation: The baraita's own gloss on the page states the reason nothing is left for the wife and children: the creditor's obligation runs only to the debtor himself.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 113b: "as the Torah did not obligate the creditor to care for the debtor's family". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same baraita the summary is drawing on, which says the items are left for the debtor "but not for his wife, and not for his sons or for his daughters, as the Torah did not obligate the creditor to care for the debtor's family." Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for example, why Rav Ḥagga's objection "Your needs are not cast upon me" arises only after the arrangement is described, or why the Gemara measures the debtor's due by the principle that all Israel are children of kings while denying his family a bed. Keep the summary's accurate picture of the Shmuel dispute and the two beds.

bava-metzia/114.summary: The Sages ask whether a creditor collecting a debt may strip a debtor bare, or must leave him something to live on, the way a priest does for a poor man who vowed his own valuation to the Temple. No one answers, until Rabba bar Avuh finds Elijah standing in a gentile graveyard and asks him; Elijah links the word "poor" in both verses. Then Elijah leads him into the Garden of Eden to gather leaves.
bava-metzia/114.question: Rabba bar Avuh throws the leaves away but still sells the scented cloak for twelve thousand dinars and hands the money to his sons-in-law, so is the account settled or only moved?
gate: the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether merit spent in this world can be returned by refusing to enjoy its proceeds, or only shifted onto someone else's account.

answer.quote: Since he knew that this was taken from his portion in the World-to-Come, he did not want to benefit from it himself, and he therefore divided the sum among his sons-in-law.
answer.explanation: The page states why he gave the money away — he refused to benefit from World-to-Come merit himself — but never says whether the merit was thereby restored or merely passed on, so the note's question survives the line.

bava-metzia/115.summary: A creditor may not walk into a debtor's house to seize collateral, though the Sages read the verse to permit entering a guarantor's house. The mishna bars taking collateral from any widow, rich or poor, while Rabbi Shimon limits the ban to a poor widow: her pledge must be returned each day, and the creditor's daily visits would give her a bad name among the neighbors. That flips the two sages' usual habits about reading reasons into verses.
bava-metzia/115.question: If a poor widow is protected because her neighbors would talk, is the law guarding her or deferring to their suspicion?

judge.reachNote: Whether a protective law serves the vulnerable party's own interest or simply defers to what others will think of her.

answer.quote: you will thereby give her a bad name among her neighbors, as they will suspect her of developing an inappropriate relationship with you
answer.where: Bava Metzia 115a (Gemara on the widow's mishna)
answer.explanation: The page supplies Rabbi Shimon's rationale — damage to the widow's reputation — which bears on the question but does not settle whether the law protects her interest or merely accommodates the neighbors' suspicion.

bava-metzia/116.summary: A house collapses, and the lower story and the upper story belonged to two different people, who now split the timber, stones and earth. Broken stones go to whoever owned the part that gave way, so the Gemara must build a case where nobody can tell how it fell: it came down at night, the stones were cleared, and the crowd that cleared them walked off. Then one owner recognizes his stones and the other says only that he does not know.
bava-metzia/116.question: If saying "I don't know" is not enough to make a man pay a hundred dinars he is accused of holding, why is it enough to cost him the stones he cannot identify?
gate: the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — when silence or ignorance counts as admission — but the page states its own answer: only where an oath obligation already exists.

answer.quote: Just as Rav Naḥman says in that context: He is liable to pay only in a case where there is a matter of an oath between them, here too
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's contradiction as a refutation of Rav Naḥman and resolves it by saying the mishna's case is one where the party who says "I don't know" is already bound to take an oath he cannot take, so he pays.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 116b: "Just as Rav Naḥman says in that context: He is liable to pay only in a case where there is a matter of an oath between them, here too". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own challenge to Rav Naḥman, and the page answers it explicitly: the stones case involves a party already liable to take an oath he cannot take, so "I don't know" costs him. Rewrite the question to start after that answer — for instance, why an unswearable oath should convert ignorance into liability at all, or why the mishna bothers to teach a case governed by an explicit oath rule. Alternatively, build the question from a different thread on the page, such as Abaye and Rava's dispute over whether recognizing some stones helps or hurts the one who recognizes them.

bava-metzia/117.summary: Two neighbors share a building, one above the other, and cracked plaster lets the upstairs washing water run down and ruin the apartment below. Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba says the upper resident repairs it; Rabbi Elai, in the name of Rabbi Ḥiyya son of Rabbi Yosei, says the lower one does. Rav Ashi's school held that even Rabbi Yosei admits liability when a man's damage travels like arrows, so the Gemara answers that the water pauses before finding the hole.
bava-metzia/117.question: If the water sits on the floor a moment before it finds the hole, at what point does the man who poured it stop being the one who shot the arrow?

judge.reachNote: Where an act ends and mere consequence begins — how much interruption of the water's path severs a man from the damage his own hands set in motion.

answer.quote: This is a case in which the water flow stops in one place, as the hole in the floor is not directly in the place where the water was poured
answer.explanation: The Gemara gives the criterion that breaks the arrow analogy — the water halting away from the point of pouring means the upper resident is not a direct cause — but it does not say where in general the line between direct and indirect action falls, so the question can still be pressed.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Ashi's school held that even Rabbi Yosei admits liability when damage travels like arrows.
summaryProblems.pageSays: But didn’t Rav Ashi say: When I was in the school of Rav Kahana we would say that Rabbi Yosei concedes in a case of his arrows.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Ashi's school held that even Rabbi Yosei admits liability when damage travels like arrows.", but the page says "But didn’t Rav Ashi say: When I was in the school of Rav Kahana we would say that Rabbi Yosei concedes in a case of his arrows.". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: the teaching that Rabbi Yosei concedes in a case of "his arrows" was said in the school of Rav Kahana and merely reported by Rav Ashi, not held by "Rav Ashi's school." Keep the rest of the summary and the question, which correctly picks up the Gemara's answer that the water stops in one place and presses on where directness ends.

bava-metzia/118.summary: A laborer hired to work with hay asks for his wages, and the employer offers him some of the hay instead; the court does not listen. Rav Naḥman tries three times to square this with a baraita that permits it, landing on the difference between a laborer who gathers ownerless hay and one who only stands and watches it. That question of whether watching alone acquires ownerless property then reopens a dispute about the Temple's watchmen over Sabbatical-year grain.
bava-metzia/118.question: Does paying the grain watchman four dinars change what he actually owns, or only how willingly he hands the crop over?
gate: the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: What a wage does: confer title on the payer, or merely secure the worker's wholehearted cooperation — the page adds a third, purely deterrent, function.

answer.quote: so that violent people should hear of this and keep away from the grain, since when they hear that the Temple is paying the watchmen
answer.explanation: The page canvasses both horns of the note's question — the first tanna's view that viewing acquires (so the wage determines for whom) and Rava's view that the wage secures a wholehearted handover — and then, in the second version backed by Ravin in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name, states that the four dinars are instituted purely to deter violent people, with viewing not effecting acquisition at all.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Metzia 118a: "so that violent people should hear of this and keep away from the grain, since when they hear that the Temple is paying the watchmen". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own, and the page answers it three ways, closing with Ravin's report that the dispute turns on the fear of violent people and that the four dinars are a deterrent. Rewrite the question so it starts from that resolution rather than reaching it — for instance, why one and the same dispute can be reread as being about acquisition, about the watchman's inner willingness, and about thieves, or what it means that a token wage can do work that has nothing to do with ownership. Keep the summary; it is faithful.

bava-metzia/119.summary: Two gardens sit one above the other, and vegetables sprout from the earth wall between them; Rabbi Shimon says whatever the upper owner can reach by stretching out his hand belongs to him. The school of Rabbi Yannai narrows it: he may reach, but he may not strain. Then comes a plant whose leaves are within reach but whose roots are not, and the question is dropped without an answer.
bava-metzia/119.question: If a vegetable belongs to whoever can reach it without straining, does a short neighbor simply own less of the wall than a tall one?

judge.reachNote: Whether a boundary of ownership can be set by the personal bodily capacity of the owner rather than by a fixed objective line.

answer.quote: And this is only so provided that he does not force himself, but simply stretches out his hand in the usual manner.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yannai's school fixes the measure as an ordinary unstrained stretch, which hints that the standard tracks the individual owner's natural reach, but the page never addresses whether a shorter owner therefore acquires less.

bava-batra/2.summary: Two partners in a shared courtyard decide to split it, and the mishna fixes the wall's thickness by local custom, six handbreadths for rough stone, with each partner giving up three from his own side. The Gemara hangs the whole chapter on one word, mehitza: if it means a partition the two of them wished for, then being watched in your own courtyard is not damage; if it means a division one can force, it is. Proof after proof is raised and turned away.
bava-batra/2.question: If being seen in your own courtyard is not damage, why must a man whose roof overlooks his neighbor's courtyard build a parapet four cubits high?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether exposure to a neighbor's gaze counts as actionable damage — but the page's final refutation already resolves this instance via predictability of use.

answer.quote: The situation is different there, as the owner of the courtyard can say to the owner of the roof: I make use of my courtyard on a regular basis.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection from Rav Naḥman's parapet ruling and answers it by distinguishing regular courtyard use from the roof owner's unpredictable, infrequent presence.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 2b: "The situation is different there, as the owner of the courtyard can say to the owner of the roof: I make use of my courtyard on a regular basis.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very last objection on the daf, and the Gemara answers it immediately: the roof case differs because the courtyard owner uses his space constantly while the roof owner goes up only rarely, so the neighbor cannot know when he is being watched. Write a question that starts from that answer instead of ignoring it — for instance, why unpredictability of the gaze rather than the gaze itself should be what makes sight into damage, or why a partition of pegs suffices to 'divide' a courtyard if privacy were the point. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful to the page.

bava-batra/3.summary: Rav Ḥisda says a person may not tear down a synagogue before the replacement is built, and Ravina keeps pressing: what if the money is already collected, what if the bricks and beams are stacked and ready? Rav Ashi blocks each case, since a chance to ransom captives could swallow the funds or the materials. His line stops only at the finished building: people do not sell their homes, and certainly not their synagogues.
bava-batra/3.question: If a community would sell its stacked bricks and beams to ransom captives, why would it not sell the building those same materials became?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that stacked materials are fungible cash while an inhabited structure is not — but the Gemara itself raises and settles this exchange.

answer.quote: Rav Ashi said to him: People do not sell their residences, and certainly not their synagogues.
answer.explanation: Ravina raises precisely the note's objection — that a built synagogue might also be sold for captives — and Rav Ashi answers it directly.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 3b: "Rav Ashi said to him: People do not sell their residences, and certainly not their synagogues.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Ravina's own objection, which Rav Ashi answers on the page with "People do not sell their residences, and certainly not their synagogues" — so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to press on something the page leaves unsettled, such as why the two stated reasons (negligence versus the disruption of prayer) yield different rulings when another synagogue exists, or why visible cracks or government action lift the concern about negligence entirely. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

bava-batra/4.summary: Herod, who blinded Bava ben Buta with a garland of porcupine hide, sits before him in disguise and tries three times to goad him into cursing the king. Bava ben Buta refuses each time, and when Herod reveals himself and asks for a remedy, the blind sage tells him to rebuild the Temple. The Gemara then asks how he could advise a murderer, since Daniel was punished for counseling Nebuchadnezzar toward charity, which delayed the king's downfall a full year.
bava-batra/4.question: If advising a tyrant to do one good thing earned Daniel the lions' den, what makes Herod's rebuilt Temple the exception?

judge.reachNote: When is it permitted to help a wicked ruler do good, given that aiding him may prolong his power — the page names both the slave's obligation and the Temple's necessity.

bava-batra/5.summary: Ronya's field was surrounded on all four sides by fields belonging to Ravina, who built partitions and then asked Ronya for half the cost, then for a cheaper reed price, then just a watchman's wage; Ronya paid nothing. Ravina sent his sharecropper to take a cluster of dates, and when Ronya shouted in protest, Ravina called the shout proof that he was glad of the fence. Rava told Ronya to settle for the watchman's wage or be charged half.
bava-batra/5.question: Does a man shouting at someone stealing his dates prove he wanted the fence, or only that he wanted his dates?

judge.reachNote: What a person's spontaneous conduct reveals about consent to and benefit from a neighbor's unrequested improvement.

answer.quote: Ronya said to him: If it were only a goat, doesn't one need merely to chase it away [le'akhluyei]? No partition is required.
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the note's objection through Ronya, who argues the shout shows at most a need for chasing off animals rather than for a wall, and Ravina then retreats to claiming only a watchman's wage — but the page never settles whether the shout proves benefit from the partitions.

bava-batra/6.summary: Abaye sets two houses facing each other across a public street, and rules that each owner fences half his roof, offset so the two halves do not line up. Someone might argue that the street already exposes you, so build the whole fence yourself and leave me out of it. The reply sorts kinds of exposure: strangers see you by day, standing, and only if they bother to look up, while the man opposite sees you always.
bava-batra/6.question: If one neighbor offers cash to cover the entire fence and is still refused because the added weight would sink his own roof, what is actually being divided here, the cost or the load?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a shared obligation may be about splitting the physical burden rather than the expense, which is exactly the Gemara's stated reasoning.

answer.quote: What is the reason you do not want to build a fence? It is because the added weight will damage your house’s foundation. My foundation too will be damaged
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly rejects the offer of cash compensation by explaining that what each neighbor is being made to bear is the structural burden of the fence, not merely its cost.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 6b: "What is the reason you do not want to build a fence? It is because the added weight will damage your house’s foundation. My foundation too will be damaged". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 6b, where the Gemara says the refusal is because the added weight damages the foundation and "My foundation too will be damaged" — so cost-versus-load is settled on the page. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on something still unresolved, for example why the privacy obligation is discharged by each man's own roof rather than by whatever arrangement actually blocks the sightline. Alternatively build the question off the Gemara's ranking of day/night, standing/sitting, and looking/not looking exposure, and ask what counts as being seen.

bava-batra/7.summary: A house has sunk into the ground; the downstairs owner wants to demolish and rebuild, and the upstairs owner refuses every offer, telling him to crawl in and out on his stomach. Rav Ḥama rules the upstairs neighbor can block the work, and rules the same way for a man whose new wall darkens his neighbor's windows. Then two brothers split an estate, one taking the hall and one the garden, and Rav Ashi says they priced bricks and beams but never airspace.
bava-batra/7.question: If the brothers never put a price on the airspace, was the light coming through the hall's windows part of what one brother inherited, or something he had merely been getting for free?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether light and airspace are owned property or merely an unpriced benefit — but the page answers it: Rav Ashi says airspace was never assessed and each brother retained it, and 7b rules with Rav Ḥama/Shmuel that brothers have no right of windows.

answer.quote: Nor do they have the right of windows against each other, i.e., the right to prevent the other from building a wall facing his windows
answer.explanation: The page states Shmuel's rule, which Rav Ḥama follows and which Ravina rules as halakha, that brothers who divide an estate acquire no claim to light through their windows, so the light was not part of the inheritance.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 7b: "Nor do they have the right of windows against each other, i.e., the right to prevent the other from building a wall facing his windows". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is settled later on the same page: Rav Ashi says each brother retained his own airspace, and 7b records Shmuel's rule that brothers have no right of windows, with Ravina ruling the halakha follows Rav Ḥama. Ask instead about what stays uneasy after that ruling — for example, why the claim "I took this share on condition that I would live there the way our fathers lived there" is set aside, or why blocking a stranger's light counts as damage even for a straw shed while a brother may darken a hall at will.

bava-batra/8.summary: Rav Na akhman bar Rav  Hisda collected the poll tax from Torah scholars, and was told he had violated verses from all three parts of the Bible. The page keeps circling who pays for what: orphans are charged for digging a cistern that may come up dry, while Sages are said not to need the city's protective wall. Then Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi opens his storehouses in a drought and bars the unlearned from entering.
bava-batra/8.question: Was Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi moved to feed everyone by the argument that even dogs and ravens are fed without having learned anything, or only by the discovery that the man he fed had been a scholar all along?

judge.reachNote: Whether sustenance is owed by merit of learning or simply by being a living creature in need — but the page settles which motive produced the change of policy.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then said: Let everyone enter, as there may also be others who hide the fact that they are true Torah scholars
answer.explanation: The page states that the general opening of the storehouses came only after the investigation revealed Yonatan ben Amram's identity, and it gives Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's stated reason, while the dog-and-raven plea moved him to feed only that one man.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 8a: "Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then said: Let everyone enter, as there may also be others who hide the fact that they are true Torah scholars". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is explicitly answered a few lines later: he fed the one man out of pity at the dog-and-raven plea, but opened the doors to all only after learning that scholars may hide themselves. Rewrite so the question starts from that stated reason rather than asking what the page already tells us. For instance, ask why the fear of turning away a concealed scholar, rather than the plea of bare hunger, was what changed the rule, or press on Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's linked claim that suffering comes only through ignoramuses.

bava-batra/9.summary: Rav Huna says charity collectors investigate how poor a man is before giving him food, but clothe anyone in rags without asking questions. Rav Yehuda says the reverse, and both hang their view on the same verse in Isaiah, reading "share your bread with the hungry" as either examine him first or hand it over at once. Nearby, Rav Pappa turns away a beggar already going door to door, until Rav Sama asks whether the man should starve.
bava-batra/9.question: If one verse can be read both as check him first and as feed him immediately, what is really deciding which reading wins?

judge.reachNote: Whether the verse is generating the ruling or merely dressing a prior judgment about which suffering is more urgent — shame or hunger.

answer.quote: It is taught in a baraita in accordance with the opinion of Rav Yehuda: If a poor person said: Cover me with clothing, the charity collectors examine him
answer.explanation: The page settles which reading prevails by citing a baraita that matches Rav Yehuda, but it does not say what makes one exegesis of the verse more compelling than the other, so the question remains largely open.

bava-batra/10.summary: A Roman governor, Turnus Rufus, asks Rabbi Akiva why, if God loves the poor, He does not feed them Himself, then answers with a parable: a king jails a slave and orders him starved, and whoever feeds him angers the king. Akiva swaps the slave for a son, and the punishment for a gift. Later the page ranks giving, preferring coins dropped in a communal purse where neither donor nor recipient learns the other's name.
bava-batra/10.question: If a man who gives charity so that his sons will live is called fully righteous, what exactly was Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai protecting when he hid the dream from his nephews?
gate: the question brings in "Yoḥanan", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Zakkai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What is lishma worth, if charity given for one's own benefit already counts as full-fledged righteousness?

answer.quote: I said, It is better that they perform a mitzva for its own sake. Had you known from the start that you were fated to lose that amount of money
answer.explanation: The page names what Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai was preserving — the mitzva being done for its own sake — though it never squares this with the later ruling that giving "so that my sons will live" is full-fledged righteousness.

bava-batra/11.summary: Binyamin the righteous, supervisor of the charity fund, swore it was empty, then fed a starving woman and her seven sons from his own pocket; when he fell ill the angels argued twenty-two years back onto his life. The rest of the page measures space: a shared courtyard is split only if each owner gets four by four cubits, and each doorway onto it earns four more cubits for unloading a pack animal. That reason then gets tested against porticos, chicken coops, and half-roofed houses.
bava-batra/11.question: If the four cubits exist only so someone has room to unload a donkey at his door, why does a man with two doorways get eight cubits rather than the one space he can actually stand in?

judge.reachNote: Is the four cubits a need-based allowance for unloading, or an ownership entitlement that attaches to each doorway regardless of use?

answer.quote: The dung in a courtyard which the residents wish to use is divided among them according to the number of entrances that open into the courtyard
answer.explanation: The page shows that entrances serve as a measure of one's share in the courtyard (as opposed to billeting, which follows the number of people), which bears on why doorways are counted rather than actual standing room, but it never states why two entrances yield eight cubits when the stated purpose is unloading.

bava-batra/12.summary: Sumakhos rules that a man who sells "part of a vineyard" without specifying must hand over at least enough land to plant three kav of seed, and Rabbi Yosei answers that this is nothing but words of prophecy, meaning he sees no reasoning behind it. The insult then turns into a claim: Rabbi Avdimi says prophecy passed from the prophets to the Sages. Rav Ashi's proof is that a Sage's ruling later turns up as law given to Moses at Sinai.
bava-batra/12.question: If a Sage can supply the reasoning for his ruling, which is exactly how Rav Ashi rules out the blind man stumbling onto a skylight, in what sense is the ruling prophecy rather than argument?

judge.reachNote: Whether reasoned halakhic argument and revelation are rivals or the same faculty once prophecy moves from prophets to Sages.

answer.quote: But does the Sage not offer a reason for his statement? The fact that he demonstrates an understanding of the issue indicates that he does not arrive at his idea by chance, but rather by prophecy.
answer.explanation: The page uses the Sage's ability to give a reason only to rule out blind chance, and asserts rather than explains how reasoned wisdom counts as prophecy, so the note's question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/13.summary: Rav Yehuda says a joint owner who wants out can tell his partner: name a price, and I will buy your share or sell you mine; Rav Naḥman says there is no such rule. It is tested on a slave whose one owner freed his half, on a poor and a rich brother who inherit a bathhouse, and on two inherited maidservants, one who cooks and one who weaves. The sharpest case is the man who offers to take less than half a courtyard and is refused.
bava-batra/13.question: When one partner offers to take the smaller half of a courtyard, why does the other get to call that a gift and refuse it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a partner may refuse an advantage he did not choose, because unearned benefit is itself a burden.

answer.quote: If you want me to compensate you with money for the difference between my share and your share, I have no money to give you. And if you wish to give it to me as a gift, I am not at ease with that
answer.explanation: The Gemara states Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's reasoning outright: the other party has no money to equalize the shares and refuses to be a gift-recipient, citing "But he who hates gifts shall live."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 13b: "If you want me to compensate you with money for the difference between my share and your share, I have no money to give you. And if you wish to give it to me as a gift, I am not at ease with that". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 13b — the refuser has no money to compensate and will not accept a gift, per Proverbs 15:27 — so it cannot stand as written. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard: e.g., why an unwanted gift counts as a real injury when the giver freely offers less for himself, or how this squares with Rav Yehuda's rule that one partner can force a buy-or-sell on the other. Keep the summary, which is accurate.

bava-batra/14.summary: Rabbi Meir measures the Ark with a six-handbreadth cubit and finds two handbreadths of empty space beside the tablets, just enough for the Torah scroll Moses wrote. Rabbi Yehuda uses a shorter cubit, ends up with no room inside, and rests the scroll on the chest the Philistines sent back, alongside the Ark. Then the arithmetic bites: a scroll two handbreadths thick will not slide into a gap of exactly two handbreadths, and Rav Ashi's fix is to roll part of it separately.
bava-batra/14.question: Does rolling a small section of the scroll on its own actually get it into the Ark, or does it just move the missing space somewhere the tape measure cannot reach?

judge.reachNote: Whether a harmonizing answer actually dissolves a physical constraint or merely relocates the difficulty out of sight.

answer.quote: Rav Ashi said: A small section of the scroll was wound separately and then placed on top of the scroll.
answer.explanation: The page offers Rav Ashi's device as its resolution of the two-handbreadth problem, but it never tests or explains how the separately wound section saves space, so the note's challenge can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/15.summary: A list of who wrote which biblical books runs into trouble at the end of Deuteronomy: could Moses have written the verse reporting his own death? Rabbi Yehuda says Joshua added the last eight verses; Rabbi Shimon says God dictated them and Moses wrote them in tears. The same anxiety about what is real drives a long argument over Job, called a mere parable by one sage and proved an actual man by another from his name and his hometown.
bava-batra/15.question: If Job is certainly real because the verse gives his name and his city, why can the sages place him anywhere from Jacob's household to the court of Ahasuerus?
gate: the question brings in "Ahasuerus", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: It reaches the idea that insisting a figure is real (name, city) does nothing to fix him in time, since each dating rests only on a verbal echo in his own book.

bava-batra/16.summary: Job loses his flocks, his children and his skin, and the sages spend the page reading his complaints line by line. Rava finds heresy hiding in them: Job did not sin with his lips but he sinned in his heart, and Rav answers several of Job's sentences with the retort that dust should be put in his mouth. Then the same Rava rules that a person in pain is not held to what he says.
bava-batra/16.question: If distress excuses everything Job said, why do the sages still weigh each of his sentences for hidden blasphemy?

judge.reachNote: Whether words spoken in agony can still be read as evidence of what a man believes, and why scrutiny continues after forgiveness is granted.

bava-batra/17.summary: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob head three lists here: men the evil inclination never ruled, men who died by a kiss rather than at the hand of the Angel of Death, men the worm never reached. Then the mishna turns to digging, and a pit must stay three handbreadths from the wall of a neighbor's pit. Abaye and Rava split over a boundary with no pit yet on the far side: Abaye sees no damage, Rava hears the hoe already loosening the neighbor's earth.
bava-batra/17.question: If nobody has dug on the other side of the line yet, does a neighbor's merely possible future pit have any claim on what you do today?

judge.reachNote: Whether a neighbor's potential future use of his land is a present-day legal interest, or only actual existing damage counts.

answer.quote: the neighbor can say to him: Just as you changed your mind and dug a pit, I too might change my mind and dig a pit
answer.explanation: Rava states that the neighbor's possible future pit does constrain the digger, but Abaye holds the opposite and the page leaves the dispute unresolved, so the question can still be honestly asked.

bava-batra/18.summary: Lime, salt, and rocks must be kept three handbreadths from a neighbor's wall, and the Gemara asks what the rule is when no wall has been built yet. One proposed proof after another collapses the same way: the mishna names a wall or a cistern not to permit digging elsewhere but to report what harms what, that heat cracks walls, that tree roots reach twenty-five cubits. Then mustard and bees, which damage each other, force the real question: must the damager move, or the damaged?
bava-batra/18.question: When two neighbors harm each other in equal measure, the bees eating the mustard and the mustard spoiling the bees, is there anything left to decide which one has to move?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real principle of the sugya—whether the burden of distancing falls on the damager or the damaged—but that principle is stated and resolved on the daf itself.

answer.quote: since the initial planting of the mustard was permitted, the owner of the bees should distance them from the mustard
answer.explanation: The page resolves mutual damage by asking who was there lawfully first: because the mustard was planted permissibly, the bee owner must move, and the Rabbis further deny mutuality by holding that bees do not damage mustard.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 18b: "since the initial planting of the mustard was permitted, the owner of the bees should distance them from the mustard". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: the page says that since the mustard was planted permissibly the bee owner must move, and the Rabbis reply that bees do not damage mustard at all. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled—for instance, why Rabbi Yosei, who holds the damaged party must distance himself, argues from the Rabbis' own premise, or why the buyer case is needed to make mutual damage possible in the first place. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

bava-batra/19.summary: A launderer's pond gets three handbreadths from the neighbor's wall if clothes only soak in it, four cubits if they are actively scrubbed. Rabba bar bar Ḥana rules a man may urinate right against another's wall, citing Ahab's punishment against "those who urinate against the wall"; a baraita demanding three handbreadths refutes him conclusively, and the verse is then reread as referring to dogs. Later, a wafer plugging a window between rooms fails to shrink the gap that lets corpse impurity through, because animals would still eat it.
bava-batra/19.question: If the baraita can win by rerouting the verse from men to dogs, what was that verse proving when Rabba bar bar Ḥana cited it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of how much evidentiary weight a prooftext carries and what happens when its referent is reread, but the page already states the proof it carried.

answer.quote: As the verse employs the term “those who urinate against the wall” to mean males, it seems that urinating against a wall was a common practice.
answer.explanation: The page spells out exactly what Rabba bar bar Ḥana's prooftext was meant to establish — that the phrase denotes males, showing the practice was ordinary and hence permitted — before the baraita and the dog reading undo it.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 19b: "As the verse employs the term “those who urinate against the wall” to mean males, it seems that urinating against a wall was a common practice.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page itself states what the verse was proving for Rabba bar bar Ḥana — that "those who urinate against the wall" means males, so the practice was common — so the question is answered a line later. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing: for example, why the Gemara first deflects two baraitot by saying they speak of urine poured from a chamber pot and only the third counts as a conclusive refutation, or why a stone wall needs only one handbreadth while a brick wall needs three. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

bava-batra/20.summary: A baraita lists what can sit in a window and stop ritual impurity from passing between rooms: plucked grass, cloth scraps, a bird, a gentile, salt, an earthenware vessel, a worn Torah scroll. Shmuel holds that anything with a use will be carried off, so the Gemara strips each item of its usefulness: poisonous grass, a lean animal nobody will buy, a bony bird that scratches. The gentile ends up a tied prisoner, because anyone else would simply be released.
bava-batra/20.question: If a thing counts as part of the wall only for as long as nobody wants it, what becomes of the barrier the moment someone finds a use for it?

judge.reachNote: Whether an object's halakhic status as part of a structure rests on its present physical presence or on the likelihood that someone will want it and take it away.

answer.quote: according to Shmuel, who says that an item that has a use is not considered part of the window and does not reduce the dimensions
answer.explanation: The page states Shmuel's principle — a usable item is not counted as part of the window — which bears on the question, but it never treats the case of a use discovered after the barrier is in place, and the Torah scroll answer ("one who determines that its repository will be there") only shows intent can fix the item's status.

bava-batra/21.summary: Yehoshua ben Gamla is remembered for the good because he placed a teacher of children in every town, so a boy without a father to teach him could still learn Torah from age six. Rava and Rav Dimi of Neharde'a then argue over hiring: take the teacher who covers more material sloppily, or the one who covers less but gets it right. Rav Dimi's proof is Joab, who slaughtered Edom's males because he had learned zakhar, males, for zekher, remembrance.
bava-batra/21.question: Joab's old teacher insists he read the word correctly and the student simply heard it wrong, so whose error was it, and why does the page refuse to say whether Joab killed him?

judge.reachNote: Who bears responsibility for a lesson that was said right but heard wrong — and whether an irreversible error deserves an irreversible punishment.

answer.quote: The teacher had read it the proper way, but he failed to notice that his student had learned it incorrectly.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly assigns the fault — the teacher pronounced correctly but failed to catch the student's mislearning — but it never explains why it leaves the killing unresolved, reporting only that "there are those who say that Joab killed him, and there are those who say that he did not."

bava-batra/22.summary: Rav Dimi of Neharde'a brings dried figs by ship, and the Exilarch tells Rava to reserve the market for him if he turns out to be a Torah scholar. Rava sends Rav Adda bar Abba, who tests Rav Dimi with a question about an elephant that swallowed a wicker basket and passed it out whole, judges him ignorant, and lets the figs rot. When Rav Adda bar Abba dies, five sages each announce that the death was on his own account.
bava-batra/22.question: When five different sages each say "I punished him," is each one confessing to a killing or claiming credit for it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a sage's slighted honor is itself lethal, and that owning a death can be simultaneously guilt and a claim of standing.

answer.quote: Rav Yosef said: I punished him, i.e., I am to blame for his death, as I cursed him.
answer.explanation: The Gemara glosses Rav Yosef's claim as an admission of blame, but the parallel statements are framed as grievances ("he was punished on my account because he did not exhibit the proper respect for me"), so the page leaves the confession-versus-credit tension unresolved.

bava-batra/23.summary: Bloodletters set up under Rav Yosef's palm trees, and crows drawn to the blood flew up and ruined the dates. Abaye objects twice: the damage is indirect, and the bloodletters have long-established use of that spot. Rav Yosef answers that the rule denying established use in damage cases was said about smoke and about a bathroom, then adds that he is sensitive, so crows count as smoke for him. The rest weighs a found dove chick's nearest dovecote against the biggest one.
bava-batra/23.question: If Rav Yosef can make crows into smoke by declaring himself sensitive, what keeps every neighbor from setting the threshold at his own nerves?

judge.reachNote: Whether the threshold for actionable nuisance is an objective category (smoke, bathroom) or the particular plaintiff's sensitivity.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Yosef answers that the rule denying established use in damage cases was said about smoke and about a bathroom.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Abaye inquired further: But wasn’t it stated with regard to that statement of Rav Naḥman that Rav Mari said it is referring specifically to smoke

summaryProblems.claim: Abaye objects twice (indirect damage; established use).
summaryProblems.pageSays: Abaye inquired further: But wasn’t it stated with regard to that statement of Rav Naḥman that Rav Mari said it is referring specifically to smoke

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Yosef answers that the rule denying established use in damage cases was said about smoke and about a bathroom.", but the page says "Abaye inquired further: But wasn’t it stated with regard to that statement of Rav Naḥman that Rav Mari said it is referring specifically to smoke". Say what the page says. The summary says "Abaye objects twice (indirect damage; established use).", but the page says "Abaye inquired further: But wasn’t it stated with regard to that statement of Rav Naḥman that Rav Mari said it is referring specifically to smoke". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: it is Abaye, not Rav Yosef, who raises that Rav Naḥman's rule was limited to smoke and a bathroom, and that is his third objection, not Rav Yosef's answer. Rav Yosef's only reply to it is that he is sensitive, so these are like smoke and a bathroom to him. Keep the question as is; it reaches the real issue and the page leaves it open.

bava-batra/24.summary: A sealed barrel of wine is found floating in a river, and Rav permits the wine if the nearest town is mostly Jewish, while Shmuel forbids it because the current could have carried it from Dekira, where most residents are gentiles. Rav answers that the river's slack bays would have sunk a barrel traveling that far. Ravina then permits a barrel hidden in a vineyard of orla, forbidden young grapevines, reasoning that thieves do not stash loot in the field they robbed.
bava-batra/24.question: Is a guess about how thieves behave a firmer basis for permitting the wine than counting how many vineyards in the region are not orla?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what kind of probability grounds a permission: a behavioral inference about how people act versus a statistical majority.

answer.quote: It is different there, as, if thieves had stolen the barrel from that very vineyard they would not have hidden it there.
answer.explanation: The Gemara does supply the thief-behavior reasoning as the ground for Ravina's ruling in place of the majority-of-vineyards argument, but it never weighs which basis is the firmer one, so the comparison the question asks can still be pressed.

summaryProblems.claim: The barrel found floating in the river was sealed.
summaryProblems.pageSays: In the case of a barrel of wine that was found floating in a river, and the status of the wine was unknown

judge.feedback: The summary says "The barrel found floating in the river was sealed.", but the page says "In the case of a barrel of wine that was found floating in a river, and the status of the wine was unknown". Say what the page says.

bava-batra/25.summary: A tannery, where hides are soaked and scraped, must sit fifty cubits from the city, placed to the east so the prevailing wind carries the stench away. Rabbi Akiva bars the west side outright, and the Gemara reads his word "frequent" not as wind but as the Divine Presence, said to rest in the west. Then the proof wobbles: perhaps the stars bow while walking backward, and other sages hold the Presence is everywhere.
bava-batra/25.question: If Rav Sheshet could pray in any direction he pleased, what makes the west too good for a tannery?
gate: the question brings in "Sheshet", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a zoning rule can rest on a contested claim about where God dwells, once sages hold the Presence is in every place.

answer.quote: the Divine Presence is found on the western side, and therefore it is inappropriate to set up a tannery there with its foul odors
answer.explanation: The page states why the west is off-limits for a tannery, but it never reconciles that reason with Rav Sheshet's and others' view that the Divine Presence is everywhere, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/26.summary: A tree has to be planted four cubits, roughly six feet, from a neighbor's field, and the reason given is room to turn an ox and plow without trespassing. Rav Yosef told Rava bar Rav Ḥanan to cut down palms whose birds kept dropping into his vineyard; Rava bar Rav Ḥanan answered that felling a fruit-bearing palm is forbidden destruction, citing a father whose son died for cutting a young fig tree. Then he offered Rav Yosef the axe.
bava-batra/26.question: If cutting down a fruit-bearing palm is destruction serious enough to cost a man his son, how does it become permissible the moment the neighbor swings the axe instead?

judge.reachNote: Whether the ban on destroying fruit trees is an objective prohibition on the act or a liability that attaches to the particular actor who benefits or bears the risk.

bava-batra/27.summary: A tree's roots are said to draw nourishment sixteen cubits out, and that distance decides whether its fruit is really yours for first fruits, the first-ripened produce brought to the Temple. The Gemara squeezes Ulla's number against a mishna's arithmetic, then tests it on a tree straddling the border of Eretz Yisrael with a rock splitting its roots. Two travelers report Rabbi Yoḥanan in flat contradiction: the owner is a robber, or Joshua parceled out the land so nobody would be fussy.
bava-batra/27.question: Can the same roots make a man a robber in Rav Dimi's report and a rightful owner in Ravin's, and does the page offer any way to choose between them?
gate: the question brings in "Dimi's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Ravin's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether title to fruit follows the physical fact of where roots feed or a communal waiver built into the original apportionment of the land.

answer.quote: one brings first fruits and recites the verses, as it was on this condition that Joshua apportioned Eretz Yisrael to the Jewish people
answer.explanation: The page gives a rationale for Ravin's version of Rabbi Yoḥanan (Joshua's condition that people not be particular), which bears on the conflict but never adjudicates between the two reports or explains how the same roots yield opposite rulings.

bava-batra/28.summary: The mishna sets three years of working a property as the proof that it belongs to you, and lists what counts: houses, water pits, dovecotes, bathhouses, olive presses, slaves. The Gemara traces the number three to the goring ox, which becomes a known danger after three gorings, and then strains the comparison: three figs in one day, a caper bush ripening over three days, alfalfa cut three times in a month. Rabbi Yishmael accepts three harvests instead of three years.
bava-batra/28.question: If each goring must stand fully apart from the next, why should fruit already sitting on a caper bush, merely finishing its ripening, be treated as three separate events at all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — what makes three acts count as three separate events rather than one continuous use — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: at least the fruit is here and it is in the process of finishing its ripening during the three days
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the caper-bush case and rejects it for precisely the reason the note asks about — the fruit is already present and merely ripening, so it is unlike the fully independent gorings.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 28b: "at least the fruit is here and it is in the process of finishing its ripening during the three days". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question assumes the caper bush counts as three separate events, but the page explicitly rules it out because the fruit is already there and only finishing its ripening, unlike independent gorings. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it. A better angle might press on where the line falls: the alfalfa cut three times in a month is rejected not for concurrency but because seizing it is 'not the normal way of farming it' — so ask what work the standard-of-use criterion is doing once the ox analogy has already been stretched.

bava-batra/29.summary: Rava tries three times to explain why working another man's field for three years without protest establishes ownership. Each version rests on the original owner: he waives his rights, or he grows particular by year three, and Abaye knocks each down, once by raising the bar Elyashiv household, who protest against anyone who merely walks along their boundary. Rava's last answer shifts the clock onto the buyer, who stops carefully guarding his purchase document after three unchallenged years.
bava-batra/29.question: If the three years are really a measure of how long ordinary people tolerate a stranger on their land, why should the bar Elyashiv household, who object to a footstep on the boundary, be held to the same three years as everyone else?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a legal presumption may be calibrated to an individual owner's temperament or must be a single uniform measure — but the page states this answer outright.

answer.quote: you have subjected your statement to the varying circumstances of each case, as there will be a different length of time needed to establish the presumption of ownership
answer.explanation: Abaye raises exactly this bar Elyashiv difficulty and the page answers it: a rule keyed to each owner's temperament is untenable, which is why Rava abandons the tolerance rationale for the document one the note itself reports.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 29a: "you have subjected your statement to the varying circumstances of each case, as there will be a different length of time needed to establish the presumption of ownership". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is simply Abaye's bar Elyashiv objection restated, and the page answers it on the spot — a rule that varies with each owner's temperament is untenable, which is why Rava drops the tolerance theory. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing: for example, why the document-preservation reason still lets a protest lodged before strangers count ("your friend has a friend"), when the whole point was that this possessor was never told to keep his deed. The maidservant used in alternate years and the beit rova dispute are also live openings.

bava-batra/30.summary: A man sells everything he owns "of the house of bar Sisin," then claims one parcel only carries that name and was never included; Rav Naḥman gives it to the buyer, since the seller should have said so up front. The rest of the page is a run of land disputes before Rava, where the squatter's evidence keeps getting talked away. A visit of thirty days a year, advice to go buy the field, an offer to purchase it back: each excuse holds.
bava-batra/30.question: If signing the bill of sale ends a man's claim but telling the buyer "go purchase the land" does not, what exactly does a signature do that speech cannot undo?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — why deeds bind a litigant while words do not — but the page states that very distinction explicitly.

answer.quote: by signing the bill of sale the claimant performed an action indicating that the field was not his for the benefit of the possessor of the field, but here
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself answers the note's question by distinguishing a binding action done for the possessor's benefit from mere speech, since "a person is apt to casually say statements."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 30b: "by signing the bill of sale the claimant performed an action indicating that the field was not his for the benefit of the possessor of the field, but here". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later on 30b, where the Gemara says a signature is an action performed for the possessor's benefit while speech is something people say casually. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, press on why an action done for another's benefit should cost a man his claim, or why casual speech before witnesses counts for nothing when presumptive ownership itself stands "in place of a document." Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-batra/31.summary: Two men each claim the same field came down from their own ancestors, and one also brings witnesses that he worked it for the years that establish possession. When the possessor rewords his claim, saying he bought the land and merely relied on it as if ancestral, Ulla permits the reinterpretation and the sages of Neharde'a refuse, while a claim first voiced outside court smells coached. Rav Nahman then tells Rava he will not reverse his own ruling, and goes out and reverses it.
