bava-batra/81.question: If honoring the doubt means consecrating the fruit, having a priest redeem it, and separating tithes in case it is ordinary produce after all, when does a doubt cost more than it is worth?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that acting out of doubt forces a chain of hedges, and asks at what point the hedging costs more than the doubt is worth.

bava-batra/82.summary: Someone who buys three trees in another man's field acquires the ground beneath them, the space between them, and enough room outside for a fig picker standing with his basket. Rabbi Elazar objects: this buyer has no right of way through the field to reach his trees, since the strip he bought counts as separate land. Rabbi Zeira draws the odd conclusion that a man who buys only two trees does have a path.
bava-batra/82.question: If the third tree is what turns a patch of someone else's field into your own separate land, why should that purchase leave you with no legal way to walk to it?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that acquiring separate ownership inside another's field cuts you off from claiming use of the rest of it — but the page already states this as its reason.

answer.quote: He has no path, even though he has no other means of gaining access to the trees, as the ground he acquired along with the trees is considered another land
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright why the three-tree buyer lacks a path: the strip he acquired is legally separate land, so he has no claim on the surrounding field, and Rava adds that the mishna follows the Rabbis who hold one sells sparingly.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 82b: "He has no path, even though he has no other means of gaining access to the trees, as the ground he acquired along with the trees is considered another land". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the page answers two lines later: the strip is "another land," so no claim on the surrounding field, and Rava grounds the mishna in the Rabbis' view that one sells sparingly. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating it. A better target is Rabbi Zeira's inversion — why the weaker purchase (two trees) yields a right of way while the stronger one (three trees, plus land) forfeits it — or Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's distinction between a pit, which does not weaken the land, and a tree, which does.

bava-batra/83.summary: Buying three trees in a field can carry the ground under them, and the Sages argue over the spacing that turns three trees into one unit; Rava fixes it at four to sixteen cubits apart. Rav says a straight line is enough, Shmuel wants a tripod, on the reasoning that a seller would not give up ground he could still sow between. Rav Hamnuna asks about three Roman thorny shrubs, where nothing can be sown, and is told shrubs are not important.
bava-batra/83.question: If the ground goes to the buyer because nothing can be sown between his trees, why does a stand of unsowable thorny shrubs leave the ground with the seller?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether ground follows trees because nothing can be sown between them or because the trees themselves are significant — but the page resolves it.

answer.quote: Those Roman shrubs are not significant, as they are merely shrubs and not trees, and therefore the ground is not acquired when one purchases them.
answer.explanation: The Gemara answers Rav Hamnuna's exact objection by saying the criterion is not sowability alone but the significance of trees, which shrubs lack.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 83b: "Those Roman shrubs are not significant, as they are merely shrubs and not trees, and therefore the ground is not acquired when one purchases them.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what Rav Hamnuna asks, and the page answers it in the next line ('Those Roman shrubs are not significant... these trees are important'), which the summary itself already reports. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains unsettled, e.g. what makes a tree 'important' enough to drag the ground with it, or why significance rather than sowability should govern what the seller is presumed to relinquish. Avoid reposing an objection the page itself resolves.

bava-batra/84.summary: A seller who promised reddish-brown wheat, sheḥamtit, and delivered white wheat lets either side back out, and the Gemara turns that rule into evidence about the sky. Rav Pappa reasons that since the mishna sets white against sun-colored, the sun itself must be red, and that weak eyesight is why nobody sees the redness at midday. An objection from leprous marks, which are white yet compared to the sun, is answered by calling the resemblance partial.
bava-batra/84.question: Can a rule about who may cancel a wheat sale really settle what color the sun is, or has the argument quietly stopped being about wheat?

judge.reachNote: Whether legal language about goods can serve as evidence for facts about the natural world.

answer.quote: And according to that which entered our mind initially, that the sun is white, doesn't it redden in the morning and evening?
answer.explanation: The Gemara keeps the alternative that the sun is white alive and explains its redness otherwise, which bears on whether the mishna's wording really settles the sun's color, but it never addresses whether a sale rule can decide a question of nature.

bava-batra/85.summary: Rav and Shmuel say a person's vessels acquire whatever is placed in them anywhere except the public street, while Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish include the street too. Rav Pappa dissolves the fight: the second pair meant an alleyway, where you are allowed to leave your things. Then Rav Sheshet asks whether a buyer's basket works inside the seller's house, and Rav Huna answers from a divorce case that Rav Naḥman says has been qualified past all use.
bava-batra/85.question: If a place counts as yours only where you have permission to leave your things, is ownership here about rights or about nobody minding?

judge.reachNote: Whether a vessel acquires because its owner holds a right to that spot or merely because the place's owner does not mind.

answer.quote: It is because a person, including a husband, is not particular neither about the place of her lap nor about the place of her basket
answer.explanation: Rava grounds Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling in the owner's lack of objection rather than in a formal grant of rights, which bears directly on the question but does not settle it for the buyer-in-seller's-domain case, where the dilemma is left unresolved.

bava-batra/86.summary: A buyer's own basket sitting in the seller's shop may or may not close a sale, and the Gemara finds no clean proof either way. The argument shifts to whether goods are acquired by dragging them or only by lifting them, tested against a thief who takes a purse on Shabbat. If he lifts it first he owes the owner money; if he drags it out the door, theft and the capital offense land in the same instant, and he pays nothing.
bava-batra/86.question: If the purse ends up in the same thief's hands either way, why should the moment he lifted it decide whether the owner is ever repaid?

judge.reachNote: Whether the instant liability attaches should govern the victim's restitution, when the loss to the owner is identical either way.

answer.quote: Based on the principle that one who is liable to receive two punishments receives only the greater of the two
answer.explanation: The page states the rule that makes the timing decisive — sequential liabilities both stand, simultaneous ones merge into the greater — but it never justifies why the owner's restitution should depend on that sequence.

bava-batra/87.summary: A seller of wine or oil must let three extra drops fall into the buyer's jug after pouring. If he then tips the barrel on its side, the final dregs stay with him, which puzzled Rabbi Elazar: a separate ruling holds that the dregs of teruma, the priestly portion of produce, still belong to the priest. Rav Yitzḥak bar Avdimi answers with Rabbi Abbahu's reasoning about despair, since a buyer writes off a few drops and a non-priest cannot write off teruma.
bava-batra/87.question: If the buyer has already given up on the last few drops, what is holding up the seller's obligation to drip three of them?

judge.reachNote: Asks where the line falls between a quantity still owed as part of the measure and a quantity so small the buyer is deemed to have waived it.

bava-batra/88.summary: A man lifts a thigh of meat in a butcher shop to inspect it, and a horseman snatches it from his hands; Rav Yeimar rules he must pay the butcher, since lifting a fixed-price item closes the sale. The same rule wrecks a pumpkin seller's revenge: his customers had already lifted the pumpkins, so declaring them consecrated to Heaven accomplished nothing. Later the page argues over how far a scale must tilt toward the buyer.
bava-batra/88.question: If the merchant who shaved his measures cannot repent only because he cannot identify the people he shortchanged, what is he supposed to do when one of them walks back into his shop?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the bar to repentance here is practical (unidentifiable victims) rather than the sin's intrinsic gravity, which invites asking whether partial restitution reopens repentance.

bava-batra/89.summary: A seller in a town where grain is heaped above the rim of the measure may not level it flat, even if he offers a lower price in exchange; the court refuses the deal, because local practice defines what counts as a perfect and just weight. The same logic governs whether scales may tilt a handbreadth toward the buyer. Then Shmuel sends Karna to teach that inspectors supervise measures but not prices, and Karna teaches the opposite.
bava-batra/89.question: If Karna was following Rabbi Yitzḥak's view that inspectors do supervise prices, why does the page let a horn grow in his eye rather than settle who was right?
gate: the question brings in "Yitzḥak's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When a student has a valid tannaitic source on his side, does defying the teacher who sent him still carry consequence — authority of the teacher versus correctness of the ruling.

bava-batra/90.summary: Hoarding grain to wait for prices to climb lands a seller in the same verse as usurers and shopkeepers who shrink their measures. Shmuel's father sold early, when produce was cheap; Shmuel held his back and sold late at the early price, and word came from Eretz Yisrael, the land of Israel, that the father's way was better. Still, Rav allows hoarding produce from one's own field, and Rabbi Yosei had his servant Fuga stockpile three years' worth.
bava-batra/90.question: If Shmuel charged no customer a coin more than his father did, what exactly was worse about his way?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that harm can lie in effect on the market as a whole rather than in the price charged to any one buyer — but the page states that answer.

answer.quote: A market price that has been eased and starts out low will remain eased, with little increase over the course of the year.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks "What is the reason for this?" about the preference for the father's practice and answers that selling early keeps the year's market price low, while withholding produce keeps prices high and hard to lower.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 90b: "A market price that has been eased and starts out low will remain eased, with little increase over the course of the year.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: the Gemara asks why the father's way is better and replies that an early low price keeps the whole year's market eased, while a high starting price is not easily lowered. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, press on how Rav's permission to hoard one's own field produce, or Rabbi Yosei's three-year stockpile, sits with a standard that judges a seller by his effect on market prices. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

bava-batra/91.summary: The Sages forbid buying and reselling wine, oil, and flour inside Eretz Yisrael, since a middleman between grower and buyer drives the price of food up. A baraita permits leaving the land only when grain costs double its usual rate, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai says Elimelech and his sons died precisely for leaving. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha rejects that flatly: they would have stayed for bran, and were punished for not praying for their generation.
bava-batra/91.question: If Rabbi Yohanan remembers grain selling cheaply while people in Tiberias swelled from hunger, what does the price of grain actually measure about whether a person can stay?
gate: the question brings in "Yohanan", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Tiberias", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a price is only a proxy for purchasing power, and that the law measures a person's actual ability to eat rather than a market rate.

answer.quote: But when money is expensive, i.e., it is difficult to earn money for sustenance, even if the price of four se’a of grain stood at a sela, one may leave
answer.explanation: Rabba bar bar Ḥana in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name states that the grain price alone does not govern; what matters is whether money can be earned, and the Tiberias memory is brought immediately to illustrate that very point.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 91b: "But when money is expensive, i.e., it is difficult to earn money for sustenance, even if the price of four se’a of grain stood at a sela, one may leave". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered a few lines above the Tiberias memory, where Rabbi Yoḥanan himself says that when money is hard to earn one may leave even at four se'a for a sela — the memory is brought as proof of that rule, not as a puzzle about it. Rewrite the question around something the page leaves standing: for instance the clash between Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai, who says Elimelech was punished for leaving, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa, who says he would have stayed for bran and was punished instead for not praying for his generation. Aim at what changes when the leaders' sin is relocated from departure to silence.

bava-batra/92.summary: A man buys an ox and it turns out to be a habitual gorer. Rav voids the sale, since the majority of people purchase oxen for plowing and this one cannot plow; Shmuel says the seller can answer that he sold it for slaughter, because majorities settle ritual questions, not money. The Gemara whittles the case down until the only thing at stake is which party must go to the trouble of reselling the animal.
bava-batra/92.question: When Ravina rescues the majority rule by adding that most virgin weddings become public knowledge, is that a real fact about this woman's case, or a way to keep the rule from ever being tested?
gate: the question brings in "Ravina", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a competing presumption genuinely describes the case or merely shields the majority rule from being tested.

answer.quote: Rather, one must modify the above argument to say that the majority of marriages of women who marry as virgins generate publicity of that fact
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself tests Ravina's added presumption and forces him to soften it from 'anyone' to 'the majority', which bears on whether the addition is a solid fact or a patch, without settling the note's question.

bava-batra/93.summary: Rav holds that a court may decide money cases by what is usually true; Shmuel holds that it may not. The challenges come fast: an ox that gored a cow found with a dead fetus beside her, a grazing ox standing next to a corpse, and Rabbi Au0127a's rutting camel rampaging among other camels, which he says is plainly the killer. The sharpest split is over flaxseed, where two sages both follow a majority and disagree about which majority to count.
bava-batra/93.question: If most flaxseed by volume is bought for planting but most buyers of flaxseed want it for something else, which of those two majorities tells you what the sale was?

judge.reachNote: What counts as a majority — heads of buyers or bulk of goods — when deciding what a transaction was for.

answer.quote: They said to him, i.e., to Rabbi Yosei: Many, i.e., a majority of people, purchase flaxseeds for purposes other than planting. Consequently, the sale stands.
answer.explanation: The page gives one side's answer — the majority of purchasers governs, so the sale stands — but it presents this only as the rejoinder to Rabbi Yosei's volume-majority and never decides between the two measures.

bava-batra/94.summary: A buyer of wheat is expected to accept a quarter-kav of stray matter, one twenty-fourth of a se'a, in every se'a he buys. Rav Huna rules that if there is more, the buyer sifts the entire batch and hands everything back, and the Gemara cannot decide whether that is strict law or a penalty on a seller suspected of mixing dirt in. Proofs from diverse seeds, a disputed cash deposit, and a note written with interest are each pushed away.
bava-batra/94.question: If nobody can tell whether the seller mixed the dirt in deliberately or it fell in during processing, why should he take back dirt he may never have added?

judge.reachNote: Whether a duty to give back rests on proven wrongdoing or simply on what the buyer's money purchased.

answer.quote: Some say that this is the strict halakha, as one who gives money for produce gives it for good-quality produce containing no impurities at all.
answer.explanation: The page answers the question directly: on the strict-halakha view the seller's intent is irrelevant, since the buyer paid for clean produce and, once he troubles himself to sift, he never agreed to accept any impurities at all.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 94a: "Some say that this is the strict halakha, as one who gives money for produce gives it for good-quality produce containing no impurities at all.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines into the Rav Huna passage: the first "some say" explains that the seller takes everything back as strict law, because money was paid for produce with no impurities, so his intent never enters the matter. A rewrite should either build on that answer or ask about something the page leaves standing, for instance why the Gemara rejects proofs in both directions with opposite suspicions of the seller ("who can say that the seller did not mix in the entire amount intentionally?" against "who can say that the seller intentionally mixed in anything?"). Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

bava-batra/95.summary: A buyer who receives more land than the sale stated, or more impurities than the norm, raises one question: does the seller take back only the excess, or the whole discrepancy? The Gemara tests Rav Huna's answer against overcharging by exactly one-sixth and against a contractor whose planting lost more than ten trees per hundred. Then it turns to a cellar of wine, where ten souring barrels per hundred are expected, unless the buyer says he needs the wine for cooking.
bava-batra/95.question: If a buyer never mentions what he wants the wine for, is his silence consent to ten souring barrels or an ordinary expectation that all hundred will be drinkable?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether unstated purpose leaves a buyer bound by market custom or by the plain terms of the sale — but the page already poses and debates exactly this.

answer.quote: Rav Aḥa and Ravina disagree about this. One says: The buyer must accept ten barrels of souring wine per hundred, and the other one says: The buyer need not accept any
answer.explanation: The note's question is the very dilemma the Gemara raises, and the page states both answers together with the baraita readings behind each.

summaryProblems.claim: Ten souring barrels per hundred are expected unless the buyer says he needs the wine for cooking.
summaryProblems.pageSays: This particular wine cellar, and the buyer said to him: I need the wine for cooking, then the seller is obligated to give him wine that is all of good quality, but the buyer accepts upon himself ten barrels

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 95b: "Rav Aḥa and Ravina disagree about this. One says: The buyer must accept ten barrels of souring wine per hundred, and the other one says: The buyer need not accept any". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Ten souring barrels per hundred are expected unless the buyer says he needs the wine for cooking.", but the page says "This particular wine cellar, and the buyer said to him: I need the wine for cooking, then the seller is obligated to give him wine that is all of good quality, but the buyer accepts upon himself ten barrels". Say what the page says. The question simply restates the Gemara's own dilemma, which the page raises explicitly and answers with the dispute of Rav Aḥa and Ravina plus the reasoning each derives from the two baraitot; ask something that remains after that dispute is on the table. Also fix the summary: when the seller says "this particular cellar" and the buyer does say he needs wine for cooking, he still accepts ten souring barrels per hundred, so mentioning cooking does not simply cancel the allowance.

bava-batra/96.summary: A man tastes a barrel of wine to be sure it can still be designated as teruma, the portion set aside for a priest, and later finds vinegar. Rabbi Yoḥanan says souring begins at the top, where he tasted, so the three days after the inspection were certainly wine; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says it begins unseen at the bottom, so the three days before the discovery were certainly vinegar. The same teaching, read twice, runs in opposite directions.
bava-batra/96.question: When a barrel smells of vinegar and tastes of wine, which sense gets to say what is in it?

judge.reachNote: Which sensory sign constitutes a thing's legal identity — smell as the first evidence of change, or taste as the substance itself.

answer.quote: The Sages of the South hold that as long as the wine still tastes like wine, it is regarded as wine.
answer.explanation: The page does state a position in which taste governs identity, but it stands alongside the opposite ruling ("is regarded as vinegar") and the Gemara closes with "There is no definitive resolution of the dispute," so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/97.summary: Water poured over spent grape skins makes tamad, and the page keeps asking at what point that liquid counts as wine. One baraita tracks first, second, and third soakings of skins from priestly wine; to isolate a case where only wine status decides, the Gemara ends up with a cow drinking the batches and dripping some onto food. Then Rav says the cup for sanctifying Shabbat must be fit for the altar, and every candidate for exclusion gets chipped away.
bava-batra/97.question: If almost every flawed wine still counts after the fact when poured on the altar, why should a bad smell alone disqualify the cup for Shabbat?

judge.reachNote: Whether the cup of a mitzva is held to the altar's standard, and whether 'valid after the fact' is good enough for honoring a mitzva.

answer.quote: With regard to all of these types of wine, one may not bring them as a libation, and if one brought one of them as a libation, it is disqualified.
answer.explanation: The page places foul-smelling wine in the class that is invalid as a libation even after the fact — unlike the earlier candidates that were valid after the fact — and adds the reason that "it is disrespectful to use inferior wine for a mitzva."

summaryProblems.claim: Every candidate for exclusion in Rav's statement gets chipped away.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rather, Rav’s statement serves to exclude wine that has a foul odor.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 97b: "With regard to all of these types of wine, one may not bring them as a libation, and if one brought one of them as a libation, it is disqualified.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Every candidate for exclusion in Rav's statement gets chipped away.", but the page says "Rather, Rav’s statement serves to exclude wine that has a foul odor.". Say what the page says. The page already answers this: foul-smelling wine sits in the baraita's list of wines that are disqualified as libations even after the fact, and the Gemara adds the Malachi verse that inferior wine is disrespectful for a mitzva. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for instance, why the honor-of-the-mitzva standard can be stricter than the altar's own after-the-fact leniency, or why diluted and uncovered wine get argued about while smell needs no argument. Also fix the summary's claim that every excluded candidate is chipped away, since the sugya settles on foul odor (and alternatively uncovered wine).

bava-batra/98.summary: A buyer's wine turns to vinegar, and the argument is over who absorbs the loss. Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, says that if it soured while still sitting in the seller's own jugs, the buyer can hand it back and demand his money. Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef disagrees on strange grounds: wine sours because of its owner's bad luck, and a haughty man's wine betrays him, so the buyer is stuck.
bava-batra/98.question: If souring is a verdict on the owner's character, whose character is on trial when the buyer's wine sits in the seller's jug?

judge.reachNote: If souring tracks a person's mazal, the question is whether fortune attaches to ownership or to possession — exactly the split between Rav Ḥiyya's buyer-owner and Rav Kahana's middleman.

answer.quote: Accordingly, since the wine soured after the buyer purchased it, he cannot place the blame upon the seller.
answer.explanation: Rav Ḥiyya bar Yosef's rule is glossed as pinning the souring on the buyer as owner from the moment of purchase, regardless of whose jug it sits in, though the page never squarely resolves the tension the note presses, and the later line "it is possible that the poor fortune of the middleman caused it to sour" pulls the fortune toward the one holding the wine.

bava-batra/99.summary: Shmuel does arithmetic on the Holy of Holies and finds the room too small for its own contents. Two gold cherubs stood over the Ark, and their outstretched wings alone take up the full twenty cubits of the room's width, so Shmuel concludes that the cherubs occupied no physical space. Six sages then offer ordinary fixes: bodies tucked under the wings like chickens, overlapping wings, a diagonal from corner to corner, a room wider at the top.
bava-batra/99.question: If each of the six objections shows an ordinary way the cherubs could have fit, what is left holding up the claim that they took up no space at all?

judge.reachNote: What carries a claim once its derivation is dismantled — received tradition or scriptural arithmetic?

answer.quote: This matter is a tradition handed down to us by our ancestors: The space occupied by the Ark of the Covenant and the cherubs
answer.explanation: The page grounds the no-space claim in a received tradition (Rabbi Levi/Rabbi Yoḥanan) and a supporting baraita about ten cubits of empty space on each side, independent of Shmuel's verse-based proof, though it never says how the six objections affect that proof.

bava-batra/100.summary: A field owner who lets the public cut a second path through his field cannot later demand it back, and the mishna lets people use both routes. Rabbi Eliezer goes further, saying that a public which picks its own path through private land keeps it, acquired simply by walking, and Rabbi Elazar grounds this in God telling Abraham to walk the land. The Gemara itself asks whether that makes the public robbers.
bava-batra/100.question: If walking a field is enough to acquire it, what separates a public that has worn a path through someone's land from a crowd of thieves?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea—where possession by use stops and theft begins—but the page already draws that line explicitly.

answer.quote: Rav Giddel said that Rav said: Rabbi Eliezer refers only to a case where the public lost a thoroughfare in that field, e.g., the field was plowed over
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection—"are the members of the public entitled to be robbers?"—and immediately answers that Rabbi Eliezer speaks only where a preexisting public thoroughfare was lost, so the public is restoring, not seizing.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 100a: "Rav Giddel said that Rav said: Rabbi Eliezer refers only to a case where the public lost a thoroughfare in that field, e.g., the field was plowed over". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it outright with Rav Giddel's report that Rabbi Eliezer speaks only of a lost thoroughfare. Write a question that starts after that answer—for instance, why walking should acquire at all when the Rabbis require a formal act, or why Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina concedes walking works for a vineyard path in particular. The summary is sound but should mention the answer so the question cannot simply repeat the page.

bava-batra/101.summary: The mishna specifies a rock-cut burial chamber six cubits wide and eight long, a cubit being about a forearm, with thirteen niches dug into its walls for bodies. Two of those niches sit beside the entrance, and no one can place them without either standing corpses upright, which Rabbi Yoḥanan calls a burial fit for donkeys, or letting niches collide at the corners. Rav Huna's fan-shaped arrangement is checked against the diagonal of a square and declared an error.
bava-batra/101.question: Is a layout that only works when the corner niches hold non-viable newborns a real solution to the geometry, or an admission that the plan does not fit?

judge.reachNote: Whether resolving a difficulty by restricting the case to a rare, miniature instance counts as answering the problem or as conceding it.

answer.quote: The Gemara provides an alternative solution to the problem of the niches at the corners overlapping. Or if you wish, say as Rav Sheisha, son of Rav Idi, said
answer.explanation: The page presents the non-viable-newborn reading as a genuine alternative solution to the overlap problem, though it never weighs whether such a narrowing concedes that the plan fails in ordinary cases, so the question's edge survives.

summaryProblems.claim: No one can place the two entrance-side niches without either standing corpses upright or letting niches collide at the corners.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Ashi said: It is possible to do this where, when constructing the niches that extend diagonally away from the chamber, one deepens them

judge.feedback: The summary says "No one can place the two entrance-side niches without either standing corpses upright or letting niches collide at the corners.", but the page says "Rav Ashi said: It is possible to do this where, when constructing the niches that extend diagonally away from the chamber, one deepens them". Say what the page says. The summary says the two entrance niches cannot be placed without either vertical burial or overlapping corners, but the page gives Rav Ashi's answer that the diagonal niches are simply dug lower down, and that solution should appear. Keep the sequence honest: objection, Rav Ashi's deepening, Rav Huna's palm-branch layout refuted by the diagonal calculation, then Rav Sheisha's non-viable newborns. The question itself is good and can stay largely as written once the summary no longer overstates the impasse.

bava-batra/102.summary: A man digging finds three corpses in a row, and the spacing decides their fate: four to eight cubits apart and the ground is presumed an old graveyard, not to be disturbed. Buried closer than that, Rabbi Shimon holds the middle ones are ignored and the outer two still make a graveyard; the Rabbis disagree. In a crowded vineyard the two sides swap, and the difference offered is that a corpse shoved in at twilight was meant to be moved, while vines are planted to stay.
bava-batra/102.question: If the body buried in haste at twilight is precisely the one that can be treated as not there, what became of the intention to come back and move it?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that presumed intention, not actual fact, can decide whether a body or a vine counts as legally present.

answer.quote: their corpses were originally buried there on a temporary basis, but then they were never reinterred
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the temporarily buried corpses were in fact never moved, which is what the question asks about the fate of the intention to rebury.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 102a: "their corpses were originally buried there on a temporary basis, but then they were never reinterred". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered a few lines up: the baraita explanation says the temporary burials "were never reinterred," so the unfulfilled intention is the page's own premise, not a puzzle. Ask instead about the asymmetry the Gemara builds: why an intention that was never acted on is enough to erase the middle corpse, while the vineyard owner's plan to uproot weak vines is not enough to erase the middle vines. Or press on the Rabbis' separate reason, that burying bodies that close is a disgrace, and what that adds beyond the intention argument.

bava-batra/103.summary: A field sold as a beit kor, the area needed to sow a kor of seed, may be pocked with crevices and studded with rocks. If they run ten handbreadths deep or high they are not measured with the field; anything less counts as the cracks of the earth and the spines of the earth, and is included. Rav Pappa then changes the reason for sales: a buyer will not pay for one plot that looks like two.
bava-batra/103.question: When does a dip in the ground stop being a crack in the earth and become a second plot: when nothing will grow in it, or when the buyer's eye sees two fields instead of one?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether land is measured by what can grow in it or by how it looks to the purchaser — but that is the very distinction the page draws between consecration and sale.

answer.quote: Because a person buying a field does not want to give his money for the purchase of one plot when it appears to him like two or three different plots
answer.explanation: The page explicitly resolves the disjunction the question poses: for consecration the criterion is fitness for sowing (water-filled crevices), while for a sale Rav Pappa rules that ten handbreadths excludes the crevice regardless of water, precisely because the buyer sees two or three plots.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 103a: "Because a person buying a field does not want to give his money for the purchase of one plot when it appears to him like two or three different plots". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what Rav Pappa's statement already answers, and the summary itself quotes that answer, so the reader is handed the resolution before asking. Rebuild the question on what the page leaves open after Rav Pappa: why a buyer's eye should set the measure for sales while fitness for sowing sets it for consecration, or why ten handbreadths of appearance can undo land that grows grain perfectly well. Alternatively work from the unresolved dilemmas — rocks in a ring, a row, an angle — where the page admits it cannot say when scattered stone stops being part of a field.

bava-batra/104.summary: The mishna lets a seller who handed over too much land choose: take money for the surplus, or take the surplus land back. The Gemara then tests that against price swings, and the buyer pays the lower figure either way, today's rate if land has fallen, the old rate if it has risen. Rav Ashi asks what would count as separating the surplus from the seller's own adjoining field: a pit, a water channel, a public road, a row of palm trees.
bava-batra/104.question: If the buyer ends up paying the cheaper rate whether land rose or fell since the sale, whose power is actually being enhanced?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whose interest a rule is designed to protect when the choice belongs to one party but the pricing consistently favors the other.

answer.quote: the buyer pays money in order to enhance the power of the seller. In other words, the Sages allowed the seller to choose whether to take back the surplus land
answer.explanation: The page states that the seller's power is the one enhanced and rebuts the baraita that seemed to enhance the buyer's power by reading it as a price-fluctuation case, but it never addresses the note's sharper point that the pricing rule consistently favors the buyer.

bava-batra/105.summary: A man in Tzippori rented a bathhouse for twelve gold dinars a year, one gold dinar per month, and then the year gained a thirteenth month. Ben Nanas says the last expression governs; the Sages call the contradiction a doubt and split the extra month's rent. Shmuel sharpens it: the split only happens if the landlord comes to collect mid-month, since whoever already holds the money keeps it.
bava-batra/105.question: If the same contract pays out differently depending on whether the landlord knocks on the first of the month or the last, is the case being decided at all?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether possession-based default is really a ruling on the contract or a refusal to rule — the page answers that it is the latter.

answer.quote: Because the party who is awarded the money was seen as already being in possession of it, and in a case of uncertainty, money is left in the hands of the party enjoying possession.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself explains that the timing-dependent outcome is not an adjudication of the contract's meaning but the default rule that unresolved doubt leaves money with whoever holds it.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 105b: "Because the party who is awarded the money was seen as already being in possession of it, and in a case of uncertainty, money is left in the hands of the party enjoying possession.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 105b, which says outright that in a case of uncertainty money is left with the party in possession — so the timing-dependent outcome is admittedly not a decision on the contract's meaning. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard: e.g. why Shmuel treats an explicit second clause as pure doubt rather than a retraction, or why Rav thinks possession should never be needed because the last expression always governs. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-batra/106.summary: A seller promises a field of a beit kor, roughly the area sown with a kor of seed, and walks the buyer around its borders; the mishna lets a shortfall under one sixth stand. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda split over a gap of exactly one sixth. Then Rav Pappa buys land described as twenty griv, measures it at fifteen, sues, and Abaye tells him he saw the plot and took it as is.
bava-batra/106.question: If a buyer who has seen the field is bound by what he saw, what is the seller's stated measure worth at all?

judge.reachNote: What a stated measure means once the buyer has inspected the plot — a guarantee of quantity or a description of quality.

answer.quote: What he meant was that the field is as good and as fruitful as one that is fit for planting twenty se’a.
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa raises exactly the note's objection — "the seller said to me that the field is fit for planting twenty se’a, and it is not" — and Abaye answers that the stated measure was a claim about quality, not area.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 106b: "What he meant was that the field is as good and as fruitful as one that is fit for planting twenty se’a.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very objection Rav Pappa raises and Abaye answers on 106b, where the stated "twenty se'a" is recast as a claim about the field's fruitfulness rather than its area. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than reaching it, for instance pressing on why Abaye's familiarity exception does not swallow the mishna's one-sixth rule, or on the tension between Rav Huna's and Rav Yehuda's readings of "until it is calculated at one-sixth." The summary is faithful and can stand largely as is.

bava-batra/107.summary: Three appraisers go down to value a field being seized for a debt, and each names a different figure: eighty dinars (a dinar is a silver coin), one hundred, and one hundred and twenty. The page tests three ways to split the difference, including the rule of Aḥerim, who take the gap between the extremes, divide it by three, and add that to the lowest estimate. Rav Huna rules that way, and Rav Ashi answers that nobody understands why.
bava-batra/107.question: If a formula settles what a debtor's field is worth but no one can explain how it works, is that a reason to follow it or a reason to drop it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rule's authority rests on its being intelligible or merely on its being taught and workable.

answer.quote: We do not even understand the reason of Aḥerim; shall we then establish the halakha in accordance with their opinion?
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi voices one side of the note's question — an unexplained formula should not be adopted — but Rav Huna twice rules by it anyway and the page never resolves between them, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/108.summary: A fence between two fields is flanked by a wide ditch and a narrow one, set a handbreadth apart so an animal cannot stand in either and jump. The mishna then sorts relatives into four groups by who inherits from whom, and the Gemara immediately quarrels with the order: why start with a father inheriting from his son, which means starting with a son's death? The answer is that this rule is derived, not written, and therefore dear.
bava-batra/108.question: Is a rule more precious because it had to be dug out of a verse, even when putting it first means opening the list with a father burying his son?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a law wrested from a verse by derivation is cherished more than one written plainly — but that is exactly the page's stated answer.

answer.quote: since the halakha that a father inherits from his son is learned through a derivation and is not explicitly mentioned in the verse, this halakha is dear to him; therefore, he listed it first
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very objection the note raises (beginning with a calamity) and resolves it by stating that a derived halakha is dear to the tanna and so listed first.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 108b: "since the halakha that a father inherits from his son is learned through a derivation and is not explicitly mentioned in the verse, this halakha is dear to him; therefore, he listed it first". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates the Gemara's own answer, which the summary already gives: the derived halakha is dear to the tanna, so he listed it first. Rewrite so the question begins after that answer and asks what still presses — for instance, why affection for a derivation should govern the order of a legal list at all, or why the second objection (that Scripture itself puts the son's inheritance first) is satisfied by the same reply. Keep the summary, which the page supports.

bava-batra/109.summary: Rava says only a father's family counts as "family" when the Torah assigns an inheritance to a dead man's nearest kinsman. A verse in Judges seems to break that: a man of the tribe of Levi is called "of the family of Judah," apparently after his mother. The answer is odder than the problem, that he was Moses' grandson, and the text reassigned him to Manasseh and Judah because he served idols as they did.
bava-batra/109.question: If a verse can swap a man's ancestry for the idolater he resembles, what is left of the rule that family means the father's family?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether Scripture's moral attributions of ancestry can coexist with a halakhic rule that lineage is strictly paternal.

answer.quote: since he acted as Manasseh, who came from the tribe of Judah, acted, the verse linked him to Judah by stating that he was "of the family of Judah," but he was, in fact, a Levite
answer.explanation: The page insists the scriptural relabeling is a moral linkage only and that the man's actual lineage remains Levite, which defends Rava's rule, though it never reflects on how a verse may speak so loosely.

bava-batra/110.summary: Men from the tribe of Dan find Jonathan, a descendant of Moses, serving as priest at Micah's idol, and press him on how Moses' grandson ended up there. He answers with a family tradition: better to hire yourself out to idol worship than to depend on charity. The Gemara says he misheard it, since the phrase meant strange work, labor that feels beneath you, the way Rav told Rav Kahana to skin a carcass for pay.
bava-batra/110.question: When King David noticed how precious money was to Jonathan and made him ruler over the Temple treasuries, what about that arrangement earns him the name Shebuel?
gate: the question brings in "King", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Shebuel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that a man's vice (love of money) can be channeled into sanctioned service and count as repentance, but the page states the naming reason outright.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: He is called Shebuel in order to allude to the fact that he repented and returned to God [shav la’el ] with all his heart.
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the name question and answers that Shebuel marks Jonathan's repentance and return to God.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 110a: "Rabbi Yoḥanan says: He is called Shebuel in order to allude to the fact that he repented and returned to God [shav la’el ] with all his heart.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same daf, where Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that Shebuel means he repented and returned to God; drop it. Build a question from something the page leaves unresolved instead, such as the tension in Jonathan's inherited tradition being honored in a distorted form, or why David's remedy for greed was to put the greedy man in charge of the treasuries. Aim at the idea that the sages read a distasteful act as misheard instruction rather than rejecting it.

bava-batra/111.summary: A baraita reads the plural in "from the tribes of the children of Israel" as a daughter who inherits from her father's tribe and her mother's. From there the first tanna argues that a son, stronger in his father's estate, must also outrank his sister in his mother's; Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav caps that reasoning, since a derived rule cannot outrun its source. Rav Nahman then bullies two judges into retracting rulings that followed Zekharya.
bava-batra/111.question: If Rabbi Yehuda Nesia's question about the firstborn's double portion was so easily resolved that Rabbi Yannai walked away, why does it take Abaye, Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak, and finally Rava three separate attempts to answer it?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Nesia's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yannai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Abaye", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yitzhak", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Rava", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What counts as an 'easily resolved' difficulty, when the resolution in fact takes three successive verse-derivations to survive challenge.

answer.quote: But one can still say that this statement applies in a case of a widower who married a virgin, so that he already has a firstborn from his previous marriage
answer.explanation: The page shows why each derivation needed replacing — every earlier verse-reading was defeated by a further marital case — but it never addresses the tension with Rabbi Yannai's dismissal of the difficulty as easily resolved.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Nahman bullies two judges into retracting rulings that followed Zekharya.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya thought to perform an action, i.e., issue a ruling, in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Nahman bullies two judges into retracting rulings that followed Zekharya.", but the page says "Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya thought to perform an action, i.e., issue a ruling, in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav.". Say what the page says. Fix the last summary sentence: only Rabbi Tavla had actually ruled and was ordered to retract, while Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya merely 'thought to perform an action' and was shamed by the threat to check with Rav Huna. Keep the question, but sharpen it so it acknowledges that each derivation was overturned by a further case (bachelor/widow, widower/virgin) and asks what that says about Rabbi Yannai's dismissal.

bava-batra/112.summary: The argument is whether a husband inherits his wife's land, and the proof comes from stray verses: Yair owning land his father Seguv never had, and Pinehas burying his father Elazar on a hill of his own. Rav Pappa objects that both men could simply have bought their fields from someone. Abaye answers that purchased land reverts to its original owner in the Jubilee Year, so Elazar would end up lying in a grave that is not his.
bava-batra/112.question: Does the assumption that a righteous man would never be buried in ground that reverts to someone else count as evidence about inheritance law, or only about what the arguers could not bring themselves to picture?
gate: gloss "the Jubilee" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether moral implausibility (a righteous man in a borrowed grave) functions as legal proof or only as a limit on the sages' imagination.

answer.quote: Rather, say that in his capacity as a priest he came into possession of this land as a dedicated field.
answer.explanation: The page does not discuss whether the piety-based argument counts as legal evidence, but it shows Rav Pappa treating it as binding enough that he abandons the purchase option and looks for a different mode of acquisition, which bears on the question without settling it.

bava-batra/113.summary: Rabba bar Ḥanina reads the phrase "on the day that he causes his sons to inherit" to mean inheritances may be distributed only in daylight. Abaye objects that a man who died at night would then leave no heirs, so the rule must be about judges, who sit only by day. Three people visiting a sick man may sign his will as witnesses or, being three, act as a court, which Rav Ḥisda limits to a daytime visit.
bava-batra/113.question: If the same three visitors at a sick man's bedside may choose to be witnesses or to be a court, what actually decides which one they become?

judge.reachNote: It reaches toward the idea that the same act takes its legal character from the intent of those performing it — but the page already says the choice is theirs "if they wish."

answer.quote: if the visitors wish to do so they may write his will and sign it as witnesses. And if they wish, they may act in judgment
answer.explanation: The page states outright that what decides is the visitors' own wish, together with their being three, which is the very thing the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 113b: "if the visitors wish to do so they may write his will and sign it as witnesses. And if they wish, they may act in judgment". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same line the summary paraphrases: Rav Yehuda says the three act as witnesses or as a court "if they wish," so their own choice is what decides. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for example why inheritance is "placed together to be considered a matter of judgment" at all, so that distributing an estate needs a court sitting by day rather than mere witnesses, or Rav Ashi's claim that a son is not "another" because he extends his mother.

bava-batra/114.summary: Three men come to visit a sick man who wants to dictate his will; by day they may write it, sign as witnesses, and also rule on it as judges, but at night only witness it. That ruling feeds a dispute about deals: Rabba says a party can back out while both sit in the same place, Rav Yosef while they are still discussing the matter. Rav Ashi presses both sides, since the dying man might still change his mind.
bava-batra/114.question: If a dying man's instructions only become binding once the visitors change the subject or stand up and sit down again, what is it that actually makes a mind made up?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea beneath the case: what constitutes a finalized intention, and whether finality is a state of mind or something the surroundings certify.

bava-batra/115.summary: When a man dies with no son, the page reads the Hebrew ein, "he has no," as ayyein alav, "investigate with regard to him": search out a son's descendants before the estate passes to a daughter or to brothers. Abaye says that search can run back to Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and no further, since a tribe never disappears completely. Then Rabban Yo\u1e25anan ben Zakkai argues with Sadducees who let a daughter inherit alongside a son's daughter, and mostly insults them.
bava-batra/115.question: Does the verse about Zibeon and Anah actually answer the old man's claim, or does Rabban Yo\u1e25anan ben Zakkai simply call him a name twice?
gate: the question brings in "Zibeon", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Anah", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a scriptural equation of grandchildren with children answers an a fortiori argument about a daughter inheriting alongside a son's daughter, or only changes the subject.

answer.quote: it is clear that grandchildren are equal to children, contrary to the Sadducees’ assertion
answer.explanation: The page states how the Zibeon–Anah verse is meant to refute the Sadducees, but it also records the Sadducee's retort that "the verse you quoted has no bearing on that claim," and breaks off at "Imbecile," leaving the rejoinder unstated.

bava-batra/116.summary: A Sadducee argues that if a granddaughter inherits, a daughter surely should, and the Sages, having beaten the argument, mark the twenty-fourth of Tevet as a minor festival. From there the talk turns to men who die without a son, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai reads divine wrath into the verse passing inheritance to a daughter. The attribution then shifts back and forth, because Rabbi Yoḥanan lost ten sons and carried a bone of the last one to console mourners.
bava-batra/116.question: When Rabbi Yoḥanan held out his tenth son's bone to the bereaved, was he refusing the harsh reading of the verse or living underneath it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's act of consolation is a protest against a doctrine he transmits or a way of living inside it.

answer.quote: This statement, with regard to the bone of his son, is his, while that statement, with regard to the verse, is his teacher’s.
answer.explanation: The Gemara resolves the tension by assigning the harsh verse-reading to Rabbi Yoḥanan's teacher and the consoling bone to Rabbi Yoḥanan himself, which bears on the question without saying whether he was rejecting or enduring the teaching.

bava-batra/117.summary: A baraita offers three answers to who actually received a share in the land of Israel: the generation that left Egypt, the generation that entered it, or both, with a man counted in both groups taking two portions. Rabbi Yonatan keeps the verse about fathers by reversing ordinary inheritance, so that the dead inherit from the living. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi pictures two priestly brothers whose sons collect teruma, the crop portion given to priests, pool it, split it evenly, and hand it back down.
bava-batra/117.question: If a man died in the wilderness and never saw the land, in what sense did the field his son plowed ever belong to him?

judge.reachNote: What ownership can mean when the owner never possessed, saw, or used the thing owned—title as pure legal fiction versus title as holding.

answer.quote: the portions of land received by those who entered Eretz Yisrael were transferred to their fathers who left Egypt, and then inherited by the current generation
answer.explanation: The page supplies a mechanism—retroactive transfer to the Exodus generation, then inheritance downward—but it states the mechanism rather than explaining in what sense a dead man who never entered could own a field, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/118.summary: Rav Pappa presses Abaye with a run of questions on whether the land was apportioned to the generation that left Egypt or the one that entered it, and each biblical complaint has to be recounted to fit. Abaye argues that since only Zelophehad's daughters and Joseph's descendants protested being shortchanged, no one else was left out. The rejection is sharp: Joseph's descendants protested and lost, and their failed protest was recorded anyway, as advice about the evil eye.
bava-batra/118.question: If Joseph's line is beyond the evil eye's reach, covered like fish in the sea, why does Joshua tell his descendants to go hide in the forest?
gate: the question brings in "Joshua", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Does a promise of protection from harm cancel the duty of ordinary prudence, or does prudence still bind even the immune?

answer.quote: Joshua said to them: Go and conceal yourselves in the forests so that the evil eye will not have dominion over you.
answer.explanation: The page gives Joshua's stated reason and then records the descendants' retort that Joseph's line needs no such caution, but it never resolves why Joshua urged concealment on a family he presumably knew to be immune.

bava-batra/119.summary: Zelophehad died in the wilderness before the land was parceled out, and his daughters claim his father Hepher's share plus the extra portion a firstborn son takes. The argument turns on whether a portion of land counts as already possessed before anyone stepped onto it, and the Gemara says Moses was unsure of exactly that. The same passage pairs the daughters with the man caught gathering wood on Shabbat: one law arrived through the deserving, one through the guilty.
bava-batra/119.question: If the law on how a Shabbat violator is executed was going to be written either way, what did the wood gatherer do to earn being the case it was written through?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the person through whom a law enters the Torah is chosen by desert, but the page states that idea outright.

answer.quote: merit is brought about by means of one who is meritorious and liability by means of one who is liable
answer.explanation: The page states the very principle the question asks for — the wood gatherer was the vehicle because he was liable, and it adds that he "was found guilty" and "deserved that a portion concerning a negative matter be written through him."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 119b: "merit is brought about by means of one who is meritorious and liability by means of one who is liable". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 119b: liability comes about through one who is liable, and the wood gatherer was found guilty and so deserved the negative portion. Write a question that starts from that principle rather than asking for it — for instance, press on what it means that Moses already knew the verdict and only the mode of death was open, or on the asymmetry between the daughters' initiative and the gatherer's passivity in "earning" a portion. Alternatively, build a question from the land-possession thread (morasha as both inheriting and bequeathing) that the summary already sets up.

bava-batra/120.summary: The five daughters of Zelophehad are named in one verse by age and in another by wisdom. Rabbi Ami takes that as an order of seating: in judgment and study the wisest sits highest, at a meal the oldest does. Then Shmuel says the command that a daughter who inherits land marry inside her father's tribe was only good advice, and Rava limits it to that one generation, reading "this is the matter" as a fence around a single moment.
bava-batra/120.question: If the restriction on whom these heiresses could marry was only good advice, why does it sit in the verse in the language of a command?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the gap between a verse's imperative form and merely advisory force — when does Scripture command and when does it counsel?

answer.quote: This mitzva applied to everyone except for the daughters of Zelophehad, who were explicitly permitted to marry members of any tribe.
answer.explanation: Rabba's objection and resolution treat the commanding language as a real mitzva binding on that generation, with Zelophehad's daughters as the sole exception, which bears on the question but does not directly explain why the counsel to them is phrased imperatively.

bava-batra/121.summary: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel called the fifteenth of Av one of the two most joyous days of the year, when the daughters of Jerusalem went out in borrowed white garments, and the Gemara asks what happened on it. Six answers pile up: tribes allowed to intermarry, Benjamin readmitted, the wilderness deaths halting, road guards to Jerusalem removed, Beitar's slain finally buried, woodcutting for the altar ended. Benjamin's readmission turns on reading an oath narrowly: the men swore for themselves, not their children.
bava-batra/121.question: If an oath can be escaped by noticing that the men of Israel swore only "none of us" and never mentioned their children, what was the oath ever worth?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of an oath's scope versus its binding force — whether precise wording limits obligation or guts it.

answer.quote: The verse states: "None of us," and not: None of our children; therefore, the oath applied only to the generation that had taken the oath.
answer.explanation: The page gives the interpretive mechanism and states that the oath did bind its takers' generation, which bears on the question but does not address what such an escapable oath is worth.

bava-batra/122.summary: Joshua's division of the land ran on two receptacles, one holding the names of the twelve tribes and one the names of twelve regions. Elazar the High Priest, wearing the Urim VeTummim, the oracular stones of the breastplate, announced aloud which pair would come up, and only then drew them. The baraita also insists the tribes paid each other money to even out the portions, since nobody would accept worse land for free.
bava-batra/122.question: If Elazar names Zebulun and Akko before his hand goes into the receptacle, what work is the lottery still doing?
gate: the question brings in "Zebulun", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Akko", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a lot can function as public confirmation of an already-known divine will rather than as a device of chance.

answer.quote: How can these texts be reconciled? One indicates that the land was divided by lottery and the other indicates that the land was divided with the Urim VeTummim.
answer.explanation: The baraita raises the same tension between lot and oracle and resolves it by having both operate together, with the lot confirming Elazar's prophetic announcement, but it never says in so many words what independent work the lot performs.

summaryProblems.claim: The tribes paid each other money to even out the portions, since nobody would accept worse land for free.
summaryProblems.pageSays: is that to say we are dealing with fools [beshufetanei] who would agree to take inferior-quality land in exchange for more money?

summaryProblems.claim: The baraita insists the evening-out was done with money.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Yehoshua says: The tribes compensated each other with land by giving extra land to those whose portions were in less advantageous locations.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The tribes paid each other money to even out the portions, since nobody would accept worse land for free.", but the page says "is that to say we are dealing with fools [beshufetanei] who would agree to take inferior-quality land in exchange for more money?". Say what the page says. The summary says "The baraita insists the evening-out was done with money.", but the page says "Rabbi Yehoshua says: The tribes compensated each other with land by giving extra land to those whose portions were in less advantageous locations.". Say what the page says. Fix the last sentence: the Gemara rejects the idea that money compensated for inferior-quality land (that would make the tribes fools) and locates the compensation in distance from Jerusalem, with Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disputing whether it was paid in money or in extra land. The lottery question is good and can stand, but sharpen it against the baraita's own attempt to reconcile lot and Urim VeTummim so the reader sees what still remains unexplained.

bava-batra/123.summary: A firstborn son inherits a double portion, and the argument here is over the arithmetic: twice what each brother gets, or twice what all the others get together. Logic runs both ways, so verses decide it, and the proof is tested on Joseph, whose two sons counted as two tribes; Rav Pappa asks why "one portion above your brothers" could not mean one palm tree. The page then asks why Jacob moved the birthright to Joseph, and lands on Rachel handing her secret signs to Leah.
bava-batra/123.question: If Rachel won the birthright back for her son by undoing the very signs Jacob gave her to outwit Laban, was his deceit defeated or completed?
gate: the question brings in "Laban", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether righteous deceit achieves its end precisely by being surrendered — the signs meant to defeat Laban win the birthright only when Rachel gives them up.

answer.quote: But because of the modesty that Rachel possessed, the Holy One, Blessed be He, returned the status as firstborn to her.
answer.explanation: The page states that Rachel's modesty in giving away the signs won back the firstborn status, which bears on the question's outcome but never addresses whether Jacob's deceit was thereby defeated or fulfilled.

bava-batra/124.summary: A father dies and the estate grows on its own: a calf is born, a palm tree thickens, silt washes onto a field. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gives the firstborn a double share of that growth, while the Rabbis limit him to what was in his father's hands at death, since the verse's word "giving" makes the double portion a gift. The same word cuts back: a firstborn who inherits his father's debt repays double, and may decline both.
bava-batra/124.question: If the firstborn can walk away from the double portion once the estate turns out to carry debts, is it an inheritance or just an offer?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether the firstborn's extra share is inherited automatically or received like a gift that can be refused — but the page names that idea outright.

answer.quote: Since the inheritance is referred to as a gift, he has the right to refuse it.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly explains that the word "giving" classifies the double portion as a gift, which is precisely why the firstborn may decline it, answering the note's inheritance-or-offer question.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 124a: "Since the inheritance is referred to as a gift, he has the right to refuse it.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered in so many words on the daf: the Gemara says the double portion is called a gift and therefore may be refused. Rewrite the question to press on something the page leaves open — for example, why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi treats self-generated growth as reaching the father's hands while a debt owed to him does not, or what it means that Rabbi Ḥiyya tells each judge to decide for himself. Keep the summary, which is faithful.

bava-batra/125.summary: A dying man leaves all his property to his grandmother, and after her death to his heirs. His married daughter dies before the grandmother does, and when the grandmother dies the daughter's widower claims the property as his wife's heir. Rav Huna grants it to him, Rav Anan refuses, and the Sages of Eretz Yisrael keep Rav Anan's ruling while throwing out his reason: the daughter never possessed the property, since her great-grandmother could still have sold it.
bava-batra/125.question: If the reason Rav Anan gave is rejected as wrong, in what sense is the ruling still his?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the distinction between a ruling's outcome and its reasoning, and what it means to be 'in accordance with' a sage whose logic is rejected.

answer.quote: The halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav Anan that the husband does not inherit the property. But not due to his reasoning
answer.explanation: The page states that what is retained from Rav Anan is the bottom-line result that the husband does not inherit, and it goes on to show where the two reasonings diverge (the case of a son), but it never addresses directly why a ruling is still credited to a sage whose stated reason is discarded.

bava-batra/126.summary: Mar Zutra, a firstborn, split a basket of peppers from his father's estate evenly with his brothers, then asked Rav Ashi for his double share of everything else. Rav Ashi refused: waiving the extra portion once waives it everywhere, because the firstborn already holds that portion before the estate is divided. The mishna then says a father who declares his firstborn will take no double portion has said nothing, yet the same father, calling it a gift, can do exactly that.
bava-batra/126.question: If calling it a gift accomplishes what the father is forbidden to declare outright, what is the rule against stipulating against the Torah actually stopping?

judge.reachNote: Whether a Torah rule bars the result or only the legal instrument — form versus substance in overriding inheritance.

answer.quote: there, the woman knew of his stipulation and waived her rights. Therefore, the stipulation stands. Here, the son whose portion was reduced did not waive his portion.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains that a stipulation against Torah inheritance fails absent the affected party's waiver, which bears on what the rule protects, but it never explains why labeling the transfer a gift succeeds where the declaration fails.

bava-batra/127.summary: Two wives of one man give birth to sons in hiding, so no one knows which boy was firstborn; Rava rules that each writes the other an authorization so they can jointly claim the double share. Told that Rabbi Yannai limited this to sons once recognized and later mixed up, Rava hires a crier to announce that his own teaching was an error. The page then asks whether a father's bare word can name a firstborn against what the court already assumes.
bava-batra/127.question: Why is a father believed when he names a firstborn nobody thought was the firstborn, while a man who calls someone his son at the customs house is assumed to be dodging the slave tax?

judge.reachNote: When is a man's bare word about another person's status trusted — does a verse's grant of credibility survive a plain motive to lie?

answer.quote: his latter statement is deemed credible, as he presumably says that the other is his son only to evade paying a tax for possessing a slave
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason the customs-house speaker is disbelieved (a motive to lie) and separately grounds the father's credibility in "He shall acknowledge him to others," but it never sets the two cases side by side, so the comparison the question draws can still be asked.

bava-batra/128.summary: Rabbi Abba sends a string of rulings to Rav Yosef bar Ḥama, one of which holds that a man who knew a field's boundary before he went blind can no longer testify about it. Three sages push back and keep widening the opening: Shmuel allows boundaries, Rav Sheshet a cloak measured by its length and width, Rav Pappa even a piece of silver identified by weight. A baraita about sons-in-law, deafness and insanity then refutes all three at once.
bava-batra/128.question: If a blind man can name the weight of the silver in his hand, what is the court holding out for when it still refuses to hear him?

judge.reachNote: Whether testimony rests on a witness's capacity to identify or on a categorical status of fitness that ability cannot substitute for.

answer.quote: Anyone whose initial state or his ultimate state, i.e., his state at the time of the incident or at the time of his testimony in court, is one of disqualification
answer.explanation: The baraita's principle states that blindness disqualifies as a matter of status at either moment, which bears on the question but never explains why demonstrated identifying ability does not suffice.

bava-batra/129.summary: A man on his deathbed who says a field "will be given" to one son can override the ordinary shares, but if he only says that son "will inherit it," his words do nothing. The sages then argue how far a single "given" stretches: across one field, two fields, two recipients. The resolution is measured in time, since a statement finished within the span it takes to greet one's teacher counts as one continuous sentence.
bava-batra/129.question: If a man can undo or extend his own words within the breath it takes to greet his teacher, why does accepting an idol bind him the instant he says it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea behind toch kedei dibbur: whether speech is binding only once it is complete, or whether some utterances commit a person the moment they leave his mouth.

bava-batra/130.summary: A man says his daughter will inherit where he has a son, and the mishna, the core teaching, rules he has said nothing, since the Torah fixes the order of heirs. Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka allows a father to hand everything to one son among his sons, and Rava grounds this in the verse about the day a man causes his sons to inherit. The page then turns to a different worry: which is stronger evidence, a sage's stated rule or a case he actually decided?
bava-batra/130.question: Rava tells his students that after his death they must neither tear up his rulings nor follow them, so what is a ruling that can be neither destroyed nor used?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a ruling's authority rests on its author's living reasoning, leaving an undefended text in limbo — neither refuted nor usable.
