answer.quote: Do not tear it up, as had I been there, perhaps I would have told you a valid explanation that you would have accepted;
answer.explanation: The page gives Rava's reason for preserving the ruling, but breaks off before explaining why it also may not be relied upon, so the paradox the question names is only half resolved.

bava-batra/131.summary: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that a man on his deathbed who signs over all his property to his wife has given her nothing; he has made her a steward, a caretaker, so that his heirs will honor her. The same reading holds even for a minor son lying in his crib, who would manage the estate only once grown. Ravina and Rav Avira, both citing Rava, then split over daughters, wives and brothers.
bava-batra/131.question: If writing over everything is read as appointing a caretaker rather than an heir, what words were left to a man who actually meant to give his wife the whole estate?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a presumption about intent can override the plain words of a deed, leaving the giver's actual wish unsayable.

answer.quote: Rather, we learned that they will take the money of the marriage contract, as a gift. When a bequeathal is worded in this manner, it is valid in any event
answer.explanation: The page shows that wording a transfer as a gift ("they will take") rather than as inheritance makes it effective, and it also lists circumstances where a gift is assumed (betrothed or divorced wife), but it never states what language a dying man must use to overcome the steward presumption for his wife.

bava-batra/132.summary: A dying man deeds all his property to his wife, and then a creditor turns up holding a loan note older than the gift. The Rabbis say she must tear up her marriage contract, the sum owed her at widowhood or divorce, keep the deed, and watch the creditor take the property, leaving her bald from here and from there. Rav Naḥman rules that way, saying the public honor of the gift was worth the risk to her.
bava-batra/132.question: Who decided that being publicly handed everything was worth more to her than the money she was owed, and was she ever asked?

judge.reachNote: Whether a court may impute consent and read a beneficiary's own interest for her, against the Gemara's own admission that she 'did not intend to waive payment'.

answer.quote: it is beneficial to her that it be publicized that he wrote a document granting her all of that property, and she was willing to risk not receiving payment
answer.explanation: The Gemara supplies the reasoning that the publicity of the gift outweighed the marriage contract, but it is an assessment made for her by the Sages, and the page never says she was consulted or consented.

bava-batra/133.summary: A mishna rules that a man who signs his property over to strangers and leaves his sons nothing has done a valid thing, though the Sages are displeased with him. The Gemara tests this against Yosef ben Yo'ezer, who consecrated a vessel of dinars, silver coins, to the Temple rather than leave it to his badly behaved son; that son later bought a fish, found a pearl in it, and sold it to the Temple for seven such vessels. The treasurers' receipt is reported two ways.
bava-batra/133.question: If the same seven vessels of coins end up in the Temple treasury either way, why should the wording of the receipt, that the son bestowed six or that he removed seven, decide whether his father was right to cut him out?
gate: the question uses "the Temple treasury", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether the way an act is recorded, rather than its net result, can settle a moral or halakhic verdict.

answer.quote: they said disparagingly that he removed seven, by inference, Yosef ben Yo'ezer did not act well when he left him out of his inheritance, as he caused money to be removed from the Temple treasury
answer.explanation: The page explains why each wording carries a verdict (bestowal credits the son, removal frames the treasury as losing), and then sets the story aside because the two accounts clash, but it never addresses the note's point that the seven vessels reach the treasury either way.

summaryProblems.claim: The vessel of dinars held silver coins.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Yosef ben Yo'ezer had a vessel [illiyyata] full of dinars, and he arose and consecrated it to the Temple treasury

judge.feedback: The summary says "The vessel of dinars held silver coins.", but the page says "Yosef ben Yo'ezer had a vessel [illiyyata] full of dinars, and he arose and consecrated it to the Temple treasury". Say what the page says.

bava-batra/134.summary: A mishna rules that a man who says "this is my son" is believed, and the Gemara asks what that credibility actually accomplishes. Shmuel's answer is that since he could divorce his wife and thereby free her from levirate marriage, marriage to her late husband's brother, he is believed that a son exists. The logic strains when he claims he divorced her on a past date: Rav Mari and Rav Zevid split over whether half a statement can stand.
bava-batra/134.question: If a man is believed only because of what he could still do today, is he being believed about his son at all, or only about his own power?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that credibility may rest on a person's legal power rather than on belief in the fact he asserts.

answer.quote: Since it is in his power to divorce her and thereby render her exempt from levirate marriage, he is deemed credible with regard to this claim as well.
answer.explanation: The page grounds the credibility in the husband's present power rather than in the truth of the claim, which bears on the question but does not settle whether he is believed about the son itself.

bava-batra/135.summary: A dying man, presumed to have brothers and no children, is asked whom his wife may marry after him, and he answers that she is fit even for a High Priest. That would free her from levirate marriage to a surviving brother, and Rava argues she is permitted, comparing her to a freed captive woman allowed to marry a priest despite rumors of witnesses far away. Abaye objects both times, and both times Rava tells Rav Natan bar Ami to be concerned anyway.
bava-batra/135.question: If Rava still thinks his own reasoning is correct, why does he leave the widow unable to remarry?
gate: gloss "levirate marriage" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is the gap between a reasoning one finds convincing and a ruling one is willing to issue where a woman's remarriage is at stake.

answer.quote: Be concerned about it. There may be a dispute with regard to this issue, as the resolution cannot be relied upon.
answer.explanation: The page states Rava's own reason for retreating: his harmonization of Rabbi Yoḥanan's two statements is only a proposed resolution and cannot be the basis of a practical ruling, as Abaye had just objected ('shall we arise and rely on answers in a halakhic ruling?').

summaryProblems.claim: Rava argues the woman is permitted by comparing her to a freed captive woman allowed to marry a priest despite rumors of distant witnesses.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Yosef responded: In any event, now the witnesses are not present before us, so this possibility does not need to be taken into account.

summaryProblems.claim: The captive-woman comparison belongs to the same case as the dying man who said his wife is fit for a High Priest.
summaryProblems.pageSays: There was a certain man who was presumed by us, i.e., the court, to have no brothers, and he said at the time of his death that he has no brothers.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 135a: "Be concerned about it. There may be a dispute with regard to this issue, as the resolution cannot be relied upon.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rava argues the woman is permitted by comparing her to a freed captive woman allowed to marry a priest despite rumors of distant witnesses.", but the page says "Rav Yosef responded: In any event, now the witnesses are not present before us, so this possibility does not need to be taken into account.". Say what the page says. The summary says "The captive-woman comparison belongs to the same case as the dying man who said his wife is fit for a High Priest.", but the page says "There was a certain man who was presumed by us, i.e., the court, to have no brothers, and he said at the time of his death that he has no brothers.". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words on the page: Rava himself says the concern is that his resolution of the contradiction cannot be relied upon for a ruling, after Abaye asks whether one may rule on the basis of harmonizing answers. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled, such as why a resolution good enough to explain Rabbi Yoḥanan is not good enough to act on. Also fix the attribution: the captive-woman analogy is Rav Yosef's, in a second, separate case about a man presumed to have no brothers, not Rava's argument about the dying man's wife.

bava-batra/136.summary: A healthy man deeds his property to his sons but wants to keep eating its produce until he dies, so Rabbi Yehuda requires the words: from today and after my death. Rabbi Yosei says the document's date already proves that; Rav Pappi claims the clause order in the deed matters, and Rav Ḥanina of Sura scoffs until Abaye's and Rava's scribes turn out to know the distinction. Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish then split over whether owning the produce amounts to owning the field.
bava-batra/136.question: If the Sages had to go ask working scribes what a reversed phrase in a deed accomplishes, who is actually deciding the law here?

judge.reachNote: Where legal authority actually sits when the drafting practice of working scribes outruns the Sages' own knowledge of what a formula does.

answer.quote: he need not write: From today and after my death, as the act of transfer is mentioned in any event
answer.explanation: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua (and the version taught by Rav Zevid of Neharde'a) sets aside the scribes' word-order distinction and rules that any mention of transfer suffices, showing the Sages retain the ruling power even after consulting the scribes — but the page never addresses head-on why the scribes' knowledge was probative in the first place.

bava-batra/137.summary: A man hands his property to one person and says that after that person dies it passes to a second. Two baraitot seem to have Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel each contradicting himself over whether the first holder may sell; the Gemara splits what he may do from the start from what stands once done. Abaye then calls the man who advises such a sale a cunning wicked person, though the sale holds.
bava-batra/137.question: If the sale is valid, what exactly has the advisor done wrong by suggesting it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the gap between what the law will enforce after the fact and what a person is permitted to do in the first place.

answer.quote: Although Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the sale is valid, he does not permit one to do so ab initio, as that would deprive the second designated recipient
answer.explanation: The page states explicitly that the wrong lies in doing ab initio what deprives the second recipient, even though the completed sale stands.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 137a: "Although Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the sale is valid, he does not permit one to do so ab initio, as that would deprive the second designated recipient". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the very line the summary paraphrases: the page says the advice deprives the second recipient and is forbidden ab initio even though the sale holds. Ask something the page leaves open instead, for instance why the blame falls on the advisor rather than the seller, or how the same 'ab initio versus after the fact' split works when the first recipient emancipates slaves or makes shrouds. Keep the summary, which tracks the page well.

bava-batra/138.summary: A man is handed a deed granting him another person's property, and among the property are slaves; he says he does not want them. The timing of that refusal decides everything: shout at the moment the deed arrives and nothing transfers, stay silent and shout only later and the slaves are already his, and he must sell or free them to be rid of them. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reads the late shout backward, as proof he never accepted.
bava-batra/138.question: When someone stays quiet while a gift is arranged and objects only once it lands in his hands, is he revealing what he wanted all along or changing his mind?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether a later act reveals a prior state of mind or undoes a completed one — but the page already states both sides of it as the machloket.

answer.quote: And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that his ultimate actions prove the nature of his initial intent; he never intended to acquire the slaves.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly frames the two alternatives the question offers — the first tanna reads the late shout as retraction ("the fact that he is shouting indicates that he is retracting his initial acceptance") and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reads it as proof of original intent — so the question merely restates the recorded dispute.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 138a: "And Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that his ultimate actions prove the nature of his initial intent; he never intended to acquire the slaves.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara already spells out: the first tanna calls the late shout a retraction, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel calls it evidence of original intent, and the summary itself reports both. Rewrite so the question starts after that dispute rather than reproducing it — for instance, why the recipient's excuse ("As long as they did not enter my possession, to what end will I shout?") is or is not a good reason to excuse silence, or why the first tanna is content to leave an unwilling owner holding slaves who may eat teruma. Keep it anchored in the slaves-and-refusal case.

bava-batra/139.summary: A woman borrows money by word of mouth, spends it, then marries and brings her property into the marriage. Is her husband a purchaser of that property, who cannot be dunned for an unwritten loan, or an heir, who can? Rav Ashi's answer is that the Sages made him both and applied whichever status leaves him better off, except against buyers who knew she had a husband and bought anyway.
bava-batra/139.question: If those buyers brought their loss on themselves by ignoring the husband, what about the creditor who lent to a woman who had no husband yet?

judge.reachNote: Whether "whichever status is better for him" is limited by whether the other party could have protected itself — assumption of risk as the hinge of the rule.

answer.quote: the Sages equated the husband with an heir, and the Sages equated him with a purchaser. And they deemed him as whichever is better for him
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi's rule would govern the creditor case too (the husband counted a purchaser, so the oral loan is uncollectable), but the page never applies it to the pre-marriage creditor or weighs whether that creditor's loss was self-caused, so the question can still be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Ashi's "whichever is better for him" rule has an exception "against buyers who knew she had a husband and bought anyway"
summaryProblems.pageSays: With regard to the case of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, where the wife sold the property, the Sages equated him with a purchaser, due to his potential loss

summaryProblems.claim: The only limit on giving the husband the better status is the knowing buyers
summaryProblems.pageSays: With regard to Ravin's halakha, concerning the sustenance of the husband's father-in-law's widow, due to the potential loss of the widow, the Sages equated him with an heir.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Ashi's "whichever is better for him" rule has an exception "against buyers who knew she had a husband and bought anyway"", but the page says "With regard to the case of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, where the wife sold the property, the Sages equated him with a purchaser, due to his potential loss". Say what the page says. The summary says "The only limit on giving the husband the better status is the knowing buyers", but the page says "With regard to Ravin's halakha, concerning the sustenance of the husband's father-in-law's widow, due to the potential loss of the widow, the Sages equated him with an heir.". Say what the page says. State Rav Ashi's rule as the page does: the husband gets whichever status spares him loss, and the buyers in Rabbi Yosei's case are precisely where he is treated as a purchaser — their self-caused loss is the reason their loss does not override it. The real counterweight on the page is the widow, for whose sake he is treated as an heir. Then build the question on that accurate footing, e.g. on why a third party's foreseeability decides whose loss counts.

bava-batra/140.summary: When a dead man's estate is too small to feed his daughters and still leave something for his sons, the daughters are sustained and the sons go begging. Rabbi Yirmeya stacks up harder cases: does a widow's right to food shrink the estate, or a stepdaughter's promised support, or an unpaid debt to a creditor? Rabbi Abbahu tells him to come back tomorrow, then answers only one of them: a widow outranks a daughter, and the daughter goes to the doors.
bava-batra/140.question: If the rule for a small estate exists so that daughters will not have to beg, what makes it tolerable that adding a widow sends the daughter to those same doors?

judge.reachNote: If the small-estate rule exists to spare the vulnerable from begging, the analogy merely shifts who begs, which asks what the rule is actually protecting — a person or a rank.

answer.quote: The Sages established the status of the widow in relation to the daughter as equivalent to the status of the daughter in relation to the brothers
answer.explanation: The page states the ranking by analogy — widow displaces daughter just as daughter displaces brothers — but gives no reason why sending the daughter to the doors is tolerable, so the question survives the answer it names.

bava-batra/141.summary: A man promises one hundred dinars, silver coins, to his child if his wife bears a son, and two hundred if she bears a daughter. The Gemara asks whether he really prefers a daughter, and splits the answer: a son carries the name and the land, a daughter needs more support. Then Rav Huna rules that a gift to an unborn child takes effect for nobody, and rather than match the mishna to a sage, he says he does not know who taught it.
bava-batra/141.question: Why does Rav Huna call the mishna unattributable and presumably corrupt instead of accepting any of the five readings the Gemara keeps offering him?

judge.reachNote: Underneath is whether a fetus can be a legal recipient at all, since a gift needs an act of acquisition while an inheritance falls in by itself.

answer.quote: Inheritance is different, since, unlike a gift, it comes into the possession of the heir by itself, without a formal act of acquisition.
answer.explanation: The page itself raises each proposed attribution for the mishna and states the reason Rav Huna cannot accept it, this being one of the explicit rejections, so the question's 'why not accept any of them' is answered line by line.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 141b: "Inheritance is different, since, unlike a gift, it comes into the possession of the heir by itself, without a formal act of acquisition.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question: for each of the suggested attributions (Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka, the combination, 'whoever informs me', and the already-born case) the Gemara states the reason it fails, which is why Rav Huna stands by 'I do not know who taught our mishna.' Rewrite the question so it starts after those rejections, for instance on why an inheritance can fall to a fetus while a gift cannot, given that both end up in the same hands. Also check the count of proposals in the question, since the page offers six, not five.

bava-batra/142.summary: The argument is whether an unborn child can be given property. Rav Huna says no, Rav Nahman says yes only if the giver delays the transfer until birth, and Rav Sheshet says yes either way, proving it from a convert who died while his wife was pregnant, whose estate strangers had already seized. Then Shmuel calls for ten men so a ruling will be well publicized, declares that a fetus does acquire, and the page concludes the opposite.
bava-batra/142.question: Why would Shmuel gather ten men to publicize a ruling that the page then flatly reverses?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the gap between a sage's deliberate act of publicizing a ruling and the anonymous halakhic conclusion that overrides it.

bava-batra/143.summary: A man says to another, you and a donkey shall both acquire my property, and three sages split over the result: half, nothing, or everything. Rav Sheshet argues from a cucumber separated as teruma, the priest's portion, whose inner part may be bitter and unfit, that an unfit partner does not spoil the fit one. Later the same problem returns in wills: what does a father mean by my sons when he has one son and a daughter?
bava-batra/143.question: If the giver is credited with knowing a donkey cannot acquire, why isn't a father credited with knowing how many sons he has?

judge.reachNote: Whether a speaker's words are construed against what he must have known to be true, or read as plain and therefore ambiguous language.

answer.quote: Come and hear a proof that one does refer to a single son using the plural term sons, as it is written: "And the sons of Dan: Hushim"
answer.explanation: The page addresses why the father's plural is not read against his knowledge of his family, since ordinary usage does call a single son "sons," leaving his intent genuinely doubtful — but it never compares this to crediting the donkey-giver with knowledge, so the question survives.

bava-batra/144.summary: Rabbi Ḥanina says a father who designates a house for his eldest son's wedding has given him the house, with no deed and no words required. The page then hunts for what cancels the gift: the father's storeroom left inside, a dovecote, a pot of small fried fish. Mar Zutra hung a sandal in the house at his son's wedding, and he also counts this rule among those the Sages enacted without explaining how they work.
bava-batra/144.question: If a father's unspoken fondness is enough to hand over a house, why is one sandal on a hook enough to take it back?

judge.reachNote: A gift resting wholly on inferred intent can be undone by any sign of contrary intent — the question asks whether that asymmetry is coherent.

answer.quote: Mar Zutra married off his son, and hung a sandal in the house, to indicate that he did not intend to give the house as a gift.
answer.explanation: The page explains that such small objects function as signals of the father's contrary intent, and Rabbi Yirmeya's storeroom case says the same ('just as his father did not intend to give him the storeroom, neither did he intend to give him the house'), yet it never addresses why a presumption strong enough to transfer a house without words yields to a single token, and Mar Zutra himself lists this halakha among those with 'no explanation of their process.'

bava-batra/145.summary: Gifts of groomsmen, the presents a friend brings to a wedding, are treated here as a debt a court can collect, though it falls due only at the giver's own wedding. Five rules follow from that: paying back more than you got is not interest, the Sabbatical Year does not cancel the debt, and a firstborn takes no double share. Rav Kahana then ranks excuses for missing the feast, and Abaye prices the discount for skipping dinner.
bava-batra/145.question: If the man who was never even told about his friend's wedding still has to pay the gift back, what is his grievance actually worth?
gate: gloss "the Sabbatical Year" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches toward whether a wrong that does not cancel a debt still has a price — but the page prices it explicitly.

answer.quote: In this case, since he did not partake of the wedding feast, he is entitled to deduct a sum from the reciprocal gift.
answer.explanation: The line immediately after the grievance states that the uninvited man deducts from what he repays, and Abaye then fixes the amounts (nothing up to a dinar, half up to four dinars, thereafter by prominence).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 145a: "In this case, since he did not partake of the wedding feast, he is entitled to deduct a sum from the reciprocal gift.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered two lines later: he deducts from the repayment, and Abaye gives the exact scale. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance, why the deduction is pegged to the food he did not eat rather than to the slight of not being told, or why a debt that only falls due at your own wedding escapes both interest and the Sabbatical release. Keep the summary; it is faithful.

bava-batra/146.summary: A betrothed man sends presents to his father-in-law's house, and the mishna asks who keeps them if the marriage never happens. Eat a groom's feast there worth a dinar, a silver coin, and the presents stay; eat nothing, and they come back. One man sent four hundred wagons of wine, silver, gold and fine wool, drank a cup of hot drink at the door, and died, and Rav Ashi guesses the cup held a ground pearl.
bava-batra/146.question: If a swallow of hot drink at the doorway is enough to keep a hundred wagons of silver, why does Rav Ashi need to imagine a thousand-dinar pearl dissolved in it?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a token act of consumption works by its symbolic force or only above a fixed monetary threshold — but the page settles it before the question is asked.

answer.quote: Can you learn from this incident that the presents cannot be claimed even if he ate or drank less than the value of a dinar
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises exactly the note's difficulty — a cup of hot drink is worth less than a dinar, which would contradict Rava's dinar minimum — and Rav Ashi's ground-pearl suggestion is the answer that keeps the incident consistent with the dinar threshold.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 146a: "Can you learn from this incident that the presents cannot be claimed even if he ate or drank less than the value of a dinar". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question assumes a swallow at the doorway is by itself enough, but the page says the opposite: Rava fixes a dinar minimum, the Gemara objects that a cup of hot drink is worth less, and Rav Ashi's pearl is the stated answer. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than re-asking it — for instance, press on why a token act of eating should need a monetary floor at all, or on why the Sages of Usha sorted by whether presents are consumable rather than by value. The summary can also note Rava's dinar rule, since it is what makes the pearl necessary.

bava-batra/147.summary: A person on his deathbed can hand over property just by saying so, with none of the formal transfer a healthy person needs. Rabbi Zeira, Rav Naḥman and others hunt for a source: an extra word in the inheritance rules of Numbers, or Isaiah telling the ailing Hezekiah to instruct his household. Then Rav Naḥman says the rule comes from the Sages, not the Torah, invented so a dying man is not unhinged by seeing his wishes ignored.
bava-batra/147.question: If the deathbed gift is only a rabbinic device to spare a dying man's peace of mind, what work is that concession still doing once the Sages hand it the force of Torah law anyway?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of a rabbinic enactment given the force of Torah law and what remains of the distinction once that force is granted.

bava-batra/148.summary: A man gives a palm tree to one person and keeps the fruit for himself, and the Sages ask whether he also kept the spot on the tree where the fruit grows. Rava, citing Rav Naḥman, says he did, because a person who holds something back holds it back generously; the same reasoning lets a seller who keeps the upper story also keep the air for projections over the courtyard. The page then turns to a dying man's gifts and partial retractions.
bava-batra/148.question: Why should the same carve-out mean more when a man keeps the fruit for himself than when he assigns it to a second person?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that a self-directed reservation is read expansively while a grant to another is read narrowly — but the page states that idea outright.

answer.quote: The reason is that anything that one reserves with regard to himself, he reserves generously, and therefore he reserves for himself not only the fruit itself, but also the place
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly gives the reason for the distinction between reserving for oneself and assigning to a second person, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 148a: "The reason is that anything that one reserves with regard to himself, he reserves generously, and therefore he reserves for himself not only the fruit itself, but also the place". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks for the very reason the page supplies, and the summary itself already repeats it ("a person who holds something back holds it back generously"), so it is answered before it is asked. Write a question that starts from that principle rather than requesting it — for example, why generosity toward oneself should be presumed when the same words in a gift to another are read narrowly, or how the unresolved dilemmas about consecrating and abandoning property sit with the assumption that a man always keeps something back for himself.

bava-batra/149.summary: Issur the convert had twelve thousand dinars, silver coins, on deposit with Rava when he lay dying. His son Rav Mari cannot inherit, having been conceived before his father's conversion, so Rava works through every route by which the money might still reach him and closes each one, including declining to show up as the bailee. Then Rav Ika asks why Issur cannot simply admit the coins are his son's, and a document of admission appears from Issur's house.
bava-batra/149.question: Rava himself mapped out every path to the money before Rav Ika found the one he had missed, so was Rav Ika teaching claims, or just finishing Rava's own argument?

judge.reachNote: Where does analyzing the law end and coaching a litigant begin, when the analyst is also the interested party's opponent.

answer.quote: Rava became angry, and said: They are teaching people legal claims and causing me loss.
answer.explanation: The page records Rava's own charge that Rav Ika was teaching litigants claims, but it never weighs that against the possibility that Rav Ika merely completed the enumeration Rava had begun, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/150.summary: A gift of "my movable property" hands over the utensils but not the wheat and barley; "all my movable property" adds the grain and the upper millstone, which is sometimes lifted, but not the lower one. Say "everything that can be moved" and the lower millstone goes too. A Canaanite slave, a non-Jewish slave, breaks the sorting: Rav Ashi says the city-sale case proves nothing, since land that moves differs from land that does not.
bava-batra/150.question: If a deed granting a slave all of his master's property frees him, why does holding back a sliver of land leave him owned: because he counts among the things held back, or because the deed was never a release at all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a document's effect comes from what it transfers or from what kind of instrument it is — but the page decides it.

answer.quote: The reason the slave is not emancipated if the master reserved part of the property for himself is not that the slave is included in the property that the owner reserved
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi explicitly chooses between the two options the question offers, rejecting the "slave is among the reserved property" reading in favor of the deed not being a bill of manumission.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 150b: "The reason the slave is not emancipated if the master reserved part of the property for himself is not that the slave is included in the property that the owner reserved". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and settled on the page: the mishna offers "perhaps he reserved the slave for himself as well" and Rav Ashi answers that the real reason is that the deed "is not a bill of manumission that completely severs the bond." Write a question that starts after that answer, or take up something the page leaves unsettled — for instance whether a slave is movable property or land, where Rav Naḥman calls him movable property while Rav Ashi shows the city-sale mishna proves nothing either way. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

bava-batra/151.summary: A run of women hand over property while sick or about to remarry, and the gifts keep coming undone. Rav Zutra's mother deeded her estate to her son so a new husband could not take it; she married, was divorced, and Rav Huna ruled she could reclaim it. The move worth watching is that saying why you are giving turns an outright gift into a conditional one, and silence about motive would have made it stick.
bava-batra/151.question: If a sick person's unspoken expectation of dying can unwind even a completed act of acquisition, what stops any giver with regrets from saying that is what they meant?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a giver's stated or provable motive, not the formal act, is what fixes whether a gift is final.

answer.quote: Inquiring into the matter, Rav Naḥman said to the witnesses: How did the act of transferring the property take place?
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman does not accept a bare claim of deathbed intent but examines witnesses to the words actually spoken ("Woe, that woman is dying!"), which bears on the question without fully settling it.

bava-batra/152.summary: A dying man writes a deed handing over his property, and the deed also records a formal act of acquisition, the ritual gesture that seals a healthy person's gift. Rav says the recipient now rides two horses: the gift cannot be retracted if the man recovers, yet a debt owed to him still transfers as only a deathbed gift can. Shmuel says he does not know what to rule, and both men are then caught contradicting themselves.
bava-batra/152.question: When Rav Naḥman answered Rava's objection with nothing but a motion of his hand and Rava went silent, was Rava reading the gesture or supplying the answer himself?
gate: the question brings in "Naḥman", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Rava's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Rava", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a teaching can pass wordlessly and that the student's report is the only record of what was taught.

answer.quote: Rava said to him: He indicated that the statement of Rav Yehuda is referring to a case where the giver was clearly enhancing the legal
answer.explanation: The page reports Rava's own account of what the gesture meant, which bears on the question but does not settle whether the content came from Rav Naḥman's hand or from Rava's reconstruction.

bava-batra/153.summary: A dying man's gift deed says the gift is given "in life and in death," and Rav and Shmuel split over which phrase controls. If it takes effect only at death, recovery lets him retract it; Rav Naḥman ducked one such case, sending the litigant out of Neharde'a rather than rule against Shmuel on Shmuel's home ground. Rava ruled by his own view, then had his scribe write a sham ruling to be rid of a woman who kept saying he judged wrong.
bava-batra/153.question: If Rava was certain his ruling was correct, why did he need a fake one to get the woman out of his court, and why did wetting his clothes not spare his ship?

judge.reachNote: A judge confident in his law still cannot end a case by law alone, and a wronged litigant's curse operates outside the court's authority.

answer.quote: She did not accept the ruling, and she constantly troubled him, saying that he had not judged her case properly.
answer.explanation: The page explains why a ruse was needed — the woman refused to accept the correct ruling and kept harassing Rava — but says nothing about why immersing his clothes failed to avert the curse, only that "even so he was not saved from the sinking of his ship."

bava-batra/154.summary: A deed of gift is contested, and the argument is over what would settle it: witnesses testifying the giver was healthy, or just confirming the signatures on the document are genuine. A case from Bnei Brak tests this, where a man sold inherited land and died, and his family claimed he had been a minor; Rabbi Akiva refuses to exhume the body. The discussion ends by reversing opinions in the mishna, the baraita, and finally between Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish.
bava-batra/154.question: When a reading can only be sustained by flipping the mishna, then the baraita, then the names of the two men arguing, what is left that the sources were supposed to prove?

judge.reachNote: When a tradition is re-attributed to save a sage's consistency, what work is the cited text still doing as proof?

bava-batra/155.summary: A man in Bnei Brak sold land he had inherited from his father and then died, and his relatives asked Rabbi Akiva whether the body could be exhumed to check whether he had been a minor; Akiva refused to disgrace a corpse over a money claim. Behind that sits a dispute over whether an heir may sell at eighteen or at twenty. Before Rava, relatives coach a young seller to throw date pits into the judge's house, and the buyers coach him back.
bava-batra/155.question: If Rava accepted a line the buyers had fed the boy because he understood it once it was explained, what could the relatives have shown that would have counted as incompetence?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that competence is measured by comprehension rather than decorum — impudence is not incompetence — though the page already hints at the contrast.

answer.quote: The reason for Rava's ruling was that there, Rava observed excessive mental incompetence in the behavior of that individual, as he was emancipating his slaves.
answer.explanation: The page gives one concrete instance of conduct Rava did treat as disqualifying incompetence (emancipating his slaves, i.e., squandering the estate), which bears on the question without laying out a general standard.

bava-batra/156.summary: A woman on her deathbed said her brooch, worth twelve hundred dinars, should go to her daughter, and the Sages upheld it with no formal act of acquisition. The Rabbis cite this as proof that a dying person's words transfer property; Rabbi Elazar answers that the ruling was not law at all, since her sons were wicked and the court bent the case against them. The evidence of their wickedness is that they let thorns grow in a vineyard.
bava-batra/156.question: If the Sages gave the brooch to the daughter because her brothers were wicked, how is anyone later supposed to tell which rulings state the law and which quietly punish somebody?

judge.reachNote: When a court rules against wicked litigants rather than by law, the ruling's value as precedent collapses — how is a later reader to sort binding law from targeted equity?

answer.quote: Consequently, when ruling in this matter the Sages did not act in accordance with the halakha, but allowed the mother of the sons of Rokhel to give this valuable piece
answer.explanation: The page explicitly labels this one ruling as a departure from halakha, which bears on the question but offers no general criterion for telling law from punishment in other cases.

bava-batra/157.summary: A house collapses on a father and his son, and no one can tell who died first, which decides whether the son's creditors reach the father's estate; Beit Shammai split the property, Beit Hillel leave it with the father's heirs. The Gemara turns the case into Shmuel's question: can a borrower place a lien on property he does not yet own? Every proof brought is deflected as Rabbi Meir's view alone.
bava-batra/157.question: If each source offered to settle Shmuel's question can be waved off as Rabbi Meir speaking, what kind of text could ever answer it?

judge.reachNote: It asks what counts as admissible proof when any proof-text can be quarantined by assigning it to a single tanna, i.e., whether a dilemma so framed is answerable at all.

bava-batra/158.summary: A house collapses on a husband and his wife, and no one knows which died first, so each set of heirs argues the other spouse died earlier. Beit Shammai split the disputed property; Beit Hillel leave each item where it already stood, which only relocates the question of where a wife's dowry already stood. When the collapse kills a son and his mother, both schools agree to split, and Rabbi Akiva dissents anyway, drawing ben Azzai's complaint.
bava-batra/158.question: Rabbi Zeira dropped his opinion after moving to Eretz Yisrael and credited the air there, while Rabba in Babylonia took up the very view Zeira had abandoned, so what exactly changed his mind?
gate: the question brings in "Zeira", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Eretz", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yisrael", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Rabba", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Babylonia", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a sage's change of view may rest on where he stands rather than on a stated argument, and asks what a reason really consists of.

answer.quote: Since the inheritance was initially in the possession of that tribe of the mother, it is not removed from their possession in order to transfer it to the son's heirs
answer.explanation: The page supplies Abaye's substantive reason for the view Rabbi Zeira came to adopt, though it never says this reasoning is what persuaded him, offering only his own quip about the air of Eretz Yisrael.

bava-batra/159.summary: A son sells some of his father's land while the father is still alive, dies first, and then the son's own son takes that land back from the buyers. The Gemara calls this hard to justify and tries four times to substitute a different difficult case, including a man who signed a document and only later became the son-in-law of the person he testified for. Every substitute is rejected, and the verse from Psalms that would have rescued the first case is demoted to a blessing.
bava-batra/159.question: If "In the place of your fathers shall be your sons" is only a blessing and not a rule, what is left holding up the grandson's claim against buyers who already paid his father?

judge.reachNote: Whether a grandson's right to land flows directly from his grandfather or only through his father, and what that means for buyers who paid the father.

bava-batra/160.summary: A mishna sorts legal documents into two kinds: a plain one, where the witnesses sign on the written side, and a tied one, folded and sewn shut, where they sign on the back and three witnesses are needed rather than two. Three sages each root the tied document in a verse from Jeremiah or Deuteronomy, and the Gemara knocks down all three, calling the practice the Sages' own invention. Its stated purpose was stalling quick-tempered priests who divorced their wives impulsively and then regretted it.
bava-batra/160.question: Why do three sages each dig a verse out of scripture for a document format the Gemara ends up admitting the Sages invented themselves?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of asmakhta — why rabbinic enactments get dressed in scriptural clothing when everyone concedes the Sages made them.

bava-batra/161.summary: Rami bar Ḥama keeps inventing ways to forge a tied document, the folded kind whose witnesses sign on the reverse side. Cut off the last line and you also cut away the words "Reuven, son of," leaving a signature that still reads as valid. Each patch invites a new attack, until Mar Zutra ends it: all the witnesses' signatures must finish on one line, so cropping the bottom mangles every name at once.
bava-batra/161.question: If a drawn fish or a single letter can serve as a signature, why is signing with your father's name the one thing the page assumes nobody would dare?

judge.reachNote: What makes a signature legally identifying — arbitrary personal mark or actual name — and why filial honor limits what a person may appropriate as his mark.

answer.quote: A person is not so insolent as to use his father’s name as a distinguishing mark.
answer.explanation: The Gemara does give a ground for the assumption — insolence toward one's father — though it never explains why an arbitrary fish or letter is unobjectionable while a father's name is, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bava-batra/162.summary: Rav Amram holds that nothing new may be learned from a document's final line, since the holder could squeeze in a forged clause above the witnesses' signatures. A baraita backs him: two blank lines between text and signatures void the document, one blank line does not. Hizkiyya then says the gap can be plugged with signatures of relatives, who cannot testify, and compares it to a sukka roof whose hole is filled with unfit material.
bava-batra/162.question: If relatives' signatures are worthless as testimony, why does filling the gap with them stop a forger who could simply write above them?

judge.reachNote: Does a document's validity turn on the legal quality of what fills the gap, or merely on the physical occupation of space?

answer.quote: If a sukka had a gap in its roofing of three handbreadths it is disqualified, but if the gap is filled in with unfit material
answer.explanation: Ḥizkiyya's sukka analogy indicates that filler need not be legally fit to count as filling the space, which bears on the question but does not spell out why a forger could not write above the relatives' signatures.

bava-batra/163.summary: A deed with too much blank space between its text and the witnesses' signatures can be padded with forged lines, so the rabbis measure the gap by handwriting, not by a scribe's small neat script, since a forger works alone. Rav Yitzhak ben Elazar, Ulla and Rabbi Abbahu each size the fatal gap differently, down to whether a lamed and a final khaf fit above and below. Then comes the trick of filling the blank with ink or dots.
bava-batra/163.question: If every forgery scheme on the page finally collapses because the signed witnesses can be asked what they actually signed, why measure blank lines at all?

judge.reachNote: Whether a document's trustworthiness rests on its physical form being unforgeable or on the living witnesses who can be interrogated about what they signed.

answer.quote: perhaps the holder of the document may forge additional lines and write whatever he wants, and the witnesses have already signed at the bottom
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason the gap before the signatures must be measured — the real witnesses' signatures would appear to attest to the added lines — but it never confronts the note's point that the later cases are all resolved by relying on what the witnesses signed upon, so the question survives.

bava-batra/164.summary: A sheet of parchment scraped clean can be written on again, so the Gemara works through how a forger might erase a loan document and write himself a better one above the original witnesses' signatures. Each defense draws a counter: witnesses must see the erasure first, or write a note about it between their two signatures, or the court erases a test parchment for comparison. Rabbi Yirmeya shuts the whole procedure down because a court might botch it.
bava-batra/164.question: If a double erasure really can be detected, why should a genuine document be voided out of worry that some court will run the test badly?

judge.reachNote: Whether the law should prefer a simple bright-line invalidation over a technically sound but fragile procedure, because the institution applying it may err.

answer.quote: We are concerned for the possibility of an erring court. If such complicated procedures were used in order to declare a document valid, there would be
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yirmeya's reason for rejecting the verification procedure — fear of a court misapplying it — and elsewhere undercuts the premise that a double erasure is reliably detectable, but it never weighs that risk against invalidating a genuine document.

bava-batra/165.summary: Rabbi Yirmeya, expelled from the study hall, receives a question from the scholars of Eretz Yisrael and answers it so well that they bring him back. Four Sages report four different questions: whether one signed witness and one speaking witness combine, whether two courts combine, whether judges from two courts combine, whether a court verifying a document must note that one of its three judges has died. Each version opens with the same self-deprecation and lands on the same answer: combine them.
bava-batra/165.question: If no one could agree on what was actually asked, what exactly did the Sages hear in the answer that made them open the study hall to him again?

judge.reachNote: What restores a scholar's standing: the content of a ruling, or the bearing in which he offers it.

answer.quote: And it was because of this fitting answer, to whichever version of the dilemma that is adopted, that the Sages brought Rabbi Yirmeya
answer.explanation: The page names the cause of his readmission — the fitting answer, whatever the version — but does not say what in the answer the Sages found fitting, so the question can still honestly be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Each of the four versions lands on the same answer: combine them.
summaryProblems.pageSays: That they are required to write: We were sitting in a group of three judges, and one of the judges is no longer alive.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Each of the four versions lands on the same answer: combine them.", but the page says "That they are required to write: We were sitting in a group of three judges, and one of the judges is no longer alive.". Say what the page says. Fix the claim that all four versions end in "combine them" — Ravina's version ends with the ruling that the court must write that one of the three judges has died. The question is also close to being answered by the line "because of this fitting answer, to whichever version of the dilemma that is adopted"; sharpen it so it presses on what the page leaves unsaid, such as why an answer's worth could be independent of which question it answered.

bava-batra/166.summary: A document reading "gold, in dinars," with no number, is read for the smallest plausible sum, because the holder of the document is at a disadvantage. That dinarei means golden dinars and dinarin silver ones is proved from an incident: pairs of birds for offerings by women after childbirth cost a fortune, so Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel swore not to lie down until the price dropped, then taught a lighter rule. Whether a fly could have eaten a stroke of ink, turning kuf into samekh, is left standing.
bava-batra/166.question: Did Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel teach that the extra offerings were not required because that was the law, or because he had already sworn the price would fall by nightfall?

judge.reachNote: Whether a halakhic ruling can be driven by market pressure and a prior vow rather than by independent legal reasoning.

bava-batra/167.summary: Abaye tells a man corroborating his signature to write it at the top of a sheet, since anything blank below invites someone to fill in a debt above it. Two forged bills of sale reach him, and he catches both by spacing: a vav, a narrow Hebrew letter, with too much room around it, then a vav squeezed in. A third forger copied Rav Aḥa bar Adda's shaky hand by steadying himself on a wobbly footbridge rope.
bava-batra/167.question: Abaye noticed the odd spacing, but the forgery was only established by a confession he extracted by binding the man, so what was the document worth as evidence on its own?

judge.reachNote: Whether physical irregularity in a document is itself proof of forgery, or only grounds for suspicion that must be converted into an admission.

bava-batra/168.summary: A gang of Arabs came to Pumbedita, seized people's land, and forced the owners to hand over the deeds. Landowners who had not yet been robbed asked Abaye for duplicate deeds, and he refused, since two deeds for one field could let a buyer collect compensation twice. Badgered until he wanted to be rid of them, he told his scribe to produce a document written over an erasure, which makes it worthless.
bava-batra/168.question: Is a deed that a frightened landowner thinks will protect him, but which the judge has quietly made void, better than being told no?

judge.reachNote: Whether a judge may satisfy a petitioner with a deliberately worthless document rather than hold to a refusal he has already explained.

answer.quote: The landowners kept badgering Abaye to write the duplicate documents, until, in order to be rid of them, he said to his scribe
answer.explanation: The page gives Abaye's motive for producing the void deed rather than simply refusing again, which bears on the question but never says whether the useless deed is preferable to a plain no.

bava-batra/169.summary: A buyer who has lost his bill of sale can have the court write him a replacement, but without the guarantee clause, the seller's promise to reimburse him if the land is later taken from him. Rav Safra explains the fear: holding two deeds, a buyer could collect that reimbursement twice, seizing fields from people who bought from the same seller afterward. The proposed fix, a receipt kept by the seller, fails because the victims never think to ask him.
bava-batra/169.question: When an agent buys land for a woman without a guarantee and Rav Naḥman orders him to buy it himself and then sell it to her with his own guarantee, is that repairing his mistake or punishing it?
gate: the question brings in "Naḥman", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether an agent who overstepped is made whole-maker or wrongdoer: does 'I sent you for my benefit, not my detriment' undo the deal or transfer the loss onto him?

answer.quote: Nevertheless, you agreed to purchase the land without a guarantee. Therefore, go yourself and purchase the land from him without a guarantee, and then sell it to this woman
answer.explanation: The page gives Rav Naḥman's stated reasoning, that the agency is void because it was to her detriment while the agent is held to the terms he personally consented to, which bears on the question without deciding whether the ruling is restorative or penal.

bava-batra/170.summary: A buyer holds a bill of sale for land but cannot show he lived there three years uncontested, and Abaye and Rav Dimi trade explanations of which proof the baraita means. The argument ends up at a different question: must a litigant back up a claim he did not need to make? Rabbi Abba, sued for a debt, says he repaid in front of two named men, and the judge tells him to bring them.
bava-batra/170.question: If a debtor who says nothing is believed when he claims he repaid, why should naming the two men who watched him pay leave him worse off?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a litigant is bound by a claim he never needed to make, but the page resolves exactly that exchange.

answer.quote: I, too, am saying only that you are required to verify your claim if you can; if you cannot, you will not be required to pay.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa's closing line states directly that naming the witnesses does not leave the debtor worse off — he must try to bring them, but loses nothing if he cannot.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 170b: "I, too, am saying only that you are required to verify your claim if you can; if you cannot, you will not be required to pay.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the page's last lines, where Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa concedes that the debtor need only verify if he can and pays nothing if he cannot. Ask instead about what stays unsettled after that concession — for instance, why a volunteered, unnecessary claim should trigger any duty of verification at all, or why the Gemara must reverse the names in one of the two baraitot to keep Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel consistent.

bava-batra/171.summary: A creditor has lost his promissory note and still wants his money; the debtor answers that he will pay only when the note is produced and torn. Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef offers to write a receipt instead, and Rabbi Abba objects that Rav and Shmuel forbid receipts. Abaye then points out the risk runs both ways: a lost receipt lets a creditor collect twice, and Rava's reply is a verse, not an argument.
bava-batra/171.question: If both a lost note and a lost receipt can cheat someone, why does Rava settle the matter with a line from Proverbs rather than a reason?
gate: the question brings in "Proverbs", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When two parties both stand to be cheated, is the risk allocated by reasoning or by their unequal standing before the law?

answer.quote: Rava said to Abaye: Yes, it is preferable, because, as it is written: "The borrower is a servant to the lender" (Proverbs 22:7).
answer.explanation: The page gives Rava's reply and glosses it as a substantive principle — "The debtor's interests are subordinated to those of the creditor" — which bears on the question without explaining why a verse rather than an argument settles the symmetry Abaye raised.

bava-batra/172.summary: A promissory note reaches Rav Huna's court saying only that so-and-so borrowed a hundred dinars, silver coins, "from you," with no creditor named. Rav Huna says the phrase fixes nothing: it could mean the Exilarch, head of Babylonian Jewry, or King Shapur. Rabba answers from the mishna about two men in one city both called Yosef ben Shimon, arguing that since each may sue outsiders, no one worries a note fell and was found by another.
bava-batra/172.question: If Rabba's proof rests on how unlikely it is that one Yosef ben Shimon's note fell into the other's hands, why should holding a document prove whose debt it is in the first place?

judge.reachNote: Whether physical possession of a written obligation can establish who the obligation runs to, when the document itself names no one.

answer.quote: Here too, the term: From you, in a promissory note indicates that man from whose possession it emerges.
answer.explanation: Rabba's own answer to why possession identifies the creditor is the analogy to Abba Shaul's "I divorced her today," read together with his statement that "We are not concerned for the possibility of a promissory note falling from its rightful owner," though the deeper question of possession as proof is not fully settled.

bava-batra/173.summary: The mishna says a creditor who lent money on the strength of a guarantor cannot collect from that guarantor. Rabba and Rav Yosef explain that the guarantor can say he was handed a man and has handed that man back, and Rav Naḥman snaps that such reasoning belongs to Persian judges who rule by whim. Rav Ashi later grounds the guarantor's obligation in something softer: the satisfaction he feels at being trusted enough for the loan to happen.
bava-batra/173.question: If what binds a guarantor is the pleasure of being trusted, what binds the one who took no pleasure in it?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether obligation rests on a subjective inner benefit or on something else, probing the asmakhta problem Rav Ashi's answer leaves behind.

bava-batra/174.summary: Moshe bar Atzari guaranteed his daughter-in-law's marriage contract, the money owed her if her husband divorces her or dies, and his son, the husband, was broke. Abaye suggests advising the son to divorce her outside of court, let her collect the sum from his father, then remarry her. The objection lands fast: Abaye himself calls that sort of legally sound advice wicked, and the answer offered is that fathers and Torah scholars are different.
bava-batra/174.question: If pushing a father to pay out for his own son is not wickedness, what exactly made the same clever advice wicked when someone else gave it?

judge.reachNote: When does technically permissible advice become wickedness — does it turn on who bears the loss, or on who benefits?

answer.quote: the first recipient can sell the property, which would thereby deprive the second recipient from receiving it
answer.explanation: The page indicates the harm in the wicked case (a third party is deprived) and distinguishes the son/Torah scholar case, but it never states in so many words what makes advice wicked, so the question can still be pressed.

bava-batra/175.summary: A creditor is strangling a debtor in the marketplace when a bystander says to leave him alone and he will cover the debt; Ben Nannas rules that bystander owes nothing, since the money was never lent on his word. Rabbi Yishmael, who had held such a late guarantor pays from his unsold property, concedes and sends students to learn monetary law from him. The Gemara then splits over whether a borrower's land is pledged to his creditor by Torah law at all.
bava-batra/175.question: If the man in the marketplace only got loose because someone promised to pay, why does that promise cost the rescuer nothing?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that a guarantee binds only where the lender parted with money in reliance on it, but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: the person who intervened is exempt from paying, as the creditor did not loan the money in the first place based on his trust of the one who intervened
answer.explanation: Ben Nannas himself gives the reason the note's question asks for: the obligation tracks the creditor's reliance at the moment of the loan, not the later rescue.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bava Batra 175b (Mishna): "the person who intervened is exempt from paying, as the creditor did not loan the money in the first place based on his trust of the one who intervened". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same lines the summary paraphrases: Ben Nannas says the rescuer is exempt because the creditor did not lend based on his trust. Rewrite so the question starts from that reason and presses on what it costs, for instance why reliance at the moment of lending should matter more than the benefit the debtor actually received, or how that squares with Rabbi Yishmael's view that a guarantor signing after the note still pays from unsold property. Aim the question at the principle the dispute turns on rather than at the outcome the mishna already explains.

bava-batra/176.summary: A note in the debtor's own handwriting, with no witnesses signed on it, lets the creditor collect only from property the debtor still holds, not from land already sold off. A guarantor's liability then hangs on a single word: "So-and-so is a guarantor" may stand apart from the witnesses' signatures, while "And so-and-so is a guarantor" is bound into the document. A guarantee given while a creditor is strangling the debtor still binds, Rabbi Yishmael holds.
bava-batra/176.question: Why should one letter of conjunction decide whether witnesses vouched for a guarantee, while a promise squeezed out of a bystander to stop a strangling needs no such scrutiny?

judge.reachNote: What makes an obligation binding — formal integration into a witnessed text, or the real commitment of the person at the moment he speaks?

answer.quote: If the debtor was being strangled, and in addition an act of acquisition was performed with the guarantor, the guarantor becomes obligated
answer.explanation: The page bears on the question by showing that the strangling-scene guarantee is not simply taken on trust — it is tied to an act of acquisition (and the closing halakha limits when no act is needed) — and it separately explains the conjunction rule as making the clause "an integral part of the document, so that the signatures of the witnesses relate to it as well," but it never confronts the asymmetry the question raises.

sanhedrin/2.summary: Sanhedrin opens by tallying how many judges each case needs: three for the half damages when an ox gores, twenty-three for capital cases, seventy-one to declare an optional war. Twenty-three is assembled from verses: ten judges arguing to convict, ten arguing to acquit, two more because conviction needs a majority of two, and one so the court is never even. The Gemara then asks why robbery and injury are listed apart from monetary law, and answers that only those need ordained experts.
sanhedrin/2.question: Does a lion that killed a person deserve the same twenty-three judges as a human defendant, or is killing it on the spot itself the mitzva?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).
the question uses "mitzva", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether a killer animal is a defendant owed process or a danger to be removed on sight.

answer.quote: Rabbi Eliezer says these dangerous animals do not need to be brought to court; rather, anyone who kills them first merits the performance of a mitzva.
answer.explanation: The mishna itself states both alternatives the question offers — twenty-three judges (Rabbi Akiva and the anonymous ruling) versus Rabbi Eliezer's ruling that killing them is itself a mitzva — so the question only restates a dispute already spelled out on the page.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sanhedrin 2a: "Rabbi Eliezer says these dangerous animals do not need to be brought to court; rather, anyone who kills them first merits the performance of a mitzva.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question just repeats the mishna's own dispute, which the page states in full (Rabbi Eliezer versus Rabbi Akiva), so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to probe something the page leaves unsaid — for example, why the beast that gored is tried like a person when the verse only compares the manner of death, or why the mishna needs a court at all for an animal that cannot be warned or deterred. Alternatively, ask about the derivation of twenty-three, where the two-vote margin for conviction sits oddly with the added judge that breaks ties.

sanhedrin/3.summary: Strictly, the Torah's "one manner of law" should require the same rigorous questioning of witnesses in loan cases as in capital cases, but the Sages waived it, and waived the need for expert judges too, so lenders would not stop lending. The Gemara pushes: then untrained judges who rule wrongly should also be exempt from paying compensation. No, it answers, that would frighten lenders even more, so the same worry cuts both ways. Rav A	tha adds that one judge suffices by Torah law.
sanhedrin/3.question: If three ordinary judges are trusted because one of them is probably learned, why must they pay for a mistake that expert judges would be forgiven?

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is that liability for error is what keeps a court authorized by leniency from becoming careless — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: If the judges will be exempt from paying compensation in the event that they err in their judgment, this lack of accountability will lead all the more so to having many of those who sit idly on street corners assume the role of judges.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection about the three-layman court and answers that exempting them would flood the courts with unlearned idlers (and earlier, in the parallel case, that it would lock the door before borrowers even more).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sanhedrin 3a: "If the judges will be exempt from paying compensation in the event that they err in their judgment, this lack of accountability will lead all the more so to having many of those who sit idly on street corners assume the role of judges.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is asked and answered verbatim on the page: exempting lay judges from liability would invite idlers to sit as judges (and would deter lenders all the more). Write a question that starts after that answer — for example, why accountability for error is the price of an authorization the Sages themselves granted, or why the same "locking the door" worry is used both to relax the rules and to tighten them. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate, but fix the garbled name "Rav A	tha."

sanhedrin/4.summary: A verse about the court that "shall condemn" is pronounced as a plural but written so it could be read as singular, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi counts five judges from it while the Rabbis count three. The Gemara widens this into one question: are the Torah's vowels authoritative, or the bare consonants? It lines up five sages on the vowels' side, then tries to dissolve every dispute, until a baraita on the four compartments of the head phylacteries pries it open again.
sanhedrin/4.question: If the ban on cooking a kid in its mother's milk rather than her fat finally rests on the plain fact that cooking is done in liquid, what work was the vocalization rule doing there at all?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether a hermeneutic principle retains any force once a plain, common-sense reading of the verse can do the same work.

answer.quote: Rather, Rav Aḥa, son of Rav Ika, said: The reason all agree that there is a prohibition to cook a young goat in its mother's milk and not in its mother's fat
answer.explanation: The page supplies the replacement reason (cooking is done in liquid) and shows why the vocalization answer was abandoned — "even when there is no difference in the way the words are written, some say that the tradition... is authoritative" — but it never says what the vocalization answer was still accomplishing once the simpler reason is available.

sanhedrin/5.summary: A judge who rules wrongly pays restitution to the side he cost, unless the litigants accepted him or he holds permission from the Exilarch, the Jewish ruler in Babylonia. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi licenses Rav to teach and to judge monetary cases, but refuses him the right to declare a blemished firstborn animal fit to eat, even though Rav apprenticed to a shepherd to learn blemishes. One explanation offered: he knew too much, and others would copy him badly.
sanhedrin/5.question: If the sharpest expert is barred from ruling because ordinary people will misapply what he permits, what expertise is left safe to use?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that public authority may be limited not by a sage's ignorance but by the gap between his knowledge and the people's, so that mastery itself becomes a hazard.

sanhedrin/6.summary: A judge who rules alone and gets it wrong still binds the litigants, and pays them out of his own pocket. From there the page turns to mediation, talking two sides into a settlement instead of ruling: one view calls the mediator a sinner and has Moses saying that judgment should pierce the mountain, another calls mediation a mitzva, a commandment, the only judgment with peace inside it. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya splits it by timing: offer compromise before you see who will win, never after.
sanhedrin/6.question: If mediation is a mitzva, why does it become forbidden the moment the judge can tell who is in the right?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the clash between truth-at-all-costs judgment and peace: once the judge knows the truth, withholding it to buy peace may itself be a betrayal of judgment.

answer.quote: Before the resolution of the contention is revealed, you can cast it off. Once the resolution of the contention is revealed, you cannot cast it off.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya grounds the timing rule in Proverbs 17:14, but this restates the cutoff rather than explaining why a mitzva of mediation lapses once the outcome is clear, and the page closes still asking what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa's 'mitzva' means.

sanhedrin/7.summary: Aaron watches Hur killed for opposing the Golden Calf and decides that a calf the people can repent for beats a second murder in the sanctuary; still, Rabbi Tanhum bar Hanilai holds that praising Aaron for this compromise provokes God. The page then turns to judges afraid of their own verdicts: a sword between the thighs, Gehenna underneath. Rav Huna would summon ten rabbis from Rav's study hall so each carried only a splinter of the beam.
sanhedrin/7.question: If a mistaken verdict hangs a prisoner's collar around every neck in the room, does calling in ten more judges thin the blame or simply spread it to more people?

judge.reachNote: Whether moral responsibility for a verdict is divisible like a beam into splinters, or whether it attaches whole to each person who sits in the room.

answer.quote: I do this so that only a small part of the responsibility, comparable to a splinter from a beam, will reach each of us
answer.explanation: Rav Huna states his own rationale — that added judges reduce each one's share of responsibility — but the page never resolves the tension with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's collar hanging around all ten necks, so the question can still be asked honestly.

sanhedrin/8.summary: A man accuses his bride of having committed adultery while betrothed, twenty-three judges convene for a capital case, and then no witnesses turn up. He asks that same court to hear the money claim instead: cut the sum in her marriage contract down to the rate for a non-virgin. Rabbi Meir says three judges are enough now; the Rabbis keep all twenty-three, and Rava explains that as concern for the honor of the judges already seated.
sanhedrin/8.question: Once the case has shrunk to a quarrel about money, whose interest keeps twenty-three judges in the room, hers or theirs?

judge.reachNote: Whose dignity a court procedure protects — the litigant's or the institution's — is a real idea, but the page names the answer outright.

answer.quote: the court of twenty-three judges must be reconvened, out of concern for their honor, since they had already begun to hear the case
answer.explanation: Rava states plainly that the twenty-three remain for the sake of the seated judges' honor, not the woman's interest, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Sanhedrin 8a (Rava's explanation): "the court of twenty-three judges must be reconvened, out of concern for their honor, since they had already begun to hear the case". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks whose interest keeps the twenty-three judges seated, and the page answers it in the same sentence the summary already paraphrases: the honor of the first judges. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard — for instance, how a court's own honor can outweigh the rule that a money claim needs only three, or why Rabbi Meir sees no affront at all in disbanding them. Alternatively, build the question off the later attempts (Abaye, Rav Pappa) to explain the same dispute without invoking judges' honor.

sanhedrin/9.summary: If one member of a group of witnesses turns out to be a close relative or otherwise disqualified, the whole testimony collapses, even in a group of a hundred. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi limits that: a relative who keeps quiet and does not warn the offender never joined the group, so two brothers and a stranger who watched a killing still yield a valid pair. Rava then splits one man's words: he is believed about the man who assaulted him, not about himself.
