answer.quote: Shmuel teaches us that although the intent of the plaintiff is for them to testify, the witnesses are liable only if he tells them so explicitly.
answer.explanation: The page states flatly that known intent is insufficient and explicit speech is required, but it never explains what the spoken demand contributes, so the question survives.

shevuot/33.summary: Ravina rescues an earlier case with two witnesses married to two sisters, which makes them unfit to testify together; the sisters are dying, but not yet dead. The same "not yet" drives the dilemma here: a fine, a penalty fixed by the Torah, vanishes if the defendant admits to it, so do witnesses who falsely swear they know nothing about one deny anything worth money? Every proof from the mishna gets rerouted to the non-fine part: the stolen principal, a daughter's humiliation, pebbles.
shevuot/33.question: If each fine in the mishna can be reread as something else, is the dilemma about swearing away knowledge of a fine being answered or just kept out of reach?

judge.reachNote: Whether a liability that would evaporate on the defendant's admission counts as 'money' now, and whether the Gemara settles that or only clears the texts out of its way.

answer.quote: In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita? It is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
answer.explanation: The page's last attempted proof (the slander baraita) is likewise deflected — by attributing it to Rabbi Elazar, for whom the dilemma does not arise — so the page shows the dilemma repeatedly sidestepped rather than resolved.

shevuot/34.summary: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili reads a verse about a witness who saw or who knew as meaning testimony built on sight alone or knowledge alone, which he says happens only in monetary cases. That pulls in Rabbi Aḥa, who blames a rampaging camel for the dead camel found beside it, and Shimon ben Shataḥ, who chased a man into a ruin and found him holding a dripping sword over a convulsing body. Without two witnesses he could not execute; a snake bit the man instead.
shevuot/34.question: If a rampaging camel's owner pays on circumstantial evidence alone, why does the man holding the dripping sword walk out of court and die only by snakebite?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that the threshold of proof differs between money and life, but the page already states that reason and even names Rabbi Aḥa as the dissent.

shevuot/35.summary: A plaintiff who swears witnesses in the name of heaven and in the name of earth binds no one, but swearing them by the Gracious One or the Compassionate One makes them liable. Abaye reads those adjectives as standing for God, since nothing else gets called gracious, while heaven and earth are real things in their own right. The page then sorts which written names may be erased, and which of Abraham's uses of "my lords" addressed God rather than three visitors.
shevuot/35.question: If "gracious" and "compassionate" are adjectives that can be scraped off a page like any ordinary word, why does an oath sworn in their name hold?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between a word's written sanctity and its power to bind an oath, but the page resolves it explicitly.

answer.quote: Although gracious and compassionate are not names of God, the reference in the mishna is to an oath in the name of God.
answer.explanation: Abaye's resolution, which the note's own summary paraphrases, explains that the mishna means an oath by "He Who is Gracious," i.e. God, so the erasable adjective is not itself the name sworn by.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 35b: "Although gracious and compassionate are not names of God, the reference in the mishna is to an oath in the name of God.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what Abaye already answers, and the summary itself reports that answer, so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to press on what remains hard after Abaye, for instance Rava's challenge about heaven and earth and why the existence of independent entities called heaven and earth should decide whether the swearer meant God. Alternatively build the question from the erasure rules or the sota verbal analogy dispute between Rabbi Ḥanina bar Idi and the Rabbis.

shevuot/36.summary: The page hunts for words that bind a person like an oath without the word oath ever being said, among them arur, amen, and a plain no. Rabbi Elazar derives that no can be an oath from God's promise that the flood waters shall never return, and Rava adds that it binds only when said twice. Then Rav Yehuda tells Rav Kahana, reciting the mishna's curse, to shift it into the third person so it does not sound aimed at his teacher.
shevuot/36.question: If a single no is only speech and a doubled no is an oath, what does the second no add that the first one lacked?

judge.reachNote: What turns ordinary speech into binding speech — whether repetition supplies deliberateness, or merely mirrors the verse's own doubling.

answer.quote: as it is written: “All flesh shall not be excised any more by floodwaters” (Genesis 9:11), and it is again written: “And the waters shall no more become a flood”
answer.explanation: The page grounds the doubling requirement in the two repeated flood verses, but it gives only the scriptural source, never saying what force the second utterance adds, so the question still stands honestly.

shevuot/37.summary: Rav Kahana asks what happens when a man swears falsely that he never received a deposit and witnesses forewarned him first: lashes, a guilt-offering, or both. Rabba then argues that if witnesses can prove the debt anyway, the false oath is merely words that change nothing, so no offering is owed, and the Gemara hunts proofs against him until the refutation is called conclusive. Rabbi Yohanan splits it differently: witnesses can die, but a promissory note stays put.
shevuot/37.question: If witnesses stand ready to expose the lie, so that swearing it changes nothing about who pays whom, is it still a false oath?

judge.reachNote: Does a denial count as a false oath when it could never have changed the outcome — the page asks this and settles it against Rabba.

answer.quote: One who denies a monetary claim to which there are witnesses is liable to bring a guilt-offering for a false oath on a deposit.
answer.explanation: The page poses exactly this question through Rabba, declares his position conclusively refuted, and then states Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling that denial before witnesses is still liable.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Yohanan's distinction rests on the fact that witnesses can die while a promissory note stays put.
summaryProblems.pageSays: This cannot be the reasoning of Rabbi Yoḥanan, as it also occurs that a promissory note becomes lost.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 37b: "One who denies a monetary claim to which there are witnesses is liable to bring a guilt-offering for a false oath on a deposit.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rabbi Yohanan's distinction rests on the fact that witnesses can die while a promissory note stays put.", but the page says "This cannot be the reasoning of Rabbi Yoḥanan, as it also occurs that a promissory note becomes lost.". Say what the page says. The question is the very question the page raises and settles: Rabba holds the denial ineffective, the Gemara calls his refutation conclusive, and Rabbi Yoḥanan rules one who denies before witnesses is liable. Ask instead about what remains hard after that ruling — e.g. why a promissory note is treated as a lien on land and so escapes liability while live witnesses do not. Also fix the attribution: the 'witnesses die, notes stay put' reason is Rav Pappa's and Rav Huna rejects it, substituting the lien-on-land reason.

shevuot/38.summary: Five people sue one man over deposits, and he denies all of their claims in a single breath. Whether he owes one guilt-offering or five turns on one small word: whether he said "nothing of yours, and nothing of yours," or left the "and" out. Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan read Rabbi Meir in opposite directions, and to keep Shmuel's reading alive the Gemara strikes the conjunction out of the mishna's own wording three separate times.
shevuot/38.question: If Shmuel's reading survives only by editing the word "and" out of the mishna again and again, when does the text get to stand as it was taught?
gate: gloss "guilt-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: How far an amora may rewrite the received text to save his reading before the attribution itself must give way.

answer.quote: According to Shmuel, the mishna is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself objects that the tanna cannot err so repeatedly, and resolves it by dropping the emendations and reassigning the mishna to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who holds both phrasings specific.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 38a: "According to Shmuel, the mishna is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Meir.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already raises this exact protest — "could it be that this tanna errs so much as he teaches the mishna?" — and answers it by declaring the mishna not Rabbi Meir's but Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's. Write a question that starts after that move rather than one the Gemara voices itself: for example, why reattributing the whole mishna is a cheaper price than conceding Rabbi Yoḥanan's reading, or why the Gemara returns to emending Rabbi Meir's own statement even after saying the mishna is not his. Keep the summary's sharp focus on the single conjunction.

shevuot/39.summary: Before administering an oath, the judges warn the defendant that a false oath is never cleared, and that punishment reaches his family and the whole world, even righteous people who had no chance to protest. The Gemara asks why this commandment alone made the world tremble, when other sins carry excision or execution. The oath is imposed according to the court's understanding because of the man in Rava's court who hid coins in a hollow reed, handed it over, swore he had paid, and took the reed back.
shevuot/39.question: If a false oath brings even a light punishment on righteous people who never heard it and could not have stopped it, what exactly is being punished?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of collective or cosmic liability: whether the punishment tracks guilt at all, or whether a false oath is a corrosion the world absorbs regardless of fault.

answer.quote: the righteous people both here, in his family, and here, in the rest of the world, are punished with a light punishment, even though they did not behave inappropriately
answer.explanation: The page states flatly that the righteous who could not protest receive a light punishment, and distinguishes this from the guarantor-liability of those who could have protested, but it never explains what in them is being punished, so the question remains askable.

shevuot/40.summary: Much of the argument turns on whether a claim for a gold dinar means that coin itself or anything worth that much, and on whether admitting to barley answers a claim of wheat and barley. At the end Rav Naḥman says a defendant who denies the whole debt still takes an oath of inducement, a rabbinic oath, since people rarely sue without cause. The objection: people rarely lie to a creditor's face.
shevuot/40.question: If denying a loan outright is read as stalling for time rather than lying, leaving the denier fit to testify, why does the identical denial about a deposit disqualify him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a false denial is judged by the intent it reveals, not by its falsity alone — but the page states that distinction outright.

answer.quote: A debtor who denies the debt may be avoiding payment until he has enough money, whereas a bailee who denies having been given a deposit clearly intends to steal the item.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly distinguishes the two denials: the debtor is presumed to be delaying payment, while the bailee is presumed to be stealing, which is why only the latter is disqualified.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 40b: "A debtor who denies the debt may be avoiding payment until he has enough money, whereas a bailee who denies having been given a deposit clearly intends to steal the item.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 40b, which says the debtor may be avoiding payment until he has money while the bailee clearly intends to steal. Rewrite the question to start from that distinction rather than ask for it — for instance, press on why a presumption about a debtor's motive should decide his fitness as a witness, or how this sits with the oath of inducement being imposed on that same stalling debtor. The summary is sound and can stay.

shevuot/41.summary: Rav Asi and Shmuel argue over whether money lent in front of witnesses must be repaid in front of witnesses, and the page fills with cases testing it. One creditor had demanded repayment before two men who had studied law, then claimed the cash he took was only a deposit; Rav Nahman answered that he and Rav Sheshet had studied plenty, so hand it over now. Rava rules that denying the loan entirely counts as denying repayment.
shevuot/41.question: If the debtor who names two witnesses who deny everything is excused as merely forgetful, why is the debtor who says he never borrowed given no room to be mistaken?

judge.reachNote: When is a litigant's false statement treated as a lie that fixes liability, and when as an ordinary lapse of memory that costs him nothing?

answer.quote: Since there is testimony that he borrowed the money, and he admits that he did not repay it, he is liable to repay the debt.
answer.explanation: The page gives Rava's reason for holding the loan-denier liable — his own words concede non-payment — but it never sets that reason against the forgetfulness allowance of the next case, so the contrast the question raises still stands.

shevuot/42.summary: A borrower tells his lender that he will believe him over himself if the lender ever claims the debt is unpaid, then repays in front of witnesses and hears the lender deny it. Abaye and Rava say the lender still collects; Rav Pappa asks whether trusting a man over yourself means trusting him over witnesses. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, answers that counting heads matters for appraising value, never for testimony.
shevuot/42.question: If numbers carry no weight in testimony, why does the second version of the story let a man who trusted his lender like three witnesses go free once four watched him pay?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — when a count of people is testimony (where two equal a hundred) and when it is mere weight of opinion — but the page supplies exactly that distinction.

answer.quote: by mentioning a larger number than what is necessary for testimony, the realm of opinions, in which three people carry greater weight than two
answer.where: Shevuot 42a (second version of the incident, Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua)
answer.explanation: The page itself states that by naming three — more than testimony requires — the debtor shifted the stipulation from the realm of testimony into the realm of assessed opinions, where four outweigh three.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 42a (second version of the incident, Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua): "by mentioning a larger number than what is necessary for testimony, the realm of opinions, in which three people carry greater weight than two". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same page: naming three witnesses, more than testimony requires, moves the stipulation into the realm of opinions where numbers do count. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for example, press on why a debtor's careless choice of a number should change the legal category of what he agreed to, or what it means that the same men can be witnesses for one purpose and assessors for another. Keep the summary, but make clear that Rav Huna's 'two are like a hundred' rule is what the second version then qualifies.

shevuot/43.summary: A man claims he handed over a house full of produce; the other says he has no idea how much came in. Rava holds there is no oath unless both the claim and the partial admission are counted by size, weight, or number, so a claimed large candelabrum answered by a small one is two different objects, not a partial admission. Ten litra of weight against five is different, Rabbi Abba bar Memel says, because the heavier one can be scraped down.
shevuot/43.question: If a large candelabrum and a small one are simply two different objects, why does the fact that a ten-litra candelabrum could be scraped down to five make them one?

judge.reachNote: When is an admission a 'part' of a claim rather than a different object — quantity within one substance versus two distinct things.

answer.quote: one can scrape a ten-litra candelabrum and reduce it to a five-litra one. Therefore, he admitted to a part of the claim
answer.explanation: The page gives Rabbi Abba bar Memel's reason — reducibility means the smaller weight is contained in the larger, so the admission is to part of the very claim — though it does not spell out why physical reducibility should establish identity, so the question can still be pressed.

shevuot/44.summary: A creditor takes an object as security for a loan and then loses it, and the argument is whether he can still collect the whole debt. Rav Yosef holds that anyone guarding a found object counts as a paid guardian, liable for loss, because while busy with that mitzva, a commandment, he is excused from others that would cost him money. Rabbi Eliezer counters that a creditor who uses the collateral is guarding it for himself, not performing a commandment at all.
shevuot/44.question: If the creditor's wages are only the commandments he was spared from paying for, what is he paid when no such expense ever comes up?

judge.reachNote: It probes whether the 'wage' of the perutah-of-Rav-Yosef is an actual saving or a notional status that attaches regardless of circumstance.

shevuot/45.summary: A customer tells a storekeeper to hand his laborers a sela in small coins; the storekeeper says he paid them, the laborers say they got nothing, and the mishna has both sides swear and collect from the customer. Ben Nannas objects that one of them is certainly lying, so neither oath should be taken. The Gemara then asks why a hired worker swears and collects at all, and settles on an employer too distracted by his workers to remember paying.
shevuot/45.question: If the whole reason for the worker's oath is that the employer probably forgot, whose doubt is that oath actually settling?

judge.reachNote: Whose uncertainty an oath is designed to resolve — the court's, the claimant's, or the payer's peace of mind — which the page addresses explicitly.

answer.quote: The oath was instituted to alleviate the concerns of the employer, to ensure him that he is not being cheated.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection — if the employer is presumed to have forgotten, let him simply pay without an oath — and answers that the oath exists to settle the employer's worry that he is being cheated.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 45a: "The oath was instituted to alleviate the concerns of the employer, to ensure him that he is not being cheated.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 45a, where the Gemara asks the same thing and replies that the oath was instituted to alleviate the employer's concern that he is not being cheated. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and probe what remains hard — for example why a worker's oath reassures an employer who is presumed forgetful, or why witnesses at payment or prepayment were rejected as alternatives. Alternatively build the question off the Rav/Shmuel miggo limitation or Rava's challenge about the bailees' oath.

shevuot/46.summary: A craftsman says the agreed fee was two coins; the man who hired him says one. Shmuel rules that the employer swears and the craftsman loses the difference, since the worker's oath was set up for employers too distracted to recall whether they paid, and nobody forgets a price he set. An older teaching about a cloak left for mending complicates this, letting the craftsman swear and collect so long as the claim is fresh.
shevuot/46.question: If an employer is trusted to remember exactly what wage he fixed, why is he presumed to forget whether he handed the money over?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of why the law assigns different presumptions of memory to two moments in the same transaction — but the page states that reason outright.

answer.quote: With regard to the fixing of wages, people certainly remember. The Sages instituted the oath taken by the worker where he claims he has not been paid in a situation where it is reasonable to presume that the employer is distracted and apt to forget.
answer.explanation: Shmuel's ruling itself states the very distinction the question asks about: wage-setting is memorable, while the moment of payment is one in which the employer is presumed distracted.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 46a: "With regard to the fixing of wages, people certainly remember. The Sages instituted the oath taken by the worker where he claims he has not been paid in a situation where it is reasonable to presume that the employer is distracted and apt to forget.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question just restates the page's own reasoning as a puzzle: Shmuel explicitly says people remember the fixing of wages while the employer is 'distracted and apt to forget' about paying. Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for example, why Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis differ over whether a rabbinically mandated oath can itself be transferred to the worker, or why possession of the cloak flips the burden of proof. Keep the summary, which is faithful.

shevuot/47.summary: A man snatches a piece of cast metal and admits it, claiming the metal was his own; one witness saw the grab, but a court does not force payment on a single witness, and a self-declared snatcher is not permitted to swear. Rabbi Ami lists the three rulings and rejects all of them. Underneath sits an older dispute: when nobody can take the oath, Babylonian sages say it returned to Sinai and the court acts no further, while Rabbi Abba makes the defendant pay.
shevuot/47.question: If the man cannot swear precisely because his own admission makes him look like a robber, why should that admission leave him owing nothing on the Babylonian view?

judge.reachNote: Whether being disqualified from an oath is itself a ground for liability, or whether a court that cannot administer an oath simply has nothing left to do.

answer.quote: The litigant who is robbing the other will be punished by God, not the court.
answer.explanation: The page gives the Babylonian rationale — the wrongdoer is left to divine punishment rather than court-enforced payment — but never confronts why the defendant's own admission fails to generate liability, so the question can still be pressed.

shevuot/48.summary: A lender dies holding a promissory note, and his children come to collect from the dead borrower's children. Rav and Shmuel say they cannot: the father himself owed an oath to those orphans, and an oath cannot be passed down. Rabbi Elazar says the heirs swear they know of nothing paid and collect. The Sages mailed the question to Eretz Yisrael twice and got impatience back. Rav Ḥama finally rules that a judge who decides either way has decided, and it stands.
shevuot/48.question: If the law was settled neither way, what is a family meant to do with a note the court will neither collect on nor tear up?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of a right that survives in law but is unenforceable in court when the halakha is deliberately left unresolved.

answer.quote: A judge who rules in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Elazar has ruled, and his ruling cannot be voided.
answer.explanation: The page's closing story shows the practical route left open to such a family — a ruling by a judge who follows Rabbi Elazar stands and cannot be overturned — though it does not say what the family does in a court that follows Rav Pappa's practice of neither collecting nor tearing.

shevuot/49.summary: The final daf of Shevuot sorts four bailees, unpaid, borrower, paid, and renter, and asks which of their lies about a missing ox matter. A bailee who swears the ox died when it was really stolen brings no guilt-offering, because the lie changed nothing: he owed the same either way. Liability tracks money saved, not falsehood, which is why the flat answer "I do not know" can be the costliest thing a borrower says.
shevuot/49.question: Why should a borrower who swears the ox died when it was stolen walk away clean, while the one who swears he knows nothing owes an offering, when both spoke falsely under oath?

judge.reachNote: The idea is real — oath liability measures money saved rather than falsehood — but the page states it outright as its governing principle.

answer.quote: Anyone who takes an oath to be lenient with himself is liable; if he takes an oath to be stringent with himself, he is exempt.
answer.explanation: The mishna's closing principle, reinforced by the borrower rulings ("exempt... since the oath did not render him exempt from liability to pay" versus "liable... as he took an oath that would render him exempt from liability to pay"), states exactly why the false detail costs nothing and "I do not know" costs an offering.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Shevuot 49b: "Anyone who takes an oath to be lenient with himself is liable; if he takes an oath to be stringent with himself, he is exempt.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words, and the summary itself already repeats the answer ("liability tracks money saved, not falsehood"), so the question has nothing left to ask. Build the new question on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance Rav and Shmuel's dispute over whether these same exempt bailees still owe a sin-offering for an oath on an utterance, or Rabbi Ami's claim that a court-administered oath never carries that liability. Keep the summary's accurate framing but let the question push past the principle rather than restate it.

avodah-zarah/2.summary: The mishna bars business with gentiles for the three days before a gentile festival, on the theory that a good deal sends the gentile off to thank his idol. Rabbi Yehuda permits collecting a debt, since that causes distress; the Rabbis reply that relief from a debt is its own kind of joy. The Gemara then drifts into a courtroom at the end of days, where Rome claims its bathhouses and markets were built to free Jews for Torah.
avodah-zarah/2.question: When the nations argue that they too would have accepted the Torah had a mountain been held over their heads, why does the reply skip that claim entirely and turn to the seven Noahide mitzvot?
gate: the question brings in "Noahide", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "mitzvot", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether a claim about what one would have done under compulsion is answered by argument or by one's record with obligations freely accepted.

answer.quote: With regard to the seven Noahide mitzvot that preceded the giving of the Torah that even you accepted, where is the proof that you fulfilled them?
answer.explanation: The page gives God's reply and hints at its logic — the Noahide mitzvot were accepted uncoerced and still unfulfilled — but never states why the coercion claim itself goes unanswered.

avodah-zarah/3.summary: The nations of the world ask God for a second chance at the Torah, and He assigns them one cheap commandment, building a sukka, the temporary branch-roofed hut of the festival. Then He heats the summer sun over them until each one kicks his hut and walks out. The page objects that God was said not to deal tyrannically, and that a Jew suffering in a sukka may also leave; the answer offered is only that leaving is allowed, kicking is not.
avodah-zarah/3.question: If the heat was severe enough to excuse anyone from sitting there, is kicking the hut on the way out really the thing that condemns them?

judge.reachNote: Whether judgment falls on failure to perform a mitzva or on the contempt shown in how one abandons it.

answer.quote: Granted that one is exempt from performing the mitzva and is permitted to leave his sukka, but should one kick it?
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very difficulty of Rava's exemption and answers that the fault lies in the kicking rather than the leaving, but it does not explain why that gesture alone is decisive, which is what the note presses on.

avodah-zarah/4.summary: A rooster's crest turns white in the morning sun, and Abaye reads that as the sign of the daily moment when God is angry, a moment the Gemara measures at one part in 53,848 of an hour. Balaam, the page says, could find that instant and time his curses to land inside it. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi tried the same trick on a heretic who pestered him, watched a rooster by his bed, and fell asleep.
avodah-zarah/4.question: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads his own nap as proof that cursing is improper, but what would he have concluded if he had stayed awake and the curse had worked?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage may read the accident of his own failure as a verdict on the act he intended, or whether the norm stands independent of outcome.

answer.quote: And moreover, it is inappropriate to cause the punishment of another, as it is written: “Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good”
answer.explanation: This second reason does not depend on the nap at all, so it hints that he would hold cursing improper regardless of outcome, but the page never addresses the counterfactual of a successful curse.

avodah-zarah/5.summary: Reish Lakish says to be grateful to the ancestors who made the Golden Calf, since without that sin the people would have stayed angel-like and produced no children. The Gemara pushes back, citing Adam shown every future generation and its sages, and the claim gets softened twice: the children would have been born but counted for nothing, and the decreed "death" may only mean poverty. Then Moses, forty years late, calls them ingrates for never asking God for a fearing heart.
avodah-zarah/5.question: If the sin at the Golden Calf is what made room for later generations to exist, what exactly is left in it to repent for?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sin that turns out to have made later life possible is still a sin one must repent for.

answer.quote: Do not say that if our ancestors had not sinned we would not have come into the world, as we still would have been born
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself retracts the premise that the sin was necessary for later generations to exist, which undercuts (but does not directly address) the question of what remains to repent for.

avodah-zarah/6.summary: Two reasons are floated for barring business with gentiles in the days before their festivals: the gentile profits, rejoices, and thanks his idol, or the seller places a stumbling block before the blind. The test case is a gentile who already owns an animal of his own. Then a baraita objects: do not hand a cup of wine to a nazirite, a man under a vow not to drink, even though he could reach it himself. The answer is a river between them.
avodah-zarah/6.question: Does the river reading rescue the verse about the stumbling block, or empty it, since almost everything we hand to someone could have been reached without us?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether liability for enabling sin requires that the enabler be genuinely necessary, or whether such a test drains the prohibition of content.

answer.quote: Here we are dealing with a case where they are standing on the two sides of a river, and therefore the recipient could not have taken it himself.
answer.explanation: The page limits the prohibition to cases where the giver's help was instrumental, which bears on the question but does not address whether that narrowing hollows out the verse.

avodah-zarah/7.summary: Naḥum the Mede, a sage from Media, rules that one may sell a male, elderly horse to gentiles in wartime, since it cannot be used in battle. Three of his rulings, on the horse, on dill and tithes, and on trading before a gentile festival, meet the same flat response from the other Sages: better this matter were lost and never said. Rav Aḥa bar Minyumi presses Abaye about it, and the single ruling Abaye offers in Naḥum's defense gets taken away too.
avodah-zarah/7.question: If the Sages wanted Naḥum the Mede's rulings lost, why are all three of them preserved here word for word?

judge.reachNote: Why a tradition that preserves everything verbatim also preserves the verdict that a ruling should have been lost — rejection recorded rather than erased.

answer.quote: Abaye said: There is one instance in which we act in accordance with his opinion
answer.explanation: The page raises the kindred complaint ("Do they wish to erase all the halakhot taught by the Sages of Media?") and Abaye's reply shows Naḥum's rulings are kept because one may yet be followed, but it never explains why the three rejected rulings themselves are recorded verbatim, and Rav Aḥa immediately strips that defense away.

avodah-zarah/8.summary: A mishna lists the festivals of gentiles during which business is barred: Kalenda, Saturnalia, Kratesis, the king's birthday, and the day a king dies. The Gemara fixes the first two at the eight days after and before the winter solstice, then traces them to Adam, who fasted eight days in terror as daylight shrank and feasted eight days when it came back. Same dates, same count: Adam kept them for Heaven, later generations for idols.
avodah-zarah/8.question: If Adam's eight days and Rome's eight days land on the same dates, is a festival made by the calendar or by the one keeping it?
gate: the question brings in "Rome's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — whether a festival's character lies in its date or in the worshipper's intent — but the baraita on Adam states that answer in the very line the summary paraphrases.

answer.quote: He, Adam, established these festivals for the sake of Heaven, but they, the gentiles of later generations, established them for the sake of idol worship.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that identical days differ by the intent of the one keeping them, and Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling that "it is prohibited to engage in business only with its worshippers" confirms that the prohibition tracks the celebrant rather than the date.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 8a: "He, Adam, established these festivals for the sake of Heaven, but they, the gentiles of later generations, established them for the sake of idol worship.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the page's own closing line about Adam already answers, a line the summary itself repeats ("Adam kept them for Heaven, later generations for idols"). Take that answer as the starting point and ask what it leaves unsettled — for instance, why Rav Ashi must prove from the mishna's phrase "with that man" that subjects of a celebrating power are exempt, if intent alone decides. Or press on Rav Yitzḥak son of Rav Mesharshiyya, who withdrew after twelve months because his own importance made the gentile rejoice: there the Jew's standing, not the host's intent, creates the problem.

avodah-zarah/9.summary: Rav Pappa offers a fix for a tanna, one who recites memorized traditions, who has lost track of the year: ask a scribe how he dates documents, then add twenty. A scribe who forgets does the reverse, deducting twenty from the tanna's count, and a pun keeps the direction straight. The same page runs a six-thousand-year clock, two thousand waste, two thousand Torah, two thousand for the Messiah, with years quietly disappearing from the last set.
avodah-zarah/9.question: If redemption was close enough in the year 400 to make a field worth a thousand dinars a bad buy at one dinar, what is a person supposed to do in the year 500?
gate: the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Under the case lies the problem of how people are supposed to live and transact once a dated promise of imminent redemption has come and gone.

avodah-zarah/10.summary: Antoninus asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whether he will enter the World-to-Come, then argues against himself with verses saying no remnant will be left of the house of Esau. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi narrows both verses: only those who act as Esau acted, and only some of Edom's kings. A baraita then names the two men the verses exclude, Antoninus and Ketia, son of Shalom, who talked an emperor out of destroying the Jews and was condemned for winning the argument.
avodah-zarah/10.question: The same Antoninus kills a servant at each end of his secret tunnel to keep his visits hidden, so what exactly counts as performing actions similar to those of Esau?

judge.reachNote: Whether a person is judged by lineage or by deeds, and if by deeds, which deeds actually mark one as 'of the house of Esau' when a benefactor of Torah also kills servants casually.

avodah-zarah/11.summary: When a king dies, his bed and his utensils are burned so that no one else can use them. Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis argue over whether a gentile king's death counts as a festival only when it includes such a burning; the Gemara decides the fire is not idolatry at all, since Jeremiah promised Zedekiah one, but a measure of the dead man's importance. The same honor extends to heads of the Sanhedrin: Onkelos burned goods worth seven thousand dinars, silver coins, for Rabban Gamliel the Elder.
avodah-zarah/11.question: If the reason for the fire is that nobody else should use the king's things, what was Onkelos burning seven thousand dinars' worth of goods for, at the death of a man who was not a king?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that destruction at a death is measured by the deceased's standing and by what was personally his — but the page states both halves of this itself.

answer.quote: The Gemara answers: Say that Onkelos burned items that were valued at seven thousand dinars in Tyrian coinage.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection — "Why, then, did Onkelos burn money?" — and resolves it by saying he burned utensils valued at that sum, while the preceding line already extends the practice from kings to "the heads of the Sanhedrin."

summaryProblems.claim: The seven thousand dinars were silver coins.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Onkelos the convert burned seven thousand dinars in valuable Tyrian coinage

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 11a: "The Gemara answers: Say that Onkelos burned items that were valued at seven thousand dinars in Tyrian coinage.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The seven thousand dinars were silver coins.", but the page says "Onkelos the convert burned seven thousand dinars in valuable Tyrian coinage". Say what the page says. The question is asked and answered verbatim on the daf: the Gemara itself objects "Why, then, did Onkelos burn money?" and answers that he burned items valued at that sum, having just said the practice extends to heads of the Sanhedrin. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance why the Rabbis treat the burning as a gauge of the gentiles' regard for the king when the same burning is a Jewish custom for Zedekiah. Also drop the unsupported "silver coins"; the page says Tyrian coinage.

avodah-zarah/12.summary: A thorn lodges in a man's foot while he stands before an idol, and an early teaching says he may not bend down to pull it out, because he looks like he is bowing. The same holds for coins he has dropped and for a spring running past the idol, even when going thirsty is dangerous. The way out is not privacy but posture, since Rav holds such rules apply even in the innermost chambers.
avodah-zarah/12.question: If the prohibition holds even in a room where nobody is watching, whose eyes is the man with the thorn in his foot bending under?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that prohibitions of appearance ('marit ayin') survive the absence of any viewer, so the standard is the act's shape, not a spectator's gaze.

answer.quote: Rather, say: If he is not seen as one who bows down to an object of idol worship, i.e., he turns his side or back to the idol
answer.explanation: The Gemara resolves the tension by redefining "not seen" as a matter of bodily orientation rather than an observer's presence, but it never says whose perception the prohibition guards against once no one is there to perceive.

avodah-zarah/13.summary: On the day the tax is reduced for anyone who wears a rose wreath in honor of an idol, a Jew in that market is stuck: wear it and he derives benefit from idol worship, refuse and his full tax funds it. Rabbi Natan's answer is to destroy whatever was bought there, cutting an animal's hooves off below the knee. Abaye defends this against the rule about animal suffering by citing Joshua's order to destroy horses.
avodah-zarah/13.question: Why does an animal consecrated when there is no Temple get locked in a room to starve, so as not to degrade it, while an animal bought at a pagan fair has its hooves cut off?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that sanctity changes which modes of destruction are permitted — but the page itself states that reason.

answer.quote: There, in the case of a consecrated animal, the method employed is different, because cutting the animal's hooves would cause the degradation of sacrificial animals.
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks precisely this contradiction between the two baraitot and Abaye answers that a consecrated animal may not have its hooves cut because that degrades sacrificial animals, with Rava adding that it looks like blemishing.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 13b: "There, in the case of a consecrated animal, the method employed is different, because cutting the animal's hooves would cause the degradation of sacrificial animals.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own contradiction, and Abaye and Rava answer it explicitly on 13b (degradation of sacrificial animals; it appears as blemishing). Rewrite so the question starts after that answer, or pick a genuinely unresolved thread on the page — for instance, why Rav Ashi replaces "bringing him under the wings of the Divine Presence" with "reducing the gentile's possessions," when the purchase money itself enriches the seller. Keep the summary, which is accurate.

avodah-zarah/14.summary: A gentile who calls out "who has a white rooster" may not be sold one, since white roosters are burned for idols, while a man pointing at several birds at once, or one preparing a feast for his son, may be sold whatever he picks. Rav Ashi presses the edges: what if he asks for a damaged white rooster, which nobody sacrifices, or accepts a black one instead? Perhaps artifice. Both dilemmas stand unresolved.
avodah-zarah/14.question: If even taking the black rooster might be a ruse, what could a buyer ever do to prove he means nothing by it?

judge.reachNote: Whether any outward act can establish intent once the law is willing to suspect pretense behind every act.

answer.quote: in the case of a gentile who is preparing a feast for his son or who has a sick person in his house, it is permitted to sell it to him
answer.explanation: The baraita names circumstances outside the buyer's words — a wedding feast or a sick person at home — that establish innocent intent, though the page leaves Rav Ashi's dilemmas about the buyer's own conduct unresolved.

summaryProblems.claim: white roosters are burned for idols
summaryProblems.pageSays: he does not need it for idol worship, as gentiles do not sacrifice defective animals

judge.feedback: The summary says "white roosters are burned for idols", but the page says "he does not need it for idol worship, as gentiles do not sacrifice defective animals". Say what the page says.

avodah-zarah/15.summary: The ban on selling large livestock to gentiles turns out to rest on the seller, not the buyer: near sunset on Friday he tells the buyer to test the animal, it walks at his familiar voice, and he has driven a laden beast on Shabbat. Rav Ashi cuts through the competing cases with a rule, that where an innocent motive can be assigned, one assigns it. Rabba sold a donkey to a Jew suspected of reselling to gentiles, conceded to Abaye, and chased him without catching him.
avodah-zarah/15.question: Rabba ran three parasangs and never overtook the buyer, so what became of a sale its own maker had just decided was forbidden?
gate: the question uses "parasang", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a seller's responsibility does not end at the handover — a sale learned to be forbidden leaves the seller chasing an act he can no longer undo.

avodah-zarah/16.summary: Shields lead the list of things one may not sell to gentiles, since a soldier whose weapon is spent can still kill with a shield; others say he simply flees. Rav Adda bar Ahava bars blocks of Indian iron, good only for forging weapons, while Rav Ashi observes that finished weapons are sold to the Persians, who protect them. Horses, a fattened ox, and a lion that does no labor follow.
avodah-zarah/16.question: If raw Indian iron is barred because weapons come out of it, what makes the finished weapon safe to sell once the buyer is the power protecting you?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the principle that the ban tracks danger to us rather than the lethality of the object itself, so the buyer's identity can outweigh the item's use.

answer.quote: And as for the fact that nowadays we do sell all weapons, Rav Ashi said: We sell the weapons to the Persians, who protect us.
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason weapons may be sold — the buyers are the protecting power — but never explains why that consideration does not equally license selling them Indian iron, so the tension the question raises remains open.

avodah-zarah/17.summary: Rabbi Eliezer blames his arrest by the Roman authorities on a single moment of pleasure he took in a clever scriptural reading he once heard in the marketplace of Tzippori. Later the page follows Elazar ben Durdayya, who begged the mountains, the sun and the stars to pray for mercy on his behalf, was refused by each, and wept until he died. A Divine Voice calls him Rabbi, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi weeps that one man earns the World-to-Come over years and another in one moment.
avodah-zarah/17.question: Why does one moment of enjoying a clever interpretation cost Rabbi Eliezer so much, while a lifetime of visiting prostitutes costs Elazar ben Durdayya only an afternoon of weeping?

judge.reachNote: What makes a sin costly is not its volume but its kind and one's proximity to it — nearness to heresy outweighs a lifetime of ordinary transgression.

answer.quote: those who go to her do not return, and even if they return, they do not attain the paths of life
answer.explanation: The page holds that heresy is the sin from which there is effectively no safe return, which bears on why mere pleasure taken in a heretic's teaching was costly for Rabbi Eliezer, though it does not directly resolve the comparison with Elazar ben Durdayya, whose death the page explains separately as being 'similar to heresy.'

avodah-zarah/18.summary: The Romans wrap Rabbi Ḥanina ben Teradyon in his Torah scroll, pack branches around him, and lay water-soaked tufts of wool on his heart so he will burn slowly. His students tell him to open his mouth and let the fire in and end it; he refuses, saying the one who gave him his soul should take it. Then the executioner offers to pull off the wool in exchange for the World-to-Come, and Ḥanina swears to it.
avodah-zarah/18.question: Why may Ḥanina not breathe in the fire to shorten his own dying, yet may swear an oath that gets the executioner to shorten it for him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the line between actively destroying oneself and consenting to another's removal of what prolongs one's dying.

answer.quote: It is preferable that He who gave me my soul should take it away, and one should not harm oneself to speed his death.
answer.explanation: The page gives Ḥanina's reason for refusing his students' advice — a ban on harming oneself — which bears on the distinction but never explains why permitting (and swearing to reward) the executioner's act is different.

avodah-zarah/19.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says a person can learn Torah only from the part of it his heart desires, and Levi, sitting right in front of him, takes him at his word and leaves to go study Proverbs instead of Psalms. Rav Ḥisda later tells his students he is afraid to say the thing he is about to say: that one who learns from a single teacher sees no blessing. They leave for Rava.
avodah-zarah/19.question: Did Rav Ḥisda's correction, that he meant reasoning and not the received texts, come because it was true, or because his students were already out the door?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's qualification is a genuine distinction or a rationalization produced by the consequences of his own teaching.

avodah-zarah/20.summary: A missing vav and a missing yud in the words lo tehonnem (Deuteronomy 7:2) are read as three separate bans: no letting gentiles acquire land in Eretz Yisrael, no undeserved gifts, no praise. Rav forbids saying how beautiful a gentile woman is, yet Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, on a Temple Mount step, saw one and quoted a psalm of praise to God. The answer given is that he thanked the Creator, not her, and glanced only by accident.
avodah-zarah/20.question: If the launderer is safe because he is absorbed in his work, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is safe because he addressed God, what exactly is left of the prohibition on looking?

judge.reachNote: Whether the prohibition governs the physical act of looking or only the intent and desire behind it, and how much survives once intent excuses.

answer.quote: Rather, he is occupied with his work, and therefore his mind will not entertain sinful thoughts.
answer.explanation: The page supplies a criterion behind both exemptions — the ban targets looking that leads the mind to sinful thoughts, and the Gemara likewise says Rabban Gamliel "did not intentionally look" — but it never states what scope remains of the prohibition once these carve-outs stand.

avodah-zarah/21.summary: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei disagree over whether a Jew may sell or only rent houses and fields to gentiles in Eretz Yisrael, in Syria, and farther away. Fields carry two problems, helping gentiles settle the land and dropping it from tithes; houses look like two as well, until Rav Mesharshiyya says the mezuza on the doorpost binds the resident, not the house. Abaye then caps responsibility: a stumbling block two steps removed is not yours.
avodah-zarah/21.question: If three gentile households count as a settlement, is the neighbor who sells first really uninvolved in what the next two sellers do?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of how far causal responsibility for another's sin extends, but the page already fixes the limit at one remove.

answer.quote: We are commanded about placing a stumbling block before the blind (see Leviticus 19:14), but we are not commanded about placing a stumbling block before someone who may place it before the blind.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely the worry that one Jew's sale plus two neighbors' sales creates a settlement, and Abaye resolves it by ruling that liability does not extend two stages removed from the act.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 21a: "We are commanded about placing a stumbling block before the blind (see Leviticus 19:14), but we are not commanded about placing a stumbling block before someone who may place it before the blind.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply re-asks the Gemara's own challenge, which Abaye answers in the very next line and which the summary itself already reports. Write a question that starts from Abaye's limit rather than reopening it, for instance probing why the tithe and settlement concerns justify decrees stretching all the way to fields outside Eretz Yisrael while indirect causation here is waved off. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

avodah-zarah/22.summary: Saffron growers split a field so that a gentile partner worked it on Shabbat and a Jew worked it on Sunday, and Rava let them divide the profits evenly. A baraita appears to forbid exactly that unless the arrangement was stipulated when the partnership began; Ravina raises it, and Rava is embarrassed. Then the page rewrites the scene: Ravina was actually supporting Rava, and the embarrassment, the Gemara says flatly, never happened.
avodah-zarah/22.question: If the gentile does the same Shabbat work either way, why should saying so in advance change whose labor the Jew is profiting from?

judge.reachNote: Whether whose labor a profit represents is fixed by the physical work or by the terms agreed in advance.

answer.quote: The reason one may not do so is that it turns out that when the gentile worked on Shabbat, he was laboring partly on behalf of his Jewish partner.
answer.explanation: The page gives the ground of the distinction — unstipulated splitting or later reckoning makes the Shabbat labor count as done on the Jew's behalf — but it never explains why an advance stipulation removes that, so the question can still honestly be asked.

avodah-zarah/23.summary: A mishna says gentiles are suspected of bestiality, yet a baraita allows buying an animal from them for the altar. The Gemara's sharpest move is a financial one: a seller would not spoil a costly red heifer by loading sacks on it for a moment's convenience, so why would he spoil it for a moment's pleasure? The answer given is that appetite is not a calculation. A captive woman's case is settled the same way, by the ransom her captor stands to lose.
avodah-zarah/23.question: If money is enough to stop a man from placing a bundle of sacks on a valuable heifer, why does the page take for granted that money cannot stop him from anything else?

judge.reachNote: Whether money deters a man reliably, or only where no appetite is engaged — the limit of economic reasoning about human conduct.

answer.quote: There, with regard to bestiality, his inclination overcomes him, and he is apt to engage in bestiality with the heifer despite the fact that he knows it is to his disadvantage
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the exact objection — that a gentile would not forfeit money for slight pleasure — and answers that desire overrides financial calculation, which the note's summary already restates as "appetite is not a calculation."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 23a: "There, with regard to bestiality, his inclination overcomes him, and he is apt to engage in bestiality with the heifer despite the fact that he knows it is to his disadvantage". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the page explicitly answers, and the summary even quotes that answer ("appetite is not a calculation"), so the note contradicts itself. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance, why the same monetary logic is trusted to protect a captive woman from a captor whose inclination is presumably no weaker, or why the Rabbis' verse from Isaiah displaces the whole cost-benefit argument. Keep the summary's financial thread, but let the question press where the page stops.

avodah-zarah/24.summary: Rabbi Eliezer will not allow a red heifer, the all-red cow burned to make purification ash, to be bought from a gentile, on the suspicion that someone had sexual relations with it. The heifer bought from Dama ben Netina's herd pushes the worry backward: Jews guarded it from birth, then from conception, then guarded its mother from conception too. Asked about the mother's mother, the answer is only that suspicion stops there.
avodah-zarah/24.question: If the doubt can be pushed back one generation and then another, what makes the heifer's grandmother the place where the worry is allowed to stop?

judge.reachNote: Where a chain of possible contamination is allowed to stop — how far back a legal doubt must be chased before it is declared unreasonable.

answer.quote: The Gemara challenges: And let us be concerned that perhaps someone engaged in bestiality with the mother of the heifer’s mother. The Gemara responds: We are not concerned to such an extent.
answer.explanation: The page states that the chain of doubt stops at the grandmother but offers no reason beyond the bare assertion that concern does not extend that far, which is what the question presses on.

avodah-zarah/25.summary: Three sages count how long the sun stood still for Joshua: twenty-four hours, thirty-six, or forty-eight, split between hours of travel and hours of suspension. The page then turns to the road, where a Jew walking with a gentile keeps him on his weapon side, stays uphill of him, never bends down before him, and names a destination past his real one, as Jacob told Esau he was heading to Seir and went to Succoth. Rabbi Akiva's students said Akko, stopped at Keziv, and the bandits praised them.
avodah-zarah/25.question: If the bandits worked out the trick as soon as the students stopped at Keziv, what exactly were they calling fortunate?

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is that a permitted deception is itself a mark of the teacher's training, admired even by the men it defeated.

answer.quote: The bandits were impressed with the wisdom that the students demonstrated in evading harm.
answer.explanation: The page explicitly glosses the bandits' blessing as admiration for the students' wisdom in evading harm, and quotes their words "they were never harmed by an evil person," so the question of what they praised is stated outright.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 25b: "The bandits were impressed with the wisdom that the students demonstrated in evading harm.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: it says the bandits were impressed with the wisdom the students showed in evading harm, and that Akiva's students were never harmed by an evil person. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled, for example why the Gemara grounds the licence to misstate one's destination in Jacob's words to Esau rather than in a plain rule about danger, or what it means that safety here depends on a lie rather than on avoiding the road altogether. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

avodah-zarah/26.summary: A Jewish woman may not deliver or nurse a gentile woman's child, and the Gemara then argues over whether a gentile midwife may be trusted with a Jewish one, Rabbi Meir fearing a hand pressed on an infant's temple. Rav Yosef keeps proposing that payment makes such help permitted, since refusal breeds enmity; Abaye keeps supplying an excuse instead. One excuse, needing the ladder for a son on the roof, later returns as a way to strand a man in a pit.
avodah-zarah/26.question: If everyone involved can tell that the ladder and the courthouse appointment are pretexts, does the excuse actually prevent the enmity Rav Yosef was worried about?

judge.reachNote: Whether the halakha cares about the gentile's actual goodwill or only about the Jew having a plausible thing to say.

answer.quote: Since the Jew can provide a legitimate excuse for refusing to aid the gentile, there is no need to extract him from the pit.
answer.explanation: The page asserts that a sayable excuse is enough to dissolve the enmity concern, but it never tests whether a transparent pretext actually placates the gentile, so the note's question can still be asked.

avodah-zarah/27.summary: A mishna allows a Jew to bring an animal to a gentile healer but not his own body, even for the small wound left by bloodletting. The Gemara then considers a patient certain to die without treatment and permits the risk, citing four starving lepers who walked into an enemy camp rather than sit and wait. But when a snake bit ben Dama, Rabbi Yishmael blocked a heretic's cure and called the resulting death pure.
avodah-zarah/27.question: If a dying man may gamble on a gentile doctor because short remaining life does not outweigh a chance at cure, what made ben Dama fortunate to die with his proof-verse unfinished?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether the value of a chance at life outranks exposure to spiritual danger — but the page states the answer outright.

answer.quote: Heresy is different, as it is enticing. In other words, it is prohibited to accept medical treatment from a heretic
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the ben Dama incident as an objection to the 'certain death' leniency and resolves it by distinguishing heresy, which entices, from ordinary gentile medicine.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 27b: "Heresy is different, as it is enticing. In other words, it is prohibited to accept medical treatment from a heretic". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 27b: heresy is different because it is enticing, so the 'certain death' leniency does not extend to a heretic healer. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for example, press on why the danger of being drawn after heresy is weighed more heavily than the near-certain loss of life, or on Rabbi Yishmael's further move that 'he shall live by them' applies only in private. The summary is accurate and can largely stand.

avodah-zarah/28.summary: The argument is about where an internal injury begins, since only a life-threatening one allows treatment that would otherwise break Shabbat, and the test case is a toothache. Rabbi Yohanan, sick with tzafdina, a bleeding gum disease, got a remedy from a gentile matron healer only after swearing not to reveal it, then taught it publicly the next day. The Gemara saves his oath by parsing its words, then adds that he had warned her from the start.
avodah-zarah/28.question: If Rabbi Yohanan told the matron at the outset that he would publish her remedy anyway, what was the oath she extracted from him actually worth?

judge.reachNote: An oath taken in a form the taker privately reads as empty, and what honesty toward a gentile healer requires beyond avoiding desecration of God's name.

answer.quote: his vow meant: I will not reveal it to the God of the Jews, which indicates: But I will reveal it to His people
answer.explanation: The Gemara construes the oath so that it never barred disclosure to Jews, which bears on how much the matron's oath actually bound him, but it never addresses what the oath was worth to her or whether such an evasion is honest.

avodah-zarah/29.summary: A list of foods that endanger a person after bloodletting, the standard treatment of draining blood, opens the page: milk, cheese, onions, cress. Rav Ḥana bar Bizna, having his hair cut in a side street of Neharde'a, hears the barber say his throat is appealing to the razor, and blames himself for ignoring Rabbi Meir. Later Rabbi Yishmael presses Rabbi Yehoshua twice on why gentile cheese is banned, and Rabbi Yehoshua answers by asking how he reads a verse in Song of Songs.
avodah-zarah/29.question: Did Rabbi Yehoshua switch to Song of Songs because he had no answer about the cheese, or because he had one he did not want to give?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a decree's stated reason may be withheld or unstateable, and that a teacher may redirect rather than concede.

avodah-zarah/30.summary: Wine left uncovered is treated as dangerous here, on the theory that a snake may drink from it and leave venom behind. The Sages sort through cases: cooked wine, wine diluted with water, wine that has soured for three days, a cress dish with vinegar in it, and a snake that carried water in its mouth to dilute wine before drinking it. Rav Ashi cuts in: clever reasoning is no way to settle a question of danger.
avodah-zarah/30.question: Rav drank water from a widow's house because she keeps her late husband's habits, and Shmuel refused because the fear of a man is no longer on her, so was either of them actually reasoning about water?
gate: the question brings in "Shmuel", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a danger ruling is really a judgment about the liquid or a judgment about the character and habits of the household it comes from.

answer.quote: Granted that they are not particular about the halakha of exposure, but in any event they are particular about cleanliness, and will cover it for hygienic reasons
answer.explanation: The page supplies each sage's stated reason, and Shmuel's Aramean ruling shows the reasoning does track whether the water actually gets covered, but the page never addresses whether the widow rulings are about the water rather than the woman, so the question survives.

avodah-zarah/31.summary: A Jew deposits his wine with a gentile, and the argument turns on what counts as locked away: a designated corner, a key, one seal, or a seal within a seal. Rava gets physical about it, describing a basin smeared with clay over a barrel's mouth, a basket fastened down, a wineskin lying stopper-downward in a sack. Then Rabbi Yirmeya shifts the ground entirely: sealed barrels are trusted among the winepresses, where a crowd is watching and the seller fears losing Jewish customers.
avodah-zarah/31.question: If what actually protects the wine is the seller's fear of being seen, what work is the seal doing at all?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Whether security comes from a physical barrier or from the social pressure and economic self-interest of the person holding the goods.

answer.quote: When Samaritans are not particular about a gentile’s touch, this is only with regard to open barrels, but with regard to sealed barrels, they are particular.
answer.explanation: The page explains that the seal marks the class of barrels the Samaritan guards, which bears on what the seal contributes, but it never states what the seal adds once Rabbi Yirmeya reduces the trust to fear of being watched at the winepresses.

avodah-zarah/32.summary: Hadrian planted vines in soil no one had ever tilled, and the wine went into white jugs that soaked it up; the jugs were smashed, and travelers carried the shards and steeped them in water for a drink. The Sages then ask whether such a shard may be propped under a bed leg, since nobody is drinking anything. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yoḥanan split over it, and one answer holds that the wine is still recognizable inside the pottery.
avodah-zarah/32.question: If the wine can still be seen in the shard, is propping a bed on it use of the pottery or use of the wine?

judge.reachNote: Whether benefit from a vessel that has absorbed a forbidden substance counts as benefit from the substance itself.

answer.quote: In this case, no benefit whatsoever is derived from the wine absorbed within the shards, but the shards themselves are being used to support the bed.
answer.explanation: The page itself frames the bed-leg dilemma by stating outright that the benefit is from the shards and not at all from the absorbed wine, which is precisely what the note asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 32a: "In this case, no benefit whatsoever is derived from the wine absorbed within the shards, but the shards themselves are being used to support the bed.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already settled by the page, which says plainly that no benefit is derived from the absorbed wine and that only the shards support the bed. Build the new question on something the page leaves unresolved, such as why jugs may be sold freely while wineskins may not, or why 'a substantive prohibited entity' turns mere desire for the item's continued existence into a prohibition. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

avodah-zarah/33.summary: Bar Adi the Arab seized wineskins from Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef, kept wine in them, and gave them back; the remedy offered is three days of water, poured out and refilled every day. From there the page sorts containers by how much they drink: tarred skins, jugs returned to the furnace until the tar softens, dung vessels that burst when set in the sun, natron that never purges. Cups get counted, prohibited the first and second time a gentile drinks, permitted the third.
avodah-zarah/33.question: If a smooth glazed jug is too slick to hold on to a gentile's wine, why does anyone still wonder whether it holds on to leaven at Passover?
gate: the question brings in "Passover", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a vessel's absorbency is one fixed property or is judged differently depending on which prohibition (gentile wine vs. leaven) is at stake.

avodah-zarah/34.summary: Rabbi Akiva came to the city of Ginzak and was asked three questions he could not answer, one of them whether clay jars belonging to gentiles are forbidden forever. The study hall answered that such jars are permitted once twelve months have passed unused. Then five sages in a row apply that same span to wine yeast, jugs, Arab canteens, Aramean grape pits, and brown and black jugs, as though a year empties anything of wine.
avodah-zarah/34.question: Is twelve months a measurement of how long absorbed wine actually lingers in clay, or a round number that quietly promises every vessel will eventually come clean?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether a rabbinic time period measures a physical reality or serves as a uniform convention applied by analogy.

answer.quote: Grape residues are considered moist for all of the first twelve months after the grapes were pressed, and dry after the first twelve months.
answer.explanation: Shmuel ties the twelve-month span to an actual physical change from moist to dry, which bears on the question without settling whether the same span for jars, canteens and yeast tracks real absorption or is a conventional round year.

avodah-zarah/35.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua, asked why cheese made by gentiles is forbidden, changes the subject to a verse from Song of Songs and tells Rabbi Yishmael to press his lips together and stop asking. Ulla explains that in Eretz Yisrael the reason for a new decree was withheld for twelve months, lest someone who disagreed treat it with contempt. The Gemara guesses anyway: snake venom, pig fat, vinegar from gentile wine, sap from a tree's first three years.
avodah-zarah/35.question: If a reason is withheld so that no one will hold the rule in contempt, what is left to hold onto once the sages are reduced to guessing at it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rabbinic decree's authority rests on its stated reason or on the fact of its enactment alone.

answer.quote: The ordinance prohibiting the cheese of gentiles was a new decree, and therefore one does not scrutinize its origins.
answer.explanation: The page says the decree's newness itself is what obliges obedience without probing its reason, which bears on the question but does not resolve what remains once the Sages themselves only conjecture the reason.

avodah-zarah/36.summary: Rav and Shmuel argue over why oil handled by gentiles was ever forbidden: Shmuel blames residue absorbed in the vessels, Rav says Daniel himself decreed it. That raises a problem, since a court cannot void another court's ruling unless it is greater in wisdom and number, yet Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted the oil. The escape is practical: the ban never spread among most Jews, and a decree most people cannot keep does not hold.
avodah-zarah/36.question: If a decree only binds when most people actually keep it, who gets to declare that it never took hold?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a decree's force depends on popular acceptance, and asks who is competent to judge acceptance — but the page names the Sages' own inspection.

answer.quote: Our Sages sat and inspected the matter of gentiles’ oil and determined that its prohibition had not spread among the majority of the Jewish people
answer.explanation: The page states that the later Sages themselves investigated and ruled on whether the prohibition had spread, which is precisely the question of who declares that a decree never took hold.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 36a: "Our Sages sat and inspected the matter of gentiles’ oil and determined that its prohibition had not spread among the majority of the Jewish people". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: the Sages sat, inspected, and determined that the oil prohibition had not spread, relying on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance, why non-compliance can unmake the oil decree while the other eighteen matters stand even if Elijah's court came to rescind them, or what it means that a law's validity is decided by whether people in fact kept it.

avodah-zarah/37.summary: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, walking and leaning on the shoulder of his attendant Rabbi Simlai, mentions that his court permitted the oil of gentiles the previous night. Simlai suggests bread is next, and the objection raised is not about bread but about arithmetic: Yosei ben Yo'ezer got the nickname Yosef the Permissive for three lenient rulings, so two is still safe. Oddly, one of Yosei's three, that touching a corpse makes a person impure, sounds strict, and the Gemara labors to show it loosened something.
avodah-zarah/37.question: If permitting gentile bread would be correct, what does it mean that the objection raised is the running tally of how many things the court has already permitted?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the tension between a ruling's correctness and a court's standing: leniencies are weighed by their cumulative effect on authority, not one by one on the merits.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia said to him: If so, people will call us a permissive court.
answer.explanation: The page states the motive behind the counting — fear of the court acquiring the reputation Yosei ben Yo'ezer earned — but it never reflects on why a correct ruling should yield to a tally, so the note's question can still honestly be asked.

avodah-zarah/38.summary: A gentile singes the hair off an animal's head, and Rabbi Yoḥanan permits eating even the fully cooked tip of the ear, because the man meant to remove hair, not to cook. The same reasoning covers meat a Jew sets on coals and a gentile turns, permitted so long as no single party did the whole job. Then a dispute over an egg roasted by a gentile ends with Rav Zevid dead from a cup of spiced vinegar.
avodah-zarah/38.question: The Exilarch's attendants hand Rav Zevid that cup right after he overrules the lenient answer about the egg, and the page reports his death and moves straight on to caper buds and leeks, so what is being said there without being said?
gate: the question brings in "Exilarch's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: a ruling's cost is borne by the ruler, and the Gemara lets a death stand as silent comment on needless stringency.

answer.quote: Due to the stringency Rav Zevid sought to impose, the attendants gave Rav Zevid a cup [negota] of spiced vinegar to drink, and he died as a result.
answer.explanation: The page itself supplies the causal link between Rav Zevid's stringency and the fatal cup, though it leaves unstated what the juxtaposition is meant to teach, so the question is only partly answered.

summaryProblems.claim: Meat turned by a gentile is permitted so long as no single party did the whole job.
summaryProblems.pageSays: it is not prohibited unless its cooking from beginning to end was performed by the hand of a gentile
