summaryProblems.claim: The intent reasoning of the singed head ('he meant to remove hair, not to cook') is what covers the turned-over meat case.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Lest you say that hastening the cooking process is a significant matter, and therefore food whose preparation is expedited by a gentile is prohibited

judge.feedback: The summary says "Meat turned by a gentile is permitted so long as no single party did the whole job.", but the page says "it is not prohibited unless its cooking from beginning to end was performed by the hand of a gentile". Say what the page says. The summary says "The intent reasoning of the singed head ('he meant to remove hair, not to cook') is what covers the turned-over meat case.", but the page says "Lest you say that hastening the cooking process is a significant matter, and therefore food whose preparation is expedited by a gentile is prohibited". Say what the page says. Correct the rule: the page prohibits only food whose cooking was done by a gentile from beginning to end, so a Jew doing the whole job is fine — "no single party did the whole job" inverts it. Also drop the claim that the singed-ear intent reasoning covers the turned-meat case; there the page argues from hastening not being significant. The question is workable, but note that the page already ties the cup to "the stringency Rav Zevid sought to impose," so ask what remains unexplained beyond that stated link.

avodah-zarah/39.summary: Rav Ashi held a suspicious fish up to the daylight to find thin scales, and shut another in a white vessel so its dark scales would show when it shed them. The page then shifts from inspecting the food to trusting the seller: a dead sage's gentile slave may still be bought from, and a sage's wife is credited when she sells sky-blue dye for ritual fringes. Reliability, it turns out, is inherited by household.
avodah-zarah/39.question: If a woman who tied phylacteries on one husband's arm later tied tax-seals on another's, what exactly was being trusted when she was trusted as a ḥaver's wife?

judge.reachNote: Whether trustworthiness is a personal commitment or a presumption borrowed from the household one happens to be in.

answer.quote: with regard to a ḥaver that died, his wife and children and members of his household remain in their presumptive status until they are suspected of engaging in inappropriate deeds
answer.explanation: The baraita frames the trust as a revocable presumptive status attached to the household, and Rabbi Yehuda's dispute plus the tax-collector story show it was never a personal commitment, but the page never states outright what was being relied upon in her assurance.

avodah-zarah/40.summary: Salted fish arrive in pieces, and the argument is how much of a kosher sign a buyer needs: a head, a spine, both, or one scaly fish in a hundred. A ship of small salted fish reaches Sikhra, Rav Huna bar Ḥinnana sees scales and permits the cargo, Rava answers that the scales may be leftovers from an earlier catch, and shofarot go out from both courts at once. Rav Ashi then refuses both to prohibit and to permit.
avodah-zarah/40.question: If two courts blow shofarot over the same boat on the same day, what is the man standing on the dock at Sikhra supposed to do with the fish?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: What binds a person when two courts of equal standing publicly rule opposite ways on the same object.

answer.quote: And I do not prohibit the fish, as Rav Pappa said to me that Rav Huna permitted it, but I also do not permit the fish
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi's response to the clashing rulings is abstention rather than a directive, so the page shows a sage's own conduct but never tells an ordinary buyer at the dock what to do.

avodah-zarah/41.summary: A statue holding a staff, a bird, or an orb is treated as an idol, since each signals dominion over the world; a sword, a crown, and a ring get added later. Rav Ashi asks what to make of a statue clutching excrement, and the answer never comes. Then Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish argue over idols that broke on their own, with Dagon, fallen and handless on his threshold, as the test case.
avodah-zarah/41.question: If Dagon's worshippers simply moved their reverence to the threshold he fell on, what would ever count as proof that a broken idol had been abandoned?

judge.reachNote: What counts as evidence that worshippers have given up on an idol — presumption from the idol's own helplessness versus proof of actual revocation.

answer.quote: who is to say that its owner certainly revoked it? It is a conflict between an uncertainty as to whether or not it was revoked, and a certainty
answer.explanation: The Gemara does set a standard — nothing short of certainty of revocation can override the certainty that the object was worshipped — but it never says what evidence would establish that certainty for a broken idol, so the question survives.

avodah-zarah/42.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan fires objection after objection at Reish Lakish, who holds that an idol which breaks on its own is permitted. Stones from a heap worshipped as Mercury and paved into roads, shavings off a statue, a dragon figure found with its head severed: in each case a Jew's hand keeps the fragment forbidden, and each time the answer is Rava's decree, lest the Jew lift the idol and thereby acquire it. Then leaves fall on their own, and a bird builds a nest.
avodah-zarah/42.question: If bending an idol out of shape revokes its status when a gentile does it but not when a Jew does, what exactly is being undone, the idol or something in the person?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether revocation is an act done to the object or a status tied to who may hold and disown it.

answer.quote: But the Sages issued a decree that such an idol retains its idolatrous status, lest a Jew first lift it up and then attempt to revoke its status.
answer.explanation: Rava holds that a Jew's bending actually does revoke the idol and the difference is only a rabbinic precaution about acquisition, which bears on the note's question without settling what revocation itself consists of.

avodah-zarah/43.summary: Rabban Gamliel kept diagrams of the moon's shapes on a tablet in his attic and showed them to witnesses who could not describe the new moon they had seen. The Gemara asks how that squares with the ban on making images of God's attendants, and Abaye offers three answers, each knocked down by another baraita. The rescues offered instead are odd: gentiles made them for him, the figures were in pieces, or making an image in order to learn is different.
avodah-zarah/43.question: If a statue of the king standing inside the Neharde'a synagogue raised no suspicion because the public is not suspected, why must Rav Yehuda disfigure the face on his own ring?
gate: the question brings in "Neharde'a", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that an appearance-based prohibition depends on who is watching — a private owner arouses suspicion where a public setting does not.

answer.quote: A public institution is different; the public is not suspected of having idolatrous intentions. Rather, it is assumed that the statue is there exclusively for ornamental purposes.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the Neharde'a synagogue against the suspicion rule and resolves it by distinguishing public institutions from an individual like Rav Yehuda, whose ring therefore remains suspect.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 43b: "A public institution is different; the public is not suspected of having idolatrous intentions. Rather, it is assumed that the statue is there exclusively for ornamental purposes.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it outright with the public/private distinction, so a reader who finished the daf would not still be asking it. Rewrite the question to probe something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why the same protruding figure is forbidden on the finger but permitted for sealing, or why suspicion of the onlooker, rather than the image itself, decides the law. Keep the summary; it tracks the page accurately.

avodah-zarah/44.summary: A gentile philosopher, Proclus ben Plospus, asks Rabban Gamliel why he is bathing in the bathhouse of Aphrodite in Akko. Gamliel waits until he is outside, then gives three answers: the bathhouse came first, the statue is mere decoration, and people urinate in front of it. Four sages each call one of those answers a dodge, and Rav Ḥama bar Yosef defends each, against the counterexample of Peor, an idol worshipped by defecating before it.
avodah-zarah/44.question: If the answer Proclus walked away with needs four rescues from later sages, was it an answer or a way of ending the conversation?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of when a reply is reasoning and when it is only a way of closing off a challenge from an outsider.

answer.quote: Rabban Gamliel gave a deceptive response to that officer, Proclus. And I, Rav Ḥama, say that the response was not deceptive but truthful.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself frames the dispute over whether Gamliel's reply was evasive or genuine, but it leaves the two positions standing rather than settling whether Proclus received a real answer.

avodah-zarah/45.summary: Gentiles worship a mountain; the mishna says the mountain stays permitted, since nobody made it, but gold or silver plating laid on it is forbidden. A tree is harder: an ashera counts as human handiwork, so the Gemara argues over a tree someone planted for ordinary reasons and only later worshipped. Rabbi Akiva reads the verse's mountains, hills and leafy trees not as legal categories at all, but as a map of where idolatry tends to be found.
avodah-zarah/45.question: If planting a tree years before anyone bowed to it is enough human involvement to condemn it, why isn't the gold someone hammered onto a mountain enough to condemn the mountain?

judge.reachNote: How much human agency it takes to draw a natural object into an idol's status — whether what a person does to a thing can change the thing or only the addition.

answer.quote: Everyone agrees that the status of the coating of a mountain is not like the mountain itself and is forbidden
answer.explanation: Rav Sheshet states that the gold coating is forbidden in its own right while the mountain stays permitted, but the page never explains why added human handiwork condemns a planted tree yet cannot condemn the mountain it is fixed to.

avodah-zarah/46.summary: Rami bar Ḥama asks whether the stones of a mountain someone bowed to may be used to build the altar in the Temple. Rava argues from payment given to a prostitute, barred from the Temple even when attached to the ground; Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, runs the identical argument backward and reaches the opposite result. Rava's answer is a rule rather than a refutation: when both directions are open, infer the stringency.
avodah-zarah/46.question: If the same two cases can be arranged to prove either leniency or stringency, is choosing the strict one reasoning, or just a way of stopping the argument?

judge.reachNote: When symmetrical a fortiori inferences cancel out, is the preference for stringency a form of reasoning or an admission that reasoning has run out?

answer.quote: There, Rabbi Akiva does not employ a real a fortiori inference. Rabbi Eliezer himself taught him this halakha, which he knew as a tradition, but he had forgotten
answer.explanation: The Gemara defends Rava's default-to-stringency rule against Rav Pappa's counterexample by denying that Rabbi Akiva's leniency was a genuine inference at all, which bears on the question but never says whether the rule is itself reasoning or a device for ending debate.

avodah-zarah/47.summary: Reish Lakish asks whether a palm branch cut from a tree that someone bowed to can still be waved for the Sukkot mitzva, or whether it is spoiled forever. A proof is tried from blood a slaughterer must cover with dust: if wind covers it and it blows open again, he covers it anew, so disqualification is not permanent. The proof collapses, since that rule there adds an obligation and here it would permit.
avodah-zarah/47.question: If once disqualified does not mean always disqualified when the ruling makes a man cover the blood a second time, why should the same logic be distrusted when it would hand him back his palm branch?

judge.reachNote: Whether a principle held only in doubt may be applied to permit as freely as it is applied to obligate.

answer.quote: Or perhaps is he uncertain, and therefore, when that ruling leads to stringency, we say that there is no disqualification with regard to mitzvot
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this asymmetry — that an uncertain principle may be invoked only where it produces stringency — but offers it as a possibility and closes with "The question shall stand unresolved," so the question survives the page.

avodah-zarah/48.summary: A tree planted from the start for idol worship, an ashera, is forbidden whole, while a tree planted ordinarily and only later bowed to may lose just its new growth. The Gemara then measures shade: the shade under the tree's own height, and the fainter shade stretching past it, and asks which one a person may sit in. Rav Sheshet, who was blind, asked his attendant to hurry him past an ashera on the only road home.
avodah-zarah/48.question: Rav Sheshet was permitted to walk under that tree, and ran anyway so no one would learn the wrong rule from him, but what does a passerby actually learn from watching a man run?

judge.reachNote: Conduct as public instruction: whether a hurried body can transmit a legal distinction that words would have to spell out.

answer.quote: lest others misunderstand the circumstances and learn from him that it is permitted for one to walk underneath an ashera even when there is another way
answer.explanation: The page states why Rav Sheshet ran, but never explains what content an onlooker is supposed to derive from the sight of a man running, so the question survives the answer it cites.

avodah-zarah/49.summary: Wood from an ashera, a tree worshipped as an idol, heats an oven, and the bread baked in it is forbidden, even once it is mixed in with ordinary loaves. Rabbi Eliezer says one can set aside money equal to the value of the wood and throw it into the Dead Sea; the Rabbis answer that idolatry has no monetary redemption. Then a man whose wine was mixed with a barrel of libation wine is told by Rav Ḥisda to throw four dinars in the river.
avodah-zarah/49.question: If objects tied to idol worship cannot be bought back, what did four dinars sinking in a river actually do for the rest of that man's wine?

judge.reachNote: Whether benefit derived from idolatry can be quantified in money and thereby cancelled — a real idea, but the page decides it.

answer.quote: Rav Ḥisda says: Even in the case of a barrel of libation wine, the wine in the other barrels is permitted once the value of the forbidden barrel has been cast
answer.explanation: The page resolves the tension the question raises by ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer rather than the Rabbis, and Rav Ḥisda extends that redemption even to libation wine, which is exactly why his four dinars permitted the rest.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 49b: "Rav Ḥisda says: Even in the case of a barrel of libation wine, the wine in the other barrels is permitted once the value of the forbidden barrel has been cast". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question treats "no monetary redemption for objects forbidden due to idol worship" as the settled rule, but the page explicitly rules the opposite — Ze'eiri and Rav Ḥisda hold the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer, and Rav Ḥisda applies it to libation wine — so the four dinars are already explained. The summary should say that the halakha was decided in Rabbi Eliezer's favor, since that is what makes the river story intelligible. Then ask something the page leaves open, such as why the Gemara needed both the bread and the shuttle cases, or why Rav Adda bar Ahava would limit redemption to bread alone.

avodah-zarah/50.summary: King Yannai's house fell into ruin, gentiles set up stones there dedicated to Mercury (a heap built by throwing stones in worship), and other gentiles later paved paths and streets with those same stones. Some Rabbis walked around the streets; some walked on them. Rabbi Yoḥanan ends the argument not with a verse but by pointing at a person: Rabbi Menaḥem, who would not even look at the image stamped on a coin, walks there, so why detour?
avodah-zarah/50.question: If the most scrupulous man in the room is the proof that something is permitted, what happens when it turns out he simply never considered the question?

judge.reachNote: Can the practice of an exceptionally scrupulous person function as legal proof, or must a permission rest on stated reasoning?

answer.quote: And the one who does not withdraw from those paths says: In order for idol worship to prohibit an offering I require the offering to be like those offerings sacrificed inside the Temple
answer.explanation: The Gemara does not leave the leniency resting on Rabbi Menaḥem's conduct alone — it supplies a substantive reason for each side (Rav Giddel's no-nullification verse for the withdrawers, the Temple-parallel requirement for the lenient ones) — yet it never addresses what would follow if the scrupulous man had simply never thought about it, so the note's question survives.

avodah-zarah/51.summary: A roadside shrine to Mercury is a heap of stones, and each passerby throws another one on. Rava presses Rav Nahman: a thrown stone does not scatter the way blood sprinkled on the altar does, so what makes the pile forbidden? The answer offered is that every stone counts twice, as part of the idol and as an offering to the stone before it, which leaves the newest stone permitted, if anyone could pick it out.
avodah-zarah/51.question: If the last stone thrown really is permitted, does that permission mean anything when nobody can tell which stone it is?

judge.reachNote: It reaches the idea of a permission that is real in law but unrecoverable in practice, and whether such a ruling has any force.

answer.quote: If you know which one it is, you may go and take it, as it is indeed permitted.
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman's reply makes the permission explicitly conditional on being able to identify the last stone, which bears on the note's question without settling what such an unusable permission is worth.

avodah-zarah/52.summary: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul asks Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whether vessels from the temple of Onias, a rival shrine the Sages did not class as idolatrous, may be used in the Temple in Jerusalem. He rules that they are forbidden, then admits he once knew the verse behind the ruling and has forgotten it. Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul objects from a verse about King Ahaz's vessels, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi seizes it as his lost proof, reading "prepared" as buried rather than immersed.
avodah-zarah/52.question: If the verse only supports the ruling once "we have prepared" is turned from immersion into burial, what was it that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had actually remembered?

judge.reachNote: What a remembered proof-text amounts to when the verse only yields the ruling after being reread against its plain sense — tradition guiding derivation rather than following from it.

answer.quote: That verse is the forgotten source of the halakha that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi stated
answer.explanation: The page identifies the Chronicles verse as the very source Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had forgotten, but it never explains what he retained of it such that the reinterpretation of "we have prepared" counts as recovery rather than construction.

avodah-zarah/53.summary: A gentile can void an idol's status by cutting off the tip of its ear or nose, or by smashing its face with a hammer so no stone is removed. Spitting or urinating in front of it does not count, since scorn passes and worship can resume. The page then asks why Joshua's generation had to burn the asherim, trees used in idolatry, rather than make the owners revoke them; the answer offered is that after the Golden Calf, gentile worshippers acted as agents for Jews.
avodah-zarah/53.question: If gentiles worshipping a tree count as agents of Jews because of the Golden Calf, what would ever bring that agency to an end, when no one can say which tree was worshipped when?

judge.reachNote: Whether agency in idolatry, once revealed by intention, has any limit in time or only an evidentiary bar to ever proving it ended.

answer.quote: But any ashera that was worshipped from that point forward, after the Jewish people repented and no longer engaged in idol worship, should be permitted
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself proposes that repentance would end the agency, but then answers "Who can prove when each ashera was worshipped?" so the question of a real endpoint survives, as the note's own wording concedes.

avodah-zarah/54.summary: Philosophers in Rome ask the Jewish sages why God, who forbids idol worship, does not simply destroy the things people worship. The sages answer that people bow to the sun, moon and stars, and the world needs those; destroying only the useless idols would just prove the survivors divine. The same reasoning stretches to stolen wheat that sprouts anyway and a child conceived in adultery: the world runs its course, and judgment waits.
avodah-zarah/54.question: If the world simply follows its course, why does Reish Lakish picture God as dragged in to form each adulterous child against his will?
gate: the question brings in "Reish", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Lakish", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether 'the world follows its course' means God withdraws from the sinner's act or is unwillingly implicated in completing it.

answer.quote: Is it not enough for the wicked that they treat My die for a sela coin as if it were ownerless [pumbi], using it without My permission and against My will
answer.explanation: The page gives the content and complaint behind the image — God's stamp used without permission — but never reconciles it with the baraita's 'the world follows its course,' so the question can still be asked honestly.

avodah-zarah/55.summary: Zunin asks Rabbi Akiva why people go to idol temples with broken limbs and come back whole, when both of them know idols are empty. Akiva answers that suffering is sworn to leave a person on a fixed day, and it keeps that oath even if the sick man happens to be standing in a shrine, like a custodian who will not deny a deposit just because the depositor was careless. Rav Yehuda adds that an idol which brings rain for a human sacrifice works because heaven lets the nations be misled.
avodah-zarah/55.question: If the sufferings depart on schedule precisely so as not to break faith, why is the man then left walking away convinced the idol cured him?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — why heaven lets deceptive evidence for idolatry stand — but the page states that idea a few lines later.

answer.quote: God allowed the nations to be misled [sheheḥelikan] by matters that seemingly indicate that idol worship is effective in order to expel the nations from the world
answer.explanation: The page explicitly explains why a false impression of idolatry's efficacy is left standing — heaven permits the misleading, and Reish Lakish adds that one who wishes to become impure is given an opening — which is precisely what the note asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 55a: "God allowed the nations to be misled [sheheḥelikan] by matters that seemingly indicate that idol worship is effective in order to expel the nations from the world". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered further down the same daf: Rav teaches God "allowed the nations to be misled" and Reish Lakish that one who comes to become impure is given an opening. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking what it already resolves — for instance, press on the tension between the sufferings' scrupulous faithfulness to their oath and heaven's willingness to let the man be deceived by the same departure. Keep the summary as it is; it is accurate.

avodah-zarah/56.summary: Grape juice becomes wine at some point, and the page offers three candidates: when it descends into the collection vat, when the seeds float on top, or when it is siphoned into barrels. Tithing, the produce set aside for priests and Levites, begins at one of those moments, while a gentile's touch makes the wine forbidden as an idolatrous libation earlier, a deliberate stringency. Then a six-year-old who had learned the tractate rules that a Jew may tread grapes alongside a gentile whose hands are tied.
avodah-zarah/56.question: Why should the same liquid count as finished wine sooner when idolatry is at stake than when tithes are?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that 'completion of work' may be fixed differently depending on which body of law is asking.

answer.quote: No, the prohibition of wine used for a libation is different, as the Sages were stringent concerning it and render the wine forbidden even before the seeds float.
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks this very question about the mismatch between the libation mishna and the tithe rulings and answers that libation wine is treated stringently, so it is forbidden at an earlier stage.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 56a: "No, the prohibition of wine used for a libation is different, as the Sages were stringent concerning it and render the wine forbidden even before the seeds float.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered flatly on 56a, where the Gemara itself raises the three-tanna problem and replies that libation wine is different because the Sages were stringent about it — and the summary even repeats that answer. Rewrite the question to start from that stringency rather than ask for it: for instance, why treating grape juice as wine early for idolatry does not also make it wine for tithes, or why Rava is willing to accept three tanna'im instead of using the stringency answer. Alternatively build the question off the returned wicker basket or the child's claim that a gentile's foot does not render wine a libation.

avodah-zarah/57.summary: A gentile climbing a palm tree in Biram brushed a Jew's wine with the tip of a branch, and Rav let the owners sell it, though he also held that even a one-day-old gentile baby's touch renders wine forbidden as an idol's libation. The baraita pressed against him draws the line elsewhere: adults know idol worship and its accessories, minors do not. The page ends with two courts blowing shofarot, one permitting a sale, one forbidding it.
avodah-zarah/57.question: When a shopkeeper in Meḥoza angrily dumped the stirred bucket into his barrel, and one court's shofarot said sell while another's said don't, what was the owner supposed to do with the wine?
gate: the question brings in "Meḥoza", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a law can be left publicly unresolved, with rival courts each broadcasting a binding ruling to the same wine.

avodah-zarah/58.summary: Rava has his attendant bolt the gates so he and Rav Huna can settle whether wine a gentile merely stirred is off limits for profit as well as for drinking. Abaye's baraita about a confiscator who plunged his hand into a barrel he thought held oil refutes Rava conclusively. Later two sages, served in the dark by a man who turned out to be a gentile, split, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says both rulings are sound.
avodah-zarah/58.question: If the wine's fate hangs on whether the pourer assumed rabbis drink wine or beer, and nobody ever asked him, what were the two sages actually ruling on?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition can turn on an unverified presumption about another person's state of mind rather than on any established fact.

answer.quote: the one who prohibited the wine properly deemed it prohibited, and the one who permitted it properly deemed it permitted, as both opinions are viable
answer.explanation: The page does state that each sage ruled on a viable presumption about what the gentile assumed he was pouring, and it later adds that force-poured wine without libation intent was never decreed prohibited, but it never addresses the note's puzzle that the pourer's actual assumption was never ascertained.

avodah-zarah/59.summary: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba visits Gavla and says nothing about three things he sees there: Jewish women pregnant by men circumcised for conversion but not yet immersed, wine that gentiles had diluted, and bitter lupine beans that gentiles cooked and Jews ate. Rabbi Yoḥanan sends him back to forbid all three. Then the Gemara argues that lupines are too lowly to reach a king's table and should be permitted, leaving the ban resting only on the locals' ignorance.
avodah-zarah/59.question: Why should the same bowl of lupines be forbidden in Gavla and permitted at a scholar's table, if the beans themselves were never the problem?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a prohibition can attach to the eater's learning rather than to the food itself — but the page supplies that idea and its reason explicitly.

answer.quote: due to the prohibition of food cooked by gentiles, as they are not people well-versed in Torah, and any leniency would be misunderstood and applied too extensively
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the lupines are barred in Gavla only because the residents are unlearned and would over-extend any leniency, while the closing line adds "But in the case of people well-versed in Torah, the lupines are permitted."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 59a: "due to the prohibition of food cooked by gentiles, as they are not people well-versed in Torah, and any leniency would be misunderstood and applied too extensively". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered twice in the same passage: the ban rests on the locals not being well-versed in Torah, so any leniency would be misapplied, and the Gemara closes by permitting lupines to the learned. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance why Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, who saw all three practices, said nothing at all until Rabbi Yoḥanan told him to, or why the wine diluted without any gentile touch still needs the nazirite maxim to forbid it.

avodah-zarah/60.summary: A gentile pours wine from a barrel while a Jew holds the cup, and Rav Pappa forbids the wine, since it left the barrel by the gentile's force. Reverse the roles and it is fine, unless he tilts the cup. When a barrel splits and a gentile throws his arms around it, he counts as a brick holding it shut, and the wine stays permitted for drinking.
avodah-zarah/60.question: If a man who climbs alive out of the wine vat forbids the wine by his gratitude alone, and a barrel hurled in by an angry man leaves it fit to drink, is libation wine made by the hands or by the mind?

judge.reachNote: Whether wine is disqualified by the gentile's physical contact or by his idolatrous intention — the page sets both standards side by side without choosing.

answer.quote: With regard to any form of contact through which a zav renders an object ritually impure, in a case where a gentile has that same type of contact with wine, he renders it wine used for a libation.
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi offers a purely physical contact standard, and Rav Pappa's rescued-gentile ruling offers an intent standard, but the page ends on Rav Huna's unresolved objection rather than deciding between hands and mind.

summaryProblems.claim: When a barrel splits and a gentile throws his arms around it, he counts as a brick holding it shut, and the wine stays permitted for drinking.
summaryProblems.pageSays: deemed it permitted to sell the wine to gentiles, as the wine was rendered prohibited only for drinking but not with regard to deriving benefit

summaryProblems.claim: The brick reasoning applies to the gentile who encircled the split barrel with his arms.
summaryProblems.pageSays: But where the barrel split widthwise and the gentile held the top and bottom halves together, it is permitted even for drinking.

judge.feedback: The summary says "When a barrel splits and a gentile throws his arms around it, he counts as a brick holding it shut, and the wine stays permitted for drinking.", but the page says "deemed it permitted to sell the wine to gentiles, as the wine was rendered prohibited only for drinking but not with regard to deriving benefit". Say what the page says. The summary says "The brick reasoning applies to the gentile who encircled the split barrel with his arms.", but the page says "But where the barrel split widthwise and the gentile held the top and bottom halves together, it is permitted even for drinking.". Say what the page says. The summary merges two distinct rulings: the barrel that split lengthwise and was hugged shut yields wine permitted only for sale and benefit, not drinking, while only the widthwise split, where the gentile holds the halves together, is permitted for drinking on the brick reasoning. Rewrite so those two cases stay separate. The question itself is strong and reaches the real tension between contact and intent, so keep it, though note that Rav Ashi's zav standard already puts one side of that answer on the page.

avodah-zarah/61.summary: A Jew treads a gentile's grapes so the wine can be sold to Jews, then leaves the barrels in the gentile's own house; wine a gentile handles is barred, on the assumption he poured some to an idol. Everything turns on whether he might be seen. An open window counts as public, so does a trash heap, so does a palm tree someone might climb, and Rav Aha and Ravina split over a palm tree with its top cut off.
avodah-zarah/61.question: If a fruitless palm keeps a man honest only because someone might climb it hunting a lost animal, how slim can the chance of being watched get before it stops working?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the prohibition rests on a probabilistic deterrent — being possibly observed — and asks where that probability becomes too thin to deter.

answer.quote: If the gentile can be caught as a thief if he touches the wine, the wine is permitted. Since he is afraid of being caught he does not have
answer.explanation: Rava's ruling gives one measure of how much fear of exposure suffices — enough that the gentile lacks presence of mind to make a libation — but the page leaves the fruitless-palm dispute between Rav Aḥa and Ravina unresolved, so the question of how remote the chance may be still stands.

avodah-zarah/62.summary: A gentile hires a Jewish laborer to help produce wine meant for pouring out to an idol, and the mishna forbids the Jew from benefiting from the pay. The Gemara tries twice to explain why the money itself is tainted, fails both times, and Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that it is simply a penalty the Sages imposed. Later a man rents out his ship to haul gentile wine, is paid in wheat, and Rav Ḥisda tells him to burn it and bury it.
avodah-zarah/62.question: If the forbidden wage is only a penalty the Sages chose to impose, why must the wheat be destroyed as thoroughly as the stone that killed a condemned man?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition that exists only as a Sages' penalty carries the same real, physical consequences as an intrinsically forbidden object.

avodah-zarah/63.summary: A man promises a prostitute a particular lamb and hands it over three years later, and the question is whether that lamb is still payment barred from the altar. The argument turns on the exact moment it became hers: the words he spoke, the act of pulling the animal, or the lamb already standing in her courtyard. The page closes with a man hired to smash barrels of wine poured for idols, who needs those barrels intact until he swings.
avodah-zarah/63.question: Can the barrel smasher's wage be clean when, right up to the moment he swings, he has an interest in those barrels surviving?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a temporary stake in an idolatrous object's survival taints a wage earned by destroying it.

answer.quote: Rav Naḥman said: He may break them, and let a blessing come upon him.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this dilemma about the breaker's interest in the barrels surviving and Rav Naḥman rules that the act is permitted and praiseworthy, with the stated reason that any action reducing impropriety is permitted.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 63b: "Rav Naḥman said: He may break them, and let a blessing come upon him.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is simply the Gemara's own dilemma, which the page answers a line later with Rav Naḥman's ruling that he may break them and a blessing should come upon him. Ask instead about what stays hard after that ruling, or about the reason given for it, such as why 'reducing impropriety' outweighs the breaker's interest here but 'hoeing together with a gentile' in a field of diverse kinds is still questioned. Alternatively build the question on the lamb material, where the page leaves Rav Hoshaya's dilemma about mere consecration unresolved.

avodah-zarah/64.summary: A Jew is owed a hundred dinars, silver coins, by a gentile who sells an idol and brings the money; that payment is permitted. But if the gentile first says to wait until he sells the idol, the money is forbidden, because the creditor now wants the idol to survive until the sale. That wish is the whole difference, and it nearly collapses when a convert splits his father's estate with his gentile brother, taking cash while the brother takes the idols.
avodah-zarah/64.question: If a creditor's hope that an idol stays intact long enough to be sold taints the money, why is the convert's identical hope excused only by the worry that he might otherwise go back to his old life?

judge.reachNote: Whether wanting an idol to survive is itself the taint, or whether that criterion can be suspended for policy reasons.

answer.quote: The inheritance of a convert is different, as the Sages were lenient with regard to it, as a rabbinic decree, lest he return to his corrupted ways
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa states outright that the convert's case is a special rabbinic leniency, after the page has explicitly tried and rejected the substantive distinctions (shards, Hadrianic earthenware) that the question implicitly asks about.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 64a: "The inheritance of a convert is different, as the Sages were lenient with regard to it, as a rabbinic decree, lest he return to his corrupted ways". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates Rav Pappa's own answer — the convert is excused by a rabbinic leniency lest he return to his corrupted ways — so the page answers it in so many words. Ask something the page leaves standing instead: for example, why the earlier attempts (value spread among shards, Hadrianic earthenware) were thought worth making at all if desire that the object not be stolen or lost defeats them, or what "desires its preservation" has to mean if it can be defeated by the idol being breakable. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page closely.

avodah-zarah/65.summary: Rav Yehuda sends a gift to a gentile named Avidarna on a festival day, arguing that a man he knows does not worship idols falls outside the ban. Rava does the same for a powerful minister, bar Sheshakh, and finds him sitting neck-deep in rose water with naked prostitutes, who asks whether the World-to-Come has anything finer. Rava answers that there, unlike here, no fear of the government hangs over anyone. A royal officer then summons bar Sheshakh to the king.
avodah-zarah/65.question: If bar Sheshakh had just conceded that Rava was right and wished him well, why is it his own eye that bursts under the curse he pronounced?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the irony that the man who conceded Rava's point turns out to be the eye that wished evil — a blessing spoken by a hostile mouth recoiling on its speaker.

avodah-zarah/66.summary: New wine poured as a libation to an idol falls onto grapes, and the question is whether any drop forbids them or only enough to be tasted. Abaye sorts mixtures by flavor, Rava by name, and since wine and grapes share a flavor but not a name, each ends up strict in one case and lenient in the next. The same pair then argues over smell, sniffed from a barrel's bunghole, the hole used for smelling wine.
avodah-zarah/66.question: If bread baked over burning cumin stalks is permitted because the stalks are gone, why should the smell of wine still sitting in the barrel be any more real?

judge.reachNote: Whether a smell counts as a substantial benefit depends on whether its source still exists — the very distinction Abaye draws on the page.

avodah-zarah/67.summary: Forbidden vinegar spills into split beans and spoils them, and the rule is that a flavor which makes food worse does not forbid the dish. Shmuel narrows it: cold beans are improved by the vinegar first, so heating them afterward forbids the pot, while Reish Lakish argues over a dish already short on salt. Rabbi Meir counters from gentile pots, purged by fire though their stale flavor could only hurt the food; Rabbi Shimon disagrees.
avodah-zarah/67.question: If vinegar that improves cold beans still forbids them once the heat turns it sour, at what moment is a dish's flavor actually decided?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether a mixture is judged by the flavor at the moment of contact or by its final taste — but the page names the answer (the initial flavor) in the same sentence the note summarizes.

answer.quote: it becomes like a dish that some added ingredient first enhanced its flavor and ultimately detracted from it, and it is rendered forbidden, as the initial flavor that was imparted was beneficial
answer.explanation: The page states outright that the moment of decision is the first imparting of flavor, since the initial beneficial flavor is what renders the heated dish forbidden.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 67a: "it becomes like a dish that some added ingredient first enhanced its flavor and ultimately detracted from it, and it is rendered forbidden, as the initial flavor that was imparted was beneficial". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the page has already said: the beans are forbidden because "the initial flavor that was imparted was beneficial," so the deciding moment is stated. Rebuild the question from the tension the page leaves open instead — Reish Lakish's lenient version says that "since now, in any event, the forbidden substance detracted from its flavor, it is permitted," which judges by the present state, against Shmuel's judging by the first contact. Or press on Rabbi Meir's inference from gentile pots, where a flavor that can only harm still prohibits.

avodah-zarah/68.summary: Forbidden vinegar falls into cold split beans and makes them worse, and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon argue over whether an ingredient that spoils a dish can still forbid it. Then a mouse drowns in a barrel of beer and Rav forbids the beer; Rav Sheshet says a mouse is so repulsive that its prohibition was already a surprise, so it forbids even when it ruins. Rav Shimi objects that field mice are royal delicacies. Rava cannot explain Rav's reasoning.
avodah-zarah/68.question: Was Rav's ruling about the flavor a mouse leaves in beer at all, or about the fact that a mouse was in it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition tracks the flavor a forbidden thing imparts or the identity of the forbidden thing itself.

answer.quote: it is a novelty that the Torah prohibits the flavor from a mouse at all, as it is repulsive and people distance themselves from consuming it
answer.explanation: Rav Sheshet explains Rav's ruling as resting on the mouse's special, repulsive status rather than on ordinary flavor rules, but Rava then declares Rav's actual reason unknown, so the question can still be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Forbidden vinegar falls into cold split beans and makes them worse.
summaryProblems.pageSays: as vinegar enhances the flavor of cold split beans, and it is consequently forbidden according to Rabbi Meir

judge.feedback: The summary says "Forbidden vinegar falls into cold split beans and makes them worse.", but the page says "as vinegar enhances the flavor of cold split beans, and it is consequently forbidden according to Rabbi Meir". Say what the page says. Fix the vinegar detail: the page says vinegar improves cold split beans, and only after they are heated does it detract, which is why Ulla calls it a case of enhancing first and detracting later; the detriment-from-the-outset case is plain split beans without the 'cold' qualifier. Keep the mouse thread, and when framing the question acknowledge that Rav Sheshet already offers the 'mouse is a novelty' answer and Rava still cannot decide, so the question should ask what remains unsettled after that.

avodah-zarah/69.summary: A mouse falls into a barrel of vinegar, and the rabbis argue how much vinegar it takes to swamp the taste of it: fifty times its volume, a hundred and one, finally sixty. The mishna then turns to wine left in a gentile's hands on a wagon, a ship, or in a shop, permitted unless the Jew announced he was leaving for a long while. Everything hinges on whether the man left behind thinks he might be walked in on.
avodah-zarah/69.question: If the mere chance of being surprised keeps a gentile from touching barrels on a ship, why does the bunghole, the small smelling hole in a barrel, undo the whole arrangement?

judge.reachNote: What actually restrains a person entrusted with another's goods: the risk of being caught, or the ease and undetectability of the act itself.

answer.quote: It is because of the bunghole, the hole in a barrel through which one smells the wine, which the gentile might widen a bit to drink from it.
answer.explanation: The page gives the bunghole as the reason wine is no longer entrusted in sealed barrels, but it does not explain why the fear of being surprised, which governs the mishna's cases, fails to deter here.

avodah-zarah/70.summary: A gentile is found standing among a Jew's barrels in a locked house, and Rava rules by sightlines: barrels visible through a crack in the door are permitted, the ones out of view are not. Case after case turns on what the gentile assumed about being watched, down to a man hiding from a roaring lion who figures a Jew may be hiding behind him. The wine's status rests on a stranger's private guess.
avodah-zarah/70.question: Why should a gentile who can explain his presence render the wine forbidden, while one who looks caught in the act leaves it fit to drink?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that wine's status depends on the gentile's fear of observation rather than on any actual act, but the page states that rationale outright.

avodah-zarah/71.summary: A gentile's touch turns wine into libation wine, which a Jew may not sell or profit from, so Rav told wine shopkeepers to take the dinars, silver coins, before measuring anything out. Ameimar holds that a gentile acquires goods by pulling them; Rav Ashi denies it and reads Rav's advice as his proof. The rebuttals then get very small: the jug's inner airspace, its bottom, a leftover drop on its mouth.
avodah-zarah/71.question: If the shopkeeper lends a gentile the coins and takes those same coins straight back, has anything changed besides the name of the transaction?

judge.reachNote: Whether the halakhic form of a transaction (loan repayment vs. sale price) is a real change or only a relabeling of the same exchange.

answer.quote: lend them dinars and then take those dinars back from them, so that it will be a loan provided to them that they are repaying
answer.explanation: The page states what the maneuver accomplishes — the money changes status from payment for libation wine to repayment of a debt — but it does not address whether that reclassification is more than nominal.

avodah-zarah/72.summary: A Jew measures wine through a funnel into a gentile's jug, then uses the same funnel for a Jew's jug, and the leftover drops in the funnel raise the question of whether a falling stream links what is above to what is below. Proof after proof is offered and each one collapses, since every clause implies the opposite of the clause beside it. Rav Hisda's advice to wine sellers is simply to pour in broken spurts.
avodah-zarah/72.question: If a stream of wine is too thin a thread to connect one vessel to another, why is a gentile's hand on a siphoning tube enough to forbid the whole barrel behind it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real distinction between a stream as a 'connection' and a gentile's force or contact reaching wine by suction — but the page draws that distinction itself.

answer.quote: It is different there, as all of the wine in the barrel is drawn toward the large tube and the small tube, and so it is as though the gentile had touched all of the wine
answer.explanation: Rava himself is asked exactly this question and answers that the barrel is forbidden not by the stream's connection but because all the wine is drawn toward the tubes, as if the gentile touched it all.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 72b: "It is different there, as all of the wine in the barrel is drawn toward the large tube and the small tube, and so it is as though the gentile had touched all of the wine". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim by Rava at the end of 72b: the barrel is forbidden because all the wine is drawn toward the tubes, as if the gentile touched it all, not because a stream connects. Rewrite the question to start after that answer — for example, why the Sages let a gentile's mere force forbid poured wine while refusing to decree on the wine left in the barrel, or why the stream question stays unresolved when every mishnaic clause cuts both ways. The summary is accurate and can stand largely as is.

avodah-zarah/73.summary: A drop of wine poured out for an idol forbids a whole cistern of ordinary wine, but spilled into water it forbids only if the taste carries. Rabbi Yohanan's move is arithmetic: when a pitcher of water also falls in, treat the permitted wine as though it were not there, leaving water against forbidden wine alone, and the water outnumbers it. The page then asks why untithed produce is held as strictly as idol wine.
avodah-zarah/73.question: If the permitted wine can be counted as though it were not there, what keeps that same accounting from dissolving any forbidden drop anywhere?

judge.reachNote: When may a legal fiction of treating permitted matter as nonexistent be deployed, and what stops such an accounting device from voiding the prohibition it is meant to measure.

answer.quote: one considers the permitted substance of the same type as though it were nonexistent so that the substance of the other type can nullify
answer.explanation: The page states that the disregarding works only because a permitted substance of a different type (the water) is present and large enough to nullify, and it also records Ḥizkiyya's refusal of the principle and Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda's requirement that the water fall in first — limits that bear on the question without fully settling why the device does not swallow every prohibition.

avodah-zarah/74.summary: The mishna lists forbidden things that stay forbidden no matter how small the trace, among them wine poured for an idol, an ox sentenced to stoning, and meat cooked in milk. The Gemara pins down the criterion, arguing each item is both significant enough to be counted on its own and forbidden to derive any benefit from. Later Rav, sent to inspect a winepress bought from a gentile, calls its pitch too smooth to absorb wine, then spots a crack underfoot full of it.
avodah-zarah/74.question: Did Rabbi Ḥiyya already suspect that a press this smooth could hide a soaked crack, or did he only know that fast rulings draw complaints?

judge.reachNote: Whether a teacher's warning encodes concrete prior knowledge of the trap or only a general discipline of slow, checkable ruling.

answer.quote: And this is what my uncle [ḥavivi] meant when he said to me: See to it that you do not cause people to complain against me in the study hall.
answer.explanation: The page reports Rav's retrospective realization that Ḥiyya's warning was apt, which bears on the question but never states whether Ḥiyya specifically suspected a wine-soaked crack rather than merely counseling caution.

avodah-zarah/75.summary: A pot bought from a gentile is purged in boiling water, a spit and grill are heated white-hot, a knife is polished, and a baraita adds that all of them still need immersion in a ritual bath of forty se'a. Since the source verse concerns metal spoils taken from Midian, an earth-and-dung pot is exempt, while glass counts because broken glass can be melted and made again. Mar bar Rav Ashi watched his father immerse a silver goblet held as a gentile's pledge, and never learned why.
avodah-zarah/75.question: If a pledged goblet counts as yours because the gentile seems unlikely to reclaim it, what happens the day he comes back with the money?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether obligation follows formal acquisition or merely the expectation that possession will become permanent.

answer.quote: whether this was because he maintained that possessing a utensil as collateral is considered like a purchase, or because he saw that the gentile's intention was to leave it
answer.explanation: The page raises the two possible rationales for immersing pledged utensils but leaves the matter unresolved and says nothing about what happens if the gentile redeems the pledge.

avodah-zarah/76.summary: A spit bought from a gentile has to be heated white-hot, but a spit used for sacrificial meat needs only purging in boiling water, and Rav Amram asks why. Rav Sheshet answers that one absorbed forbidden food while the other absorbed permitted food that only later became forbidden. Rava objects that whatever went in, what comes out is forbidden taste, and several rescues of the distinction fail before Rav Ashi revives it by calling flavor without substance a lenient thing.
avodah-zarah/76.question: If the taste seeping out of a spit is forbidden either way, why should it matter what that food was on the day it soaked in?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition is fixed by the status of the food when absorbed or by its status when it re-emerges.

answer.quote: at the time it expels flavor, the forbidden food is nonexistent in its substantive form. Since the forbidden substance expelled from the utensil is not the forbidden food itself but only its flavor, it is treated leniently
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi explicitly answers Rava's objection: because only flavor and not substance emerges, the status of the food at the moment of absorption is what counts.

summaryProblems.claim: Several rescues of Rav Sheshet's distinction fail before Rav Ashi revives it.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Pappa said that there is another resolution to the contradiction between mishnayot

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Avodah Zarah 76a: "at the time it expels flavor, the forbidden food is nonexistent in its substantive form. Since the forbidden substance expelled from the utensil is not the forbidden food itself but only its flavor, it is treated leniently". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Several rescues of Rav Sheshet's distinction fail before Rav Ashi revives it.", but the page says "Rav Pappa said that there is another resolution to the contradiction between mishnayot". Say what the page says. The question is exactly the objection Rav Ashi answers on the page ('at the time it expels flavor, the forbidden food is nonexistent in its substantive form'), so it cannot stand as written. Either press on what remains unsettled after that answer — why flavor alone should be judged leniently when it still renders food forbidden — or turn to untouched material, such as Rav Pappa's crustiness criterion or Rav Akavya's dough rim and the principle 'as it absorbs it so it expels it.' Also correct the summary: Rava's, Abaye's and Rav Pappa's proposals are alternative resolutions of the contradiction, not failed rescues of Rav Sheshet's distinction, and Rav Pappa's is never refuted.

horayot/2.summary: A court rules by mistake that forbidden fat is permitted; an ordinary person eats it on the court's word and owes no sin-offering. A judge who knew the court erred, or a student qualified to rule, eats the same fat and is liable. Abaye presses the point: a scholar of Ben Azzai's caliber could not have blundered, so his act was deliberate. The answer offered is that his error lay elsewhere, in thinking he must heed the Sages even when certain they are wrong.
horayot/2.question: If a scholar's only mistake was believing he had to obey a court he knew was wrong, is that obedience or is that the sin?
gate: gloss "sin-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: When does submitting to communal authority stop counting as obedience and become the sin one answers for?

answer.quote: erred with regard to the mitzva of heeding the statements of the Sages. Due to that error, they are liable to bring an offering.
answer.explanation: The page locates the scholar's unwitting error in the mitzva of heeding the Sages and rules him liable on that basis, but it does not settle whether his deference was itself the transgression or merely a mistaken premise, so the note's question can still be asked honestly.

horayot/3.summary: A court rules that forbidden fat is permitted, a minority of the people eat it, the court reverses itself and then errs again, and a second minority eats. Whether those two minorities combine into the majority that turns this into a communal sin, atoned for by a bull, is left unresolved, as are versions pairing fat with blood, or fat with idol worship. Later Rabbi Yehoshua says the chain on a condemned man's neck hangs on all ten judges, and Rav Huna seats ten reciters beside him.
horayot/3.question: If the weight of a ruling really splits into splinters among ten judges, where does the rest of the beam go?

judge.reachNote: Whether shared responsibility divides a fixed burden or replicates whole in each judge — the kolar on every neck against the splinter from the beam.

answer.quote: the chain [kolar] placed around the neck of the person taken to his punishment is suspended around the neck of all of them, i.e., they are all responsible
answer.explanation: The page sets out the competing picture — each judge bears the whole responsibility, not a fraction — but never says what becomes of the portion Rav Huna's splinter image leaves over, so the question survives.

horayot/4.summary: A court that rules there is no prohibition of labor on Shabbat at all brings no offering; a court that rules only that carrying out to the public domain is permitted does. Ulla finds this in "and the matter is hidden," reading the final mem twice so the phrase means part of a matter. Shmuel adds another exemption, for errors so obvious even the Sadducees, who read only the written Torah, would catch them, which pushes the Gemara to shrink the mishna's examples to ever finer slips.
horayot/4.question: If a court that denies Shabbat outright goes free, and a court whose error a schoolchild could catch goes free, what sort of mistake is the bull actually brought for?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what makes an error a 'ruling' at all rather than mere ignorance, but the page names that criterion outright.

answer.quote: A court is not liable to bring an offering unless it issues an erroneous ruling concerning a matter with which the Sadducees do not agree.
answer.explanation: The page states the positive criterion the question asks for — liability attaches to a fine, non-obvious detail of a mitzva — and then illustrates it repeatedly (initial stage of atypical intercourse, throwing between domains, bowing without extending arms and legs).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Horayot 4a: "A court is not liable to bring an offering unless it issues an erroneous ruling concerning a matter with which the Sadducees do not agree.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what kind of error the bull is brought for, and the page answers it directly: only a matter the Sadducees would not agree to, i.e. a detail of a mitzva that is not explicit in the written Torah, with the Gemara supplying example after example. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why forgetting a schoolchild's verse counts as no ruling while a subtle oral-Torah error counts as one, or Rav Yosef's still-open dilemma about abolishing plowing. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

horayot/5.summary: A court that knows it issued a mistaken ruling but has forgotten which ruling is exempt from the communal bull offering, since the verse requires that the sin became known to the court itself. That sits oddly beside Rabbi Eliezer, who holds a man who ate one of two forbidden pieces of meat and cannot say which still brings a sin-offering. The rest turns on counting how many times Leviticus says "congregation," and whether one tribe counts as one.
horayot/5.question: If a man who cannot recall which forbidden piece he swallowed still owes an offering, why does a court that admits it erred go free simply because it cannot name its own mistake?
gate: gloss "sin-offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether liability for an unwitting sin requires knowing that you sinned or knowing which sin you committed.

answer.quote: Here, in the baraita, it is different, as it is written: “And the sin that they sinned became known” (Leviticus 4:14). The verse underscores that the judges must be aware
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely the note's tension with Rabbi Eliezer and resolves it twice — first by saying the baraita is not Rabbi Eliezer's view, then by Rav Ashi's verse-based distinction requiring the judges to know the specific sin.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Horayot 5a: "Here, in the baraita, it is different, as it is written: “And the sin that they sinned became known” (Leviticus 4:14). The verse underscores that the judges must be aware". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and answered on the page: the Gemara first says the baraita is "not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer," and then Rav Ashi distinguishes the court from the individual because the verse demands that "the sin that they sinned became known." Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for instance, why the parallel individual verse, "or if his sin that he sinned became known to him," is read instead to exclude one who acts unawares, rather than to demand the same specific knowledge. The summary should also mention Rav Ashi's resolution so the question does not appear to ignore it.

horayot/6.summary: Ezra's returning exiles bring twelve goats as sin-offerings, animals offered to atone for an unwitting sin, and the Gemara asks how that can work when the idol worshippers of Zedekiah's day are long dead and an offering whose owner has died may not be sacrificed. Rav Pappa answers that a congregation never dies. The proof stumbles twice before landing on the elders who had seen the first Temple and wept louder than the young men shouted.
horayot/6.question: If a sin-offering exists for sins done unwittingly, what is left of that boundary once deliberate idol worship can be covered by a one-time emergency ruling?
gate: the question uses "sin offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Asks whether the unwitting/intentional distinction that defines the sin-offering survives when exigency can suspend it.

answer.quote: It was a provisional edict issued in exigent circumstances to enable them to sacrifice a sin-offering to atone for an intentional sin.
answer.explanation: The page states the emergency-ruling mechanism the question already assumes, and supports it by noting the rams and lambs were likewise a provisional edict, but it never addresses what remains of the unwitting/intentional boundary once such edicts are allowed.

horayot/7.summary: The argument opens by asking whether the anointed priest, the High Priest, resembles the whole community or the king when he sins after his own mistaken ruling. Logic pulls both ways, since he shares a bull offering with the community but shares goats and guilt-offerings with the king, so a verse settles it: he is treated like the community. The sharper trouble comes later, when he rules on fat covering the innards and the court rules on fat on the intestines.
horayot/7.question: If two rulings come from different verses but end in the same offering, has the priest sinned alone or with everyone else?
gate: gloss "guilt-offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What individuates one ruling from another: the Torah source of the prohibition or the offering it generates.

horayot/8.summary: Rav Ḥilkiya of Hagronya asks why a verse is needed to say that a whole city and a single person bring the same offering for unwitting idol worship. He runs through the animals: a bull is taken, a bull with a goat is taken, a goat belongs to the king's case, a female goat to the individual. The answer is that without the verse the city might have swapped bull and goat, or been left with nothing to bring.
horayot/8.question: If every animal was already spoken for, what would it mean for a whole city to owe an offering that does not exist?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is obligation without any possible means of discharging it, i.e., a liability with no remedy — but the page names that very outcome.

answer.quote: perhaps the majority of a city that unwittingly engaged in idol worship must bring an offering, but it has no remedy, because there is no unique offering that it can bring
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself spells out what an obligation with every animal taken would mean — a city bound to bring an offering yet left with no remedy — which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Horayot 8a: "perhaps the majority of a city that unwittingly engaged in idol worship must bring an offering, but it has no remedy, because there is no unique offering that it can bring". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in the same line the summary already paraphrases: the Gemara says the city "has no remedy, because there is no unique offering that it can bring." Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for example, why each class of sinner must have an offering of its own rather than sharing one, or what the Gemara gains by rejecting Rav Ḥilkiya's objection with a reversal of bull and goat. Keep the summary as is; only the question needs replacing.

horayot/9.summary: The sliding-scale offering, a sheep from the wealthy, two doves from the poor, a measure of flour from the very poor, applies only to a person who can swing between wealth and poverty. That excludes the king and the High Priest, though if the High Priest happens to have no money, the other priests are to make him rich from their own property. Ravina asks about a king struck with leprosy and removed from office; since he would pay from his personal treasury, he stays exempt.
horayot/9.question: If the High Priest's wealth has to be handed to him by his fellow priests, in what sense was he ever a man who cannot become poor?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether the exemption rests on personal wealth or on an office whose status is maintained by others' property.

answer.quote: Make him great from the property of his brethren, who will provide him with enough property to render him wealthy.
answer.explanation: The page states the mechanism that guarantees the High Priest's wealth, which bears directly on why he is treated as one who cannot become poor, though it does not address the conceptual tension the question raises about wealth that is conferred rather than owned.

horayot/10.summary: A king who sinned before his coronation brings the sin-offering of an ordinary person, and the Gemara hunts for the verse that blocks the obvious inference. The word asher in "when a king sins" then opens a long run on straight paths and crooked walkers: two men roasting Paschal lambs, one dutiful and one greedy, an analogy Reish Lakish throws out as unfair. It lands on Lot in the cave, convicted by a dot over a single letter.
horayot/10.question: If Lot and his daughters walked the same road that night, what makes their intention enough to call them righteous and his second night of drinking enough to call him a transgressor?

judge.reachNote: One road, two walkers: intent alone decides whether the same act makes a person righteous or a transgressor.

answer.quote: With regard to Lot, who intended his action for the sake of a transgression, it is written: "And transgressors will stumble in them."
answer.explanation: The page itself supplies the distinction the question asks for — the daughters acted for the sake of a mitzva while Lot acted for the sake of transgression — and then explains that his drinking a second night proves intent: "He should have derived from it that on the following night he should not drink."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Horayot 10b: "With regard to Lot, who intended his action for the sake of a transgression, it is written: "And transgressors will stumble in them."". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara already answers — the daughters intended a mitzva, Lot intended transgression, and his second night of drinking is what the dotted vav is brought to prove. Rewrite it to press on what remains hard after that answer: e.g. why the daughters' mistaken belief that the world was destroyed is credited as mitzva-intent at all, or why the Gemara rejects the Paschal-lamb and dark-house analogies and insists the case must involve a single shared path. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

horayot/11.summary: A man eats half an olive-bulk of forbidden fat, the fat of an ox or a sheep that may not be eaten, is then crowned king, and finishes the rest. Since a king's sin-offering, the animal brought to atone for an unwitting transgression, is a male goat rather than the commoner's female goat, the two halves do not combine. Rava then asks what happens if the crown comes and goes between bites, and the attempt to settle it from the case of an apostate is rejected.
horayot/11.question: If a coronation can split one act of eating into two halves that never add up, is the offering atoning for the act or for the person?

judge.reachNote: Whether the sin-offering is keyed to the transgressive act itself or to the legal identity of the person who must atone.

answer.quote: Therefore, the verse teaches us that the status of a king is not like that of a commoner.
answer.explanation: The page ties the non-combining of the two halves to the eater's changed status, and the dispute over whether liability follows "the time of knowledge" or "the time of the performance of the sin" bears directly on act-versus-person, but the Gemara leaves the related dilemma standing unresolved, so the question survives.'

horayot/12.summary: When a High Priest was temporarily disqualified, the other priests appointed Yosef ben Eilim of Tzippori in his place. Rabbi Yosei reports that once the first priest returned, Yosef was barred from serving as High Priest, since two of equal rank would breed jealousy and bitterness, and barred from serving as an ordinary priest, since sanctity is raised and never lowered. Rabbi Meir holds instead that the substitute keeps all the obligations of the high priesthood.
horayot/12.question: Yosef ben Eilim did nothing wrong and ended up with no post at all, so whose jealousy is the rule guarding against?

judge.reachNote: Institutional peace and the one-way ratchet of sanctity outweigh the innocent substitute's own claim to a post.

answer.quote: Neither as a High Priest, due to enmity, jealousy, and bitterness that would be engendered if there were two High Priests with equal standing in the Temple.
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason as the rivalry that two co-equal High Priests would generate, though it does not say explicitly whose jealousy is feared or address the unfairness to Yosef, so the question can still be pressed.

horayot/13.summary: A bull for the anointed priest's error is offered before the bull for the congregation's, and the ranking runs on down to people: whom to rescue first, whom to ransom from captivity. Then the mishna breaks its own ladder, since a mamzer, born of a forbidden union, who is a Torah scholar precedes an ignorant High Priest. It closes with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel demanding sharper deference than Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Natan receive, and the two plotting to expose him on a tractate he does not know.
horayot/13.question: If learning outranks lineage and office, what exactly is Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel defending when he insists that people rise for him differently than for Rabbi Meir?

judge.reachNote: Whether rank in Israel rests on learning or on office, and what an officeholder retains once wisdom is declared supreme.

answer.quote: Shouldn’t there be a conspicuous distinction between me and them in terms of the manner in which deference is shown?
answer.explanation: The page gives Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's own stated motive — that the office of Nasi must be visibly distinguished from his subordinates — but it does not resolve how that squares with the mishna's ruling that Torah wisdom surpasses all else, so the question can still be asked honestly.

horayot/14.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi cites rulings without naming the sages behind them, and his son asks why they drink these men's water but never say their names; the answer is that those sages once tried to strip his father's house of its standing. The son argues the old grudge died with them, and his father half yields, teaching the ruling in the name of Rabbi Meir without ever saying "Rabbi Meir said." The rest weighs the walking library against the incisive mind, and leaves one such comparison unresolved.
horayot/14.question: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi finally says "the Sages said in the name of Rabbi Meir," has he conceded his son's point or found a way around it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a half-attribution honors the truth of a teaching or merely preserves a grudge under cover of form.

answer.quote: who is humble, taught: The Sages said in the name of Rabbi Meir. But he did not say directly: Rabbi Meir said.
answer.explanation: Rava's comment marks the attribution as deliberately partial — even the humble Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi stopped short of naming Rabbi Meir outright — which bears on the question without settling whether this counts as concession or evasion.

zevachim/2.summary: The mishna opens with an animal slaughtered while the slaughterer had a different offering in mind: it stays fit for sacrifice and eating, but the owner has not discharged his obligation, with the Paschal offering and the sin offering as exceptions. Rava sets this against a bill of divorce written without naming the wife, which is void, while slaughter with no stated intent counts as correct. His resolution is that a consecrated animal already stands designated for its purpose; a wife does not.
zevachim/2.question: Why should a consecrated animal be presumed to be headed for its own purpose while a marriage is presumed to be headed nowhere in particular?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of designation-by-status standing in for stated intent — but that is the very resolution the page supplies.

answer.quote: Ordinary slaughtered offerings stand designated for their own sake. From the time that the offering is consecrated, its presumed end is that it will be slaughtered
