answer.quote: Rabbi Yoḥanan says: This cannot serve as a proof with regard to the halakhot of consecrated matters.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan states the distinction itself — chained derivation works for the rest of the Torah but not for consecrated matters, and proves it from the guilt offering's explicit juxtapositions — yet the page never gives a reason why consecrated matters are different, so the note's 'why' still stands.

zevachim/50.summary: Three offerings must be slaughtered on the north side of the Temple courtyard, and the page asks why the Torah states it for each one separately instead of letting one teach the others. Behind it lies a larger question: may a law that was itself learned by inference go on to teach a third law by another kind of inference? The chain finally breaks when an argument is rejected as the grandchild of an inference rather than its child.
zevachim/50.question: If a conclusion drawn from a conclusion still counts, why should the very next link in the chain be too far?

judge.reachNote: How far a derivation may travel from its scriptural source before the chain of inference loses authority.

answer.quote: It is not the son of an a fortiori inference, but the grandson of an a fortiori inference, which cannot be used.
answer.explanation: The page states the rule that a second-generation a fortiori inference is disqualified, and then repairs the argument so it is only the "son" of an inference, but it never explains why one further link is too far.

zevachim/51.summary: A baraita asks why blood of an offering that was left out overnight, once placed on the altar, is not taken back down. Its answer runs in a chain: from meat of a peace offering, eaten for two days and one night, to the portions burned on the altar, to the blood, each link serving as the model for the next. Then the Gemara concedes that a verse about the burnt offering resting on the altar all night covers all of it.
zevachim/51.question: If one verse already keeps every disqualified offering on the altar, what is the chain of derivations still doing there?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what exegetical chains are for once a verse settles the law — but the page answers it with 'mere supports.'

answer.quote: which amplified it, teaching that many types of disqualified offerings may be left upon the altar. The derivations written in the baraita are mere supports for those halakhot.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself states that once the verse is relied upon, the baraita's chain of derivations functions only as supports (asmakhta), which is exactly what the note asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 51a: "which amplified it, teaching that many types of disqualified offerings may be left upon the altar. The derivations written in the baraita are mere supports for those halakhot.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in so many words: the derivations are "mere supports" once the verse from Leviticus 6:2 is relied upon. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than asking for it. For instance, press on why the Gemara nonetheless used this baraita as proof that a matter derived via a paradigm can teach via a paradigm, if its derivations are only supports.

zevachim/52.summary: After blood is sprinkled on the inner altar inside the Sanctuary, whatever is left is poured at the base of the outer altar. The page argues whether skipping that pouring ruins the offering, and notices that Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva build the same inference except that Akiva adds four words about atonement. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi carries the strict view to its end: a second bull, slaughtered, and all the inner sprinkling done over again.
zevachim/52.question: If the leftover blood is precisely the part that effects no atonement, why should spilling it cost a whole second bull?

judge.reachNote: Can a rite that effects no atonement still be indispensable to the offering — is essentiality the same thing as atoning power?

answer.quote: One Sage, Rabbi Yishmael, holds that failure to pour the remainder of the blood does disqualify the offering. And one Sage, Rabbi Akiva, who adds the words
answer.explanation: Rav Adda bar Ahava ties the dispute to the extra phrase "does not come for atonement," showing the strict view does not treat non-atoning status as decisive, but the page never states why a non-atoning remnant should be essential enough to require a second bull.

zevachim/53.summary: A priest climbs the altar ramp with blood on his index finger, and Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar argue whether he must hit the exact edge of each corner or anywhere within a cubit of it. A red line painted around the altar's middle divides blood placed high from blood placed low. The page ends with geometry becoming geography: the southeast corner had no base because that one cubit of ground belonged to Judah, not Benjamin.
zevachim/53.question: Why should an invisible line between two tribes' portions, drawn generations earlier, disqualify one corner of an altar that all of them shared?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that ritual fitness can depend on inherited land allotment rather than on the altar's own structure or sanctity.

answer.quote: Because it was not in the portion of land of the one who tears, i.e., the tribe of Benjamin
answer.explanation: The page states that the tribal boundary is the reason the southeast corner lacked a base, but it never explains why a tribal portion should govern the altar's fitness, so the note's question survives.

zevachim/54.summary: A priest climbing the altar ramp pinches a bird's head off with his thumbnail at the southeast corner, the one corner said to have no base. If there is no base, he is working over empty air, outside the altar's domain; Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak answers that when the tribes divided the land, the airspace there went to Benjamin while the ground stayed Judah's. Rav and Levi then argue over what having no base means: missing stone, or stone that blood may not touch.
zevachim/54.question: If Benjamin holds only the air above that corner and Judah holds the stone beneath it, where is the bird's blood actually being offered?

judge.reachNote: Whether sacred space can be split vertically — air consecrated to one tribe, ground to another — and which layer a rite actually happens in.

answer.quote: The airspace of what would become the southeast part of the altar is in the portion of the tribe of Benjamin, so the pinching of the bird offering was performed within the domain of the altar.
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's condition resolves the domain problem for the pinching itself, and the baraita says the priest "would squeeze out its blood on the wall of the altar," but the page never says whose portion that blood-presentation counts as, and Levi even holds "no blood was sprinkled on that side."

zevachim/55.summary: Shmuel rules that peace offerings slaughtered before the doors of the Sanctuary were opened are disqualified, since the verse places their slaughter at the entrance, and a locked entrance is not one. The Gemara then tests the edges: a curtain over the doorway still counts as open, and two small openings eight cubits high, plus a niche behind the Sanctuary, made far corners of the courtyard count as facing it. Being "before the Tent of Meeting" turns out to be something carpentry can arrange.
zevachim/55.question: If cutting two small wickets into a wall makes the far western corner of the courtyard count as facing the entrance, what work is the word "entrance" still doing?
gate: gloss "peace offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Whether "at the entrance" names a real relation to the Sanctuary or a legal status that construction can confer on any spot.

answer.quote: This means when the entrance of the Sanctuary is open, and not when it is locked.
answer.explanation: The page shows one job the word "entrance" keeps doing — it requires a functioning, open doorway in time — but it never confronts why spatial facing can be engineered by wickets and a niche while openness cannot be waived.

zevachim/56.summary: The Temple courtyard measured 187 cubits by 135, and side chambers built on unconsecrated ground open into it. Priests may eat the most sacred offerings inside those chambers, yet Rava holds they may not slaughter there and incur no karet, the penalty of being cut off, for entering while impure. Later the page takes up a peace offering on the night after its second day: Ḥizkiyya calls it still valid, Rabbi Yoḥanan calls it already rejected.
zevachim/56.question: If the peace offering's meat may no longer be eaten on that second night but may not be burned until morning, what is it during those hours?
gate: gloss "peace offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What is the standing of consecrated meat that has fallen out of the time for eating but has not yet entered the time for burning — limbo or already rejected?

answer.quote: Ḥizkiyya says that the offering is valid because on the evening preceding the third day, the peace offering has not yet been removed from its previous status and designated for burning
answer.explanation: The page supplies two competing characterizations of the meat's status in those hours — Ḥizkiyya's "not yet removed from its previous status" and Rabbi Yoḥanan's "rejected from being eaten" — but leaves the status itself contested rather than defining it.

zevachim/57.summary: The Sages in the vineyard at Yavne, their study hall, are asked how long priests may eat the meat of a firstborn animal given to them. Rabbi Tarfon likens it to peace offerings, eaten two days and one night; Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, a student there for the first time, likens it to sin and guilt offerings, eaten one day and one night. Both cite the same rule, judge from the most similar case, and reach opposite answers.
zevachim/57.question: If both men agree that a case should be judged from the case it most resembles, what makes a firstborn more like a peace offering than like the other gifts a priest receives?

judge.reachNote: When two sages both reason from 'the most similar case' and reach opposite results, what actually fixes similarity — shared sanctity, shared mode of giving, or a verse.

answer.quote: The verse juxtaposes firstborn offerings with a breast and thigh of peace offerings. Just as peace offerings are eaten for two days and one night, so too, a firstborn offering
answer.explanation: Rabbi Akiva breaks the deadlock not by ranking the resemblances but by citing a verse that ties the firstborn to peace offerings, so the page settles the dispute without ever saying what makes the firstborn intrinsically more like a peace offering.

zevachim/58.summary: Offerings of the most sacred order are supposed to be slaughtered in the northern part of the Temple courtyard, so the mishna asks about one slaughtered on top of the altar itself. Rabbi Yosei calls it valid; Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, splits the altar, its northern half fit and its southern half not. Rabbi Zeira, unwilling to accept a claim no mishna supports, goes out and finds one, measuring four cubits from the altar's southwest corner, until someone counts those cubits differently.
zevachim/58.question: If the same four cubits can be tallied two ways to place the altar in the north or dead center of the courtyard, did Rabbi Zeira find his proof or build it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a proof sought out to confirm a claim already held is discovery or construction — the page's own four cubits can be tallied either way.

zevachim/59.summary: Rav rules that when the altar is damaged, animals slaughtered in the courtyard are disqualified, and then admits the verse behind the ruling has been forgotten. Rav Kahana travels from Babylonia and hears Rabbi Shimon quote a line about slaughtering on an altar of earth, read as: slaughter when the altar is whole, not when it is lacking. Rabbi Yoḥanan goes further, holding that even animals not yet slaughtered are set aside for good.
zevachim/59.question: If Rav taught the ruling for years without its verse, what was the ruling standing on until Rav Kahana went looking?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: Asks what authority a halakha carries when its scriptural source is lost but the ruling is still taught.

answer.quote: We have a verse as the source for this halakha but we have forgotten which one it is
answer.explanation: The page says only that Rav held a received tradition that a verse existed, which bears on the question without saying what authority the ruling rested on in the interim.

zevachim/60.summary: Rabbi Elazar rules that when the altar is damaged, priests may not eat the leftover flour of a meal offering, reading "beside the altar" as a limit in time rather than place: only while the altar is whole. Abaye pushes the rule down to offerings of lesser sanctity, by a chain of verses tying second-tithe produce to a firstborn animal. Rabbi Yirmeya, hearing this in Eretz Yisrael, calls the Babylonians fools from a dark land and points to the wilderness.
zevachim/60.question: If sacrificial food stayed fit to eat while the whole Tabernacle traveled dismantled in the wilderness, why should a damaged altar standing in place spoil a priest's meal?
gate: gloss "second-tithe" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Tabernacle", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the altar disqualifies eating because it is physically absent or because it must be intact — is the altar a place or a condition?

answer.quote: this first baraita is referring to offerings of the most sacred order, and that second baraita is referring to offerings of lesser sanctity
answer.explanation: The page raises the very tension the question names and offers a resolution by sorting the two baraitot into most-sacred versus lesser-sanctity offerings, but Ravina then reopens it ("Both this baraita and that baraita are referring to offerings of lesser sanctity") and the answer is left unfinished at the end of the daf.

zevachim/61.summary: Rav Huna says the altar at Shiloh was built of stone, which collides with a report that the fire fallen from Heaven in Moses' day rested on the copper altar until Solomon replaced it. The answers keep that fire half-present: it threw sparks toward the stone altar, or it came and went like a guest. The page then asks why the Second Temple altar was enlarged by four cubits on two sides, and offers two unrelated reasons.
zevachim/61.question: If the extra cubits were added so that poured wine could drain through the altar itself, why does Rav Yosef still need the departed heavenly fire to explain them?

zevachim/62.summary: The returning exiles could trace the Temple's outline from the vestiges of its foundations, but the altar left no such mark. Rabbi Elazar says they saw a vision of the archangel Michael offering sacrifices on the spot; Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani says incense scented the whole House while that one place smelled of burnt flesh. An early teaching holds that the altar's corner, ramp, base and square shape are indispensable, while its length, width and height are not.
zevachim/62.question: If offerings can be brought even when no Temple stands, why does the altar's exact spot need an angel, a prophet, or a smell to fix it?

judge.reachNote: The altar's place, not the building around it, is what carries the service — so location is fixed while measurements are negotiable.

answer.quote: one who testified to them that one sacrifices offerings even if there is no Temple, provided that there is a proper altar
answer.explanation: The page's phrase "provided that there is a proper altar" indicates that the altar, not the House, is what makes offering possible, which bears on why its site had to be fixed, though the page never states why the location specifically is indispensable while its dimensions are not.

zevachim/63.summary: Rabbi Elazar holds that a handful of flour may be scooped from a meal offering inside the Sanctuary, the inner room, not just in the outer courtyard. Rabbi Yoḥanan pushes further: the courtyard, of lesser holiness, should not outrank the holier room, so peace offerings slaughtered inside are valid. But a baraita needed a separate verse to let besieged priests eat offerings in the Sanctuary, and the answer turns on a servant's manners: one works before his master, not eats.
zevachim/63.question: If a priest can slaughter in the inner room because no lesser space should outrank a holier one, why does eating there need a verse of its own?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the 'lesser sanctity cannot outrank greater' inference depends on the act being service rendered before the Master, not merely on the holiness of the space.

answer.quote: in the case of eating sacrificial food, which is different because a person does not eat in the presence of his master, we do not say the rationale
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly distinguishes slaughter (service performed before one's master) from eating, which is why eating in the Sanctuary requires its own verse.

Rava answers with a verb form: the verse says the leftover blood shall be drained, by itself, so it must be sprinkled low enough to run down.

Rabbi Akiva blocks the inference by rereading the word "priest" to mean the priest's own body, his thumbnail, and the page then argues over how deep the cut may go.

zevachim/66.summary: A priest who squeezes out the blood from a bird burnt offering's body but not its head has still done it right; the reverse disqualifies. Ravina admits there is no proof in the wording, only the reasoning that most of the blood sits in the body. The mishna then sorts bird offerings by height on the altar, rite, and intent, and Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua split over whether a burnt offering handled entirely as a sin offering still makes benefiting from it a misuse of Temple property.

Rava notices that Eliezer still had a fourth case in hand, one with a deviation about the owner too, and never used it.
zevachim/67.question: If Rabbi Eliezer had another counterexample available, does his silence mean he was persuaded, or only that he was finished arguing?

zevachim/68.summary: A woman whose bird offerings got so scrambled that nobody knows which was sacrificed as what must bring seven more, and Rabbi Yehoshua caps it with a proverb: a live sheep makes one sound, a dead one seven, from its horns, shinbones, skin and guts. zevachim/69.summary: A priest pinches the nape of a bird offering, and the bird turns out to be a tereifa, fatally wounded and unfit; Rabbi Meir says an olive-bulk of its meat does not make a swallower impure, Rabbi Yehuda says it does. Rabbi Meir argues from the lighter case: if slaughtering an animal keeps even a wounded one from counting as a carcass, pinching a bird should too. Rabbi Yosei caps the inference, and the Gemara then claims Meir was reading a verse all along.
zevachim/69.question: Rabbi Meir is credited with a verse he never quoted, so is the Gemara explaining his ruling or quietly swapping in better reasoning for it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of attributed reasoning: when the Gemara supplies a verse a sage never cited, is it recovering his logic or rebuilding it to survive an objection.

answer.quote: Rabbi Meir does require that a fortiori inferences conform to this principle. But he does not actually infer his opinion a fortiori; rather, he found a verse and interpreted it.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that Meir's real basis is a verse (Leviticus 11:46) rather than the a fortiori argument, but it never addresses whether this is a recovery of his reasoning or a reconstruction imposed on him, so the note's question survives.

zevachim/70.summary: One word, tereifa, meaning an animal with a fatal injury, drives the opening argument over why the verse bothers to say that the fat of a carcass and the fat of a tereifa may be used for any other service. Rava's answer is that it stacks liability, two prohibitions in a single bite. Later Rabbi Elazar reports that Rabbi Meir deems a goose or chicken pinched at the nape pure, though such birds are never offerings, and Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a goat's broken neck.
zevachim/70.question: If pinching the nape keeps a chicken that could never be an offering from imparting carcass impurity, is the act doing the work or the animal?

judge.reachNote: Whether a ritual act purifies by its own form or only because the animal belongs to a species for which that act is meaningful.

answer.quote: It is because they are species of birds and the napes of some birds are pinched; but a goat is not
answer.explanation: The Gemara, in weighing Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma, offers the reasoning that pinching works for geese and chickens because they belong to a species whose napes are pinched, which bears on whether act or animal does the work but is left as an unresolved side of a dilemma.

zevachim/71.summary: The mishna lists animals that can never reach the altar: an ox sentenced to stoning for killing a person, an animal used for bestiality, one given as a prostitute's payment, the offspring of a ram and a goat. Mix a single one of these into a flock of proper offerings and the whole mixture is doomed, even one in ten thousand. The Gemara then spends the page asking why a nearly identical ruling already appears in tractate Temura.
zevachim/71.question: Why does one condemned ox swallow ten thousand fit animals, when in almost every other mixture the majority swallows the minority?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of nullification itself: why certain prohibitions are not diluted by a majority but instead spread to everything they touch.

answer.quote: The halakha is stringent with regard to them, as they are items from which deriving benefit is prohibited
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi gives a reason for the stringency — these are items from which benefit is forbidden, so they are not nullified in a majority — but the page never explains why that category resists nullification, so the question can still be pressed.

zevachim/72.summary: One forbidden animal mixed into a group of valid offerings does not dissolve into the majority, and the Gemara presses on why not. The answer offered is that animals are significant, since they are counted one by one, which drags in an older dispute over fenugreek bundles grown illegally in a vineyard: does counted mean always sold by unit, or only sometimes? Rabbi Yoḥanan reads it strictly, Reish Lakish loosely, and Rav Pappa must find another tanna.
zevachim/72.question: If a sealed barrel of wine is too much itself to vanish among two hundred others, why should a single animal lose its identity just because herds are sometimes sold by the lot?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether market practice (how an item is customarily sold) is a sound measure of an item's individual significance, i.e. what makes a thing too much itself to dissolve into a majority.

answer.quote: And the Rabbis say: Only six items are sufficiently significant to render their mixture prohibited. Rabbi Akiva says: There are seven.
answer.explanation: The page indicates that sealed barrels of wine resist nullification because they belong to a short closed list of significant items, which does not include animals, but it never justifies why the 'exclusively counted' criterion should draw the line there, and Rav Pappa's reply only reassigns the mishna to another tanna.

zevachim/73.summary: A litra of untithed dried figs, pressed onto the opening of one barrel among many holding tithed figs, cannot be traced to its barrel. The Sages argue whether figs sold by the piece can ever be diluted into a majority, and the same question governs a disqualified animal mixed into a herd of fit ones. Then someone proposes shuffling the animals, drawing one out, and calling it a member of the majority; Rava blocks it with a decree, revising his reason twice.
zevachim/73.question: If Rava has to abandon two explanations before settling on a decree made only to protect another decree, what is really keeping these animals off the altar?

judge.reachNote: Whether the animals are barred by something real in them (significance, permanent rejection) or only by a chain of protective decrees.

answer.quote: living creatures that become disqualified are permanently rejected from being sacrificed on the altar, and this animal was rejected when it was part of the mixture
answer.explanation: After Rava's decrees are whittled down, the page supplies a substantive ground — the animal's permanent rejection (and, per Rav Ashi, that living creatures are significant and not nullified) — though it is offered to defend a different Rava statement, so the question can still be asked honestly.

zevachim/74.summary: A ring used in idol worship falls into a hundred permitted rings, and then one ring drops into the Great Sea. Rav rules the rest are permitted, because the ring that sank is assumed to be the forbidden one. Rabba and Rav Yosef then split over a fig: too small for its departure from the pile to be noticed, which for Rabba means the same trick no longer works.
zevachim/74.question: If the missing ring can be assumed to be the forbidden one, why should it matter whether anybody saw it go?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether the leniency rests on a probabilistic assumption about the lost item or on what bystanders can observe — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: the halakha is lenient only in the case of a barrel of teruma, as its falling is noticeable, and everyone will know that the other barrels were permitted due to the one that fell
answer.explanation: The page explicitly explains that noticeability matters because onlookers must be able to see why the remainder was permitted, so they will not permit mixtures where nothing fell out.

Rabbi Ami shuts the door, saying the priest cannot hand over more than he received.

zevachim/76.summary: Priests may eat offerings roasted or boiled and may season them with teruma, the portion set aside for priests, even though that shortens the window in which the teruma can be eaten. The test case is oil of teruma cooked into Sabbatical Year vegetables, and whether squeezing the oil back out counts as a fix.

answer.explanation: Ravina asserts that squeezing constitutes a remedy, but the page never explains in what sense it works, and Rav Yosef's two-pronged reply (too hard wastes produce, too little is ineffective) leaves the force of Ravina's claim unexplained.

zevachim/77.summary: Limbs of a sin offering, which priests are supposed to eat, get mixed up with limbs of a burnt offering, which belong on the altar fire. Rabbi Eliezer burns the whole pile and declares the sin offering's meat to be firewood; the Rabbis say let it all rot and burn it outside. Watch where the Rabbis draw their line: they allow the firewood fiction for sin offering meat, but not for a blemished animal's limbs, because those are repulsive.
zevachim/77.question: If a sin offering's flesh can be reclassified as firewood, why can't the same words be said over the limbs of a blemished animal?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of a legal fiction — when may a forbidden substance be redescribed as fuel — but the page already states the answer, and the note's own summary repeats it.

answer.quote: these limbs are repulsive, and therefore they may not be brought upon the altar, even as wood
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks how the Rabbis distinguish the two mixtures and answers that blemished limbs are repulsive while sin offering flesh is not, which is exactly the note's question.

summaryProblems.claim: The Rabbis say let it all rot and burn it outside.

zevachim/78.summary: Water mixed into an offering's blood stays fit for sprinkling on the altar as long as the mixture still looks like blood. Rabbi Yoḥanan narrows that: only if the water fell into the blood. Pour blood into water and each drop is swallowed as it lands, so nothing is left to present, though Rav Pappa says blood that falls into water can still require covering, since its cancellation was only temporary.
zevachim/78.question: If a drop of blood lost in water can return to itself once enough blood joins it, why can the same mixture never come back for the altar?

judge.reachNote: Whether nullification is a permanent loss of identity or a temporary state that can be undone, and why the purpose of the act (mitzva vs. altar service) should decide.

answer.quote: The blood is not nullified by the water because there is no permanent rejection with regard to mitzvot, i.e., its nullification was merely temporary
answer.explanation: The page limits the reversal of nullification to the domain of mitzvot (covering the blood), which hints at why presentation blood is not revived, but it never states why offering blood is permanently rejected, so the question can still be asked.

zevachim/79.summary: A broken earthenware flask has soaked up the urine of a zav, a man whose discharge makes him a source of ritual impurity. Rinse it with water three times and it is clean; pour in urine of a ritually pure person ten times and it stays impure, since a substance is not nullified by its own kind. Rabbi Yehuda then holds that flax woven by a menstruating woman keeps her spittle's impurity however much water you add, and Rav Pappa answers that spittle clings.
zevachim/79.question: If three rinses of water empty the flask of urine, what makes spittle in damp flax different in kind rather than merely harder to rinse out?

judge.reachNote: Whether resisting nullification is a property of the substance's kind or only of how stubbornly it is lodged in the vessel or fabric.

answer.quote: Spittle is different, as it is thoroughly absorbed and adheres to the flax, and therefore washing the flax with water does not nullify the spittle.
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa states the reason spittle resists water — it is absorbed and adheres — but the page never says whether this is a categorical difference or merely a difference of degree, which is what the note asks.

zevachim/80.summary: Blood from two offerings spills together into one cup, and the priest must dash it on the altar, where some offerings call for one application of blood and others for four. Rabbi Eliezer says give four, Rabbi Yehoshua says one, and each charges the other with breaking the verse that forbids adding to or subtracting from a commandment. Rabbi Yehoshua breaks the tie by claiming that adding is something you do, while falling short is only something you fail to do.
zevachim/80.question: If one verse forbids both adding and diminishing, why should the priest who does too much be worse off than the one who does too little?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that an act weighs more than an omission under a single prohibition — but that is precisely the page's stated answer, which the summary already repeats.

zevachim/81.summary: Blood of a sin offering belongs above the red line painted around the altar, blood of a burnt offering below it, so a mixture of the two looks unusable. Rabbi Eliezer says place it above and treat the wrong blood as water; the Rabbis say pour it all into the courtyard drain. Rava narrows the fight to cups that got switched, not blood actually stirred together, and Abaye asks what happens once only leftovers remain.
zevachim/81.question: If the mixture had no remedy, why do both sides agree that the priest who placed it without consulting anyone gets credit for what he did?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that an act already done improperly is reckoned with after the fact rather than voided, which is why the page must explain the concession.

answer.quote: once the priest has placed blood from the mixture above the red line, all that remains is a mixture of remainders, which are placed in the same location
answer.explanation: The explanation from Eretz Yisrael accounts for the universal concession by recasting the case so that whatever is left after the first placement all belongs in one place, though the page never states outright why the improper placement already made should count for the priest.

zevachim/82.summary: A priest collects the blood of one sin offering in two cups, and one cup is carried into the Sanctuary, where that blood does not belong. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says the cup left in the courtyard stays fit, reasoning that blood taken out of the courtyard never spoils what remains behind. The Rabbis answer with the verse about blood brought into the Tent of Meeting, and each side keeps flipping the other's inference back on it.
zevachim/82.question: If blood carried out of the courtyard leaves the cup behind it fit, why should blood carried into the Sanctuary ruin the cup that never moved?

judge.reachNote: The idea is the asymmetry between going out and going in — why a disqualification can spread inward but not outward — which the page settles as a verse-imposed limit rather than logic.

answer.quote: This teaches that only blood that enters the Sanctuary disqualifies the blood in the courtyard, but the blood that leaves the courtyard does not disqualify the blood in the courtyard.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili raises exactly the note's symmetry objection, and the Rabbis answer it by scriptural decree: the verse singles out blood brought inside as the only case that spoils the rest.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 82a (Gemara on the two-cup mishna): "This teaches that only blood that enters the Sanctuary disqualifies the blood in the courtyard, but the blood that leaves the courtyard does not disqualify the blood in the courtyard.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very objection Rabbi Yosei HaGelili raises and the Rabbis answer on this page with the verse from Leviticus 6:23, so it reads as already resolved. Rewrite it to start from that answer and press on what remains hard: e.g. why a verse-decreed asymmetry in blood does not carry over to intent or to meat, since the page shows both a fortiori inferences blocked by other verses. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

zevachim/83.summary: A priest sprinkles sin offering blood on the golden altar inside the Sanctuary, then carries the remainder back toward the Curtain, and Rava cannot decide whether that return counts as forbidden bringing in. The dilemma stands unresolved. The rest turns to unfit things placed on the altar anyway: Rabbi Yehoshua keeps whatever the fire can consume, Rabban Gamliel whatever can ascend, and their whole disagreement comes down to disqualified blood and the wine libations poured alongside an offering.
zevachim/83.question: Why does a handful of flour that was never placed in a service vessel have to come back down, while fats offered too early, before the blood was sprinkled, get to stay?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Under the case lies the idea that fitness for the altar depends on whether what is missing is intrinsic to the item or an external act performed elsewhere.

answer.quote: These sacrificial portions described by Ulla do not lack the performance of an action with regard to themselves that will render them fit for the altar; they lack only the sprinkling
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly distinguishes the two cases the question contrasts: the portions lack only an independent act (sprinkling), while the handfuls lack an act upon themselves (placement in a service vessel).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 83b: "These sacrificial portions described by Ulla do not lack the performance of an action with regard to themselves that will render them fit for the altar; they lack only the sprinkling". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words on 83b, where the Gemara distinguishes items lacking an action upon themselves from items lacking only the independent act of sprinkling. Write a question that starts after that distinction rather than one it resolves — for instance, probing why sanctification in a vessel counts as intrinsic to the handful while the blood's sprinkling stays external to the fats. The summary is accurate and can stay largely as is.

zevachim/84.summary: A mishna lists items that stay on the altar even once they are found unfit: blood or limbs left out overnight, an offering that became impure, blood collected and sprinkled by a priest unfit to serve. Rabbi Shimon draws the line by where the flaw arose, so an animal that was payment to a prostitute, or a tereifa, or born by caesarean section comes down. The Gemara later concedes the baraita's analogies are only supports for an expansive verse.
zevachim/84.question: Why should a flaw introduced by the priest's own hand during the service keep an offering on the fire, while a blemish the animal arrived with sends it off?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether sanctity attaches to the process or to the animal's origin — but the page names that idea as its own answer.

answer.quote: any unfit offering whose disqualification occurred in sanctity, i.e., in the course of the Temple service, the sacred area renders the offering acceptable
answer.explanation: The mishna states Rabbi Shimon's reason outright — a flaw that arose during the service is absorbed by the sacred area, while an animal unfit from the start is not — and the Gemara on 84b asks the note's question in so many words ("what did you see as reason to include those and exclude these?") and answers with the same in-sanctity/not-in-sanctity line.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 84a (Mishna): "any unfit offering whose disqualification occurred in sanctity, i.e., in the course of the Temple service, the sacred area renders the offering acceptable". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the mishna and the Gemara on 84b already answer: disqualification "in sanctity" is absorbed because "the sacred area renders the offering acceptable." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer and presses on what it leaves unsettled — for instance why Rabbi Akiva keeps blemished animals on the altar though their blemish predates the service, or why Rabbi Ḥanina's father rejected them, or why Rabbi Yehuda needs analogies at all if the sanctity rule would cover his cases.

zevachim/85.summary: A disqualified animal's innards are carried down off the altar and rinsed of their dung, and the Gemara asks why bother washing something that can never go back up. One answer: a priest who chances on them might otherwise burn them, dung and all, and repulsive things are not offered to Heaven. The objection lands at once, that rinsing is what sets the trap, and the reply is only that sacred meat should not lie about like a carcass.
zevachim/85.question: If rinsing the innards is the very thing that makes another priest likely to burn them by mistake, is sparing them from lying like a carcass worth setting that trap?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the weighing of the dignity of consecrated items against the risk of causing another person to sin.

answer.quote: Even so, rinsing disqualified innards is preferable, so that the sanctified offerings of Heaven shall not be lying as a carcass.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the identical stumbling-block objection and resolves it by asserting that avoiding the appearance of a carcass takes precedence, though it never explains why that consideration outweighs the risk to the priest.

zevachim/86.summary: Bones, tendons, horns and hooves still attached to an offering's flesh burn on the altar with it; once separated, they come down even from the top of the pyre. Rabba adds that bones which fell off before the blood was sprinkled lose their sanctity entirely, fit for carving knife handles. The page then turns to a half-burnt limb knocked off the altar: before midnight the priest puts it back, after midnight he does not, and Rav explains by splitting the night in half.
zevachim/86.question: If a limb dried hard by the fire is treated as finished at midnight, what has actually changed about it at that hour?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a fixed hour, not a physical change, can complete an offering's consumption — but the page says this in so many words.

answer.quote: since the mitzva of burning has been performed and the limbs are considered to have been entirely consumed
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that nothing physical changes at midnight — the limb is deemed consumed because the night's designated time for the mitzva of burning has passed, as Rav's division of the night explains.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 86b: "since the mitzva of burning has been performed and the limbs are considered to have been entirely consumed". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: it says the limbs are treated as consumed because the mitzva of burning has been performed, with Rav dividing the night into a half for burning and a half for removal. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than asking for it — for instance, about the case the page raises at the end, where a limb dislodged before midnight is only returned after midnight, or about why Rav's midnight division survives Rav Kahana's objection while his ash-removal timing does not. The summary itself is accurate and can stay largely as is.

zevachim/87.summary: Limbs of an offering burning on the altar fire sometimes slip off, and the question is when they count as already consumed, so nobody has to put them back. Rabba sets the line at the second midnight, Rav Ḥisda at dawn, and Rav Yosef holds that midnight finishes them wherever they happen to be lying. The discussion then asks whether the air above the altar is altar, and whether a priest dragging a limb up the sloping ramp ever lets it leave.
zevachim/87.question: Is a limb counted as consumed because the fire has done its work, or because midnight has passed, even if it spent that hour on the ground?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether 'consumed' is a physical fact about the fire or a legal fact about time — but the page rules on exactly that.

answer.quote: the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav Yosef, i.e., the passing of midnight renders all limbs consumed, regardless of their location at that time
answer.explanation: The page explicitly decides that midnight, not the fire's work or the limb's place on the altar, is what renders limbs consumed.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 87a: "the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav Yosef, i.e., the passing of midnight renders all limbs consumed, regardless of their location at that time". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is settled on the page: Rav Yosef's view, that midnight consumes the limbs wherever they lie, is ruled to be the halakha. Ask instead about what still presses after that ruling — for instance Abaye's answer that Rabba and Rav Ḥisda still argue about fatty limbs, where the surrounding fat delays burning, which quietly lets physical reality back into a purely time-based rule. Alternatively ask why limbs on top of the altar escape disqualification for being left overnight while limbs on the courtyard floor do not.

zevachim/88.summary: Rabbi Inini bar Sason matches each priestly garment to a sin it atones for: the tunic for bloodshed, the linen trousers for forbidden sexual relations, the mitre, a headdress, for arrogance, and the High Priest's robe, hung with gold bells, for malicious speech. The objection comes fast, since Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that bloodshed and malicious speech are atoned only by the heifer whose neck is broken and by the incense. The answer splits cases: slander in public against slander in private, murder witnessed against murder unknown.
zevachim/88.question: If a man killed on purpose and escapes execution only because no witness warned him first, what is the tunic actually settling?

judge.reachNote: What is left for atonement to do when guilt is known and undischarged because the court's hands are tied.

answer.quote: It is referring to a case where he murdered intentionally but witnesses did not forewarn him of the consequences of committing murder.
answer.explanation: The page supplies exactly the case the question starts from — intentional murder without forewarning — and says the tunic atones there, but it never spells out what that atonement accomplishes once the land's atonement is said to require the murderer's blood.

zevachim/89.summary: The daily offering goes first because it is brought more often than the additional Shabbat or New Moon offerings, and the mishna builds a whole queue from there: sin offering before guilt offering, guilt offering before thanks offering, firstborn before animal tithe. Each rank comes with a reason, and the Gemara answers nearly every one with a reason pointing the other way. Its reply each time is just that the mishna's factor matters more.
zevachim/89.question: If a guilt offering must be worth at least two shekels and a sin offering has no minimum value at all, what makes the extra placements of blood the weightier claim?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: When two ranking criteria conflict, what makes one criterion outrank the other — is there a principle behind 'of greater importance' or only assertion?

answer.quote: Even so, the fact that the sin offering requires more placements of the blood on the altar is of greater importance.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very objection about the guilt offering's fixed two-shekel value and replies only by asserting that the blood placements outweigh it, without explaining why that factor is weightier.

zevachim/90.summary: A bird sin offering, an animal burnt offering, and an animal tithe, one animal in ten from the flock, all come due at the same time. Each outranks one of the others and is outranked by the third, so the rules of precedence close into a circle. The Sages in Babylonia cut it by putting the tithe first, since it requires slaughtering; in Eretz Yisrael they start with the bird, and both answers stand.
zevachim/90.question: If each of the three outranks one and loses to another, is the sequence a rule at all, or only a decision about where to enter the circle?

judge.reachNote: Whether precedence is a genuine ordering of sanctity or merely a procedural choice once the criteria conflict irreconcilably.

answer.quote: Here, in Babylonia, they explained that the fact that the animal tithe offering is a type of offering that requires slaughtering is of greater importance than the other factors.
answer.explanation: The page breaks the circle by ranking one criterion above the others (and Eretz Yisrael by a different weighting), which bears on whether precedence is principled, but it never addresses whether the resulting sequence is a rule or merely a chosen entry point.

zevachim/91.summary: A priest holding two offerings has to decide which to handle first: the more frequent one, or the one of greater sanctity. Five proofs are brought, from the extra Shabbat offerings to reciting the blessing on wine before the blessing of the day at kiddush, and each is knocked down the same way: the day's holiness attaches to both items, so neither is holier. Then a priest slaughters the infrequent offering out of turn, and someone stirs its blood while he waits.
zevachim/91.question: If the sanctity of a day spreads to everything offered on it, is there any case left where sanctity and frequency actually clash?

judge.reachNote: If holiness of a day soaks into everything offered that day, the category 'greater sanctity' may never stand opposite frequency at all, and the whole dilemma could be empty.

answer.quote: We raise the dilemma only with regard to a clash between a frequent offering and one of greater sanctity, but we do not raise the dilemma with regard to a common offering.
answer.explanation: Rava's line confirms the Sages still hold a genuine frequent-versus-holier clash in view even after every day-sanctity proof is deflected, but the page never supplies a case where the two demonstrably collide, so the question survives.

zevachim/92.summary: A priest's garment catches a spray of blood from a sin offering, and the verse requires laundering it in a sacred place. The argument is over which sin offerings count: a bird sin offering, killed by pinching the nape rather than with a knife, is excluded, even though its blood is also described as sprinkled. The deciding move is a tally of resemblances, since internal and eaten animal offerings share more traits, the bird loses.
zevachim/92.question: When one verse both includes and excludes, and the tiebreaker is a count of shared features, who decides which features are worth counting?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that analogy by counting resemblances presupposes an unstated judgment about which resemblances are significant.

answer.quote: Those features that are common to internal sin offerings and eaten animal sin offerings are more numerous than the features common to bird sin offerings and eaten animal sin offerings.
answer.explanation: The page states the tiebreaker rule — the side with more shared features wins — but never says who determines which features are eligible to be counted, so the question can still honestly be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: The garment sprayed with blood is a priest's garment.
summaryProblems.pageSays: In the case of the blood of a sin offering designated for presentation that was sprayed on a garment, that garment requires laundering

judge.feedback: The summary says "The garment sprayed with blood is a priest's garment.", but the page says "In the case of the blood of a sin offering designated for presentation that was sprayed on a garment, that garment requires laundering". Say what the page says.

zevachim/93.summary: Blood from a sin offering sprays onto a garment, and the Torah requires laundering that spot inside the Temple courtyard. Rami bar Ḥama asks about blood still fit until the instant it lands on an already impure garment: does impurity arriving at the moment of contact count the same as impurity that came first? The answer runs through water mixed with ashes of a red heifer, sprinkled on a woman impure from a corpse, which goes impure on contact and purifies her anyway.
zevachim/93.question: If the blood left on the priest's finger came out of the same bowl a moment earlier, what makes it unfit for the next sprinkling?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Fitness of blood depends on where it sits (in the sacred vessel) rather than on its substance or origin.

answer.quote: he must sprinkle of the blood that is mentioned in this matter, which is the blood in the vessel
answer.explanation: The baraita's derivation from "Sprinkle of the blood" states that only blood still in the vessel may be sprinkled, which is exactly why Rava (and Rabbi Elazar) rule the remainder on the finger unfit.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 93b: "he must sprinkle of the blood that is mentioned in this matter, which is the blood in the vessel". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question outright: "Sprinkle of the blood" is read to mean the blood in the vessel, so the remainder on the finger is excluded. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance, the tension Rava must resolve between that rule and the baraita about blood spraying "before he sprinkled," or the mishna where the priest wipes his hand on the heifer. Also consider a question tied to the summary's own thread about impurity arriving at the moment of contact, since the summary and question currently point at different sugyot.

zevachim/94.summary: Blood from a sin offering that sprays onto a garment must be laundered, and inside the Temple courtyard. Whether leather counts as something one launders drives the argument: Rav let a student pour water on his shoes on Shabbat, so Rava tries soft leather against hard, drops that, and settles on rubbing as the line. Having already taught in public that laundering a shoe on Shabbat is permitted, he sets up an interpreter and announces the error.
zevachim/94.question: What made the shoe ruling require a public retraction, when Rava had abandoned three earlier positions on the same page without announcing anything?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the difference between revising a position inside an argument and retracting a practical ruling already given to the public.

answer.quote: Rava taught in public: It is permitted to launder a shoe on Shabbat.
answer.explanation: The page marks this ruling, unlike his earlier reasoning within the discussion, as something he had "taught in public," which bears on why the correction was also made publicly, but it never states that reason outright.

zevachim/95.summary: Blood from a sin offering that sprays on a garment must be laundered inside the Temple courtyard, and a garment that became impure outside is torn first to strip it of impurity. Reish Lakish says the High Priest's robe cannot be torn, so it is fed through the gate in strips under three fingerbreadths, the size below which cloth counts as a garment, and washed piece by piece. But proper laundering takes seven scouring agents, and one of them is urine.
zevachim/95.question: If urine is too unfit to enter the Temple at all, how does absorbing it into a mouthful of tasteless saliva make it fit?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether a substance disqualified from the Temple loses that disqualification when it is absorbed and no longer discernible on its own.

answer.quote: Rather, it must be explained that the urine is absorbed in tasteless saliva, which comes from one who has not eaten since waking
answer.explanation: The page supplies the saliva-absorption resolution and, in rejecting an earlier version of it, hints at the logic that absorbed urine is "not discernable separately," but it never explains why absorption removes the unfitness for the Temple.

zevachim/96.summary: Rav Yitzhak bar Yehuda explains why he left Rami bar Hama for Rav Sheshet: Rami answers questions by reasoning, so any mishna a student finds can knock the answer down, while Rav Sheshet answers by quoting a mishna, and then it is one source against another. Challenged to prove himself, Rami reasons that a pot needs scouring only where sin offering meat cooked, as a garment is laundered only where blood sprayed. A baraita says otherwise, and he concedes.
zevachim/96.question: If one source can always be met by another source, is quoting a mishna really safer than reasoning your way to the same answer?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what makes an answer durable: citation that can only be matched by a rival source versus reasoning that a single source can overturn.

answer.quote: it is a dispute between one mishna and another mishna, which does not necessarily refute the mishna that he cited
answer.explanation: Rav Yitzḥak bar Yehuda himself states why a cited mishna is safer — a clash of two mishnayot leaves his teacher's answer standing — though the page never tests whether that stalemate is really an advantage, so the question can still be pressed.

zevachim/97.summary: A copper pot that cooked a sin offering has to be scoured and rinsed, because taste of the meat soaks into the metal and may not be eaten past its time. Rabbi Tarfon says a pot used from the start of a pilgrimage Festival needs no scouring until the Festival ends. The Gemara drops his verse-based reason and offers another: each day's fresh cooking scours out what the previous day left behind.
zevachim/97.question: If every day's meat purges the day before it, what is left in the pot on the last day that still needs scouring?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that ongoing use can itself function as purging, so absorbed taste is a running account rather than a fixed residue.

answer.quote: Therefore, only after the Festival, when the vessel is not being used, must the pot be scoured and rinsed.
answer.explanation: The page states that the purging-by-use works only while the vessel is in continual service, so scouring is required once the Festival ends — but it never spells out what specifically remains absorbed from the final day's cooking, so the question can still be asked honestly.

zevachim/98.summary: Rava asks what happens when sin offering blood lands on a garment already soaked through with the blood of a burnt offering, and he decides such a garment needs no laundering. The same reasoning about absorption becomes a question about ritual immersion: blood on a garment blocks the water, unless the wearer is a butcher who never minds blood. Then comes a man who works as both butcher and fat seller, wearing both stains, and the question is left standing.
zevachim/98.question: Does a man used to blood and used to fat mind the two of them together, or does his habit cover everything he wears at once?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Asks whether being unfussy is substance-by-substance or a general disposition of the person — i.e., what 'particularity' about interposition really measures.

zevachim/99.summary: A verse about the sin offering, "The priest who effects atonement shall eat it," is read as a rule about who receives a portion of sacrificial meat. The rule is tested and bent: the whole priestly watch eats without performing the rite, minors eat but receive nothing, and a blemished priest who can never serve gets a share anyway. By the end the test is not fitness to serve but fitness to eat, settled by a High Priest whose relative has just died and is not yet buried.
zevachim/99.question: If a blemished priest who can never serve still receives a share, why does a priest who immersed today and will be fit by nightfall receive none?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real axis of the passage — fitness to serve versus fitness to eat right now — but the Gemara poses and resolves it in so many words.

zevachim/100.summary: A person whose relative has died but is not yet buried is an acute mourner, and the page asks whether he may still eat the Passover lamb that night. Rabbi Shimon seems to say both yes and no, so Rav Mari, Abaye and Rava split the cases: died before midday or after, before the blood of the offering was sprinkled or after. Into this comes Yosef the priest, whose wife died on Passover eve and who refused to bury her.
zevachim/100.question: If burying his own wife was a mitzva Yosef the priest was already obligated to perform, why did it take a vote of his colleagues to make him do it?
gate: the question uses "mitzva", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the clash between two mitzvot on one person and whether a community may compel someone into the one he is shirking.

answer.quote: he did not want to become impure, as he wanted to offer the Paschal offering; and his brethren the priests voted and rendered him impure
answer.explanation: The page gives Yosef's motive for refusing (the competing Paschal offering) and states the derived rule that others coerce a reluctant priest, but it never explains why a formal vote was the mechanism or how the clash of obligations was adjudicated in his case.

zevachim/101.summary: On the eighth day of the Tabernacle's inauguration, two of Aaron's sons died, and a goat brought as a sin offering was burned instead of eaten. Rabbi Nehemya says Aaron burned it because he was an onen, a mourner whose dead is not yet buried; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say it had become ritually impure, since two other goats that day were not burned. Both sides script the same verses as a cross-examination that ends with Moses conceding he had forgotten the law.
zevachim/101.question: If the ruling only surfaced when Aaron reasoned it out loud from the rules for second tithe, in what sense was it ever Moses's to forget?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question uses "second tithe", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether a law recovered by reasoning is a rediscovery of revelation or a new derivation — and what "forgetting" Torah means.

answer.quote: Rather, he said: I heard it, and I forgot it, as the verse indicates by stating: "Moses heard."
answer.explanation: The page asserts that Moses had indeed received this halakha and forgot it, deriving that claim from the word "heard," though it does not address how a law reached by Aaron's a fortiori inference counts as previously received.

zevachim/102.summary: A priest who immersed in a ritual bath that morning is not fully pure until sunset, and he asks the priest distributing sacrificial food for a share to eat in the evening. Three times he reasons from one offering to another; three times the pure priest ends it with a verse tying the food to the priest who performed the service. He leaves with nothing, and the page says Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, worked this out in the bathroom.
zevachim/102.question: If the priest who immersed that day meets every argument with a good counterargument and still goes home empty-handed, what is his reasoning actually for?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the standing of a fortiori logic once a verse decides the matter: does losing reasoning still do work?

answer.quote: The priest who immersed that day left in disappointment, with his a fortiori inferences upon his head, as they did not help him.
answer.explanation: The page states that his inferences failed him, and later shows they were not worthless — his refutation in the firstborn case is precisely why Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, "did not include this exchange in his story" — so it bears on the question without fully answering what his reasoning is for.

zevachim/103.summary: A verse gives the priest the hide of a burnt offering he sacrifices, and the page argues over which burnt offerings count. Excluded are one bought with coins left over from another offering, one brought by a convert who died with no heirs, and one folded into a gift of all a person's property to Temple upkeep. The second mishna asks about hides of disqualified offerings; Rabbi Ḥanina, the deputy High Priest, testifies he never saw one burned, and the Rabbis answer that not seeing proves nothing.
zevachim/103.question: If Rabbi Ḥanina spent his working life in the Temple and never once saw a hide carried out to the burning place, what would count as evidence that it ever happened?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether the absence of an observed case can settle a law — testimony of experience versus rule-derived halakha.

answer.quote: The claim: We did not see, is no proof; rather, if after flaying it is discovered that the animal was unfit before it was flayed
answer.explanation: The Rabbis reject Rabbi Ḥanina's argument from never having seen it and state the rule that would in fact send a hide to the burning place, but they never say what would count as positive evidence that it ever occurred, so the question survives.

zevachim/104.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, argue over whether sprinkling an offering's blood on the altar wins acceptance for the hide by itself, even when the flesh is disqualified and burned. Rabbi Ḥanina, the deputy High Priest, claimed he never saw a hide sent out to be burned, and the Gemara hunts for a case that would prove him wrong. The answer lands on an animal later found to have a fatal wound in its intestines: nobody knew, so the sprinkling held.
zevachim/104.question: If the wound in the intestines was already there, why should nobody having noticed it be enough to make the hide the priests' own?

judge.reachNote: Whether the validity of a rite is measured by the objective state of the animal or by what was known to the priest when he acted.

answer.quote: the sprinkling of the blood nevertheless effects acceptance, because the wound was unknown at the time of the sprinkling
answer.explanation: The page gives ignorance at the moment of sprinkling as the operative reason, but it asserts rather than justifies why unawareness should override the animal's actual disqualified status, so the note's question can still honestly be asked.

zevachim/105.summary: A bull to be burned is carried out of the Temple courtyard slung on poles, and an earlier teaching says the priests at the front, already past the wall, have their garments rendered impure while those still inside do not. Rabbi Elazar asks what happens if the animal leaves and is then brought back in; Rabbi Abba bar Memel reads the pole case as the answer. Ravina denies it: the rear priests are clear only because they have not yet left the camp.
zevachim/105.question: If three of the five men carrying a bull out have crossed the wall but most of the bull is still inside, which majority decides?

judge.reachNote: Whether impurity status tracks the bearers who carry a thing or the thing being borne — whose 'majority' constitutes the act of leaving.

answer.quote: Do we follow the majority of the people handling the offering, who have left the courtyard, or do we follow the animal, the majority of which did not yet leave?
answer.explanation: The page poses exactly this dilemma in the name of Rabba bar Rav Huna but then states, "The dilemma shall stand unresolved," so no resolution is given.

zevachim/106.summary: The Torah threatens karet, excision, for anyone who slaughters an offering outside the Temple courtyard, yet the page struggles to find a verse that plainly forbids the act. Rabbi Avin argues from the lighter case: if an act carrying no punishment was still banned outright, an act carrying punishment surely was banned too. Ravina and Rav Ashi test that reasoning on forbidden fat, watch it fail again and again, and the inference is dropped for a shared word, "bring."
zevachim/106.question: If the Torah already threatens to cut a man off for slaughtering outside the courtyard, why does the page refuse to let that punishment stand as proof the act was forbidden?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the principle that a stated punishment does not by itself establish a prohibition — warning and penalty must both be written.

answer.quote: But from where do we derive its prohibition? One is liable only in a case where the Torah specifies both the prohibition and the punishment.
answer.explanation: The page states outright the governing rule that a punishment counts only when the Torah also supplies an explicit prohibition, which is precisely why karet alone cannot prove the act was forbidden.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 106a: "But from where do we derive its prohibition? One is liable only in a case where the Torah specifies both the prohibition and the punishment.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks why punishment alone cannot prove prohibition, but the page states that rule in so many words ('One is liable only in a case where the Torah specifies both the prohibition and the punishment'). Rewrite the question to start from that stated rule and press on something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why a verbal analogy on the word 'bring' is an acceptable substitute for an explicit warning when an a fortiori inference is not. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

zevachim/107.summary: A baraita sorts out which places count as "outside the camp" for the penalty of slaughtering an offering away from the Temple, ruling out the south of the courtyard, since offerings of lesser sanctity may be slaughtered there. Ulla adds the roof of the Sanctuary, where nothing may be slaughtered, and Rava objects that the animal was still brought to the Tent of Meeting. Then Rav Mari's case: body outside the courtyard, neck inside, and liability anyway.
zevachim/107.question: If the cut is what the verse is particular about, why is a man liable when the animal's body lies outside the courtyard and the knife works on a neck that is inside it?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Where does an act of slaughter happen — at the blade's point of contact, or wherever the animal's body lies?

answer.quote: Rather, say instead that the term “in the camp” is written to include liability for slaughtering an offering where its body is entirely outside the courtyard but its neck is inside
answer.explanation: The page supplies the scriptural ground for the ruling — the redundant phrase "in the camp" must be including just such a case — but it never reconciles this with its own principle that "The Merciful One is particular about the slaughter," so the question can still be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Mari's case is body outside the courtyard, neck inside.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Mari said in defense of Rava: No, the term “in the camp” is written to include liability for slaughtering an offering in a case where its body is entirely inside

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rav Mari's case is body outside the courtyard, neck inside.", but the page says "Rav Mari said in defense of Rava: No, the term “in the camp” is written to include liability for slaughtering an offering in a case where its body is entirely inside". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: Rav Mari's own case was body inside the courtyard with the neck outside, and it is the Gemara that rejects this as obvious and substitutes body outside with neck inside. The question itself is good and can stand as written once the summary names whose case it is. Since the page does offer a ground for the ruling (the otherwise redundant "in the camp"), consider having the question press on the tension with "the Merciful One is particular about the slaughter" explicitly.

zevachim/108.summary: Rabbi Yosei holds that one is liable for offering a sacrifice outside the Temple courtyard only if he built an altar there; Rabbi Shimon says a rock or a stone is enough. Each side reads the other's proof verse away: Noah's altar becomes merely an elevated place, and the rock where Manoah offered a kid becomes a one-time order from an angel. A baraita adds that the corner, ramp, base and square shape are required for the great public altar but not a small private one.
zevachim/108.question: If Noah's altar counts as nothing more than a raised piece of ground, and Manoah's rock as a one-off emergency, what is actually left to tell an altar apart from a stone?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what makes a place an altar at all — structure, designation, or mere elevation — once both scriptural anchors are explained away.

answer.quote: The corner, the ramp, the base, and the square shape are all indispensable for the validity of a great public altar, but they are not indispensable
answer.explanation: The closing baraita names the features that define an altar, but since it declares them dispensable for a small private altar, it bears on the question without settling what distinguishes altar from stone.

zevachim/109.summary: A burnt offering is burned whole on the altar, so half an olive-bulk of its flesh and half an olive-bulk of its fats combine into the single olive-bulk that makes a person liable for burning it outside the Temple courtyard. A peace offering's meat is eaten rather than burned, so those halves do not combine. Then the measure splinters: an olive-bulk of incense brings liability, but wine poured outside is exempt below three log, several olive-bulks' worth.
zevachim/109.question: If an olive-bulk of incense burned outside is enough for liability, why is a pour of wine just short of three log, many olive-bulks of it, nothing at all?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "peace offering's" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: What fixes a minimum measure: a fixed volume (olive-bulk) versus the completeness of the act of offering as the Torah defines it.

answer.quote: The term “to sacrifice it” indicates that one is liable for the sacrifice of a complete offering outside the courtyard but one is not liable for the sacrifice of an incomplete offering outside.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the reason for the wine exemption — liability attaches only to a complete offering, and less than three log is an incomplete libation — while incense is complete at an olive-bulk since "the Torah does not specify the amount to be burned."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 109b: "The term “to sacrifice it” indicates that one is liable for the sacrifice of a complete offering outside the courtyard but one is not liable for the sacrifice of an incomplete offering outside.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: the baraita derives from "to sacrifice it" that only a complete offering incurs liability, so a sub-three-log libation is an incomplete pour while an olive-bulk of Sanctuary incense counts as a complete burning because the Torah fixes no amount there. Rewrite the question to start from that answer — for instance, why the Rabbis refuse to carry the olive-bulk measure from Sanctuary incense over to libations or to the inner-sanctum incense, which is exactly Rava's move against Abaye. Keep the summary's flesh-and-fats contrast; it is accurate.

zevachim/110.summary: Rabbi Elazar holds that pouring out the water libation of Sukkot outside the Temple courtyard makes a person liable, and Rabbi Yoḥanan traces this to Rabbi Akiva, who read the plural word "libations" in a verse as covering water alongside wine. Reish Lakish objects: if water comes from the same word as wine, why is it restricted to the festival, and why no minimum of three log, a liquid measure? The reply is that the water libation came to Moses at Sinai, unwritten.
zevachim/110.question: If the water libation reached Moses at Sinai with no verse behind it, what is Rabbi Akiva doing when he finds it hiding inside a plural noun?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of how a scriptural derivation and an unwritten Sinaitic tradition can both be offered as the ground of one mitzva.

answer.quote: According to Rabbi Asi, the mitzva of the water libation is not derived from the same source as the wine libation
answer.explanation: The page presents the Sinai tradition as an alternative source that displaces the shared-verse derivation for Rabbi Elazar, but it never explains what Rabbi Akiva's exegesis of the plural "libations" is then accomplishing, so the question survives.

zevachim/111.summary: A bird offering is killed by pinching the nape with a thumbnail; a knife disqualifies it. So pinching inside the courtyard and burning the bird outside brings liability, while slaughtering it inside and burning it outside brings none, and outside the courtyard the pairing flips. Rabbi Shimon then states a rule that matches nothing in the mishna, and the Gemara tries four readings, discards them all, floats night slaughter and a non-sacred cup, and finally rewrites the sentence.
zevachim/111.question: When a sage's stated rule fits none of the cases in front of him, is it more honest to supply a case he never mentioned or to change the words he said?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the interpretive choice between inventing an unstated case to save a sage's words and altering the words to save the sense.

zevachim/112.summary: The page sets a rule for when killing an offering outside the Temple courtyard carries no penalty: whatever is unfit to be brought to the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. That covers the red heifer, burned in its pit on the Mount of Olives, and the scapegoat sent off a cliff. Rabbi Shimon then splits the cases by time, holding that a temporary blemish or a too-young dove still breaks a prohibition. The Rabbis refuse that middle ground entirely.
zevachim/112.question: If a dove will be fit for the altar once its wings turn golden, is killing it outside already an offense against something, or is it simply not yet an offering at all?
gate: gloss "the scapegoat" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether future fitness for the altar already gives an animal sacrificial status now, or whether status begins only at the moment of actual fitness.
