answer.quote: Rabbi Shimon says: For pigeons whose time of fitness has passed one is exempt, and for doves whose time of fitness has not yet arrived he is in violation of a prohibition.
answer.explanation: The mishna directly resolves the note's question, with Rabbi Shimon holding the too-young dove's slaughter outside violates a prohibition (because it will later be fit) and the Rabbis holding that without karet there is no prohibition at all.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 112b: "Rabbi Shimon says: For pigeons whose time of fitness has passed one is exempt, and for doves whose time of fitness has not yet arrived he is in violation of a prohibition.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim by the mishna the summary already paraphrases: Rabbi Shimon says the too-young dove's slaughter outside violates a prohibition without karet, and the Rabbis deny any prohibition. Ask instead about what the dispute leaves unsettled — e.g. why the Rabbis reject a prohibition that carries no karet when the mishna elsewhere freely exempts unfit animals, or what "fit to come after the passage of time" implies for an animal premature only for its impure owner. Keep the question on ground the page does not itself close.

zevachim/113.summary: The mishna says burning the red heifer, whose ash purifies anyone who touched a corpse, outside its pit carries no liability, and Reish Lakish reads "pit" as ground inspected for buried graves. Rabbi Yohanan counters that all of Eretz Yisrael counts as inspected, and the argument turns into a fight over whether Noah's flood reached the land at all. From there: boiling floodwater, a beast too large for the ark, and Babylonian dust made of the dead.
zevachim/113.question: If Eretz Yisrael needs no inspection for hidden graves, why were children born and raised on stone courtyards built over a hollow space to keep them pure?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that a rite can demand a stricter purity standard than the law itself requires, but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: The Sages established a higher standard for purity in the case of the red heifer, but generally speaking there is no concern for hidden sources of impurity in Eretz Yisrael
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely the courtyard-and-oxen mishna as an objection to Rabbi Yoḥanan and answers that the red heifer rite was held to a stricter purity standard than ordinary matters.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 113a: "The Sages established a higher standard for purity in the case of the red heifer, but generally speaking there is no concern for hidden sources of impurity in Eretz Yisrael". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Reish Lakish's own objection from the Jerusalem courtyards, and the page answers it explicitly: the Sages set a higher purity standard for the red heifer. Rewrite the question to start from that answer rather than repeat it — for instance, ask what it means for a rite to demand precautions the law says are unnecessary, or press on why Rabbi Yoḥanan still needs 'outside its pit' to mean inside Jerusalem's walls. Keep the summary as is.

zevachim/114.summary: A dove too young to be offered, an animal with a blemish that will heal, and a lamb whose mother was slaughtered this morning are all unfit now and fit later. Rabbi Shimon says slaughtering them outside the Temple courtyard breaks a prohibition, learned from Moses telling Israel that obligatory offerings must wait for Shiloh; the Rabbis exempt. At the close, Rabbi Ḥilkiya says a leper's premature guilt offering brings liability only when slaughtered for the sake of a different offering.
zevachim/114.question: Why should slaughtering the leper's guilt offering under the wrong name make a man liable, when slaughtering it as itself leaves him exempt?
gate: gloss "guilt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether liability tracks what the animal actually is now or what it could validly become under a different name.

answer.quote: This is because it was fit to be sacrificed not for its own sake inside the Temple courtyard, as a guilt offering that was slaughtered not for its own sake is fit for sacrifice
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Ḥilkiya's reason outright — slaughtering it under another name is liable because such a guilt offering is fit inside — and then handles the follow-up by requiring uprooting of its status.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Zevachim 114b: "This is because it was fit to be sacrificed not for its own sake inside the Temple courtyard, as a guilt offering that was slaughtered not for its own sake is fit for sacrifice". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and answered in the same paragraph it comes from: the page says liability attaches because a guilt offering slaughtered not for its own sake is fit inside, and then explains that for-its-own-sake slaughter lacks the needed uprooting of status. Build the new question on what remains hard after that answer — for instance Rav Huna's objection that a thing should not be unfit when done for its own sake yet fit when done for another's, or why an intention alone is what makes the animal count as fit. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

zevachim/115.summary: A woman after childbirth brings her burnt offering before her days of impurity are over, and a leper brings his guilt offering before his time arrives. The Gemara asks whether someone who slaughters such an animal outside the Temple courtyard is liable, and the answer hinges on whether the animal could have been offered inside at all. Then the page turns to the era before the Tabernacle, when firstborn sons did the slaughtering, and to Aaron's silence when his sons die.
zevachim/115.question: Moses tells Aaron that his sons died to sanctify God's name and Aaron says nothing; is that silence agreement, or simply all that was left to him?
gate: gloss "guilt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: What silence before a divine blow means — consent, or the only response left when protest is futile.

zevachim/116.summary: A gentile may build a private altar wherever he likes and sacrifice on it, since the verse banning slaughter outside the Temple is addressed to Aaron, his sons, and the children of Israel. Rav Asi says a Jew may not assist or act as agent in such an offering; Rabba says instructing is permitted. Then Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur, sends Rava an animal, and Rava specifies the youths, the untouched silt, the new wood, the new fire.
zevachim/116.question: If Rava chose the pair of youths, the spot, the wood, and the source of the fire, what was left in the act that made it instruction rather than assistance?

judge.reachNote: Where the line falls between teaching a permitted act and participating in one forbidden to oneself.

answer.quote: and the two youths will sacrifice the offering for her, for the sake of Heaven
answer.explanation: The page shows that the actual sacrificial act was performed by gentile youths, so the Jews' role stayed on the side of direction, but it never explains where directing ends and assisting begins, so the question still stands.

zevachim/117.summary: Rava insists all three camps stood at Shiloh, and that the Levite camp there differed only in no longer sheltering someone who had killed by accident. The page then moves to Gilgal, where a person could sacrifice on a private altar, and asks what belonged on one. Rabbi Meir permits the offerings of a nazirite, one who vows off wine; the Rabbis answer that once the vow is made, those offerings are compulsory.
zevachim/117.question: Once a man has bound himself by a vow nobody forced on him, is what follows still something he chooses?

judge.reachNote: Whether an obligation freely undertaken is still 'voluntary' once it binds — the boundary between choice and compulsion.

answer.quote: While one assumes the status of a nazirite voluntarily, once he has become a nazirite he is required to bring the offering.
answer.explanation: The Rabbis state exactly the position that a self-imposed vow converts what follows into a compulsory act, though Rabbi Meir on the same page holds the opposite, so the question remains a live dispute rather than settled.

zevachim/118.summary: During the years the Tabernacle stood at Shiloh, meat from offerings of lesser sanctity could be eaten anywhere Shiloh could be seen, a rule drawn from a verse warning against offering sacrifices in every place you see. Then the definition frays: must the whole Tabernacle be visible, or is a glimpse enough? Rav Pappa asks about a spot where a person sees Shiloh standing but not sitting, and Rabbi Yirmeya about a streambank, and no one answers.
zevachim/118.question: If sacred meat may be eaten wherever Shiloh can be seen, does a person lose the right by sitting down?

judge.reachNote: Whether the permission to eat attaches to the place as such or to the eater's actual line of sight at the moment of eating.

zevachim/119.summary: A single verse tells Israel they have not yet come "to the rest and to the inheritance," and the sages split over which sanctuary each word names. Rabbi Yehuda hears rest as Shiloh and inheritance as Jerusalem; Rabbi Shimon flips them; the school of Rabbi Yishmael says both mean Shiloh. That gap between two words is what let people sacrifice on their own altars while the Tabernacle stood at Nov and Gibeon, and Manoah's kid, burned on a rock, gets explained away as an emergency permit.
zevachim/119.question: If a kid offered on a rock outside Shiloh can always be called a one-time emergency measure, what evidence could ever count against the reading it seems to contradict?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether the "emergency measure" move makes a reading immune to disproof — the cost of an escape clause in exegesis.

answer.quote: the verse should have stated: For you have not as yet come to the rest and inheritance [menuḥa naḥala]. The Gemara concedes that this is difficult.
answer.explanation: The page never limits when a "provisional edict" may be invoked, but it does show what counterevidence looks like for these same positions — an unanswered linguistic objection the Gemara lets stand as difficult — so the question is touched but not settled.

zevachim/120.summary: The last page of Zevachim asks whether a place holds on to what passes through it: an offering consecrated for a private altar that was brought inside the public altar's partition and then carried out again. Rabba says the altar sanctifies only what suits it, but the partition, the Gemara suggests, absorbs even what does not belong there. Two dilemmas on this are left standing. Later, Rav and Shmuel read Saul's great stone against the sheep slaughtered that night.
zevachim/120.question: Why should a partition take permanent hold of an offering that the altar inside it would refuse to consecrate?

judge.reachNote: Whether sanctity inheres in a place's boundary or only in the fitness of the object, and whether crossing a line changes a thing permanently.

answer.quote: the partition nevertheless absorbs the offering and it is sacrificed there. Consequently, all the halakhot of the public altar apply to that offering
answer.explanation: The page offers a rationale — the partition absorbs what is actually sacrificed within it, unlike the altar which consecrates only what is fit for it — but it presents this only as one side of a dilemma that 'shall stand unresolved,' so the question remains askable.

menachot/2.summary: Menachot opens with meal offerings: the priest removes a handful, puts it in a vessel, brings it to the altar, burns it. If he does any of this intending a different meal offering, the mishna says the offering stays valid but the owner still owes another one. Rabbi Shimon pushes back, arguing that a dry sinner's offering handled for the sake of an oil-mixed one gives itself away by sight, while every slaughtered animal looks the same, so only intent distinguishes them.
menachot/2.question: If a false intention is ignored because the flour in the pan visibly contradicts it, why should naming the wrong owner, which nothing visible contradicts, be the thing that ruins the offering?
gate: no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real principle — improper intent only disqualifies when the performed rites do not visibly refute it — but the page states that principle outright.

answer.quote: The intent to sacrifice an offering for the sake of another owner does not include a change in the sacrificial rites and it therefore disqualifies the offering.
answer.explanation: Rabba, answering Abaye, states exactly the principle the question asks for: intent that is not recognizably false (change of owner) disqualifies, while intent contradicted by the visible mode of preparation does not.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 2b: "The intent to sacrifice an offering for the sake of another owner does not include a change in the sacrificial rites and it therefore disqualifies the offering.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words by Rabba's reply to Abaye, which says that intent not recognizably false disqualifies while intent contradicted by the mode of preparation does not; ask something the page leaves open instead, for example why Rabbi Shimon's reason-based reading can override a disqualification the Torah derived from sin and guilt offerings, or why pinching a bird offering above the line is not treated as visibly self-refuting. The summary should also not state the mishna's leniency as covering every meal offering, since the sinner's offering and the offering of jealousy are disqualified.

menachot/3.summary: Rabba's rule, that an intent obviously false doesn't disqualify, gets stress-tested by a parade of animals: a black goat versus a white ram, a lamb whose tail hides its sex, a first-year lamb that looks second-year. Each time the question is whether a bystander could tell, and mostly the answer is no. Rava then anchors everything to one verse about the meal offering, and Rav Ashi splits intent for a vessel from intent for an offering.
menachot/3.question: If the imagined onlooker is sharp enough to suspect a priest of slaughtering in the wrong part of the courtyard, why is he too inattentive to notice whether the animal is male or female?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the 'recognizably false intent' test depends on a fictional observer whose attentiveness the Gemara adjusts case by case.

answer.quote: Rather, discerning between males and females is not on people’s minds, i.e., they do not take notice of the offering’s gender
answer.explanation: The page gives its reason for discounting gender, but never reconciles that inattentive onlooker with the same onlooker who is imagined suspecting a priest of slaughtering in the wrong part of the courtyard, so the note's tension survives.

menachot/4.summary: A handful lifted for the wrong offering usually leaves a meal offering valid but useless to its owner. The page hunts the exceptions: the sinner's meal offering and the meal offering of jealousy, each called "it" in its verse, then Rav adds the omer and the guilt offerings of a nazirite and a leper, which came to make someone fit and did not. Rabbi Yirmeya ranks making fit above atoning, until money left by a dead nazirite complicates the ranking.
menachot/4.question: If a guilt offering for robbery came to atone and did not atone, why does it stay valid while the leper's guilt offering does not?
gate: gloss "the omer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real distinction between offerings that atone and offerings that render a person fit — but the page states that distinction outright.

answer.quote: We find that the Torah differentiates between those guilt offerings that atone and those that render fit, and the halakha is more stringent
answer.explanation: The Gemara poses the note's exact question about the robbery and misuse guilt offerings and Rabbi Yirmeya answers that rendering fit is treated more stringently than atoning, proving it from offerings brought after the owner's death.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 4b: "We find that the Torah differentiates between those guilt offerings that atone and those that render fit, and the halakha is more stringent". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is asked and answered on the daf itself: the Gemara raises the robbery guilt offering objection and Rabbi Yirmeya replies that rendering fit is more stringent than atoning. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer — for instance, why Rav Pappa has to narrow the rule to a "fixed manner of rendering fit" once the nazirite's burnt and peace offerings come after death, or what makes the nazirite's path to wine less fixed than the leper's path to the camp. Keep the summary; it tracks the page.

menachot/5.summary: A priest lifts the handful from the barley omer while thinking of some other offering. Rav disqualifies it, Reish Lakish burns the handful but keeps the remainder off the priests' table until a second omer is brought, and Rava says intent cannot spoil an offering as irregular as this one. The argument turns on timing: does an offering due later that same day already count as being in its time?
menachot/5.question: If something scheduled for later today already counts as timely, why is the leper's sin offering slaughtered out of turn left overnight to decay instead of being stirred and saved?
gate: the question uses "sin offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether an obligation due later the same day already counts as being in its time — the very principle the page tests and then abandons.

answer.quote: It is that he holds that the illumination of the eastern horizon on the morning of the sixteenth of Nisan permits the new crop to
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises exactly this objection in Rav Pappa's name and resolves it by discarding the "same day" principle altogether, re-grounding Reish Lakish in the illumination of the eastern horizon (after first offering "The halakhot of a leper are different").

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 5a (end): "It is that he holds that the illumination of the eastern horizon on the morning of the sixteenth of Nisan permits the new crop to". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection: Rav Pappa raises it from the leper's sin offering, and the page answers it twice — first that "the halakhot of a leper are different," then by dropping the same-day principle entirely in favor of the illumination of the eastern horizon. Ask something the page leaves standing, such as why Rava treats the omer's novelty (barley, not wheat) as making it an item "unfit for the Temple service" so that improper intent cannot touch it, or why an offering that is itself what permits the new crop can be burned before that permission exists.

menachot/6.summary: Sages spend the first half arguing whether a verse is even needed to bar a tereifa, an animal with a fatal injury, from the altar. Every a fortiori inference from blemished animals and those born by caesarean section gets built and knocked down, until the difference lands on one thing: those defects are visible, a tereifa's may not be. Then the mishna lists who may not remove the handful, and Rav says a non-priest's handful goes back.
menachot/6.question: If a handful taken by a non-priest can be poured back and lifted again by a priest, in what sense was the offering ever disqualified?
gate: banned phrase: "a fortiori".

judge.reachNote: It reaches for whether a botched rite is a permanent fact or a reversible state, but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: It means that the non-priest has disqualified the meal offering until such time as he returns the handful to the meal offering
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the note's objection from the mishna and answers that "disqualified" means disqualified only until the handful is returned and a fit priest removes a new one.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 6b: "It means that the non-priest has disqualified the meal offering until such time as he returns the handful to the meal offering". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered almost verbatim on the page, which itself challenges Rav from the mishna and replies that the offering is disqualified only "until such time as he returns the handful." Rewrite the question around something the page leaves unsettled, for example Rav Naḥman's dilemma: if a non-priest's removal is a real sacrificial rite it should disqualify at once, and if it is not, why should placing the handful in a vessel change anything. Keep the summary, which the page supports.

menachot/7.summary: Returning the handful to the bowl it came from should let the vessel sanctify it again and disqualify it. The way out offered here: lay it on the wall of the vessel, tilt, and let it drop in by itself, as though a monkey had returned it. The argument then turns to whether a vessel resting on the ground may be used, and it is settled from what the shewbread mishna leaves out: nobody lifts the Table.
menachot/7.question: One mishna's failure to mention lifting the vessel proves nothing, while the shewbread mishna's identical silence decides the case, so what makes one silence speak?
gate: the question brings in "One", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When is an omission in a source probative — silence counts only where the source is otherwise exhaustive about that very detail.

answer.quote: There, on 12a, the tanna did not delve into the number of priests involved in the service of a meal offering. Here, on 99b
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself distinguishes the two silences: the mishna on 12a never enumerates priests at all, whereas the shewbread mishna does count priests, so its omission of a Table-lifter is meaningful.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 7b: "There, on 12a, the tanna did not delve into the number of priests involved in the service of a meal offering. Here, on 99b". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page explicitly answers this question: the 12a mishna never enumerates priests, while the 99b shewbread mishna does count them, so only there is the omission telling. Write a question that starts from that distinction rather than one the Gemara resolves a few lines later — for example, press on whether Rava's later dilemma (deriving the handful from the meal offering or from the collection of blood) sits comfortably with the conclusion drawn from silence.  Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

menachot/8.summary: The High Priest's griddle-cake offering comes as a full tenth of an ephah and is then split, half burned in the morning and half in the evening. Rabbi Yoḥanan reads the verse to require a whole measure before any halving; Rabbi Elazar says a thing sacrificed in halves can be sanctified in halves. The sharper move arrives with Rabbi Yosei: if one intends to add more flour, each bit is sanctified as it enters the vessel.
menachot/8.question: If half a measure becomes holy only because the person means to add the rest, what is doing the sanctifying, the vessel or the intention?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what actually effects consecration — the physical service vessel or the offerer's declared intent about a measure not yet complete.

answer.quote: But at a time when his intention was initially to add, each initial bit of flour is sanctified by the vessel.
answer.explanation: The baraita as qualified by Rabbi Yosei says the vessel does the sanctifying, with the intention to add serving as the condition that lets it act on a partial measure, so the question's core alternative is addressed but the role left to intention is not spelled out.

menachot/9.summary: A meal offering comes up short of its full measure before the priest removes the handful. Rabbi Yoḥanan says the owner fetches more flour from home and fills it; Reish Lakish says the service vessel already sanctified it, so it is ruined, until a mishna about a leper's log of oil, refillable before pouring, refutes him. The fight then moves to a remainder that goes lacking after the handful is taken, with broken shewbread as evidence.
menachot/9.question: If the handful may be burned on account of a remainder that has gone lacking, but the priests then may not eat what is left of it, what is that burning actually accomplishing?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether a sacrificial rite retains its point when the effect it exists to produce — permitting the remainder for the priests — can no longer occur.

answer.quote: it is unfit and the priest does not burn the handful, as the handful serves to render the remainder permitted
answer.explanation: The page states that the handful's burning functions to permit the remainder, which bears on the question but never explains what it accomplishes once Ze'eiri and Rabbi Yannai bar the remainder of the remainder from consumption.

menachot/10.summary: The leper's purification says the oil goes on the right thumb and big toe, but the verses already said where the blood went, so the words look wasted. Rava's move is to spend them elsewhere: "right hand" supplies the right hand for removing the handful, "right foot" the shoe in halitza, "right ear" the slave pierced with an awl. Then a broader rule is tested: does mentioning a finger or a priest always mean the right hand?
menachot/10.question: If the oil's placement was already obvious from the earlier verse, why must the extra words purchase a rule somewhere else rather than simply repeat?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the assumption that no scriptural word is idle, so surplus wording must be spent on a halakha elsewhere — but the page states that principle outright.

answer.quote: Rather, these verses are the source of verbal analogies for other halakhot.
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the note's question ("Why do I need all of these verses?") and answers that the surplus words are not repetition but sources of verbal analogies, with the school of Rabbi Yishmael's rule ("was repeated only for the sake of a matter that was introduced for the first time") covering the remaining repeated verses.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 10a: "Rather, these verses are the source of verbal analogies for other halakhot.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates Rava's own query, which the page answers explicitly: the redundant words are sources of verbal analogies, and repeated passages are repeated only for the sake of the new matter in them. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for example why Rabbi Shimon needs both "finger" and "priesthood" together when priesthood alone already implies a priest acting, or why an indispensable rite like conveying the limbs is exempted from the right-hand rule. Build the question on a tension the Gemara raises but does not settle.

menachot/11.summary: A stone, a grain of salt, or a pinch of frankincense caught up in the priest's fist ruins the handful, because the measure comes up short. From there the page maps the hand itself: three fingers fold over the palm, the thumb wipes flour off the top, the little finger off the bottom. Rav Pappa then asks whether a sideways or upside-down scoop still counts, and the answers never come.
menachot/11.question: If a single grain of salt is enough to spoil the handful, how can the page leave unsettled whether scooping with the fingertips counts as a handful at all?

judge.reachNote: The page is exact to a grain about quantity yet leaves the manner of taking unfixed — measure as a definable requirement versus form as something only recognizable, not legislated.

answer.quote: the removal of the handful from a meal offering should be performed ab initio in the manner that people usually remove a handful,
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa's framing bears on the question — the normal manner is obvious as the ideal, and only the after-the-fact status of odd scoops is left open — but it never explains why an exact measure tolerates an unresolved method.

menachot/12.summary: The mishna's machinery of piggul intent runs on which rite carried which thought. The Gemara narrows to a stranger case: if the remainder of a meal offering shrank below a full measure, can burning the handful still render it piggul? Rava argues yes from Rabbi Hiyya's wording, Abaye takes that proof apart, and then Rava abandons his own claim as "nothing," citing a broken loaf of shewbread that disqualifies all the rest.
menachot/12.question: If Abaye goes on to dismantle the shewbread proof as well, is Rava's abandoned position left standing, or only left unproven?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the difference between a position being refuted and a position merely losing its proof — what a sage's retraction is worth once the counter-proof collapses.

answer.quote: But according to Rabbi Akiva, who says that sprinkling is effective with regard to an item that left the Temple, even in the case of a lacking measure, burning is effective
answer.explanation: Abaye's closing line reasserts, at least according to Rabbi Akiva, the very substance of Rava's retracted claim, though the page never says what becomes of the retraction itself.

menachot/13.summary: A priest lifts his handful from a meal offering while intending to burn the frankincense the next day. Rabbi Yosei says the offering is unfit but not piggul, the intent that makes an offering rejected and its eater liable to karet, because handful and frankincense are separate permitting factors: either may be burned first. The Rabbis counter that the two are fixed in one vessel, and what sits in one vessel counts as a single unit.
menachot/13.question: If the handful and the frankincense can be burned in either order, does sharing one vessel really make them one thing?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What makes two items one entity — functional independence in how they are offered, or physical containment in a shared vessel?

answer.quote: But in a situation where they were fixed in one vessel, as is the case with regard to the handful and the frankincense, they are considered like one unit
answer.explanation: The page gives the Rabbis' reason — fixation in a single vessel makes the two permitting factors one unit — but it never confronts that reason against Rabbi Yosei's point that either may be burned first, so the question can still honestly be asked.

menachot/14.summary: Two loaves of Shavuot, two lambs, and a priest thinking about tomorrow. The argument is whether piggul intent, the plan to eat an offering past its proper time, about one loaf reaches the other; after several attempts to pin Rabbi Yosei down, Rabbi Yoḥanan says the verse makes the loaves one body and two bodies at once. Which they are depends on the priest: intent covering both mixes them, intent about one leaves them apart.
menachot/14.question: If the priest's intent can split the two loaves into separate bodies, why does Rabbi Yehuda insist that a communal offering cannot be divided when one loaf becomes impure?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the unity of a paired offering is fixed by its status as a communal offering or is made and unmade by the priest's intent.

answer.quote: as no communal offering is divided. That is, it is either fit in its entirety or unfit in its entirety.
answer.explanation: The mishna gives Rabbi Yehuda's stated reason for indivisibility, and the Gemara locates the dispute (impurity before sprinkling; Rav Pappa's frontplate), but it never reconciles this with Rabbi Yoḥanan's claim that intent can render the loaves two bodies.

menachot/15.summary: A thanks offering slaughtered with intent to eat it the next day renders its loaves piggul, but intent aimed at the loaves alone leaves the offering fit. The proposed reason, that the loaves are themselves called a thanks offering, fails once the Shavuot lambs come up, since nobody calls two loaves lambs; what is left is rank, the bread comes on account of the animal. Rav then rules half an olive-bulk of intent from each side still ruins the loaves.
menachot/15.question: If intent about the loaves cannot touch the offering at all, why does intent about the offering get to supply the missing half measure that condemns the loaves?

judge.reachNote: Whether subordination ('brought on account of') is a one-way channel that can also supply a partial measure, or only a direction of contamination.

answer.quote: The bread is brought on account of [gelal] the thanks offering, but the thanks offering is not brought on account of the bread
answer.explanation: The page supplies the general ground of the asymmetry — the animal is the primary element and the bread subordinate to it — but it never states why that subordination lets the offering's half-measure intent combine to condemn the loaves, and in fact leaves the a fortiori challenge to Rav standing.

menachot/16.summary: A meal offering is made permitted by two burnings, the handful and the frankincense. Rabbi Meir holds that intent to eat the remainder the next day during either burning renders the whole offering piggul, a rejected offering carrying karet; the Rabbis want that intent during both. Rav adds the wrinkle worth watching: if the priest spoke his intent at the handful and then burned the frankincense in silence, the silence carries the first intent forward. Shmuel disagrees, and the baraitot are pulled apart over it.
menachot/16.question: When the priest says nothing during the second burning, is his silence a continuation of what he already intended or an empty stretch that means nothing at all?
gate: gloss "karet" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether an unspoken act inherits the intent that preceded it, or whether each rite must carry its own declared intent.

answer.quote: as anyone who performs the rites in such a manner performs them in accordance with his initial intent
answer.explanation: Rav states the continuity principle that silence carries forward the earlier intent, but Shmuel disputes it and the page's proofs and final "this poses a difficulty" leave the matter unresolved, so the question can still honestly be asked.

menachot/17.summary: A meal offering goes up in two pieces: the handful and the frankincense. If the priest burns the handful while intending to burn the frankincense the next day, is the whole thing piggul, disqualified by intent to use it past its time? Rav says no, since the handful is not what permits the frankincense; the reply is that the two were fixed in one vessel, which fuses them into one item, unlike two lambs slaughtered separately.
menachot/17.question: If sitting together in one vessel is enough to make handful and frankincense a single thing, what would it take for two lambs of the same offering to count as one?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What constitutes two sacrificial items as a single entity — shared vessel, shared permitting factor, or something else.

answer.quote: as it was not fixed in one vessel with the other lamb, and therefore each animal stands independent of the other
answer.explanation: The Gemara names the criterion of unity (fixation in one vessel) and says the lambs lack it, but it never says what, if anything, could make two lambs count as one.

menachot/18.summary: A priest slaughters an offering intending to leave some of its blood until the next day. Debating whether Rabbi Yehuda held this disqualifies by all opinions, the Gemara tells of Yosef the Babylonian, who asked Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua the same question five times in one day and whose face only lit up when told that Rabbi Eliezer deems it unfit. The second half asks which meal offering rites a non-priest may perform: pouring oil, mixing, breaking loaves.
menachot/18.question: Yosef the Babylonian agrees the offering is fit, so what exactly was returned to him when he learned that one sage, somewhere, ruled otherwise?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What a scholar loses when a received tradition has no corroborating witness, and what confirming it restores even if he does not follow it.

answer.quote: He meant that Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua had in any event returned to him that there is some opinion in the world concerning the unfitness of the offering
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself asks what Yosef meant by "returned to me that which I had lost" and answers that what was restored was the knowledge that such an opinion exists at all, vindicating the tradition he had received.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 18a: "He meant that Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua had in any event returned to him that there is some opinion in the world concerning the unfitness of the offering". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is explicitly answered on the page: the Gemara asks what Yosef meant by "you have returned to me that which I had lost" and answers that he was given back the knowledge that such an opinion exists in the world. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled, e.g. why Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua at first thought his own halakhot "were not accurate," or why the mishna's clauses on pouring and mixing are read so differently. Also fix the timeline: the five askings run from evening through the next late afternoon, not within one day.

menachot/19.summary: The phrase "with his finger," sitting between collecting the blood and placing it on the altar, raises the question of whether a word reaches backward as well as forward. From there Rav's rule that the words "law" and "statute" mark a rite as indispensable gets tested against the nazirite, the leper, and the two goats of Yom Kippur, and is rewritten twice. Shmuel then refuses to learn permanent practice from the Tabernacle's one-time consecration.
menachot/19.question: If a single one-time offering teaches nothing for all generations, why does the princes' offering, written out twelve times, suddenly teach?

judge.reachNote: Whether sheer repetition can convert a one-time, time-bound event into a norm binding for all generations.

answer.quote: There, with regard to the offering of the princes, it is different, as the verse is repeated twelve times, once with regard to each and every prince.
answer.explanation: The page states that the twelvefold repetition is what lets Shmuel derive a lasting halakha from the princes' inauguration, but it does not explain why repetition overcomes the objection that a temporary situation teaches nothing, so the question can still honestly be pressed.

menachot/20.summary: Salt is the thread: whether a meal offering is unfit when no salt was added, and which offerings need salting at all. Abaye tries to read the mishna as a case where a non-priest salted the handful, and Rav Yosef answers that a non-priest could never get near the altar. Later the Gemara decides blood needs no salt while burnt offering limbs do, by tallying how many traits each shares with a meal offering.
menachot/20.question: When burnt offering limbs win over blood because they share six traits with the meal offering rather than two, is that an argument or just a longer list?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: Whether analogy is decided by the weight of a resemblance or merely by the tally of resemblances.

answer.quote: These characteristics shared by the meal offering and the limbs of the burnt offering are more than those shared by the blood and the meal offering.
answer.explanation: The page does state that the decision rests on the greater number of shared traits, but it never defends counting as a mode of reasoning, so the note's challenge survives the line it quotes.

menachot/21.summary: The page starts with which offerings need salt and slides into a harder question: if salted blood counts as cooked, why does a verse have to exempt blood from salting at all? The answer is that a priest might sprinkle a mere pinch for the mitzva. Then Abaye presses Rava on congealed blood, Rava is silent, and Rav Pappa extends liability even to a donkey's congealed blood, since comparable blood could be placed on the altar.
menachot/21.question: Why should eating a congealed drop of a donkey's blood make someone liable because some other blood, from a sin offering, could have gone on the altar?
gate: gloss "mitzva" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.
the question uses "sin offering", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether the prohibition on blood tracks this particular blood's fitness for the altar or the fitness of blood of its type in general.

menachot/22.summary: The opening argument is about altar wood: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon says it need only come from communal supplies, Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua says it must never have been used, which forces a rereading of Araunah's threshing sledges as brand new. Then a mishna on handfuls of meal offerings mixed together, where Rabbi Yehuda invalidates mixtures of thick and loose oil. Rabbi Yoḥanan claims both sides read one verse about the bull's and goat's blood, and the Gemara twice fails to separate the readings.
menachot/22.question: If the verse about the bull's blood and the goat's blood supports either rule equally well, and the Gemara admits twice over that it cannot tell them apart, what is still holding Rabbi Yoḥanan's explanation up?
gate: gloss "meal offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that one verse may underdetermine two rules, and asks what an attributed derivation rests on once its distinguishing argument collapses.

answer.quote: But now that the verse taught us this halakha through a case of a mixture of items that ascend to the altar, it is understood that the reason it is not nullified
answer.explanation: The Gemara does supply a reason each tanna's reading is preferred — the verse's chosen example points to that criterion — but it then twice concedes "This is difficult," so the note's question still stands.

menachot/23.summary: A handful of flour mixed into another meal offering, carcass meat mixed into slaughtered meat: when does the smaller quantity disappear into the larger? Rav Hisda and Rabbi Hanina agree that sameness depends on what one substance could become, but they aim in opposite directions, one measuring the larger quantity, the other the smaller. Rava's separate puzzle, about oil squeezed onto the wood before the handful is laid on it, is left standing.
menachot/23.question: If carcass meat and slaughtered meat sit in the pot looking identical, why should anything turn on which one could someday rot into the status of the other?

judge.reachNote: What makes two substances 'the same' for nullification: how they look now, or what they could yet become.

answer.quote: But where it is not possible for one to become like the other, it is nullified, since the two are not considered the same substance.
answer.explanation: The Gemara, via Rabbi Ḥiyya's reading of Rabbi Yehuda, states that potential to become the other is what makes two items count as the same substance, though it never explains why potential should outrank identical appearance, which the page itself raises as Rabbi Yehuda's criterion.

menachot/24.summary: Two half-measures of flour sit in one vessel without touching. Does the vessel join them, so that impurity in one spreads to the other, and may the priest scoop his handful from one on behalf of the other? Rava reads a baraita about a tenth split between two vessels to argue yes; Abaye counters with a hen trough and a partition that stops short of the rim, and the later cases of a lost half and its replacement stay unresolved.
menachot/24.question: If the priest's intention settles what the handful permits, why is it still unknown which of the leftover half-measures may be eaten?

judge.reachNote: Intention can fix what an act is for without fixing which physical portion it applies to — the limits of intent against factual indeterminacy.

answer.quote: he removes it to permit the remainder of the tenth of an ephah, and not the remainder of the extraneous half-tenth
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi's answer bears directly on the question — intention is aimed at permitting a tenth's remainder generally, which is why the identity of which half was permitted still cannot be known — though the page states the residual uncertainty as a conclusion rather than explaining it further.

summaryProblems.claim: The later cases of the lost half and its replacement stay unresolved.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Ashi said: These questions present no difficulty, since with regard to the removal of the handful, the matter is dependent on the intention of the priest.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The later cases of the lost half and its replacement stay unresolved.", but the page says "Rav Ashi said: These questions present no difficulty, since with regard to the removal of the handful, the matter is dependent on the intention of the priest.". Say what the page says. Fix the ending of the summary: the page leaves Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemmas and Rava's 'saturated with impurity' dilemma unresolved, but the lost-half-and-replacement cases get rulings from Rava and Abaye and Rav Ashi answers the objections to Abaye. Since the question already builds on Rav Ashi's intention answer, push it past what the page states — e.g. ask why intention, which fixes the purpose of the handful, cannot also fix which of the two halves it permits.

menachot/25.summary: A gold plate on the High Priest's forehead makes an impure offering acceptable, but not one that left the courtyard. The Gemara asks why impurity in particular, and settles on a test: the frontplate covers a prohibition that was lifted somewhere, since impure communal offerings are permitted when the whole community is impure. Rabbi Zeira pushes back with private altars, Rabbi Ile'a with the left hand on Yom Kippur, and Abaye answers each with a phrase of the verse.
menachot/25.question: Ravina and Rav Sheila split over which moment of intent ruins the offering, the making impure or the sprinkling, so why should knowing matter at one moment and not the other?
gate: the question brings in "Ravina", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Sheila", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea beneath the dispute: at which moment does willfulness attach, so that the penalty for deliberate wrongdoing falls on contracting impurity or on the sprinkling that uses it.

menachot/26.summary: Rav Nau0125man bar Yitzu0125ak claims that everyone, even Rabbi Shimon, requires the handful to be sanctified in a service vessel. Three baraitot are brought against him; two are explained away, the third holds, and his view is conclusively refuted. Along the way, a baraita about carrying the handful up by hand or by vessel, right hand or left, is read disjunctively to save one sage and straightforwardly to save another.
menachot/26.question: If the same baraita rescues Rabbi Yehuda son of Rabbi u0124iyya when read disjunctively and Rabbi Yannai when read plainly, what decides which reading it actually is?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yannai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: When one text can be read two ways, each rescuing a different sage, what constrains the reading — the text itself or the position it is meant to save?

answer.quote: Rabbi Yannai could say to you: I stated my ruling in accordance with the opinion of the tanna who taught that the burning of the fats and the limbs
answer.explanation: The Gemara says only that each amora aligns himself with a tanna who reads the baraita his way, which bears on the question but gives no criterion for deciding which reading the baraita truly bears.

menachot/27.summary: Failure to burn even the smallest part of the priest's handful of flour disqualifies the whole meal offering, and the mishna runs that all-or-nothing rule down a long list: wine libations, the two Yom Kippur goats, the two Shavuot loaves, the four species of the lulav. Then Rav Ḥanan bar Rava narrows it. If a person owns all four species, he may take them one at a time. A baraita disagrees, insisting on a single bound bundle.
menachot/27.question: If the Rabbis rule an unbound lulav fit, what is left of the baraita's claim that nothing is accepted until everything is bound into one bundle?

judge.reachNote: The idea is that a stated requirement can survive as adornment ("I will beautify Him") once it is no longer a condition of validity — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: The Rabbis agree that although failure to bind the three species does not render them unfit for performing the mitzva, the performance of the mitzva is more beautiful
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly resolves the tension: the binding baraita reflects Rabbi Yehuda ("Whether the different species must be taken together is a dispute between tanna'im"), and for the Rabbis binding survives as a matter of beautification rather than validity.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 27a: "The Rabbis agree that although failure to bind the three species does not render them unfit for performing the mitzva, the performance of the mitzva is more beautiful". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on the same daf: the Gemara calls binding a tannaitic dispute and says the Rabbis keep binding as beautification, not validity. Read to the end of the lulav passage and ask something that starts from that answer — for instance, why Rabbi Yehuda's hyssop-bundle analogy should govern the lulav at all, or what it means that the homiletic image of Israel bound in one bundle rests on a law the Rabbis treat as optional. Keep the summary; it is accurate.

menachot/28.summary: The Candelabrum needed all seven of its branches and all seven lamps; the absence of one voids the rest. Gold carries extra demands: a single beaten block, an exact talent of weight, goblets, knobs, and flowers. Made from other metals, it may be assembled from fragments and left plain, and the Rabbis say the Hasmonean kings began with iron spits coated in tin, moved up to silver, and only later to gold.
menachot/28.question: If a Candelabrum of iron spits coated in tin served in the Temple, what were the talent of gold and the twenty-two goblets ever for?

judge.reachNote: If the detailed gold specifications drop away for cheaper metals, are they the mitzva itself or only the standard for those who can afford it?

answer.quote: If the one who is fashioning the Candelabrum has no gold, he may bring even a Candelabrum made of silver, of copper, of iron, of tin, or of lead.
answer.explanation: The page shows that lesser metals are a fallback for one who lacks gold, and that the talent-weight and goblets bind only "if the Candelabrum is fashioned of gold," which bears on the question without fully settling what the gold specifications are for.

menachot/29.summary: Rav rules that a letter whose ink touches its neighbor is unfit, and two men bring in phylacteries, the boxed parchments worn on head and arm, where a hole has broken a letter's leg. Rabbi Zeira sends for a child of average intelligence to read the damaged word and decide it. From those same small strokes, Moses is shown God tying crowns on letters for Rabbi Akiva, then shown Akiva's flesh weighed in a butcher shop.
menachot/29.question: God tells Moses to be silent twice, once when he asks why the Torah comes through him and not Akiva, and once when he asks about Akiva's death; is the same silence answering both questions?

judge.reachNote: Whether an unexplained divine will is one answer covering both the choice of Moses over Akiva and Akiva's death, or two different refusals.

answer.quote: God said to him: Be silent; this intention arose before Me.
answer.explanation: The page gives the identical formula in both exchanges, so it supplies the same stated reason twice, but it never says whether that silence means the same thing in each case.

menachot/30.summary: A baraita asks how Moses could have written the words "And Moses the servant of the Lord died there." Rabbi Yehuda says Joshua wrote from that verse onward; Rabbi Shimon refuses, since the scroll placed beside the Ark could not lack a letter, and says God dictated while Moses wrote the ending in tears, not repeating the words aloud. Rav rules that a single reader must take those last verses in synagogue, and the Gemara turns the tears into the very difference that justifies it.
menachot/30.question: If Moses wrote every letter himself, what still sets the verses about his own death apart enough that no second reader may share them?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that how a text was received, not only who wrote it, can give it a distinct halakhic status.

answer.quote: since they differ from the rest of the Torah in one way, as Moses wrote them without repeating the words, they differ from the rest of the Torah in this way as well
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly states that the manner of writing (without repeating) is the difference that keeps these verses from being split between two readers, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 30a: "since they differ from the rest of the Torah in one way, as Moses wrote them without repeating the words, they differ from the rest of the Torah in this way as well". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks for the distinction the page already supplies in so many words, and the summary itself reports that answer ("turns the tears into the very difference that justifies it"), so the question is closed before it is asked. Write a question that starts from Rabbi Shimon's answer and presses on what is still hard: e.g. whether a difference in how Moses received the words, rather than in the words themselves, should have any consequence for public reading. Alternatively, pivot to Rav's rulings about finishing a scroll mid-line or to the claim that buying a scroll is "snatching a mitzva."

menachot/31.summary: A tear running into two lines of a Torah scroll's parchment can be sewn shut, Rav says; a tear into three lines cannot. Talk turns to the mezuza, an inscribed parchment fixed to a doorpost, where uneven lines are fit so long as the writing does not widen like a tent or narrow like a tail. Rav Ḥisda puts the last two words, "above the earth," alone on the final line, and the Sages split over whether they belong at its end, under "the heaven," or at its far start.
menachot/31.question: If the same two words can be set under "the heaven" to show closeness or across the line to show distance, what is the scribe deciding when he chooses where to put them?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the physical layout of a text can itself be an act of interpretation of the words it carries.

menachot/32.summary: Rabbi Meir wrote the mezuza's two Torah passages in the open manner, starting the second on a new line, though a Torah scroll runs them together closed. Arguing over what Rav actually endorsed, Abaye brings Rav's rule that custom holds: if Elijah announced that ḥalitza, the ceremony freeing a childless widow by removing her brother-in-law's sandal, may not use a sandal, the Sages would not listen. The two versions of the statement differ only over whether a shoe may be used at the outset.
menachot/32.question: If people's habit with a sandal can outweigh an announcement from Elijah himself, what could ever dislodge a custom?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the question of whether settled practice can outrank authoritative instruction, and what authority is left to overturn it.

answer.quote: If Elijah comes and says that one performs ḥalitza with a shoe, the Sages listen to him
answer.explanation: The page shows the limit of the principle — Elijah is heeded where no fixed practice has taken hold (the shoe), and refused only where one has (the sandal) — but it never says what could dislodge an entrenched custom, so the question still stands.

menachot/33.summary: A mezuza is the parchment scroll fixed to a doorpost, and the argument here is about exactly where it goes: inside the entrance's own airspace, a handbreadth above the ground, in the handbreadth nearest the street. Rav Naḥman tells the Exilarch, head of Babylonian Jewry, to hang the doors first, since the hinge socket decides which room counts as inside. Rava says it belongs nearest the public domain, and two reasons compete: so a person meets it on entering, or so it guards the house from outside.
menachot/33.question: If the side door Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi alone used to enter the study hall needed no mezuza because one follows the entrance people are accustomed to using, why should a doorway one man walks through daily count for less than one a crowd uses?
gate: the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "HaNasi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Does mezuza obligation attach to a doorway by its public character and customary traffic, or by the fact that someone actually lives and passes through it?

answer.quote: That entrance was the one through which all were accustomed to enter the study hall. By contrast, the entrance that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi used was a side entrance
answer.explanation: The page states the rule that exempts the private side entrance — follow the entrance people are accustomed to using — but never explains why habitual public use, rather than one man's daily use, generates the obligation, which is exactly what the question presses on.

menachot/34.summary: A mezuza, the small parchment fixed at a doorway, goes on the right as you enter, and Rabba's reason is that a person lifts his right foot first when he starts walking. A baraita then asks why not carve the passages into the doorpost stones themselves, the way the Torah was written on stones at the entry to the land. Rav Aha presses the plain words, upon the doorposts; Rav Ashi answers that the writing must be finished before it is placed there.
menachot/34.question: If the verse says to write the words on the doorposts, why should a comparison to other acts of writing outweigh what the verse actually says?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real tension between a verse's straightforward sense and a verbal analogy that overrides it — but the page names and resolves that tension itself.

answer.quote: The verse states: “And you shall write them [ukhtavtam],” which means that it should first be complete writing [ketiva tamma]
answer.explanation: Rav Aḥa asks precisely the note's question about the plain meaning of "upon the doorposts," and Rav Ashi answers it directly with the reading of ukhtavtam as "complete writing" preceding placement, backed by the baraita's rule that writing for all generations is derived from writing for all generations.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 34a: "The verse states: “And you shall write them [ukhtavtam],” which means that it should first be complete writing [ketiva tamma]". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Rav Aḥa's own objection, which Rav Ashi answers on the page (and which the summary itself reports), so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to ask about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why the verbal analogy is still needed once "and you shall write them" already requires finished writing, or why writing "performed in all generations" is the decisive criterion for choosing between two equally available comparisons. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

menachot/35.summary: The page piles up physical requirements for phylacteries, the leather boxes holding scriptural passages that are worn on the arm and head. The base, the passageway for the straps, the protruding letter shin, the black outer straps, the square shape, the dalet and yod in the knots: each is called a law given to Moses at Sinai. Then a strap tears, and Rav Ashi settles whether it may be sewn from inside by telling his questioner to go see what people do.
menachot/35.question: If the shape of a knot came down at Sinai, why is a torn strap's repair decided by watching what people already do?

judge.reachNote: Where does authority for the details of a mitzva come from — revelation at Sinai or the settled practice of the community?

menachot/36.summary: Phylacteries run through the page. Speaking between the arm straps and the head box costs a second blessing and, in one baraita, counts as the sort of sin that sends a soldier home from the ranks of war. The argument then moves to nightfall, where Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yoḥanan split over whether wearing them after sunset breaks a positive mitzva or a prohibition, and Ravina watches Rav Ashi don them in the dark and claim he is only guarding them.
menachot/36.question: Rav Ashi believed night was a fit time for phylacteries and said so to no one but gave Ravina a cover story instead, so what makes a ruling too true to announce?
gate: gloss "mitzva" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The gap between what a sage holds to be true and what he is willing to teach publicly.

answer.quote: rather, Rav Ashi holds: This is the halakha, that night is an appropriate time for phylacteries, but a public ruling is not issued to that effect
answer.explanation: The page states the fact that Rav Ashi held night valid yet withheld public instruction, but never gives a reason why such a true ruling is not announced, so the question survives.

menachot/37.summary: Most of the argument is about where phylacteries sit: the weak arm, read out of yadkha spelled with a heh, and the crown of the head, the spot soft on a newborn. Then Peleimu asks which head a two-headed man uses, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi tells him to leave or be excommunicated. Moments later a man walks in with a two-headed firstborn, and an elder rules ten sela, five per skull.
menachot/37.question: Was the question ridiculous when Peleimu asked it, and what changed when a father with a two-headed son walked through the door?

judge.reachNote: When does a hypothetical stop being idle speculation and become law — the difference between a question asked for sport and the same question asked by someone who must act.

answer.quote: A child with two heads is like one that was ravaged, as he will certainly not live.
answer.explanation: The page's later remark that such a child cannot survive bears on why the phylacteries dilemma was dismissed as unreal, but it never states why the rebuke turned into a ruling once a real father appeared.

menachot/38.summary: The mishna says sky-blue and white fringe strings do not hold each other hostage: one without the other still works. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi read "that you may look upon it" in the singular and said each needs the other, so the Gemara bends the mishna into a rule about which color goes in first. Rava dismisses that and asks whether the cloth's color really sets the order, then says the mishna is about strings that snapped and are still long enough to knot.
menachot/38.question: Why does the Gemara strain so hard to read the mishna as agreeing with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, when at the end it produces a tanna who flatly says you affix white strings if you have no sky-blue?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the interpretive principle behind harmonization: why a mishna is stretched to fit one authority when a dissenting tanna is available to own it.

menachot/39.summary: Rav and Rabba bar bar "Hana sit together as a man walks past in a cloak of sky-blue wool whose corner fringes are all winding, with no loose strings hanging below. Rav calls the cloak beautiful and the strings not beautiful; his companion calls both beautiful. The split turns on two verses, one saying "twisted cords" and one saying "a thread": either the fringe needs both wound and loose portions, or either form alone will do.
menachot/39.question: When Rav says the strings on the passing man's cloak are not beautiful, is he calling them invalid or merely badly made?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's aesthetic language ('not beautiful') encodes invalidity or only sub-optimal performance of a mitzva.

answer.quote: And Rav holds that actually, we also require loose strings in addition to the windings
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks what principle underlies the dispute and answers that Rav holds loose strings are required, so his "not beautiful" expresses a genuine legal requirement (unfitness), not mere poor craftsmanship.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 39b: "And Rav holds that actually, we also require loose strings in addition to the windings". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already resolves this: the Gemara explicitly explains that Rav 'holds that actually, we also require loose strings in addition to the windings,' so the strings are unfit, not merely inelegant. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than asking it. For instance, ask why Rav phrases a disqualification in the language of beauty, or how his ruling here sits with the earlier statement in his name that fringes wound in their majority — or even with a single set of windings — are still fit.

menachot/40.summary: A linen cloak still needs ritual fringes, says Beit Hillel, even though the sky-blue tekhelet strings are wool and wearing wool with linen together is forbidden. The Gemara then hunts for why the Sages in Jerusalem discouraged it anyway, and every proposed fix gets knocked down: send ten men into the marketplace wearing them, announce it in the public lecture, test the dye, write letters to the dye producers. Rava settles on a torn corner stitched with linen thread and the leftover thread reused as fringes.
menachot/40.question: If the halakha follows Beit Hillel that a linen cloak is obligated, what is Rabbi Zeira doing untying the fringes off his own linen cloak?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "obligated: obligated to do what?" Name the object.
the question brings in "Zeira", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question uses "halakha", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is the gap between a Torah obligation and a rabbinic decree that makes a sage strip the mitzva off his own garment — but the page names that reason explicitly.

answer.quote: Because of this rabbinic decree, Rabbi Zeira untied the ritual fringes and removed them from his linen cloak.
answer.explanation: The page states outright that Rabbi Zeira removed his fringes because of the rabbinic decree Rava had just explained (the torn corner stitched with linen thread), so the question is answered in so many words.

summaryProblems.claim: The proposal to write letters to the dye producers gets knocked down along with the other fixes.
summaryProblems.pageSays: here, with regard to the mitzva of ritual fringes, which is merely a positive mitzva, is it not all the more so correct that letters can be relied on?

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 40b: "Because of this rabbinic decree, Rabbi Zeira untied the ritual fringes and removed them from his linen cloak.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The proposal to write letters to the dye producers gets knocked down along with the other fixes.", but the page says "here, with regard to the mitzva of ritual fringes, which is merely a positive mitzva, is it not all the more so correct that letters can be relied on?". Say what the page says. The question is answered on the page: the line "Because of this rabbinic decree, Rabbi Zeira untied the ritual fringes" gives the reason directly, so ask something the page leaves standing — for instance why a decree built on one man's possible mending of a torn corner is allowed to strip a Torah obligation from every linen cloak. Also fix the summary: the letters proposal is not knocked down; Rava defends letters (we rely on them for leap years and karet-level prohibitions), which is precisely why he must supply a new reason for the decree.

menachot/41.summary: An angel finds Rav Ketina wearing a linen cloak, which carries no obligation of fringes, and asks what will become of the sky-blue strings if he wears exempt garments in every season. Rav Ketina objects that Heaven does not punish for merely skipping a positive commandment, and the angel answers that in times of anger it does. The Gemara then rereads the whole exchange: the angel was not stating law, only asking whether Ketina was hunting loopholes.
menachot/41.question: If the linen cloak really carried no obligation, what was the angel accusing Rav Ketina of?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: It gestures at whether fringes bind the man or the garment, but the page's own resolution — evading a mitzva through technically exempt garments — is already restated in the summary itself.

answer.quote: Rather, this is what the angel is saying to Rav Ketina: Are you seeking ploys [tatzdeki] to exempt yourself from performing the mitzva of ritual fringes?
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly resolves the difficulty by saying the angel charged Rav Ketina not with violating an obligation but with contriving exemptions, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 41a: "Rather, this is what the angel is saying to Rav Ketina: Are you seeking ploys [tatzdeki] to exempt yourself from performing the mitzva of ritual fringes?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the angel accused Rav Ketina of, but the page answers it in so many words — "Are you seeking ploys to exempt yourself" — and the summary even repeats that answer in its last sentence. Write a question that starts after that resolution, for instance on the tension between the angel's warning and Shmuel's later ruling that the mitzva pertains to the garment, or on why a shroud is exempt because it is not made "to cover yourself" while a garment in a box is obligated. Keep the summary, which is accurate.

menachot/42.summary: Rav Naḥman finds Rav Adda bar Ahava tying strings onto a garment while reciting a blessing over making ritual fringes, and objects that no such blessing exists. That sends the page hunting for a rule about when the maker of a ritual object blesses, testing it against circumcision, a sukka built by gentiles, and phylacteries written by a woman or a minor. The answer offered: one blesses at the act that completes the mitzva, so fringes depend on whether the obligation sits on the cloak or on the man.
menachot/42.question: If the same three words, "that they prepare for themselves," can be taught as barring gentiles from making fringes and as permitting it, what decides which version Rav actually said?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a sage's transmitted words are chosen partly to keep him consistent with himself, but the page already states that criterion.

answer.quote: We teach it in this way, according to which there is no contradiction: Rav Yehuda says that Rav says: From where is it derived that if ritual fringes are attached
answer.explanation: Rav Mordekhai tells Rav Ashi that his version of Rav's ruling is the one taught precisely because it leaves no contradiction with Rav's other statement, and the page grounds it in the extra word "lahem," so the criterion the question asks for is supplied.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 42b: "We teach it in this way, according to which there is no contradiction: Rav Yehuda says that Rav says: From where is it derived that if ritual fringes are attached". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is settled on the page: Rav Mordekhai says the version is taught "in this way, according to which there is no contradiction," and the reading rests on the word "lahem." Ask instead about the principle the page actually builds, e.g. why blessing should attach to the act that completes a mitzva rather than to the act the Torah restricts to Jews, given that gentile-written phylacteries are unfit yet the writer says no blessing. Or press on the fringes dispute itself: what turns on the obligation resting on the cloak versus on the man.

menachot/43.summary: Two tests distinguish real tekhelet, the sky-blue dye for ritual fringes, from imitation, one an overnight soak in an aged solution, the other a baking in hard leavened barley dough. Wool brought by a sage from Mashkhei failed the first and passed the second; Rav Au0127ai said it cannot be neither tekhelet nor indigo, so the two tests must run in sequence. Later comes the question of who owes fringes, and why a blind person's garment counts while a night garment does not.
menachot/43.question: If a blind person's fringes are obligated because other people can see them, whose looking does "that you may look upon it" actually mean?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "obligated: obligated to do what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether the fringe mitzva is grounded in the wearer's own sight and remembrance or in the garment's public visibility.

answer.quote: I include the garment of a blind person, which is visible to others, even though the blind person himself cannot see it, and I exclude a nighttime garment, which is not visible even to others
answer.explanation: The page gives the criterion of visibility to others as the reason for the blind person's inclusion, which bears on whose seeing counts, but it never resolves how that squares with the verse addressing the wearer, especially since the Rabbis read "that you may look" as the wearer's own seeing leading to remembering Shema.

menachot/44.summary: The ḥilazon, the sea creature whose blood makes the sky-blue dye for ritual fringes, surfaces once in seventy years, so the dye is scarce and costly. Rabbi Natan proves that every small mitzva pays off in this world with a story: a man who sent four hundred gold coins to a prostitute overseas climbs to her golden bed, and his fringes slap his face. He stops; she later sells her property, converts under Rabbi Ḥiyya, and the same beds are set up again, permitted.
