Then Rabbi Ḥanina and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute whether the shewbread was an open box or a rocking boat.
menachot/94.question: If every objection to the rocking boat can be answered by adding a protrusion to the base or bending the panels inward, what evidence could ever settle the shape of the bread?

judge.reachNote: When each objection to a reconstruction can be met by adding a detail, the dispute becomes underdetermined — what could count as evidence at all?

answer.quote: It is in accordance with the opinion of the one who said the shewbread was like a rocking boat, i.e., Rabbi Yoḥanan.
answer.explanation: The page's closing move shows one kind of evidence that can favor a view — Rabbi Yehuda's tradition that loaves and panels lean on each other fits only the boat — but it never addresses whether such patched objections can settle the shape, so the question survives.

menachot/95.summary: When the camp moved through the wilderness, the Tabernacle was dismantled and the golden Table carried off with its loaves on it. One sage holds the bread was disqualified once the courtyard curtains came down; another holds it stayed sacred while it rested on the Table, and each brings a verse. After verses are traded both ways, Ravin arrives from Eretz Yisrael and reports there was no dispute at all: one spoke of loaves left on the Table, one of loaves removed from it.
menachot/95.question: If the dismantled Tent of Meeting keeps enough sanctity to preserve bread sitting on the Table, why is the rest of the sacrificial food disqualified the moment the curtains are rolled up?
gate: the question brings in "Tent", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Meeting", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What actually carries sanctity on the move — the place (courtyard/Tent) or the vessel (the Table) the offering rests on.

answer.quote: This Master, who stated that the shewbread is not disqualified during the journeys, stated his ruling with regard to loaves that are arranged on the Table
answer.explanation: Ravin's resolution locates the exemption in the loaves' resting on the Table rather than in any residual sanctity of the dismantled Tent, which bears on the question without ever stating why the remaining sacrificial food is disqualified.

menachot/96.summary: Twelve loaves of shewbread overhung the gold Table they sat on, so the priest folded the extra upward, two and a half handbreadths per side for Rabbi Yehuda, two for Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yoḥanan counts how high above the Table the holiness reaches, and the Gemara defends his number by tucking everything in: rods sunk into the loaves, hornlike protrusions folded under, gaps too small to count. Then the Table turns out to be carried, lifted with its loaves to show pilgrims bread still hot after a week.
menachot/96.question: If the bread came off the Table a week later exactly as it went on, why the rods, the wind gap, and the worry about mold?

judge.reachNote: Whether one may rely on a standing miracle, or must still take ordinary precautions as though the bread would spoil.

menachot/97.summary: A vessel plated in gold normally takes its status from the covering, which would make the shewbread Table susceptible to impurity like a metal vessel. The Gemara escapes this by citing Ezekiel, where one object is called an altar of wood and then named as the Table, so the hidden acacia decides. Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Elazar read the doubled name another way: with no Temple standing, a person's table atones when the poor are fed from it.
menachot/97.question: If the gold that everyone sees usually decides what a vessel is, why does the acacia that nobody sees decide this one?

judge.reachNote: Whether a vessel's identity follows what the eye sees (the covering) or what Scripture declares it essentially to be.

menachot/98.summary: A cubit of six handbreadths is called medium, which implies larger ones existed: two rods kept in the Shushan chamber, one half a fingerbreadth longer than Moses' cubit, one a full fingerbreadth longer. The reason given is accounting. Artisans took payment measured by the small cubit and returned their labor measured by the large one, so they could never be charged with misusing consecrated property, and the shorter rod was reserved for silver and gold.
menachot/98.question: If the safeguard against misusing Temple property works by paying artisans for less than they actually built, why is that loss treated as acceptable?

judge.reachNote: A safeguard against misappropriation of consecrated property is purchased at the worker's expense; the question asks how that cost is justified.

answer.quote: Since silver and gold were valuable, the difference between the two measurements was set at only half a fingerbreadth, so that the artisans would not suffer too great a loss.
answer.explanation: The page shows the Sages did weigh the artisans' loss and capped it for costly materials, but it never explains why imposing any loss at all is justified, so the question still stands.

menachot/99.summary: Eight priests swap the shewbread on the golden Table, four sliding the old loaves out as four push the new ones in, handbreadth for handbreadth, so bread is never absent. Rabbi Yosei disagrees: remove it all in the morning, replace it toward evening, and "always" is still satisfied, as long as the Table is not bare overnight. Rabbi Ami reads that leniency back into Torah study, one chapter in the morning and one at night.
menachot/99.question: If "always" can survive a whole day of an empty table, what work is the word still doing?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — what continuity means when it is measured in days rather than moments — but the page (and the note's own last clause) already supplies the answer.

summaryProblems.claim: four sliding the old loaves out as four push the new ones in
summaryProblems.pageSays: two with the two arrangements of the new shewbread in their hands and two with the two bowls of frankincense in their hands

judge.feedback: The summary says "four sliding the old loaves out as four push the new ones in", but the page says "two with the two arrangements of the new shewbread in their hands and two with the two bowls of frankincense in their hands". Say what the page says. The question is answered two lines later in the very baraita the summary paraphrases: "always" means the Table must not be left overnight without bread, and the summary itself already says so. Ask instead about what remains strange after that answer — e.g. why Rabbi Ami thinks a rule about an object resting on a table can be transferred to the mind of a person studying, or why the mishna's opinion insists on handbreadth-for-handbreadth continuity if a night's measure would do. Also fix the count: only two of the four incoming and two of the four outgoing priests handle loaves; the others carry the bowls of frankincense.

menachot/100.summary: A handful of a meal offering lifted at night cannot simply be poured back and re-scooped, because the service vessel has already gripped it: consecrated enough to be ruined, not enough to be offered. Rabbi Zeira objects from the shewbread, which sits on the Table from a Sunday and is not spoiled overnight. Rabba separates a night from whole days; Mar Zutra says bread laid out at the wrong time is as if a monkey had arranged it.
menachot/100.question: If a vessel can sanctify a handful at the wrong hour just enough to destroy it, why does the Table do nothing at all to loaves set down on the wrong day?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: How far the reach of a service vessel's sanctity extends in time — the gap between 'too early' by hours and 'too early' by days.

answer.quote: But if a rite is performed several days earlier it is considered a rite whose time has not yet arrived.
answer.explanation: Rabba answers precisely this question: a night before the day counts as one unit so the vessel sanctifies, but days in advance do not, so the Table does not sanctify the loaves.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 100a: "But if a rite is performed several days earlier it is considered a rite whose time has not yet arrived.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is simply Rabbi Zeira's objection, which Rabba answers on the same page by distinguishing a rite done the preceding night from one done days early. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer: for instance, press on what it means for the handful to be "consecrated enough to be disqualified but not to be sacrificed," or on why Rava needs the priest to physically remove the loaves before nightfall while Mar Zutra can say a misplaced arrangement is as if a monkey did it.

menachot/101.summary: Consecrated wood, frankincense, and service vessels are not redeemed, and one answer offered is plain scarcity: wood with a worm in it is disqualified, so usable wood is hard to come by. The second half asks what counts as food for purposes of ritual impurity, and Rabbi Shimon's test is whether you could feed it to someone else. The argument then runs on potential: wheat consecrated while still growing, a red heifer redeemable even on its pyre.
menachot/101.question: If the flour could have been redeemed at any moment and turned back into ordinary food, why should the fact that nobody actually redeemed it settle what it is?

judge.reachNote: Whether a thing's status is fixed by what was actually done to it or by what could still be done to it.

answer.quote: But is there a mitzva to redeem these meal offerings?
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely the note's objection and resolves it: potential redemption counts as actual only where there is a mitzva to redeem, as with the red heifer, and there is no such mitzva for a meal offering.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 101b: "But is there a mitzva to redeem these meal offerings?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page itself asks this question — "How can the flour be considered as not having a time in which it is fit for consumption merely because he has not redeemed it" — and answers it twice, first with "In any event, now he has not redeemed it," then with the distinction that only an item there is a mitzva to redeem counts as already redeemed. Rewrite the question to start after that answer: for instance, why a mitzva to redeem should be what converts mere possibility into accomplished fact, or why the same logic does not then apply to blood that stood to be sprinkled with time left in the day. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

menachot/102.summary: Rabbi Shimon holds that blood standing to be sprinkled counts as already sprinkled. Rav Ashi narrows this sharply: an animal that could have been redeemed by a spoken sentence counts as redeemed, but a sprinkling that merely could have happened counts as nothing. Pressed with cases of misuse and a ram brought for a sin that turned out never to have been committed, he splits the question, since misuse turns on sanctity and impurity turns on whether meat ever became food.
menachot/102.question: If a redemption that never happened counts as done because the words would have been easy, why does a sprinkling the priest had all day to perform count as nothing?

judge.reachNote: When does a potential act count as already performed — is it the ease of the act, or the change it actually effects in the object's status?

menachot/103.summary: A man vows a meal offering of barley, which no voluntary meal offering may be; the mishna has him bring wheat, while Rabbi Shimon exempts him because "he did not pledge in the manner of those who pledge." The Gemara then separates barley from lentils: barley is a plausible error, since the sota's meal offering is barley, so the words read as a mistake rather than a retraction. Lentils nobody confuses, so there the second half cancels the first.
menachot/103.question: If the barley vow stands only because a person might honestly confuse it with the sota's offering, is he bound by what he said or by what others decide he must have meant?

judge.reachNote: Whether a vow is constituted by the words uttered or by the intent the words are presumed to carry once they are recognized as an error.

answer.quote: Had I known that one cannot vow in this manner to bring barley for a meal offering, I would not have vowed in this manner but rather in that manner
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan's explanation has the vower himself declare the intent behind the erroneous words, which bears on the words-versus-intent question without settling whether the vow binds by speech or by reconstructed meaning.

menachot/104.summary: A vow of five log of wine matches no libation: three log go with a lamb, four with a ram, six with a bull. The Gemara allows four to be offered and the odd log to go to communal gift offerings, then stalls on eleven log: two rams and a lamb, or one short of two bulls? Elsewhere the meal offering is called the poor person's, credited as if he offered up his soul, yet someone who forgot what he pledged brings sixty-tenths of an ephah.
menachot/104.question: If the meal offering belongs to the person with little, what becomes of that person when a half-remembered vow costs sixty-tenths of an ephah?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: resolving doubt by maximal stringency ignores the means of the very person whose offering the Torah singled out as the poor man's soul-gift.

menachot/105.summary: A man vowed a meal offering and forgot which kind he named; the mishna has him bring all five. Rabbi Yirmeya says that cannot fit Rabbi Shimon, who allows half loaves and half wafers, leaving eleven more combinations to cover. Abaye answers with a spoken condition, borrowed from the man unsure he is a leper, who brings one animal and declares it a guilt offering if he is and a peace offering if he is not.
menachot/105.question: Can a sentence spoken over an animal decide which offering it is, when the man saying it does not know what he owes?
gate: gloss "guilt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "peace offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether words alone can determine which offering an animal or meal offering is when the owner's obligation is unknown — but the page answers it.

answer.quote: of uncertainty one may bring an offering and stipulate with regard to its type ab initio only for the remedy of a man
answer.explanation: The page states outright that a spoken condition can fix an offering's identity under uncertainty, and then sets its limits — ab initio only where a person needs purification, and with the stricter eating time imposed.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 105b: "of uncertainty one may bring an offering and stipulate with regard to its type ab initio only for the remedy of a man". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very question the page takes up and settles: Rabbi Shimon's stipulation does work, limited to the remedy of a man and with the stricter eating time. Rebuild the question around what is still hard after that answer — for instance why the leper's stipulation needs the excuse of 'remedy of a man' while the forgotten meal offering may be stipulated even ab initio, or how one handful can be assigned to loaves and wafers at once. Keep the summary as it stands; it is accurate.

menachot/106.summary: Someone vowed a meal offering of a certain number of tenths of an ephah and forgot the number. The Rabbis say bring one offering of sixty-tenths; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says bring sixty offerings in sixty vessels, 1,830 tenths in all, and 9,150 if the type was forgotten too. The Gemara then offers explanation after explanation for what the two sides are actually arguing about: non-sacred flour in the courtyard, mixing obligation with gift, how much oil, small offering for large.
menachot/106.question: If the surplus flour can simply be declared a gift offering, why does the donor have to hand the sorting over to the priest's hand, so that whatever it happens to reach becomes the obligation?

judge.reachNote: The idea is how an undifferentiated mass of flour can be retroactively split into obligation and gift by deferring designation to the priest's act.

answer.quote: since the tenths that fulfill an obligation and the tenths that are a gift are mixed together in a single vessel, when the priest removes a handful, isn't he removing a handful
answer.explanation: The page presents Rava's device of tying the designation to wherever the priest's hand reaches precisely as the answer to Abaye's objection that in a single mixed vessel the handful would otherwise be taken from obligation-flour for the gift and vice versa.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 106a: "since the tenths that fulfill an obligation and the tenths that are a gift are mixed together in a single vessel, when the priest removes a handful, isn't he removing a handful". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: Rava explains that the donor defers designation to the priest's hand because the obligation-tenths and gift-tenths are mixed in one vessel and cannot otherwise be told apart. Rewrite the question so it starts from that answer and asks what remains hard, for example whether a designation that only takes effect through the priest's grab is a real designation, or how this squares with the later worry about which handful may be burned first. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

menachot/107.summary: Vows made in vague words get decoded here: say "gold" and maybe you meant a lump, not a coin, until Rav Pappa notes nobody mints gold perutot. Pledged iron is measured by a spike for keeping ravens off the altar, pledged copper by a hook for scraping lamp wicks. The sharp move comes with the forgetful vower, who must cover every possibility: one of each animal, or 140 log of oil, the Sukkot-on-Shabbat maximum.
menachot/107.question: If the value of a small bull is contained in a large one, is a person who vowed small and brought large giving more than he promised, or something other than what he promised?

judge.reachNote: Whether a vow is a quantity of value that a larger gift subsumes, or a description that a different animal simply fails to match.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says: He has not fulfilled his obligation, as the offering that he brought did not correspond to his vow.
answer.explanation: The page itself frames the two horns of the note's question as the tannaitic dispute: the first opinion says he has fulfilled "as the value of a small bull is included in the value of a large bull," while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the offering "did not correspond to his vow."

summaryProblems.claim: The possibility that "gold" means a lump rather than a coin stands until Rav Pappa notes nobody mints gold perutot.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Elazar said: The case of the baraita is where he said the word coin.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Menachot 107b: "Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says: He has not fulfilled his obligation, as the offering that he brought did not correspond to his vow.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The possibility that "gold" means a lump rather than a coin stands until Rav Pappa notes nobody mints gold perutot.", but the page says "Rabbi Elazar said: The case of the baraita is where he said the word coin.". Say what the page says. The question restates a dispute the page already spells out in both directions, so it reads as answered rather than open; ask instead what remains hard after Rebbi's position, for example why the collection-horn count or the bull-and-calf ruling should follow from treating size as a description rather than a value. Fix the gold clause: the "lump" objection is resolved by Rabbi Elazar's point that he said the word coin, while Rav Pappa answers only the perutot objection.

menachot/108.summary: Half the page argues over the Temple's six collection horns and what becomes of leftover coins; Rabbi Elazar holds that surplus from the High Priest's griddle-cake meal offering simply rots. Then the mishna turns to vague vows: a consecrated bull goes blemished, and "one of my lambs" leaves everyone guessing which lamb. The Gemara rules that a person consecrates generously, and then hears that a seller of "a house from among my houses" may point to the one that collapsed.
menachot/108.question: If "a bull from among my bulls" means the best bull he owns, why may a man who sold "a house from among my houses" hand over the house that just fell down?
gate: gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that ambiguous wording ('one from among my X') may be construed generously when consecrating but in the giver's favor when selling.

menachot/109.summary: A vow to bring a burnt offering "in the temple of Onias" in Egypt drives the argument: Rava reads the vower as offering a gift he never consecrated, since he lives nearer Egypt than Jerusalem. Later the mishna's phrase "needless to say" about idolatry implies that Onias' temple was not idolatrous at all. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda then tell the same story of two priestly brothers with trickster and victim swapped, and the altar's status flips with them.
menachot/109.question: If the story of the two brothers yields the same conclusion about jealousy whichever one did the tricking, what makes the Egyptian altar idol worship in one telling and an altar to God in the other?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Egyptian", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The shared moral about jealousy is detachable from the altar's halakhic status, so something other than the plot must decide whether Onias built for Heaven or for idols.

answer.quote: Mar Kashisha, son of Rav Ḥisda, said to Abaye: What does Rabbi Meir do with this verse of Rabbi Yehuda?
answer.explanation: The page locates the hinge of the dispute in Isaiah 19:19 — Rabbi Yehuda reads it as sanctioning an altar to God in Egypt, and the Gemara asks how Rabbi Meir reassigns it (Abaye: to Hezekiah's gentile princes) — but it never says what within the brothers' story makes the altar idolatrous rather than holy.

menachot/110.summary: The final page of Menachot collects readings that turn study into service: scholars who learn the halakhot of the Temple are credited as though it stood in their days, and one who studies the law of the sin offering as though he brought one. Rava objects to the wording and pushes further, saying such a person need not bring the offering at all. The mishna then flattens bull and meal offering alike, provided the heart is directed toward Heaven.
menachot/110.question: If learning the law of the sin offering counts as bringing one, what is left for the person who slaughters an actual offering while his mind is elsewhere?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "meal offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether it is directed intent rather than the physical act that makes an offering an offering — and what that leaves of ritual performed absent-mindedly.

answer.quote: the verse states: "With your will you shall slaughter it" (Leviticus 19:5), i.e., sacrifice intentionally, in the form of a purposeful action
answer.explanation: The page rules that slaughter performed unawares is disqualified and that intentional action is indispensable, so the distracted slaughterer's offering does not count, though the page never weighs this against the credit given to study.

chullin/2.summary: Chullin opens with a mishna that says everyone may slaughter an animal, except a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor. Rav Acha and Rav Ashi then fight over one word: does "everyone" mean permitted from the start, or only valid after the fact? They trade cases of substituting animals, vows, sukka and fringes, until Rabba bar Ulla resolves it by reading in a ritually impure man who slaughters with a long knife so he never touches the meat.
chullin/2.question: If an impure man is believed afterward when he says he never touched the flesh, why is he not trusted to pick up the knife in the first place?

judge.reachNote: Why retrospective trust in a person's report does not become prospective permission to act — the gap between ab initio caution and after-the-fact reliance on his word.

answer.quote: with regard to sacrificial animals, he may not slaughter them ab initio even with a long knife, lest he come into contact with the flesh
answer.explanation: The page states the reason for barring him ab initio (the worry that he will touch the flesh) alongside the after-the-fact acceptance of his claim, but it never explains why his own testimony is credited afterward yet not relied upon in advance.

chullin/3.summary: The mishna says everyone may slaughter an animal, then turns around and lists people whose slaughter is suspect, and four sages take turns deciding who "everyone" is meant to include: a Samaritan, a Jew who eats unslaughtered carcasses for convenience, anyone who can recite the rules, anyone who has cut two or three times without fainting. Every reading runs aground on the same phrase in the mishna. The oddest test: hand the Samaritan an olive-bulk of the meat and watch whether he eats it.
chullin/3.question: Does the Samaritan's eating prove the animal was slaughtered properly, or only that he believes it was?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that another's self-interested scrupulousness can serve as evidence of a fact one cannot verify oneself.

answer.quote: Since Samaritans are meticulous with regard to the meat that they eat and eat meat only from an animal that was slaughtered properly, the Jew may partake
answer.explanation: The page gives the rationale for the olive-bulk test — Samaritan eating habits are trusted as reliable — but it does not distinguish proof of proper slaughter from the Samaritan's own confidence, so the question can still be pressed (especially given Rav Ashi's view that Samaritans are void converts).

summaryProblems.claim: Every reading runs aground on the same phrase in the mishna.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara answers: Supervision is necessary in the case where the one who slaughtered the animal is not before us so that we can examine him.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Every reading runs aground on the same phrase in the mishna.", but the page says "The Gemara answers: Supervision is necessary in the case where the one who slaughtered the animal is not before us so that we can examine him.". Say what the page says. Fix the claim that every reading founders on the phrase "any of them who slaughtered": that phrase defeats Abaye, Rava and Rav Ashi, but Ravina's two versions answer it by positing that the slaughterer is no longer before us to be examined or questioned — which is exactly why Ravina parted from the others. Keep the question; it can be sharpened by naming what the olive-bulk test actually leans on, the Samaritan's own standards rather than the Jew's inspection.

chullin/4.summary: A Jew finds a string of birds held by a Samaritan and does not know whether they were slaughtered properly, so he cuts off one bird's head and offers it to the Samaritan to eat. The Gemara keeps finding holes: maybe only that one bird was kosher, so the birds are hidden under the Jew's garment; maybe the Samaritan marked it, so the head is crushed unrecognizable. The test works only when the man being tested cannot tell which bird he is swallowing.
chullin/4.question: If the whole procedure depends on making it impossible for the Samaritan to cheat, what is left of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's claim that he is the more exacting one?
gate: the question brings in "Shimon", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Gamliel's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between a halakha built to defeat deception and a tanna's praise of the tested party's scrupulousness — trust versus verification.

answer.quote: Once it is known that they embraced observance of a mitzva, they embraced the mitzva and one may rely upon them.
answer.explanation: The page states that reliance on Samaritans rests on their having embraced a given mitzva, which bears on Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's claim but does not explain why a tamper-proof test is still required.

chullin/5.summary: Rav Anan says a Jew who worships idols can still slaughter meat others may eat, and the argument hunts for proof in what people actually ate. Ravens brought Elijah bread and meat, said to come from Ahab's slaughterhouse, but that proof is waved off: Elijah ate at God's word. Rabbi Zeira then reasons that since Rabbi Yoḥanan ate a Samaritan's slaughter, and God does not let the righteous stumble into forbidden food, he must have heard the ban and rejected it.
chullin/5.question: If a righteous man's dinner counts as evidence about the law, what could ever show that he simply got it wrong?

judge.reachNote: Whether the observed practice of the righteous is evidence of the law or merely protected conduct that proves nothing about it.

answer.quote: Since he ate the meat according to the word of God, the case of Elijah is different, and no proof may be cited from there.
answer.explanation: The page does show one way a righteous person's eating is discounted as legal evidence (special divine instruction), but it never entertains that such a figure simply erred — indeed Rabbi Zeira's reasoning assumes the opposite, so the question survives.

chullin/6.summary: At an inn in Ya'ei, Rav Asi eats eggs cooked in wine while Rabbi Zeira refuses them, worried the wine is demai, produce that may never have been tithed. Rather than conclude that Rav Asi ate something forbidden, Rabbi Zeira reasons that God does not let the righteous stumble, then goes out and hunts down a source permitting such mixtures. The rest of the discussion tests that leniency against women suspected of swapping ingredients, and each time supplies a motive.
chullin/6.question: Did Rabbi Zeira search the sources to find out whether Rav Asi had erred, or because he had already decided he had not?

judge.reachNote: Whether halakhic inquiry is open-ended investigation or a search for confirmation of a conclusion already reached on theological grounds.

answer.quote: Now, since even with regard to the animals of the righteous, the Holy One, Blessed be He, does not generate mishaps through them, is it not all the more so true
answer.explanation: The page narrates Rabbi Zeira's a fortiori conviction that the righteous do not stumble before he 'emerged, analyzed, and found' the permitting baraita, which bears on his motive without stating it outright, so the question can still be pressed.

chullin/7.summary: Rabbi Zeira argues that Rabbi Meir could not have eaten an untithed leaf by mistake, since God does not let even the animals of the righteous stumble. The proof is a donkey that refused its barley at an inn until the hosts separated the portions of produce owed to priests and Levites. The same Rabbi Pine"has ben Ya'ir later accepts a dinner invitation from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, then rejects every remedy his host offers for the dangerous white mules in the yard.
chullin/7.question: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi offers to sell the mules, abandon them, lame them, kill them, and each is blocked by a real prohibition, so was there any answer that would have gotten his guest to the table?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a scrupulous piety can make every available course forbidden, leaving the host with no lawful way to satisfy his guest.

chullin/8.summary: Shmuel rules that slaughtering with a knife heated white hot is valid, because the blade cuts the windpipe and gullet before the heat can sear them into a fatal wound. The same race shows up with a red hot skewer: a person struck with one ends up with half a boil and half a burn, and the two kinds do not combine to reach the split bean measure that makes a mark impure. The proof from the knife fails, since a blade cuts where a blunt rod strikes.
chullin/8.question: When a blow and a burn land in the same instant, is deciding which one came first a question of fact or a question of what the law needs to count?

judge.reachNote: Whether the 'which came first' race is a physical finding about knives and rods or a legal construct shaped by what the halakha needs to count together.

answer.quote: Cutting with a sharp blade is different from striking with a blunt object
answer.explanation: The Gemara distinguishes cutting from striking on physical grounds, which bears on whether priority is a matter of fact, but it never resolves the skewer dilemma, so the question can still be asked.

summaryProblems.claim: A person struck with a red hot skewer ends up with half a boil and half a burn.
summaryProblems.pageSays: it is a case where initially there was a boil half the size of a split bean on the person’s skin

summaryProblems.claim: The outcome is settled: the two halves are a boil and a burn and do not combine.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Or perhaps the effect of the heat comes first and then the effect of the blow comes and nullifies the effect of the heat

judge.feedback: The summary says "A person struck with a red hot skewer ends up with half a boil and half a burn.", but the page says "it is a case where initially there was a boil half the size of a split bean on the person’s skin". Say what the page says. The summary says "The outcome is settled: the two halves are a boil and a burn and do not combine.", but the page says "Or perhaps the effect of the heat comes first and then the effect of the blow comes and nullifies the effect of the heat". Say what the page says. Fix the skewer case: the half-measure boil was already on the skin before the white-hot skewer struck, and the outcome is an unresolved dilemma, not a ruling. Say both horns — half boil plus half burn that do not join, versus half boil plus half boil that do — and note that both attempted proofs are rejected. The question can stay as is.

chullin/9.summary: Rav Huna holds that once an animal is slaughtered it keeps a presumption of being permitted, even if something later raises doubt. Rabbi Abba tests this with a wolf that carries off the innards and brings them back punctured, since maybe the hole was there first and the animal was a tereifa, fatally flawed, all along. Rav Huna is unworried, yet a fig pecked by a bird is forbidden, because a snake may have left venom in it.
chullin/9.question: If the same doubt about an old hole leaves the animal permitted but the fig forbidden, what makes a possible poisoning weigh more than a possible forbidden meal?

judge.reachNote: Whether risk to life and ritual prohibition are weighed by the same standard of doubt — an idea the page itself states and then debates.

answer.quote: Are you comparing danger to prohibition? Danger is different, and one rules stringently in cases involving danger.
answer.explanation: Rav Huna answers the note's exact question in so many words, and Rav Ashi later brings "additional proof that danger is more severe than prohibition."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 9b: "Are you comparing danger to prohibition? Danger is different, and one rules stringently in cases involving danger.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks the very thing Rav Huna answers on 9b ("Danger is different, and one rules stringently in cases involving danger"), so it reads as unanswered only to someone who stopped mid-page. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what stays hard after it — for instance Rava's objection that doubt in prohibition is also ruled stringently, or why the sota derivation should limit impurity doubt but not the doubt about exposed water. Keep the fig-and-wolf contrast as the setup, but aim the question past the line the page already supplies.

chullin/10.summary: A man slaughters an animal and afterward finds his knife notched. Rav Huna says the notch may have come from the hide of the neck, so the slaughter fails; Rav Ḥisda pins it on a bone the man broke later and rules the meat permitted, since an uncertainty does not override a certainty. The distinction that carries the argument is where the flaw sits: the knife became defective, the animal did not, so the animal keeps its presumption of permissibility.
chullin/10.question: If a notched knife can be blamed on any neck bone you like, what stops you from blaming the last of Rav Yosef's thirteen animals and eating all of them?
gate: the question brings in "Yosef's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a leniency-by-attribution has no natural stopping point, but the page already states and resolves that very objection.

answer.quote: since we attribute the notch to the neck bone as a leniency, from where is it ascertained that it is on the neck bone of the first animal that it was notched?
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's exact objection and answers that nothing stops it — "Perhaps it is on the neck bone of the last animal that it was notched, and all of the animals are permitted" — which is why Rav Yosef's ruling is assigned to Rav Huna.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 10b: "since we attribute the notch to the neck bone as a leniency, from where is it ascertained that it is on the neck bone of the first animal that it was notched?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection on 10b, answered there by reassigning Rav Yosef's ruling to Rav Huna; a reader who finishes the daf would not still be asking it. Rewrite with a question the page leaves standing — for instance why a flaw in the knife should leave the animal's presumption of permissibility intact when a flaw found on an immersed person destroys his presumption of purity, or why deference to a Sage is required only for the first examination. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

chullin/11.summary: Ten sages line up to prove that one may rely on a majority that cannot be counted, such as the assumption that most animals have no hidden fatal defect. Each picks a case where the law itself blocks the examination that would settle the doubt: the head of a burnt offering, the Paschal lamb whose bones may not be broken, the scapegoat torn to pieces on the rocks. Nearly every proof is knocked down, and at the end someone suggests the majority applies only where examination is impossible.
chullin/11.question: If a majority is relied on only when looking is forbidden or impossible, is it a claim about what is probably true, or just a rule for what to do when you cannot check?
gate: gloss "the scapegoat" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Asks what rov actually is — an epistemic judgment that the case probably resembles the majority, or a default for action adopted only when verification is blocked.

summaryProblems.claim: Nearly every proof is knocked down.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara answers: Even so, there is no steward [apotropos] for restraining sexual immorality, and the identity of his father is not based on certainty.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Nearly every proof is knocked down.", but the page says "The Gemara answers: Even so, there is no steward [apotropos] for restraining sexual immorality, and the identity of his father is not based on certainty.". Say what the page says. Fix the claim that nearly every proof fails: only three are dismissed with "Therefore, no proof can be cited from here" (the burnt offering's head, the Paschal bone, the fat tail), while the objections to Rav Sheshet, Rabba bar Rav Sheila, Rav Aḥa, Rav Mari, Rav Kahana and Ravina are themselves rebutted and those proofs stand. Say instead that a string of proofs is tested, some discarded and most sustained, before Rav Ashi's slaughter case draws the qualification. Keep the question as it is.

chullin/12.summary: A man tells his agent to slaughter a chicken, comes home, and finds a chicken slaughtered. Rav Nahman permits it, but rules that produce found already set aside as teruma, the priests' portion, does not count; Rav Dimi presses him on the inconsistency. The answer is that no agent is presumed to have done his job: the chicken is fine because whoever slaughtered it was probably expert, while a stranger separating another man's teruma separates nothing.
chullin/12.question: If the chicken is permitted only because some unknown hand was probably expert, what work is the agent doing here at all?
gate: banned phrase: "what work".

judge.reachNote: Whether a permission rests on a person's assigned responsibility or merely on statistics about strangers — and what agency still contributes once the majority does the work.

answer.quote: Actually, there is no presumption that an agent performs his assigned agency, and in the case of slaughter, even if perhaps another person heard him instruct the agent
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman's resolution states outright that the agency carries no presumption and the permission rests on the majority of slaughterers being expert, though the page never says why the instruction to the agent is mentioned at all or what remains of it.

chullin/13.summary: A minor cannot form an intention that the law recognizes, yet he can carry produce up to the roof, and Rabbi Yoḥanan says that if he turns the produce over so dew will wet it, his intent counts. The same puzzle reaches slaughter, where a child drags an animal meant to be burned whole on the altar to the north side of the Temple courtyard and kills it there. Whether such readable intent works by Torah law or only rabbinic law stays disputed.
chullin/13.question: If turning the produce over shows plainly what the child wanted, why should that intent count by rabbinic law but not by Torah law?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what legal intent is: whether visible action can stand in for a mind the law refuses to credit, and on whose authority.

answer.quote: in a case where his thought is apparent from his actions, by Torah law he does not have effective thought, and by rabbinic law he has effective thought
answer.explanation: The page states the very split the question asks about as Rabbi Yoḥanan's resolution, though it never gives a reason for the split, so a reader could still ask why.

summaryProblems.claim: Whether such readable intent works by Torah law or only rabbinic law stays disputed.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves the dilemma: They have the capacity to perform an action and it is effective, even by Torah law.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Whether such readable intent works by Torah law or only rabbinic law stays disputed.", but the page says "And Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves the dilemma: They have the capacity to perform an action and it is effective, even by Torah law.". Say what the page says. Drop the claim that the Torah-versus-rabbinic status of readable intent stays disputed; in Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's version Rabbi Yoḥanan resolves it, ruling that such intent is ineffective by Torah law and effective by rabbinic law. Build the summary on that resolution, and then pitch the question at what the page leaves unstated, such as why the Sages would credit an intent the Torah refuses to credit, or why a minor's action counts by Torah law while his mind never does.

chullin/14.summary: A person who slaughters an animal on Shabbat or Yom Kippur is liable to death, yet the mishna says the slaughter works. Rav adds that the meat may not be eaten that day, and calls this Rabbi Yehuda's view; the Gemara then spends the whole page hunting for which of Rabbi Yehuda's rulings he meant. Gourds cut for cattle, a broken bowl, juice seeping from grapes, a sooty old lamp: each analogy is offered and each one is knocked down.
chullin/14.question: If an animal is already food while it is alive, what exactly came into being at the moment of slaughter that was not there when Shabbat began?

judge.reachNote: Whether slaughter produces a newly-born item (nolad) or merely separates food that was already there — the note names the idea, but the page states both sides of it.

answer.quote: Since it was prohibited when Shabbat began as the limb of a living being, it remains prohibited for the entire Shabbat.
answer.explanation: The page itself asks what changed and answers it twice: Abaye says nothing new came into being since it is "merely food that was separated," and Rav Sheshet answers that what was absent at the onset of Shabbat was permitted status, the animal then being a forbidden limb of a living being.

summaryProblems.claim: Each analogy is offered and each one is knocked down, including the sooty old lamp.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara answers: Yes, as we learned in a baraita that Rabbi Yehuda says:

summaryProblems.claim: Juice seeping from grapes is offered as an analogy for Rav's ruling and then knocked down.
summaryProblems.pageSays: we heard that it is Rabbi Yehuda who says: Food that was separated is permitted

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 14b: "Since it was prohibited when Shabbat began as the limb of a living being, it remains prohibited for the entire Shabbat.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Each analogy is offered and each one is knocked down, including the sooty old lamp.", but the page says "The Gemara answers: Yes, as we learned in a baraita that Rabbi Yehuda says:". Say what the page says. The summary says "Juice seeping from grapes is offered as an analogy for Rav's ruling and then knocked down.", but the page says "we heard that it is Rabbi Yehuda who says: Food that was separated is permitted". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words on the page: Abaye says slaughtered meat is "merely food that was separated" rather than an item that came into being, and Rav Sheshet says what was true at the onset of Shabbat was that the animal was forbidden as a limb of a living being. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled, or about what still pinches after Rav Sheshet's answer. Also fix the summary: the lamp analogy is not knocked down — the page ends with the Gemara defending it ("The Gemara answers: Yes") — and the seeping-liquids mishna is brought by Abaye against Rav, not as another analogy in Rav's favor.

chullin/15.summary: An animal slaughtered on Shabbat to feed a critically ill person leaves extra meat, and the argument turns to whether a healthy person may eat any of it that day. Rav's distinction rests on chewing: food was edible raw before Shabbat, so it was never set aside from use, while a live animal's meat could not be chewed and so was. Rav Dimi of Neharde'a reverses the outcome, since no olive-bulk of meat can be had without slaughtering the whole animal.
chullin/15.question: If the leftover meat is permitted because the animal could not be slaughtered in part, why is the leftover food in the pot forbidden on the mere suspicion that someone cooked extra?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the contrast between permission that follows from physical necessity and prohibition that follows from suspicion of abuse — but the page states that contrast outright.

chullin/16.summary: A knife fixed to a potter's wheel slaughters validly, since the potter's foot on the pedal drives it; a knife on a waterwheel does not, once the wheel is past its first turn. Rav Pappa runs the same line through a killing: a man who bound another and diverted a stream onto him is liable if the water struck by direct force, exempt if it traveled on and drowned him later. One yardstick for both.
chullin/16.question: If the released water counts as the man's own arrow on the first turn of the wheel, what changes by the second turn that makes it no longer his?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: At what point does a chain of motion a person set going stop counting as his own act.

answer.quote: killed by secondary force after the water flowed on its own, it is not by his direct action; rather, it is merely an indirect action
answer.explanation: The page names the criterion — once the water 'flowed on its own' the deed is indirect rather than the man's direct act — but it labels the shift rather than explaining why the released water stops being his arrow, so the question can still be asked.

chullin/17.summary: Shmuel's father would cut notches into knives and send them to Eretz Yisrael to learn which flaw ruins a slaughter; the answer came back that the disqualifying notch is like a saw, teeth pointing up, ripping the throat on the backstroke. Rava sorts notches into three kinds: one that catches, one that only entangles, one that rises and falls harmlessly. Then the sages test blades in sunlight, on water, with a strand of hair, on a fingernail, on the tongue.
chullin/17.question: If showing a knife to a Torah scholar is only a rabbinic custom kept up out of deference to him, why does Rav Ḥisda reach for Saul's words to call the examination Torah law?
gate: the question brings in "Saul's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of scriptural verses cited as support rather than derivation, but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: Indeed, it is a requirement by rabbinic law, and the verse is cited as a mere support for that practice, not as a source.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the tension between Rabbi Yoḥanan's deference rationale and Rav Ḥisda's verse, and resolves it by saying the verse is only an asmakhta, not a Torah source.

summaryProblems.claim: The disqualifying saw-like notch rips the throat on the backstroke.
summaryProblems.pageSays: whose teeth point upward, as it rips the simanim with every draw of the knife back and forth

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 17b: "Indeed, it is a requirement by rabbinic law, and the verse is cited as a mere support for that practice, not as a source.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The disqualifying saw-like notch rips the throat on the backstroke.", but the page says "whose teeth point upward, as it rips the simanim with every draw of the knife back and forth". Say what the page says. The question is closed by the page itself, which says the knife-showing rule is rabbinic and Saul's verse is "a mere support for that practice, not as a source" — so the rewrite needs a question the page does not settle. Consider asking about something still unresolved, such as why the examination methods multiply (sun, water, hair, tongue, nail) or why Rav Ashi disputes only the three-sides part and the attribution to Rava. Also fix the summary: the saw-like notch rips the simanim with every draw back and forth, not only on the backstroke.

chullin/18.summary: Rabbi Zeira moves from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael and eats meat from an animal whose knife slipped above the top ring of the windpipe, a slaughter Rav and Shmuel called invalid. Challenged about his home authorities, he does not defend the meat; he attacks the chain of transmission, saying Rav Yosef learns from anyone, even students who misquote. Rav Yosef, stung, names his own meticulous teacher, while Abaye and Rav Ashi argue that a traveler who never means to return sheds his old stringencies.
chullin/18.question: Rabbi Zeira never says the slaughter was valid, only that the ruling reached him through a sloppy transmitter, so was that an objection or a way to keep eating?

judge.reachNote: Whether discrediting a ruling's transmitter counts as halakhic argument or as cover for a practice one has already adopted.

answer.quote: that statement applies only in a case where his intent is to return. Rabbi Zeira was not one whose intent was to return.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself presses why Rabbi Zeira ignored the stringencies of his home place and supplies independent justifications (Abaye's subordination of Babylonia, Rav Ashi's no-intent-to-return), which bears on whether his transmission remark was the real ground, though it never says whether the remark was objection or excuse.

summaryProblems.claim: Abaye and Rav Ashi both argue that a traveler who never means to return sheds his old stringencies.
summaryProblems.pageSays: But when one ascends from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael, this principle does not apply. Since we, the residents of Babylonia, are subordinate to them in terms of halakha

judge.feedback: The summary says "Abaye and Rav Ashi both argue that a traveler who never means to return sheds his old stringencies.", but the page says "But when one ascends from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael, this principle does not apply. Since we, the residents of Babylonia, are subordinate to them in terms of halakha". Say what the page says. Separate the two answers: Abaye says the stringency rule simply does not apply when one ascends from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael, since Babylonia is subordinate in halakha, while only Rav Ashi invokes the traveler's intent to return. Keep the rest of the narrative as is, and let the question acknowledge that the Gemara already supplies grounds for Rabbi Zeira's eating beyond his jab at Rav Yosef's sources.

chullin/19.summary: A slaughterer's knife strays above the large ring of cartilage partway through the windpipe, and the argument is over which third of the cut decides the case. Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda both report rulings in Rav's name, and each reports the opposite of the other, valid when the middle third was cut properly, invalid when the middle third was the stray one. The test both sides use is where the animal's life left it.
chullin/19.question: Rav Ḥisda's reason for telling Rav Huna not to retract is that retracting would wreck his own earlier ruling, so is consistency a fact about the animal or only about Rav Huna?

judge.reachNote: Whether halakhic consistency is a claim about the animal's condition or a demand placed on the ruling sage's own record.

answer.quote: life left the animal with the cutting of the second third of the windpipe, it left the animal in the course of diverting the knife
answer.explanation: Rav Ḥisda grounds the demand for consistency in a criterion about the animal itself — where life left it — so the page bears on the question, though it never addresses whether coherence is owed to the case or to the ruler.

chullin/20.summary: Pinching, melika, is how a priest kills a sacrificial bird: he cuts from the nape with his thumbnail rather than with a knife at the throat. Much of the argument is about where the cut may start and whether the nail may be drawn back and forth or must press through in one motion. Then Ze'eiri says a broken neck bone with most of its flesh cut makes a carcass, and Rava asks how pinching can consecrate a bird already dead.
chullin/20.question: If cutting one windpipe or gullet is enough to kill a bird, what is the priest doing when he keeps pinching through the second one?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — an act done on an already-dead bird must accomplish something other than killing — but the page names that something outright.

answer.quote: There, he continues pinching in order to fulfill through it the mitzva of separation between the head and the body in the bird burnt offering.
answer.explanation: Rava states explicitly that pinching past the first siman serves the mitzva of separating head from body, which is precisely what the note asks about.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 20b: "There, he continues pinching in order to fulfill through it the mitzva of separation between the head and the body in the bird burnt offering.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words at the end of 20b: Rava says the priest continues pinching to fulfill the mitzva of separation between head and body. Build the new question on what remains hard after that answer — for instance why the two simanim count as "part of the mitzva of slaughter" for separation while the skin does not, even though a minority of simanim left uncut still leaves the slaughter valid. Keep the summary as it stands; it tracks the page.

chullin/21.summary: A priest killing a bird offering pinches its neck from behind with his thumbnail, and the argument here is how deep the cut goes: spinal column and neck bone first, then the gullet or windpipe, one for a sin offering, two for a burnt offering. Rabbi Zeira objects that one version leaves the priest pinching a bird already dead. The discussion then moves to bodies, where a person whose neck bone and surrounding flesh are cut counts as a corpse while still twitching.
chullin/21.question: If movement no longer proves life, what is the severed lizard's tail doing when it convulses?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that twitching and convulsion are not evidence of life, so halakhic death is decided by structural severance rather than by observed movement.

answer.quote: like the tail of a lizard that was severed that convulses even though it is not alive
answer.explanation: The page asserts that the severed tail's convulsing is motion without life, which is the premise the question probes, but it never explains what the motion is or why it occurs.

chullin/22.summary: The mishna rules that doves are fit for the altar only when mature and pigeons only when young, so the same age never works for both. The Gemara fixes the line by plumage: doves count once their feathers glisten gold, pigeons stop counting once theirs turn yellow. That leaves a bird in between, and Rabbi Zeira asks whether it is merely a doubtful case or a third thing, belonging to neither category, that can never be brought at all.
chullin/22.question: Is the yellowing bird disqualified because something real in it has changed, or only because the verse says "of doves" and not all doves?

judge.reachNote: Whether a disqualification reflects a genuine change in the object or is a decree of the verse that creates a category.

answer.quote: They are unfit as doves because they are not sufficiently old and as pigeons because they are no longer young.
answer.explanation: The baraita gives a real developmental reason for the disqualification alongside the scriptural exclusion, though it does not settle whether the verse or the bird's state is doing the work, which Rava's proof then presses in the other direction.

chullin/23.summary: Rabbi Zeira asks about a palges, a sheep too old to be a lamb and too young to be a ram, somewhere between twelve and thirteen months. If a man vowed a burnt offering of a ram or of a lamb and brought a palges, has he paid his vow, or is a palges a third thing belonging to neither class? The same shape returns with siur, dough neither matza nor leavened bread; both dilemmas end unresolved.
chullin/23.question: When bar Padda has the man stipulate "if it is a ram" and "if it is a lamb," why should the possibility he never names be the one that does not exist?
gate: the question brings in "Padda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the silences in a legal formula are evidence about what its author thinks exists, or merely about what he chose to say.

chullin/24.summary: A short mishna says there is something that keeps priests fit for Temple service while it disqualifies Levites, and something that works the other way around. The baraita fills it in: blemishes disqualify priests but not Levites, while Levites age out at fifty and priests do not. From the gap between the verses' twenty-five and thirty, the Sages get five years of apprenticeship, and a rule that a student with nothing to show after five years never will.
chullin/24.question: If a Levite is finished at fifty because he can no longer carry the Tabernacle's boards, why does a priest go on serving until his hands and feet shake?
gate: the question brings in "Tabernacle's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether fitness for service tracks the physical work required of the tribe or is simply a scriptural category assigned to each group.

answer.quote: Therefore, the verse states: “Which pertains to the Levites,” and not which pertains to the priests.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the very inference that priests should also age out and rejects it on the strength of the verse, which restricts the disqualification of years to Levites, while a separate verse ties that disqualification to the era of carrying the Tabernacle on their shoulders.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 24a: "Therefore, the verse states: “Which pertains to the Levites,” and not which pertains to the priests.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already asks and answers this: the baraita entertains the a fortiori inference that years should disqualify priests too, and rejects it with "which pertains to the Levites," and not the priests, plus the verse limiting the years-disqualification to the era of carrying the Tabernacle. Write a question that starts from that answer rather than one the baraita disposes of. For instance, ask about the tension between a purely textual limit for Levites and the functional tests the Gemara then uses for priests and for Levites in the Temple, trembling hands and a changed voice.

chullin/25.summary: A mishna states that what stays pure in wooden vessels becomes impure in metal ones, and the reverse. The Sages explain the reversal: an unfinished wooden vessel that can already hold something is susceptible to impurity, while an unfinished metal one is not until its crafting is done. Rabbi Yoḥanan attributes this to metal being made for honored uses; Rav Naḥman to its price, and they split over cups carved from animal horn.
chullin/25.question: Does an object become what it is the moment it can do its job, or only when its maker stops working on it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea beneath the wood/metal reversal: is identity conferred by present function or by the completion of the craftsman's intent.

answer.quote: since metal vessels are crafted for uses of honor, they are not considered vessels until their completion
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan (and Rav Naḥman's price rationale) explain why metal waits for completion while wood counts once fit for use, which bears on the question but does not settle the general principle of when a thing becomes itself.

chullin/26.summary: Temed is water poured over grape dregs, and whether it counts as wine or is still just water decides if it can be bought with second-tithe money, produce money that must be spent on food in Jerusalem. Rav Naḥman says that if the temed later ferments, it was produce all along, revealed after the fact. Rava counters from a ritual bath case, where a drop of milk in drawn water still looks like water, so go by appearance.
chullin/26.question: If a cup of temed left on the shelf can settle what the liquid already was at the moment of purchase, at what point did it actually become wine?
gate: gloss "second-tithe" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Does later evidence reveal what a thing always was, or does status track what the thing is now (taste and appearance)?

answer.quote: the matter was revealed retroactively, such that when the temed was purchased it was produce fit to be purchased with second-tithe money
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman's reasoning states that later fermentation retroactively establishes that the liquid was already produce at purchase, while Rava's appearance-based reading holds that before fermentation it is water — so the page frames both sides of the timing question without fixing a moment when it "became wine."

chullin/27.summary: The mishna rules that cutting one of the neck's two pipes, windpipe or gullet, makes a bird's slaughter valid, while an animal needs both, and most of a pipe counts as all of it. Three sages then prove from the Torah that slaughter belongs at the neck, reading one verb as bends, flows, or speaks. Each proof is picked apart (why not the tail, the nose, the tongue?), and each ends in the same admission: it is tradition.
chullin/27.question: If every one of the three scriptural readings collapses under a single objection and the rule turns out to rest on tradition anyway, what are the three sages doing?

judge.reachNote: Asks what a scriptural derivation is for when the law is admittedly received by tradition — the status of a verse as support rather than source.

answer.quote: The verse serves to teach that one should not sever the head completely from the animal’s body and render it a broken animal.
answer.explanation: After each derivation collapses into tradition, the Gemara salvages a residual teaching for the verse, which bears on but does not fully explain why three sages advanced scriptural proofs at all.

chullin/28.summary: A duck in Rava's house arrives for slaughter with its neck filthy with blood, and nobody knows whether its windpipe was severed or its gullet perforated beforehand. Behind that duck sits a dispute about birds, where Rav Naḥman holds that cutting either the gullet or the windpipe suffices and Rav Adda bar Ahava holds that only the gullet works. The Gemara calls Rav Adda conclusively refuted, then withdraws the refutation, and settles the question only through Rav Yosef's plan for the bird.
chullin/28.question: Why does a stained duck in one household settle a question that a baraita called a conclusive refutation could not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward what kind of evidence settles law — a distinguishable textual proof about pinching versus a live ruling on an ordinary bird — but the page states that distinction outright.

answer.quote: perhaps it is different there with regard to pinching, as in that case there is the spine and the neck bone that are cut initially
answer.explanation: The page itself explains why the pinching baraita cannot settle the matter — it concerns a case where the spine and neck bone are already cut — and therefore turns to the duck, an actual non-sacred slaughter, asking "What then is the halakha in the case of slaughter?"

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 28a: "perhaps it is different there with regard to pinching, as in that case there is the spine and the neck bone that are cut initially". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question: it says the pinching baraita may be different "as in that case there is the spine and the neck bone that are cut initially," then explicitly asks what the halakha is for slaughter and brings the duck. Write a question that starts after that answer — for instance, why Rava's praise of his son's plan counts as a ruling on the Naḥman/Adda dispute at all, or why Rabbi Yehuda's veins are read as puncturing rather than cutting despite the word sheyishḥot. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

chullin/29.summary: Rav is said to hold that a windpipe cut exactly halfway counts as if most of it were cut, and the Gemara hunts for cases that would prove him wrong. Rava rescues him by distinguishing tereifa, a fatally injured animal, from slaughter, but Abaye turns the reasoning around and the defense collapses. So the Gemara moves the whole dispute elsewhere: a nation split evenly, half ritually impure on the fourteenth of Nisan, arguing over who brings the Paschal offering and when.
chullin/29.question: If half the people are impure, what makes that half a congregation rather than simply a very large number of individuals?

judge.reachNote: When does a mass of individuals become a single collective body, such that the law addresses it as a congregation rather than as many persons?

answer.quote: The status of half the people is that of a congregation, not that of a collection of individuals.
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks Rav's reason and answers from Numbers 9:10–11 that an impure congregation is not deferred, asserting that half the people count as a congregation, but it never states what makes half qualify as a congregation rather than a large body of individuals.

chullin/30.summary: Rav rules that a siman, one of the two pipes in the neck, cut in two or three separate spots is still a valid slaughter; Shmuel answers that slaughter must be clear and obvious, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish anchors that in Jeremiah's sharpened arrow. Later a bull is cut exactly that way, and Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta walks into the shop and buys the best meat, arguing by eating. Rava, meanwhile, shoots birds out of the air.
chullin/30.question: If an arrow is the model for a slaughter that is clear and obvious, why does Rava's actual arrow leave everyone guessing which way it cut the bird's neck?

judge.reachNote: The arrow is the Torah's image of a clean, visible cut, yet a real arrow's cut cannot be inspected — so what does "clear and obvious" demand, appearance or verifiability?

answer.quote: And perhaps when the arrow cut the bird’s neck it performed an inverted slaughter, with the arrow concealed in the neck
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely this worry about Rava's arrow, but its reply breaks off mid-sentence at "We see," so no answer is actually stated on this page.

chullin/31.summary: A knife that falls by itself and cuts an animal's throat in the correct way is still not valid slaughter, since the verse is read as excluding what was slaughtered on its own. But the Gemara infers from that same line that a knife a person drops does work, even with no thought of slaughtering at all. Rabbi Natan needs no intent; the Rabbis want at least intent to cut, and Rava reports Natan's answer: the verse says slaughter, not cut.
chullin/31.question: If a knife falling on its own produces nothing edible, what changes when a human hand lets go of the very same knife?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that human agency, apart from any intent, may be what turns a cutting event into an act of slaughter.

answer.quote: the slaughter is valid is due to the fact that it comes due to the action of a mentally competent person
answer.explanation: In explaining why Rava had to state his ruling twice, the Gemara names the feature that distinguishes a dropped or thrown knife from one that falls on its own — it proceeds from a competent person's act — though this is voiced inside a hypothetical about what one might have thought, so the question of what that agency supplies can still be pressed.

chullin/32.summary: A mishna asks how long a slaughterer may pause mid-cut before the slaughter is ruined: the knife falls and he picks it up, or he tires and another man finishes. The Sages measure the fatal interval differently, by the time it takes to slaughter a second animal, or to cast one to the ground first, or to lift it and lay it down. Asked which measure fits a bird, Rav says he never felt close enough to his uncle Rabbi Ḥiyya to ask.
chullin/32.question: Why would Rav, who learned the whole topic from Rabbi Ḥiyya, hold back the one question that would have settled it?

judge.reachNote: Transmission of Torah runs through personal relationships, so a link in the chain can be lost not for want of knowledge but for want of closeness.

answer.quote: When we studied this topic I did not feel sufficiently intimate with my beloved uncle, Rabbi Ḥiyya, such that I could ask him that question
answer.explanation: The page states Rav's own reason — he lacked sufficient intimacy with Rabbi Ḥiyya — but says nothing about why that closeness was lacking or why it was needed to ask, so the question can still be pressed.

chullin/33.summary: Rav A a bar Yaakov holds that once the windpipe and gullet are cut, a Jew may eat the innards of a still convulsing animal, but a gentile may not, since for a gentile meat becomes permitted only at death. Rav Pappa sat before him and wanted to object that nothing permitted to a Jew is forbidden to a gentile, then kept quiet, since a reason had been given. A baraita then permits both to cut an olive-bulk from the neck, salt it, and eat.
chullin/33.question: Was Rav Pappa right to swallow his objection just because Rav A a bar Yaakov had supplied a reason, when the baraita contradicts the ruling anyway?

judge.reachNote: Does a sage's having stated a reason for his ruling insulate it from objection, or must the objection still be pressed when sources contradict it?

answer.quote: It is taught in a baraita not in accordance with the opinion of Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov
answer.explanation: The page shows that the ruling Rav Pappa declined to challenge is in fact contradicted by a baraita, which bears on whether his silence was warranted, but it never evaluates Rav Pappa's deference itself.

chullin/34.summary: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua argue over whether a person who eats impure food takes on the same degree of impurity as what he swallowed. Eliezer's proof is the carcass of a kosher bird: touching it does nothing, but swallowing it makes a person's clothes impure. Yehoshua refuses the analogy, calling that bird a novel ruling that cannot serve as a paradigm, and counters with measures: food goes impure at an egg-bulk, an eater only after half of a half-loaf.
chullin/34.question: When does a rule that behaves like nothing else, a bird carcass harmless to touch and defiling to swallow, count as evidence, and when is it just an oddity to be quarantined?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the underlying question of when a halakhic anomaly (ḥiddush) can generate inference and when it must be sealed off as exceptional.

answer.quote: we do not derive other cases from the case of the carcass of a kosher bird, because it is a novel ruling that cannot serve as a paradigm
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yehoshua's bare principle that a novelty cannot ground an inference, but it gives no criterion for when such an anomaly may or may not serve as evidence, and Rabbi Eliezer's reply shifts to the measures argument rather than answering the novelty objection.

chullin/35.summary: An animal is slaughtered and no blood emerges, and Rabbi Shimon says the slaughter itself made the meat able to catch ritual impurity, since food only becomes susceptible once wetted by a liquid. Rav Asi reads him strictly: slaughter, never blood. The Gemara brings four proofs and dismantles each, because Rabbi Shimon's rulings that blood of an animal dead of natural causes and blood from a wound do not count still leave slaughter blood undecided.
chullin/35.question: If the same blood pours out whether a person kills the animal or it simply dies, why should one flow count as a liquid and the other not?

judge.reachNote: What makes blood count as a liquid for susceptibility — the manner of death versus the substance itself.

answer.quote: What is different with regard to blood of animals that are killed that they render food items susceptible to ritual impurity? It is due to the fact that it is written
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises exactly this distinction and answers it from the verse about drinking "blood of carcasses," which shows killed-animal blood counts as a drinkable liquid.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 35b: "What is different with regard to blood of animals that are killed that they render food items susceptible to ritual impurity? It is due to the fact that it is written". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very one the Gemara asks and settles at the end of the page, where the distinction is derived from the verse "drinks blood of carcasses" and the parallel verse about pouring blood "as water." Rewrite so the question starts from that scriptural answer instead of ignoring it — for instance, why a verse about drinking should determine what counts as a liquid, or why the "pour it as water" verse is read as permitting benefit rather than as conferring susceptibility. Keep the summary's framing of Rav Asi and the rejected proofs, which the page supports.

chullin/36.summary: Blood from a freshly slaughtered animal splashes onto a gourd of teruma, the produce set aside for priests, and the question is whether that wetting makes the gourd able to contract ritual impurity.
