answer.explanation: The page offers a purely textual derivation (the definite article pointing to "the most important thigh") alongside the wrestling reconstructions, which bears on whether the narrative grip is doing the legal work, but it never addresses whether the scene is being reconstructed to fit a rule already held.

chullin/92.summary: Pharaoh's imprisoned butler dreamed of a vine with three branches, and the sages here read that vine six different ways: princes, Torah, Jerusalem, the manna and the well, the three pilgrimage Festivals. Rabbi Yehoshua knocks down Rabbi Eliezer's reading of the branches as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob on a technicality: a dream shows the future, and they were already born. Then Reish Lakish maps the vine onto the people, with scholars as grape clusters and ignoramuses as the leaves that shelter them.
chullin/92.question: If the clusters of grapes would not survive without the leaves, why does the word from Eretz Yisrael have the grapes pray for the leaves rather than rank the leaves first?
gate: the question brings in "Eretz", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yisrael", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Dependence does not translate into precedence: the ignoramuses sustain the scholars, yet the duty created is intercession by the sustained, not a reversal of standing.

answer.quote: Let the clusters of grapes pray for the leaves, as were it not for the leaves, the clusters of grapes would not survive.
answer.explanation: The page gives the reason the grapes must pray for the leaves — their dependence on them — but never addresses why the instruction takes the form of prayer rather than reordering the ranks, which is what the question asks.

chullin/93.summary: Most of the page maps forbidden fat and blood inside a slaughtered animal: five sinews in the tail, membranes on the spleen and the kidney, veins in the foreleg that Rava says are banned only because they are full of blood. Rabbi Yoḥanan disclaims expertise, saying he is not a butcher and not the son of a butcher, but he remembers what the study hall said. At the end, butchers' credibility flips twice, and the reason given is forgetting.
chullin/93.question: If butchers became trustworthy only because they forgot the lenient opinion and grew used to the harder scraping, is that trust in the butchers or trust in their forgetting?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that halakhic credibility is grounded in the difficulty of the task and in habit rather than in the person's honesty or knowledge.

chullin/94.summary: A Jew who sends a gentile a thigh of meat still holding the sciatic nerve, the sinew Jews may not eat, may be giving a gift that looks more generous than it is. From there the page collects cases of misleading: Shmuel's attendant paying a ferryman with a non-kosher chicken, a wine barrel with oil floated at its mouth, an empty oil jug offered for show. Then the line shifts, and a butcher's vague announcement passes, because the buyers fool themselves.
chullin/94.question: If a buyer who misreads a vague announcement has only fooled himself, why did Rav Safra feel he had to tell Mar Zutra that nobody had come to greet him?
gate: the question brings in "Safra", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Mar", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Zutra", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question does reach the real idea — where active deception ends and letting a person mislead himself begins — but the page supplies Rav Safra's motive and Rava's rebuttal outright.

answer.quote: Rav Safra said to Rava: But if I would not have said so we would have misled him.
answer.explanation: The page has Rav Safra state his own reason for speaking up — that silence would have amounted to misleading Mar Zutra — which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 94b: "Rav Safra said to Rava: But if I would not have said so we would have misled him.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few words later on the page: Rav Safra says he spoke because otherwise "we would have misled him," and Rava replies that Mar Zutra misled himself. Rewrite so the question starts from that exchange rather than asking for a motive the page states. A better target is the tension between Rava's permission to let a gentile buyer fool himself and the earlier decrees that forbid sending an uncut thigh or selling tereifa precisely because someone might draw a wrong conclusion.b.rn.gt.pkt.hs.dbl.tst.chk.brk.vld.trc.nrm.qst.lbl.txt.itm.evt.mtx.ptr.srv.nod.exp.cnt.dat.grp.flg.rec.set.map.arr.str.num.bin.sum.ttl.val.idx.buf.tmp.cur.ref.obj.key.tag.pos.dir.len.max.min.avg.std.err.log.dbg.inf.wrn.crt.fat.ok.no.yes.on.off.up.dn.lt.gt.eq.ne.le.ge.and.or.not.xor.add.sub.mul.div.mod.pow.sqrt.abs.sgn.flr.cei.rnd.trn.mn.mx.cmp.swp.srt.rev.fnd.ins.del.upd.qry.cmt.rbk.beg.end.nxt.prv.fst.lst.all.any.non.som.mny.few.lot.big.sml.new.old.hot.cld.wet.dry.hi.lo.in.out.pre.pst.mid.top.bot.lft.rgt.ctr.ful.emp.opn.cls.run.stp.pau.res.rst.ini.fin.sav.lod.imp.exp.cpy.cut.pas.und.red.zom.zoi.fit.sel.mov.rot.scl.flp.mir.grd.snp.lck.unl.hid.shw.viz.inv.act.ina.ena.dis.chg.mod.rdy.bsy.idl.wat.slp.wak.die.liv.brn.gro.mat.age.hlt.ill.cur.hrt.kil.rev.spw.tel.war.jmp.fly.swm.crl.wlk.rnn.snk.hop.dig.cut.chp.brn.frz.mlt.boi.evp.cnd.sub.dep.dis.abs.ref.rfr.rfl.dif.int.uni.sub.sup.equ.neq.les.gre.ltq.gtq.tru.fal.nul.udf.nan.inf.eps.pi.e.phi.tau.deg.rad.grn.sin.cos.tan.asn.acs.atn.snh.csh.tnh.exp.log.ln.lg.sqr.cub.rot.trn.shf.msk.bit.byt.wrd.dwd.qwd.oct.hex.dec.bcd.asc.utf.uni.chr.str.txt.doc.pag.lin.col.tab.spc.nwl.crt.lf.eof.nul

chullin/95.summary: A butcher tells a man he quarreled with that the fine cut he ate came from a tereifa, an animal with a fatal defect, which he had sold off to a gentile shop. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refuses to ban all gentile butcher meat over one spiteful man. That pulls the page toward Rav's harsher view, that meat left out of sight is forbidden, a rule Rav never stated outright; it was inferred from two animal heads fished from a river.
chullin/95.question: If Rav himself admitted that at that river crossing forbidden meat was the more common kind, should an afternoon at a gentile port have become a general rule about every unwatched piece of meat?

judge.reachNote: Whether a ruling driven by one place's local majority of forbidden meat can be stretched into a universal rule about unwatched food.

answer.quote: There is room to say that this incident cannot serve as a precedent for a general policy, because that location was a port of gentiles
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection and answers that the river-port incident may not generalize, since most meat there was non-kosher and Rav might permit where the majority is kosher.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 95a: "There is room to say that this incident cannot serve as a precedent for a general policy, because that location was a port of gentiles". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the exact objection the Gemara raises and resolves on 95a, where it says the gentile port cannot serve as a precedent because forbidden meat was more common there. Rewrite so the question starts after that answer: for example, ask why the Sages preserved an inferred stringency at all once its factual basis was localized, or press on how Rav's own practice (eating only fresh, sealed, or triangle-marked meat) squares with a rule he never stated. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

chullin/96.summary: Two witnesses who describe a killer by his distinguishing marks are not believed, but two who say they recognized his face are, and the man is executed on their word. The page uses this, along with a blind man who knows his wife without seeing her marks, to rank recognition above identifying marks, even though a lost item is not returned on recognition alone. Then it moves to scraping out the sciatic nerve, where Shmuel tells a butcher he nearly served forbidden meat.
chullin/96.question: If a recognized face is enough to put a man to death, why is it not enough to get a lost cloak back?

judge.reachNote: Why the same act of recognition counts as proof in one area of law and not in another — whether reliability or something else (stakes, claimant self-interest) sets the standard.

chullin/97.summary: A young goat was roasted with its forbidden fat in the synagogue of the town of Maon, and Rabbi Yoḥanan told the people to peel the meat away and eat down to the fat. The problem sharpens with meat cooked in milk, since no Jew may taste that mixture to check whether the flavor carried, so Rava turns to a gentile cook's palate. Where no taster is available, the fallback is sixty times as much permitted food.
chullin/97.question: If flavor is the real test, what happens when the gentile cook's tongue and the sixty-to-one measure would give opposite answers?

judge.reachNote: Whether prohibition tracks actual perceptible flavor or a fixed formal ratio that stands in for it.

answer.quote: a type of food mixed with food not of its own type when the mixture may be forbidden and it is a case where there is no gentile cook available
answer.explanation: The page arranges taster and sixty-to-one as a hierarchy — sixty applies only where no tasting is possible — which bears on the conflict but never states what to do if the two measures did disagree.

chullin/98.summary: A half-olive-bulk of forbidden fat, about the volume of an olive, falls into a pot of kosher meat, and the argument is how much permitted food it takes to cancel it. Rav Ashi holds out for sixty times the volume and tells his son not to treat measures lightly. Then two sons of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permit mixtures at forty-five and forty-three, each citing a father who once permitted less than sixty.
chullin/98.question: If sixty is the number derived from the nazirite's ram, what lets a son permit at forty-three because his father once permitted at forty-five?
gate: the question uses "nazirite", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether a measure derived from a verse binds a judge, or whether a father's practical precedent can license assessing by eye below the derived number.

answer.quote: Rabbi Ḥanina said: Rabbi Ḥiyya did not make this statement to set a halakhic principle, but merely as an exaggeration.
answer.explanation: The Gemara notices that a figure below sixty conflicts with the sixty-fold rule and defuses it in Rabbi Ḥiyya's case as non-halakhic exaggeration, but it never explains the forty-seven/forty-five/forty-three rulings of the Nasi's household, so the note's question survives.

summaryProblems.claim: A half-olive-bulk of forbidden fat is 'about the volume of an olive'.
summaryProblems.pageSays: There was once a certain half-olive-bulk of forbidden fat that fell into a pot of kosher meat.

judge.feedback: The summary says "A half-olive-bulk of forbidden fat is 'about the volume of an olive'.", but the page says "There was once a certain half-olive-bulk of forbidden fat that fell into a pot of kosher meat.". Say what the page says. Fix the measure: a half-olive-bulk is half an olive's volume, which is exactly why Mar bar Rav Ashi proposed thirty half-olive-bulks and his father insisted on sixty. Keep the question about precedent versus the derived sixty, but sharpen it against the page's own handling of a low number, where Rabbi Ḥanina writes off Rabbi Ḥiyya's 'thirty' as exaggeration while the forty-five and forty-three rulings stand unexplained.

chullin/99.summary: Split beans of teruma, the portion set aside for priests, get cooked with ordinary lentils, and the question is how many lentils it takes to cancel them: sixty times their volume, a hundred, or a hundred and one. Abaye presses Rav Dimi with the case, Rav Dimi falls silent, and Abaye supplies an answer for him about leaven being unusually potent. Later, Rabbi Ami sends people asking about a thigh cooked with its sciatic nerve to a colleague who permits it.
chullin/99.question: Is Rabbi Ami's habit of routing questioners to a lenient colleague, whose ruling he does not accept, a kindness or a dodge?

judge.reachNote: Whether a judge may route a case to an authority whose leniency he rejects — deference to others' ease versus owning one's own ruling.

answer.quote: Rabbi Ami himself did not hold accordingly, but he did not wish to rule stringently for others.
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Ami's motive for the referral — unwillingness to impose his own stringency on others — which bears directly on the question, though it does not settle whether that counts as kindness or evasion, and the closing ruling that sciatic nerves impart no flavor adds a further wrinkle.

chullin/100.summary: A mishna rules that the ban on the sciatic nerve, the thigh sinew named in Jacob's wrestling story, applies only to kosher animals, while Rabbi Yehuda extends it to non-kosher ones because Jacob's sons were forbidden the nerve while camel meat was still open to them. The Gemara objects that Yehuda holds elsewhere that a second prohibition cannot land on food already forbidden. The resolution offered: the nerve binds gentiles too, so it adds something new and takes hold.
chullin/100.question: If the nerve's prohibition sticks only because it also binds Noah's descendants, why should a rule aimed at gentiles change anything about meat a Jew may already not eat?
gate: the question brings in "Noah's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Asks whether a prohibition's wider scope over other people gives it independent force on a person already bound by another ban.

answer.quote: Since the prohibition of eating the sciatic nerve adds an additional stringency that did not exist with regard to non-kosher meat, it takes effect even though there was an already existing prohibition.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the mechanism — a prohibition with broader scope counts as an added stringency and so can attach — but it does not explain why the added reach over gentiles should affect a Jew's liability, so the question can still be pressed.

chullin/101.summary: The sciatic nerve, the thigh tendon forbidden after Jacob wrestled through the night, drives a long argument about whether one prohibition can land on meat already forbidden for another reason. To keep Rabbi Yosei HaGelili consistent, the Gemara reverses the names in a teaching about labor done on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbat, and Rava explains that strange year as a decree sent during persecution. Then the Rabbis deny Jacob's sons were ever called children of Israel.
chullin/101.question: If the ban on the sciatic nerve was really spoken at Sinai, why is it written back into the night Jacob was injured, and why does that placement carry no weight?
gate: the question brings in "Sinai", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Where a law is narrated versus when it legally took effect — placement as explanation rather than enactment.

answer.quote: but was written in its place, after the incident of Jacob wrestling with the angel, to allow the Jewish people to know the reason the sciatic nerve was forbidden
answer.explanation: The baraita states exactly why the Sinai-given prohibition is written at the Jacob narrative, and adds that since it took effect only at Sinai "there is no proof that it ever applied with regard to non-kosher animals," which is why the placement carries no legal weight.

summaryProblems.claim: The Rabbis deny Jacob's sons were ever called children of Israel.
summaryProblems.pageSays: And the Jewish people were not called “the children of Israel” until they received the Torah at Mount Sinai.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 101b: "but was written in its place, after the incident of Jacob wrestling with the angel, to allow the Jewish people to know the reason the sciatic nerve was forbidden". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The Rabbis deny Jacob's sons were ever called children of Israel.", but the page says "And the Jewish people were not called “the children of Israel” until they received the Torah at Mount Sinai.". Say what the page says. The question is answered almost verbatim on the page: the baraita says the prohibition was stated at Sinai but written in its place so Israel would know why the nerve was forbidden, and that therefore it proves nothing about non-kosher animals. Build the question from something the page leaves unresolved instead — for instance Rav Ashi's "Was the Torah given piecemeal?" reply, or Rav Ashi's suggestion that meat-impurity may be the more stringent prohibition. Also fix the summary: the Rabbis say the people were not called "children of Israel" until Sinai, not that they were never so called.

chullin/102.summary: A baraita argues about a man who eats a live kosher bird so small and scrawny that its entire body holds less than an olive-bulk of meat. Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, holds that a living creature already counts as a bundle of limbs, so swallowing it whole is eating a limb from a living animal; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requires the limb be severed first. Rava then makes the whole thing turn on what the eater was thinking.
chullin/102.question: If Rava is right that one man is lashed and another goes free for swallowing the same small bird, what exactly did the second man fail to do?

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition attaches to the deed itself or to the deed as construed by the eater's intention.

answer.quote: There can be different outcomes for different people who perform the same act, as this individual's action is judged according to his thought and that individual's action is judged according to his thought.
answer.explanation: Abaye raises the note's exact objection and Rava answers it outright: the second man failed only in his thought, since each man's act is judged by what he intended (to eat it limb by limb or whole).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 102b: "There can be different outcomes for different people who perform the same act, as this individual's action is judged according to his thought and that individual's action is judged according to his thought.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Abaye's challenge, and Rava answers it on the page: each man's action is judged according to his own thought. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved, for example why thought can turn a whole bird into a set of limbs for one eater but not for another, or why Rabbi Elazar's thought-based exemption runs in the opposite direction from Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's thought-based liability. Keep the summary's accurate framing of the baraita and the scrawny bird.

chullin/103.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish argue over how many sets of lashes a man earns for eating a limb torn from a living animal that is also a tereifa, an animal with a fatal defect. The dispute then narrows to a measuring problem: the forbidden bite must be an olive-bulk, so what if he splits it inside his mouth and swallows the halves separately? Rabbi Yoḥanan counts the throat's pleasure, Reish Lakish counts what reaches the stomach.
chullin/103.question: If a person swallows half an olive-bulk, vomits it, and swallows it again, is the eating measured where the food is tasted or where it finally arrives?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether eating is defined by pleasure at the throat or arrival in the stomach — but the page names and settles it.

answer.quote: let him resolve the dilemma from that which Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said, which indicates that we follow the throat.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this dilemma about vomiting and re-eating and resolves it in favor of following the throat, since the throat derives pleasure from a full olive-bulk.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 103b: "let him resolve the dilemma from that which Rabbi Asi said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said, which indicates that we follow the throat.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and decided on the page: Rabbi Elazar's dilemma about vomiting and re-eating is resolved by Rabbi Asi's report that we follow the throat. Ask something the page leaves standing — for instance, why pleasure at the throat should count as eating when nothing whole ever reaches the stomach, or why Reish Lakish's stomach standard leaves almost no way to be liable for a limb from a living animal, forcing Rav Kahana's swallowable bone. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

chullin/104.summary: A mishna rules that someone who vows off meat may still eat fish and grasshoppers, which leaves open whether birds count as meat at all. Rabbi Akiva decides categories by what a shopper's agent would bother to ask about: sent for vegetables, he comes back asking about gourds, never about legumes, so gourds are vegetables. The Gemara then fights over whether birds and cheese may sit on one table, and whether the Sages stack one precaution on another.
chullin/104.question: If what counts as meat or as a vegetable is settled by what an errand-runner thinks worth asking about, does the category shift when shopping habits shift?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that halakhic categories may be defined by ordinary usage rather than by fixed nature, and asks whether that makes them mutable.

chullin/105.summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue over whether one wipes the mouth with bread after eating meat or rinses it with water, and the Gemara ends by saying both required both and never disagreed at all. Rav Ḥisda holds that meat before cheese needs a pause while cheese before meat needs none, and meat lodged between the teeth still counts as meat. Then Abaye lists habits he once explained as mere tidiness, and Rabba replaced every reason with a hidden danger.
chullin/105.question: When Rabba tells Abaye that sweeping up crumbs guards against poverty rather than mess, and that the gutter hides a demon rather than dirty water, has anything about what a person does actually changed?

judge.reachNote: Whether a practice's stated reason is decorative or actually governs how far the practice extends.

answer.quote: After the man ate, he brought a hoe, uprooted the grass, and threw it into the river.
answer.explanation: The page does not state a principle about reasons changing practice, but the crumb story (and the foam remedy, "He should sink the foam inside the beverage and then drink it") shows the deeper reason pushing conduct well past ordinary tidiness, so the question can still be honestly asked.

chullin/106.summary: A storekeeper who sold different meat to his Jewish and gentile customers watched a guest sit down without washing his hands, took him for a gentile, and served him pig. Rav Dimi and Ravin told that story and its companion, about a host with lentils left on his mustache, in competing versions, and Rabbi Abba always taught the harsher one. Later the page cannot settle whether washing before fruit is required, a mitzva, optional, or arrogant.
chullin/106.question: What makes rinsing your hands before eating fruit mere cleanliness to one sage and arrogance to another?

judge.reachNote: When a pious-looking act has no legal basis, keeping it can read as piety or as pretension — the question reaches that.

answer.quote: The obligation of washing hands before eating non-sacred food is due to an ancillary decree on account of teruma
answer.explanation: The page supplies the rationale that grounds washing before bread (a safeguard for teruma), which bears on why washing for fruit could be seen as baseless stringency, but it never states why Rabbi Oshaya calls it cleanliness while Rav Naḥman calls it arrogance.

chullin/107.summary: Shmuel, as a boy, is found crying because his teacher struck him for feeding the teacher's son without first washing his hands. Earlier the page tests the same question from several angles: eating with a cloth over the hands, worn wineskin scraps used as gloves, an attendant fed slices of bread while he works. The ruling splits the pair apart, requiring the one being fed to wash while the one doing the feeding need not.
chullin/107.question: If the worry is hands touching food, why must the man who touches nothing wash, while the hands actually holding the slice go unwashed?

judge.reachNote: Is handwashing tied to contact with food, or to the act of eating itself?

answer.quote: The reason for the washing there is not on account of the food specifically. Rather, it is due to an evil spirit named Shivta
answer.explanation: Abaye's Shivta explanation removes the food-contact rationale from the feeder's case, which bears on the asymmetry, but the page never says why the non-touching eater must nonetheless wash.

chullin/108.summary: A single drop of milk falls into a pot of meat, and the mishna asks whether the piece it landed on is sixty times the drop or less. Rav says the piece itself becomes non-kosher meat in its own right, so it can forbid every other piece in the pot, because a food is not nullified by its own type. The argument then narrows to whether meat you could still wring the absorbed milk out of stays forbidden.
chullin/108.question: If the milk can still be squeezed back out of the meat, why does Rav treat the meat itself as forbidden rather than just the milk it is holding?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the real idea — whether an absorbed prohibition transforms its host into a forbidden substance or stays a separable foreign substance — but the page already answers it.

answer.quote: Rather, Rav must maintain that even an item that can be wrung to remove the forbidden substance is forbidden.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself poses the note's question ("why should this piece of meat itself become non-kosher?") and resolves it by stating that Rav holds a wringable item remains forbidden, so the meat itself is non-kosher and not merely a container for milk.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 108a: "Rather, Rav must maintain that even an item that can be wrung to remove the forbidden substance is forbidden.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own question, answered a few lines later with "Rather, Rav must maintain that even an item that can be wrung to remove the forbidden substance is forbidden." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer and asks what remains hard, for instance why Rav then permits the large pot of milk into which an olive-bulk of meat fell, or why the boiling-pot and removal-before-cooling conditions are needed. Keep the same idea — when absorbed flavor turns a food into a forbidden substance in its own right — rather than restating a point the page settles.

chullin/109.summary: An udder is torn open and its milk squeezed out before cooking, and the mishna says that if someone skipped that step and cooked it anyway, no meat-and-milk prohibition was broken. A baraita explains why: milk inside a suckling calf's stomach counts as milk because it left the teat, while milk still in the udder's flesh never did. Yalta then argues that for everything forbidden there is a permitted lookalike, and asks for the taste of meat in milk.
chullin/109.question: If the milk in an udder is not milk at all, what is Rav Nahman actually serving Yalta when she asks for a dish that tastes forbidden?
gate: the question brings in "Nahman", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a permitted lookalike satisfies desire by flavor while the halakhic category (milk vs. not-milk) stays untouched.

answer.quote: The Torah prohibits the consumption of meat cooked in milk; I wish to eat a dish that tastes like meat cooked in milk.
answer.explanation: The page states that Yalta asked only for the taste, and that Rav Naḥman answered with roasted udders, but it never confronts the tension the note names — that the udder's milk is by definition not milk.

chullin/110.summary: Rav forbade eating udders, which hold milk inside meat, and Rav Yitzhak bar Avudimi says he never taught that; Rav had simply found a town where women asked how much milk to cook meat in, and fenced the gap. Sura kept the ban, Pumbedita did not, so when Rami bar Tamrei found Sura's discarded udders on the eve of Yom Kippur he roasted and ate them. Hauled before Rav Hisda, he has an answer for every charge, and one answer stops a stranger's flogging.
chullin/110.question: Does Rami bar Tamrei's knack for finding the exemption look different when it frees the man tied to the pillar than when it gets him his roasted udders?

judge.reachNote: The same legal sharpness that excuses oneself from fringes, phylacteries and a local stringency can also shield another man from the lash — is evasion a different thing when it serves someone else?

answer.quote: Rav Ḥisda said to Rami bar Tamrei: I see that you are very sharp.
answer.explanation: Rav Ḥisda's praise, delivered right after the flogging is halted, is the page's only verdict on Rami's ingenuity, but it does not distinguish the self-serving evasions from the rescue, so the question still stands.

chullin/111.summary: A liver cooked with other meat may or may not bleed into it, and the page leaves the question open, working instead through roasting spits, whether liver sits above or below the meat, and a dripping pan where liver blood floats on the fat rather than sinking under it. The sharper move comes later: how would anyone know whether flavor actually crossed over? Rava says taste it, and since no Jew may taste blood, Rav Pappa proposes a gentile cook's palate.
chullin/111.question: If a gentile cook's tongue can settle whether blood passed from a salting bowl into the food cooked in it, why did Rabbi Ami break his bowl instead of having it tasted?
gate: the question brings in "Ami", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a prohibition absorbed in a vessel can be settled empirically by a palate, or whether the vessel itself is treated as permanently compromised.

answer.quote: Rava responded: Indeed, a gentile cook can discover whether the food in the bowl has absorbed the taste of blood. When I said my statement I was referring to a case where there is no gentile cook available.
answer.explanation: The page concedes that a gentile cook's tasting works and limits Rava's stringency to where none is available, which bears on the question but never explains Rabbi Ami's breaking of his bowl.

chullin/112.summary: Shmuel holds that a loaf is prohibited if unsalted roasted meat was cut on it, since blood from the meat soaks into the bread. The conditions then narrow fast: only if the meat is ruddy, only if the stain passes through to the other side, only if the liquid is viscous rather than runny. Three sages meet the same loaf: Shmuel throws it to his dog, Rav Huna hands it to his attendant, and Rava eats it, calling the red liquid meat wine.
chullin/112.question: If the loaf is permitted, as the Gemara concludes, what is happening when Rav Huna will not eat it himself and gives it to the man who serves him?

judge.reachNote: The question gestures at the idea of a personal stringency being passed off onto a subordinate, but the page already names Rav Huna's fastidiousness as the reason.

answer.quote: In fact, the loaf is permitted for consumption, and Rav Huna is different, as he is of delicate constitution and did not want to eat the loaf himself.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very objection the note asks and resolves it by saying the loaf is permitted and Rav Huna merely had a delicate constitution, so he passed it to his attendant.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 112a: "In fact, the loaf is permitted for consumption, and Rav Huna is different, as he is of delicate constitution and did not want to eat the loaf himself.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, which the page answers outright: the loaf is permitted and Rav Huna was simply of delicate constitution. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than restating it — for instance, ask what it means that a sage's private fastidiousness can be discharged by handing the food to his attendant, or press on why Shmuel's dog and Rava's "meat wine" sit beside a single permitted loaf. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

chullin/113.summary: Salting draws blood out of meat, so the Gemara asks what the brine carries from one piece to the next, starting with a kosher fish salted together with a non-kosher one. Rav Sheshet salted meat one piece at a time, and the Gemara shrugs that off, since blood leaving one side of a single piece could be absorbed by the other. Shmuel, citing Rabbi Ḥiyya, says breaking a slaughtered animal's neck too early traps blood, weighs the meat down, and cheats buyers.
chullin/113.question: If the trapped blood only matters because customers pay by weight, is there anything wrong with the meat a butcher keeps for himself?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether trapped blood is a monetary wrong against the buyer or a dietary prohibition in the meat itself — the Gemara's own unresolved dilemma.

chullin/114.summary: The verse "in its mother's milk" appears three times in the Torah, and the Gemara hands each repetition a job: one extends the ban to cow and ewe milk, one to the milk of the kid's older sister, one to cooking a mother's own meat in her own milk. Each time, someone first tries to reach the rule by arguing from the easier case, and each time the argument is broken by a stray counterexample: mules, freed slaves, seeds sown in the ground.
chullin/114.question: Why should the mating rules of a mule, or the status of a freed slave and her enslaved brother, count as evidence about whether a goat may be cooked in its mother's milk?

judge.reachNote: Whether an a fortiori inference is a formal claim about any fruit/mother pairing, so that a counterexample from mules or slaves can defeat a food prohibition.

answer.quote: the hypothesis that if two fruit cannot be paired, one can learn by a fortiori inference that the fruit cannot be paired
answer.explanation: The page explains that the mule and slave cases are brought as tests of a general formal hypothesis about fruit-with-fruit versus fruit-with-mother pairings, and are dismissed when the prohibition turns out to stem from something else (paternity, manumission), so the question of why such domains count is addressed but not fully settled.

summaryProblems.claim: Each of the three derivations is broken by a stray counterexample: mules, freed slaves, seeds sown in the ground.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav Ashi said: It is needed because one can say that the refutation of the a fortiori inference is present from the outset

summaryProblems.claim: One of the three repetitions of the verse does the job of extending the ban to the milk of the kid's older sister.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Yes, it is indeed so; the halakha with regard to the older sister is derived from the common denominator of the mother and a cow.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Each of the three derivations is broken by a stray counterexample: mules, freed slaves, seeds sown in the ground.", but the page says "Rav Ashi said: It is needed because one can say that the refutation of the a fortiori inference is present from the outset". Say what the page says. The summary says "One of the three repetitions of the verse does the job of extending the ban to the milk of the kid's older sister.", but the page says "Yes, it is indeed so; the halakha with regard to the older sister is derived from the common denominator of the mother and a cow.". Say what the page says. The summary's pattern claim is wrong: the first two a fortiori inferences are refuted by the mother's uniqueness (she may not be slaughtered with the kid on the same day), and the mule, slave and seed counterexamples all belong to the single third derivation and are each rejected before Rav Ashi settles it with "two separate bodies that were never unified." Also note that the Gemara retracts the older-sister assignment, conceding it can be derived from the mother and cow together, so the extra verse is reassigned to the mother's own meat and milk. Keep the question's line of attack, but let the summary show that these outlandish cases are proposed and then knocked down.

chullin/115.summary: Food cooked in violation of Shabbat stays permitted to eat, which strains the principle that anything made by a practice God calls abominable should be banned. The Gemara works down a list: grain threshed by a muzzled cow, seeds sown as diverse kinds, the offspring of crossbred animals, a mother bird set free by court order, each permitted for its own reason. Then Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan argue over the verse behind the ban on meat cooked in milk, and whether it forbids selling it too.
chullin/115.question: If a sin was committed in both cases, why does grain from a muzzled cow's threshing stay permitted while meat cooked in milk may not even be sold to someone else?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a sin in the making does not by itself contaminate the product — but the page says precisely that, resolving it by text over logic.

answer.quote: and yet benefit from the products of these actions is permitted. One cannot refute a verbal analogy with logical reasoning.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the muzzled-cow/ox-and-donkey cases as proof that a committed sin does not imply the product is forbidden, and answers that meat in milk is prohibited for benefit by textual derivation (verbal analogy and verses), which logical parity cannot overturn.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 115b: "and yet benefit from the products of these actions is permitted. One cannot refute a verbal analogy with logical reasoning.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already asks and answers this: it invokes plowing with ox and donkey and the muzzled cow to show that a sin committed does not make the product forbidden, and concludes that meat in milk is different only because its benefit prohibition rests on a verbal analogy and explicit verses, which logic cannot refute. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why a textual derivation should outweigh an a fortiori inference, or why Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan need separate verses for eating and for benefit. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

chullin/116.summary: Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili both read the verse about cooking a kid in its mother's milk as excluding birds, though they split over wild animals and over whether bird meat in milk is barred by rabbinic decree at all. A baraita reports that in Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's locale people simply ate it. Levi was served a peacock's head cooked in milk, said nothing, and later told Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi he assumed the local sage had permitted it.
chullin/116.question: If Levi only guessed that Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira had permitted bird in milk there, was his silence at the table a ruling he never actually made?
gate: the question brings in "Beteira", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a visiting sage's silence before a practice he cannot forbid amounts to endorsing a ruling he never issued.

answer.quote: If so, I could not prohibit it to them, and I certainly could not excommunicate them for following their ruling.
answer.explanation: Levi himself explains his silence as an inability to prohibit or excommunicate in another sage's locale rather than as a positive permission, which bears on the question without settling whether silence counts as a ruling.

chullin/117.summary: Rav Mari asks Rav Zevid why a sheep's fatty tail, which the Torah calls "fat," may be eaten when forbidden fat may not. Rav Zevid replies that only what an ox, a sheep and a goat all have counts as forbidden fat, and neither ox nor goat carries such a tail. Rav Ashi instead says the tail is never called plain "fat"; that answer is rejected, since then taking it from an offering would not be misuse of Temple property.
chullin/117.question: If a fat tail is fat enough that benefiting from it on an offering counts as misuse of Temple property, what keeps it off the list of fats forbidden at the table?

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether a Torah label ("fat") fixes an item's status, or whether the prohibition's scope is set by what the three species share.

answer.quote: This teaches that the Torah designates as forbidden fat only an item that is found equally in an ox, and a sheep, and a goat
answer.explanation: Rav Zevid explicitly states why the fatty tail is permitted at the table even though it is called "fat" — the prohibition covers only fat common to ox, sheep, and goat.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 117a: "This teaches that the Torah designates as forbidden fat only an item that is found equally in an ox, and a sheep, and a goat". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is exactly what Rav Zevid answers on the page ("only an item that is found equally in an ox, and a sheep, and a goat"), and the summary itself already reports that answer, so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to ask about something the page leaves unresolved — for instance, why the tail can be full "fat" for the altar and misuse of consecrated property while being less than fat for the eating prohibition, or what the Gemara's rejection of Rav Ashi shows about when a name in a verse governs status. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

chullin/118.summary: A hide with no olive-bulk of flesh on it does not carry the impurity of an animal carcass, but a hide with an olive-bulk attached does, even if a person touches only its outer side. From there the page sorts appendages into handles, the part held while eating, and protection, the part that shields the food. A pomegranate's protrusion counts as protection; its flower does not, since it only guards the guard.
chullin/118.question: Why should a pomegranate's flower count for nothing, when the protrusion it shields counts only because it shields the fruit?

judge.reachNote: How far derivative status carries: does something that protects a protection share the protection's legal standing, or does the chain stop at one remove from the food?

answer.quote: But its flower does not join together with the pomegranate in that regard because it does not provide protection for the fruit; rather, it provides protection for the protection
answer.explanation: The page states the operative reason — the flower guards only the guard, not the fruit — but it never justifies why the chain of protection stops after one step, so the question can still be asked.

chullin/119.summary: Half an olive-bulk of corpse flesh on the end of each of two bones, with only the bare ends under a roof, can make the house impure. The argument sorts these attachments into two kinds, a handle you grip and a covering that shields the food, each with its own minimum of attached flesh: an olive-bulk, a bean-bulk, or less. Then Reish Lakish asks what a single hair is good for, and the question of hairs piercing a hide arrives.
chullin/119.question: If hair really penetrates all the way through the hide to touch the flesh, is any parchment ever whole, or does ink filling the hole simply let the problem go unnoticed?

judge.reachNote: Underneath is whether legal wholeness is physical integrity or functional appearance — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: Any perforation over which the ink passes and which it covers is not considered a perforation that invalidates the writing.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection about writing phylacteries on a perforated hide and resolves it by ruling that a hole covered by ink is not a disqualifying perforation, which is the second alternative the note's question proposes.

summaryProblems.claim: Reish Lakish asks what a single hair is good for.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara adds: So too it is reasonable to explain that the person is impure because hair is considered protection

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 119b: "Any perforation over which the ink passes and which it covers is not considered a perforation that invalidates the writing.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Reish Lakish asks what a single hair is good for.", but the page says "The Gemara adds: So too it is reasonable to explain that the person is impure because hair is considered protection". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words by the ruling that ink covering a perforation does not invalidate the writing, so it cannot stand as posed. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for example why hair that pierces the hide counts as protection for the flesh rather than protection on top of protection, or what work is left for a single hair once Rabbi Ela's 'awn among many awns' reading is adopted. Also do not attribute the 'for what function is one hair fit' challenge to Reish Lakish; the page puts it in the Gemara's mouth.

chullin/120.summary: A baraita rules that someone who coagulates blood and eats it, or melts forbidden fat and swallows it down, is liable. The objection is blunt: the Torah writes eating, and swallowing a liquid is drinking. Reish Lakish answers by reading the word "soul" in three separate verses, on forbidden fat, on leavened bread, and on a bird's carcass, to include drinkers, and the Gemara then works hard to show that none of the three could have been derived from the other two.
chullin/120.question: If coagulating blood counts because the eater turned it into food, why does melting fat into a liquid not turn it out of a prohibition written as eating?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Whether a person's act of changing a substance's form can create or dissolve the category of 'eating' the Torah prohibits.

answer.quote: Reish Lakish said: One is liable even for drinking the melted forbidden fat of an animal.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the note's objection—"Eating, and not drinking, is stated in the Torah"—and answers it with Reish Lakish's homiletical reading of "soul" to include one who drinks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 120a: "Reish Lakish said: One is liable even for drinking the melted forbidden fat of an animal.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates the Gemara's own objection, which the page answers outright with Reish Lakish's derivation from the word "soul"—and the summary itself already reports that answer. Ask instead about something the passage leaves standing: why three separate scriptural inclusions are needed rather than one governing principle about liquefied prohibitions, or why a carcass melted in the sun escapes where fire-melted does not. Keep the question rooted in a line the page states but does not explain.

chullin/121.summary: A Jew slaughters a non-kosher animal for a gentile, and the animal keeps twitching. The page holds that it already imparts the impurity of food but not yet the impurity of a carcass, while Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Yoḥanan argue over whether a gentile may eat a limb cut from it. Rabbi Zeira's fix is that such an animal has left the category of living without entering the category of dead, and Abaye then rules strictly in both directions.
chullin/121.question: If the twitching animal counts as dead for impurity of food and as alive for the prohibition of bestiality at the same moment, is Abaye deciding what it is, or only what to do when nobody can say?

judge.reachNote: Whether a ruling under indeterminate status fixes what a thing is, or only what to do while its status cannot be fixed.

answer.quote: Abaye resolved the dilemma and said: It is proper to treat this case stringently.
answer.explanation: The page reports Abaye's ruling as a stringency rather than a determination of status, which bears on the question but leaves open whether stringency is a verdict about the animal's nature or only a policy under doubt.

chullin/122.summary: A mishna lists the skins soft enough to count as flesh for ritual impurity, including a corpse's skin, a domesticated pig's, the hump of a young camel, and the skin of a calf's head. Ulla says human skin is actually pure by Torah law, and the Sages declared it impure only so that no one would tan a dead parent into a mat. A camel's youth is measured by work, as long as it has not carried a burden; a camel old enough but never loaded is left unresolved.
chullin/122.question: If human skin is clean by Torah law, why is the remedy to call it impure rather than simply to forbid making the mats?

judge.reachNote: Why the Sages legislate through the category of impurity as a deterrent instead of issuing a direct prohibition against a repugnant act.

chullin/123.summary: A mishna asks when the hide being flayed off an animal stops counting as flesh for ritual impurity, and the answer turns on what the flayer intends to make: a carpet, or a leather jug. Rav says the flayed portion is pure once it no longer serves as a handle, while Rabbi Asi keeps one handbreadth impure because that is where the hand grips. The Gemara then tests this against how a person actually holds a hide mid-work.
chullin/123.question: If that handbreadth of skin is impure only because a flayer's hand tends to land there, what is it when he puts down the knife and walks away?

judge.reachNote: Whether a thing's impurity-status tracks its ongoing use as a handle or a fixed classification set by the normal manner of work.

answer.quote: it is more comfortable for the one flaying the hide to grasp the edge of the hide rather than the handbreadth of hide that is nearest to the flesh
answer.explanation: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Asi's handle-status by what a flayer would typically grip at that stage rather than by an actual grip, which bears on but does not settle what happens when flaying stops altogether.

chullin/124.summary: A hide from an animal that died on its own, with an olive-bulk of flesh still stuck to it, makes whoever touches a single hair on the hide impure. Ulla reports that Rabbi Yoḥanan limited this: if a person cut the flesh off with a knife, the hide nullifies it. Rav Naḥman swears he would reject that even from Rabbi Yoḥanan's own mouth, and the argument turns out to hinge on which clause of the mishna the ruling was attached to.
chullin/124.question: If the same sentence from Rabbi Yoḥanan is outrageous when attached to the first clause and unremarkable when attached to the second, was Rav Naḥman rejecting the ruling or the man who carried it to him?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's refusal to accept a tradition targets its content or the authority of whoever carried it.

answer.quote: Rabbi Ami said to him: If so, Rav Naḥman was justified in his surprise at the halakha of Rabbi Yoḥanan.
answer.explanation: The page settles the matter: once Rabbi Ami learns the ruling was reported on the first clause, he endorses Rav Naḥman's objection as substantive — and adds he would refuse it even from Joshua son of Nun — so the rejection was of the ruling, not of the reporter.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 124a: "Rabbi Ami said to him: If so, Rav Naḥman was justified in his surprise at the halakha of Rabbi Yoḥanan.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Rav Oshaya's jibe about the Nasi's son-in-law is rebutted when Rabbi Ami says Rav Naḥman was justified and that he too would refuse the ruling from Joshua son of Nun. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance why the same words are outrageous on the first clause and tame on the second, or what Rav Pappa's thin layer of flesh does to the disagreement once it dissolves it.

chullin/125.summary: A thigh bone from a human corpse makes whoever touches it impure, sealed shut or perforated, while the same bone from an animal carcass is clean unless there is a hole to reach the marrow. The argument turns on whether marrow inside a bone can still grow flesh back outside it, which would make the bone a whole limb. Rabbi Elazar offers a palm tree as the memory aid: scraped lengthwise it heals, scraped around the circumference it does not.
chullin/125.question: If a scraped bone counts as a limb because its marrow might still grow flesh back, is it being judged by what it is or by what it could become?

judge.reachNote: Whether limb-status attaches to what a body part now is or to the future flesh its marrow could still generate.

answer.quote: Even if it is not attached to flesh or marrow, a bone scraped in such a manner still has the ability to heal. But if one scraped it widthwise it will not heal
answer.explanation: Rabbi Elazar's ruling states the operative criterion is the bone's remaining capacity to heal, which bears on the question of potential versus present state, though the page never reflects on that distinction as such.

chullin/126.summary: A sealed thigh bone from an animal carcass can be touched without contracting ritual impurity, since the bone closes off the marrow inside; a hole as narrow as a strand of hair changes that. Rabbi Zeira presses Abaye: by that reasoning an animal still in its hide should transmit nothing, and Abaye answers by counting orifices, the eyes, the nostrils, the mouth. Then Rav Oshaya asks about a bone someone merely intends to perforate, and rules it already impure.
chullin/126.question: If the marrow stays unreachable until the hole is actually made, why should the plan to drill it be enough?

judge.reachNote: Whether a trivial act one plans to do counts as already done, so that status follows intended condition rather than present physical access.

answer.quote: A thigh bone lacking perforation is not considered to be lacking the necessary action for it to impart impurity.
answer.explanation: The page gives Rav Oshaya's ruling and the category it turns on — whether perforation counts as a still-missing action — but never explains why a merely intended act should suffice while the marrow is still unreachable.

chullin/127.summary: A limb dangles from a living animal, still joined by a connector the size of a strand of hair, and the Mishna asks what it is. A verse about a carcass that falls settles one half: nothing imparts carcass impurity until it drops off completely. Yet the same limb counts as severed for food impurity, and Shmuel extends this to figs that dry on their tree, detached for impurity but attached for Shabbat.
chullin/127.question: If lifting the hanging limb does not lift the animal with it, what is left that makes Rabbi Meir call them one and the same?
gate: the question brings in "Meir", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What makes two attached things count as one object — continuity of substance, or the practical test of whether one moves with the other?

answer.quote: Rabbi Meir, holds that although if one grasps and lifts the small part the large part does not ascend with it, the small part is still considered one and the same
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Meir's position that mere physical connection suffices despite the lifting test, but it never gives his reason, and the passage ends with Rabbi Yoḥanan raising a contradiction against exactly that position.

chullin/128.summary: Abaye asks about a cucumber planted in an unperforated flowerpot that grows out past the rim, half of it detached food and half attached to the ground. Rabbi Yirmeya adds a gourd where only the half someone bowed to is forbidden, Rav Pappa a fig branch hanging by its bark, Rabbi Zeira a stone in a wall shared by two houses with a leprous mark on one side. Each asks whether one half is a handle carrying impurity into the other; all four stand unresolved.
chullin/128.question: If bowing to half a gourd forbids only that half, at what point do the two halves stop being one gourd?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea beneath all four dilemmas: what makes a single object halakhically one thing rather than two when its parts have different statuses.

answer.quote: If when one grasps the small piece, the large piece ascends with it, it is considered one and the same; but if it does not ascend with it, it is not
answer.explanation: Rabbi Meir's lifting test earlier on the page offers one criterion for when two parts count as one item, but the page never applies it to the gourd and leaves the handle dilemma unresolved.

chullin/129.summary: A lump of hardened leaven that its owner sets aside to sit on stops being bread and becomes a seat. The Gemara runs the same reasoning through dough stuck to a kneading bowl, food offered to an idol, fat covering the kidney of a carcass, and seeds spread as a roof: in each case the item stopped being food and "performed the role of wood." What a thing is turns on the job it is doing.
chullin/129.question: If a mass of leaven becomes furniture the moment its owner decides to sit on it, what keeps anyone from reclassifying any food just by changing his mind about it?

judge.reachNote: Whether halakhic status follows the owner's intent or the function the object is actually performing.

answer.quote: Rava said that if a food item serves a function other than food, the principle that if it will eventually contract a severe form of impurity
answer.explanation: The page's operative test is that the item must actually serve a non-food function ("performed the role of wood"), which bears on the question but never states what limits a mere change of mind, so the question can still be asked.

chullin/130.summary: Whoever slaughters a non-sacred ox or sheep owes a priest three parts of it: the foreleg, the jaw, and the maw. The Gemara tries hard to prove that consecrated animals should owe them too, chasing through male goats, old goats, purchased animals, and orphaned ones, until a verse shuts it down. Then Rav Ḥisda: eat those gifts or ruin them before handing them over, and you pay nothing, since any priest will do and no one priest can sue.
chullin/130.question: If the verse calls the gifts a matter of judgment, what sort of debt is it that no one in the world has standing to collect?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is an obligation owed to a whole class rather than to any person, so no one can sue on it — but the page states this resolution outright.

answer.quote: No, they are a judgment with regard to distributing them through judges, i.e., the court dictates to the owner to which type of priests he should give
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly the note's objection from "mishpat" and answers that the judgment concerns distribution, not extraction, while also stating the debt's character as "money that has no claimants" because any priest may receive it.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 130b: "No, they are a judgment with regard to distributing them through judges, i.e., the court dictates to the owner to which type of priests he should give". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection, and the page answers it on 130b: "mishpat" means distribution through judges, not extraction, and the gifts are "money that has no claimants." Rewrite so the question starts after that answer rather than before it. For example, press on why Rav Ḥisda must call both Rabbi Eliezer's ruling and the Rabbis' opposing ruling merely "an attribute of piety," or on the tanna who treats unseparated gifts as already the priest's property while Rav Ḥisda treats them as ownerless money.

chullin/131.summary: A certain Levite made a habit of snatching the priestly portions of slaughtered animals, the foreleg, jaw, and maw, from children carrying them to priests on their fathers' behalf. Rav objected but ordered nothing: he cannot decide whether Levites count among "the people" who owe those portions, so nothing is collected from a Levite either. Baraita after baraita looks decisive, and each is reread as really concerning first tithe, a tenth of the crop, or first shorn wool.
chullin/131.question: If nobody can collect the foreleg and jaw from a Levite because nobody knows whether he owes them, why does that same doubt not stop him from grabbing what others owe?

judge.reachNote: Uncertainty shields a possessor from a claim but should not itself generate a right to seize — doubt does not cut both ways.

answer.quote: Therefore, he exempts the Levites from giving their own gifts, in accordance with the principle that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant.
answer.explanation: The page explains the exemption by burden of proof resting on the claimant, which bears on the asymmetry the question raises but never addresses the Levite's snatching of others' gifts, which Rav merely rebukes ('Is it not enough...').

summaryProblems.claim: Each seemingly decisive baraita is reread as really concerning first tithe or first shorn wool.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rav could say to you that although this baraita is in fact contrary to his opinion

judge.feedback: The summary says "Each seemingly decisive baraita is reread as really concerning first tithe or first shorn wool.", but the page says "Rav could say to you that although this baraita is in fact contrary to his opinion". Say what the page says. Fix the last summary sentence: only some of the baraitot are reinterpreted as first tithe or first sheared wool, while the baraita about slaughtering for a Levite is conceded to contradict Rav and is instead answered by making the status of Levites a dispute between tanna'im. Note too that Rav's own resolution is the burden-of-proof principle, and that Mareimar rules the halakha follows Rav's uncertainty. The question itself is strong and can stand.

chullin/132.summary: The foreleg, the jaw and the maw of a slaughtered ox or sheep go to a priest, and much of the page is about who slips out of that obligation. A priest short of money is advised by Rabbi Tavla to buy into Israelite butchers' animals, since jointly owned animals are exempt, so the butchers would take him as a partner for nothing. Rav Naḥman charged the butcher anyway, holding that a priest who opens a butcher shop owes the gifts like anyone else.
chullin/132.question: If joint ownership with a priest really exempts an animal, what exactly was wrong with the partnership Rabbi Tavla arranged?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that the priestly exemption attaches to a role (owner vs. recognized butcher) rather than to bare ownership, but the page spells this out.

answer.quote: But here, he has already established a butcher shop and is therefore obligated to give the gifts without delay.
answer.explanation: The page states Rav Naḥman's reason explicitly: the priest had set up shop as a butcher, and a priest-butcher owes the gifts (exempt only for two or three weeks before he is known as a butcher), so the partnership did not help.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 132b: "But here, he has already established a butcher shop and is therefore obligated to give the gifts without delay.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: Rav Naḥman cites Rabbi Aḥa bar Ḥanina that a priest who becomes a butcher owes the gifts, and says this priest had already opened a shop. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains puzzling, for instance why the obligation tracks being known publicly as a butcher rather than who owns the animal, or how that squares with the mishna's exemption for jointly owned animals. Keep the summary as is; it matches the page.

chullin/133.summary: Abaye, who was a priest, tells how he gave up collecting the foreleg, jaw and maw that an animal's owner owes a priest. First he seized them, then only asked for them, then only accepted them, and finally took nothing except on the eve of Yom Kippur, so his priestly status would not be doubted. Later Rava eats gifts an attendant hands over under pressure from the host, and the rebuking verse shows up in Rav Safra's dream.
chullin/133.question: If the verse in the dream was aimed at Rava, what was Rav Safra, who refused the meat, supposed to do with a reproach that was never addressed to him?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rebuke can be genuinely 'delivered' to one who did nothing wrong, and what the innocent recipient owes it.

answer.quote: Rava was rebuked as a result of this incident and therefore was not granted heavenly communication. The verse was therefore proclaimed to Rav Safra instead.
answer.explanation: The page explains why the verse was routed to Rav Safra (Rava was cut off from heavenly communication), but never says what Rav Safra himself was meant to do with a reproach not aimed at him.

chullin/134.summary: A convert owns a cow, and nobody can say whether it was slaughtered before or after he converted, so the mishna exempts him from the priestly gifts of foreleg, jaw and stomach: the claimant must bring proof. Reish Lakish objects with grain found in ant holes behind the harvesters, where Rabbi Meir awards doubtful gleanings, stalks dropped in reaping and left for the poor, to the poor. Rava answers that doubts about money are decided leniently, doubts touching a prohibition strictly.
chullin/134.question: If a doubt that costs only money is settled in favor of whoever already holds the property, why does the poor person's uncertain grain in the ant hole go the other way?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of who a doubt favors — the current holder versus the prior presumptive status of the property — but the page states that very answer.

summaryProblems.claim: Rava answers Reish Lakish's objection by distinguishing monetary doubts (lenient) from doubts touching a prohibition (strict).
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rava said in response: Here, in the case of gifts of the priesthood, the halakha is lenient because the cow of a convert maintains the presumptive status of exemption

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rava answers Reish Lakish's objection by distinguishing monetary doubts (lenient) from doubts touching a prohibition (strict).", but the page says "Rava said in response: Here, in the case of gifts of the priesthood, the halakha is lenient because the cow of a convert maintains the presumptive status of exemption". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few lines on: Rava resolves the gleanings contradiction by saying the standing crop has a presumptive status of obligation while the convert's cow has a presumptive status of exemption, so ask something that survives that answer. Also fix the summary: the money-versus-prohibition distinction is Rava's later reply to Abaye about the convert's dough, not his reply to Reish Lakish's gleanings objection. A better question might press on Reish Lakish's verse-based rule to "be righteous with that which is yours" and why generosity toward the poor does not extend to the priests.

chullin/135.summary: The mishna gives the priest the first wool sheared from a flock: at least five sheep by Beit Hillel's count, and enough wool to fashion a small garment. Dye the wool before handing it over and the obligation vanishes, since dyeing changes the wool into the owner's own; launder it and the debt stands. The Gemara then spends its strength on one singular pronoun, "your flock," arguing over whether two partners in a sheep count as a "you" at all.
chullin/135.question: If dyeing the wool cancels the priest's gift because the owner has made the wool his own, what keeps anyone from reaching for the dye pot first?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a rule granting acquisition through physical change builds an escape hatch into the very obligation it defines.

chullin/136.summary: Rabbi Ilai reads the singular "your" so strictly that jointly owned sheep escape the first sheared wool, the fleece owed to a priest. The Gemara answers with plural verses: tithe, a tenth of the crop given away, first fruits, ritual fringes, a parapet on the roof; the spare singular word then excludes something else, like synagogues. Then Abaye presses Rava on how far the comparison between wool and teruma, the priest's share of produce, actually runs, and Rava sometimes blocks it and sometimes concedes.
chullin/136.question: When Rava blocks the wool-and-teruma comparison with a verse in one case and simply answers "yes, that is the halakha" in the next, what is doing the deciding?
gate: the question uses "halakha", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Asks what governs the scope of a verbal analogy: how far a comparison between two gifts runs, and what stops it.

answer.quote: “He shall add its fifth part to it,” and not to the first sheared wool. “And die because of it,” and not because of the first sheared wool.
answer.explanation: The page shows that Rava blocks the analogy only where a verse supplies an explicit exclusion and otherwise says "Yes, that is the halakha," but it never states this as a governing principle, so the question can still be asked honestly.

chullin/137.summary: The gift of first sheared wool to the priest applies only to sheep, and the page works hard to say why: an ox's hair makes sackcloth rather than clothing, and goats' hair is plucked rather than shorn. Beit Shammai set the minimum flock at two, Beit Hillel at five, Rabbi Yosei at four, each counting sheep in a different verse. Later Rabbi Yoḥanan tells Isi bar Hini that the mishna's "any amount" is not the ruling.
chullin/137.question: If the mishna says the obligation applies to any amount of wool and Rabbi Yoḥanan says sixty sela, what is someone who has only the mishna actually holding?
gate: the question uses "sela", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what the plain text of a mishna is worth against a transmitted halakhic conclusion — but the page states that answer itself.

answer.quote: If so, i.e., if the halakha could be understood by a simple reading of the mishna, what is the difference between my knowledge and yours?
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan answers Isi's exact objection by saying the mishna-only student holds the mishna's wording while he holds the halakhic conclusion, which is the note's question.

summaryProblems.claim: The reason only sheep are obligated is that an ox's hair makes sackcloth and goats' hair is plucked rather than shorn.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rather, the Gemara provides a different source for the mishna’s statement. The reason that the mitzva of first sheared wool applies only to sheep is as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Chullin 137b: "If so, i.e., if the halakha could be understood by a simple reading of the mishna, what is the difference between my knowledge and yours?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The reason only sheep are obligated is that an ox's hair makes sackcloth and goats' hair is plucked rather than shorn.", but the page says "Rather, the Gemara provides a different source for the mishna’s statement. The reason that the mitzva of first sheared wool applies only to sheep is as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few words later on the page: Rabbi Yoḥanan tells Isi that he knows only the mishna's statement while Rabbi Yoḥanan knows the halakhic conclusion. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance why the Gemara keeps the mishna's "any amount" on the books at all once figures like sixty or six sela are fixed, or why five sheep can be learned from a verse in Prophets while four is learned from the Torah. Also fix the summary: the page rejects the ox-sackcloth and plucked-goats reasoning and grounds the sheep-only rule in "to serve," i.e. wool fit for the priestly garments.

chullin/138.summary: A man shears one sheep and sells it, shears the next and sells that one too, until he holds five fleeces and no sheep. Five sheep trigger the gift of first shorn wool to a priest; Rav Ḥisda says he owes it, having owned them while shearing, while Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya exempts him, since "your flock" must apply when the fifth fleece completes the measure. Rav Ḥisda saves a related case by having a gentile hand over his sheep for thirty days.
chullin/138.question: If a man can shed the gift by selling each sheep the moment it is shorn, is the obligation attached to the shearing or only to the fifth fleece?

judge.reachNote: When does a quantity-based obligation attach: at each act of shearing, or only at the instant the required measure is reached?

answer.quote: at the time that the measure of five fleeces is completed, we require the term "your flock" to apply, since the obligation takes effect at that stage
answer.explanation: The page lays out both sides of exactly this alternative — Rav Ḥisda anchoring the obligation to ownership at shearing, Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya to the moment the five-fleece measure is completed — but leaves the dispute unresolved.

chullin/139.summary: A chicken donated to the Temple for upkeep escapes its owner's house and nests in an orchard, and the question is whether a finder must shoo the mother off before taking the eggs, as Deuteronomy requires for ordinary birds. Shmuel and Rabbi Yoḥanan say the bird stays holy wherever it wanders, since everything sits in God's treasury already. Reish Lakish first said its holiness lapses when it bolts, then reversed himself after hearing his teacher.
chullin/139.question: If a runaway chicken and a stolen hundred dinars are already in God's treasury wherever they are, what does handing them to the Temple treasurer actually change?

judge.reachNote: If divine ownership is already total, physical delivery must be doing something other than transferring ownership — namely fixing human liability.

answer.quote: the valuation money is non-sacred until it enters the possession of the Temple treasurer, and that the owner bears responsibility for it until that time
answer.explanation: The page indicates that in certain formulations (valuations, and Rabbi Yoḥanan's "incumbent upon me" case) the handover to the treasurer is what ends the owner's liability and turns the money sacred, though it does not squarely reconcile this with the God's-treasury principle for the chicken and the lost dinars.

chullin/140.summary: Rav Kahana reads "the young you may take for yourself" to mean a mother bird need only be sent away when the fledglings or eggs could end up on your table, not in your dog's bowl. Rav Hoshaya then asks about a man who reaches into a nest and severs only part of the windpipe and gullet of the fledglings: left that way they become unfit, but he could still finish the cut. The dilemma stands.
chullin/140.question: Does a half-slaughtered fledgling count as food because the man can still finish the cut, or as dog's fare because that is what it is at this moment?

judge.reachNote: Whether status is fixed by a thing's present condition or by what its owner still has the power to make of it.

chullin/141.summary: A mother bird resting on her nest must be sent away before the eggs or fledglings are taken, and the argument turns to what sending actually requires. Rav Huna says he holds her by the feet and releases her; Rav Yehuda says by the wings, since wings are how a bird walks. One man clipped a bird's wing, released her, and caught her again; Rav Yehuda had him flogged and told him to wait for the feathers.
chullin/141.question: If clipping a bird's wing before releasing her earns lashes, what makes Rava's ring of nets, placed far enough from the nest to avoid suspicion, different?
gate: the question brings in "Rava's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What counts as really sending the mother away — a release that restores her flight, versus a technically permitted later recapture.

answer.quote: he acted in accordance with the opinion of the Rabbis, and the lashes administered by Rav Yehuda were not for transgressing a Torah prohibition; rather, they were rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness
