answer.explanation: The page explains the clipper's punishment as rabbinic lashes for acting inappropriately (a defective sending), and separately explains Rava's nets as "positioned far from the nest in an unusual manner that did not arouse suspicion," so the materials for a contrast are present without the Gemara ever drawing it.

chullin/142.summary: A mishna says that sending away a mother bird from her nest costs at most an issar, a small copper coin, yet the Torah promises long and good days for it. Rabbi Yaakov saw a boy sent by his father to fetch fledglings do exactly that, then fall from the roof and die. The Gemara keeps trying to save the promise: maybe he thought of idol worship, maybe the return trip is riskier, maybe the ladder was simply rotten.
chullin/142.question: If a rickety ladder is enough to explain the boy's death, what is left of Rabbi Yaakov's proof that the reward waits in another world?
gate: "Rabbi Yaakov" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.

judge.reachNote: Whether a natural, mundane explanation of a death dissolves or merely relocates the theological proof that reward is deferred to the World-to-Come.

answer.quote: If it is so that there is reward for performance of mitzvot in this world, it should be effective for the son and protect him
answer.explanation: The page supplies a general form of reply — genuine this-worldly reward should have shielded the boy from whatever caused his fall — but it never applies this to the rickety-ladder concession, so the note's challenge to the proof still stands.

bekhorot/2.summary: Bekhorot opens with five ways a gentile can hold a stake in a donkey: buying its unborn young, being sold them, partnership, and two caretaking deals where the offspring is split. In all five the young animal is exempt from firstborn status, the rule that a first-born animal is sanctified and must be redeemed from a priest. The page asks whether an unborn donkey is like a damaged animal that cannot work, which Rabbi Yehuda permits selling to a gentile, or like a sick one that will recover.
bekhorot/2.question: Is an unborn donkey judged by what it cannot do now, or by the work it will grow up able to do?

judge.reachNote: The question does name the underlying idea — present incapacity versus natural potential — but the page states the resolution outright.

answer.quote: And a fetus is also similar to one who is able to be cured, as it ultimately will be capable of working. Learn from it that Rabbi Yehuda deems the sale of a fetus to a gentile prohibited.
answer.explanation: Rav Ashi resolves the dilemma explicitly: the fetus is judged by the work it will eventually do, so selling it is prohibited, and the same reasoning appears earlier ('since it is in its natural state, and will become capable of working after growing up').

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 2b: "And a fetus is also similar to one who is able to be cured, as it ultimately will be capable of working. Learn from it that Rabbi Yehuda deems the sale of a fetus to a gentile prohibited.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is settled on the page: Rav Ashi rules that a fetus counts as curable because it will grow up able to work, so its sale is prohibited. Write a question that starts from that resolution and asks what remains unsettled — for instance why the Rabbis' worry is about people confusing one sale with another rather than about the animal's capacity, or why a sale of fetus-rights alone stays an open dilemma even after the fetus is deemed 'curable.' Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

bekhorot/3.summary: A firstborn male animal in a Jew's flock belongs to the priest and may not be sheared or put to work, but a gentile's share in the animal cancels that status. The Gemara asks how small a share suffices: Rav Huna says even the animal's ear, while Rav Ḥisda and Rava demand a part the animal could not live without. Rav Mari bar Raḥel sold the ears of unborn firstborns to a gentile, kept the restrictions anyway, and his animals died.
bekhorot/3.question: If selling an ear to a gentile really does cancel the firstborn obligation, does the page's answer, that others would copy Rav Mari badly, mean a permitted device becomes wrong once someone else may imitate it wrongly?

judge.reachNote: Whether an otherwise valid legal device becomes forbidden because onlookers may copy it defectively and stumble.

answer.quote: Due to this concern, Rav Mari should not have transferred ownership of the ears to a gentile, and consequently his animals died.
answer.explanation: The page states, for this case, that the imitation concern made the device improper, though it does not generalize the principle the question raises.

bekhorot/4.summary: A firstborn donkey or firstborn son must normally be redeemed from a priest, but in the wilderness the Levites themselves replaced Israel's firstborn sons, and Levite sheep replaced their firstborn donkeys. Abaye and Rava disagree over whether the mishna's inference frees the Levites' own animals from redemption or frees the Levites themselves. Rav Safra presses both readings: a Levite who owned no lamb, a Levite baby under a month old, and Aaron, whose name is dotted in the verse to show he was never counted.
bekhorot/4.question: If release from redeeming firstborns came from taking part in that exchange, why should a Levite who owned no lamb, or a baby too young to be counted, be released as well?

judge.reachNote: Does exemption flow from actually participating in the swap, or from belonging to the class of Levites — the page chooses class over participation.

answer.quote: The verse states: "The Levites" (Numbers 3:45), to teach that all of the Levites were juxtaposed with each other. Therefore, even a firstborn Levite who did not abrogate
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly Rav Safra's difficulty about Levites who did not take part in the exchange (Aaron, and by the same logic the uncounted infant) and resolves it by juxtaposing all Levites to one another.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 4a: "The verse states: "The Levites" (Numbers 3:45), to teach that all of the Levites were juxtaposed with each other. Therefore, even a firstborn Levite who did not abrogate". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: after the Aaron challenge the Gemara derives from the word "the Levites" that all Levites are juxtaposed, so even one who abrogated nothing is himself abrogated. Rewrite the question around something the page leaves standing — for instance why a single Levite lamb can free many Israelite donkeys while the surplus firstborn sons still needed silver, or what Reish Lakish gains by saying sanctity lapsed only after the counting. Keep the summary, which is accurate.

bekhorot/5.summary: Kontrokos, a Roman officer, works out the silver Moses collected for the Tabernacle, half a shekel from each of 603,550 men, and finds twice as much collected as delivered. He asks Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai whether Moses was a thief, a gambler, or simply bad at arithmetic. The answer is that the Sanctuary's maneh, a unit of weight, was double the ordinary one, and the Gemara then hunts for a verse proving that, rejecting two before settling on Ezekiel.
bekhorot/5.question: If the doubled maneh answers the officer's question about Moses, why does the Gemara reject two verses before finding one that proves the doubling?

judge.reachNote: An answer that silences an outside challenger is not yet an answer the Gemara can rest on; it must be anchored in a verse that admits no alternative reading.

answer.quote: But perhaps the total amount of shekels does equal the amount of a talent, but the verse calculates the general amounts, i.e., the hundreds of talents, in talents
answer.explanation: The page states the grounds on which each of the first two proofs is rejected (the verse's counting habits could explain the small-coin figures), though it never says why a scripturally derived source was needed once Kontrokos was satisfied.

bekhorot/6.summary: A long argument over why only donkeys, and not horses or camels, carry firstborn status runs into cases of a cow that gives birth to something donkey-shaped. Then the page swerves: how does anyone know that milk is permitted at all? Milk is treated as a novelty, either spoiled blood or something drawn from a living animal, and proof after proof is rejected until David's ten cheeses, sent to a battlefield where nobody trades, settle the matter.
bekhorot/6.question: If it took cheeses carried to a war camp to establish that milk may be eaten, what were people doing with milk while the proof was still missing?
gate: gloss "firstborn status" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: It reaches the gap between settled practice and scriptural derivation: the Gemara searches for a verse to license something everyone was already eating.

bekhorot/7.summary: The mishna's rule that what emerges from a non-kosher animal is non-kosher gets tested on donkey urine, asked about because it is turbid like milk, or, in a second version, because people drink it to cure jaundice. Rav Sheshet forbids it. Then comes the objection: bee honey is permitted precisely because bees carry nectar through their bodies without producing it, and the answer is that honey is a scriptural exception rather than an application of the rule.
bekhorot/7.question: If nectar that merely passes through a bee stays permitted, what really makes water passing through a donkey different, other than a verse?

judge.reachNote: Does a substance's status follow its source (what animal it came out of) or its production (whether the body actually made it)?

answer.quote: any type [min] of non-kosher substance is included. And these fluids, i.e., the urine of a donkey, are also a type of non-kosher substance
answer.explanation: The page grounds the prohibition of donkey urine in the mishna's categorical "min hattamei" inference and its resemblance to donkey milk, and explains honey only as Rabbi Ya'akov's scriptural exception, so the question of what substantively distinguishes pass-through nectar from pass-through water remains askable.

bekhorot/8.summary: A baraita sorts animals by mating and gestation: a chicken hatches in twenty-one days, a viper carries for seventy years. The snake's seven years is pried from the word order of its curse, animals before beasts, with the harshest available reading chosen because a curse should sting. Then the emperor sends Rabbi Yehoshua ben Ḥananya to Athens, where he buys a butcher's head for half a dinar and answers riddles about salting spoiled salt.
bekhorot/8.question: Rabbi Yehoshua buys the butcher's head, then trades it back for directions to a place the butcher says gets informants killed, so was that a bargain or a threat?
gate: gloss "dinar" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether a purchase made by wordplay gives a sage a real claim, and whether a worthy mission licenses squeezing a frightened bystander.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: If you wish for me to let you be, go and show me the entrance to the school of the sages of Athens.
answer.explanation: The page narrates the exchange as leverage over the head Rabbi Yehoshua claims to own, but it never labels the act or judges it, so the note's question can still be asked honestly.

bekhorot/9.summary: The mishna sorts donkeys: a first-time mother bears twin males, and one lamb goes to the priest; a male and a female leave nobody able to prove which came first, so the owner keeps the lamb. The Gemara then splits over whether an unredeemed firstborn donkey is forbidden, Rabbi Yehuda saying yes and Rabbi Shimon no. Ulla's reasoning rests on the lamb being worth less than the donkey, which Rav Neḥemya's boiled vegetables unsettle.
bekhorot/9.question: If a small, blemished lamb can redeem a donkey, why did Rav Neḥemya's boiled vegetables have to match the donkey's full value?
gate: no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: The idea is whether the Torah's insistence on a lamb is about the species of the redeeming object or about permitting redemption at a discount.

answer.quote: Ulla is not saying, i.e., referring to, a case where the donkey is redeemed at its full value. Rather, when we say the Torah is particular that the donkey be redeemed with a lamb, the reference is to redeeming it not at its full value
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself explains that only a lamb may redeem for less than the donkey's worth, so any other item, like Rav Neḥemya's vegetables, must equal the full value.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Neḥemya's boiled vegetables unsettle Ulla's reasoning that the lamb is worth less than the donkey.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara answers: Ulla is not saying, i.e., referring to, a case where the donkey is redeemed at its full value.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 9b: "Ulla is not saying, i.e., referring to, a case where the donkey is redeemed at its full value. Rather, when we say the Torah is particular that the donkey be redeemed with a lamb, the reference is to redeeming it not at its full value". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rav Neḥemya's boiled vegetables unsettle Ulla's reasoning that the lamb is worth less than the donkey.", but the page says "The Gemara answers: Ulla is not saying, i.e., referring to, a case where the donkey is redeemed at its full value.". Say what the page says. The question is answered a few words later on the same daf: the Gemara says Ulla means redemption at less than full value, which is why vegetables had to be worth the donkey's whole worth. Read to the end of that exchange and ask something that survives it, for instance why the Torah would care about a discount at all, or why a blemished or tiny lamb still counts while other property does not. The summary should also not present the vegetables as leaving Ulla unsettled, since the Gemara resolves the challenge.

bekhorot/10.summary: A firstborn donkey not redeemed with a lamb has its neck broken from behind with a cleaver and is buried, and the argument here is whether anyone may still derive benefit from the carcass, and whether the carcass counts as food for contracting ritual impurity. The Rabbis float an odd idea: the ban on eating a thing is itself the intent that makes it food. Mishnayot about crows, camels and unslaughtered birds knock the idea down, and then it comes back.
bekhorot/10.question: If a carcass becomes food only when someone means it to be eaten, can the bare fact that eating it is forbidden ever stand in for that intention?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the real idea: what confers food status — a person's intention, or the significance a prohibition itself lends an object.

answer.quote: According to Rabbi Shimon, intent to eat it is required in order to render it susceptible to the impurity of food, while according to the Rabbis the prohibition to eat it in this case serves as intent
answer.explanation: The page states outright that in the learn-to-slaughter case the Rabbis (and Rabbi Eliezer) hold the prohibition itself substitutes for intent, while Rabbi Shimon requires actual intent, which is exactly what the question asks.

summaryProblems.claim: The crow case comes from a mishna and is one of the sources that knocks down the 'prohibition serves as intent' idea.
summaryProblems.pageSays: As it is taught in a baraita that Rabbi Yosei says: Nimos, the brother of Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi, once related to me that in the case of one who slaughters a crow

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 10b: "According to Rabbi Shimon, intent to eat it is required in order to render it susceptible to the impurity of food, while according to the Rabbis the prohibition to eat it in this case serves as intent". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The crow case comes from a mishna and is one of the sources that knocks down the 'prohibition serves as intent' idea.", but the page says "As it is taught in a baraita that Rabbi Yosei says: Nimos, the brother of Rabbi Yehoshua HaGarsi, once related to me that in the case of one who slaughters a crow". Say what the page says. The question is the page's own stated dispute and is answered in so many words on 10b, so it cannot stand as an open question. Rewrite it to press on what remains hard after the answer — e.g. why Rava first declares that everyone denies that prohibition serves as intent, yet the idea survives only where the animal was slaughtered to practice slaughtering, or why 'indicators of a kosher animal' should matter more than intent. Also fix the crow: it comes from a baraita of Nimos and it revives the idea rather than refuting it.

bekhorot/11.summary: A firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb, and the argument is over how small that lamb may be. Rav Yosef allows a lean one worth a single small coin, a ma'a; Rabbi Tarfon offers a scale by temperament, sela for the generous, shekel for the miserly, a ragya in between. The two are reconciled by who is asking: the man who comes for advice hears three dinars, the man who acts on his own has already discharged his obligation with a ma'a.
bekhorot/11.question: If a scrawny lamb worth a ma'a genuinely completes the redemption, on what grounds is the man who bothers to ask told to spend three dinars?
gate: gloss "sela" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The gap between what legally discharges an obligation and what a person who seeks guidance is told to do.

answer.quote: here the reference is to one who comes to consult; he is told to give a lamb worth three dinars. There, the reference is to one who acts on his own
answer.explanation: The page draws the consult/act-alone distinction the question already concedes, and Rabbi Tarfon's disposition scale hints at the reason, but no explicit grounds for demanding more of the inquirer are stated.

bekhorot/12.summary: A firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb given to a priest, and the mishna rules out a calf, a hybrid of sheep and goat, and a koy, whose status is uncertain. The sharp case is a ben pekua, a lamb taken alive from its mother's womb after she was slaughtered: Mar Zutra calls it meat already in the pot, Rav Ashi calls it a lamb because it walks. Rav Nahman goes further: every priest is suspected of skipping the redemption, since the lamb stays with him anyway.
bekhorot/12.question: Is a lamb pulled alive from its slaughtered mother a lamb because it walks around, or meat because of how it came into the world?

judge.reachNote: Does an animal's status follow its present condition and behavior, or the manner of its coming into being?

answer.quote: Mar Zutra said that one may not redeem a firstborn donkey with a ben pekua, and Rav Ashi said that one may redeem with it.
answer.explanation: The page names both sides of exactly this dilemma and lets Mar Zutra have the last word ("what purpose does the verbal analogy of 'lamb,' 'lamb'... serve?"), but never states a settled ruling, so the question can still be asked.

bekhorot/13.summary: The argument slides from when a firstborn donkey must be redeemed, immediately or after thirty days, into a question about ownership itself: who acquires what, and by which act. Rabbi Oshaya's rule runs in mirror image, money from a gentile's hand, pulling from a Jew's, wrung out of one phrase in Leviticus. It ends with a man who buys broken gold vessels and finds an idol among them, and with a line about whose word can be relied on.
bekhorot/13.question: If backing out of a spoken deal counts as bad faith only when the other side is assumed to keep their word, what makes that assumption true to begin with?

judge.reachNote: Whether the force of a bare promise comes from the promise itself or from the reliance a community's presumed honesty makes possible.

answer.quote: in a case of a Jew who purchases an item from gentiles, as they are not assumed to uphold their verbal commitments, reneging on one's word does not constitute an act of bad faith
answer.explanation: The page states the asymmetry and grounds it in reliance — "neither party relies upon the commitment of the other in the first place" — but never says what makes the presumption of trustworthiness itself hold, so the question survives in part.

bekhorot/14.summary: The mishna sorts by timing: if the blemish came before consecration, only the animal's value is holy, and after redemption it can be shorn, worked, and its offspring counted a firstborn. Much of the Gemara then chases one spare verse about not sacrificing "an ox, or a sheep, in which is a blemish," pushing off firstborn, tithe, substitutes, and offspring until only a private altar is left. It closes conceding that one exclusionary word is difficult, and with a question unanswered.
bekhorot/14.question: Rabbi Elazar's private altar gets the verse only after every other candidate is knocked out by some other verse, so is that reading the verse or filling the last empty slot?
gate: the question brings in "Elazar's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the hermeneutic question of whether a verse's meaning is discovered or assigned by default once every other candidate is spoken for elsewhere.

answer.quote: Accordingly, Deuteronomy 17:1 must be understood as referring to a private altar of an individual, as maintained by Rabbi Elazar.
answer.explanation: The page states the conclusion that the elimination yields Rabbi Elazar's reading, but it never addresses whether derivation by elimination is genuine exegesis or merely slot-filling, so the question survives.

bekhorot/15.summary: A blemished consecrated animal, once redeemed, is read against "the gazelle and the hart": exempt from the firstborn obligation and the priestly gifts, though its fat stays forbidden. The argument then reaches a calf conceived before its mother's redemption and born after, which can be neither sacrificed nor redeemed. Rav Huna says it is shut in a chamber and starves; Rabbi Ḥanina offers a workaround, dedicating it in advance, and Rabbi Levi names the fear behind it.
bekhorot/15.question: If the mother herself may be eaten once she is redeemed, what makes her calf so dangerous that the answer is a locked chamber and starvation?

judge.reachNote: The idea under it is a sanctity that can neither be discharged on the altar nor transferred to money, so it has no exit.

answer.quote: Shall we redeem them? They cannot be redeemed, as their sanctity is not strong enough to be transferable to money for their redemption.
answer.explanation: The page states Rav Huna's own reasoning for the chamber — the calf, born of a deferred sanctity, can neither be offered nor redeemed — and Rabbi Levi supplies the further fear, "lest one raise flocks and flocks of them."

summaryProblems.claim: A blemished consecrated animal, once redeemed, is exempt from the firstborn obligation and the priestly gifts (stated without qualification).
summaryProblems.pageSays: Sacrificial animals whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration and that were redeemed, are obligated in the mitzva of a firstborn, and obligated in the gifts.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 15b: "Shall we redeem them? They cannot be redeemed, as their sanctity is not strong enough to be transferable to money for their redemption.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "A blemished consecrated animal, once redeemed, is exempt from the firstborn obligation and the priestly gifts (stated without qualification).", but the page says "Sacrificial animals whose permanent blemish preceded their consecration and that were redeemed, are obligated in the mitzva of a firstborn, and obligated in the gifts.". Say what the page says. The question is already answered in the passage the summary itself narrates: Rav Huna explains the calf can neither be sacrificed (deferred sanctity) nor redeemed (sanctity untransferable), and Rabbi Levi gives the decree about raising flocks. Ask something that starts from those reasons instead, e.g. why a sanctity too weak for the altar is still strong enough to forbid all benefit, or why the Eretz Yisrael workaround of pre-dedication is preferable to letting the animal live. Also make clear that the exemption from firstborn and gifts belongs only to animals whose consecration preceded the blemish, since the baraita rules the reverse case obligated.

bekhorot/16.summary: A Jew takes animals from a gentile under a fixed-price arrangement and splits the offspring; the question is whose animals they are. Rava rejects Abaye's split reading and says the beasts sit in the Jew's possession, yet because the gentile can seize the offspring if the mother is gone, the hand of a gentile is in the middle, and firstborn obligation lapses. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel stretches that unexercised claim ten generations down the line.
bekhorot/16.question: If the gentile never actually comes to collect, at what generation does a claim he might make stop counting as ownership?

judge.reachNote: When does a creditor's potential, never-exercised claim on an animal's body still count as ownership enough to void firstborn status?

answer.quote: Rav Huna says: Their direct offspring are exempt, but the offspring of their direct offspring are obligated.
answer.explanation: The page states the generational cutoffs for the gentile's contingent claim outright — the mishna and Rav Huna stop it after the direct offspring, Rav Yehuda after two generations, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel at ten — so the question is asked and answered on the daf.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 16b: "Rav Huna says: Their direct offspring are exempt, but the offspring of their direct offspring are obligated.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the page's own topic: the mishna, Rav Huna, Rav Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel each state exactly how many generations the gentile's potential seizure exempts, so a reader who finished 16b would say it has been answered. Rewrite so the question starts from those stated cutoffs and presses on what remains hard — for instance why a claim that reaches the offspring's body at all should ever expire with a generation, or why 'establishing the offspring in place of their mothers' adds only one generation rather than all of them. Keep the summary; it is accurate.

bekhorot/17.summary: A ewe bears twin males and both heads emerge as one. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili gives both to the priest; the Rabbis say a perfect tie never happens, so one came first. The Gemara then tests that claim against the red line painted around the altar, an impure earthenware oven split into equal halves, and a corpse found midway between two towns, and each proof is deflected rather than settled.
bekhorot/17.question: If the altar's red line can simply be painted a little wider to cover the true middle, is the claim that exactness is impossible, or only that nobody can ever confirm it?

judge.reachNote: Whether 'two things never coincide exactly' is a claim about reality or about the limits of human measurement and verification.

answer.quote: An earthenware vessel is different, since it has indentations in it, i.e., the place of the break is uneven and is therefore particularly difficult to measure precisely.
answer.explanation: The rejection of the oven proof frames the problem as one of measuring precisely rather than of exact equality being ontologically impossible, which bears on the question but never states the distinction outright.

bekhorot/18.summary: A slain man found exactly midway between two towns opens the page: can two distances in human hands coincide precisely? Then twin lambs whose heads emerged as one, with Rabbi Tarfon giving the priest the better animal and Rabbi Akiva leaving the extra fat in dispute until the priest brings proof. Rava locates the real disagreement in the courtyard: does an owner hand a priest a share of his ground so the mitzva can happen, even at a loss?
bekhorot/18.question: If an owner only grants the priest a portion of his courtyard when it costs him nothing, was anything ever transferred?
gate: gloss "mitzva" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that acquisition here rests on the owner's presumed will, so a grant that evaporates whenever it costs him may never have been a grant.

answer.quote: And Rabbi Akiva holds: Since there is a loss to the owner in this case of uncertainty, he does not transfer anything to the priest.
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Akiva's position that the loss cancels the transfer, but it does not discuss whether a grant conditioned on costing nothing counts as a genuine transfer at all, so the question can still be asked.

bekhorot/19.summary: A lamb pulled out by caesarean section never opened its mother's womb, and the one born after it was not first; Rabbi Akiva says neither counts as firstborn, while Rabbi Tarfon stays uncertain and lets both graze until blemished. The Gemara then fights over whether being a firstborn in one aspect counts at all, with Abaye and Ravina reading the same baraita in opposite directions. Buying an animal from a gentile raises a second problem: when does a mere statistic decide anything?
bekhorot/19.question: Why does a majority you could walk over and inspect, nine kosher butcher shops against one, settle a case, while the plain fact that most animals give birth in their first year settles nothing?

judge.reachNote: Asks what kind of knowledge a majority has to be before halakha will act on it: a thing you can point at versus a bare statistic.

answer.quote: When the Rabbis follow the majority, this is in a case of an evident majority, which is extant and can be examined.
answer.explanation: The Gemara names the distinction the question asks about — the majority must be present and inspectable — but it immediately challenges that answer from the levirate-marriage baraita and breaks off at "Rather, Rava says:" without explaining why presence should matter.

bekhorot/20.summary: A goat bought from a gentile may or may not have given birth before, and the priest's claim on the next male depends on the answer. Rabbi Yishmael counts by the animal's age, Rabbi Yehoshua looks for a murky discharge or an afterbirth, and Rabbi Akiva refuses the whole method, leaving uncertain cases with the owner. When Rabbi Yehoshua's ruling on milk clashes with his indifference to minorities elsewhere, the Gemara simply swaps the two names.
bekhorot/20.question: If a sage's recorded opinion can be reassigned to his opponent whenever it conflicts with what he says elsewhere, what would it take to conclude the sage was inconsistent instead?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the method question: when the Gemara harmonizes a sage with himself by re-attributing views, what constrains that move.

answer.quote: Rather, reverse the two opinions in the mishna. And in fact it is taught in that manner in a baraita
answer.explanation: The page shows the reversal is not a bare device but is corroborated by an independent baraita, which bears on the question without saying what would instead force a verdict of inconsistency.

bekhorot/21.summary: Buy an animal from a Jew, and nobody mentions whether it has already given birth. Rav reads the silence one way: a seller with nothing to lose would have bragged that the buyer owes no firstborn to a priest, so the offspring is definitely a firstborn. Rabbi Yo\u1e25anan reads the identical silence in reverse, Shmuel reads nothing into it at all, and the Gemara settles the matter by reassigning who must speak.
bekhorot/21.question: If the same silence supports three opposite conclusions, why does the firstborn become the buyer's job to ask about while the mother and its offspring stays the seller's job to disclose?

judge.reachNote: Who bears the burden when a transaction is silent: a duty on the seller to disclose versus a duty on the buyer to inquire.

bekhorot/22.summary: A miscarried congealed mass is buried and exempts later births from firstborn status, yet imparts no impurity; Rabbi Yoḥanan says the fetus inside is real, just nullified by the majority around it. Then measurement: a dead fetus imparts impurity only once its head is the size of a skein of warp threads, and Rav Huna admits he cannot say which skein fits which rule. Brine bought from someone unreliable about purity is fixed by touching mikveh water, until Rabbi Yirmeya has the nullified water revive in a pot.
bekhorot/22.question: If the water in the brine turns impure again the moment it meets more water, was it ever really nullified, or only outnumbered for a while?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempts: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea itself: whether nullification by majority changes a substance's status or merely suspends it while the numbers hold.

answer.quote: Nevertheless, the mixture may not be allowed to come in contact with water, so that it does not become susceptible to ritual impurity
answer.explanation: Abaye raises the note's very challenge ("does nullified impurity return and revive in its impure state?") and Rav Dimi answers from the teruma mishna, where produce is declared nullified yet still guarded from water, showing nullification is conditional rather than absolute — though the deeper question of whether it was ever truly nullified can still be pressed.

bekhorot/23.summary: Most of the page tests whether impurity swallowed by a majority is really gone or only dormant, waiting to meet its own kind and revive. Abaye presses Rav Dimi with case after case: red heifer ashes mixed into ordinary ashes, carcass meat mixed with slaughtered meat, and finally the buried mass of congealed blood that Rabbi Ḥiyya says defiles neither by contact nor by carrying. Rav Dimi has no answer. A second dispute measures rot by what a dog will still eat.
bekhorot/23.question: If a nullified kav of impure produce can be revived the moment it meets its own type, in what sense was it ever nullified?
gate: the question uses "kav", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether nullification annihilates a forbidden or impure substance or merely suspends it, leaving it latent and recoverable.

answer.quote: The mixture is pure in the sense that it does not impart impurity through contact, but it does impart impurity through carrying.
answer.explanation: Rav Dimi's position spells out one sense in which nullification is real and one in which it is not — the mixture loses contact impurity but retains impurity by carrying — which bears on the question without settling why revival by 'its own type' should count as nullification at all.

bekhorot/24.summary: A nursing animal bought from a gentile raises a question: is the young at its side her own, or did she take pity on another's? Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the matter stands in its presumptive status, and the Gemara cannot pin down which way he means it, so it tests the limit with a pig-like animal trailing after a sheep. Whether mercy crosses species stays unresolved; the mishna then turns to clearing wool with a cleaver before slaughter.
bekhorot/24.question: If nursing is what proves motherhood, why is the pig-like animal's status left for Elijah to decide rather than treated as a plain uncertainty about facts?
gate: the question brings in "Elijah", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: It reaches the difference between a doubt about facts (whose offspring is this?) and a doubt about law (what does the sage hold?), but the page itself draws that distinction and resolves it.

answer.quote: Actually, it is obvious to Rabba bar bar Ḥana that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. But it is uncertain if
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection about the Elijah verse and answers that the doubt is not factual but a halakhic doubt about Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's position (whether mercy extends to another species), which only Elijah can settle.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 24a: "Actually, it is obvious to Rabba bar bar Ḥana that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. But it is uncertain if". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection to the Elijah verse, and the page answers it a few lines later by saying the doubt is halakhic — whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel thinks mercy extends beyond the animal's own species. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing: for example, why the same presumption that exempts the future offspring from firstborn status does not also settle whether one is flogged for slaughtering mother and young, or what it means that the whole matter is left unresolved while practice still follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

bekhorot/25.summary: A firstborn animal may not be shorn, so what about the hair in the way of the slaughtering knife? Rav permits clearing it, and the Gemara works out why: either plucking is not shearing at all, or it is shearing done in an unusual manner, which Torah law does not forbid. The sharper case is the red heifer with two hairs red at the root and black at the tip, where Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam says to snip the tips with scissors.
bekhorot/25.question: If a rabbinic prohibition can be set aside simply because red heifers are rare, what keeps it in force for any other uncommon case?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the principle that rabbinic decrees are legislated for common situations, and asks where the boundary of that principle lies.

answer.quote: the red heifer is different, as it is uncommon, and Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam therefore maintains that the prohibition by rabbinic law was not applied
answer.explanation: The page states the rationale the question starts from — rabbinic decrees were not extended to uncommon cases — but never says what limits that leniency or keeps such decrees in force elsewhere.

bekhorot/26.summary: How long must an Israelite feed a firstborn animal before handing it over to a priest? Thirty days for a sheep, fifty for an ox, pulled from a juxtaposition of verses that the Gemara admits could just as easily be read backwards, with Rabbi Yosei holding out for three months for a lamb. The sharp move comes after: a priest who asks for the animal early may not receive it, because taking it early looks like being paid.
bekhorot/26.question: If the firstborn belongs to the priest in any case, why does asking for it a month early turn a gift into wages?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that service rendered to the giver converts an entitlement into purchased wages — but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: Since this arrangement benefits the owner of the firstborn, as he is spared the effort of taking care of the animal throughout this period, it is as though this priest has paid
answer.explanation: Rav Sheshet states exactly why early receipt counts as wages: the priest spares the owner the burden of upkeep, so the animal is effectively bought with service.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 26b: "Since this arrangement benefits the owner of the firstborn, as he is spared the effort of taking care of the animal throughout this period, it is as though this priest has paid". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered in so many words by Rav Sheshet, who explains that the early-asking priest spares the owner the upkeep and so appears to have paid for the firstborn; a reader reaching that line would not still be asking. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard — for instance why the Sages declined to penalize those who did pay teruma as wages, or why fear of over-tithing outweighs the deterrent. Alternatively build the question on the wool material, such as why shed hair and plucked hair are treated as the same test case for Akavya's leniency.

bekhorot/27.summary: Teruma grown outside Eretz Yisrael keeps getting lighter here: Rabba, a priest, nullified his in a majority of ordinary produce and ate it while ritually impure, while Rav Huna kept a vat running so each new jug of teruma wine dissolved on arrival. A menstruating woman may separate ḥalla, burn it on a skewer, then separate more, only so the category is not forgotten. Then a ferry, and a woman's question about corpse impurity.
bekhorot/27.question: Rami bar Ḥama holds the answer back until the old man returns from relieving himself, and Rav Amram comes back with Rav's ruling, which is then rejected; what did the waiting accomplish?
gate: gloss "Teruma" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Rami", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Amram", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether deference to an elder's transmitted tradition has worth apart from whether that tradition is ultimately followed.

answer.quote: He said to them that this is what Rav says: One who became impure with impurity imparted by a corpse may immerse and partake of teruma
answer.explanation: The page shows what the waiting produced — Rav Amram's transmitted ruling in Rav's name — but since the Gemara immediately says "the halakha is not in accordance with his opinion," the note's question about what the deference accomplished still stands.

bekhorot/28.summary: Much of the page turns on blemishes checked too late. Rabbi Meir bars benefit from a firstborn slaughtered before an expert saw it, penalizing whoever skipped the check, while Rabbi Yehuda permits body blemishes, since only corneas change after death. Then an erring judge: Rabbi Tarfon called a cow whose womb was removed a tereifa, the owner fed it to the dogs, and Theodosius the doctor reported that Alexandrian cows live on after exactly that surgery.
bekhorot/28.question: If Rabbi Tarfon's ruling was void from the start, so that the owner's own hand destroyed the cow, why does Rabbi Akiva bother adding that an expert for the public is exempt from paying?
gate: the question brings in "Akiva", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a ruling void on its face already shifts the loss to the owner, so an exemption for experts must be doing separate work — but the page states that work.

bekhorot/29.summary: Ila of Yavne could take four issar for ruling on a small animal's blemish and six for a large one, and he had to be paid either way, blemished or not, so nobody could say he found the blemish to earn the fee. A judge who takes wages has his rulings voided, and paid purification water sinks to the status of cave water. Still, an elderly witness gets carried on a donkey, and everyone is paid as an idle laborer.
bekhorot/29.question: If being paid whether the animal passes or fails is enough to clear Ila of suspicion, why can't a judge be hired on those same terms?
gate: gloss "issar" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the difference between a fee barred because it breeds suspicion (curable by conditions) and a fee barred categorically by Scripture.

answer.quote: just as I, Moses, learned the word of God for free, so too, you learned it from me for free, and this is also how you should act with all future generations
answer.explanation: The page grounds the judge's ban in a verse about teaching Torah for free, which bears on why no payment arrangement helps a judge, but it never compares this to Ila's suspicion-based conditions, so the question still stands honestly.

bekhorot/30.summary: A butcher lured butchers' children with nuts so they would bring him forbidden kidney fat, and Rava barred him from selling even nuts, though not water and salt. The mishna then sorts suspicions by subject: one suspected about Sabbatical-Year produce is not thereby suspected about tithes, since redemption and the requirement to eat within Jerusalem's wall make each prohibition weigh differently. Rabbi Meir refuses the sorting entirely: fail in one matter, and you are suspect in the whole Torah.
bekhorot/30.question: If breaking faith on a single detail makes a person suspect in the entire Torah, why is the butcher who sold forbidden fat still trusted with water and salt?

judge.reachNote: Does one breach of trust taint the whole person, or only the domain in which he broke faith?

answer.quote: my ruling is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one is suspected only about those items that are related
answer.explanation: Rava expressly rejects the sweeping view (Rav Pappa's water-and-salt challenge) and grounds his penalty in Rabbi Shimon's rule that suspicion extends only to items connected to the original offense, which is exactly what the note asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 30a: "my ruling is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that one is suspected only about those items that are related". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Rava tells Rav Pappa his penalty follows Rabbi Shimon, who limits suspicion to items related to the offense, and the Rabbis in the baraita likewise say one is suspected only in that particular matter. Build the question on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance, why nuts count as 'related to the prohibition' when the forbidden act was selling fat, or why Rabbi Ilai's private-stringency answer and Rabbi Yannai's accepted-and-then-suspected answer pull in opposite directions about how suspicion spreads.

bekhorot/31.summary: A ḥaver who slips back into the ways of an am ha'aretz may or may not be readmitted, depending on which Sage answers. Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya, who tied four hundred chairs for visiting Sages, was dropped when they heard he had become a tax collector; he said he had repented, and Rabba went to him while Rav Yosef stayed away. Later the page bars a man from inspecting his own firstborn, yet lets him rule on his own consecrated animals.
bekhorot/31.question: What would Rav Yosef have needed to see before he, like Rabba, walked to Rav Huna bar Ḥiyya's house?

judge.reachNote: Whether repentance can restore lost trust, or whether some acts permanently disqualify a person from ḥaver status.

answer.quote: Rav Yosef said in explanation of why he did not go: We learn in a baraita that even if such an individual resigns from his position as a tax collector he is not accepted.
answer.explanation: The page states Rav Yosef's own reason for staying away — he follows the earlier baraita, under which no resignation or repentance suffices — which answers what he would have needed to see (nothing could satisfy him).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 31a: "Rav Yosef said in explanation of why he did not go: We learn in a baraita that even if such an individual resigns from his position as a tax collector he is not accepted.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is already answered in the next line of the page, which gives Rav Yosef's reason: he holds the baraita that a former tax collector is never accepted. Ask instead about the idea underneath — why later generations reversed the ruling, or why public retraction should count as better evidence of sincerity than private, given that R. Yoḥanan rules everyone is taken back. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

bekhorot/32.summary: The animal tithe, every tenth animal counted as it passes under the rod, keeps its holiness even after it gets a blemish and is slaughtered, so its meat may not be sold outright; the workaround is to fold the meat's price into the hide, fat, sinews and horns. Rabbi Ḥiyya and Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, split over bones, and the split is resolved as local custom. Rav Ashi reads "it shall not be redeemed" as meaning: it shall not be sold.
bekhorot/32.question: If the meat can be bundled into the bones in a town where people carve bones into utensils but not in a town where the bones are discarded, is that the same prohibition in both places?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rabbinic decree's content is fixed or is defined by whatever the local market happens to treat as a saleable part of the animal.

answer.quote: the Sages did not decree that one may not sell such items after the animal’s slaughter
answer.explanation: The page gives the principle that the decree attaches only to items appraised in a live sale, and then resolves the bones dispute by locale custom, which bears on the question without stating whether the prohibition itself differs from town to town.

bekhorot/33.summary: A firstborn animal is congested with blood and will die unless someone lets it, but the cut may leave a permanent blemish. Rabbi Yehuda forbids the cut outright; the Rabbis allow it while barring slaughter on that blemish; Rabbi Shimon allows both. Someone maps the dispute onto an argument about a barrel of teruma oil of doubtful purity, and the Gemara takes the comparison apart: the barrel might yet be ruled pure, while the animal will certainly die.
bekhorot/33.question: If the congested firstborn dies untreated, what exactly has Rabbi Yehuda's refusal to cut it preserved?
gate: gloss "teruma" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether the prohibition against blemishing protects something real when the alternative is the animal's certain death, or only the actor's non-involvement.

answer.quote: here, with regard to the firstborn offering, as the individual is causing the blemish by direct action
answer.explanation: The Gemara gives Rabbi Yehuda's ground — he refuses to be the direct cause of a blemish in a consecrated animal — but never says what value that refusal secures once the animal dies anyway, so the question survives the answer only partly.

bekhorot/34.summary: A man slits his firstborn animal's ear to manufacture the blemish that would let him slaughter and eat it. Rabbi Eliezer bars him from that animal forever; the Rabbis allow it if a second blemish later appears on its own. Rava fits the Rabbis' penalty exactly to the deed: the route the man chose is the route closed to him, and the same logic covers one who cuts off his own leprous mark.
bekhorot/34.question: If the penalty is aimed at what the man did, why does the animal he mutilated go free to his son the moment he dies?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rabbinic penalty is fastened to the person who sinned or to the object he used to sin with.

answer.quote: if one improved his field in a prohibited manner and then died, his son may sow it. Apparently, the Sages penalized only him, i.e., the father
answer.explanation: Rabbi Zeira resolves Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma from the Sabbatical-Year field: the penalty attaches to the transgressor personally, not to the property, so it lapses at his death and the son is unpenalized.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 34b: "if one improved his field in a prohibited manner and then died, his son may sow it. Apparently, the Sages penalized only him, i.e., the father". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Rabbi Yirmeya asks exactly whether the son is penalized, and Rabbi Zeira answers from the Shevi'it field that the Sages penalized only the father, not the son. Ask instead about a tension the page leaves standing, for instance why the Canaanite-slave case does extend the penalty to the son while the field does not, or how Rabba and Rav Yosef's claim that Rabbi Eliezer penalizes indefinitely only "in a case which involves his property" sits with a penalty that dies with its owner.

bekhorot/35.summary: A Roman official, puzzled by a shaggy old ram, slits its ear with a dagger; the Sages permit that animal's slaughter, and when he repeats the trick on other firstborns they refuse. Children tying lambs' tails together produce the same pair of rulings. The line is intent, and the Gemara presses it: a man kicks the firstborn that chased him, and Rav Pappa is quoted in two opposite directions about a kick delivered after the chase is over.
bekhorot/35.question: If the quaestor's first cut was permitted because he did not know what he was doing, what changed in the ear the second time?

judge.reachNote: Whether disqualification tracks the animal's body or the human intent that produced the wound — a real idea, but the mishna's closing principle and the Gemara's 'speaks offhandedly' case already state it.

answer.quote: This is the principle: With regard to any blemish that is caused intentionally, the animal’s slaughter is prohibited; if the blemish is caused unintentionally, the animal’s slaughter is permitted.
answer.explanation: The mishna states outright that nothing about the ear is at issue — the animals are equally blemished ("the Sages deemed their slaughter prohibited, despite the fact that they were now blemished") and only the intent behind the wound decides.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 35a (Mishna): "This is the principle: With regard to any blemish that is caused intentionally, the animal’s slaughter is prohibited; if the blemish is caused unintentionally, the animal’s slaughter is permitted.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the mishna's own stated principle: the page says the second animals were prohibited "despite the fact that they were now blemished," so a reader already knows nothing changed in the ear. Build the question on something the page leaves live instead — for example why the Gemara needs both the gentile and the minor when its two reasons (acquiring the habit, onlookers confusing him with a Jew) pull in opposite directions, or why Rava rejects Rav Ketina's distinction between 'had a blemish' and 'a blemish was caused in it' when the bystanders' phrasing is all that stands between permitted and forbidden. Keep the summary as it is; only the question needs replacing.

bekhorot/36.summary: Priests are suspected of injuring their own firstborn animals to make them eligible for slaughter, so the argument tests whose word can be taken. Hearsay is allowed, and a priest who claims an Israelite handed him an already blemished animal is believed, on the theory that people do not lie about what can easily be checked. Then Rafram, eyes swollen nearly shut, pries them open and recognizes the animal as one he himself gave that priest.
bekhorot/36.question: If a priest was brazen enough to bring the animal back to the very man who gave it, what makes him the exception rather than the evidence?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of when one exposed liar should or should not reset a presumption of credibility for a whole class — but the page states its own answer.

answer.quote: it is only this priest who is impudent, but all other priests are not impudent
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that Rafram treated the priest as an exceptional case of impudence, precisely because he dared bring the animal to the donor himself, so no inference can be drawn about other priests.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 36b: "it is only this priest who is impudent, but all other priests are not impudent". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: Rafram held that only this priest was impudent, and that bringing the animal to the donor himself proved the case exceptional. Write a question that starts after that answer, e.g. about why a demonstrated deception is confined to the individual while the class-wide suspicion of priests causing blemishes remains in force, or about the tension with the 'likely to be revealed' reasoning the Gemara itself weakens by noting the priest volunteered the Israelite's name.

bekhorot/37.summary: One who slaughters a firstborn and sells the meat before any expert examined it must refund every coin, and the unsold meat is buried. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar narrows the refund: with carcasses and creeping animals the buyer is presumed disgusted, but with firstborn meat, untithed produce, and libation wine the seller deducts the value of the pleasure. The Gemara then asks what loss the buyer even caused, and answers that the seller could have had the blemish ruled on and eaten it himself.
bekhorot/37.question: Can a seller charge a buyer for enjoyment on the strength of a permission he never actually sought?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a merely potential permission counts as a real loss, but the page states that answer outright.

answer.quote: Had you not eaten the meat, I would have shown the animal to a Sage and he would have deemed it permitted to me.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection and answers that the seller's unexercised right to have the blemish examined counts as his loss, per Rabbi Yehuda who permits examination even after slaughter.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 37a: "Had you not eaten the meat, I would have shown the animal to a Sage and he would have deemed it permitted to me.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very objection the Gemara raises and then resolves in the next line, and the summary itself reports the answer, so it cannot stand as asked. Rewrite it to press on what remains open after that answer, for instance why the seller's claim depends on Rabbi Yehuda's view that a slaughtered firstborn can still be examined, or why the buyer's disgust matters for carcasses but not for firstborn meat. Keep the summary as it is; it tracks the page.

bekhorot/38.summary: The mishna lists eye defects that let a firstborn animal be slaughtered outside the Temple: a split eyelid, a cataract, a growth shaped like a snail or a snake, a white thread crossing into the black of the eye. To settle whether snail and snake are one blemish, the Gemara tells of an elder who taught a passing student the law, then asked the student to apply it to his own firstborn. A scholar may not rule on his own case, unless he said it before the case arose.
bekhorot/38.question: If a man cannot see blemishes in his own animal, what has changed when his own words come back to him from a student's mouth?

judge.reachNote: Whether self-interest disqualifies a ruling because of the ruler's judgment or because of who pronounces it — and whether routing the ruling through a student cures the bias.

answer.quote: he too, Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei Lakonya, was engaged in issuing this ruling of halakha at the outset, before it became relevant to him
answer.explanation: The page resolves the objection by noting the teaching preceded the case, which bears on but does not fully explain why a student's mouth changes the standing of the elder's own words.

bekhorot/39.summary: A run of dilemmas about testing a firstborn's constant tearing ends with nothing settled: is the fodder given before drinking or after, when the animal is tied or untied, in the field or in a garden next to the city? The mishna then lists blemishes anyone could see, a pierced nose, a split lip, damaged gums, and the Gemara turns to whether a missing internal organ counts as a lack at all. An animal found with one kidney: born that way, or short one?
bekhorot/39.question: If a blemish has to be visible to permit slaughtering a firstborn, why should an unseen missing kidney be enough to keep an animal off the altar?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that "blemish" (which must be seen) and "lacking" (completeness) may be two different disqualifications — but the page draws exactly that distinction explicitly.

answer.quote: a complete animal, yes, is fit as a sacrifice, but if it is lacking in any manner, even on the inside, it is not fit
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection — "it is written: 'Lameness or blindness,' which indicates that the blemish must be exposed" — and answers that the dilemma is only about disqualification from sacrifice, which rests on the separate requirement of "complete to be accepted," not on visible blemish.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 39a: "a complete animal, yes, is fit as a sacrifice, but if it is lacking in any manner, even on the inside, it is not fit". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already separates the two categories: it rules out the internal lack as grounds for slaughtering a firstborn or redeeming ("Lameness or blindness" must be exposed) and confines the dilemma to disqualification from sacrifice via "It shall be complete to be accepted." Ask instead about what stays unsettled after that answer — e.g. why the alternative reading ties "complete" to "no blemish therein" and so demands an outward lack, or why a kidney lost before the blood is collected ruins the offering while most of the flesh lost afterward does not. Keep the summary as it is.

bekhorot/40.summary: A firstborn with one testicle counts as blemished and may be slaughtered, and the argument here is how to tell. Rabbi Akiva's test is physical: seat the animal on its rump, mash the sac, and whatever is there will emerge. In Piran of Beit Menaḥem the mashing found nothing, the animal was slaughtered, and the second testicle turned up attached to the loins; Akiva still permitted the meat, while Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri accused him of feeding Israel sacrificial meat outside the courtyard.
bekhorot/40.question: If the testicle was there the whole time, was the animal ever blemished, or does a blemish only begin to exist once an examination can find it?

judge.reachNote: Whether a blemish is a fact about the animal's body or a status created by what a valid examination can reveal.

answer.quote: And Rabbi Akiva permitted the consumption of its flesh, as the testicle had not previously emerged, and Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri prohibited its consumption.
answer.explanation: The mishna gives Akiva's reason as the fact that the testicle never emerged under examination, which bears on whether blemish status tracks detectability, but the page never states the underlying principle or resolves the dispute with Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri.

bekhorot/41.summary: The mishna lists conditions that do not permit slaughtering a firstborn outside the Temple: moist boils, old age, a foul odor, an animal that killed a person on the word of a single witness. The discussion then turns to an animal with both male and female organs, and asks why that female organ is not simply a crack, a blemish the Torah names. Abaye and Rava insist only bone can crack, not flesh, while Rabbi Yishmael calls it the largest blemish there is.
bekhorot/41.question: Rava ends the page by asking why a tumtum, if it is certainly one sex or the other, cannot be valuated as one, and nobody answers him, so what would an answer even look like?

judge.reachNote: Whether a status that is 'certainly one of two' can be cashed out in practice, or whether uncertainty blocks any concrete legal consequence.

bekhorot/42.summary: The argument is whether a tumtum, whose genitals are concealed, is a distinct third category or simply a male or female whose sex is unknown. Six baraitot list the tumtum beside the hermaphrodite as unfit, and six times the Gemara answers identically: strike the word, the source meant only the hermaphrodite. The seventh source counts its items as five, so striking would leave four, and an orphaned animal is slotted into the tumtum's place instead.
bekhorot/42.question: If the word can be deleted from six sources, what really saved the seventh besides the accident that it counted to five?

judge.reachNote: How far a text may be emended to protect a position, and what counts as real textual resistance versus a mere counting accident.

answer.quote: No, everyone agrees with regard to the statement that a tumtum is a distinct entity that there is no doubt that this is incorrect.
answer.explanation: The page eventually resolves the whole tumtum-as-distinct-entity question by relocating the dispute to whether the urination site settles male or female, but it never says what made the five-item baraita resist deletion beyond its count, so the note's question can still be asked.

bekhorot/43.summary: The mishna says every blemish that disqualifies an animal also disqualifies a priest, then adds blemishes no animal could have: a pointed head, a turnip-shaped head, a hammer-like forehead, a head with a dent. Rabbi Yoḥanan grounds these in a verse read as requiring a priest equal among the seed of Aaron, meaning he looks like the other priests. The Gemara sorts the disqualifications into tiers: a genuine blemish profanes the service, while merely looking unlike the others breaks a positive command without profaning anything.
bekhorot/43.question: If a crooked spine or a missing eyebrow changes nothing about how the rite is performed, what exactly is damaged when such a priest serves anyway?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a disqualification can attach to a priest's appearance rather than to his capacity to perform the rite, and asks what such a disqualification protects.

answer.quote: A priest who is not equal among the seed of Aaron who performs the Temple service transgresses this prohibition.
answer.explanation: The page states the legal consequence — no profanation of the service, but violation of the positive mitzva that equal priests serve — without saying what about appearance makes it matter, so the question can still be asked.

bekhorot/44.summary: The page sorts the eye blemishes that bar a priest from Temple service: eyes set above or below their place, eyes that take in the ground floor and the upper story at once, eyes that will not open in sunlight. Rava gives each word in Leviticus a separate job, so that "in his eye" catches a priest whose eyes merely look unusual. Then Rav Huna illustrates "different eyes" by pointing at Rav Yehuda, who took offense.
bekhorot/44.question: When Rav Huna needed a living example of different eyes and pointed at the colleague in the room, was he demonstrating the category or showing what it costs?

judge.reachNote: Teaching a category of bodily blemish by pointing at a living colleague turns a definition into an injury; the question reaches the cost of using a person as an illustration.

answer.quote: In order to illustrate this blemish, Rav Huna pointed with his finger while saying: The term: Different eyes, is referring to an individual
answer.explanation: The page states that the pointing was done to illustrate the blemish, and separately reports that Rav Yehuda took offense, so it supplies both halves of the note's either/or without weighing Rav Huna's awareness of the cost.

bekhorot/45.summary: The mishna lists the leg and hand defects that bar a priest from Temple service: bowlegs, a heel that protrudes backward, flat goose feet, fingers grown together. The argument sharpens over a sixth finger on each hand and foot. Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis both read the verse about the Philistine champion with twenty-four digits, one hearing praise and the other a defect, and Rabbi Yosei rereads Rabbi Tarfon's apparent blessing to a six-fingered man as an insult.
bekhorot/45.question: If one verse about twenty-four fingers and one sentence from Rabbi Tarfon can both be heard as compliment or as insult, what is deciding the hearing before the words arrive?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a prior judgment about whether extra digits are strength or defect governs how the verse and Rabbi Tarfon's words are heard.

bekhorot/46.summary: Ravina dissolved a public vow that had barred a children's teacher from teaching, because the man hit the children too hard and no replacement was as meticulous. The mishna then sorts sons who are firstborn for inheritance but not for redemption from a priest, and the Gemara narrows to a fetus that pushes out its head and draws it back. Reish Lakish splits the cases: that forehead counts as birth everywhere except inheritance, which wants a recognizable face.
bekhorot/46.question: If a forehead is enough to make a child born for every other purpose, why should a father's power to recognize a face be what decides who gets the double portion?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that birth for ritual purposes may be defined differently than identification for transmitting property, but the page states that reason outright.

summaryProblems.claim: Ravina dissolved the vow because the man hit the children too hard.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Ravina had his vow nullified and reinstated him, as they did not find another teacher who was as meticulous as he was

judge.feedback: The summary says "Ravina dissolved the vow because the man hit the children too hard.", but the page says "Ravina had his vow nullified and reinstated him, as they did not find another teacher who was as meticulous as he was". Say what the page says. The question is the very one the Gemara asks and answers on 46b with the verse "he shall recognize the firstborn," so it must be replaced. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved, for example why Rabbi Yoḥanan holds a forehead suffices even for inheritance despite the recognition verse, or why the Sages demand a nose for remarriage testimony but not for the firstborn. Also fix the opening line: the hitting was why the vow was imposed, while the nullification rested on there being no equally meticulous replacement and on teaching being a mitzva.

bekhorot/47.summary: A man fathers sons, then converts. Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that a son born afterward takes no double portion, since the earlier boys were already "the first of his strength"; Reish Lakish rules that the convert counts as newly born, so those sons drop out of the reckoning. The same two sages split the same way over whether he has already fulfilled the command to be fruitful and multiply, and the Gemara explains why neither dispute settles the other.
bekhorot/47.question: If a convert is treated as newly born, what is he to the sons he fathered and raised before?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that halakhic rebirth at conversion severs legal kinship while lived fatherhood remains, asking what status the severed relationship retains.

answer.quote: The case of a gentile is different, as he has no lineage [ḥayis], i.e., this man is not considered his father’s son at all.
answer.explanation: The page states that a gentile father has no halakhic lineage tie to his son, which bears directly on what pre-conversion sons are to their father, though it is said of a gentile father of a Jewish-born child rather than of a convert's earlier sons.

bekhorot/48.summary: Twin boys, nobody knows which came out first, and the father dies before the five sela redemption is paid. Rabbi Meir says that once the brothers split the estate each can shrug the priest off: prove I am the firstborn. Rava rebuilds the whole dispute around an estate worth exactly five sela, where half counts as inheritance and half as purchase from one another, leaving two and a half, and the argument turns on whether part of five is worth anything.
bekhorot/48.question: If each brother can turn the priest away by demanding proof that he is the firstborn, why should the very same coins owe the priest anything while they still sit in one undivided pile?

judge.reachNote: Whether an obligation can attach to a fund when it attaches to no identifiable person — partnership property versus individual liability.

answer.quote: he can say to each of them: If I have a claim against you, I am taking the one hundred dinars that is your share in the joint field
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact objection ("The same should apply even in a case where they did not divide the property") and Rabbi Yirmeya answers that undivided brothers are partners, so the priest can claim from the joint fund under either alternative — and Rava then rejects the whole premise by rereading the mishna as a case where the father died after thirty days and the property is on lien.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 48a: "he can say to each of them: If I have a claim against you, I am taking the one hundred dinars that is your share in the joint field". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own challenge, asked and answered on the page: Rabbi Yirmeya's Yosef ben Shimon partnership reasoning, and then Rava's rereading of the mishna as a case where the property was already on lien. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved — for instance why Rava's guarantor objection (that one cannot claim from a guarantor before claiming from the debtor) should govern property that secures a Torah obligation, or why Rabbi Yehuda would insist the lien fell on the father's property when he concedes the priest forfeits half. Keep the summary's thread but hang the question on what the page argues over rather than on the step it explicitly settles.

bekhorot/49.summary: Redeeming a firstborn son for five sela turns into a question of clocks. If the son dies within thirty days the priest returns the money; if he dies on the thirtieth day itself, Rabbi Akiva calls it uncertain, so money already handed over stays with the priest and money not yet handed over need not be. Rav and Shmuel then argue over a father who pays early, stipulates that it take effect later, and whose coins are spent in the meantime.
bekhorot/49.question: If the five sela are gone by the thirtieth day, what is the priest still holding that could redeem the boy?
gate: gloss "sela" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Does a payment work by the coins being present when the obligation matures, or by the act of giving with a condition attached?

answer.quote: Rav says his son is redeemed, just as is the halakha with regard to the betrothal of a woman on the condition that it takes effect after thirty days.
answer.explanation: The page squarely addresses the squandered-money case: Rav holds the son is redeemed by analogy to conditional betrothal, Shmuel counters that here the father has no power to redeem now, and the halakha is stated to follow Shmuel.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 49a (end) / 49b: "Rav says his son is redeemed, just as is the halakha with regard to the betrothal of a woman on the condition that it takes effect after thirty days.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: Rav says the son is redeemed on the betrothal analogy, Shmuel says it is not in his power to redeem from now, and the Gemara rules like Shmuel. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing — for example why the halakha here follows Shmuel against the usual rule that Rav prevails in ritual matters, or why the mishna's inference could only be squared with Shmuel by saying the money is still extant.

bekhorot/50.summary: Redeeming a firstborn son costs his father five sela, a silver coin paid to a priest, and the page works at converting that sum into the worn-out gold dinars of Hadrian and Trajan. The arithmetic fails twice before an order of operations is found that comes out even. Rava then argues the Torah's sela is worth only three and a third dinars, and Rav Ashi sends a priest seventeen dinars and asks for change back.
bekhorot/50.question: When Rav Ashi asks the priest to return a third of a dinar and the priest asks for three dinars more, is the son redeemed in the meantime?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a mitzva paid in money may hang unresolved while the sages dispute what the required sum actually is.

bekhorot/51.summary: Five sela redeem a firstborn son, but paid in what? The mishna bars Canaanite slaves, promissory notes, and land; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, reading the verse by amplification and restriction rather than generalization and detail, bars only the notes. Then practice complicates theory: Rabbi Tarfon would take the coins and hand them back, and the redemption held, until Rabbi Ḥanina saw a father pacing in front of him waiting for the refund.
bekhorot/51.question: If a priest may return the five sela and the son stays redeemed, what exactly did the pacing father fail to do that Rabbi Tarfon's donors did?
gate: gloss "sela" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
