judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that the validity of the payment rests on the giver's wholehearted intent, not on the coins' final resting place — but the page says this in so many words.

answer.quote: Rabbi Ḥanina said to him: Evidently, you did not conclusively resolve to give the money. This is a bad matter, and therefore his son is not redeemed.
answer.explanation: The page states outright what the pacing father lacked — a conclusive resolve to give the money — which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Bekhorot 51b: "Rabbi Ḥanina said to him: Evidently, you did not conclusively resolve to give the money. This is a bad matter, and therefore his son is not redeemed.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim a line later: Rabbi Ḥanina tells the man he "did not conclusively resolve to give the money." Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than asking for it — e.g., press on how a priest's advance willingness to refund differs from a father's expectation of a refund, or why intent decides a payment the Torah wants in actual money. Keep the summary; it is faithful to the page.

bekhorot/52.summary: The firstborn takes twice only of what was in his father's hand at death, not of stalks that ripened afterward, not of debts still owed, and never from his mother's estate. A second mishna asks what the Jubilee Year undoes, and the argument turns on one word: "giving" makes the extra share a gift for Rabbi Meir and ordinary inheritance for the Rabbis. Rabbi Elazar has it come back for naught, the firstborn simply losing it.
bekhorot/52.question: If the double portion returns in the Jubilee and the firstborn is paid nothing for it, what was the birthright ever worth?
gate: gloss "the Jubilee" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Asks what a Torah-given privilege amounts to if the Jubilee can cancel it without payment — the nature of the birthright as right versus temporary holding.

answer.quote: What is the meaning of the clause: They return in the Jubilee Year? It means that they return for naught, and they forfeit that which they received.
answer.explanation: The page confirms the premise of the question — that the firstborn genuinely forfeits the extra portion with no compensation — and even voices Rav Sheshet's protest, but it never says what the birthright is then worth.

bekhorot/53.summary: The mishna says animal tithe applies in and outside Eretz Yisrael, with or without the Temple, so the Gemara asks why flocks are not tithed now. Rav Huna blames an orphaned animal slipping into the count; Rabba blames misuse of consecrated property, citing a baraita where a dedicated animal is shut in a room until it starves. The suggestion to blemish every animal in advance is dropped: the Temple may be rebuilt, and then no unblemished animals would remain.
bekhorot/53.question: If the rebuilt Temple is near enough to rule out blemishing a whole herd, what is the argument for locking a consecrated animal in and waiting for it to starve?

judge.reachNote: The Gemara uses 'soon the Temple will be rebuilt' as a live constraint in one ruling and ignores it in another, raising how seriously that expectation governs halakhic policy.

answer.quote: the presence of these items might lead to the mishap of the violation of the prohibition against using consecrated property
answer.explanation: The page states the rationale for destroying already-consecrated items (fear of misuse), but never reconciles that destruction with the same passage's confidence that the Temple will soon be rebuilt and animals will be needed.

bekhorot/54.summary: Grain of one kind cannot be tithed for grain of another, and the argument runs on into animals: cattle and sheep stay separate, while sheep and goats count as one flock. The mishna measures a flock by distance instead, sixteen mil, the reach of one shepherd's eye, read out of a verse in Jeremiah. Rav wants five animals standing in the middle to bridge thirty-two mil; Shmuel needs only one, and relocates the shepherd there.
bekhorot/54.question: If one animal in the middle can bind two flocks thirty-two mil apart, is a flock defined by the animals in it or by where the shepherd happens to stand?

judge.reachNote: Whether a group's unity comes from the animals themselves being joinable or from a single overseer's field of vision.

answer.quote: we see the shepherd as one who stands here in the middle and we apply the verse: “Who counts them” (Jeremiah 33:13), to him
answer.explanation: Shmuel's reasoning (and Rabba bar Sheila's derivation that animals passing under one shepherd's hands are one flock) leans toward a shepherd-centered definition, but Rav's requirement of five combinable animals in the middle keeps the alternative live, so the question can still honestly be asked.

bekhorot/55.summary: Animal tithe requires a flock to count as one, so the page asks what bridges a gap of thirty-two mil. One sheep in the middle works; so does the shepherd standing there; so, says Rav Pappa, do his implements, since he will have to go fetch them. Rav Ashi then asks about the shepherd's dog, which sometimes comes when called and sometimes does not, and the question is left standing.
bekhorot/55.question: If the middle counts only because the shepherd must go there himself, does a disobedient dog combine the flocks while a well-trained one does not?

judge.reachNote: The middle point links two flocks only insofar as the shepherd is bound to go there, so the question presses whether the link depends on actual necessity — and whether that necessity is measured per case or by the general nature of the thing.

answer.quote: Or perhaps, because sometimes the dog does not come when the shepherd calls it, and in such cases the shepherd himself must go and bring it, it does combine
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises both horns of exactly this doubt — the callable dog versus the dog that must be fetched — but explicitly leaves the dilemma unresolved, so the question can still be asked honestly.

bekhorot/56.summary: Purchased animals are exempt from animal tithe, derived from a verse about redeeming a firstborn son: just as the son cannot be bought, neither can your oxen and sheep. Rabbi Yoḥanan then opens a gap: buy ten fetuses while still in their mothers' wombs, and all ten enter the pen, since the exclusion bites only once an animal is fit for the altar. Rabbi Elazar defends the reading with a dream and dismisses a contradicting baraita as inaccurate.
bekhorot/56.question: If ownership acquired in the womb slips past the exemption, what is the rule against purchased animals actually keeping out?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of what an ownership-based exemption is protecting once timing of acquisition can be manipulated to evade it.

answer.quote: The verse excludes purchased animals from animal tithe only at the time of doing, i.e., from the time the animals are fit to be sacrificed in the Temple
answer.explanation: Rava (and Rabbi Elazar) state the residual scope of the exemption — it bars animals bought once they are altar-fit — but the page never says what purpose that narrowed rule serves, so the note's question can still be asked.

bekhorot/57.summary: The mishna lists what never enters the pen for animal tithe: a sheep-goat hybrid, a tereifa, an animal born by caesarean section, one under eight days old, an orphan. A baraita then puts back in animals used for bestiality, set aside for idol worship, or given as the price of a dog, reasoning that since a blemish does not disqualify a tithed animal, corruption does not either. Rabbi Yishmael ben Satriel's report about wrapping a newborn in its dead mother's flayed hide explains the orphan rule.
bekhorot/57.question: Why should an animal that was worshipped as a deity pass under the rod while a lamb seven days old does not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — which sacrificial disqualifications carry over to tithe and which do not — but the page itself poses and resolves exactly that tension.

answer.quote: Actually, the tanna does derive the verbal analogy, but these categories listed in the baraita are included by the Merciful One in the animal tithe.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises precisely this difficulty — if the verbal analogy from sacrificial animals excludes the young and the orphan, why not the idolatrous animal? — and answers that Scripture (corruption/blemish) includes those categories while the analogy still excludes the animal whose time has not arrived.

Ben Azzai will not choose between Elul and Tishrei as the new year for animals, though he elsewhere calls every sage but Rabbi Akiva unimpressive; Rabbi Yoḥanan says the two views came down as rival traditions from the prophets, so reasoning cannot touch them. The mishna then has mothers bleat outside the pen so the young walk out on their own.

bekhorot/59.summary: Counting lambs for the animal tithe, one in ten, and the argument is over how much the counting actually does. Rava holds that the tenth animal is sacred even if it never left the pen, and the Gemara tries four baraitot before giving up and reaching for a verse. Then lambs stream out of a pen with two openings, six through one, four through the other, four still inside, and Rava tallies who is exempt.
bekhorot/59.question: Why should lambs counted toward a ten that never arrived walk away exempt from the tithe for good?

bekhorot/60.summary: Animals leave the pen one by one and every tenth belongs to the tithe. The page works through miscounting: the owner calls the tenth "ninth" and the eleventh "tenth," and all three become sacred, each with a different status. The sharp move is the limit drawn from the verse, that a mistaken word sanctifies only an animal near ten, the ninth or eleventh, never the eighth or twelfth. Rava then has two animals emerge together, leaving sacred and non-sacred indistinguishable.
bekhorot/60.question: If the tenth is sanctified of its own accord, why should a wrong word spoken over the ninth make that animal holy too?

judge.reachNote: The question does reach the real idea — sanctity that arises from the animal's position versus sanctity created by the owner's word — but the page states that both operate, by scriptural derivation.

answer.quote: This indicates that the tenth animal that passes under the rod is imbued with sanctity, in addition to any animal that the owner designates as the tenth.
answer.explanation: The baraita asks exactly this ("From where is it derived that... all three of them are sanctified?") and answers from Leviticus 27:32 that the verse adds sanctity through the owner's mistaken designation alongside the automatic tenth.

bekhorot/61.question: Why can an agent's guess about how generous his sender is bind that sender, while an agent's slip of the tongue in counting sheep does not?

arakhin/2.summary: Arakhin opens with a list of who can pledge a person's fixed Torah valuation to the Temple treasury, and who can be the object of such a pledge. The Gemara treats each "everyone" in the mishna as a hunt for some unnamed case: a discriminating minor in the year before adulthood, or a repulsive man and one afflicted with boils, whom no buyer would want. Market price and fixed valuation come apart here, since the verse says "persons," and any amount of life counts.
arakhin/2.question: Why does the Gemara let one "everyone" stand as an unnecessary phrase said only for balance, while insisting every other one must be hiding a case?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the interpretive premise that no phrase in a mishna is idle, and asks what happens when the Gemara itself suspends it.

answer.quote: Actually, this statement is not necessary, but it is mentioned because the continuation: And everyone is the object of a vow, was necessary.
answer.explanation: The page gives the local reason for tolerating that one redundant clause — it rides along with its necessary partner — but never states why the "everyone" method must otherwise always yield a hidden case, so the question survives the line.

arakhin/3.summary: The Gemara works through a long list of rulings that open with the word everyone, asking each time whom that word was meant to sweep in. The answers: a day-old baby with a discharge, a minor who knows to Whom he recites a blessing, a woman sanctifying the ashes of the red heifer, a Samaritan who slaughters. Then priests, who might seem exempt from sukka, since dwelling means a man and his wife together and they are on Temple duty.
arakhin/3.question: If a priest who cannot tell the leprous marks apart is still fit to declare pure or impure once someone explains them to him, whose decision is it?

judge.reachNote: It reaches the split between formal authority to declare and the knowledge that actually decides the case.

answer.quote: This statement, that the priest is fit, is referring to a situation where if they explain to him he understands
answer.explanation: Ravina resolves when such a priest is fit, but the page never says whose ruling the declaration counts as — the expert who explains or the priest who pronounces — so only part of the question is met.

arakhin/4.summary: A priest, the argument runs, might be exempt from vows of valuation, the fixed sums Leviticus assigns to a person by age and sex; three sages propose different reasons to think so, and each is knocked down. Then the plural word "persons" is squeezed hard. A repulsive man and one covered in boils, worth nothing on the market, still carry the full fixed valuation, while a dying man who cannot stand before the priest carries none.
arakhin/4.question: If a man nobody would pay a coin for still carries the Torah's full fixed sum, why does the one too weak to stand before the priest carry nothing at all?

judge.reachNote: Valuation tracks something other than market price — the question asks what that something is, if not worth then presence or capacity.

answer.quote: anyone who is included in the category of setting, i.e., he can stand, is included in the halakha of valuation
answer.explanation: The page names the criterion that excludes the moribund — the verse's requirement of being "set before the priest" — but does not explain why mere life suffices for the boil-covered man while standing is demanded of the dying, so the question can still be pressed.

summaryProblems.claim: Three sages propose different reasons to think a priest might be exempt from valuations, and each is knocked down.

arakhin/5.summary: The Torah sets a fixed sum owed to the Temple for a person, scaled by age and sex, but it names no amount for a baby under a month old. Rabbi Meir says a man who pledges such a valuation still owes the child's market price, since people do not speak for nothing; the Rabbis say he owes nothing at all. Rav pushes Meir's logic further, to a pledged utensil and to a man who consecrates his neighbor's animal.
arakhin/5.question: When someone pledges something the law cannot deliver, is he held to the words he used or to the payment he must have meant?

judge.reachNote: The question does name the real idea — construing a failed declaration by intent rather than by its literal words — but the page states that idea outright and resolves it with Rav's rulings.

arakhin/6.summary: Two early teachings clash over whether the Temple may accept a gentile's gift, and Rabbi Yoḥanan sorts them by timing: nothing at the start of building, later only what cannot be identified as his. A gentile's candelabrum in a synagogue follows similar logic; its use may not be changed while people still recall who gave it, since he would protest and scream. Sha'azrak, an Arab merchant, gave one to Rav Yehuda's synagogue, someone switched its use too soon, and the page records who got angry.
arakhin/6.question: If a donated lamp becomes free to repurpose once the donor's name is forgotten, what was holding it in place before then, the gift or the giver?

judge.reachNote: Whether a donation is bound by the object's consecration or by the donor's standing and feelings — an idea the page names explicitly.

answer.quote: it is specifically a gentile who would protest and scream: Where is the candelabrum that I donated?
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that what restrains repurposing is the living donor's likely protest, i.e. the giver rather than any sanctity in the gift.

arakhin/7.summary: A pregnant woman sentenced to death is executed without delay, since the court treats the unborn child as part of her body. But if she has already sat on the travailing chair, the birthing stool, the court waits, because once the fetus uproots from its place it counts as a separate body. Shmuel goes further: if a woman in labor dies on Shabbat, one carries a knife through the public street and opens her abdomen on the chance the child lives.
arakhin/7.question: If labor is what turns an unborn child into a body of its own, what has actually changed in that moment besides where it is?

judge.reachNote: Asks what constitutes becoming a separate life — whether position in the birth canal marks a real change in status or only a legal marker.

answer.quote: Once the fetus uproots from its place and begins to leave the woman's body, it is considered an independent body and may not be killed together with the mother.
answer.explanation: The page gives uprooting/beginning to leave as the trigger for independent status, but it does not say what changes beyond that displacement, so the question can still be pressed.

arakhin/8.summary: A woman who bled but cannot tell whether it fell in her seven menstrual days or in the eleven days that would make her a zava, a woman with irregular discharge, counts clean days until her cycle is legible again: seventeen if she saw one day of blood, seven if she saw thirteen. Rav Adda bar Ahava asks why bother, since seven clean days already permit her to her husband. Rabba answers that the extra counting buys knowledge, not permission.
arakhin/8.question: Why spend ten more days counting to learn the name of a status when seven days have already settled what she may actually do?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether clarifying a status is worth anything once conduct is already settled — but the page states the payoff outright.

answer.quote: This is significant because if she is menstruating she can become ritually pure and permitted to her husband after seven days even if none of them are clean days
answer.explanation: Rabba's reply, which the Gemara elaborates, states exactly why the extra counting matters: knowing the status determines how her next discharge is purified (seven days with no clean days, one clean day, or seven clean days).

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 8b: "This is significant because if she is menstruating she can become ritually pure and permitted to her husband after seven days even if none of them are clean days". The question is Rav Adda's own question, and Rabba plus the Gemara's elaboration answer it in full: the knowledge is not merely nominal, since it fixes how her next discharge will be purified (seven days without clean days, one clean day, or seven clean days), and it also determines whether the zava's offering may be eaten by priests. arakhin/9.summary: The argument is about how many of a year's twelve lunar months may be stretched to thirty days and how many cut to twenty-nine. Rav Huna and Ulla read the mishna in opposite directions, but both fear the same thing: if the declared month drifts too far from the visible new moon, people will mock the court for setting dates as it pleases. The answer offered is that nobody notices a gap of one day.
arakhin/9.question: If the court's standing rests on people not noticing a one-day gap between the declared month and the moon overhead, what happens when someone does look up?

judge.reachNote: Whether the court's calendrical authority depends on matching what is visible in the sky or stands independent of sighting.

answer.quote: The new moon was visible yesterday but we did not pay attention and did not notice it.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the remaining one-day gap and answers that a person who does notice the moon will assume witnesses reported it and blame his own inattention, and on 9b Rava adds that sanctifying the month need not follow sighting at all.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 9a: "The new moon was visible yesterday but we did not pay attention and did not notice it.". arakhin/10.summary: The mishna counts Temple trumpet blasts, twenty-one on an ordinary day and forty-eight on a Friday during Sukkot, and lists the twelve days a reed flute played before the altar. Those twelve turn out to be the days an individual completes the full hallel, and the Gemara then hunts for why the list stops there: not Shabbat, not the New Moon, not Rosh HaShana when the books of life lie open, not Purim. Rava's reason for Purim is that the rescue was partial.
arakhin/10.question: If the answer to Purim is that the Jews came out of it still serving Ahasuerus, does a half-finished rescue earn half a song, or none?
gate: the question brings in "Ahasuerus", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether praise is proportional to the completeness of the redemption being praised.

arakhin/11.summary: The magreifa, a Temple instrument a cubit square with ten holes, emitted a hundred tones according to Shmuel and a thousand according to a baraita, which Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak attributes to the way baraitot exaggerate numbers. Abaye holds that a Levite singer who instead closes the Temple gates is liable to death at Heaven's hand; a baraita calls it only a prohibition.
arakhin/11.question: When Rabbi Yohanan ben Gudgeda sent Rabbi Yehoshua bar Hananya away from the Temple doors, was he sparing him a death at Heaven's hand or just enforcing a fence around a lesser rule?

the question brings in "Hananya", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

arakhin/12.summary: The Sages ask whether Levites sing when wine alone is poured on the altar, with no animal offering burning beside it. A baraita about the First Temple's destruction seems to settle it, until Rava notices that the Levites on their platform were singing Wednesday's psalm on a Sunday, so it accompanied no offering at all. The rest of the page counts Sabbatical and Jubilee cycles, trying to make two chronologies of the destructions agree.
arakhin/12.question: What turns a psalm sung on the wrong day of the week into a lamentation rather than simply a mistake?

judge.reachNote: When does an unintended utterance count as providence rather than error — the same logic by which Rabbi Yosei assigns deleterious matters to inauspicious days.

answer.quote: Rather, it was merely a portentous lamentation that came into their mouths, not a song recited over an offering.
answer.explanation: The page labels the misplaced verse a portentous lamentation that came unbidden into the Levites' mouths, but never says what distinguishes such an omen from an ordinary error, so the question can still be asked.

arakhin/13.summary: The mishna counts out minimums for Temple music, two trumpets, nine harps, one cymbal, and twelve Levites singing on the platform beside the altar. Boys entered the courtyard only when the Levites were singing, and only to sing; Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov keeps them off the platform, standing on the ground with their heads reaching between the Levites' legs. One baraita calls them helpers, soadei; the mishna calls them tzoarei, from anguish, since the grown men could not match their voices.
arakhin/13.question: If the boys' voices were what gave the music its flavor, why does the count of twelve leave them out?

judge.reachNote: What is counted as constituting the service versus what merely sweetens it — the boys supply the flavor yet are not part of the required quorum.

answer.quote: Rav Pappa says: It corresponds to the minimum number of instruments that were played: Nine harps and two lyres and one cymbal.
answer.where: Arakhin 13b (Gemara on the mishna of the twelve Levites)
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa ties the number twelve to the instruments played, which bears on why voice-only minors fall outside the tally, though the page never says this about the minors in so many words.

arakhin/14.summary: Land inherited as an ancestral field is redeemed from the Temple at a flat rate, fifty silver shekels per area that grows a kor of barley, poor sand or the fine orchards of Sebastia alike. That flat pricing returns twice more: thirty sela, a silver coin, whether the ox killed the most attractive among the slaves or the most unsightly, and fifty for a rapist or seducer. Rav Zeira objects that fifty cannot cover a king's daughter's humiliation; Abaye answers with the slave who pierces pearls.
arakhin/14.question: If nobody balks at a flat thirty sela for a slave who pierces pearls, why does a flat fifty for any young woman sound wrong to Rav Zeira?

judge.reachNote: What a fixed statutory sum is measuring: the worth of the victim, or a humiliation that varies with her standing.

answer.quote: Nevertheless, the mishna clearly indicates that there is no distinction between the two slaves, as the Torah states a fixed payment. Rather, Rav Zeira says that there is a different proof:
answer.explanation: The page raises exactly this parallel through Abaye and shows Rav Zeira retreating to a different proof, but it never explains why the flat fifty struck him as wrong in the first place, so the question survives.

arakhin/15.summary: A man who falsely claims his bride was not a virgin pays one hundred sela, a silver coin, double the fifty a rapist pays, and the mishna reads that gap as proof that the mouth sins worse than the hand. The proof offered is the spies, whose evil report about the land sealed the desert generation's fate. At the end Rava tries to define slander: saying there is always fire at so-and-so's house is plain fact, until it is said with a sneer.
arakhin/15.question: Does Rabbi Yosei's practice of saying nothing he would not say to the person's face make the words clean, or only make him bolder about them?
gate: the question brings in "Yosei's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether willingness to say a thing openly purifies the speech or merely adds brazenness to the harm.

answer.quote: Abaye said to him: All the more so it is proscribed speech, as it is both impudence and malicious speech.
answer.explanation: Abaye answers that saying it to the person's face makes the speech worse, not clean, but Rabba holds with Rabbi Yosei and the page breaks off mid-dispute without resolving it.

arakhin/16.summary: Saul curses Jonathan and throws a spear at him, and three sages read that scene for how far the duty to rebuke goes: until the person hits you, curses you, or merely snaps back. Rabbi Tarfon doubts anyone can receive rebuke, since a man told to remove the splinter from his eye answers: remove the beam from yours. Rav Huna promises Shmuel he will stop afflicting Ḥiyya bar Rav, then explains, once Ḥiyya leaves, that he was right all along.
arakhin/16.question: If Rav Huna held his tongue only to spare Ḥiyya bar Rav the humiliation while still believing himself in the right, was anything actually said between them?

judge.reachNote: Reaches toward the idea that a rebuke given privately, with restraint from ulterior motives, still counts as rebuke 'for its own sake'.

answer.quote: as Rav Huna originally rebuked Ḥiyya bar Rav only when Shmuel was not present
answer.explanation: The page explicitly states that Rav Huna did rebuke Ḥiyya bar Rav, privately and outside Shmuel's presence, which is exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 16b: "as Rav Huna originally rebuked Ḥiyya bar Rav only when Shmuel was not present". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks whether anything was said between Rav Huna and Ḥiyya, but the page answers this outright by explaining that Rav Huna had rebuked him privately, when Shmuel was not present. Build the new question on what the story leaves unsettled instead: e.g. why silence born of unwillingness to humiliate counts as 'humility not for its own sake,' or how that squares with the baraita's warning not to rebuke until the other's 'face changes.' Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page accurately.

arakhin/17.summary: A destitute man who vows the valuation of a wealthy man, the sum the Torah fixes by age and sex, pays only what a poor man can afford, while a wealthy man who valuates a pauper pays the full amount. Offerings run the other way: one who vows to cover a leper's purification offering brings sheep or birds according to the leper's means, not his own. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi resists the split, saying a poor man who echoes a rich man's vow pays the rich man's price.
arakhin/17.question: If a poor man's vow to donate a rich man's valuation shrinks to what he can actually pay, why does that same poor man, vowing to fund a wealthy leper's offering, owe the full two sheep?

judge.reachNote: Whose status fixes an obligation — the one who speaks the vow or the person who is its subject — and why Scripture splits the two domains.

answer.quote: Consequently, the verse states: “And if he is poor,” from which it is derived that the offering of the destitute leper is brought only when the leper himself is destitute.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the note's exact analogy from valuations and answers it: a verse blocks the leniency, so a poor vower for a wealthy leper must bring the wealthy leper's offering.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 17b: "Consequently, the verse states: “And if he is poor,” from which it is derived that the offering of the destitute leper is brought only when the leper himself is destitute.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page asks this very question in the baraita on 17b and answers it from the verse "And if he is poor," so the question as written is closed. Rewrite it to press on what remains after that answer — for instance, why a scriptural edict is needed at all if the vower's means never governed offerings, or why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi must redirect the same verse to exclude the opposite case (a wealthy vower for a poor leper). Keep the summary, which tracks the mishna faithfully.

arakhin/18.summary: Whether a recovered leper counts as destitute when he brings his offerings turns on what he owns, and the mishna says a father dying with ten thousand dinars, silver coins enough to make anyone rich, does not yet count. Rabbi Abbahu rewrites the case so the father is still alive; the objection that most dying people do die is answered flatly, the son stays destitute until the death. Rav Ḥisda saves the ship at sea by renting it out, since rent falls due only at the end.
arakhin/18.question: If a man whose father will be dead by morning is still destitute this morning, what is it that makes the ten thousand dinars his?

judge.reachNote: What constitutes ownership: actual possession at death versus a practically certain expectancy that statistics would already credit to him.

answer.quote: the mishna therefore teaches us that the son retains his status as destitute until the father actually dies
answer.explanation: The page fixes the moment of transfer at the father's actual death and rejects the majority-of-moribund-people argument, but it never explains what ownership consists in such that a near-certain inheritance is not yet his.

arakhin/19.summary: A man vows to donate the weight of his forearm, and Rabbi Yehuda works out that weight by sinking the arm into a full barrel of water and then refilling the displaced space with donkey flesh, sinews, and bones. Rabbi Yosei objects that water measures volume, not weight, and that matching donkey bone to human bone is guesswork anyway. Rabbi Yehuda concedes one estimates, but holds that an elaborate approximation beats a bare appraisal.
arakhin/19.question: Is a careful procedure built on an admitted guess any closer to the truth than the guess by itself?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rigorous method resting on an acknowledged approximation yields more truth than the approximation alone.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda holds that we do whatever is possible in order to be more precise.
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yehuda's rationale for the elaborate procedure, but it is one side of an unresolved dispute against Rabbi Yosei's "if one estimates, let one estimate the weight of the forearm directly," so the question can still honestly be asked.

arakhin/20.summary: Someone who pledges the valuation of his forearm has said nothing, since the Torah's fixed price, set by age and sex, applies only to a whole person. But one who pledges the valuation of his head or his liver owes the valuation of his entire self, since the soul depends on them. Rav Giddel says the forearm still owes an assessment, its market value, because Rabbi Meir holds that a person does not utter a statement for naught.
arakhin/20.question: If pledging half one's valuation merely sounds like pledging the valuation of half of oneself, why should the risk of that mix-up cost the speaker the other half?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches whether a rabbinic safeguard against verbal confusion may impose real financial loss on a speaker who committed himself to less.

answer.quote: A rabbinic decree was issued that one who says: It is incumbent upon me to donate half of my valuation, must give the value of his entire self, due to a concern
answer.explanation: The page states that the full payment is a rabbinic decree issued out of concern for confusion with the vow of "the valuation of half of me," but it does not explain why a preventive decree may impose the extra monetary loss, which is what the question presses on.

arakhin/21.summary: A mishna rules that burnt offerings and peace offerings must be brought willingly, and yet the court repossesses a man's property and pressures him until he says: I want to do so. The same formula is applied to a husband whom the Sages have obligated to divorce his wife. Rav Sheshet then presses the wording: if the man announced in advance that he acts under duress, the bill of divorce is void even after he hands it over.
arakhin/21.question: If beating a man until he says "I want to" counts as willingness, why does his earlier announcement that he was forced still cancel the divorce?
gate: gloss "burnt offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "peace offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of what makes coerced speech count as real consent, and where compelled willingness must be voiced to be effective.

answer.quote: This indicates that the court coerces him until he explicitly cancels his original declaration.
answer.explanation: The Gemara explains that the mishna's phrase "until he says: I want to do so" means the coerced husband must explicitly retract his earlier declaration of duress, which is exactly why an unretracted declaration still voids the bill of divorce.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 21b: "This indicates that the court coerces him until he explicitly cancels his original declaration.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already resolves this: the Gemara reads "until he says: I want to do so" as requiring the husband to explicitly cancel his earlier declaration of duress, which is why an unretracted declaration voids the get. Ask something the page leaves open instead — for instance why consent at the moment of separating the animal, rather than at atonement, is where Shmuel and Ulla locate the real act of will, or why a coerced "I want" suffices for an offering but a prior protest survives in divorce. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

arakhin/22.summary: A court that sells a dead man's land to pay his debts must first announce the sale, thirty days for orphans' property and sixty for consecrated property, and Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis disagree over the counts. The longer argument asks whether a court should touch minor orphans' inheritance at all, with Rav Asi allowing it only when interest is devouring the estate. Rav Naḥman says he refused such collections until he heard one line from Rav.
arakhin/22.question: Rav Naḥman changed his practice on the strength of a single sentence about orphans eating what is not theirs, so what in that sentence answered the reasons he had held for refusing?

judge.reachNote: Under the case lies whether a court acts on the formal obligation of the minors or on the moral fact that they are holding money that belongs to someone else.

answer.quote: Rav Pappa says: The repayment of a creditor is a mitzva, and minor orphans are not obligated in performing that mitzva.
answer.explanation: The page states the reasons Rav Naḥman had held for refusing (Rav Pappa's mitzva reason and Rav Huna's bundles-of-coins concern), but it never says what in Rav's line about orphans consuming what is not theirs overcame those reasons.

arakhin/23.summary: A man consecrates all his property to the Temple, but his wife's marriage contract debt is still secured against it. Rabbi Eliezer makes him vow that benefit from her is forbidden, so he cannot divorce her, let her collect from the Temple treasury, and quietly remarry her; Rabbi Yehoshua sees no such risk. Then Abaye suggests exactly that trick for Rav Huna, a broke Torah scholar whose father guaranteed the marriage contract, until Rav Huna turns out to be a priest.
arakhin/23.question: Abaye calls a man who advises selling property against a benefactor's wishes wicked, so what makes his own advice to Rav Huna different beyond the fact that Rav Huna studies Torah?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of when exploiting a legal loophole against a benefactor counts as wickedness rather than permissible advice.

answer.quote: When one is a guarantor for his son it is different, as he would forgive his son for acting in this manner, as the son will in any case inherit his property.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection from Abaye's 'wily, wicked person' and answers it with two distinctions, the first being that a father-guarantor forgives his son, quite apart from the Torah-scholar consideration the question sets aside.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 23a: "When one is a guarantor for his son it is different, as he would forgive his son for acting in this manner, as the son will in any case inherit his property.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later: the Gemara asks the same objection from Abaye's 'wily, wicked person' and answers that a father forgives his son, and additionally that helping a Torah scholar is different. Since the note only rules out the Torah-scholar answer, it must engage the father-son answer too. Rewrite so the question starts from both distinctions and probes something the page leaves unsettled, for instance why a father's presumed forgiveness of his son is enough to license collusion that the mishna's vow exists to prevent.

arakhin/24.summary: A man who dedicates all his property to the Temple keeps food and clothes for himself, and his tools, but the treasurer takes the phylacteries off his head. Rav Yeimar applied the same to a sale, telling the court to remove a man's phylacteries, small leather boxes of scripture worn on head and arm, and give them to the buyer. The mishna also bars waiting for market day or hauling a pearl to the city; value is fixed where the thing is, now.
arakhin/24.question: If a person would never knowingly sell the phylacteries he is wearing, what makes them part of the sale anyway?

judge.reachNote: Whether a transfer of 'all property' is measured by what the owner would have intended or by what objectively belongs to him, even items on his body used for a mitzva.

answer.quote: Remove his phylacteries from his head and his arm and give them to the buyer, as they are included in his property.
answer.explanation: Rav Yeimar's ruling gives the page's reason — the phylacteries simply count as part of the man's property — but the Gemara only asserts this against the intuition that a mitzva item worn on the body would not be sold unstated, so the question can still honestly be pressed.

arakhin/25.summary: A man consecrates his ancestral field to the Temple, and if nobody redeems it, the priests take it at the Jubilee. The mishna rules that a son who redeems it preserves it for his father, while a brother or a stranger does not, and the Gemara defends this by weighing an inherited Hebrew slave and a designated maidservant against levirate marriage. A daughter, when there is a son, is counted as another person entirely.
arakhin/25.question: If a daughter cancels levirate marriage exactly as a son does, what makes her a stranger to her father's field the moment a son exists?
gate: gloss "levirate marriage" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "the Jubilee" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Which relationship test governs standing in a father's place — exemption from levirate marriage or the right of inheritance.

answer.quote: since with regard to inheritance, when there is a son, a daughter is considered like another person, as she does not inherit a share of her father’s estate
answer.explanation: The Gemara poses exactly this dilemma and resolves it with Rabbi Yishmael's baraita that anyone counted as another person when there is a son does not preserve the field, because a daughter does not inherit alongside a son.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 25b: "since with regard to inheritance, when there is a son, a daughter is considered like another person, as she does not inherit a share of her father’s estate". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the very dilemma of Rabba bar Avuh, and the page settles it: inheritance, not levirate exemption, is the test, so a daughter is 'like another person' when a son exists. Ask something the page leaves standing instead — for example, why the son-versus-brother comparison rests on the Hebrew slave and designation cases rather than simply counting justifications, or why Rabbi Zeira's case of a woman's own field stays unresolved. Keep the summary's thread but let the question push past the line that already answers it.

arakhin/26.summary: A man consecrates his ancestral field, the inherited family land, to the Temple and never pays to buy it back, and the question is whether the priests receive it at the Jubilee, the fiftieth year when land returns to its original families. Rabbi Eliezer says they do not, unless some other person redeemed it first. Rabba explains this by reading the verse's clauses out of order, and Abaye asks whether a knife may cut the words apart like that.
arakhin/26.question: When a son has bought a field from his father who is still alive, is the land judged by what it is at the moment he consecrates it, or by what it is due to become when his father dies?

judge.reachNote: Whether a thing's legal status is fixed by what it is now or by what it is already destined to become — but the page states both answers outright.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say: Even in a case where the son consecrated the field before his father died, its halakhic status is like that of an ancestral field
answer.explanation: The page poses exactly this alternative and answers it, with Rabbi Meir judging by present status and Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon judging by what the field is due to become, a reading the Gemara then grounds in the verse "which is not of his ancestral field."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 26b (Mishna): "Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say: Even in a case where the son consecrated the field before his father died, its halakhic status is like that of an ancestral field". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates the mishna's dispute, which the page answers explicitly for each tanna, so it is already resolved for the reader. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — for instance why Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak insists Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon also hold that acquiring produce is like acquiring the item, which dissolves the neat explanation the Gemara had just offered. Alternatively, press on the two conflicting versions of Rabbi Eliezer's baraita about the owner who redeems in the second Jubilee cycle, where the page ends without deciding.

arakhin/27.summary: A man consecrated a field he did not want because its soil was poor, and the treasurer forced him to open the bidding on its redemption. He bid an issar, a small copper coin; Rabbi Yosei says it was an egg, and the treasurer told him the field was his again. Then a ladder of bidders from ten to fifty sela, a silver coin, where each one who reneges covers the ten-sela gap, unless all back out at once, in which case Rav Ḥisda splits the loss.
arakhin/27.question: If making the owner bid first exists to protect the Temple treasury, why does the mishna keep the story of the man who walked off with his field for the price of an issar?
gate: the question uses "the Temple treasury", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a procedure built to enrich the treasury is recorded together with the case in which it failed, so the law preserves its own loopholes.

answer.quote: The tanna states one reason and there are another two reasons: One reason is that since it is dear to him he would increase his bid
answer.explanation: The Gemara shows that making the owner bid first rests on three reasons, not only the treasury's one-fifth gain, which bears on the question's premise, but it never explains why the mishna preserves the issar story.

arakhin/28.summary: A person may dedicate to sacred or priestly use some of his flock, some of his slaves, some of his ancestral field, but never all of any one kind. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya reads that limit outward: if not even the Most High takes everything, a person should hold something back from other recipients too. The Gemara ties this to the ruling from Usha capping charity at a fifth, then reports a man stopped from giving more by a friend who simply would not let him.
arakhin/28.question: If a man wants to hand over more than a fifth of everything he owns, what makes it his friend's business to stop him?

judge.reachNote: Whether a limit on impoverishing oneself through generosity is a private virtue or something the community may enforce on a person against his will.

answer.quote: If for the Most High a person may not dedicate all his property, it is all the more so the case that a person should spare his property
answer.explanation: The page supplies the rationale for restraining excessive giving (and the Usha fifth-cap), but it never explains why a friend has standing to prevent another man from giving, so the question survives.

arakhin/29.summary: A man in Pumbedita dedicated all his property, a vow called herem that puts it beyond ordinary use, then came to Rav Yehuda asking how to get it back. Rav Yehuda told him to transfer the sanctity onto four dinars, silver coins worth far less than the property, and throw them in the river. One peruta, a tiny copper coin, would have sufficed; the four were for publicity, so people would know the property was permitted only because it was redeemed.
arakhin/29.question: If the coins end up in the river where nobody can use them, what separates redeeming a dedication from simply cancelling it?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that sanctity is a thing that must be relocated rather than erased, so redemption differs from nullification even when nothing of value survives.

answer.quote: Take four dinars and desacralize the dedicated property by transferring its sanctity onto them. And then throw the dinars into the river, because one may not derive benefit from them
answer.explanation: The page describes the mechanism — sanctity is moved onto the coins, which then themselves become forbidden — which bears on the difference from cancellation, but it never addresses the conceptual question of why a transfer to something immediately destroyed counts as redemption rather than annulment.

arakhin/30.summary: When a man buys back the ancestral field he sold, the page prices it at whichever figure is lower, the original sale or the current value, and derives that leniency from the Hebrew slave, who is redeemed the same way. A Sage pushes back: a man sinks to selling his movable goods, then his fields, his house, his daughter, and finally himself, all through his own transgressions, so why be generous? Abaye answers that the verse restores him anyway.
arakhin/30.question: If a man reaches slavery step by step through sins the page lists in order, why should the price of his freedom always be the cheaper one?

judge.reachNote: Whether a person whose ruin is self-inflicted still deserves the cheapest path out — a real idea, but the page states the debate and its resolution.

answer.quote: Abaye said to that Sage: But the verse subsequently restores him, i.e., it requires that one strive to redeem him from slavery.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this objection in the Sage's name — impose stringency since the slave's descent came from his own sins — and Abaye answers it, with Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak then deriving the leniency from the two verses.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 30b: "Abaye said to that Sage: But the verse subsequently restores him, i.e., it requires that one strive to redeem him from slavery.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates the Sage's objection that the page itself raises and answers, first by Abaye ("the verse subsequently restores him") and then by Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's reading of the two verses; as written a reader finds the answer a few lines below. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than reaching it — for example, press on the Gemara's own lingering objection that redemption might exist only so he not be assimilated among the gentiles while the price stays stringent, or ask why the field's leniency needs to be borrowed from the slave at all. Keep the summary, which tracks the page.

arakhin/31.summary: A house sold inside a walled city can be bought back for twelve months, after which it belongs to the buyer permanently. Buyers took to hiding on the final day so the redemption money could not reach them, and Hillel ruled that the seller may deposit the coins in the court's chamber, break the door, and walk in. Rava then reads that ordinance backward, to decide when money handed over against the recipient's will counts at all.
arakhin/31.question: If a buyer who hides can be paid against his will and lose the house anyway, why does Rava say a husband handed his two hundred dinars unwillingly has not divorced his wife?
gate: the question uses "dinar", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Whether a payment can take effect when the recipient refuses it, or whether consent is part of what makes money 'given'.

answer.quote: Rava says: It may be inferred from the ordinance of Hillel in the mishna that if one says to his wife: This is your bill of divorce
answer.explanation: The page states only that Rava derives the divorce ruling from Hillel's ordinance, without spelling out why an ordinance-based forced payment works for the house while unwilling giving fails for the get, so the tension the question raises remains standing.

arakhin/32.summary: A house sold inside a city walled since Joshua's time stays with the buyer forever if it is not redeemed within a year. So the page argues over what counts: olive presses and dovecotes are in, fields are out, a quarry is disputed, and Rabbi Shimon reads Rahab's house on the wall as inside the city. Then the stakes widen to whether Joshua's consecration of the land lapsed at exile, and Nehemiah's sukkot turn into Ezra's prayer sheltering the returnees.
arakhin/32.question: Why is Joshua faulted for not praying away the urge to idolatry when Moses is excused on the grounds that he lacked the merit of the land?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that the merit of the land makes a leader's prayer effective, but the page states that idea outright.

answer.quote: Granted, Moses, the first leader of the Jewish people, did not pray for mercy that this inclination should be removed, as at the time there was no merit of Eretz Yisrael
answer.explanation: The page itself poses and resolves the Moses/Joshua contrast, stating that Joshua is singled out precisely because he, unlike Moses, had the merit of Eretz Yisrael.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Arakhin 32b: "Granted, Moses, the first leader of the Jewish people, did not pray for mercy that this inclination should be removed, as at the time there was no merit of Eretz Yisrael". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates the Gemara's own explanation, which appears verbatim a line later ('Joshua, who had the merit of Eretz Yisrael, why didn't he pray'). Build the question on something the page leaves unresolved instead, for example the two readings of the Nehemiah verse and what is at stake in making the returnees' sanctification new or continuous, or why counting Jubilee Years to fix the Sabbatical cycle counts as counting at all. Keep the summary; it is faithful to the page.

arakhin/33.summary: A house in a village with no wall around it takes the better half of two deals. It can be redeemed the moment after it is sold, like a house in a walled city, and it still goes back to the seller in the Jubilee, the fiftieth year, when sold land returns to its first owner. Then the mishna shrinks the walled city almost to nothing: two courtyards holding two houses each count as unwalled, wall or no wall.
arakhin/33.question: If a wall only makes a city walled when gentiles built it before the conquest and the houses came after, what is the wall itself deciding?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea behind the walled-city rule: whether a wall marks a real urban reality (so houses are property, not ancestral land) or is merely a formal scriptural token.

answer.quote: It means that there are certain places that even though they have a wall, they are considered like places that do not have a wall.
answer.explanation: The page shows that a physical wall is not by itself decisive — small settlements with walls count as unwalled, and the wall must have been built by gentiles before the conquest — but it never states what the wall is actually meant to mark or measure.

arakhin/34.summary: The last daf of Arakhin closes with a priest making an argument from his own advantage: if he collects other people's consecrated fields when the Jubilee arrives, surely a field already in his hands stays his. The verse blocks it, and the Gemara then hunts for why the block was needed at all. Rami bar Hama and Rav Nahman each supply a reason the greedy inference almost worked, ending with the field split among the serving watch.
arakhin/34.question: Why should a priest hold his inherited field forever but lose the dedicated field that was handed to him, when both sit in the same hands at the same Jubilee?
gate: gloss "the Jubilee" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: What makes holding permanent — ancestral inheritance itself, or merely having the land in hand when the Jubilee comes?

answer.quote: with regard to the ancestral field of a priest that he inherited from his father, yes, it remains in the possession of that priest in perpetuity
answer.explanation: Rav Naḥman's resolution states the distinction and grounds it in the verse's juxtaposition, but it supplies the scriptural source rather than a reason why inherited land differs in kind from a dedicated field, so the question can still be pressed.

temurah/2.summary: Temurah opens with a mishna that sounds like permission and is not: swapping a non-sacred animal for a consecrated one is forbidden, yet if done, both animals are holy and the substituter takes forty lashes. The Gemara then asks whom the word "everyone" drags in. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda split over an heir, verses are counted to admit women, and Rami bar Hama pushes further, to a discriminating minor and to a gentile whose offering a Jew uses.
temurah/2.question: Rami bar Hama makes substitution hinge on whether the person can ever be flogged, so why should an animal's sanctity depend on someone else's liability to punishment?

judge.reachNote: Whether the power to create sanctity by speech depends on the speaker's accountability under the law, or only on his capacity to consecrate.

answer.quote: since no minor is subject to punishments, he cannot apply sanctity to an animal by an act of substitution, which would incur a punishment
answer.explanation: The page states the rationale linking punishability to substitution — the act is one that inherently carries a penalty — but it presents this only as one horn of Rami bar Ḥama's unresolved dilemma and never justifies why sanctity should track liability, so the question can still be pressed.

temurah/3.summary: A baraita strips gentile-consecrated animals of most consequences: no liability for misusing them, no penalty for eating them as piggul or notar, no valid substitution, each exemption read out of a verse that names the children of Israel. Then the page turns to lashes. The rule is that speech alone earns none, yet the mishna flogs a man who merely says one animal should stand in for a consecrated one, and Rabbi Yoḥanan tells his reciter to drop substitution from the exceptions entirely.
temurah/3.question: If saying the words of substitution counts as an action because the words themselves consecrate an animal, why does swearing falsely that you ate when you did not count as no action at all?

judge.reachNote: When does speech itself become a deed — only when it changes an object's status, or whenever it binds the speaker?

answer.quote: Do not teach: And one who effects substitution, in this regard, because one who effects substitution performs an action of consecration by his speech.
answer.explanation: The page states why substitution's words count as an action, and Rava explains the false oath is flogged only because the Torah explicitly includes a past-tense oath, but it never explains why oath-speech itself is not an action, so the contrast the question draws remains live.

temurah/4.summary: Separating teruma, the priest's share of the crop, before setting aside first fruits puts the farmer's gifts in the wrong order, and the argument here is whether that earns forty lashes. Rabbi Avin says no, since the skipped gift can still be separated afterward, and a prohibition that comes with its own repair carries no flogging. Abaye presses Rav Dimi with substitution, where swapping a consecrated animal also ends with both animals holy, yet the man is flogged.
temurah/4.question: Rava holds that a forbidden act simply does not take effect, so what are the lashes answering for, the damage done or the defiance alone?
gate: gloss "first fruits" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Rava", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether punishment tracks the change a forbidden act produces in the world or the bare act of disobedience — a real idea, but the page names Rava's answer outright.

answer.quote: Rava said: If one performed it, it is not effective at all. And this is the reason that he is flogged: Because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One.
answer.explanation: The page's closing line states Rava's own reason — the lashes answer the defiance of God's word, not any effect achieved.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Temurah 4b: "Rava said: If one performed it, it is not effective at all. And this is the reason that he is flogged: Because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered verbatim in the last line of 4b, where Rava says one is flogged "because he transgressed the statement of the Merciful One." Build the new question on something the page leaves unsettled — for instance, why Abaye needs the act to be effective before lashes make sense, or how the priest's greater holiness can make an otherwise rectifiable transgression floggable. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

temurah/5.summary: A man who separates teruma, the portion of a harvest given to a priest, from poor-quality produce to cover good produce has broken a prohibition, yet the mishna rules his teruma counts anyway. Abaye holds that acts done in transgression take legal effect; Rava holds they do not, and case after case is thrown at both. Every objection gets answered the same way, with a verse that makes that particular case the exception rather than the rule.
temurah/5.question: If each side can neutralize every counterexample by finding a verse that makes it exceptional, what evidence could ever settle which of them is right?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the method itself: when every counterexample is defused by a dedicated verse, what could count as proof of the underlying rule?

answer.quote: And Rabbi Ile'a likewise says that the phrase in the verse "the first part of them" is the exception that proves the rule.
answer.explanation: This line gestures at the evidentiary logic the question asks about — an explicit verse in one case implies the opposite default elsewhere — but the page never uses it to decide between Abaye and Rava, so the question still stands.

temurah/6.summary: A man robs another of wool, weaves it into garments, and keeps the garments, paying only the value of the wool. Objections like this are thrown at Abaye and Rava, who disagree over whether a transgression is effective, whether breaking a rule still produces the result the breaker wanted; each time the answer is a verse marking that case an exception. Pressed for a case where the two actually differ, the Gemara ends up allowing there may be none.
temurah/6.question: If every apparent counterexample turns out to have its own verse making it exceptional, what is either rule still ruling over?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — what a legal principle governs when every concrete case is carved out by its own verse — but the page states that answer outright: the principle survives as a presumption in the absence of a verse.

answer.quote: According to the opinion of Abaye, if there is no verse teaching otherwise, a transgression is presumed to be effective. According to the opinion of Rava, it is presumed to be not effective.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself asks what is left of the dispute once every case is settled by a verse, and answers that the two positions function as default presumptions governing any case where no verse teaches otherwise, with the sages disagreeing over which halakhot are rule and which exception.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Temurah 6b: "According to the opinion of Abaye, if there is no verse teaching otherwise, a transgression is presumed to be effective. According to the opinion of Rava, it is presumed to be not effective.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this: it says the dispute is only theoretical and that each position is the presumption where no verse teaches otherwise, so they merely differ over which halakhot are rule and which are exception. Rewrite the question to start from that answer rather than to ask for it — for instance, press on why the presumption still matters if it never decides a case, or on the fixed-interest material where Abaye's own ruling that the court repossesses seems to cut against his own principle. Keep the summary as it is; it is accurate.

temurah/7.summary: Reish Lakish argues that a man who consecrates an animal born blemished has done nothing punishable, since the animal can only ever be sold for its value, like consecrating a date palm. Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that the two cases differ: wood can burn on the altar, but an animal has unblemished counterparts that could have been brought, so the choice is disgraceful. Rava pushes further, and the page also argues over whether one act of burning can draw two sets of lashes.
temurah/7.question: If both the date palm and the blemished animal end up as nothing but money, why does swapping in the flawed animal count as disgrace and the tree not?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that identical monetary outcomes may still differ in the honor or disgrace of the act, but the page supplies exactly this answer.

answer.quote: When one consecrates a date palm, the matter is not disgraceful, as it is a type of wood that one may burn on the altar.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yoḥanan states the distinction outright — wood is itself fit for the altar, while the blemished animal has fit counterparts of its own type that the owner forsook, which is disgraceful — and the alternative version repeats it.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Temurah 7a: "When one consecrates a date palm, the matter is not disgraceful, as it is a type of wood that one may burn on the altar.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks for the very distinction Rabbi Yoḥanan gives on the page (wood is itself altar-fit; the blemished animal has fit counterparts he forsook), and the summary even repeats that answer, so the question is already closed. Rewrite it to press on something the page leaves unresolved — for instance whether Rava's extension to consecrating for libations still leaves the earlier "akin to a date palm" reasoning any force, or why disgrace of intent yields lashes at all. Keep the question anchored to a line the page states but does not explain.

temurah/8.summary: Rava, Rav Mesharshiyya and others press a single question: while the Temple stands, does a priest really own an unblemished firstborn animal, or does it belong only to the altar? One proof comes from a priestess's baby mixed up with her maidservant's baby; grown, each can tell any priest claiming their firstborn that he himself is a priest, and keep the animal until it is blemished. The page closes with Mar Zutra questioning meat served to him at Rav Ashi's house.
temurah/8.question: When the hosts insist they paid full market price, is the worry the page is chasing what the priest actually hopes to get later, or only how the sale looks to anyone watching?

judge.reachNote: Whether the prohibition guards against a real exchange of benefit or only against how the transaction appears to onlookers.

answer.quote: Here, we purchased it for its fair market value, and there is no appearance of impropriety.
answer.explanation: The page frames the concern as appearance ("looks like a priest who assists at the threshing floor") and the hosts answer that full price removes that appearance, yet the final version reopens the priest's actual hope for future firstborns and breaks off mid-sentence, so the question can still be honestly asked.

temurah/9.summary: A consecrated sheep can be swapped for a goat, a male for a female, an unblemished animal for a blemished one, and in every case the swap fails and both animals end up sacred. Rabbi Shimon insists the phrase "an animal for an animal" means strictly one for one; the Sages answer with a line in Jonah where a whole crowd of beasts is called by the singular word behema. The rest asks whether one animal can be substituted twice.
temurah/9.question: When Rabbi Shimon drops his own proof text and tells the Sages their verse proves his point too, is he reading scripture or defending a position he already held?

judge.reachNote: Whether a sage's verse is the source of his ruling or a retroactive prop for a position already fixed.

answer.quote: But when he saw that the Rabbis taught their opinion drawing support from the phrase "an animal for an animal," he said to them: You can learn the reason for my opinion from there too.
answer.explanation: The Gemara states why Rabbi Shimon shifted proof texts — he adopted the Sages' own verse once they cited it — but it does not settle whether that shift is exegesis or advocacy, so the note's question can still be asked honestly.

temurah/10.summary: Someone points at a pregnant animal and says that whatever is in its womb is a burnt offering; bar Padda holds that nothing takes hold, while Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the unborn animal is consecrated. Rabbi Yirmeya presses Rabbi Zeira with one source after another, and each time Zeira narrows the case: the pledge was only of the animal's sale value, or the offspring was already holy through its mother. The last objection is left standing.
temurah/10.question: If those unborn animals are already holy because their mothers were consecrated, what is left for the word "consecrates" to do?
gate: gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the difference between an act of dedication and sanctity inherited automatically through the mother — whether derived holiness can be described by the verb 'consecrates'.

temurah/11.summary: A man says that the hind leg of his animal is a burnt offering, and the argument is how far that holiness travels. Rabbi Yosei says the whole animal is consecrated; Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir keep it in the leg, so the animal is sold to a buyer who vows an offering with all the limbs its life depends on. Rav Ḥisda, Rava and Rav Sheshet then argue over which limbs those are, measuring by how fast the animal would die without them.
temurah/11.question: If the buyer vows a burnt offering only of the limbs the animal's life depends on, is he bringing a whole animal or most of one?

judge.reachNote: What makes an offering count as complete — the physical animal, or the scope of what the owner vowed.

answer.quote: specifically to one who says: It is incumbent upon me to bring a burnt offering with all the limbs upon which its life depends. Since the consecrated limb is not one of these, it does not detract
answer.explanation: Rava's reply addresses the very worry that the purchaser brings a deficient animal, saying the pre-consecrated limb does not diminish his vow, though the page never says outright whether the offering counts as a whole animal.

temurah/12.summary: A mishna collects rules that all turn on calculation: teruma, the priest's portion of produce, mixed into ordinary food; dough raised by teruma leaven; drawn water spoiling a ritual bath; and ashes of the red heifer stirred into water. The Gemara hunts for the sage behind each ruling. On the heifer, Rabbi Shimon notices the verse says "dust" where it means ashes, links it to the dust poured into the bitter water a suspected wife drinks, and lets either order stand.
temurah/12.question: If one clause of the verse puts the ashes in first and the next puts the water in first, why should a general habit of placing the enabling ingredient on top decide which clause is meant literally?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: When two clauses of a verse conflict, may a general presumption about how things are normally done decide which clause is read literally?

answer.quote: just as we find in every instance that the facilitating item goes above, e.g., in the case of a sota the dust, which enables the water to be used, goes on top
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the very objection (why prefer the last clause?) and answers by invoking the general rule that the enabling item goes on top, but it only asserts that rule by analogy to the sota without defending why such a habit should override the verse's own order, so the note's question survives.

temurah/13.summary: A mishna rules that doves, meal offerings, animals owned by the community or by partners, and items donated for Temple upkeep are not subject to substitution, the rule that swapping a non-sacred animal for a consecrated one makes both holy. The Gemara then hits a snag: gold armlets and rings taken from Midian are called an offering in the Torah, so why is Temple-upkeep property not an offering here? The answer splits the phrase by word order.
temurah/13.question: If the same gold bracelet counts as an offering in one verse and not in another, is the distinction between "the Lord's offering" and "an offering to the Lord" something the words carry, or something the argument needs them to carry?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the question of whether a derivation discovers a distinction latent in the verse's wording or manufactures one to save a prior ruling.

answer.quote: These items are called: “The Lord’s offering,” but they are not called: “An offering to the Lord,” which is used only with regard to offerings sacrificed upon the altar.
answer.explanation: The page supplies the phrase-order distinction the question builds on, but says nothing about whether the words themselves carry that distinction or the argument imposes it, so the question survives the answer it cites.

temurah/14.summary: The mishna contrasts offerings brought by one person with those brought by the whole community, and the Gemara keeps finding exceptions to every rule it states. Midway, Rav Dimi hears a ruling in Eretz Yisrael and says he will send it to Rav Yosef in Babylonia if he can find someone to write the letter. The objection comes fast, since Rabbi Yoḥanan held that writing halakhot burns the Torah, and the reply is that a new matter may be different, lest everything be forgotten.
temurah/14.question: If writing down an oral ruling is like burning the Torah, who decides which rulings are new enough to be worth the fire?

judge.reachNote: Who holds the authority to suspend a law in order to save the whole body of law from being lost.

answer.quote: Perhaps with regard to a new matter it is different, i.e., it might be permitted to write down new material so that it
answer.explanation: The page supplies the criterion for when writing is allowed — a new matter, lest the Torah be forgotten — but never says who is authorized to make that call.

temurah/15.summary: Five sin offerings, animals brought to atone for an unwitting sin, are listed as unfit and left to die: among them one whose owner already gained atonement with a replacement, and one whose owner has died. Rabbi Yehuda extends the rule to offerings of the whole community, and the Gemara pushes back with the twelve goats the returning exiles brought in Ezra's day. Rav Pappa answers from the half-shekels collected each Adar: a community does not die.
temurah/15.question: If coins donated by people who have since died can still buy a communal offering, why can a son not bring the sin offering his dead father left behind?

judge.reachNote: Whether a collective is a continuing legal person whose members' deaths do not interrupt it, while an individual's obligation dies with him.

answer.quote: Rather, this is Rav Pappa's reasoning for his statement that a community does not die. It is derived from the halakha of the goats sacrificed on pilgrimage Festivals
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the note's objection ("this should apply even to an individual as well") and resolves it by rejecting the verse-based reason and grounding "a community does not die" in a source that concerns only communal offerings purchased from the chamber, though it never positively explains what makes an individual's death final.

temurah/16.summary: Three thousand halakhot, points of law, were forgotten during the days of mourning for Moses, and when the people asked Joshua to fetch them back from Heaven he refused. Joshua then loses three hundred more, the people rise to kill him, and God's advice is not to teach him but to send the nation into battle. The legal half makes forgetting operational: five kinds of sin offering are left to die because nobody recalled which single case the rule covered.
temurah/16.question: If no one could remember which of the five sin offerings was meant, why did the doubt end with all five animals left to die rather than all five left to graze?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: When a tradition is lost, uncertainty about consecrated animals defaults to the destructive, stringent outcome rather than the lenient one.

temurah/17.summary: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda, holds that swapping a non-sacred animal for a consecrated one takes effect even when the swap was a mistake, and the man is lashed anyway. The Gemara hunts for what unwitting means here: he meant to say black and said white; he meant burnt offering and said peace offering; he announced he would go into the house and act deliberately, then did it absentmindedly. In each case the wrong word sticks, while the same slip in consecration does nothing.
