Rabbi Akiva uses the pair to argue that sprinkling one animal's blood frees the other's meat from liability for misuse, deriving benefit from consecrated property, even meat carried out of the courtyard. Reish Lakish says Akiva gave his student a deceptive answer, hiding that the two were slaughtered at once; Rabbi Yohanan presses a case about guilt offerings until Reish Lakish falls silent.
meilah/7.question: If the distinction Akiva left unsaid turns out to be correct, does that make his answer to his student honest, or only lucky?
gate: gloss "guilt offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether an answer that is technically correct but withholds the qualification it depends on counts as teaching truthfully.

meilah/8.summary: A bird sin offering is killed by pinching the back of its neck, and the mishna tracks its changing status: liable for misuse from consecration, then vulnerable to disqualification, then, once its blood is sprinkled, food for the priests. Two students report Rav teaching that mishna with different words. Rav Huna has "Once its blood was sprinkled"; Rav Adda bar Ahava has "Once its blood was squeezed out." Whether draining the leftover blood at the altar's base is essential turns on that one verb.
meilah/8.question: If one teacher's version of the mishna reaches us as two different sentences, how would anyone decide which words he actually said?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: how a tradition attributed to one master is authenticated when it arrives in two conflicting forms — and whether Scripture, not memory, becomes the arbiter.

answer.quote: The Gemara raises a difficulty with regard to the statement of Rav Huna. Come and hear a verse in the Torah
answer.explanation: The page does not investigate which words Rav actually said, but it does show how the rival versions are adjudicated — each is tested against Leviticus 5:9, with Rav Huna defended by a baraita of Rabbi Yishmael — so the question remains honestly askable about the wording itself.

meilah/9.summary: Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan argue over the heap of ash left on top of the altar, and whether a person who takes benefit from it is liable for misuse of consecrated property. Rav says the ash is spent once the required daily removal has been carried out; Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that carrying ash outside the camp still demands priestly garments, so it stays holy. The test case is a glowing ember that rolls off the altar, because an ember has substance.
meilah/9.question: Does an object stop being holy the moment the task it was needed for is finished, or does the care demanded in disposing of it prove it never stopped?
gate: gloss "consecrated property" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether sanctity ends with the completion of the function that created it, or whether the rules for disposal show it persists.

answer.quote: Rav says that one who derives benefit from it is not liable for misuse of consecrated property, as its mitzva has been performed and completed.
answer.explanation: The page voices both horns of the question — Rav's "its mitzva has been performed" and Rabbi Yoḥanan's garments proof — but leaves the dispute unresolved, so the question can still be asked.

meilah/10.summary: Rava rules on two things nobody may eat: meat of the holiest offerings that became impure before the blood was sprinkled, and the fats of lesser offerings once they are already burning on the altar. Someone who derives benefit from either owes nothing, though the Gemara presses the point, since a priest is commanded to burn the impure meat and to turn the fats with a fork so they burn evenly. A commandment, Rava holds, is not the same as Temple service.
meilah/10.question: If a priest is commanded to turn the burning fats with a fork, what makes that act a mitzva and not part of the service the altar is still performing?
gate: the question uses "mitzva", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: Asks what separates a commanded act performed on an offering from the sacrificial service itself — the boundary that decides misuse liability.

answer.quote: once the portions of offerings of lesser sanctity have been placed on the altar no further service is performed with them
answer.explanation: The Gemara's opening challenge gives the ground for treating the fork-turning as non-service — nothing further is done with the portions once they are on the altar and no loss to Temple property results — but Rava's own reply only asserts that "the mitzva to burn them or turn them is not considered part of the sacrificial rite," so the question of what marks the line can still be pressed.

meilah/11.summary: Rabbi Shimon says sacrificial blood carries no liability for misuse, that is, taking personal benefit from Temple property, until it drains out to the Kidron Valley, while libation wine is off limits from consecration and free once it reaches the drainpipes under the altar. Still, young priests went down once in seventy years to bring up the congealed wine from below, and burned it in sanctity. Pressed on this, the Gemara calls the supporting verse a mere support.
meilah/11.question: If the congealed wine under the altar is not consecrated by Torah law, why can it not simply be thrown out rather than burned in sanctity?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: an item can lose Torah-level sanctity yet still be handled as holy, so sanctity may linger by rabbinic decree after its mitzva is done.

answer.quote: Rather, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok concedes that even libations that reached the bottom of the drainpipes are not subject to misuse, as by Torah law they are not consecrated. And his ruling that they must be burned applies by rabbinic law.
answer.explanation: The page says the burning requirement stands by rabbinic law even though Torah law does not consecrate the drained libations, which explains its authority but not why the Sages chose burning over disposal, so the question can still be honestly asked.

meilah/12.summary: Ulla says in Rabbi Yoḥanan's name that a consecrated animal that dies before being offered drops out of the laws of misuse, the rules against using Temple property, since it can neither be sacrificed nor redeemed to feed dogs. Rav Ḥisda's objection is simple: where did the sanctity go? The argument then turns to what counts as part of a consecrated animal, and settles on blood, because the animal cannot live without it, while milk and dung are separate.
meilah/12.question: If blood belongs to the animal because the animal cannot exist without it, why does dung, which the animal also cannot live without, count as something borrowed from its food?

judge.reachNote: The idea is what counts as constitutive of a body versus what merely passes through it and is replaced.

answer.quote: In the case of this dung that comes to the animal from an external source, i.e., the food that it ate, this food goes out of the body
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly distinguishes dung as material that enters from outside and is replaced, unlike blood, which is part of the animal's own body — exactly what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Meilah 12b: "In the case of this dung that comes to the animal from an external source, i.e., the food that it ate, this food goes out of the body". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks precisely what the Gemara answers a few lines later: dung comes from an external source and is replaced by new food, while blood is part of the body itself. Read to the end of the sugya and ask something that starts after that answer. For instance, press on why milk, which the animal produces from its own body and is not replaced from outside, still fails the test, or on why the whole discussion of 'where has the sanctity gone' is settled by rabbinic-law concessions rather than by an answer.

meilah/13.summary: The mishna sorts consecrated property by what the Temple can actually use: a cistern full of water, good for kneading clay to reinforce walls but not for the altar, and a dump of manure, fit for neither and simply sold for cash. The sharper move is timing: consecrate a full dovecote and the pigeons are included; consecrate an empty one and the pigeons that arrive later are not. Rabbi Yosei objects, at least for fruit and grass.
meilah/13.question: The mishna bars any benefit from the willow branches before they are set against the altar, so what were the elders doing when they snipped pieces off for their own lulav?
gate: gloss "consecrated property" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Whether using a Temple-designated item for a different mitzva counts as deriving benefit at all, or whether mitzva use is outside the category of misuse.

answer.quote: The elders were accustomed to derive benefit from the willow branches even before their placement on the sides of the altar, by cutting small branches for use in their lulav
answer.explanation: The page states exactly what the elders did and for what purpose — taking twigs for the lulav mitzva — but it never explains how that squares with the mishna's ban on benefit before placement.

meilah/14.summary: An idol that broke apart on its own divides Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish: Yoḥanan holds benefit from the pieces stays forbidden, since only a gentile owner can cancel an idol's status, while Reish Lakish assumes the owner would give up on a god that could not protect itself. The proof runs through a bird's nest in a worshipped tree, and whose twigs built it. Rav Pappa later explains Temple repairs with ordinary materials by a workman who might sit down to rest.
meilah/14.question: If the gentile owner never saw the wreckage and never said a word, is the renunciation Reish Lakish credits him with a real one?

judge.reachNote: Whether legal nullification requires a performed act of renunciation or can be supplied by an owner's assumed state of mind.

answer.quote: as it can be presumed that its gentile owner, upon seeing that it was broken, would have nullified it
answer.explanation: The page gives Reish Lakish's rationale — a presumed nullification grounded in what the owner would conclude on seeing the broken idol — but it never addresses whether that presumption holds when the owner neither saw nor spoke, so the question survives.

meilah/15.summary: A mishna rules that consecrated items add up: benefit worth one peruta, a small copper coin, taken from several of them together makes a person liable for misuse. Rabbi Yannai then claims that by Torah law only items consecrated for Temple upkeep and burnt offerings can be misused at all, and four objections are each turned aside with the answer that those cases are only rabbinic, one of them by demoting a quoted verse to mere support. Then the position collapses entirely.
meilah/15.question: If a verse cited by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi can be brushed off as decoration three times over, what objection could ever have defeated Rabbi Yannai's claim?
gate: gloss "burnt offerings" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Yehuda", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "HaNasi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches a real idea — what makes a position refutable once every counter-case can be relabeled 'rabbinic' — but the page supplies the answer.

answer.quote: But didn't Ulla say that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Sacrificial animals that died without being sacrificed are excluded from the potential of misuse by Torah law?
answer.explanation: The page names exactly the objection that could not be deflected — Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling about dead consecrated animals, which implies live altar-animals are subject to misuse by Torah law, and which forces the Gemara to reject Rabbi Yannai's stated position outright.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Meilah 15a: "But didn't Ulla say that Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Sacrificial animals that died without being sacrificed are excluded from the potential of misuse by Torah law?". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page answers this question in so many words: the objection from Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yoḥanan, that dead consecrated animals are excluded from misuse by Torah law, is precisely the one that cannot be dismissed as rabbinic and forces the retraction. Also, the verse is demoted to 'mere support' only once, not 'three times over,' so the question's premise misstates the page. Rewrite the question to start from the objection that did work and ask why that one bites while the earlier mishnayot did not — e.g., why an inference about what is excluded when dead is harder to reclassify as rabbinic than a mishna stating liability directly.

meilah/16.summary: A dead cow supplies half an olive-bulk of flesh and a live camel the other half, and the question is whether they combine into one forbidden mouthful. Rav Asi keeps kosher and non-kosher carcasses apart, holding that the carcass prohibition cannot settle on camel flesh that is already forbidden. Then the measure shrinks: one verse slides from eating creeping animals to their impurity, and a baraita concludes that a lentil-bulk, the size that defiles by touch, is also the size that brings lashes.
meilah/16.question: If the amount of a swarming creature that defiles by touch also fixes the amount that counts as eating it, why should the eight creatures the Torah names be measured by a lentil and all the others by an olive?

judge.reachNote: Whether the measure that defiles by touch should govern the measure that counts as eating, and whether scriptural singling-out can split a measure by species.

answer.quote: he was referring only to those eight creeping animals of which the verse speaks, which are separated from all other creeping animals
answer.explanation: Rava's resolution explicitly supplies the reason for the split measure: the lentil-bulk rule applies only to the eight creatures the verse singles out, all others requiring an olive-bulk.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Meilah 16b: "he was referring only to those eight creeping animals of which the verse speaks, which are separated from all other creeping animals". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the one Rava answers on the page: he says the lentil measure applies only to the eight creatures "of which the verse speaks, which are separated from all other creeping animals," so a reader who finishes the daf has already been told why. Rewrite the question to start after Rava's answer, for instance by pressing on Rav Adda bar Ahava's objection that the same logic of separation should then enlarge the impurity measure for non-kosher animal carcasses to an egg-bulk. Alternatively, ask about the earlier thread on whether a prohibition takes effect where a prohibition already exists.

meilah/17.summary: A mishna asks whether half a lentil's volume of blood and half of flesh from a creeping animal combine to reach the minimum that transmits ritual impurity. Chasing the verse behind impure creeping-animal blood, the Gemara slides into a story: Rome bans Shabbat and circumcision, and Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai travels there to overturn the decrees, helped by a demon rather than an angel. On the road he curses his companion Rabbi Elazar for answering that very question in his teacher's presence.
meilah/17.question: Why does the page record Rabbi Shimon's promise not to punish Elazar, then report that he punished him, and leave it at that?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the tension between a sage's given word and the honor due a teacher, but the page states the resolution outright.

meilah/18.summary: A woman wears a consecrated gold chain; a man chops wood with a consecrated ax. Rabbi Akiva counts benefit worth a peruta, a small copper coin, as misuse even without damage; the Rabbis want damage, and Rava narrows the fight to a middle garment and to sheer malmala cloth too costly for its wearer to let it fray. A baraita then builds limits from teruma, the priest's portion, and the word "anyone" knocks several of them down.
meilah/18.question: If the comparison to teruma establishes that the damage and the benefit must belong to one person at one moment, what is left of it once "anyone" lets your bite and a stranger's bite three years later add up to a single peruta?

judge.reachNote: When an inclusive verse dismantles the very conditions a verbal analogy imported, how much authority does the analogy retain?

answer.quote: and misuse applies only to an item detached from the ground; and misuse is committed by the one appointing the agent in the case of an agent
answer.explanation: The page lists which halakhot the teruma analogy still supplies (detachment from the ground, liability of the appointer, the basic damage-plus-benefit pairing) even as "anyone" overrides simultaneity and single-person requirements, but it never states what remains of the analogy as such, and the baraita breaks off mid-argument at the end of the daf.

meilah/19.summary: Misuse of Temple property requires benefit worth a peruta, a small copper coin, and damage worth a peruta to the same item, so the page asks which items can be damaged at all. A consecrated gold chain around a woman's neck counts as undamageable, until Rav Kahana points out that the gold jewelry of the rich man Nun's daughter-in-law wore away. Rav Zevid blames careless owners, then concedes gold does deteriorate, only not immediately.
meilah/19.question: If gold really does wear down over years, what makes the moment of damage rather than the fact of it the thing liability hangs on?

judge.reachNote: Whether liability tracks the act's own effect on the sacred item or the item's eventual wear — i.e. what 'damage' means when it is gradual.

answer.quote: granted that gold does not have the status of an item that is damaged immediately [le'altar] when someone derives benefit from it
answer.explanation: Rav Zevid names immediacy (le'altar) as the operative distinction and admits slow deterioration, but the page never explains why the moment rather than the fact of damage governs liability, so the question survives.

meilah/20.summary: A homeowner sends an agent to serve guests consecrated meat, and the agent hands out liver instead. When each party adds something, the mishna splits liability for misuse three ways: the homeowner for the first piece he ordered, the agent for the second he added, the guests for the third they took on their own. Abaye shifts the ground of the argument: what makes the agent liable is not that liver is a different food, but that he never went back to ask.
meilah/20.question: Is the agent liable because liver is not meat, or only because he did not ask first, and if he had asked, would liver have become meat?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.
legal verb left hanging, "liable: liable to or for what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: Does liability rest on the objective category of the item or on the agent's procedural break in not returning to ask?

answer.quote: the ruling of the mishna is not due to the fact that meat and liver are considered two different types of items
answer.explanation: Abaye (endorsed by Rava) settles the disjunction by grounding liability in the agent's failure to consult rather than in liver being a separate category, but the page never addresses the note's counterfactual of what would follow had the agent actually asked.

meilah/21.summary: A homeowner sends an agent to fetch consecrated Temple money from the window in the wall; the agent brings it from there, and the homeowner then says he privately meant the chest. His claim fails, since unspoken matters in the heart are not significant matters, so the misuse of sacred funds is his. Yet Rabbi Yehuda lets another homeowner dodge liability by saying he had wanted a large etrog, not the small one the agent bought.
meilah/21.question: Why does the homeowner's private intention count for nothing when he says he meant the chest, but count for everything when Rabbi Yehuda has him say he wanted a bigger etrog?

judge.reachNote: When does a principal's unstated desire shape liability, and when is he bound only by the words he actually spoke?

answer.quote: if you had given the entire dinar as I requested, you could have brought me a much finer robe, worth at least two dinars
answer.explanation: The Gemara recasts Rabbi Yehuda's claim as an objective complaint about the value the homeowner could have received rather than a mere unspoken wish, which bears on the contrast but does not squarely resolve why one homeowner's stated desire counts and the other's does not.

meilah/22.summary: Rav Pappa sets a mishna about consecrated coins in a purse against one about wine bought from Samaritans. Rabbi Meir lets a buyer say that two log he will separate later are teruma, then drink the barrel at once; Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon forbid it, refusing retroactive designation. The sting is the purse: every peruta in it might be the sacred one, so Rabbi Yoḥanan reads the wording as pointing at the last coin left.
meilah/22.question: If wine can be drunk now on the strength of a portion its owner has not yet picked out, why can't a purse be spent the same way?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of retroactive designation — whether a later act of separation can reach back and fix which part was sacred all along.

answer.quote: Even according to Rabbi Meir, one can rely on retroactive designation only in a case where he says: That I will separate in the future
answer.explanation: The page itself draws the distinction the question asks for: the wine case works only because the owner explicitly says "that I will separate in the future," whereas with the purse each peruta might already be the consecrated one, so Rabbi Yoḥanan must reread the wording as pointing to the last coin.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Meilah 22a: "Even according to Rabbi Meir, one can rely on retroactive designation only in a case where he says: That I will separate in the future". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved three lines later on the same page, which states that Rabbi Meir's leniency depends on the words "that I will separate in the future" and that each peruta in the purse might be the consecrated one. Rewrite the question to start from that distinction rather than asking for it: for instance, why a declaration about the future should be able to fix identity in wine but not in coins, or why Rabbi Yoḥanan needs to relocate the sanctity to the last peruta instead of simply invoking retroactive designation. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

kinnim/23.summary: A woman after childbirth brings two birds, one a hatat (sin offering, slaughtered below the altar's red line) and one an olah (burnt offering, above it); an unassigned pair can go either way. Here one bird keeps escaping into a neighbor's cage, disqualifying a bird each time it leaves and each time it flies back, until the cascade through seven women wipes out whole sets. Yet a bird leaving an unassigned middle pair toward the sin offerings costs nothing: the priest simply calls it a hatat.
kinnim/23.question: If a priest can settle a stray bird's status by declaring which way it flew, why does that same power fail the women whose cages keep trading pigeons?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: a priest's word can fix what is still undesignated, but it cannot recover an identity or ownership that has been lost in a mixture.

answer.quote: An unassigned pair and an assigned pair: if one bird from the unassigned [pair] flew to the assigned [pair], then a pair must be taken for the second [bird].
answer.explanation: The page marks the line between designable (unassigned) birds and already-fixed ones, which bears on why declaration saves the middle pair but not mixed sets, yet it never states that reason outright, so the question remains askable.

kinnim/24.summary: Two women bring pairs of birds, one bird a sin offering sprinkled below the altar's red line, the other a burnt offering above, and the pairs get mixed up. A priest who never asked advice offers them anyway, and the mishnah counts what can be salvaged: usually half, but when one woman's pair is split above and below, the larger group is valid. Oddly, the unassigned pair is the only thing that survives a split offering, and it is divided between the two women.
kinnim/24.question: Why does the pair that was never assigned to anything come through the mix-up intact, while every bird already given a job is lost?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
gloss "burnt offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: Designation is what creates the possibility of error: a bird with no assigned purpose cannot be offered in the wrong place.

answer.quote: If he offered half of them above and half below, then all of them are disqualified, because I can argue that the hatats were offered above and the olot below.
answer.explanation: The page gives a reason why assigned birds are lost in a split offering — the doubt can be resolved against them — but never states why the unassigned pair alone survives, so the question still stands.

kinnim/25.summary: The final page of Kinnim keeps counting: hataot mixed with unassigned obligatory birds, and only the matching number comes out valid. Then a woman vows a pair of birds for a male child, the priest sprinkles two above and two below instead of three and one, and the replacement birds multiply from one to six depending on how precisely she spoke. Rabbi Joshua answers all this arithmetic with a dead ram whose horns, bones, hide and entrails make seven instruments.
kinnim/25.question: Why does a tractate of pure counting end by insisting that a scholar's mind grows composed with age while an ignorant elder's gets befuddled?
gate: "Rabbi Joshua" is not named on this page; name a sage only for a view the text attributes to them, in the page's own spelling.
no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: that a tractate of bare enumeration ends by claiming the counting is worth something only in a mind that ripens rather than decays.

answer.quote: Rabbi Joshua said: This is what it meant when they said: "When [the beast] is alive it possesses one sound, but when it is dead its sound is sevenfold."
answer.explanation: The page does gesture at why the counting ends in aggadah — Rabbi Joshua's parable of multiplying sound, followed by the claim that a scholar's mind grows composed — but it never states why the tractate closes on aging and intellect, so the question can still be honestly asked.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Joshua's parable is about a dead ram.
summaryProblems.pageSays: When [the beast] is alive it possesses one sound, but when it is dead its sound is sevenfold.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rabbi Joshua's parable is about a dead ram.", but the page says "When [the beast] is alive it possesses one sound, but when it is dead its sound is sevenfold.". Say what the page says.

tamid/26.summary: A priest who immersed at night walked back through a lamp-lit passage beneath the Temple, where a fire waited to warm him and an open bathroom door signaled that nobody was inside. The Gemara later asks why the elders of the priestly family slept on stone ledges jutting from the walls of the Chamber of the Hearth. Abaye answers that beds would be improper in the Temple, though the chiseled ledges raise their own trouble, since no iron tool was heard at the building.
tamid/26.question: If a warming fire, a towel and a bathroom designed for privacy all belong inside the Temple, what makes a bed the thing that crosses the line?

judge.reachNote: Where the line falls between provisions that serve the priests' service and furnishings that domesticate a sacred space.

answer.quote: Abaye said: It is not proper conduct to bring beds into the Temple.
answer.explanation: The page gives Abaye's reason for excluding beds, but never explains why a bed is improper while the warming fire, towel and bathroom of honor are not, so the comparison the question draws remains unanswered.

tamid/27.summary: The mishna had said that priests sleeping in the Chamber of the Hearth folded their sacred vestments and placed them beneath their heads. The Gemara balks, since the belt mixes wool and linen, a combination forbidden elsewhere, and even ten mattresses stacked over such a mixture would not make lying on it permitted. So it rereads "beneath" as "next to," while Rav Ashi answers instead that the belt is too stiff to count as a garment anyone enjoys.
tamid/27.question: If "beneath their heads" can be turned into "next to their heads," what keeps any inconvenient word in a mishna from sliding a few inches?

judge.reachNote: How much interpretive pressure a halakhic difficulty licenses against the plain words of a mishna.

answer.quote: So too, it is reasonable to say that the mishna permits the vestments to be placed only next to their heads. As, if you say that the mishna permits
answer.explanation: The page shows the reread is forced by an independent halakhic difficulty (diverse kinds) rather than by convenience, and it later offers rival answers that keep "beneath" literal, which bears on the question without settling how far such rereading may go.

tamid/28.summary: A Levite caught asleep on his watch was struck with a staff, and his clothing could be burned; Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov says it happened to his mother's brother. Rabbi Yoḥanan calls the early generations praiseworthy for punishing even sleep a person could not resist. Later the page explains how clearing the altar's ashes became a lottery: priests used to race up the ramp, until one shoved another and broke his leg.
tamid/28.question: If sleep no one could help still cost a watchman his burned garment, why did a priest who shoved a rival off the ramp get an ordinance instead of a punishment?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: when does the law discipline the offender and when does it instead redesign the procedure that tempted him.

answer.quote: And when the court saw that people were coming to potential danger, they instituted that the priests would remove the ashes from the altar only by means of a lottery.
answer.explanation: The page gives the court's motive for the ordinance — averting danger — but says nothing about whether the priest who shoved was punished, so the note's contrast can still be asked.

tamid/29.summary: The ash heap in the middle of the altar is said to hold three hundred kor, a dry measure of hundreds of liters, and Rava says plainly that this is an exaggeration, like the golden cup the lamb drinks from before slaughter. Shmuel counts only three such exaggerations and keeps the cup literal, since the Temple is a place of wealth. Then the priests argue over firewood: olive and vine are barred for their knots, or to spare the trees.
tamid/29.question: If three hundred priests lifting the golden vine is only a way of saying it was heavy, what makes the golden cup for the lamb the one detail to read literally?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the real idea — what separates rhetorical hyperbole from literal report in Temple descriptions — but the page states the criterion outright.

answer.quote: there, in the case of the golden cup, it is not an exaggeration, as even the cup from which the lamb was given to drink was actually made of gold
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly explains that Shmuel's list of three exaggerations excludes the golden cup, which was literally gold because "there is no poverty in a place of wealth."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Tamid 29a: "there, in the case of the golden cup, it is not an exaggeration, as even the cup from which the lamb was given to drink was actually made of gold". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the page answers, and the note's own summary already supplies the answer ("since the Temple is a place of wealth"). Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for instance, pressing on why lavishness makes the cup literal while the vine's three hundred priests and the Curtain's three hundred immersers, both also in a place of wealth, stay hyperbole. Keep the summary, which is faithful.

tamid/30.summary: The second of the day's four lotteries hands out thirteen jobs at once: the priest who wins slaughters the daily lamb, and the twelve standing to his right take the rest, down to the man carrying the wine for the libation. The mishna then lists what could be heard from Jericho, miles away: the great gate opening, ben Arza's cymbals, Gevini the crier. Rabbi Elazar ben Diglai adds his father's goats, grazing far off, sneezing at the incense.
tamid/30.question: What makes a goat's sneeze in a distant town worth recording as evidence about the incense?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the Temple's greatness is measured by how far its sights, sounds, and smells carried — with an animal's involuntary reaction serving as impartial witness.

tamid/31.summary: A priest punctures the hind legs of the slaughtered lamb behind the knees, hangs it on two hooks, and flays downward, handing off head, legs, flanks, cud and haunch until nine priests stand in line holding the pieces. A baraita says the foreleg and hind leg are bound together as Isaac was bound. Rav Huna and Rav Hisda then split over why all four legs are never tied: degradation of a sacred animal, or pagan practice.
tamid/31.question: If tying all four legs is barred because it degrades a sacred offering, why would binding the lamb with silk or a thread of gold still be a problem?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches for what rides on the two reasons for the ban — is the fault in the indignity to the offering or in the resemblance to gentile rites — but the page already sorts silk and gold onto the pagan-practice side.

answer.quote: one ties the animal with silk [beshira’ei], which would be considered to be treating the offering in the manner of the nations, but it is not degrading
answer.explanation: The Gemara states outright that silk and gold bindings are objectionable only on the pagan-practice view and are expressly not degrading, which is precisely what the question asks.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Tamid 31b: "one ties the animal with silk [beshira’ei], which would be considered to be treating the offering in the manner of the nations, but it is not degrading". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved in the next line of the page: silk and gold are a problem only for the sage who bans four-legged tying as pagan practice, and the Gemara says they are "not a degradation." Rewrite the question so it starts from that distinction rather than asking for it — for instance, why an act that harms nothing and shames nothing should still be barred merely for resembling gentile rites, or what makes the manner of tying, rather than the tying itself, the locus of the prohibition. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

tamid/32.summary: Alexander of Macedon puts riddles to the Elders of the Negev: is the sky further from earth than east is from west, who is wise, who is mighty, who is rich. When he asks what makes a person liked, they say hate the king and keep clear of those in power; Alexander says his own answer is better, then announces he will execute them. They invoke his pledge, and he drapes them in purple and gold chains.
tamid/32.question: The Elders advise staying far from kings, and moments later a king spares them and hangs gold on their necks; whose answer did that scene prove right?

judge.reachNote: Whether safety and standing come from distance from power or from proximity used well — the page stages both claims without ruling.

answer.quote: One who wants to be accepted must love the king and the authorities, but he must use his connections to perform beneficial acts for people.
answer.explanation: The page records Alexander's counter-answer to the Elders' advice, which bears on the question, but it never adjudicates which view the ensuing scene of threat, pledge, and honoring vindicated.

tamid/33.summary: The last page of Tamid runs the morning service to its end: coals shoveled from the outer altar into a gold pan, roughly a kav spilling onto the floor, incense scattered on the far side of the altar first so the priest is not burned. Sound organizes the whole operation. A thrown shovel drowns out speech across Jerusalem and summons priests to prostrate, bells announce the High Priest's exit, and trumpets and cymbals cue the Levites' daily psalm.
tamid/33.question: Why is the spot between the Entrance Hall and the altar, where the shovel is thrown to gather everyone, the one place that must be emptied of people while the incense burns?
gate: gloss "kav" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
the question brings in "Entrance", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Hall", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The same courtyard space that the shovel's noise fills with assembled worshippers must be emptied of them at the moment of atonement — nearness and exclusion in one spot.

answer.quote: “And there shall be no man in the Tent of Meeting when he goes in to make atonement in the Sanctuary, until he comes out” (Leviticus 16:17)
answer.explanation: The page supplies a scriptural derivation for clearing that area, but does not explain why this particular gathering-place is the one emptied, so the question still stands honestly.

middot/34.summary: Priests keep watch in three places and Levites in twenty-one, and an officer makes the rounds with torches; a guard who fails to rise and greet him is beaten and has his clothes burned. Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob says that happened to his mother's brother. After mapping gates and the chamber where the courtyard keys hang on a chain under a marble slab, the page ends with the one man who walks the Temple Mount leftward and is asked why.
middot/34.question: If the man circling against the crowd answers that he is excommunicated, does Rabbi Yose's added clause, that he should listen to his colleagues, comfort him or scold him one more time on his way around?
gate: the question brings in "Yose's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether a blessing that also assigns fault to the sufferer can still function as comfort, or whether consolation requires withholding the rebuke.

answer.quote: Rabbi Yose to him: you make it seem as if they treated him unjustly.
answer.explanation: The page gives Rabbi Yose's stated motive—avoiding the implication that the community wronged the excommunicated man—which bears on the note's question but does not settle whether the reworded blessing consoles or reproves the man himself.

middot/35.summary: A lattice fence, the Soreg, ten handbreadths high, ringed the Temple courts, and Greek kings had broken thirteen gaps in it; the repairs were marked by thirteen prostrations. The eastern wall was kept low so the priest burning the red heifer on the Mount of Olives could see the Sanctuary doorway as he sprinkled blood. In a text that is measurement rather than argument, Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob says of one corner chamber that he forgets its use.
middot/35.question: In a description that fixes every step at half a cubit, why preserve a chamber whose purpose nobody could any longer recall?
gate: gloss "the red heifer" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a text built entirely of exact measurements also records the gap where memory failed.

answer.quote: Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob said: I forget what it was used for. Abba Shaul says: they used to store there wine and oil
answer.where: Middot 35 (courtyard of the women, four corner chambers)
answer.explanation: The page does not explain why the forgetting is preserved, but it does immediately set Abba Shaul's surviving tradition beside Rabbi Eliezer ben Jacob's admission, which bears on the question without settling it.

middot/36.summary: The stones of the altar and its ramp were quarried from virgin soil in the valley of Bet Kerem, whole, with no iron ever lifted against them. Any flaw disqualifies a stone, but iron disqualifies by mere touch, because iron shortens a man's days and the altar lengthens them; even the whitewash goes on without an iron trowel. This is Mishnah without Gemara, so the reason stands unargued, a few cubits from the iron hooks where carcasses were hung and skinned.
middot/36.question: If iron may not so much as touch the altar because it shortens life, what makes the iron hooks in the slaughterhouse just north of it fine?

judge.reachNote: Asks how far the symbolic logic of iron-as-shortener extends: is it a property of the metal or only of what touches the altar?

answer.quote: Since iron was created to shorten man's days and the altar was created to prolong man's days
answer.where: Middot 36 (stones of the ascent and altar)
answer.explanation: The page grounds the ban in the altar's own character, which implies the restriction is altar-specific rather than a general ban on iron in the Temple, but it never addresses the slaughterhouse hooks.

middot/37.summary: Middot closes in numbers: thirty-eight cells stacked around the Hekhal, a winding ramp called the mesibbah climbing from corner to corner, a sanctuary a hundred cubits each way, narrow behind and broad in front like a lion. Workmen repairing the Holy of Holies were lowered through trapdoors in baskets so they would not look around. The last scene is people, not cubits: the Sanhedrin in the Chamber of Hewn Stone vetting priests, black garments for the rejected, a feast for the rest.
middot/37.question: Who is the feast for, if the priest dismissed in black is still walking away within earshot of the blessing?
gate: no teaser-and-colon opener ('X opens with donkeys:'); make the first sentence stand on its own.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached: a communal celebration of the purity of Aaron's seed is built on the public exclusion of the individual it just disqualified.

answer.quote: They used to make a feast because no blemish had been found in the seed of Aaron the priest
answer.explanation: The page states the stated occasion of the feast — that the priestly line was found unblemished — but says nothing about the rejected priest walking away in black while that blessing is recited, so the note's tension survives.

niddah/2.summary: Tractate Niddah opens with a dispute about how far back impurity reaches. Shammai says a woman who finds menstrual blood is impure only from that moment; Hillel says from her last self-examination, however many days earlier, so everything she handled since is impure. The Gemara presses both views against a ritual bath later measured and found short of forty se'a, and a barrel of wine later found turned to vinegar, where the change is assumed to have crept in unnoticed.
niddah/2.question: If water can trickle away and wine can sour unnoticed, why does the Gemara raise the possibility that she saw the blood depart bit by bit and then drop it for a tally of weakening factors?

judge.reachNote: Whether retroactive impurity rests on the change being gradual and unnoticeable, or merely on counting how many considerations weaken the presumption of purity.

answer.quote: The Gemara states a different answer: There, in the case of the ritual bath, there are two factors that weaken the suggestion that the items are ritually pure
answer.explanation: The page shows the gradual-change distinction collapsing under the 'bit by bit' rejoinder and a new two-factors-versus-one distinction taking its place, but it never states why the first line of reasoning is abandoned rather than defended.

niddah/3.summary: Shammai holds that a woman who finds menstrual blood is impure only from that moment; Hillel pushes the impurity back to her last examination. Hillel's proof is a basket of pure produce where the carcass of a creeping animal, which conveys impurity, later turns up in another corner; Shammai concedes the basket, but says it has a base where the carcass could hide, and a woman has none. Rava then reports a different reason: fear that couples would stop having children.
niddah/3.question: If Hillel's retroactive impurity touches only pots and produce and never bars a woman from her husband, is Shammai right that a scrupulous husband will pull away from her anyway?

judge.reachNote: Whether a purity stringency that formally leaves intimacy permitted can nonetheless chill it in practice — law's effect on conscience versus its letter.

answer.quote: the heart of a scrupulous husband might strike him with pangs of conscience over sins that he could transgress and he would separate
answer.explanation: The page states Shammai's rejoinder to Hillel's 'only pure items' answer in exactly these terms, though it never adjudicates whether Shammai's psychological claim is correct.

niddah/4.summary: A basket that held ritually pure produce is carried across the house, and the carcass of a creeping animal turns up inside it. Ḥizkiyya says the impurity stayed put, so the produce is clean; Rabbi Yoḥanan presumes impurity moved from place to place. Against him comes a loaf found on the floor beneath a shelf, ruled pure because maybe an unseen pure person set it down, while an unseen raven dropping the carcass will not do, since a raven acts without intent.
niddah/4.question: Why is an imagined pure man good enough to keep the loaf clean, while an imagined raven is not good enough to keep the produce clean?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is which imagined explanations may be posited to preserve purity — only acts of a being capable of purposeful action.

answer.quote: In the case of a person, who acts with intent, we can say that perhaps a person moved the loaf from the shelf onto the ground. By contrast, with regard to a raven
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises the raven suggestion itself and rejects it precisely because a raven lacks intent, which is the distinction the question asks about.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 4b: "In the case of a person, who acts with intent, we can say that perhaps a person moved the loaf from the shelf onto the ground. By contrast, with regard to a raven". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks exactly what the Gemara asks and answers on 4b, and the summary even supplies the answer ('since a raven acts without intent'), so it cannot stand as a question. Rewrite it to press on what remains hard after that answer — for instance why intent should matter at all when the only issue is whether the carcass could have arrived later, or why the pure-man explanation is allowed without any evidence anyone entered. Alternatively build a question from another thread on the page, such as the Rabbis' twenty-four-hour period and the two rationales for fixing it.

niddah/5.summary: A woman with a fixed cycle sits on a bed handling ritually pure items, stands up, and finds menstrual blood; she is impure, the items stay pure. The Gemara asks why the bed is mentioned at all, and Ze'eiri reads it to mean that in cases of retroactive impurity the bed itself is defiled. But doubtful impurity only sticks to something that can be questioned, so the bed qualifies only while friends are carrying it, borrowing their awareness.
niddah/5.question: If a bed standing on the ground cannot be asked anything and so stays pure in doubt, why should the same bed turn impure the moment friends lift it?
gate: no idioms in the question; say it plainly (rely on, prove, permit).

judge.reachNote: The idea underneath is whether an object borrows legal personhood from the humans involved with it — but the page states this answer outright, and then supersedes it with Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule about impurity caused by human hands.

answer.quote: the bed is considered as the extended hand of her friends. In other words, it is part of an entity that has consciousness
answer.explanation: The page explicitly explains that the carried bed counts as an extension of the friends, who do have consciousness to be asked, which is precisely what the question asks.

summaryProblems.claim: The bed qualifies as an item that can be asked only while friends are carrying it.
summaryProblems.pageSays: according to Ze’eiri a menstruating woman transmits impurity to a bed even though her friends are not carrying her in the bed

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 5b: "the bed is considered as the extended hand of her friends. In other words, it is part of an entity that has consciousness". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The bed qualifies as an item that can be asked only while friends are carrying it.", but the page says "according to Ze’eiri a menstruating woman transmits impurity to a bed even though her friends are not carrying her in the bed". Say what the page says. The question is answered verbatim on the page — the carried bed is the "extended hand of her friends," an entity with consciousness to be asked — so ask something the page leaves standing. The summary also stops one step too early: the Gemara goes on to say, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, that impurity brought about by human hands makes even a bed on the ground askable, so the "only while carried" restriction is dropped. A better question could probe why human involvement should convert an inanimate vessel into something the law treats as capable of being questioned.

niddah/6.summary: A woman who sees menstrual blood is treated as impure for the previous twenty-four hours, and Rav Huna limits that backward reach to sacrificial food, sparing teruma, the priests' portion of produce. Objections pile up, the sharpest being the maidservant of Rabban Gamliel, who baked loaves of bread and examined herself between each one. He first declares every loaf impure; when she says she checked all along, he shortens the reach to the last loaf alone.
niddah/6.question: Rabban Gamliel condemned all the loaves before learning she had examined herself between each one, so why was it left to her to say so?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that the default presumption is the worst case and the burden falls on the woman to report her own examinations, which alone shorten retroactive impurity.

niddah/7.summary: A mishna lists four women whose menstrual blood renders things impure only from the moment they see it, rather than retroactively for the previous day: a virgin, a pregnant woman, a nursing woman, and an elderly woman. Rabbi Yehoshua says he heard this tradition only about the virgin, and Rabbi Eliezer answers that he heard more. While Eliezer lived the Sages followed Yehoshua, because Eliezer leaned toward Beit Shammai; after Eliezer died, Yehoshua restored Eliezer's ruling.
niddah/7.question: If Rabbi Eliezer's tradition was the right one, what does it mean that it could only be put into practice once he was no longer alive to be followed?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between a ruling's correctness and the social authority of the sage who holds it.

answer.quote: if we act in accordance with his opinion in one matter, people will act in accordance with his opinion in other matters
answer.explanation: The Gemara asks exactly why Eliezer's ruling was not followed in his lifetime and answers that because he was a Shammuti, following him here would lead people to follow him elsewhere, and his honor made protest impossible while he lived.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 7b: "if we act in accordance with his opinion in one matter, people will act in accordance with his opinion in other matters". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks the very thing the Gemara asks and answers on 7b: they avoided ruling like Rabbi Eliezer because he was a Shammuti and people would then follow him in other matters, and his honor barred protest during his lifetime. Rewrite so the question starts from that answer rather than requesting it. For instance, press on what it means that the Sages preserved a ruling they believed correct by not practicing it, or on why protest against followers becomes possible only after a master's death.

niddah/8.summary: Rav Kahana cites a teaching that there are three kinds of virgin: a person who has not had intercourse, ground never worked, and a sycamore never cut back to spur growth. The mishna also calls a woman a virgin if she has never menstruated, so why is she absent from the list? Four sages give four different reasons, and Ravina's answer, that no buyer is particular about it, is knocked down by a baraita saying plentiful blood means plentiful children.
niddah/8.question: When the answer shifts from what a buyer is particular about to what buyers are eager to purchase, has the omission been explained, or has the subject quietly changed to what sells?

judge.reachNote: Whether a taxonomy of 'virginity' is being defined by conceptual untouchedness or by what matters to a purchaser — and whether retreating to marketability preserves the original principle.

answer.quote: when the Sage teaches the list of virgins, he includes only an item that buyers are eager to purchase. But he does not teach an item that buyers are not eager
answer.explanation: The page supplies the revised criterion that accounts for the omission, but it never addresses the note's worry that the criterion itself has quietly shifted from particularity to marketability.

niddah/9.summary: Ordinarily a woman who finds menstrual blood is treated as impure for the previous twenty-four hours, but a nursing woman is not. Rabbi Meir explains this by saying her blood spoils and becomes milk, so the exemption holds as long as she nurses, four or five years if it comes to that. Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon say instead that birth dislocates her limbs and her strength returns at twenty-four months, nursing or not.
niddah/9.question: Is the nursing exemption a claim about what her body is doing right now, or only about how long ago she gave birth?

judge.reachNote: Whether a leniency rests on a present physiological state or on a fixed period counted from an event.

answer.quote: according to the statement of Rabbi Meir the case is that menstrual blood spoils and becomes milk. Therefore, it follows that this status continues for as long as she is nursing
answer.explanation: The page lays out exactly the two options the question names — an ongoing bodily process (Rabbi Meir) versus a fixed post-partum term of twenty-four months (Rabbi Yosei and colleagues) — but leaves the dispute unresolved, so the question can still honestly be asked.

niddah/10.summary: The Gemara counts sightings of blood to fix the moment a girl who has just started menstruating loses the leniency that her impurity begins only when she sees blood, rather than reaching back a full day. Seven straight days of bleeding count as one sighting, while bleeding that stops and starts again counts as two. Cycles missed during pregnancy and during nursing are then allowed to combine, which raises the problem of the blood at the birth itself.
niddah/10.question: If a week of unbroken bleeding counts as a single sighting, why should a short pause turn the same blood into two?

judge.reachNote: What makes bleeding one 'sighting' rather than two — continuity of flow or the interruption that marks off discrete events.

answer.quote: On the contrary, if she stops and restarts it is as though she has had two sightings of menstrual blood.
answer.explanation: The page asserts that an interruption yields two sightings (and later that constant dripping is really continuous, hence one), but it never states why a pause should individuate the blood, so the question can still be asked.

niddah/11.summary: Rav Huna takes up a woman who jumps and then bleeds, three times over, and asks whether that makes a fixed menstrual cycle, a predictable onset that changes her status. Rav Ashi sharpens it: she jumps on Sunday twice and bleeds, then jumps on Shabbat and sees nothing, then bleeds on Sunday without jumping. One reading says the Shabbat jump worked late; a second version of Rav Huna reads the same facts as proof the day, not the jumping, is the cause.
niddah/11.question: If a jump that produced no blood can be credited with blood that appears the next day, what evidence could ever show the jumping was not the cause?

judge.reachNote: When a cause can be credited with a delayed effect, the causal claim becomes untestable — what would count as disproof?

answer.quote: In that case there, the matter is revealed retroactively that it is the day that causes her to menstruate, not the jumping.
answer.explanation: The second version of Rav Huna reads the very same facts as evidence that the day, not the jumping, is the cause, which bears on the question but leaves the first reading's device unfalsified and the dispute unresolved.

niddah/12.summary: Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Yehuda whether a woman should check herself with a cloth before intercourse, and the answer is no: a scrupulous husband would be tormented by what she might find and would separate from her. Rabbi Ami calls the pre-intercourse check the cloth of virtuous women; Rava rejects that reading and says virtuous women are simply the ones who do not reuse a cloth. Rav Kahana, wanting to know what sages actually did at home, asked their wives.
niddah/12.question: If one man's pangs of conscience are reason enough to skip the examination, why does Rabbi Meir's woman with no fixed cycle lose her marriage, her marriage contract, and even her worn clothes?
gate: the question brings in "Meir's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Both rulings claim to shield the husband, yet one spares him worry at the cost of certainty and the other strips the wife of every material right — whose interest is the law actually protecting?

answer.quote: She is forbidden to engage in intercourse, as perhaps she will ruin her husband if she emits blood during intercourse
answer.explanation: The Gemara does give Rabbi Meir's reasoning — the risk of causing the husband to sin, plus "since she is not fit for intercourse, she is not entitled to payment of her marriage contract" — but it never reconciles that severity with Rav Yehuda's protective leniency about the scrupulous husband's conscience.

niddah/13.summary: The mishna praises a woman who examines herself often for discharge and says a man who does the same should have his hand severed, for fear of arousal. Rav Yehuda, standing at night on a synagogue roof and needing to urinate, is told by Shmuel to hold himself and aim away, and the Gemara stacks six separate reasons why that was allowed. Later it asks whether "his hand should be severed" is a court penalty or only a curse, and reports that Rav Huna once actually severed one.
niddah/13.question: If fear of falling, awe of Shmuel, and awe of the Divine Presence each work on their own, why does the Gemara pile up six answers for one man on a roof?
gate: the question brings in "Divine", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Presence", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a permission granted against a stated prohibition may need several converging safeguards rather than one sufficient reason.

niddah/14.summary: A woman examines herself with a cloth she never checked first, puts it in a box, and finds blood on it the next morning. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi calls her a definite menstruant; Rabbi Ḥiyya calls the blood only a stain, an uncertain impurity. Ḥiyya's move is the sharp one: you agree a mark smaller than a split bean is blamed on a squashed louse, so you are already reasoning in doubt.
niddah/14.question: If a spot smaller than a split bean is written off as a crushed louse, why does a slightly larger one become a certainty rather than a bigger doubt?

judge.reachNote: Whether removing the one competing explanation for a doubt converts the case into a certainty, or only shifts the doubt.

answer.quote: this is necessary only to exclude the possibility that this is the blood of a louse; and since the possibility that it is the blood of a louse has been excluded
answer.explanation: The Gemara states Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's answer explicitly: the split-bean threshold exists solely to rule out louse blood, so once the stain exceeds it the only remaining source is her body, hence definite impurity.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 14b: "this is necessary only to exclude the possibility that this is the blood of a louse; and since the possibility that it is the blood of a louse has been excluded". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered a few lines later on 14b, where the Gemara says the split-bean size is required only to exclude louse blood, so once that is excluded the blood certainly came from her body. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what remains hard, for example why the unexamined cloth's own prior history is not itself a second competing explanation that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ignores. The summary is faithful and can stand, though it could note that the exchange is placed in Rabbi Ḥiyya's old age.

niddah/15.summary: A husband coming home after weeks away may assume his wife is ritually pure, and so permitted to him, without asking. The Gemara tests how far that assumption stretches: Rav Huna says the day her period is due breaks it, Rabba bar bar Ḥana says it does not. Then the rule that an uncertainty does not override a certainty meets a priest who looked into a pit at Rimon and was deemed pure, since scavengers had likely dragged the corpse away.
niddah/15.question: If a priest is cleared because martens and hyenas probably dragged the body off before he looked, why can a woman who certainly saw blood not be presumed to have immersed?

judge.reachNote: When may a presumption built on likelihood displace a known fact — the asymmetry between the priest cleared by probable scavengers and the wife known to have bled.

answer.quote: Do not say in the baraita that the woman certainly cast a non-viable newborn into a pit; rather, say
answer.explanation: The Gemara begins to resolve the very contrast the question draws by denying that the Rimon case involved a certainty at all, but the resolution is cut off mid-sentence at the end of the daf.

niddah/16.summary: A woman with a fixed cycle lets the expected day of her period pass without examining herself, and Rav and Shmuel split over whether a later clean examination clears her retroactively. The page then moves to the cloths used before and after intercourse, where Beit Shammai want a check each time and Beit Hillel one at each end of the night. It closes on a stranger case: a cloth examined at night and then lost.
niddah/16.question: If losing the cloth changes nothing about whether blood was there, why should that alone forbid what the same unexamined night would have permitted?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a law can turn on the survival of evidence rather than on the underlying facts — which is exactly the idea Rava states.

answer.quote: with regard to that woman who lost her cloth, her proof does not exist, and therefore they will never know if they require atonement
answer.explanation: Rabbi Ila raises precisely the note's objection, and Rava answers it: the intact cloth preserves evidence that would later obligate sin offerings, while the lost cloth leaves them permanently unable to know whether atonement is needed.

summaryProblems.claim: The page closes on a stranger case: a cloth examined at night and then lost.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Four matters the Holy One, Blessed be He, hates, and I do not love them, and they are: One who enters his house suddenly

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 16b: "with regard to that woman who lost her cloth, her proof does not exist, and therefore they will never know if they require atonement". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "The page closes on a stranger case: a cloth examined at night and then lost.", but the page says "Four matters the Holy One, Blessed be He, hates, and I do not love them, and they are: One who enters his house suddenly". Say what the page says. The question is answered outright a few lines later: Rabbi Ila asks it and Rava replies that with an intact cloth the proof exists and sin offerings can follow, while a lost cloth leaves them never knowing if atonement is required. Rewrite so the question starts from Rava's answer and probes what remains hard in it — for instance why the possibility of knowing one's liability should govern permission now. Also drop the claim that the page closes with the lost cloth, since it goes on to intercourse by day, the angel Night, and ben Sira's list.

niddah/17.summary: The mishna describes a woman's reproductive organs as a house with an inner room (the uterus), a corridor (the vaginal canal), and an upper story (the bladder). Blood found in the corridor is treated as impure, presumed to have come from the room rather than the bladder. Rav Huna splits the corridor, inward definitely impure and outward impure by doubt, since a woman who bent over might have carried blood there; Abaye answers that the same worry runs the other way.
niddah/17.question: If the worry that a woman bent forward is strong enough to make blood at the outer end impure, why does the matching worry that she staggered backward not turn the inner ruling into a doubt as well?

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a ruling must consistently follow either the presumption of origin or the concern that blood shifted — you cannot mix the two.

answer.quote: then in both this case and that, whether the blood is found in the inner or outer section of the canal
answer.explanation: Abaye himself raises the note's exact objection and resolves it: if you rule by the concern about leaning, both inner and outer blood are uncertain, while if you rule by presumption, inner is definitely impure and outer definitely pure.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 17b: "then in both this case and that, whether the blood is found in the inner or outer section of the canal". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is Abaye's own objection, which the page answers a few lines later by forcing a choice between ruling by presumption and ruling by the concern. Rewrite so the question starts from Abaye's resolution rather than reproducing his challenge — for instance, why Rav Huna would build a hybrid ruling that treats one end by presumption and the other by concern, or what is lost when Abaye's consistency makes outer blood entirely pure. Keep the summary, which tracks the page accurately.

niddah/18.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan counts three uncertainties that the Sages settled by majority and then treated as certain: blood found inside the corridor of a woman's body, an afterbirth left in a house, and a miscarried hand with discernible fingers. The Gemara keeps offering a fourth case, nine kosher butcher shops and one selling carcasses, nine dead frogs and one impure creeping animal, a woman who miscarried into a river. Each time the answer shrinks the category instead of lengthening the list.
niddah/18.question: Why is the number three defended by narrowing what counts, rather than simply admitting a fourth case?

judge.reachNote: A sage's enumeration functions as a claim about the boundary of a category, so counterexamples are answered by redrawing the boundary rather than by amending the count.

answer.quote: We say that this list of cases mentioned by Rabbi Yoḥanan is referring to matters of ritual impurity, whereas we do not say that the list includes cases that involve prohibitions
answer.explanation: The page supplies the successive narrowing criteria (impurity, impurity of a woman, only Mishna/baraita cases) but never explains why the count of three is preserved by restriction rather than revised upward.

niddah/19.summary: A mishna lists five colors of blood that render a woman ritually impure: red, black, the bright part of the crocus flower, water flooding red earth from the Beit Kerem Valley, and wine diluted two parts water to one. Before ranking colors, the Gemara has to prove that any blood is pure at all, and it does so by arguing that a rebellious elder needs something to dispute. Then the sages chase what "red" means: an ox's first cut, a squashed louse, a young man's finger.
niddah/19.question: If the only evidence that pure blood exists is that a defiant elder must have something to argue about, is that a fact about blood or a fact about disagreement?

judge.reachNote: Whether a derivation driven by the need for a disputable case establishes a substantive fact about the world or only a structural fact about halakhic controversy.

answer.quote: But here, concerning the phrase "between blood and blood," if there is no type of pure blood at all, with regard to what issue could the rebellious elder disagree
answer.explanation: The page states the rebellious-elder argument and its conclusion that the verse must allude to pure blood, but it never reflects on whether that reasoning is evidence about blood itself or only about the conditions of legal dispute, so the note's question can still be asked.

niddah/20.summary: Five shades of blood decide whether a woman is ritually impure, and the sages match them to real things: the darker ink at the bottom of an inkwell, mud from the Beit Kerem Valley, the middle leaf of a crocus. Then Rav Ashi, watching his own blood come out two different colors in two bloodletter's horns, concluded that a sage like him should not examine blood at all. Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Zeira also back away; Rabbi Elazar keeps looking.
niddah/20.question: If Rav Yitzḥak had already judged the blood pure on his own learning, why did he need Yalta's word about the other sage's sore eye before he would say so?
gate: the question brings in "Yitzḥak", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Yalta's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea under it — how much of a ruling is knowledge and how much is deference to a colleague — is real, but the page states the answer outright.

answer.quote: At first, he was reluctant to issue his ruling, in deference to Rabba bar bar Ḥana, who had said the blood was impure.
answer.explanation: The Gemara's final resolution states plainly that Rav Yitzḥak had already concluded the blood was pure from his learning but held back out of deference to Rabba bar bar Ḥana, and Yalta's report freed him to rule as he had originally thought.

summaryProblems.claim: Rav Ashi was watching his own blood come out in two different bloodletter's horns.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The bloodletter removed blood in a bloodletter’s horn from Ameimar for his first treatment.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 20b: "At first, he was reluctant to issue his ruling, in deference to Rabba bar bar Ḥana, who had said the blood was impure.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Rav Ashi was watching his own blood come out in two different bloodletter's horns.", but the page says "The bloodletter removed blood in a bloodletter’s horn from Ameimar for his first treatment.". Say what the page says. The question is answered in so many words on 20b — Rav Yitzḥak held back only in deference to Rabba bar bar Ḥana — so ask something the page leaves open, e.g. why the Gemara ultimately refuses to learn from this story that a woman's claim about a prior ruling is credible. Also fix the bloodletting detail: the blood drawn in the two horns was Ameimar's, and Rav Ashi was the onlooker who said a sage like himself should not examine blood.

niddah/21.summary: A woman discharges a shapeless piece of tissue with no blood alongside it, and the Rabbis call her pure while Rabbi Yehuda calls her impure. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak relocates the argument: the real question is whether the womb can open at all without bleeding, so that blood must have come even if nobody saw it. Later sages tear the tissue open to look inside, and Rabbi Zeira reads "in her flesh" to exempt blood found in an inserted tube.
niddah/21.question: If blood hidden inside a piece of discharged tissue still counts as blood "in her flesh," why does blood from the same body, caught in a tube, not count?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: What makes blood count as coming "in her flesh" — the path it travels, or the ordinary manner in which women bleed.

answer.quote: There, with regard to a piece of tissue, the woman is impure, as it is the manner of a woman to see blood inside such a piece of tissue.
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this comparison and answers that tissue-blood is the normal manner of a woman's bleeding whereas tube-blood is not, so only the former satisfies "in her flesh."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 21b: "There, with regard to a piece of tissue, the woman is impure, as it is the manner of a woman to see blood inside such a piece of tissue.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already asks and answers this question: the tissue case counts because "it is the manner of a woman to see blood inside such a piece of tissue," while a tube is not the normal manner. Build the new question on top of that answer — for instance, why the cracked-tissue dispute makes direct contact with the flesh decisive if ordinariness is what matters, or why Abaye insists everyone exempts the tube. Keep the summary as it is; it is faithful.

niddah/22.summary: A woman keeps discharging red items shaped like shells, and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Tzadok's father brings the case to the Sages at Yavne, who ask doctors; the doctors say she has a wound in her womb. The test set for her is soaking the items in water, since whatever dissolves was blood. Reish Lakish requires lukewarm water; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel has her mash the item with saliva against a fingernail, and the dispute turns on whether forced crumbling counts as dissolving.
niddah/22.question: If an item comes apart only when pressed between saliva and a fingernail, was it blood the whole time, or did the test make it into something it was not?

judge.reachNote: Whether a diagnostic test discloses what a thing already was or helps constitute its identity.

answer.quote: Ravina says: The difference between them is whether an item is considered blood if it can be mashed by pressing on it, or only if the item dissolves by itself.
answer.explanation: The page names exactly this disagreement — mashable versus self-dissolving — as the point between Reish Lakish and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, but leaves it unresolved, so the question can still be asked honestly.

niddah/23.summary: Rabbi Meir holds that a woman who miscarries something shaped like a cow, a wild animal, or a bird is impure as if she had given birth, and the Gemara hunts for his reason: the word "formation" used of both animals and man, or eyes set in the front of the head, as in owls. Rabbi Ami objects that Amos says God forms mountains too, so what about a discharged clod? The dispute ends up counting eyebrows and cheeks.
niddah/23.question: If Rabbi Yirmeya's question about betrothing an animal-shaped daughter was only an attempt to make Rabbi Zeira laugh, why does the page bother answering it before saying so?
gate: the question brings in "Yirmeya's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Zeira", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Why the Gemara tests a question's premise on its merits even when it judges the question unserious.

answer.quote: impure only since there are animals of its type that can live
answer.explanation: The page supplies the substantive ground that defeats Rabbi Yirmeya's premise — such a creature cannot itself live — but it never explains why it engages the question before Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov declares it a jest, so the note's question can still honestly be asked.
