niddah/24.summary: A woman miscarries a fetus whose face is flat, and the amora'im split over whether that counts as a birth at all. Rabbi Ḥiyya's sons ruled the mother impure, playing it safe; he sent them back to reverse it, since declaring her impure also hands her thirty-three days in which any blood she sees counts as pure. Rav and Shmuel then argue whether a creature with two backs and two spines can live.
niddah/24.question: When ruling someone impure also grants her a stretch of days when her blood is pure, how does anyone tell which ruling is the strict one?

judge.reachNote: Ruling 'stringently' is incoherent when a single ruling carries both impurity and licence, so decision must rest on something other than a default toward severity.

answer.quote: you should perform, i.e., issue your ruling, in accordance with the opinion of Rav, as we maintain that the halakha is in accordance with the opinion of Rav
answer.explanation: Rav Huna's reply bears on the question by abandoning the strict/lenient heuristic in favor of deciding by Rav's authority, but it does not explain how one identifies which ruling is actually the stringent one.

niddah/25.summary: Students ask Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi whether a woman who discharges a gestational sac full of flesh has the impurity of a woman after childbirth, and he says he never heard a ruling on it. Rabbi Yishmael reports his father's two-part answer, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi discards both halves because the first half happens to match a lone minority view. Rabbi Yehoshua argues from the skins God made for Adam that skin comes only after a person exists.
niddah/25.question: If the first half of Rabbi Yosei's tradition is suspect for matching a rejected minority, why does that contaminate the second half, heard from the same father?
gate: the question brings in "Yosei's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether the provenance of one clause of a transmitted tradition discredits the rest of it — guilt by association in the chain of transmission.

answer.quote: one can say that perhaps Rabbi Yosei said it in accordance with the opinion of another individual Sage, Rabbi Yehoshua.
answer.explanation: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi states the reasoning explicitly: since the first clause turned out to follow a lone Sage (Sumakhos in the name of Rabbi Meir), the second clause may likewise be a lone Sage's view (Rabbi Yehoshua), whose ruling is not halakha, so the whole tradition cannot be accepted.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 25a: "one can say that perhaps Rabbi Yosei said it in accordance with the opinion of another individual Sage, Rabbi Yehoshua.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already answers this question in so many words: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says that because the first clause turned out to follow a lone Sage, the second may likewise follow a lone Sage (Rabbi Yehoshua), whose view is rejected. Rewrite the question so it starts from that reasoning and asks what remains hard — for example, why a report that is verifiably accurate about one lone view becomes less trustworthy rather than more, or why Rabbi Yehoshua's own scriptural proof from Adam's skins does not rescue the second clause. Alternatively, build the question on a later part of the page, such as the move that makes Rabbi Yehoshua merely uncertain and his verse a mere support.

niddah/26.summary: A baraita says no afterbirth is shorter than a handbreadth, which sends the Gemara to Rabbi Oshaya's list of five things needing that measure: afterbirth, the horn blown on Rosh HaShana, the spine of a palm branch, the third wall of a sukka booth, and the hyssop used to sprinkle purifying water. Then the objections come: a toy oven, a stone oven handle, a beam over an alleyway. Each is deflected by a fresh rule about what the list never covered.
niddah/26.question: If every counterexample gets excluded by a qualification announced only after it is raised, what would a successful refutation of Rabbi Oshaya's five have looked like?

judge.reachNote: Whether a rule that acquires a new exclusion for every counterexample can still be refuted at all — the falsifiability of a closed list.

answer.quote: Rabbi Oshaya is not dealing with matters of rabbinic law. Rather, he is speaking only of matters that are written in the Torah but whose measure is not explicit in the Torah.
answer.explanation: The page eventually states the positive criterion behind the ad hoc deflections, which implies what a valid counterexample would need to be, though it never spells out what a successful refutation would look like.

niddah/27.summary: A house holding a discharged afterbirth is treated as impure, because, Rabbi Meir says, there is no afterbirth without an offspring, and the tiny offspring must have crumbled away inside the house. Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon answer that it already crumbled on the way out of the womb, so nothing impure remains. Rabbi Meir's reply is that disintegrating once is not the same as disintegrating twice.
niddah/27.question: If carrying the afterbirth into the next room is enough for Rabbi Meir to call that room pure, why isn't the trip from the womb into the first room enough?

judge.reachNote: When may we presume an unseen thing has crumbled away — how much handling does it take before we stop treating it as present?

answer.quote: disintegrated once, when the afterbirth was moved to its first location in the house, is not comparable to a case where the offspring disintegrated twice
answer.explanation: The page poses exactly the note's challenge in the Sages' words and Rabbi Meir answers it: one relocation is not enough to presume disintegration, two are.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 27a: "disintegrated once, when the afterbirth was moved to its first location in the house, is not comparable to a case where the offspring disintegrated twice". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Sages' objection, and Rabbi Meir's answer ('disintegrated once ... is not comparable to ... disintegrated twice') appears on the page — and the summary even repeats it, so the note answers itself. Write a question that starts after that reply: for instance, why a second move should make the presumption of disintegration credible when the first did not, or how Rabbi Meir can hold the house impure on the strength of an offspring nobody can find. Alternatively draw on the other thread of the page, such as Rabbi Shimon's principle that a mixed-in substance nullifies impurity.

niddah/28.summary: A fetus puts a hand out of the womb and draws it back, and Rav Huna calls that a birth, citing Tamar, whose baby put out a hand and pulled it back before his brother came out. A baraita says the mother need not be concerned about anything; Rav Naḥman reports Rav Huna's own gloss, that she keeps the strictures but gets no days in which her blood counts as pure. Abaye then demotes the verse from proof to support.
niddah/28.question: If the hand poking out only makes her a mother by rabbinic decree, why reach for Tamar's midwife at all?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of asmakhta — a verse quoted as ornament or support for a law that is really rabbinic — but the page states that resolution outright.

answer.quote: This halakha applies by rabbinic law, and the verse is cited as mere support for it, i.e., it is not an actual source.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection ("But doesn't Rav Huna cite a verse as proof...?") and answers that the Tamar verse functions only as supporting reference for a rabbinic ruling.

summaryProblems.claim: Abaye is the one who demotes the Tamar verse from proof to mere support.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara answers: This halakha applies by rabbinic law, and the verse is cited as mere support for it

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 28a: "This halakha applies by rabbinic law, and the verse is cited as mere support for it, i.e., it is not an actual source.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The summary says "Abaye is the one who demotes the Tamar verse from proof to mere support.", but the page says "The Gemara answers: This halakha applies by rabbinic law, and the verse is cited as mere support for it". Say what the page says. The page already asks and answers this question in the same paragraph, so the note cannot pose it as open; ask instead about something the answer leaves unresolved, e.g. why Rav Naḥman's gloss splits strictures from days of purity, or what work a mere support does if the halakha stands without it. Also fix the attribution: Abaye explains that the baraita speaks of Torah law, while the demotion of the verse to support is an unattributed Gemara answer.

niddah/29.summary: A fetus that emerges feetfirst or in pieces counts as born only when most of its limbs are out, which sets the mother's days of impurity; Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the head alone settles it, Rabbi Elazar does not. A baraita then fixes the exact moment as most of the head: the temples, the forehead, or the corners above the neck. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi extends majority reasoning to a woman who miscarried into a river and cannot say what she lost.
niddah/29.question: If most pregnant women deliver a fully formed offspring, why is that majority strong enough to let a pinched bird offering be eaten, but not strong enough to spare the next calf of an animal that went out to pasture pregnant and came back empty?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — when reliance on rov (majority) governs and when a counter-indication cancels it — but the page itself states both the challenge and Ravina's resolution.

answer.quote: since this animal did not discharge turbid liquids, the effect of the majority is undermined
answer.explanation: The Gemara raises exactly this contrast and answers through Ravina that the animal's failure to discharge turbid liquids (a sign accompanying most real births) weakens the majority, leaving the offspring a firstborn of uncertain status.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 29a: "since this animal did not discharge turbid liquids, the effect of the majority is undermined". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is the Gemara's own objection to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and Ravina answers it on the same daf: the missing turbid liquids undermine the majority. Rewrite the question so it starts after that answer — for example, why the Gemara had to retreat from "all animals" to "most animals" that discharge turbid liquids, or why a presumption of pregnancy is needed for the woman but a mere sign suffices to defeat the majority for the animal. Keep the summary as is; it is faithful.

niddah/30.summary: A mishna asks what happens when a woman miscarries on the fortieth day after she immersed and had relations, when nothing is yet formed, versus the forty-first, when something might be. Rabbi Yishmael reads the doubled mention of childbirth in Leviticus to mean a female embryo takes eighty-one days to form; the Rabbis answer that a period of impurity cannot measure gestation. Both sides then cite Cleopatra's dissection of condemned maidservants, and each calls the other's version proof from fools.
niddah/30.question: When the very same experiment is quoted by Rabbi Yishmael in one baraita and by the Rabbis in the other, with each side calling it the work of fools, what is actually being rejected here, the evidence or the person holding it?

judge.reachNote: Whether an empirical experiment can be rejected on its controls rather than its conclusion, and how that weighs against a scriptural derivation.

answer.quote: What is the reason the Rabbis consider this a proof from the fools? They claim that it is possible that this woman who was pregnant with a female embryo did not conceive
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly asks why each side dismisses the Cleopatra experiment as "proof from the fools" and answers in both directions that what is rejected is the experiment's reliability (possible earlier or later conception, no steward to restrain intercourse), not the disputant.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 30b: "What is the reason the Rabbis consider this a proof from the fools? They claim that it is possible that this woman who was pregnant with a female embryo did not conceive". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page itself asks and answers exactly this: it spells out why each side calls the Cleopatra experiment "proof from the fools" (an earlier pregnancy, a later conception, the unreliable steward), so the rejection is plainly of the experiment's controls, not the person. Ask instead about something the page leaves standing, such as Abaye's appeal to matching hair and fingernails as a way of certifying the eighty-day claim, or why Rabbi Yishmael treats a doubled word in the verse as outweighing dissection.

niddah/31.summary: The students of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai ask why the Torah requires a woman to bring an offering after giving birth. He answers that in the pain of labor she swears never to have intercourse again, and the offering atones for breaking that oath. Rav Yosef objects twice: she breaks the oath knowingly, not accidentally, and a broken oath calls for a lamb or goat, not the pair of birds a new mother brings.
niddah/31.question: If Rav Yosef's two objections go unanswered on the page, what is left standing of the explanation that the offering pays for an oath sworn in labor?

judge.reachNote: Asks whether a homiletic reason for a mitzva survives unanswered halakhic objections, or operates on a different plane from them.

answer.quote: she regrets her oath, that she will never again engage in intercourse with her husband, already seven days after giving birth
answer.explanation: The page never rebuts Rav Yosef, but it continues to build on the oath explanation in the very next answers about seven versus fourteen days and circumcision, which bears on what is left standing without resolving the objections.

niddah/32.summary: Rabbi Yosei, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rav Yosef each report a town where a newborn girl bled so soon after birth that she was immersed in a ritual bath before her mother. Such cases explain why the laws of menstruation reach a one-day-old girl, derived from one extra word: the "and" of "And if a woman." Elsewhere that same "and" stretches only to a girl of three years and one day, so Rava says both rules came from Sinai and the verses merely prop them up.
niddah/32.question: If both rules came down from Sinai anyway, why does the argument keep hunting for a verse and then hand it some other job, like excluding a man from impurity due to red semen?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the relation between halakha transmitted from Sinai and scriptural derivation, and the assumption that a verse may never be left with nothing to teach.

answer.quote: The verse serves to exclude a man from contracting ritual impurity due to red semen.
answer.explanation: The page does state what job the leftover verse is given once the rule itself is assigned to Sinai, though it never explains the underlying assumption that no verse may be redundant.

summaryProblems.claim: Rava says both rules came from Sinai and the verses merely prop them up.
summaryProblems.pageSays: the halakha with regard to the intercourse of a girl aged three years and one day is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai, whereas the halakha with regard to the menstruation of a one-day-old girl is derived from a verse

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rava says both rules came from Sinai and the verses merely prop them up.", but the page says "the halakha with regard to the intercourse of a girl aged three years and one day is a halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai, whereas the halakha with regard to the menstruation of a one-day-old girl is derived from a verse". Say what the page says. The summary stops at Rava's opening line and misses the Gemara's resolution: only the three-years-and-one-day intercourse rule is assigned to Sinai, while the one-day-old menstruation rule stays verse-derived. Fix that, since the question's premise ("if both rules came down from Sinai anyway") rests on the error. A reworked question can still press on why the now-spare verse must be given a fresh job, such as excluding red semen.

niddah/33.summary: A Sadducee chatting with the High Priest in the marketplace sprays saliva onto his garments, and the face of the High Priest turns green. The worry runs through the man's wife: if she miscounts her menstrual days, her husband carries her impurity onto the clothes, so the High Priest hurries to her to ask. She says Sadducee wives fear the perushim, the scrupulous ones, and show their blood to the Sages; an objection about saliva from an unreliable man is left unfinished as the page ends.
niddah/33.question: If the High Priest's garments depend on whether a stranger's wife counted her days correctly, why is her own word about it enough?

judge.reachNote: Whether a suspect person's own report about her observance can settle another's purity, and what makes such self-testimony credible.

answer.quote: they are scared of the perushim and they show their blood to the Sages when an uncertainty arises
answer.explanation: The page gives a ground for crediting her report — Sadducee wives fear the perushim and bring their blood to the Sages, and Rabbi Yosei then testifies from personal acquaintance that they all do so — but it never states why her unverified word about her own counting is legally sufficient.

niddah/34.summary: Beit Shammai hold that the menstrual blood of a gentile woman conveys no ritual impurity at all, while Beit Hillel treat it like her saliva, impure only while still moist. The Gemara defends Beit Shammai as deliberate design: leaving one substance wholly pure works as a conspicuous marker, so nobody mistakes a rabbinic decree for Torah law and burns teruma, the priestly portion, on contact. Asked why not mark the other substance instead, the answer is frequency: saliva and urine are common, blood is not.
niddah/34.question: If the whole point of the marker is to keep rabbinic decrees distinguishable from Torah law, why should the choice of which substance to leave pure turn on how often it happens to show up?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the tension between two rationales for rabbinic decrees: pedagogical signaling (keep rabbinic and Torah impurity distinguishable) versus practical need (decree where the case actually arises).

answer.quote: With regard to her saliva and her urine, which are relatively common, the Sages decreed that they are impure, but with regard to her blood, which is not as common
answer.explanation: The page gives frequency as the reason the marker falls on blood rather than saliva and urine, but it does not explain why frequency, rather than the marker's didactic purpose, should govern the choice, which is what the question presses on.

niddah/35.summary: Rav and Levi disagree over whether a woman has one source of blood or two. Rav says a single source yields both the blood that is impure in the week after a birth and the blood the Torah declares pure for the thirty-three days that follow; Levi says one source closes as the other opens. Their test case is a woman who bleeds without pause across the boundary day, and each view turns the other's leniency into stringency.
niddah/35.question: When one unbroken flow of blood crosses the day the count changes, does the calendar decide what that blood is, or does the flow?

judge.reachNote: Whether a blood's status is fixed by the Torah's calendar of days or by the physical continuity of the flow and its source.

answer.quote: There is a practical difference between them with regard to the following cases: A woman who continuously discharges menstrual blood from within seven days of giving birth to a male
answer.explanation: The page identifies exactly the continuous-flow case the question names and spells out what each of Rav and Levi would say about it, but it never rules between the calendar view and the flow view, so the question remains honestly askable.

niddah/36.summary: A woman in labor bleeds, and the argument turns on whose blood it is: hers, or her child's. Reading the phrase "her blood" in Leviticus, the Sages exclude bleeding brought on by the baby, so labor pangs during the eleven days of ziva, the stretch between menstrual periods when bleeding makes a woman a zava, leave her pure. The page ends with Rav, dying, sending Rav Asi to suppress one of his own rulings.
niddah/36.question: If Rav Asi only excommunicated Sheila bar Avina because he misheard his dying teacher's instruction, why is he the one who dies of fever after fever?
gate: the question brings in "Sheila", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Avina", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: Whether an act done in honest error still carries its full consequence — harm follows the deed, not the intention behind it.

answer.quote: And I am Sheila bar Avina, and my father's name alludes to an iron pestle [bukhna], which smashes a copper mortar
answer.explanation: The page supplies the immediate cause of Rav Asi's suffering — Sheila's retort that his ancestors' merit will smash the copper mortar — but never addresses why a good-faith mishearing should carry that consequence.

niddah/37.summary: A woman who bleeds from labor pains is not a zava, the status brought on by irregular discharge, but Rava asks whether that blood still cancels the seven bleeding-free days a zava must count. Abaye and Rava then argue over a zava who gives birth mid-count, and whether the days of impurity after birth can be counted among the clean ones. Rabbi Ḥanina offers a parable of a king and his advance soldiers; Rav Ḥisda reads the same picture backwards.
niddah/37.question: If the king's soldiers can show both that the blood belonged to the coming birth and that it did not, what is the parable actually deciding?

judge.reachNote: When an analogy can be read in opposite directions, it illustrates a position rather than establishing it — the real work is done by the textual inferences that follow.

answer.quote: The mishna is apparently a conclusive refutation of the opinion of Rav Ḥisda.
answer.explanation: The page does not settle what the parable itself proves, but it shows the dispute being decided by mishnaic inference rather than by the image, which bears on the question without answering it.

niddah/38.summary: Blood that comes with labor pains does not render a woman a zava, the status earned by bleeding three straight days outside the seven menstrual days, and Rabbi Meir builds a calendar in which a woman bleeds for 150 days and never crosses that line. The Rabbis outbid him: chain pregnancies and miscarriages together and she could bleed a lifetime, to which Meir replies that the exemption excludes a non-viable newborn. Rava then turns the phrase "her blood" against the Rabbis.
niddah/38.question: If labor blood is exempt because it comes from the child and not the mother, why should a miscarried fetus not count as a child for that purpose?
gate: legal verb left hanging, "exempt: exempt from what?" Name the object.

judge.reachNote: If the exemption rests on the blood belonging to the child rather than the mother, the question probes what makes a fetus count as 'the child' at all.

answer.quote: What is the reason? The halakha that blood emitted due to labor pains does not render a woman a zava does not apply to non-viable newborns.
answer.explanation: The page twice states the exclusion of non-viable newborns as a flat rule (also in Rabbi Meir's reply on 38a), but never explains why a nefel fails to count as a child for the exemption, so the question can still honestly be asked.

niddah/39.summary: A woman who goes without examining herself morning and evening stays ritually pure, even if she skipped the check on purpose; only an examination that finds blood changes her status. Rabbi Meir adds that a woman hiding from danger when her period is due stays pure, since fear drives away blood. The argument later lands on a hen that lays every other day, then skips two: when it resumes, does the count restart from the egg or from the old schedule?
niddah/39.question: If a hen picks its rhythm back up from the egg it actually laid, why would a woman's cycle ever be counted from a day on which she did not bleed?

judge.reachNote: Whether a cycle is anchored to the event that actually happened or to the schedule the body is presumed to keep.

answer.quote: Evidently, one counts her menstrual cycle from the first of the month, despite the fact that she did not actually experience bleeding.
answer.explanation: Rav Pappa raises exactly the note's tension against the hen analogy and answers it from Rabbi Yoḥanan's case, that the cycle is reckoned from the habitual day even without bleeding, after which Rav Huna's counter-explanation is adopted.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 39b: "Evidently, one counts her menstrual cycle from the first of the month, despite the fact that she did not actually experience bleeding.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page already stages this exact clash: Rav Pappa answers the hen argument by showing from Rabbi Yoḥanan that the count runs from the habitual day even with no bleeding, and Rav Huna then answers him back, with the sea-farers endorsing Rav Huna. Ask something the page leaves standing instead, for example what it means that a deviant sighting is dismissed as "extra blood that gathered inside her" so that it does not uproot a cycle, or why testimony brought from Eretz Yisrael decides between two readings of the same dispute. Keep the summary's framing of presumed purity and the hen, since both are accurate.

niddah/40.summary: A child delivered by caesarean section, say the Rabbis, does not start the mother's days of impurity and then purity, and she brings no offering for the birth; Rabbi Shimon says it counts like any other birth. Both sides mine the same verses in Leviticus, arguing over which phrase is spare enough to do extra work. Then, on whether a caesarean-born animal can be consecrated, the Gemara settles the matter by tallying shared traits: five features beat four.
niddah/40.question: Why should a count of five shared characteristics against four decide which verse a case is compared to?

judge.reachNote: Asks what makes a verbal analogy authoritative — whether resemblance can be weighed by counting features rather than by relevance.

answer.quote: The Gemara answers that the comparison to firstborn animals is preferable to the comparison to human childbirth because these shared characteristics are more numerous.
answer.explanation: The page states the majority-of-shared-traits rule as the deciding factor but never justifies why sheer number of shared features should govern the analogy, so the question still stands honestly.

niddah/41.summary: A baraita asks about a woman whose child is delivered by caesarean section and whose blood also comes out through the abdominal incision rather than the vagina. The anonymous first view calls that blood impure, Rabbi Shimon calls it pure, and Rav Yosef says the argument is really about whether the womb itself is an impure place. Reish Lakish ties the woman's status to her blood's, while Rabbi Yoḥanan splits them, since a menstruant is impure only when blood emerges from her genitalia.
niddah/41.question: If blood from the womb can be impure while the woman who shed it stays pure, what exactly is the impurity attached to?

judge.reachNote: Whether ritual impurity inheres in the substance (blood, the uterus as a source) or in the person who produced it, and whether the two can come apart.

answer.quote: Rather, she is subject to impurity that lasts until the evening, as a result of her body having come into contact with a discharge from the uterus, which is a source of impurity.
answer.explanation: In the parallel cases of the dislodged uterus and the two pearly drops the Gemara locates the impurity in the discharge or organ itself as a source, the woman being impure only until evening by contact, which bears on the question without resolving it for the caesarean blood dispute where Rabbi Yoḥanan deems the woman outright pure.

niddah/42.summary: Rav Shmuel bar Bisna asks Abaye whether a woman who discharges semen after intercourse is impure as one whose own body emitted it, or as one who merely touched something impure. He puts the question to Rava and to Rav Yosef, hears the same answer three times, and tells Abaye they are all spewing the same saliva. Abaye then repeats the answer, unchanged, and insists he said it well.
niddah/42.question: When Abaye gives back the answer Rav Shmuel bar Bisna has already rejected twice, what makes the third telling any different?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches toward the idea that an answer becomes real only when its scope and reasoning are stated, but the page supplies that reasoning itself.

answer.quote: Rabbi Shimon says that it is sufficient for the woman to be like the man who engaged in intercourse with her only with regard to
answer.explanation: Abaye's final reply is not a bare repetition: he explains that Rabbi Shimon's leniency is limited to the inside/outside issue, so the other two matters follow the stringent 'emission' status, which is exactly what makes the third telling different.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 42a: "Rabbi Shimon says that it is sufficient for the woman to be like the man who engaged in intercourse with her only with regard to". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The page itself states what changes in Abaye's final reply: he now delimits Rabbi Shimon's 'sufficient to be like the man' to the inside/outside question alone, leaving the count and the minimum-amount issues under the stringent 'emission' status. The summary must not say the answer was repeated unchanged, since Abaye adds this reasoning. Write a question that does not ask what the page already answers, e.g. about why the additional two matters should track emission rather than contact.

niddah/43.summary: A priest eating teruma, the portion of produce reserved for priests, feels his limbs quaking and grips himself through a cloth so no seminal emission escapes and the food he swallows stays pure. Abaye permits only a coarse cloth, fearing a soft one draws more out; Rava says once the semen is uprooted, it is uprooted. Rava then asks about a gentile whose semen was uprooted, who immerses to convert, and emits afterward.
niddah/43.question: If status is fixed at the moment a discharge is uprooted, why does the argument hesitate over that rule precisely when following it would leave someone pure?

judge.reachNote: Whether a legal principle runs symmetrically or only in the direction of stringency — the page names this as the crux.

answer.quote: one can maintain that this statement applies only when it entails a stringency, as is the case with regard to a born Jew. But here, where this would lead to a leniency
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself explains the hesitation: the rule of following the moment of uprooting may have been established only where it produces stringency, so it may not apply when it would yield purity.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 43a: "one can maintain that this statement applies only when it entails a stringency, as is the case with regard to a born Jew. But here, where this would lead to a leniency". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question restates the Gemara's own explanation, which says plainly that the rule of following the moment of uprooting may apply only where it entails a stringency. Rewrite so the question begins after that answer — for instance, asking what it means that a principle of when impurity attaches can bend with the direction of its outcome, or why the gentile convert, the zava's urine, and the gentile zava all stay unresolved. Keep the summary as is; it is accurate.

niddah/44.summary: A one-day-old baby counts as a full person on a long list: his killer is liable for murder, his birth releases his widowed mother from having to marry her dead husband's brother, and he is mourned like a grown man. The argument turns on what separates him from an unborn child, and the answer is usually the single day outside. Told that one fetus twitched three times after its mother died, Mar son of Rav Ashi calls it a severed lizard's tail.
niddah/44.question: If three movements after the mother's death prove nothing, what evidence would ever show that the unborn child died second?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of a legal presumption that no observable sign can dislodge — what counts as proof of life at all.

niddah/45.summary: A girl of eleven years and one day who makes a vow, binding herself before God, is examined to see whether she knows in Whose name she vowed; a boy is examined a year later. The Gemara presses each clause: an unusually sharp eleven-year-old is still not examined, and after twelve, saying she does not know no longer voids the vow. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar flips the ages, since a boy frequents his teacher's house and cleverness enters first.
niddah/45.question: If a girl of very sharp mind is still too young to be examined at eleven, and a twelve-year-old's claim of ignorance counts for nothing, what is the examination actually measuring?

judge.reachNote: When does law measure a real capacity, and when does it only use age as a fixed line that actual understanding cannot cross?

answer.quote: the status of the vow is determined in accordance with the examination of the child’s understanding, as stated in the mishna
answer.explanation: The page says the examination tests the child's understanding, which bears on the question but does not resolve why fixed ages override demonstrated understanding at both ends.

niddah/46.summary: Two pubic hairs turn a child into an adult, and the sages argue over hairs that appear during the twelfth or thirteenth year: too early to count, or already late enough? Rava rules they are early, then applies it. A girl of twelve examined with no hairs found may not annul the betrothal her mother and brothers arranged, since hairs may have grown and fallen out, yet that same doubt will not free her by halitza from her dead husband's brother.
niddah/46.question: Why is the suspicion that hairs once grew and fell out strong enough to lock a twelve-year-old into a marriage, but not strong enough to release her from one?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that an unresolved doubt can strip a status without conferring its opposite — but the page says this outright.

answer.quote: although the girl is not treated with the presumption that she is an adult, she does not have the certain status of a minor either
answer.explanation: The page states the asymmetry's rationale: a mere doubt removes her certain minority (so no refusal) without establishing adulthood, and it adds that Rav Pappa's leniency "applies only with regard to ḥalitza, but with regard to refusal everyone agrees that we are concerned."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 46a: "although the girl is not treated with the presumption that she is an adult, she does not have the certain status of a minor either". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The Gemara itself raises and settles this asymmetry: mere concern that hairs fell out removes her certain minor status (barring refusal) yet cannot make her an adult for ḥalitza, and it states that Rav Pappa's leniency applies only to ḥalitza. Ask instead about something the page leaves unsettled — e.g. why the concern about fallen hairs is dropped entirely when intercourse happened only before twelve, so that the whole marriage stays rabbinic, or how a girl can be held in a marriage she is presumed neither minor nor adult for.

niddah/47.summary: A mishna compares a girl's three stages to three stages of a fig, unripe, ripening, and ripe, and the sages argue over which change in the breast marks the last one. Shmuel checked those signs on his Canaanite maidservant, then paid her four dinars, silver coins, for her humiliation, on his own principle that slaves were given for service and not for shame. Rabbi Ḥiyya, asked about a man past twenty with no signs, sent him off to gain or lose weight first.
niddah/47.question: If Shmuel already held that a master may not humiliate his slave, what does paying her four dinars afterward actually settle?

judge.reachNote: Whether money can discharge a violation of a person's dignity, or only register it after the fact.

answer.quote: Consequently, if a master humiliated his Canaanite slave, he must pay him damages.
answer.explanation: The page states that Shmuel's principle itself generates a monetary liability for humiliation, so the four dinars are the damages the principle requires, though the page never says whether payment cures or merely compensates the wrong.

niddah/48.summary: The mishna sets two bodily signs of puberty in a girl: two pubic hairs, called the lower sign, and developed breasts, the upper sign. Rabbi Meir holds the upper can appear first, so a girl with breasts alone might still be a minor and neither marry her dead husband's brother nor be released from him. The Rabbis say that order is impossible, and draw the sharp conclusion: even when an examination finds no hairs, the hairs grew once and fell out.
niddah/48.question: If examiners look and find nothing, what evidence could ever unsettle the claim that the hairs were there and fell out?

judge.reachNote: When a legal presumption about the body is held to be impossible to violate, direct observation can no longer refute it — the question names that clash between rule and evidence.

answer.quote: When Rava said that one relies on this presumption, he was referring specifically to her inability from now on to perform refusal. But with regard to ḥalitza, she requires an examination
answer.explanation: The page shows that presumptions about maturity are not treated as absolute for every purpose — examination is still demanded for ḥalitza — which bears on the question without answering what could overturn the Rabbis' claim that hairs grew and fell out.

niddah/49.summary: A mishna collects pairs that run in one direction only: a hole in an earthenware vessel wide enough to let water in certainly lets water out, and a limb with a fingernail certainly has a bone inside it. The Gemara then argues over how to test a cracked pot: sink it in a tub of water, turn it upside down and cover it, set it on the fire, or on hot ash. Ulla says the real dispute is whether water forced in counts as entering.
niddah/49.question: If water gets into the pot only because you pushed the pot under, did the hole let it in, or did you?

judge.reachNote: Whether a test measures the hole's own capacity or the force applied to it — does the vessel's status depend on what it does or what is done to it.

answer.quote: The difference between their opinions is whether liquid that enters through a hole with difficulty, i.e., as the result of force, is considered entering.
answer.explanation: Ulla names exactly the issue the question raises and reports Rabbi Yehuda's view that forced entry does not count, but the page leaves it as an unresolved tannaitic dispute rather than deciding it.

niddah/50.summary: Rabbi Yoḥanan rules that endives first planted as animal fodder need a fresh decision, made after they are pulled from the ground, before they count as human food and can become ritually impure. Rava proves it from the carcass of a kosher bird, which needs a person's intent to eat it even if the owner had planned on it while it was alive. Rabbi Zeira deflects the proof; the listeners laugh at his answer, and Abaye defends him.
niddah/50.question: Why does Abaye, who pressed the sharpest objection against Rabbi Zeira, then defend a reading that requires a chicken running off to the wild and raising chicks there?

judge.reachNote: How one can argue hard against a colleague's position and still guard his standing and give his words the best possible reading.

answer.quote: Abaye said to them: A great man has stated a matter; do not laugh at him.
answer.explanation: The page states Abaye's own stated motive for defending Rabbi Zeira — deference to a great man — but never addresses why the very sage who pressed the Yavne objection now reads the case charitably, so the tension the question raises remains.

niddah/51.summary: Any produce owing pe'a, the corner of a field left for the poor, also owes tithes, according to a rule quoted from earlier. Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers with a man who declares his vineyard ownerless, picks the grapes at dawn, owes the poor their fallen grapes, and owes no tithe; Rava says such rules name kinds of produce, not every circumstance. Later, scales alone already prove a fish kosher, so why does the verse also name fins?
niddah/51.question: If an extra sign in the verse counts as glory, why does an extra exception to a rule count as a flaw to be explained away?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the asymmetry in how the Gemara treats surplus material: an extra Torah sign is glory, while an extra case outside a mishna's generalization must be neutralized.

niddah/52.summary: Two pubic hairs mark the line between child and adult, and one thing that ends at that line is a girl's right to refuse a marriage her mother and brothers arranged for her as a minor. Rabbi Yehuda would stretch the window later; then Rabbi Yishmael's daughter came to the study hall to refuse, her son on her shoulders, and wept, since refusal would make the boy retroactively born outside marriage. The Sages counted votes and closed the window at two hairs.
niddah/52.question: Did the Sages count those votes because Rabbi Yehuda's ruling was wrong, or because the woman weeping in the study hall was Rabbi Yishmael's daughter?

judge.reachNote: Whether a halakhic window gets closed by legal reasoning or by the pressure of a particular, painful case in front of the court.

answer.quote: as a result of the event involving Rabbi Yishmael’s daughter, the Sages assembled, counted the votes, and concluded: Until when may a young girl perform refusal? Until she grows two pubic hairs.
answer.explanation: The page states that the vote followed from this particular incident, and the Sages' outcry — "Could it be that with regard to a matter that that righteous Rabbi Yishmael said... his offspring would stumble upon it?" — hints at the personal dimension, but it never says outright whether the ruling was rejected as legally wrong or only because of whose daughter she was, so the question still stands.

niddah/53.summary: A woman examines herself for blood at twilight, and the argument is how long twilight lasts: the time it takes to walk half a mil before the stars appear, or, by Rabbi Yosei, the blink of an eye before them. The discussion then turns to a red stain found on a garment, which by one view makes her impure retroactively back to the last time that garment was laundered. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi prefers his opponent's ruling because it is gentler, and the Gemara doubts that it is.
niddah/53.question: If a ruling is adopted because it goes easier on the woman, what becomes of it when the Gemara shows it does not?

judge.reachNote: Whether a stated reason (leniency) governs a ruling, or the ruling is preserved by re-describing where the leniency lies.

answer.quote: Ravina says: Reverse Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s statement, so that it states: My statement appears to be more correct than that of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
answer.explanation: The page itself raises the very objection the question asks and resolves it twice — Ravina reverses the attribution, and Rav Naḥman redefines the leniency as pertaining to her ziva reckoning.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 53b: "Ravina says: Reverse Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi’s statement, so that it states: My statement appears to be more correct than that of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is resolved a few lines later on the same page: Ravina reverses Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's statement and Rav Naḥman keeps it by relocating the leniency to her ziva count. Rewrite the question so it starts from those two answers rather than asking what the page already says — for instance, why Rav Naḥman prefers straining the meaning of "fixes her situation" over simply swapping the names, or what it says about rabbinic-law stringencies that leniency alone decides. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

niddah/54.summary: A baraita counts the days a woman with a fixed bleeding pattern may be with her husband: one day of blood alternating with one clean day leaves several nights; three days of blood and three clean leaves two days, and then never again. The count runs out to cycles of a hundred days and a thousand. The mishna turns to dried substances, where the saliva of a zav, a man with an abnormal discharge, is pure once dry unless soaking restores it.
niddah/54.question: The baraita reaches the woman whose pattern is three days of blood and three days clean, records that she may never again be with her husband, and moves straight on to the next calculation; what becomes of her?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea that a halakhic calculation can arrive at a permanent prohibition and simply move on, leaving the person it describes unaddressed.

niddah/55.summary: A corpse transmits impurity whether its flesh is moist or dry, and the argument turns on how dry. Reish Lakish holds that even crumbled flesh is impure; Rabbi Yoḥanan compares a corpse to a bone, so flesh ground to flour counts as dust. Rav Adda bar Ahava then sorts the body by a bone's two traits, present from birth and never regrowing, which drops teeth, hair, and nails from the list.
niddah/55.question: If hair and nails are excluded because they grow back, why does flesh still count when Mar bar Rav Ashi's only evidence that it never truly regrows is the scar left behind?
gate: the question brings in "Mar", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.
the question brings in "Ashi's", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: What counts as 'renewal' — whether imperfect regrowth (scarred flesh) is a different kind of regrowth from hair and nails, i.e. what makes a body part permanently the person's own.

answer.quote: Mar bar Rav Ashi says: Flesh does not renew itself, as although when someone is cut his flesh regrows and heals, a scar is formed in its place.
answer.explanation: The page gives the scar as the reason flesh is not deemed self-renewing, though it does not defend why a scar is a sufficient mark of non-renewal as against hair and nails, which the question presses.

summaryProblems.claim: Rabbi Yoḥanan compares a corpse to a bone, so flesh ground to flour counts as dust.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Rabbi Yoḥanan maintains it is ritually pure, as it is unlike a bone, which does not crumble.

summaryProblems.claim: The flour/dust distinction belongs to Rabbi Yoḥanan's bone comparison.
summaryProblems.pageSays: The Gemara raises an objection to the opinion of Reish Lakish from a baraita: The flesh of a corpse that crumbled is ritually pure.

judge.feedback: The summary says "Rabbi Yoḥanan compares a corpse to a bone, so flesh ground to flour counts as dust.", but the page says "Rabbi Yoḥanan maintains it is ritually pure, as it is unlike a bone, which does not crumble.". Say what the page says. The summary says "The flour/dust distinction belongs to Rabbi Yoḥanan's bone comparison.", but the page says "The Gemara raises an objection to the opinion of Reish Lakish from a baraita: The flesh of a corpse that crumbled is ritually pure.". Say what the page says. Fix the attribution: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds crumbled flesh is simply pure because a bone does not crumble, while the flour-is-dust answer is the Gemara's defense of Reish Lakish against a baraita. Keep the Rav Adda bar Ahava thread and the question, which usefully presses on the scar as a criterion, but state the two opinions as the page assigns them.

niddah/56.summary: A dead creeping animal turns up in an alleyway, and everything that passed through since the alleyway was last swept is treated as impure. The same retroactive count applies to a bloodstain found on a woman's robe, reaching back to the last laundering. The Sages then ask what sweeping and laundering actually establish: that someone looked and saw nothing, or that anything present would have been removed. The difference shows up when a man says he swept but never looked.
niddah/56.question: If a stain looks the same after a second laundering, does that really prove it was there before the first one, or only that this particular stain is stubborn?

judge.reachNote: Whether an experimental re-test can serve as halakhic proof, or only shows the stain's own properties — evidence versus inference.

niddah/57.summary: Samaritans are believed when they say where they buried stillborn children, even though the page notes they reject the reading of the verse about not putting a stumbling block before the blind. The fix is not trust: a Samaritan priest has to be standing on the spot eating teruma, the priestly portion of produce that only a ritually pure priest may eat. The same move recurs, with a man walking back and forth across a plowed-over grave field.
niddah/57.question: If a Samaritan's word counts only once he has staked his own purity on it, is he being believed at all?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of whether accepted testimony is trust in a person or a verified circumstance — but the page resolves it by locating the credibility in their knowledge.

answer.quote: Therefore, the mishna teaches us that they are sufficiently knowledgeable, and their testimony is accepted.
answer.explanation: The Gemara itself raises the note's objection — once the priest is eating teruma on the spot "it is obvious that the Samaritan priest's testimony can be accepted. Then what is the purpose of stating this halakha?" — and answers that what is being believed is their expertise about embryo formation (and, in the animal case, murky discharge), not merely their self-endangerment.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 57a: "Therefore, the mishna teaches us that they are sufficiently knowledgeable, and their testimony is accepted.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The Gemara asks this very question ("If so, it is obvious that the Samaritan priest's testimony can be accepted. Then what is the purpose of stating this halakha?") and answers it: what is credited is their knowledge of embryo stages, not their word alone. Rewrite the question to start from that answer, or aim it elsewhere — e.g. why traversing the whole field cures the problem in the baraita while partial traversal does not, since they are "not meticulous with regard to cases of uncertainty." The summary is faithful and can largely stand, but it should not present the priest-with-teruma device as the page's last word.

niddah/58.summary: A woman finds a blood stain, and the argument turns on what else it might have come from: a slaughtered bird, sycamore sap, eye salve, a crushed louse. Rabbi Akiva clears a woman by pointing to an old wound that could reopen, telling his puzzled students that stain impurity is rabbinic and was set up to be lenient. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel then concedes his own louse rule would leave no woman pure to her husband.
niddah/58.question: If the whole business of stains was instituted to be lenient, why is a woman who is certain she walked through the butchers' market pure, while one who only thinks she might have is impure?

judge.reachNote: A rabbinic leniency that permits attributing a stain elsewhere is not the same as resolving doubt about whether the attributable circumstance even occurred.

niddah/59.summary: A bloodstain no bigger than a split bean can be blamed on a crushed louse, leaving a woman ritually pure; anything larger cannot. Rabbi Yannai allows subtraction: if a squashed louse is visible on a stain slightly over that size, deduct its blood and credit the bean-sized remainder to a second louse. Rabbi Ḥanina holds her impure. Rabbi Yirmeya presses the case where she had been handling a bean's worth of slaughtered bird's blood and the stain came out larger.
niddah/59.question: If one louse you can see licenses a second louse you cannot, what stops the reckoning at two?

judge.reachNote: How far a permitted attribution can be iterated before leniency by uncertainty devours the rule it is carved out of.

answer.quote: Therefore, the baraita teaches us that this is not so, and in such a case she is impure.
answer.explanation: The Gemara rejects the parallel move of splitting one large stain into sub-bean portions by interposing an attributable stain, which bears on how far such subtraction may be multiplied, but it never states a limit on chaining lice themselves.

niddah/60.summary: A woman lends her cloak to another woman, gets it back with a blood stain on it, and the question is whose stain it is. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel lets her pin it on the borrower who is already counting impure days, since that woman has less to lose; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says neither may shift it, so both are impure. Rav Ḥisda reads the same argument into two men on two paths, one already impure, neither remembering which he walked.
niddah/60.question: If the borrower is already counting impure days and can immerse whenever she likes, what exactly does she lose by absorbing someone else's stain, and why does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi still refuse to hand it to her?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the idea of whether a presumption of purity can be traded away against someone who still has purity left to lose.

answer.quote: as she can immerse in a ritual bath at any time, and therefore both women are like each other
answer.where: Niddah 60a (Rav Adda's objection to Rav Ḥisda)
answer.explanation: Rav Adda states the reason Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refuses the attribution: since the borrower can immerse at will, she has the same presumption of purity as the lender, so neither may be preferred, and the page elsewhere states what she loses — the stain would ruin her counting or render her "ritually impure for an extra day."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 60a (Rav Adda's objection to Rav Ḥisda): "as she can immerse in a ritual bath at any time, and therefore both women are like each other". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is answered twice over on the page: Rav Adda says Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refuses because the borrower can immerse at any time and so "both women are like each other," and the baraita and 60b spell out the loss (she must begin counting again, or is impure an extra day). Rewrite the question to start from that answer rather than ask for it — for instance, press on Rav Ḥisda's reply that a woman observing a day for a day is also "not fully pure," and what that says about whether partial impurity counts as impurity at all. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

niddah/61.summary: Three women share a bed set against a wall, and blood turns up beneath one of them; the mishna sorts out who is impure by who lay where. Rabbi Meir holds that something presumed impure stays impure however hard you look, while the Rabbis say dig down to bedrock and assume a raven carried the corpse away. Then come three stories of searches that came up empty and were later proved wrong, including a sycamore in Kefar Sava, uprooted by wind, with a skull in its roots.
niddah/61.question: If a fruitless search can always be blamed on a search that stopped too soon, what could ever count as having looked enough?

judge.reachNote: Whether a presumption of impurity can ever be defeated by evidence, or whether an unfalsifiable presumption makes examination meaningless.

answer.quote: One continues searching the relevant area until he reaches bedrock or virgin soil, beneath which there is certainly no ritual impurity.
answer.explanation: The Rabbis do state a threshold for a sufficient search — bedrock or virgin soil — but the baraitot that follow (the Shiḥin cave dug to ground 'smooth as a fingernail', the Beit Ḥoron 'bedrock' that was really soft earth, and the Sages' repeated retort 'they did not examine as much as was necessary') keep the question live.

niddah/62.summary: A stain of unknown origin gets scrubbed with seven substances in order, three rubs each: tasteless saliva from someone who has eaten nothing all night, fermented urine, natron, borit, Cimolian earth, eshlag scraped from a pearl shell with an iron skewer. If the stain stays, it was dye, and anything handled with the garment stays pure. Then the ground shifts: Rabbi Zeira says a second washing makes it impure, because repeating the scrub shows the owner was worried.
niddah/62.question: If blood that is certainly menstrual blood can be scrubbed into a mere mark and the garment called pure, is the washing removing the blood or removing the owner's concern about it?

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — whether impurity is an objective property of the substance or a function of the owner's concern — but the page names that idea and decides it.

answer.quote: Yes, the status of purity depends upon whether or not the owner of the garment is particular about the stain.
answer.explanation: The note asks whether washing removes the blood or the owner's concern, and Rav Ashi states outright — citing Rabbi Ḥiyya's case of certain menstrual blood that is nullified though not fully removed — that purity turns on the owner's particularity.

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 62b (Rav Ashi to Rabbi Abba): "Yes, the status of purity depends upon whether or not the owner of the garment is particular about the stain.". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question is stated and answered on the page: Rav Ashi tells Rabbi Abba that purity does depend on whether the owner is particular, citing Rabbi Ḥiyya's ruling that certain menstrual blood is nullified by the seven substances even when the stain remains. Rewrite the question to start from that answer and press on what it leaves unsettled — for instance, Reish Lakish's move to discard Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita entirely rather than accept that particularity governs, or Rav Pappa's case of liquid that can emerge while the owner is indifferent. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

niddah/63.summary: Tasteless saliva, one of seven substances rubbed on a stained cloth to test whether the stain is blood, counts only if the person has not eaten since evening; saying a chapter of Torah aloud weakens it. Rav Ashi defines dozing as being asleep and not asleep: the man answers when called but cannot reason, yet remembers when reminded. Later Rav Yosef, who fell ill and forgot his studies, denies ever hearing a ruling of Shmuel, and Abaye tells him he taught it himself.
niddah/63.question: If Rav Yosef knows the ruling only because Abaye recites it back to him, whose teaching is it now?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea of how a tradition is owned when the teacher's memory fails and the student restores it — echoing Rav Ashi's doze, where one cannot reason but remembers when reminded.

answer.quote: You yourself told us this halakha, and it was with regard to this following matter that you told this halakha to us
answer.explanation: Abaye ascribes the teaching back to Rav Yosef himself (with the chain 'Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said'), which bears on the question of attribution but does not settle who owns the teaching after it is returned to him by a student.

niddah/64.summary: Rav says a woman who bleeds on the fifteenth of one month, the sixteenth of the next, and the seventeenth of the next has fixed a cycle of a month and a day; Shmuel says two shifts are not enough. The Gemara wonders whether this is the same argument as whether a woman whose first two husbands died may marry a third, then drops the link. Each sage rereads a baraita to save his count.
niddah/64.question: Is the bleeding on the fifteenth the first step of the new pattern, or only the old habit that the pattern departs from?

judge.reachNote: Whether the baseline occurrence from which a new pattern departs can itself be counted as a member of that pattern.

answer.quote: Rav holds that when she experienced bleeding on the fifteenth of the month, that occasion is also one of the number, i.e., it counts as the first of the pattern
answer.explanation: The Gemara explicitly frames the Rav–Shmuel dispute as exactly the question of whether the fifteenth counts as the first instance of the pattern or, as Shmuel holds, is excluded because it was not reached by skipping, and Rav's later answer adds that when the fifteenth was her established day "the fifteenth does not count as the beginning of a new pattern."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 64a: "Rav holds that when she experienced bleeding on the fifteenth of the month, that occasion is also one of the number, i.e., it counts as the first of the pattern". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question simply restates the dispute the page already spells out — Rav counts the fifteenth as one of the three, Shmuel does not because it was not reached by skipping — so a reader hits the answer three paragraphs in. Ask instead about something the page leaves unresolved, for example why an already-established day is treated as unavailable to start a new pattern ("Since she was accustomed to experience bleeding on the fifteenth it is different"), or why an unestablished cycle of two is uprooted by a single deviation while an established one needs three. Keep the summary as is; it tracks the page.

niddah/65.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once gave a bride four nights spread across twelve months in which bleeding could be attributed to the torn hymen, and the Gemara cannot work out how he counted them. To fix the length of a "period of time" it turns to pressing baskets of palm leaf and reed that soaked up impure wine and must lie dormant, settling on twelve hours. A bride gets a night and half a day, because signing the marriage contract can drag.
niddah/65.question: Rav Ashi blocks an extra stringency by predicting that a man afraid of bleeding mid-act would avoid his wife entirely, so why doesn't that same fear undercut the rule that he separate the moment he finishes?
gate: the question brings in "Ashi", which the summary never mentions; the question must stand on the summary alone, so introduce it there or leave it out.

judge.reachNote: The idea reached is that a stringency which frightens a man out of the marital mitzva defeats itself — and whether that logic can be applied selectively.

summaryProblems.claim: The Gemara cannot work out how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi counted the four nights.
summaryProblems.pageSays: Actually, the correct explanation is that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave her one night during her days as a minor and three nights during her days as a young woman.

judge.feedback: The summary says "The Gemara cannot work out how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi counted the four nights.", but the page says "Actually, the correct explanation is that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave her one night during her days as a minor and three nights during her days as a young woman.". Say what the page says. The summary wrongly says the counting is never resolved; the Gemara works through the failed options and settles on one night as a minor and three as a young woman, with each two-month absence counting as one night. Rewrite that clause to reflect the resolution. The question itself is good and unanswered — keep it as is.

niddah/66.summary: A woman who bleeds every time she has intercourse is tested with a lead tube, its edge folded inward, holding a cosmetic brush tipped with an absorbent cloth: blood at the top points to the uterus, blood on the sides to the vaginal wall. Reish Lakish asks why she does not test early and spare herself two divorces. Rabbi Yoḥanan answers that a test could forbid her to every man, and another husband might cause no bleeding at all.
niddah/66.question: If the examination could settle the matter but might bar her from marrying anyone, is Rabbi Yoḥanan protecting her or keeping her from knowing her own body?

judge.reachNote: Whether halakha prefers leaving a status undetermined so a woman remains marriageable, over a test that would give certainty at the cost of a permanent prohibition.

answer.quote: It is preferable for her not to test herself and risk becoming forbidden to all men and instead to be divorced and remarry another, because not all fingers
answer.explanation: The page states Rabbi Yoḥanan's rationale — avoiding a result that would bar her to all men — which supports the protective reading, though the note's question about withholding self-knowledge is not itself addressed.

niddah/67.summary: A woman may not immerse in a port, because mud from the boats drawn up on shore might have stuck to her and then fallen off on the walk home. The page collects what blocks the water from reaching skin: a bloodletting scab after three days, eye mucus once it yellows, a single knotted hair, though Rabbi Yoḥanan holds two do not. Then the timing shifts, as lions in Neresh, thieves in Pappunya, cold in Pumbedita and untrustworthy gatekeepers in Meḥoza push immersion into daylight.
niddah/67.question: If night immersion is kept so that a watching daughter will not copy her mother and immerse by day on the seventh, what did the daughters of Neresh learn from mothers who immersed in daylight because of lions?

judge.reachNote: A safeguard built on what a child sees her mother do is undermined the moment the Sages themselves license the daytime practice.

answer.quote: The Gemara cites examples of Sages who permitted immersion on the eighth day due to exceptional circumstances.
answer.explanation: The page frames the Neresh, Pappunya, Pumbedita and Meḥoza rulings as danger-driven exceptions on the eighth day, which bears on the tension but never says how the imitating-daughter concern is answered there.

niddah/68.summary: A zava, a woman with an irregular discharge who must count seven clean days before immersing, examined herself on the first of those days and on the seventh and skipped the five in between. Rabbi Eliezer counts all seven for her, Rabbi Yehoshua counts only the first and seventh, and Rabbi Akiva counts only the seventh. Then Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say Akiva's position looks the most correct of the three, and rule like Eliezer anyway.
niddah/68.question: What is a sage doing when he says one opinion looks the most correct and then hands the halakha to a different one?
gate: the question uses "halakha", which the summary never introduced; gloss it in the summary first or leave it out of the question.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the gap between what argument makes most compelling and what is actually ruled as law.

niddah/69.summary: A woman who has lost track of her cycle comes before the court, and the immersions pile up: nine if she saw blood on one day, eleven if at twilight, fifteen if she saw none at all. Rava balks at that last figure and compares it to the town of Galaḥi, where a man with one ox herds the flocks one day and a man with none herds two. An orphan there followed that logic, slaughtered every ox, and gave two hides to whoever owned none.
niddah/69.question: Did the orphan of Galaḥi break his town's law or only finish it?

judge.reachNote: Whether pushing a rule to its logical conclusion is obedience that exposes the rule or a violation dressed as obedience.

answer.quote: The end of the law is like the beginning of the law: Isn’t the beginning of the law that one who has no ox is preferred
answer.explanation: The orphan himself gives the claim that he merely carried the town's rule through to its end, but the page never rules on whether this was lawful, so the question can still be asked.

niddah/70.summary: The sages of Alexandria ask Rabbi Yehoshua whether Lot's wife, turned into a pillar of salt, transmits the ritual impurity of a corpse, and whether the boy Elisha brought back to life still does. He answers both by category: a pillar of salt is not a corpse, and a living person is not a corpse, even one who was dead. Asked whether the resurrected dead will need sprinkling with the ashes of the red heifer, he stops classifying and defers.
niddah/70.question: If a revived boy is simply not a corpse, why can't Rabbi Yehoshua give the resurrected dead the same answer instead of putting it off?

judge.reachNote: The idea under it: whether clean category distinctions (corpse vs. pillar of salt vs. living person) still hold when the case lies beyond present experience, or whether some questions resist classification altogether.

niddah/71.summary: Beit Shammai hold that every woman who dies counts as a menstruating woman, and the Gemara hunts for a reason. Fear at the sight of the Angel of Death is floated, then dropped, since a discharge caused by circumstances beyond a person's control does not make a man impure. What is left is social: utensils used by women who died while menstruating were immersed, living menstruating women were embarrassed by that, so the Sages extended immersion to every woman who dies.
niddah/71.question: Does a rule invented to spare embarrassment still spare it once everyone knows that is the only reason it exists?

judge.reachNote: Reaches the idea that a legal fiction adopted to protect dignity may be self-defeating once its protective purpose is openly stated as its only basis.

niddah/72.summary: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel argue over a woman who bleeds on the eleventh day of the stretch between menstrual periods, immerses that night, and has intercourse with her husband. Beit Shammai demand consistency: if her bedding is impure, she and he also owe a sin offering. Beit Hillel answer that the eleventh day is treated like the earlier ten only as a hedge against confusion, and a hedge can push toward strictness without dragging a non-sacred animal into the Temple courtyard.
niddah/72.question: If treating the eleventh day like the other ten is only a guard against people confusing them, why does that confusion always argue for strictness and never for leniency?
gate: gloss "sin offering" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.

judge.reachNote: The question reaches the real idea — that a rabbinic hedge is directional and can only add stringency — but the page states and justifies that idea outright, and the note's own summary repeats it.

answer.quote: we will not bring them to the liability of bringing an offering, to be lenient. It would be a leniency to permit them to bring an unnecessary and therefore a non-sacred animal
answer.explanation: Beit Hillel state exactly why the confusion-decree can only run toward stringency: the lenient direction would license bringing a non-sacred animal into the Temple courtyard, and they conclude "the two are equated to be stringent, but not to be lenient."

judge.feedback: The page answers your question in Niddah 72a: "we will not bring them to the liability of bringing an offering, to be lenient. It would be a leniency to permit them to bring an unnecessary and therefore a non-sacred animal". Do not ask it as if it were open: ask what remains difficult once that answer is on the table, or ask it as a reading question and say the page answers it. The question asks what the summary itself already answers: Beit Hillel say the equation works only to be stringent because the lenient side would drag a non-sacred animal into the Temple courtyard. Build a question on what the page leaves unresolved instead — for example, Beit Shammai's parity demand ("apply your method equally") against Beit Hillel's own split between impurity and offering, or the later asymmetry where the decree makes her bedding definitely impure yet leaves her husband pure because intercourse is infrequent.

niddah/73.summary: The tractate's last page is one long baraita squeezing the laws of the zava out of a single verse in Leviticus, counting outward from menstruation to day eleven and stopping at twelve. Twice the baraita builds an a fortiori inference and then cancels it with a word: logic says a zav should render a woman he has intercourse with impure, and "She is impure" says otherwise. Rabbi Akiva gets the eleven days from verses; Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya calls them a halakha from Sinai.
niddah/73.question: If one word in the verse can cancel an a fortiori inference, why does the baraita bother building the inference first?
gate: gloss "halakha" in a few words the first time it appears; the reader has never opened a Talmud.
banned phrase: "a fortiori".

judge.reachNote: Reaches the method itself: what a rejected kal va'homer accomplishes, i.e. that a verse's force is measured by the logic it has to overturn.
